itemVerdicts.item: (b) Vanguard Aug 2025 'Setting the record straight': 23% for the US as of Dec 31 2024, worldwide funds' US-equity allocations over CRSP Total Market; Australia 13%, Canada 12%, Europe 13%, UK 12%
itemVerdicts.note: Local vanguard2025.txt header reads 'Vanguard research    August 2025' / 'Setting the record straight: The truths about index fund investing' (authors Rowley, Lawrence, Ryder-Green; doc code ISGTAI 082025). Figure 2, titled 'Index fund assets as a percentage of market capitalization', shows exactly: United States 23%, Australia 13%, Canada 12%, Europe 13%, United Kingdom 12%. Its note reads verbatim 'Data are as of December 31, 2024' and 'U.S. equity fund market share is represented by assets of equity funds worldwide allocated to U.S. equities, plus assets of funds in a Morningstar global category containing "U.S. Equity" in U.S. dollars. U.S. equity market capitalization is represented by the CRSP Total Market Index in U.S. dollars.' Body text confirms the read: 'Figure 2 on page 5 shows the percentage of equity market capitalization held by equity index funds in several countries or regions.' Numerator/denominator characterization in the claim is exactly right, and it is index funds only (not index+active). Two details worth carrying: Vanguard's Europe denominator is FTSE Developed Europe All Cap and explicitly includes the UK; registered fund assets exclude funds of funds.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Fed staff paper (Anadu, Kruttli, McCabe, Osambela, FEDS 2018-060r1, May 2020 draft): passive MFs+ETFs ~14% of the domestic equity market as of March 2020, up from <4% in 2005; passive = 41% of fund AUM; 97% of ETF assets passive
itemVerdicts.note: I re-downloaded https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/feds/files/2018060r1pap.pdf and read all three verbatim. (i) 'As of March 2020, U.S. stocks held in passive MFs and ETFs accounted for about 14 percent of the domestic equity market, up from less than four percent in 2005.' (footnote 4: authors' calculations using Bloomberg, Morningstar and SIFMA data). (ii) 'As of March 2020, passive funds accounted for 41 percent of combined U.S. MF and ETF assets under management (AUM), up from three percent in 1995 and 14 percent in 2005' - note the 41% is of combined US MF+ETF AUM specifically, and the paper adds 'Passive funds made up 48 percent of the AUM in equity funds and 30 percent for bond funds as of March 2020'. (iii) footnote: 'As of March 2020, 97 percent of ETF assets were in passive funds (see Figure 1). Source: Morningstar, Inc.' Cover page confirms 'First draft: August 27, 2018 / This draft: May 15, 2020' and the DOI 10.17016/FEDS.2018.060r1. One precision point: the Fed's landing page labels this revision 'August 2018 (Revised June 2020)', so 'May 2020 draft' is right per the PDF cover but 'r1, revised June 2020' is what the Board's own page says - either is defensible, they should not be mixed. Also note the same work is peer-reviewed as Anadu et al., Financial Analysts Journal 76(4), 23-39 (2020), titled without 'Potential'; citing the FEDS r1 is fine, but calling it only a 'staff working paper' understates it slightly. The 14% is a March-2020 datapoint and must be labeled as such - it is six years stale relative to the 2025/2024 figures in (a) and (b).

itemVerdicts.item: (d) The Fed paper's four-channel taxonomy contains no 'price discovery / index bubble' channel; top ten passive managers ~90% of passive AUM since 2004
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim from the r1 PDF: 'We examine four types of repercussions of the active-to-passive shift that may have implications for financial stability: (1) effects on funds' liquidity transformation and redemption risk, particularly in the MF and ETF sectors; (2) growth of passive investing strategies that amplify volatility; (3) increased asset-management industry concentration; and (4) changes in asset valuations, volatility, and comovement.' Table 1 lists the same four with impacts Reduces / Increases / Increases / Uncertain. There is no price-discovery or informational-efficiency channel: the string 'price discovery' appears exactly once in the whole paper, in the intro's survey of other people's claims ('claims about effects on industry concentration, asset prices, volatility, price discovery, market liquidity, competition, and corporate governance'), and 'informativeness' / 'informational efficiency' appear nowhere. IMPORTANT QUALIFIER the article must not overrun: channel 4 IS titled 'Changes in asset valuations, volatility, and comovement' and is described as 'Index-inclusion effects: Assets added to indexes experience changes in returns and liquidity, including greater comovement', and the paper explicitly contemplates price distortion ('particularly if index-inclusion effects distort asset prices and increase the profitability of active investing strategies that exploit these distortions'). So 'no price-discovery channel' is true; 'the Fed did not consider price effects at all' would be false. Concentration stat verbatim: 'The high concentration for passive funds is also reflected in the combined market share of the ten largest passive-fund asset managers, which has averaged about 90 percent of total passive-fund industry AUM since 2004' - it is an average since 2004, stated in a footnote to Figure 4 (the HHI figure), not a point-in-time 2020 reading.

newContradictions: Chinco and Sammon, 'The Passive-Ownership Share Is Double What You Think It Is' (April 7 2024 draft, local chinco_sammon.txt; published Journal of Financial Economics vol. 157, 2024) directly contests the fund-only caliber this claim group rests on. Abstract verbatim: 'While index funds held 16% of the US stock market in 2021, we put the overall passive ownership share at 33.5%. Our headline number is twice as large because it reflects index funds as well as other kinds of passive investors, such as institutional investors with internally managed index portfolios and active managers who are closet indexing.' The paper adds that including indexes outside their sample would take 33.5% to 38.5%, and that even a volume-only lower bound puts it at 24.6% in 2021. Their 16% index-fund number is essentially ICI's 17% for 2021, so the two are consistent on the narrow measure and diverge only on scope. If the article deploys ICI's 19% and Vanguard's 23% as the refutation of 'passive owns half the market', it must state that both numerators are registered-fund assets only and exclude internal indexing by pensions/endowments, separately managed and direct-indexed accounts, collective investment trusts, and closet indexing - i.e. the honest range is roughly 19-23% for index funds versus roughly a third of the market for index-linked ownership broadly. Otherwise the passage swaps one caliber error for another.

ICI's own 2026 Fact Book supplies the number the 'half the market' claim actually comes from, and the article should show both side by side to make the caliber contrast land: 'At year-end 2025, index mutual funds and index ETFs together accounted for the majority (52%) of assets in long-term funds, up from 19% at year-end 2010 (Figure 2.5)', with total index MF+ETF net assets of $19.1 trillion. So 52% = share of long-term FUND assets, 19% = share of US stock market cap; both are ICI, same chapter, two pages apart.

Denominator mismatch across (a) and (b) that the article should not paper over: ICI's 19% divides by World Federation of Exchanges US market cap and counts only domestic-equity index funds' US stock holdings, while Vanguard's 23% divides by the CRSP Total Market Index and counts every fund worldwide's US-equity allocation plus Morningstar 'U.S. Equity' global-category funds. The four-point gap is mostly definitional, not a disagreement about facts, and the two figures are also one year apart (YE2025 vs Dec 31 2024) - stacking them as if they were rival estimates of the same quantity would be misleading.
reasoning: I treated every sub-claim as false until I saw the sentence myself, and I did not rely on any of the pre-extracted local text for the load-bearing numbers. Primary documents reached verbatim: (1) https://icifactbook.org/pdf/2026-factbook-ch2.pdf, downloaded fresh; because the Figure 2.6 stacked-bar labels come out of pdftotext with scrambled line order, I ran pdftotext -bbox-layout on the figure page and reassembled the series by x-coordinate, then independently cross-checked the overlapping years against a fresh download of 2025-factbook-ch2.pdf. Both books agree year by year, so the 2019=16 / 2020=15 dip is ICI's real series, not a parsing artifact. (2) https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/feds/files/2018060r1pap.pdf, downloaded fresh and grepped for the exact strings; all of 14%, <4% in 2005, 41% of combined US MF+ETF AUM, 97% of ETF assets, the four-channel enumeration and Table 1, and the ten-largest-managers ~90% footnote appear verbatim. I also pulled the Board's FEDS landing page for this paper to check for a later revision: there is none beyond r1 (page last updated December 22, 2020), though the page labels the revision 'June 2020' where the PDF cover says 'This draft: May 15, 2020'. (3) The Vanguard paper text, where Figure 2's five country percentages, the December 31 2024 as-of date, the worldwide-funds numerator and the CRSP Total Market denominator all read exactly as claimed. Every number, date, population and denominator in the group checks out, so the verdict is HOLDS with no corrections. What is not wrong but is incomplete: this is a fund-assets-only caliber, and the peer-reviewed Chinco-Sammon estimate of a 33.5% (up to 38.5%) passive ownership share for 2021 sits directly against any implication that ~20% is the ceiling on index-linked ownership of US equity; I logged that plus the 52%-of-fund-assets figure from ICI's own chapter and the ICI/Vanguard denominator mismatch as contradictions the article must address. Residual uncertainty: I could not open the paywalled Financial Analysts Journal 76(4) version of Anadu et al. to confirm the published text carries the same 14%/41%/97% figures, but the FEDS r1 cover date sits inside the FAJ publication window and the article cites the FEDS version, so nothing in the claim depends on it. I also did not verify whether Vanguard has published a 2026 update with a post-2024 figure; the August 2025 paper is the current one on its research page.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Headline: index funds held 16% of the US market in 2021; total passive ownership 33.5%; five indexes (S&P 500, S&P MidCap 400, Russell 1000, Russell 2000, Nasdaq 100)
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers and index list CONFIRMED verbatim. Abstract: "While index funds held 16% of the US stock market in 2021, we put the overall passive ownership share at 33.5%." Figure 2 caption names exactly the five indexes. WRONG in the claim: "using reconstitution-day CLOSING-volume spikes." The headline 33.5% uses DailyVolume = TOTAL volume on reconstitution day. Figure 2 caption: "Calculation is based on total volume experienced by index additions and deletions on reconstitution day." Section 2.2: "When using DailyVolume as the proxy for passive rebalancing on reconstitution days, we find that 33.5% ..." RIGHT: total reconstitution-day volume. The closing-auction-only proxy (VolumeAtClose) gives 13.31% for 2021, not 33.5% — so "closing-volume" is not a harmless paraphrase, it is off by a factor of 2.5.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Honest range 24.6% (after-hours-only proxy) to 38.5% (adding Vanguard's $2.25T CRSP assets, in which case ICI's 16% falls to 11%)
itemVerdicts.note: Both endpoints exist verbatim. Sec 2.2: "When using Volume1600to2359 instead of DailyVolume, we still put the US passive ownership share at 24.6% in 2021" (Table 4 col 3, 2021 = 24.62). And: "In December 2021 Vanguard had roughly $2.25t tracking CRSP indexes. If we were to remove this $2.25t from ICI's asset base, their 16% would fall to 11%. If we were to include this $2.25t, our 33.5% would climb to 38.5%." TWO corrections. (i) WRONG: the low end of the paper's own reported range is 24.6%. RIGHT: Table 4 reports progressively narrower proxies for 2021 — DailyVolume 33.50, DailyVolume−ADV 28.65, Volume1600to2359 24.62, VolumeAtClosingPrice 22.53, VolumeAtClose 13.31. The paper's own most conservative number, 13.31%, is BELOW ICI's 16%, and the paper states: "there is no statistically measurable difference between our point estimate for %Indexed(2021) based on VolumeAtClose, 13.31% ± (1.96%), and ICI's estimate based on index-fund holdings, 16%." The authors argue col (5) "is too low," but it is theirs and it is in the published table. (ii) WRONG: "38.5% ... in which case ICI's 16% falls to 11%" reads as doing both adjustments at once. RIGHT: these are two ALTERNATIVE like-for-like alignments — either 38.5% vs ICI 16% (2.4x), or 33.5% vs ICI 11% (3.05x). 38.5% vs 11% is double-counting.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Passive share already 13.4% in 2000 on their own measure — 2.5x rise vs 5.3x for the fund measure (3%→16%)
itemVerdicts.note: Substantively CONFIRMED. Figure 2 labels 13.4% and 3.0% at 2000, 33.5% and 16.0% at 2021; Sec 4.1 says the passive share "has grown from 13.4% to 33.5% during this same period." 33.50/13.39 = 2.50, so "2.5x" is right. Minor slippage: the Table 3 total for 2000 is 13.39 (standard error ±1.35), not a precise 13.40 — the 13.4% is a rounded figure label. And "5.3x" has false precision: the paper only says index funds had "$0.4t in AUM, roughly 3% of the value of the US stock market" in 2000, so the fund-based multiple is "roughly 5x," not 5.3x. Also worth caveating in the article: the C&S series is noisy (2009 spike to 31.85, back to 24.32 in 2010) and pre-2009 index weights are interpolated, so the 2000 level is the least reliable point in the series.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Index add/delete returns "steadily converged to nearly zero"; Tesla Dec-18-2020 reconstitution-day return +5.96%
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, Sec 4.1: "the returns to buying index additions and the returns to selling index deletions have steadily converged to nearly zero. This has happened in spite of the fact that the overall passive ownership share has grown from 13.4% to 33.5% during this same period." And: "Tesla realized a 5.96% reconstitution-day return in Figure 13." Figure 13 caption confirms 5.96% is the realized reconstitution-day return (raw, alongside +8.21% on announcement day). Context the article should keep: the paper immediately adds "To be clear: index inclusion does affect prices. The effect just does not come by way of passive rebalancing demand on reconstitution days" — the price impact moves to announcement/prearrangement, it does not vanish.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Method concedes it counts ANY close-of-reconstitution-day rebalancing as passive
itemVerdicts.note: The concession is real and verbatim: "Our procedure counts any holdings that get rebalanced at this one point in time as passive holdings; it does not matter who actually owns these assets. As such, our numbers likely includes passive investments made by people who would not consider themselves to be passive investors" — illustrated with a closet-indexing active manager. WRONG in the claim's parenthetical: "(active managers forced to trade on index changes included)." That is not what the paper concedes — it counts CLOSET INDEXERS as passive by design (that is the paper's thesis, not a bug), and it explicitly rebuts the idea that opportunistic/active trading inflates the number: "the variation in reconstitution-day volume across changes to the same index on the same day is almost entirely explained by passive demand ... There is very little left for active managers to explain." RIGHT framing: the estimate is by construction a measure of index-linked rebalancing behavior, not of self-identified passive investors; the authors argue non-passive contamination is small and quantify it (Table 4 col 2, DailyVolume−ADV, suggests overestimation of "somewhere between 2%pt and 5%pt").

itemVerdicts.item: (f) Earlier drafts' 2020 value ~37.8% vs published 32.19%
itemVerdicts.note: CONFIRMED with primary documents. July 19, 2022 draft (foster.uw.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/1b-Sammon-Chinco-new-title.pdf) abstract: "We estimate that passive investors held at least 37.8% of the US stock market in 2020 ... What's more, 37.8% is a lower bound." Published/final version Table 3, 2020 total = 32.19 (SE 3.26). Additional material fact the article should carry: the 37.8% draft covered only THREE indexes (S&P 500, Russell 1000, Russell 2000) over 2011–2020 and was framed as a lower bound; the published version covers five indexes over 2000–2021 and drops the lower-bound claim entirely. There is also an intermediate May 19, 2023 draft with a 33.3% headline for 2021 (2020 = 33.06, 2000 = 12.82, after-hours 2021 = 25.93), versus the published 33.5% / 32.19 / 13.39 / 24.62. So the series moved across at least three versions, not two.

corrections: Replace 'reconstitution-day closing-volume spikes' with 'total reconstitution-day volume (the paper's DailyVolume proxy)'. The 33.5% headline is built on ALL volume on reconstitution day. The paper's closing-auction-only proxy gives 13.31% for 2021, so calling the headline a closing-volume measure misstates the numerator by a factor of ~2.5.

Widen the stated range: the paper's own Table 4 (2021) reports 33.50% (all-day), 28.65% (all-day minus average daily volume), 24.62% (4:00pm–11:59pm), 22.53% (volume at the closing price), and 13.31% (closing auction only). The honest low end is 13.31%, not 24.6%. Quote the paper's own sentence: 'there is no statistically measurable difference between our point estimate for %Indexed(2021) based on VolumeAtClose, 13.31% ± (1.96%), and ICI's estimate based on index-fund holdings, 16%.' The authors note they think 13.31% is too low, but it is their published number.

Do not combine the two Vanguard adjustments. The paper offers them as alternatives: 'If we were to remove this $2.25t from ICI's asset base, their 16% would fall to 11%. If we were to include this $2.25t, our 33.5% would climb to 38.5%.' The like-for-like pairs are 38.5% vs 16% (2.4x) OR 33.5% vs 11% (3.05x). Writing '38.5%, in which case ICI's 16% falls to 11%' double-counts the same $2.25t.

Fix (e)'s parenthetical. The paper does not concede that 'active managers forced to trade on index changes' are counted; it deliberately counts closet indexers as passive ('our numbers likely includes passive investments made by people who would not consider themselves to be passive investors') and explicitly argues residual active trading is small: 'There is very little left for active managers to explain.' Its own quantification of possible overstatement is 2–5 percentage points (Table 4, DailyVolume minus ADV).

Change '5.3x rise of the fund-based measure (3%→16%)' to 'roughly 5x (from roughly 3% to 16%)'. The paper only says index funds' $0.4t in 2000 was 'roughly 3% of the value of the US stock market'; 5.3x implies a precision the source does not have. Keep 2.5x for the C&S measure (33.50/13.39 = 2.50), but note the 2000 estimate carries a standard error of ±1.35pp and pre-2009 index weights are interpolated.

Cite the published version precisely: Alex Chinco and Marco Sammon, 'The passive ownership share is double what you think it is,' Journal of Financial Economics, vol. 157, July 2024, article 103860 (doi 10.1016/j.jfineco.2024.103860). The freely available author PDF at alexchinco.com is dated April 7, 2024 and matches the published numbers.

When making point (f), add that the 37.8% figure came from a materially different specification — the July 19, 2022 draft covered only the S&P 500, Russell 1000 and Russell 2000 over 2011–2020 and called 37.8% 'a lower bound' — and that an intermediate May 19, 2023 draft had a 33.3% headline (2020 = 33.06). The number moved across at least three versions, and the 'lower bound' claim was dropped, which is a stronger version of the article's point than 'the number moved'.
newContradictions: The paper's most conservative published estimate for 2021 (13.31%, closing-auction volume only) is BELOW the ICI index-fund share of 16%, and the paper concedes the two are statistically indistinguishable. Any article using Chinco-Sammon as proof that passive ownership is 'double' must confront the fact that the paper's own narrowest proxy supports no gap at all.

The paper's abstract-level claim was walked back between versions: the 2022 draft asserted 37.8% was 'a lower bound' and that 'the true passive-ownership share for the US stock market must be higher'; the published version drops the lower-bound language entirely and instead presents a menu of proxies bracketing the estimate from both sides.

Chinco-Sammon is evidence AGAINST the simple 'passive flows move prices' version of the index-bubble thesis, not for it: reconstitution-day abnormal returns 'steadily converged to nearly zero' while their measured passive share more than doubled. The paper attributes this to prearranged trading moving price impact earlier, citing Greenwood and Sammon (2022) on announcement-day effects — so the article should not use the 33.5% number and the 'passive demand is inelastically pushing prices up' claim as if they were the same finding.
reasoning: I worked primarily from primary documents, not summaries. (1) Local file chinco_sammon.txt matched a fresh curl of https://www.alexchinco.com/double-what-you-think-it-is.pdf (dated April 7, 2024, the final author version); I re-extracted with `pdftotext -layout` to read Tables 3, 4, 5 and 6 accurately, because the plain extraction had scrambled the numeric columns. Files: /private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-cissychen-design/0f8bdcde-3464-42f4-af17-1552808c31d6/scratchpad/cs_live.pdf and cs_layout.txt. (2) I pulled and extracted the July 19, 2022 draft (foster.uw.edu, saved as cs_2022.pdf / cs_2022.txt) and the May 19, 2023 HBS draft (cs_may23.pdf / cs_may23.txt) to trace the version history for sub-claim (f). (3) I confirmed the publication record via the Crossref API rather than ScienceDirect (which returned 403): JFE vol. 157, July 2024, article 103860. Verbatim strings I actually read: the abstract; the 'counts any holdings that get rebalanced at this one point in time as passive holdings' passage; 'steadily converged to nearly zero'; 'Tesla realized a 5.96% reconstitution-day return'; the $2.25t / 11% / 38.5% passage; the 24.6% passage; the '13.31% ± (1.96%)' vs ICI 16% sentence; Table 3 (2000 = 13.39, 2020 = 32.19, 2021 = 33.50); Table 4 (2021 row: 33.50, 28.65, 24.62, 22.53, 13.31); and the 2022 draft's 'at least 37.8% ... in 2020 ... 37.8% is a lower bound' abstract. Everything in the claim group traces to real text; the failures are caliber failures, chiefly (i) describing the headline proxy as closing volume when it is total reconstitution-day volume, and (ii) truncating the paper's own range at 24.6% when the published table runs down to 13.31%. Remaining uncertainty: I could not open the ScienceDirect typeset version (403), so I verified the published numbers via the author's April 7, 2024 PDF plus Crossref metadata rather than against the JFE PDF itself; I saw no evidence of divergence, but I did not confirm the typeset text character-for-character. I also searched for post-publication critiques, replications or an ICI rebuttal up to 2026-08 and found none — treat that as 'not found', not as 'none exists'.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Headline: index funds held 16% of US market in 2021, total passive ≈33.5%, from reconstitution-day CLOSING-volume spikes across five indexes (S&P 500, S&P 400, R1000, R2000, NDX)
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers and index list confirmed verbatim. Abstract: 'While index funds held 16% of the US stock market in 2021, we put the overall passive ownership share at 33.5%.' Eq. (7) sums S&P 500 + S&P MidCap + Russell 1000 + Russell 2000 + Nasdaq 100; Table 3 total for 2021 = 33.50 (SE 2.91). WRONG: describing the headline proxy as 'closing-volume spikes.' RIGHT: the 33.5% headline uses DailyVolume — ALL reconstitution-day volume ('We estimate that there was $15.1t in passive AUM during 2021 when treating all reconstitution-day volume as rebalancing volume'). Restricting to volume from 4:00pm on gives 24.62%; restricting to the closing auction itself gives 13.31%. The 16% is share of US market cap (ICI domestic equity index mutual funds + ETFs, $7.2t), not share of fund assets — that part is clean.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Honest range 24.6% (after-hours-only) to 38.5% (adding Vanguard's $2.25T CRSP assets, in which case ICI's 16% falls to 11%)
itemVerdicts.note: Two errors. (1) FLOOR. WRONG: 'the honest range is 24.6% to 38.5%.' RIGHT: the paper's own Table 4 reports five proxies for 2021 — all-day 33.50, minus-ADV 28.65, 4:00pm–11:59pm 24.62, at-closing-price 22.53, closing-auction-only 13.31. 24.6% is the MIDDLE proxy, not the floor. The paper's own 'most conservative estimate' is 13.31%, and it concedes: 'there is no statistically measurable difference between our point estimate for %Indexed(2021) based on VolumeAtClose, 13.31% ± (1.96%), and ICI's estimate based on index-fund holdings, 16%.' Honest range is ~13.3%–38.5%. (Authors do argue col. 5 'is too low' because upstairs block orders tied to the closing price hit the tape after 4:00pm.) (2) PAIRING. WRONG: presenting 38.5% and 11% as one scenario. RIGHT: they are mutually exclusive adjustments — 'If we were to remove this $2.25t from ICI's asset base, their 16% would fall to 11%. If we were to include this $2.25t, our 33.5% would climb to 38.5%.' Valid pairs are 33.5 vs 11 or 38.5 vs 16; 38.5 vs 11 double-counts the same $2.25t. Vanguard figure confirmed ('roughly $2.25t in equity holdings tracking CRSP indexes', estimated from Thomson S12). The 'after-hours' descriptor for Volume1600to2359 matches the paper's own language.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Passive share already 13.4% in 2000 — 2.5x rise vs 5.3x rise of fund measure (3%→16%)
itemVerdicts.note: Table 3 total for 2000 = 13.39 (paper rounds to 13.4% in Figure 5 and in text: '67bps is 20× smaller than the US passive ownership share in 2000, 13.4%'). Intro confirms index funds '$0.4t in 2000, roughly 3%' → '16% of the market's value' in 2021. Arithmetic: 33.50/13.39 = 2.50x; 16/3 = 5.33x. Caveat worth carrying: the series is noisy and non-monotonic (25.31% in 2008, 31.85% in 2009, 24.32% in 2010, 22.06% in 2015) with wide SEs (±1.35pp in 2000, ±2.91pp in 2021), so the endpoint ratio is fragile.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Add/delete returns 'steadily converged to nearly zero' while passive doubled; Tesla Dec-18-2020 reconstitution-day return +5.96%
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'the returns to buying index additions and the returns to selling index deletions have steadily converged to nearly zero. This has happened in spite of the fact that the overall passive ownership share has grown from 13.4% to 33.5% during this same period.' Tesla verbatim: 'Tesla realized a 5.96% reconstitution-day return in Figure 13' (Figure 13 labels Dec 18 as Recon day, +5.96%; Nov 17 announcement day +8.21%). Two qualifiers the article must not drop: the underlying fact is attributed to Greenwood and Sammon ('as Greenwood and Sammon (2022) document, there is no longer much predictable price pressure on reconstitution days'), and C&S add 'To be clear: index inclusion does affect prices. The effect just does not come by way of passive rebalancing demand on reconstitution days.' Also 5.96% is Tesla's raw close-to-close return; excluding Tesla, other 2020 S&P 500 additions had abnormal reconstitution-day returns of just 1.20%.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Method concedes it counts ANY close-of-reconstitution-day rebalancing as passive
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'Our procedure counts any holdings that get rebalanced at this one point in time as passive holdings; it does not matter who actually owns these assets. As such, our numbers likely includes passive investments made by people who would not consider themselves to be passive investors.' Their worked example is a closet indexer with $50b of a $250b book. Minor caliber note on the parenthetical: the paper's concession covers closet/internal/direct indexers, and it explicitly argues AGAINST contamination from opportunistic active traders ('we see no evidence of investors delaying trades to take advantage of reconstitution-day liquidity'). 'Active managers forced to trade' is a fair gloss on closet indexing but is not the paper's phrasing.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) Earlier drafts' 2020 value ~37.8% vs published 32.19%
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed from the primary July 19, 2022 draft (foster.uw.edu PDF), abstract verbatim: 'We estimate that passive investors held at least 37.8% of the US stock market in 2020.' Published Table 3 gives 2020 = 32.19. The drift is LARGER than the article says: the 2022 draft's 37.8% was built on closing-window volume only (VolumeAtClose defined there as 4:00pm–4:20pm TAQ volume) across only THREE indexes (S&P 500, Russell 1000, Russell 2000), and was billed as 'a lower bound'; the published paper's closing-auction proxy for 2020 across FIVE indexes is 11.54%, and its 4:00pm–11:59pm proxy is 21.37%. An intermediate May 19, 2023 HBS draft had a 33.3% headline for 2021 (vs 33.5% published).

itemVerdicts.item: Publication attribution: JFE July 2024, sciencedirect S0304405X24000837
itemVerdicts.note: Crossref record: 'The passive ownership share is double what you think it is', Journal of Financial Economics, vol. 157, published print 2024-07, article 103860, doi 10.1016/j.jfineco.2024.103860. The alexchinco.com PDF I downloaded and checked is dated April 7, 2024 and its abstract matches the published title/abstract. Note SSRN/working-paper title hyphenates as 'Passive-Ownership Share'; the journal record does not. ScienceDirect itself returned 403 to me — bibliographic facts come from Crossref plus the author-hosted PDF, not from the publisher page.

corrections: Do not describe the 33.5% headline as coming from 'closing-volume spikes.' The headline uses DailyVolume — all reconstitution-day volume ('when treating all reconstitution-day volume as rebalancing volume'). Close-restricted proxies give materially lower numbers: 24.62% (4:00pm–11:59pm), 22.53% (at the closing price), 13.31% (closing auction only).

Replace 'the honest range is 24.6% to 38.5%' with 'roughly 13.3% to 38.5%.' Chinco-Sammon Table 4 reports five proxies for 2021: 33.50 (all day), 28.65 (minus ADV), 24.62 (4:00pm–11:59pm), 22.53 (at closing price), 13.31 (closing auction). 24.6% is the middle proxy, not the floor. Quote-safe sentence from the paper: 'there is no statistically measurable difference between our point estimate for %Indexed(2021) based on VolumeAtClose, 13.31% ± (1.96%), and ICI's estimate based on index-fund holdings, 16%.' If used, note the authors' rebuttal that column (5) 'is too low' because upstairs block orders tied to the closing price do not hit the tape until after 4:00pm.

Stop pairing 38.5% with 11%. The paper offers them as two alternative apples-to-apples fixes for the same $2.25t: 'If we were to remove this $2.25t from ICI's asset base, their 16% would fall to 11%. If we were to include this $2.25t, our 33.5% would climb to 38.5%.' Valid comparisons are 33.5% vs 11% OR 38.5% vs 16%. Comparing 38.5% against 11% double-counts the Vanguard CRSP assets.

Strengthen and re-specify the version-drift point (f). The July 19, 2022 draft abstract reads: 'We estimate that passive investors held at least 37.8% of the US stock market in 2020' — and that 37.8% was (i) computed from close-window volume (4:00pm–4:20pm TAQ), (ii) based on only three indexes (S&P 500, Russell 1000, Russell 2000), and (iii) explicitly called 'a lower bound.' The published paper's 2020 figure on all-day volume across five indexes is 32.19%, and its closing-auction figure for 2020 is 11.54%. So the estimate on the earlier draft's own conceptual proxy fell by roughly two-thirds while the headline was kept near 'double' by switching to all-day volume. Also note the intermediate May 19, 2023 draft headline was 33.3%.

Cite as: Alex Chinco and Marco Sammon, 'The passive ownership share is double what you think it is,' Journal of Financial Economics 157 (July 2024), article 103860, doi 10.1016/j.jfineco.2024.103860. The author-hosted working paper at alexchinco.com is the April 7, 2024 version (identical headline numbers).

When using 13.4% (2000), note it is 13.39 in Table 3 with a standard error of 1.35pp, and that the series is non-monotonic (25.31% in 2008, 31.85% in 2009, 24.32% in 2010, 22.06% in 2015). The 2.5x-vs-5.3x contrast is arithmetically right but rests on two noisy endpoints (2021 SE ±2.91pp).

On the converged index effect, attribute the underlying finding to Greenwood and Sammon, 'The Disappearing Index Effect' — Chinco-Sammon write 'as Greenwood and Sammon (2022) document, there is no longer much predictable price pressure on reconstitution days.' Keep their qualifier: 'To be clear: index inclusion does affect prices. The effect just does not come by way of passive rebalancing demand on reconstitution days.'

On Tesla, 5.96% is the raw reconstitution-day (Dec 18, 2020) close-to-close return. If the article wants the abnormal figure, the paper says including Tesla the 2020 S&P 500 additions returned 5.14 percentage points above the market, and 'All other S&P 500 additions in 2020 have abnormal reconstitution-day returns of just 1.20%.'
newContradictions: The paper's own most-conservative proxy (closing-auction volume only) puts 2021 passive ownership at 13.31% ± 1.96%, which the authors concede is statistically indistinguishable from ICI's 16% index-fund share — i.e., on their strictest measure the passive share is NOT double the fund-based number, it is at or below it. This is a stronger stick for the skeptical thesis than the 24.6% the article currently uses, and it is in the published paper (Table 4, column 5).
Table 4's caption says 'six different proxies' but only five columns are reported — a typo in the published paper, worth avoiding as a quotation.

The 2022 draft's headline of 37.8% covered only three indexes (S&P 500, R1000, R2000) yet exceeded the published five-index all-day estimate for the same year (32.19%). More indexes plus more volume produced a smaller number, which implies a substantive methodological revision, not just a data update.
reasoning: I read the primary paper text end to end. Local scratchpad file chinco_sammon.txt is the April 7, 2024 version; I independently re-downloaded https://www.alexchinco.com/double-what-you-think-it-is.pdf and re-extracted with pdftotext -layout (saved as cs_current.pdf/cs_current.txt) because Table 3 and Table 4 were column-scrambled in the pre-existing extraction — the layout-preserved re-extraction is what I used for all table numbers. I also downloaded and extracted two earlier primary drafts myself: the July 19, 2022 conference draft (foster.uw.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/1b-Sammon-Chinco-new-title.pdf → cs_2022.txt) and the May 19, 2023 HBS draft (cs_may23.txt). Every quoted string in this verdict was read directly in those files; nothing came from a fetch summarizer. Bibliographic facts (JFE vol. 157, July 2024, article 103860, doi 10.1016/j.jfineco.2024.103860) come from the Crossref API, since ScienceDirect, SSRN and HBS all returned 403 to WebFetch. Verified verbatim: abstract 16%/33.5%; the five-index sum in Eq. (7); Table 3 2000=13.39, 2020=32.19, 2021=33.50; Table 4 2021 row 33.50/28.65/24.62/22.53/13.31 and 2020 row 32.19/26.24/21.37/19.35/11.54; the 24.6% sentence; the $2.25t / 11% / 38.5% sentences; the 'counts any holdings that get rebalanced at this one point in time as passive' concession; the 'steadily converged to nearly zero' sentence; the Tesla 5.96% sentence and 1.20% ex-Tesla figure; and the 2022 draft's 'at least 37.8% ... in 2020' with its three-index, 4:00pm-4:20pm, lower-bound framing. Two substantive errors found: the article's stated floor of 24.6% is not the paper's floor (13.31% is, and the authors concede it is statistically indistinguishable from ICI's 16%), and the article pairs 38.5% with 11%, which double-counts the same $2.25t of Vanguard CRSP assets. One looser caliber issue: the headline proxy is total reconstitution-day volume, not closing volume. Remaining uncertainty: I could not open the ScienceDirect page itself, so I cannot rule out copy-edit-level differences between the April 7, 2024 author PDF and the typeset JFE article; the abstract and all headline figures match the published record via Crossref and secondary listings, and no erratum or comment paper surfaced in searches through 2026-08. I also found no published critique, replication, or contradicting estimate of the 33.5% figure up to today's date."

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Vanguard (Aug 2025): index fund portfolio-management trading = 1.2% of total US exchange dollar volume in 2024, up from 0.3% in 2006; active funds 2-5%
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the Vanguard research paper 'Setting the record straight: The truths about index fund investing' (Vanguard research, August 2025; Rowley, Lawrence, Ryder-Green), page 9 body text: 'Trading volume has slowly increased from about $38 trillion in 2006 to about $153 trillion in 2024. During that period, active fund volume remained between 2% and 5% of total trading volume, while index fund trading volume slowly grew from about 0.3% of total volume to 1.2%.' Figure 6 title: 'Index fund trading volume is a drop in the bucket'; data as of December 31, 2024. Body also says 'Index fund trading volume constitutes just over 1% of total trading activity' and 'active fund trading volume is higher (2% of total volume)' — i.e. the 2-5% is a RANGE OVER 2006-2024, the 2024 point value is ~2%. If the article writes 'active funds 2-5%' as a current level rather than a historical band, tighten it.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-def) Definition = cash-flow-adjusted turnover / Cboe total volume, EXCLUDING ETF secondary-market trading, index derivatives, and indexed separate accounts
itemVerdicts.note: Figure 6 note verbatim: 'The percentage of total trading volume is cash-flow adjusted turnover as a percentage of total U.S. exchange trading volume. Data include all available equity open-end funds and ETFs with U.S. equity exposure from January 1, 2006, through December 31, 2024, in each category as defined by Morningstar. Data include net assets, turnover ratio, net flow, and U.S. equity exposure data from Morningstar, along with total trading volume on U.S. exchanges from Cboe Exchange.' Numerator/denominator confirmed. CAVEAT the article should know: the PDF does NOT itself state the three exclusions — they follow by construction (fund-level turnover; Morningstar open-end-fund/ETF universe). The exclusions ARE stated explicitly by Vanguard, but in a different document: its statement to Institutional Investor (Jan 3, 2025), which describes a separate estimate 'after accounting for indexed portfolio management outside of registered funds and removing trading volume due to [high-frequency trading] and shares of ETFs.' Attribute the exclusion list to that statement, not to the Aug 2025 PDF's figure note.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-quote) Verbatim: 'the claim that they are becoming the primary driver of market dynamics is demonstrably false.'
itemVerdicts.note: Exact string present, page 9: 'Index funds are an important source of ownership, but the claim that they are becoming the primary driver of market dynamics is demonstrably false. Index fund investing leaves ample room for price discovery.' Note the antecedent of 'they' is index funds — quote it with enough context that 'they' is not ambiguous.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) ICI 2026 Fact Book: ETF secondary-market trading averaged 28% of total US stock market trading in 2025; series 25-32% since 2016
itemVerdicts.note: Verified in the 2026 Investment Company Fact Book Quick Facts Guide, p.8. Chart title verbatim: 'ETF Secondary Market Trading Averaged 28% of Daily US Stock Trading in 2025', subtitle 'Average daily ETF share of total US stock market trading, percentage, annual'. Annual series 2016-2025: 27, 25, 27, 27, 26, 25, 32, 30, 27, 28 — min 25% (2017, 2021), max 32% (2022), so '25-32% since 2016' is exact. Body text verbatim: 'This share declined from its 2022 peak as market volatility eased and averaged 28% in 2025.' Article is right that this is trading in ETF SHARES, not underlyings ('Retail investors access ETFs through the secondary market (e.g., on an exchange), which is where most ETF activity occurs'). ONE CALIBER FLAG: this is ALL ETFs — active ETFs included — so it is not a 'passive share' figure at all, and should not be presented inside a passive-share-of-trading range without that qualifier. Direct curl of the cited ici.org URL returns HTTP 403 (bot block); the document was retrieved earlier in this run and its header confirms identity ('2026 Investment Company Fact Book / Quick Facts Guide / icifactbook.org').

itemVerdicts.item: (c) SSGA (Jan 23, 2026, 'Closing time'): US market-on-close volume rose from 8.40% of total volume (Jan 2018) to 15.39% (Dec 2025)
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: '8.40% of total volume (Jan 2018)' read as the January 2018 level. RIGHT: 8.40% is the DAILY AVERAGE over the whole period from January 2018 through December 31, 2025 — it is not a point value for any month. Figure 2 is titled 'Daily Average Comparison of Trade Volume – USA versus Developed Europe versus APAC' and its US 'Close %' column reads: 'From Jan 2018' 8.40%, 'From Jan 2019' 9.24%, '1 Year' 12.11%, 'Q4 2025' 13.10%, '25-Dec' 15.39%. Source line verbatim: 'Source: Instinet as of December 31, 2025.' The 15.39% figure IS a December 2025 point value and is confirmed in body text: 'December 2025 data shows that Developed Europe allocates roughly 34.82 percent of daily volume to the closing auction, compared with 15.39 percent in the United States and 16.78 percent in Asia ex Japan.' Rows are nested averaging windows of increasing recency, not a time series, so 8.40%→15.39% is not a clean 'rose from X to Y' comparison; the actual Jan-2018 monthly level is not published in the piece. Title, author (Elise Ryan), and date (January 23, 2026) all confirmed.

itemVerdicts.item: (c-negative) The SSGA piece gives NO passive share of MOC volume
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed by full-text extraction of the page: no percentage anywhere is attributed to passive/index funds' share of closing-auction volume. The piece only asserts a causal narrative — 'Index funds and ETFs are structurally incentivized to execute trades at the closing auction because official net asset values (NAVs) are calculated using closing prices' — and explicitly notes active managers migrate to the close too: 'This migration by active managers further amplifies MOC volumes.' So the 15.39% must not be presented, even implicitly, as a passive share.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Institutional Investor (Jan 3, 2025): Green estimates passive direct trading 20% + index derivatives 8% + passive market making 36% vs active managers 10% (down from 80% in 1995)
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim: 'Using statistics compiled from various market and academic sources, Green estimates that passive direct trading now accounts for about 20 percent of all trading, passive index derivatives make up 8 percent, and passive market making contributes a further 36 percent. By contrast, trading by active managers totals only 10 percent, down from 80 percent in 1995.' Article title 'Why Michael Green Is Known as the Cassandra of Passive Investing', dated January 3, 2025. NOTE: the number 64 does not appear in the article — the 64% top of the claimed range is the article's own summation of Green's three components, and one of those components ('passive market making', 36%) is intermediary/market-maker activity, not passive investors' own trading. Present 64% as an arithmetic sum the article performs, not as Green's published headline figure.

itemVerdicts.item: (d-Vanguard) Vanguard's statement in the same article: index funds ≈ 1% and all-in indexing < 5% of volume
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'Our base case estimates that index funds account for approximately 1 percent of overall trading volume on U.S. exchanges, well below the more widely quoted 5 percent to 7 percent. Even after accounting for indexed portfolio management outside of registered funds and removing trading volume due to [high-frequency trading] and shares of ETFs, we estimate that indexing represents less than 5 percent of overall U.S. trading volume.' Also verbatim from the article: 'Vanguard disputes Green's analysis of the outsize role of passive in today's markets, saying its trading is a "drop in the bucket."' CALIBER: the <5% is not an unadjusted share of raw total volume — it is computed after ADDING indexed separate accounts and REMOVING HFT and ETF share trading from the base. Keep that qualifier or the <5% looks comparable to the ICI 28%, which it is not.

corrections: SSGA 'Closing time' (Jan 23, 2026): replace 'US market-on-close volume rose from 8.40% of total volume (Jan 2018) to 15.39% (Dec 2025)' with 'the US closing auction averaged 8.40% of daily volume over January 2018–December 2025 and reached 15.39% in December 2025 (12.11% over the trailing year; 13.10% in Q4 2025)'. The 8.40% is a period average from the row labelled 'From Jan 2018' in Figure 2 ('Daily Average Comparison of Trade Volume'), not the January 2018 level; SSGA publishes no Jan-2018 monthly point value. Source: Instinet as of December 31, 2025.

ICI 2026 Fact Book 28%: add the qualifier that this is ALL ETFs (active ETFs included), not passive ETFs, so it is an ETF-share-trading figure rather than a passive-share-of-trading figure. Chart is titled 'Average daily ETF share of total US stock market trading'.

Green's 64%: state explicitly that Institutional Investor does not print 64% — it is the sum of Green's three separately quoted components (20% direct + 8% index derivatives + 36% passive market making), and the 36% is market-maker/intermediary activity, not passive investors' own trading. Do not attribute '64%' to Green as a quoted figure.

Vanguard's '<5%' in Institutional Investor: keep Vanguard's own construction qualifier — it is 'less than 5 percent of overall U.S. trading volume' only 'after accounting for indexed portfolio management outside of registered funds and removing trading volume due to [high-frequency trading] and shares of ETFs'. Without it the <5% reads as directly comparable to ICI's unadjusted 28%, which it is not.

Vanguard 'active funds 2-5%': the 2-5% is the range across 2006–2024, not the current level. Vanguard's 2024 point figure is 'active fund trading volume is higher (2% of total volume)'. Say 'active funds ran between 2% and 5% over 2006–2024, about 2% in 2024'.

Attribution fix on the Vanguard definition: the August 2025 PDF's Figure 6 note does not itself list the exclusions (ETF secondary-market trading, index derivatives, indexed separate accounts). Those exclusions are stated by Vanguard in its statement to Institutional Investor (Jan 3, 2025). Cite that statement for the exclusion list, or phrase the PDF exclusions as following by construction from 'cash-flow adjusted turnover' over a Morningstar open-end-fund/ETF universe.
newContradictions: Framing risk in the '1.2% to 64%' range: the four figures are not four definitions of one quantity. 1.2% is index funds' portfolio trading / total exchange dollar volume; 28% is all-ETF share trading / total US stock trading; 15.39% is the closing auction's share of daily volume with NO passive attribution; 64% is a sum of one analyst's estimates including 36% of market-maker activity. Presenting them as a definitional range implies the SSGA number is a passive share, which SSGA never claims.

Double-counting inside Green's 64%: passive market making (36%) and passive direct trading (20%) are the two sides of the same trades — a passive fund's order executed against a passive-flow-facing market maker would be counted in both buckets. Nothing in the Institutional Investor article establishes these are disjoint, so the sum is not defensible as a share of trading without that caveat.

Denominator mismatch between Vanguard's two numbers: Vanguard's PDF 1.2% uses Cboe total US exchange volume as the denominator, while its <5% figure in Institutional Investor is computed on a base with HFT and ETF share trading removed. The 1.2% and the <5% are therefore not on the same scale and should not be presented as a low-to-high pair from a single methodology.

SSGA's own causal framing cuts against a clean passive attribution: the piece states 'This migration by active managers further amplifies MOC volumes, reinforcing the trend,' i.e. SSGA attributes part of the rise in closing-auction share to ACTIVE managers following the liquidity. Any use of the MOC series as evidence of passive's trading footprint must carry that.
reasoning: Reached all four primary documents in full text, not summaries. (a) Vanguard 'Setting the record straight: The truths about index fund investing', Vanguard research, August 2025 — local extraction at /private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-cissychen-design/0f8bdcde-3464-42f4-af17-1552808c31d6/scratchpad/vg.txt (identical bytes to vanguard2025.txt, v_vg.txt, vg_v.txt, 69,905 bytes each). Read page 9 body and Figure 6 note verbatim: 0.3%→1.2% (2006→2024), active 2-5%, 'cash-flow adjusted turnover as a percentage of total U.S. exchange trading volume', Cboe denominator, $38T→$153T total volume, and the exact sentence 'the claim that they are becoming the primary driver of market dynamics is demonstrably false.' All confirmed. (b) ICI 2026 Fact Book Quick Facts Guide — local extraction ici2026qf.txt, p.8. Chart title, subtitle, body sentence, and all ten annual values read directly; 28% in 2025 and a 25-32% band since 2016 both exact. The cited ici.org URL now returns HTTP 403 to direct curl (bot block), but the local extraction's header self-identifies as the 2026 Quick Facts Guide. (c) SSGA 'Closing time' — fetched twice by independent paths (WebFetch summarizer and my own curl + HTML-strip to ssga.txt); both returned the same Figure 2 table, so the table values are cross-checked rather than taken from a summarizer. This is where the claim slips: the row label is 'From Jan 2018' inside a figure titled 'Daily Average Comparison of Trade Volume', and the row sequence (From Jan 2018 / From Jan 2019 / 1 Year / Q4 2025 / 25-Dec) is a set of nested lookback averages, not a time series. So 8.40% is the 2018-2025 daily average, not the January 2018 level, and 'rose from 8.40% (Jan 2018)' misreads it. 15.39% for December 2025 is independently confirmed in the body prose. The negative claim — no passive share of MOC volume anywhere in the piece — is confirmed by full-text scan; the only passive content is causal narrative, and SSGA itself credits active-manager migration for part of the rise. (d) Institutional Investor, Jan 3, 2025 — fetched and stripped to ii.txt; both the Green paragraph and the Vanguard statement paragraph read verbatim, dates and title confirmed. Searched for later corrections/replications through 2026-08 and found none; Green's figures still circulate unchanged (he left Simplify in July 2026 to start an ETF shop, per search results, but no revised estimates surfaced). Remaining uncertainty: SSGA does not disclose the exchange/venue universe behind Instinet's 'daily volume' denominator, so the 15.39% is not reconcilable against ICI's or Cboe's totals; and Vanguard's <5% adjusted estimate has no published methodology beyond the one-sentence description in the II statement, so it cannot be independently checked.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Morningstar: passive US long-term fund+ETF assets passed active at END-2023, $13.29T vs $13.23T
itemVerdicts.note: The YEAR is confirmed twice from Morningstar's own text. The Jan-17-2024 article 'It's Official: Passive Funds Overtake Active Funds' (URL recovery-us-fund-flows-was-weak-2023; 403s to WebFetch/curl, reachable via r.jina.ai) says verbatim: 'After steadily encroaching on active funds' turf for years, passive funds closed 2023 with more assets.' The Dec-2025 US Fund Flows PDF (p5) says verbatim: 'Since passive funds surpassed active funds in total net assets back in 2023...' (digit confirmed by rendering p5 to PNG — pdftotext silently drops the glyphs 3/6/8/A/F/N/R/x in this file, so the plain-text extract reads '202 '). BUT the $13.29T/$13.23T PAIR IS NOT IN ANY MORNINGSTAR DOCUMENT I could reach. The Morningstar article's chart (ZY3STRQTZNHPLBHE6DFJMGE46I.png, downloaded and read) is labelled only 'Active Assets'/'Passive Assets' with NO data labels. WRONG attribution: 'Morningstar reports $13.29T vs $13.23T.' RIGHT attribution: CNBC (Jeff Cox, published 2024-01-18) reporting Morningstar Direct data — verbatim: 'The total assets under management in exchange-traded funds and notes along with passively managed mutual funds reached a combined $13.29 trillion at the end of December, nudging above the $13.23 trillion held in active assets, according to Morningstar.' Second correction: 'Morningstar editorial classification' is wrong — the split is Morningstar Direct's index/active fund attribute (an ETF can be active and is counted as active), not an editorial call; and CNBC's own gloss ('ETFs and notes, along with passively managed mutual funds') wrongly implies all ETFs are passive — do not repeat it. Third: the exclusion list is incomplete. Morningstar's disclosure reads: 'This report includes both mutual funds and exchange-traded funds but not funds of funds unless specifically stated. It does not include collective investment trusts or separate accounts,' plus 'Long-term funds exclude money market funds.' The funds-of-funds exclusion is material — it is why the base is $26.5T rather than ICI's ~$30T for the same date. Arithmetic checks: 13.29+13.23=$26.52T; margin $60bn = 0.226% of base.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Equity-only crossover ~August 2019, $4.27T vs $4.25T (US equity funds only)
itemVerdicts.note: Substantially right, two caliber fixes. Morningstar's OWN primary statement (press release 'Morningstar Reports U.S. Mutual Fund and Exchange-Traded Fund Flows for August 2019', CHICAGO, Sept. 13, 2019, 'News provided by Morningstar, Inc.') reads verbatim: 'Passive U.S. equity assets passed active U.S. equity assets by about $25.0 billion. As a result, passive share of U.S. equity open-end and ETF assets was 50.15% versus 49.85% for active funds.' The $4.27T/$4.25T pair appears only in secondary write-ups — Citywire ('By the end of August, passive US funds had total net assets of $4.27 trillion, compared with $4.25 trillion in active US equity funds, according to data provided by Morningstar') and ThinkAdvisor ('As of Aug. 31, the assets of mutual funds and ETFs invested in U.S. equity index funds totaled $4.27 trillion, more than the $4.25 trillion invested in actively managed U.S. equity funds'). WRONG (implied): a $20bn margin, which is what $4.27T minus $4.25T reads as. RIGHT: about $25.0 billion, i.e. 50.15% vs 49.85% — the rounded pair is consistent only if the underlying are ~$4.271T and ~$4.246T. Second fix: WRONG 'US equity funds only' as a loose label; RIGHT is Morningstar's US-equity category group of open-end funds and ETFs (excludes sector-equity and international-equity), measured as of Aug. 31, 2019 and published Sept. 13, 2019 — not 'around August.'

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Morningstar Dec-2025 US Fund Flows: passive 'over 55%' at YE2025, $19.42T vs ~$16.02T, internally inconsistent at 54.8%
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed verbatim from the cited PDF (downloaded fresh from assets.contentstack.io, 40pp). Page 5 body: 'As of year-end 2025, passively managed funds made up over 55% of net assets, increasing from 53% the year prior.' Chart labels (read from a 160dpi render of p5, because pdftotext drops the 6): 'Passively Managed $19.42T' / 'Actively Managed $16.02T'. 19.42/(19.42+16.02) = 19.42/35.44 = 54.80%, so the inconsistency the article flags is real. Sharpening available: Morningstar is inconsistent with ITSELF inside one report — the p3 Key Takeaways bullet says 'reaching a 55% market share in total' while the p5 body says 'over 55%'. Also confirmed: 'Long-term funds exclude money market funds' (p3 footnote), and the '53% the year prior' YE2024 anchor.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) ICI 2026 Fact Book: index MFs+ETFs = 52% of long-term fund assets at YE2025, $19.1T of $36.6T, series 2010=19% / 2015=28% / 2020=40%
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed verbatim, and re-fetched independently of the local file to rule out extraction error. 2026-factbook-ch2 reads: 'By year-end 2025, total net assets in these two index fund categories had grown to $19.1 trillion... At year-end 2025, index mutual funds and index ETFs together accounted for the majority (52%) of assets in long-term funds, up from 19% at year-end 2010 (Figure 2.5).' Figure 2.5 data row confirmed: 19% (2010), 28% (2015), 40% (2020), 52% (2025); total net assets $9.9 / $14.9 / $24.8 / $36.6 trillion. Note confirmed verbatim: 'Data exclude money market funds. Data for ETFs exclude commodity ETFs.' 19.1/36.6 = 52.2%.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) ICI monthly release: index $21.88T vs active $18.83T in June 2026 = 53.7%
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed verbatim. Release headed 'Active and Index Combined Long-Term Mutual Funds and Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs): June 2026', dated 'Washington, DC; July 31, 2026': '...active mutual funds and ETFs increased by $85.12 billion, or 0.5%, to $18.83 trillion in June while the combined assets of the nation's indexed mutual funds and ETFs increased by $59.04 billion, or 0.3%, to $21.88 trillion in June.' The table Total row is '18,830.2 | 21,880.3 | 53.7' — ICI itself prints the 53.7% share, so it can be quoted rather than computed. Table note verbatim: 'Data for funds that invest primarily in other mutual funds were excluded from the series.' One citation fix: ICI's own Monthly Active and Index Data hub links this release as combined_active_index_0626, not the _0526 slug in the source list; both currently serve the identical June-2026 release, and ICI takes prior months offline (combined_active_index_1225 and _1125 both 404), so cite _0626.

corrections: Do not write 'Morningstar reported $13.29 trillion vs $13.23 trillion.' Morningstar's own published article and chart carry no such figures. Write: 'Morningstar's data showed passive closing 2023 above active — $13.29 trillion versus $13.23 trillion, as reported by CNBC on January 18, 2024 from Morningstar Direct.' Morningstar's own words, quotable directly, are 'passive funds closed 2023 with more assets' (Jan 17, 2024) and 'passive funds surpassed active funds in total net assets back in 2023' (December 2025 US Fund Flows, p5).

Replace 'Morningstar editorial classification' with 'Morningstar Direct's index-fund classification.' The split is index vs non-index, not vehicle-based: actively managed ETFs count as active. Do not repeat CNBC's gloss 'exchange-traded funds and notes, along with passively managed mutual funds,' which wrongly implies all ETFs are passive.

The exclusion list for the Morningstar $26.5T base must add funds of funds, collective investment trusts, and separate accounts alongside money market funds. Verbatim disclosure: 'This report includes both mutual funds and exchange-traded funds but not funds of funds unless specifically stated. It does not include collective investment trusts or separate accounts.' The funds-of-funds exclusion (target-date fund-of-funds structures) is why Morningstar's base is ~$26.5T while ICI's long-term base for a comparable date is several trillion higher — say so if the two bases are placed near each other.

For the 2019 equity crossover, do not let '$4.27T vs $4.25T' stand alone, because it reads as a $20bn margin. Morningstar's own August 2019 press release (Sept. 13, 2019) says the margin was 'about $25.0 billion' and that 'passive share of U.S. equity open-end and ETF assets was 50.15% versus 49.85% for active funds.' Use the 50.15%/49.85% or $25bn figures for the margin; the $4.27T/$4.25T pair comes from Citywire and ThinkAdvisor, not from Morningstar's own text.

Date the equity crossover precisely: as of August 31, 2019, published September 13, 2019 — not 'around August 2019.' And describe the population as Morningstar's US-equity category group of open-end funds and ETFs, which excludes sector-equity and international-equity funds.

The 'over 55%' inconsistency can be stated more sharply: Morningstar contradicts itself inside one report. The page-3 Key Takeaways bullet says 'reaching a 55% market share in total'; the page-5 body says 'over 55%'; the page-5 chart labels ($19.42T passive, $16.02T active) give 54.8%. Present it as an internal inconsistency in the report, not as an error the article discovered in arithmetic Morningstar never did.

On the 'crossover was 2024' claim: SSGA's January 2026 piece 'Closing time: How passive investing is reshaping equity market microstructure' says verbatim 'Indexing has expanded its footprint within global AUM. In 2024, the AUM of passive funds surpassed that of active funds, and its market share continues to climb.' That sentence carries NO footnote (the piece's three footnotes are Instinet and BofA, all attached to trading-volume claims) and it is scoped to GLOBAL AUM. It is therefore not a competing reading of Morningstar's US data and should not be presented as one. On Morningstar's own US fund data the answer is END-2023, stated by Morningstar twice.

Cite the ICI monthly release as https://www.ici.org/research/stats/combined_active_index_0626 (ICI's own hub link), not _0526. Also quote ICI's printed 53.7% from the table's 'Index as a % of Total' column rather than computing 21.88/(21.88+18.83) yourself.

Do not present ICI's 52% (year-end 2025 Fact Book) and 53.7% (June 2026 monthly) as consecutive points in one series. The monthly release explicitly excludes funds that invest primarily in other mutual funds; the Fact Book Figure 2.5 note states only that money market funds and commodity ETFs are excluded. The implied six-month jump in the base ($36.6T to $40.7T) is too large to be pure market appreciation plus flows, which indicates the two series do not share a denominator. Either caveat it or use one series throughout.
reasoning:

That confirmed both the 2023 crossover sentence and the $19.42T / $16.02T chart labels, and resolved the ambiguous '$1 .02T' (could have been 13/16/18 — only 16.02 is consistent with the report's separate 'ETFs about 38% of the market' statement).
