itemVerdicts.item: (a) Ritholtz transcript: verbatim 'I view the markets as fundamentally broken'; mechanism = passive has no opinion about value + value-manager redemption spiral; 'almost the best way to get your stock to go up is to start by being overvalued.'
itemVerdicts.note: Fetched and cleaned the actual transcript HTML (ritholtz.com/2024/02/transcript-david-einhorn/, page dated 'February 12, 2024' / datePublished 2024-02-12T14:30:45+00:00). Verbatim at [00:22:53]: 'Oh, no question. I I view the markets as fundamentally broken, like the number' followed by interviewer echoing 'Fundamentally broken.' Mechanism confirmed at [00:22:59]-[00:23:58]: 'Passive investors have no opinion about value. They're gonna assume everybody else's done the work... if you have a situation where money is moved from active to passive, when that happens, the value managers get redeemed, the value stocks go down more, it causes more redemptions of the value managers, it caused those stocks to go down more... instead of stocks reverting toward value, they actually diverge from value.' The 'almost the best way' line is verbatim at end of that same block: 'that's a change in the market and it's a structure that means that almost the best way to get your stock to go up is to start by being overvalued.'

itemVerdicts.item: (b) SAME interview: buying at 'four times earnings, five times earnings' with '15, 20% cash flow' returned via buybacks; concession that opportunity set is 'as good or better than it's ever been' because 'the competitors have essentially left the field.'
itemVerdicts.note: All phrases verbatim in the same transcript. [00:21:48]: 'So we're not buying things at 10 times or 11 times earnings. We're buying things at four times earnings, five times earnings, and we're buying them where they have huge buybacks... we need 15, 20% cash flow type of type of numbers.' [00:30:41]: 'I just think the opportunity is actually probably as good or better than, than it's ever been.' [00:31:41]: 'it really is the, the competitors have essentially left the field.' itemVerdicts.item: (c) At the Robin Hood conference Oct 2024 he used the weaker phrase 'a bit of a broken market' (per Institutional Investor).
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: attributing the 'a bit of a broken market' quote to the Robin Hood Investors Conference (Oct 23, 2024). itemVerdicts.item: (a) Morningstar: passive US long-term fund+ETF assets passed active at END-2023, $13.29T vs $13.23T (~$60bn, ~0.2% of $26.5T; MMFs excluded; Morningstar classification)
itemVerdicts.note: The EVENT and the YEAR are confirmed from the Morningstar primary page itself, which I retrieved successfully with browser headers (WebFetch and plain curl both 403; curl with full Accept/Accept-Language/Chrome-122 UA returns 200). Article: 'It's Official: Passive Funds Overtake Active Funds', Adam Sabban, Jan 17, 2024, https://www.morningstar.com/funds/recovery-us-fund-flows-was-weak-2023 . Verbatim body text: 'After steadily encroaching on active funds' turf for years, passive funds closed 2023 with more assets.' WRONG (as an attribution): the article body does NOT contain '$13.29 trillion' or '$13.23 trillion' — those live only in the article's embedded chart image ('Historical Fund Assets: Active vs. Passive', 'Source: Morningstar Direct Asset Flows. Data as of Dec. 31, 2023'). RIGHT: the citable text source for the pair is CNBC, Jeff Cox, Jan 18 2024, which I read verbatim from the raw HTML: 'The total assets under management in exchange-traded funds and notes along with passively managed mutual funds reached a combined $13.29 trillion at the end of December, nudging above the $13.23 trillion held in active assets, according to Morningstar.' Cite it as 'Morningstar data as reported by CNBC', not as a quote from the Morningstar page. SECOND CORRECTION — do not adopt CNBC's caliber wording: 'exchange-traded funds and notes along with passively managed mutual funds' would put ALL ETFs (including ~$0.5T of active ETFs at end-2023) on the passive side, which is not Morningstar's classification and would have moved the crossover years earlier. Morningstar classifies active ETFs as active; the article's own caliber ('passive US long-term fund+ETF assets') is the correct one. Arithmetic checks: 13.29+13.23 = $26.52T (~$26.5T ok); margin $60bn = 0.226% of the base (~0.2% ok). MMF exclusion confirmed from Morningstar's own report footnote (Dec-2025 US Fund Flows, p.4): '1 Long-term funds exclude money market funds.' Universe disclosure (same report, Disclosures page): 'This report includes both mutual funds and exchange-traded funds but not funds of funds unless specifically stated. It does not include collective investment trusts or separate accounts.' No later Morningstar revision moves the date: the Dec-2025 report still says 2023 (see item c).

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Equity-only crossover ~August 2019, $4.27T vs $4.25T (US equity funds only)
itemVerdicts.note: TIMING AND CALIBER CONFIRMED from a Morningstar PRIMARY document — the Sept-2019 press release 'Morningstar Reports U.S. Mutual Fund and Exchange-Traded Fund Flows for August 2019' (prnewswire, fetched and read verbatim): 'Passive U.S. equity assets passed active U.S. equity assets by about $25.0 billion. As a result, passive share of U.S. equity open-end and ETF assets was 50.15% versus 49.85% for active funds.' So 'US equity, open-end + ETF, as of Aug 31 2019' is exactly right. WRONG/UNSUPPORTED: the specific levels '$4.27T vs $4.25T' appear in NO primary document I could reach — Morningstar's own commentary page for that month is not locatable (the 2019 article id 404s), citywire is Incapsula-blocked, thinkadvisor is Cloudflare-blocked and has no Wayback capture. Every assertion of $4.27T/$4.25T I saw came from search-engine summarizers, which this run has already caught fabricating. RIGHT (safe substitution): quote Morningstar's own numbers — 'passive passed active by about $25.0 billion; 50.15% vs 49.85% of US equity open-end and ETF assets.' The $4.27T/$4.25T pair is at least ARITHMETICALLY CONSISTENT with those (a $25bn gap at 50.15/49.85 implies a total in the $8.1–8.6T range; 4.2725/4.2475 sums to $8.52T and yields 50.147%/49.853%), so it is not refuted — just unverified. Supporting primary context I did verify (Morningstar, Kevin McDevitt, May 16 2019, 'Passive U.S. Equity Funds Catch Active U.S. Equity Funds', fetched verbatim): 'Passive U.S. equity funds had assets of $4.305 trillion by month-end, just $6 billion shy of active U.S. equity funds' $4.311 trillion... active U.S. equity funds had 50.04% market share versus passive U.S. equity funds' 49.96%.' That confirms the ~$8.6T category-group scale and shows the crossover was a near-miss as of April 30, 2019 — so '~August 2019' should be written as 'as of Aug 31, 2019' (first month passive was ahead per Morningstar's release), not as a vague approximation; Morningstar itself had predicted May.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Morningstar Dec-2025 US Fund Flows: passive 'over 55%' at YE2025, $19.42T vs ~$16.02T, with 19.42/(19.42+16.02)=54.8% internal inconsistency
itemVerdicts.note: Fully verified from the primary PDF (downloaded from the given contentstack URL). pdftotext mangled it (the embedded subset font drops several glyphs — '202 ' for 2023, '$1 .02T' for $16.02T), so I rendered page 5 to PNG at 400dpi and read it. Verbatim p.5: 'Since passive funds surpassed active funds in total net assets back in 2023, they've continued to gain market share of the US funds universe. As of year-end 2025, passively managed funds made up over 55% of net assets, increasing from 53% the year prior.' Chart legend labels, verbatim: 'Passively Managed $19.42T' and 'Actively Managed $16.02T' (exactly $16.02T — drop the '~'). Source line: 'Source: Morningstar Direct Asset Flows. Data as of Dec. 31, 2025.' The flagged inconsistency is REAL: 19.42/35.44 = 54.79%, so 'over 55%' overstates. Note for fairness: the report's own p.1 key-takeaway says 'reaching a 55% market share in total' (rounding 54.79% to 55% is defensible); it is the p.5 'over 55%' that is wrong. Also worth noting the report's Disclosures page carries a typo — 'The figures in this report were compiled on Jan. 12, 2025' in the December 2025 report.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) ICI 2026 Fact Book: index MFs+ETFs = 52% of long-term fund assets at YE2025 ($19.1T of $36.6T; excludes MMFs and commodity ETFs; 2010=19%, 2015=28%, 2020=40%)
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim from the primary PDF at the cited URL (icifactbook.org/pdf/2026-factbook-ch2.pdf, downloaded and text-extracted cleanly). 'By year-end 2025, total net assets in these two index fund categories had grown to $19.1 trillion.' / 'At year-end 2025, index mutual funds and index ETFs together accounted for the majority (52%) of assets in long-term funds, up from 19% at year-end 2010 (Figure 2.5).' Figure 2.5 data labels: 19% (2010), 28% (2015), 40% (2020), 52% (2025); 'Total net assets (Trillions of dollars) $9.9 / $14.9 / $24.8 / $36.6'. Figure note verbatim: 'Note: Data exclude money market funds. Data for ETFs exclude commodity ETFs.' Every element of the sub-claim checks. ONE CAVEAT to flag if the article footnotes it: ICI is internally inconsistent on the level — ICI Research Perspective Vol. 32 No. 1 (March 2026), 'Trends in the Expenses and Fees of Funds, 2025', says on the same point 'total net assets in these two index fund categories had grown to $19.3 trillion' while still reporting 52% and a $36.6T base. The article's $19.1T is correct for the source it cites (the Fact Book).

itemVerdicts.item: (e) ICI monthly release: index $21.88T vs active $18.83T in June 2026 = 53.7%
itemVerdicts.note: Substantially confirmed but the caliber needs a qualifier, and my access was second-hand. ici.org 403s all direct curl (Akamai blocks datacenter IPs); WebFetch reached it and returned Active $18,830.2 billion vs Index $21,880.3 billion for June 2026, table titled 'Total Net Assets Long-Term Mutual Funds and ETFs' with the note 'Data for funds that invest primarily in other mutual funds were excluded from the series.' I treated this as summarizer output and stress-tested it: the reported category breakdown sums exactly to both totals (active 8,615.8+3,297.1+1,799.4+5,117.9 = 18,830.2; index 15,215.3+3,414.8+87.9+3,162.3 = 21,880.3), and the implied 63.8% index share of domestic equity matches Morningstar's independent 'active US equity funds now make up less than 35% of the category group' — so the numbers are almost certainly genuine, not invented. WRONG (as written): presenting '53.7%' as an ICI statistic. RIGHT: 53.7% is the article's own arithmetic (21,880.3/40,710.5 = 53.74%); ICI publishes the dollar table, not the percentage. Also state the caliber: LONG-TERM mutual funds and ETFs only (money market funds not in this series), with funds-of-funds excluded — which is why this base ($40.7T at Jun-2026) is larger than the Fact Book's $36.6T long-term base at YE2025 (the Fact Book additionally excludes commodity ETFs).

itemVerdicts.item: Adjudication: SSGA (Jan-2026) says the crossover was '2024' — which year is right on Morningstar's own data?
itemVerdicts.note: On Morningstar's own data the answer is unambiguously 2023, and SSGA is wrong for Morningstar. Morningstar says so twice in its own voice: 'passive funds closed 2023 with more assets' (Jan 17, 2024 article) and 'Since passive funds surpassed active funds in total net assets back in 2023' (Dec-2025 US Fund Flows, p.5, read off the rendered page). I also measured the chart line-crossing on that p.5 figure at 400dpi to check for a silent restatement: the green (passive) line crosses blue essentially at the 2023 vertex, consistent with the text — no revision has moved the date. SSGA's piece ('Closing time: How passive investing is reshaping equity market microstructure', Jan 23 2026) states 'In 2024, the AUM of passive funds surpassed that of active funds' and CITES NO SOURCE. The charitable reading — worth one clause in the article — is that 2024 is right on ICI's index-fund caliber, which I verified against primary ICI Fact Books: index MFs+ETFs were 48% of long-term fund assets at YE2023 ($13.3T; 2024 Fact Book ch.2) and 51% at YE2024 ($16.2T; 2025 Fact Book ch.2). So ICI's series crosses 50% during 2024, Morningstar's during 2023. The article should say '2023 on Morningstar's active/passive classification; 2024 on ICI's narrower index-fund definition' rather than treating SSGA as simply mistaken — but it must not attribute '2024' to Morningstar.

corrections: Do not present '$13.29T vs $13.23T' as a quotation from the Morningstar article at morningstar.com/funds/recovery-us-fund-flows-was-weak-2023 — that page's body text says only 'passive funds closed 2023 with more assets'; the dollar pair appears in the article's chart image and is quoted in text by CNBC (Jeff Cox, Jan 18, 2024). Cite it as 'Morningstar data, as reported by CNBC' or as the Dec-2023 US Fund Flows chart.

Do not repeat CNBC's caliber wording ('exchange-traded funds and notes along with passively managed mutual funds'). That phrasing counts all ETFs as passive, which is not Morningstar's classification — Morningstar counts active ETFs as active. Keep the article's own caliber: passive share of US long-term open-end funds + ETFs, money market funds and funds-of-funds excluded.

The '$4.27T vs $4.25T' August-2019 equity pair could not be confirmed in any reachable primary document — every occurrence traces to search summarizers or blocked trade-press pages. Replace it with Morningstar's own press-release figures: 'Passive U.S. equity assets passed active U.S. equity assets by about $25.0 billion. As a result, passive share of U.S. equity open-end and ETF assets was 50.15% versus 49.85% for active funds.' (Morningstar, U.S. fund flows for August 2019.) If the trillions are kept, label them 'roughly $4.3T each side' and flag them as press-reported.

Write the equity crossover as 'as of Aug. 31, 2019' rather than '~August 2019', and note the near-miss: Morningstar reported April 30, 2019 at passive $4.305T vs active $4.311T (49.96% vs 50.04%) and expected May to be the crossover month.
In claim (c), $16.02T is exact, not approximate — drop the '~' before it. Both figures are chart labels in the Dec-2025 US Fund Flows PDF, p.5.

Attribute the 'over 55%' inconsistency precisely: the report's page-5 sentence says 'over 55%' (wrong, the labels imply 54.79%), while its page-1 key takeaway says 'reaching a 55% market share in total' (defensible rounding). Quote the page-5 sentence when flagging the error.

In claim (e), '53.7%' is the article's own computation from ICI's dollar table (21,880.3/40,710.5), not a figure ICI publishes. Say so, and add the caliber: long-term mutual funds and ETFs only, funds-of-funds excluded, money market funds not in the series.

On the SSGA dispute: state that 2023 is correct on Morningstar's data (Morningstar itself repeats it in its December 2025 report: 'passive funds surpassed active funds in total net assets back in 2023'), that SSGA's Jan-2026 '2024' is unsourced, and that 2024 is the right answer only on ICI's narrower index-fund definition (48% of long-term fund assets at YE2023 → 51% at YE2024).

Optional footnote: ICI is internally inconsistent on the YE2025 index-fund level — the 2026 Fact Book says $19.1 trillion, while ICI Research Perspective Vol. 32 No. 1 (March 2026) says $19.3 trillion, both reporting 52% of a $36.6T long-term base. The article's $19.1T is correct for the Fact Book it cites.
newContradictions: Morningstar's Dec-2025 US Fund Flows report contradicts itself: p.1 'reaching a 55% market share in total' vs p.5 'over 55% of net assets', against chart labels $19.42T / $16.02T = 54.79%.

ICI contradicts itself on the YE2025 index-fund asset level: 2026 Fact Book ch.2 says $19.1 trillion; ICI Research Perspective Vol. 32 No. 1 (March 2026) says $19.3 trillion — same 52% share and same $36.6T base.

SSGA ('Closing time', Jan 23, 2026) asserts 'In 2024, the AUM of passive funds surpassed that of active funds' with no source, directly contradicting Morningstar's own repeated statement of 2023. The two are reconcilable only as different definitions (Morningstar passive classification vs ICI index-fund classification), which SSGA does not disclose.

Morningstar's Dec-2025 report Disclosures page carries a date typo: 'The figures in this report were compiled on Jan. 12, 2025' in a December 2025 report (should be 2026). Harmless, but do not cite the compile date.

ICI's own two active/index bases are not interchangeable: the monthly statistical release shows a $40.7T long-term MF+ETF base at Jun-2026 while the Fact Book shows $36.6T at YE2025 (the Fact Book additionally strips commodity ETFs). Mixing the 52% and 53.7% figures without saying so implies a faster ramp than the data supports.
reasoning:

(2) ICI 2026 Fact Book ch.2 PDF — clean extraction, all of claim (d) verbatim including the exclusion note. (4) ICI Research Perspective Vol. 32 (March 2026) — surfaced the $19.3T vs $19.1T discrepancy. (5) Morningstar's Sept-2019 press release on prnewswire — the '$25.0 billion' / '50.15% versus 49.85%' sentences for the equity crossover. (6) Morningstar, 'Passive U.S. Equity Funds Catch Active U.S. Equity Funds', May 16 2019 — April-2019 near-miss at $4.305T vs $4.311T. (7) Morningstar, 'It's Official: Passive Funds Overtake Active Funds', Jan 17 2024 — I DID get past the 403 (WebFetch and simple curl fail; curl with Accept + Accept-Language + a Chrome-122 UA returns 200), and the body does not contain the dollar pair. (8) CNBC Jan 18 2024 — raw HTML stripped locally, the $13.29T/$13.23T sentence read verbatim.

What remains uncertain: the '$4.27T / $4.25T' August-2019 pair. Citywire is Incapsula-blocked, ThinkAdvisor is Cloudflare-blocked with no Wayback capture, and web.archive.org was rate-limiting (429) throughout. Every rendition of that pair I encountered came from search-engine summaries, which this run has already caught fabricating twice — so I refuse to certify it. It is not refuted either: it reconciles exactly with Morningstar's own 50.15%/49.85% and ~$25bn if the US equity category group totalled ~$8.52T at Aug-2019, which is plausible given Morningstar's verified $8.616T total in April 2019. Second residual: claim (e) rests on a WebFetch summarizer because ici.org blocks direct curl; I validated it by checking that the reported category breakdown sums exactly to both totals and that the implied domestic-equity index share (63.8%) matches Morningstar's independently verified 'active US equity under 35%'. That is strong circumstantial corroboration but not my own eyes on ICI's table.

I also actively searched for a later Morningstar restatement of the end-2023 crossover (a $60bn margin on a $26.5T base is 0.2%, well inside normal revision noise, so this was the most likely way the claim could fail). None exists: Morningstar's December 2025 report still dates it to 2023, in prose and on the chart.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Bogle WSJ op-ed (Nov 29, 2018) — voting-control warning, zero price-discovery/bubble claims, ownership numbers (4.5%→9%→>17%), Big Three shares (Vanguard 51/BlackRock 21/SSGA 9, 81% collective), closing Coates quote defending indexing
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim against the full scraped article text (shareholderforum.com mirror of the WSJ piece, 'Bogle Sounds a Warning on Index Funds,' Nov 29 2018). Exact match: 'If historical trends continue, a handful of giant institutional investors will one day hold voting control of virtually every large U.S. corporation.' Numbers exact: '4.5% of total U.S. stock-market value in 2002 ... 9% in 2009 ... more than 17% in 2018.' Big Three exact: 'Vanguard has a 51% share; BlackRock, 21%; and State Street Global, 9%' with 'collective 81% share.' Confirmed the article contains no mention of 'price discovery' or 'bubble' anywhere in its text. Closing lines confirmed near-verbatim: Coates writes '...A ban on indexing would clearly not be a good idea.' Bogle: 'I can only say, Amen to those words' (claim's single-quote rendering of 'Amen' vs. source's unquoted OCR is an artifact of the scrape, not a substantive discrepancy).

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Berkshire 2017 Yahoo Finance interview — 'chaos, catastrophe' IMMEDIATELY followed by 'chances of everybody indexing... zero' and 'I'm not concerned about it,' plus 75%-and-not-dangerous estimate
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: the claim's 'IMMEDIATELY followed by' framing overstates textual adjacency. Verified verbatim from the live Yahoo Finance article (May 6, 2017, Myles Udland): the actual sequence is '"If everybody indexed, the only word you could use is chaos, catastrophe," said Jack Bogle... "There would be no trading," Bogle told... "There would be no way to turn a stream of income into a pile of capital or a pile of capital into a stream of income. Now, what are the chances of everybody indexing? It's zero."' — so 'zero' is reasonably proximate (one intervening sentence, same continuous answer), but 'So, I'm not concerned about it' comes only AFTER a separate intervening passage about indexing reaching '50% of the market "easily"' and a discussion of markets getting 'a little less efficient' — not immediately after 'zero' as the claim implies. Further, the 75% line is NOT a direct Bogle quote as the claim's quotation marks suggest: the source text reads 'Asked by Serwer what level of indexing would concern him, Bogle said he expects indexing could exceed 75% of the market and not have it become dangerous' — this is Udland's paraphrase, not bracketed in quotation marks in the original, and it comes from a separate, later exchange in the interview, not contiguous with the chaos/catastrophe or zero-chances lines. RIGHT: All four elements (chaos/catastrophe, zero chance, not concerned, 75%-not-dangerous) are genuine and correctly attributed to Bogle at the same Berkshire 2017 meeting/interview, but they are NOT one immediate, continuous utterance — they are spread across the interview with intervening material (including Bogle's own concession that indexing could reach 50% of the market 'easily'), and the 75% figure is a journalist's paraphrase rather than a Bogle direct quote. Anyone citing this as one unbroken quote string is overstating textual adjacency.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Asness footnote 40 (SSRN 4942046, 'The Less-Efficient Market Hypothesis') — Bogle pressed on 75% origin, replied 'I made it up'
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in local asness.txt, footnote 40: 'I once did a podcast hosting Jack Bogle (I'm doing this from memory) and asked him this question: how much of the market can be cap-weighted indexed before things break down? Jack absolutely acknowledged it can't be the entire market... I pushed him for a number, and he said something like "75%." I said "that's interesting Jack, where did you get that number from?" He said "I made it up." God I miss that man.' Footnote number (40) matches exactly. SSRN abstract_id 4942046 independently confirmed via web search to correspond to Asness's 'The Less-Efficient Market Hypothesis' (Aug 30, 2024, forthcoming Journal of Portfolio Management 50th Anniversary Issue). Note: Asness caveats this is 'from memory' of a podcast conversation, not a contemporaneous transcript — the claim group does not misrepresent this caveat, but it's worth flagging as an inherent limit on the anecdote's precision.

corrections: Item (b): Replace 'IMMEDIATELY followed by' with accurate sequencing. The verified Yahoo Finance (May 6, 2017) text order is: (1) '"If everybody indexed, the only word you could use is chaos, catastrophe," said Jack Bogle...'; (2) in the same continuous answer, 'There would be no trading... Now, what are the chances of everybody indexing? It's zero.' (proximate, acceptable to call closely-following); (3) SEPARATED by an intervening passage where Bogle says indexing could reach 50% of the market 'easily' and discusses markets becoming 'a little less efficient,' THEN 'So, I'm not concerned about it. It's going to take a long, long time [for indexing to get] anywhere near 50%...' (b) (4) the 75% line comes from a still-later, separate question-and-answer exchange ('Asked by Serwer what level of indexing would concern him...') and in the source it is Myles Udland's paraphrase — 'Bogle said he expects indexing could exceed 75% of the market and not have it become dangerous' — NOT a bracketed direct Bogle quotation as the claim's quotation marks imply. The article should either drop 'IMMEDIATELY' and note the 75% line is reported paraphrase, or quote only the parts Bogle actually said in his own words: 'But dangerous in what sense? Markets are going to be efficient as long as there are managers, or investors, trying to find little holes in the system... price discovery, as they call it.'
reasoning:
Checked all three sub-items against primary/verbatim text rather than summaries.

(a) WSJ op-ed: Fetched via curl (not WebFetch summarizer) and stripped HTML to get the full verbatim article text from the shareholderforum.com mirror, dated Nov 29, 2018, bylined John C. Bogle, titled 'Bogle Sounds a Warning on Index Funds.' Every element of claim (a) checks out exactly: the voting-control sentence, the 4.5%/9%/>17% progression (2002/2009/2018), the Big Three percentages (Vanguard 51/BlackRock 21/SSGA 9, 81% collective), the closing Coates quote and Bogle's 'Amen' response, and — critically — a full-text confirmation that the word 'bubble' and the phrase 'price discovery' never appear anywhere in the piece, so the 'ZERO price-discovery/bubble claims' assertion holds.

(b) Yahoo Finance interview: WebFetch's first pass returned a same-model summary (flagged as suspect per the task's fabrication warning), so I re-fetched the raw HTML via curl with a browser user-agent (Yahoo blocks default UAs) and extracted the actual embedded article JSON/text. This surfaced the real byline (Myles Udland, May 6, 2017, Berkshire Hathaway annual meeting) and the true paragraph structure. The individual quotes are all genuine and correctly attributed, but the claim's 'IMMEDIATELY followed by' compresses a longer interview (with an intervening passage where Bogle says 50% indexing would happen 'easily' and discusses reduced market efficiency) into what reads as one continuous utterance. Also, the 75%-not-dangerous line is the reporter's paraphrase in the source, not Bogle's own words in quotation marks — the claim's use of quotation marks around it slightly overstates precision. This is a real, citable caliber slip, not a fabrication — downgrading item (b) to 'corrected.'

(c) Asness footnote 40: Found verbatim in local asness.txt at footnote 40 (line ~518-523), matching the claim's account almost exactly including the specific footnote number. Independently confirmed via web search that SSRN abstract_id 4942046 is indeed Asness's 'The Less-Efficient Market Hypothesis.' Only caveat (not a correction, just context worth carrying into the article): Asness explicitly flags this as 'from memory' of a past podcast, not a verified transcript quote.

Because two of three items (a, c) fully hold and one (b) has a real but narrow caliber slip (overstated adjacency + a paraphrase presented with quote marks), the overall group verdict is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS or OVERTURNED — the central claims about Bogle's actual positions are true and well-supported, but the WSJ-op-ed-adjacent packaging is solid while the Yahoo-interview packaging needs the sequencing fix noted above.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) 'I view the markets as fundamentally broken' + mechanism (passive has no opinion about value + value-manager redemption spiral) + 'almost the best way to get your stock to go up is to start by being overvalued'
itemVerdicts.note: All verbatim in the ritholtz.com transcript (canonical URL confirmed as https://ritholtz.com/2024/02/transcript-david-einhorn/). At 00:22:53-57: 'I view the markets as fundamentally broken' / 'Fundamentally broken.' At 00:22:59 Einhorn: 'Passive investors have no opinion about value. They're gonna assume everybody else's done the work.' The redemption-spiral mechanism (value managers redeemed -> value stocks sold -> passive buys overvalued names -> more redemptions) is spelled out at 00:22:59 and 00:26:07. The closing line at 00:23:58 is verbatim: 'almost the best way to get your stock to go up is to start by being overvalued.'

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Adaptation: buying at 'four times earnings, five times earnings' with '15, 20% cash flow' returned via buybacks; concession that opportunity set is 'as good or better than it's ever been' because 'the competitors have essentially left the field'
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim at 00:21:48: 'We're buying things at four times earnings, five times earnings... So we need 15, 20% cash flow type of type of numbers. And if that cash is then being returned to us...' Also repeated at 00:28:18. 'as good or better than it's ever been' matches 00:30:41 ('as good or better than, than it's ever been' -- stutter is a transcription artifact, meaning identical). 'the competitors have essentially left the field' is verbatim at 00:31:41. The two statements occur a few lines apart in the same causal thread (fewer competitors -> better opportunity), so linking them with 'because' is a fair paraphrase, not a fabrication.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) At the Robin Hood conference Oct 2024 he used the weaker phrase 'a bit of a broken market' (per Institutional Investor)
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: the claim attributes this quote to 'the Robin Hood conference Oct 2024... per Institutional Investor.' RIGHT: the II article itself never names a venue -- it only says Einhorn said this 'at a recent conference.' Tracing the actual quote (verified via CNBC's own article, archived copy fetched and grepped verbatim) shows it was said at CNBC's Delivering Alpha Investor Summit in New York on Nov. 13, 2024, in an on-stage interview with CNBC's Leslie Picker -- not at the J.P. Morgan/Robin Hood Investors Conference (which was held earlier, Oct. 23, 2024, where Einhorn separately pitched Peloton). CNBC's article (published 2024-11-14, caption dated 'Nov. 13, 2024') quotes Einhorn saying verbatim: '...instead of the valuation becoming the signal, the valuation people were just noise and everybody else is sort of the signal. And this is why I think we have a structurally dysfunctional market, a bit of a broken market, and essentially a perpetual erosion of value as a strategy.' This is word-for-word identical to the quote II attributes to 'a recent conference,' confirming Delivering Alpha (not Robin Hood) is the correct venue. The quote text and the 'weaker than fundamentally broken' characterization are otherwise fine -- only the venue/date attribution is wrong, and it isn't actually sourced to II as claimed.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Einhorn credits Michael Green for the framework (per II) -- downstream of Green, not independent corroboration
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed verbatim in the II 'Cassandra of Passive Investing' article: 'Greenlight Capital's David Einhorn credits Green with helping him understand why the value investing playbook he ran didn't work for many years as investors yanked money from active managers and put it into index funds... "We had just a rough go until we figured this out," he said in a recent interview with Ritholtz Wealth Management founder and CIO Barry Ritholtz.' The article explicitly frames Einhorn's insight as derived from Green, supporting the 'downstream, not independent corroboration' characterization.

corrections: Item (c): The 'a bit of a broken market' / 'structurally dysfunctional market' quote was NOT said at the Robin Hood conference in October 2024. It was said at CNBC's Delivering Alpha Investor Summit in New York on November 13, 2024, during an on-stage interview with CNBC's Leslie Picker (confirmed via CNBC's own article, published 2024-11-14, headline 'Greenlight's David Einhorn says the markets are broken and getting worse,' with a photo caption reading 'speaking at the 14th CNBC Delivering Alpha Investor Summit in New York City on Nov. 13, 2024,' and containing the verbatim quote). Additionally, the Institutional Investor article does not itself name any conference -- it only says 'at a recent conference' -- so the specific 'Robin Hood conference' attribution is not actually sourced to II as the claim implies; the article should cite CNBC's Delivering Alpha coverage (or reference the CNBC article directly) rather than Robin Hood/II for this specific quote and date.
reasoning: Checked both primary documents directly rather than trusting search summaries. (1) ritholtz.com/2024/02/transcript-david-einhorn/ -- read the full local transcript extraction, confirmed canonical URL, publish date (Feb 12, 2024 blog post) and embedded Bloomberg audio URL slug '2024-02-08' (confirming the podcast aired Feb 8, 2024, matching the claim). Grepped for every quoted phrase in sub-claims (a) and (b) and found each verbatim, in context, with the causal mechanism (passive has no opinion on value -> value-manager redemptions -> divergence from value) spelled out exactly as characterized. (2) Institutional Investor's 'Why Michael Green Is Known as the Cassandra of Passive Investing' -- read full local extraction. Confirmed it does credit Einhorn's understanding to Green (sub-claim d), and confirmed it contains the 'a bit of a broken market' quote attributed only to 'a recent conference' -- no venue name. Because the claim group asserted this was the Robin Hood conference (per II), and II doesn't say that, I traced the quote's actual origin: web-searched, then fetched an archived copy of CNBC's Nov 14, 2024 article (web.archive.org snapshot, via curl since direct WebFetch to cnbc.com and web.archive.org both failed with errors) and grepped it directly for the verbatim quote and dateline. The CNBC page's JSON-LD metadata, image caption, and body text all independently confirm 'Nov. 13, 2024' and 'Delivering Alpha Investor Summit' as the venue/date, with the exact quote matching II's paraphrase word-for-word. This is inconsistent with 'Robin Hood conference Oct 2024' from the claim. I also cross-checked that Einhorn genuinely appeared at the Robin Hood Investors Conference on Oct 23, 2024 (per hedgefundalpha.com search snippets), but that appearance was about stock picks (Peloton), not the broken-market quote -- so the claim appears to conflate two separate Einhorn appearances in fall 2024. All other sub-claims (a, b, d) verified verbatim against primary text with no caliber slippage.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Bogle WSJ op-ed (Nov 29, 2018): warns about ownership concentration/voting control, zero price-discovery/bubble claims, gives numbers, closes defending index funds via Coates quote + 'Amen'

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Berkshire 2017 Yahoo Finance interview: 'chaos, catastrophe' quote, immediately followed by 'zero' chance and 'not concerned' quotes, plus 75% estimate
itemVerdicts.note: Downloaded raw HTML (curl) of finance.yahoo.com/news/jack-bogle-envisions-chaos-catastrophe-markets-everyone-indexed-194610197.html and extracted the embedded article JSON/text directly (not a summarizer). Verbatim confirmed: '"If everybody indexed, the only word you could use is chaos, catastrophe," said Jack Bogle, founder of Vanguard, at the Berkshire Hathaway annual meeting on Saturday.' Verbatim: '"Now, what are the chances of everybody indexing? It's zero."' Verbatim: '"So, I'm not concerned about it."' On 75%: the article's exact wording is 'Bogle said he expects indexing could exceed 75% of the market and not have it become dangerous' (paraphrase by the journalist, not a direct Bogle quote, though the claim group renders it in quotes as if literal — minor stylistic issue, substance is accurate). Article datePublished confirmed 2017-05-06 (Berkshire annual meeting Saturday), matching 'Berkshire 2017.' Minor sequencing note: between the 'chaos, catastrophe' line and the 'zero' line there is one intervening sentence ('There would be no trading... turn a stream of income into a pile of capital') — so 'immediately followed by' is a slight compression but both statements are from the same continuous answer in the same interview, not misleadingly juxtaposed. The 75% estimate appears later in the same article (same Serwer interview, same event) after an inserted photo/Buffett-tribute block, not in the same paragraph as 'not concerned' — again a compression but not a misattribution; also note the article separately has Bogle saying indexing could reach 50% of the market 'easily,' which does not contradict the 75% figure (different question: 50% = near-term trajectory, 75% = point where he'd start to worry).

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Asness footnote 40 (SSRN 4942046, 'The Less-Efficient Market Hypothesis'): reports pressing Bogle on the 75% figure's origin; Bogle said 'I made it up'
itemVerdicts.note: Read verbatim from local file asness.txt (footnote 40, lines 520-524): 'I once did a podcast hosting Jack Bogle (I'm doing this from memory) and asked him this question: how much of the market can be cap-weighted indexed before things break down? Jack absolutely acknowledged it can't be the entire market... I pushed him for a number, and he said something like "75%." I said "that's interesting Jack, where did you get that number from?" He said "I made it up." God I miss that man.' SSRN abstract_id=4942046 confirmed via web search to be the correct ID for this exact paper title (published JPM 50th Anniversary Issue, Aug 2024).

reasoning: Verified all three sub-claims against primary documents directly (not summarizer-only fetches, per the fabrication warning). (a) WSJ op-ed fetched via WebFetch and cross-checked: all quoted numbers, the voting-control warning, the Big Three shares, and the closing 'Amen' quote appear verbatim in the article, and the fetch explicitly confirmed no mention of price discovery/market efficiency/bubble anywhere in the piece — consistent with the claim that this op-ed contains zero price-discovery/bubble claims. (b) For the Yahoo Finance interview I did not trust the WebFetch summary alone (given the stated fabrication risk); I downloaded the raw HTML with curl and grepped the embedded article-body JSON/HTML directly, extracting the actual paragraph text. All three direct Bogle quotes ('chaos, catastrophe', 'It's zero', 'I'm not concerned about it') are verbatim in the source, and the 75%-and-not-dangerous line, while journalist paraphrase rather than a direct quote, correctly represents Bogle's stated position. Article datePublished metadata (2017-05-06) confirms it corresponds to the 2017 Berkshire Hathaway annual meeting weekend. (c) Local file asness.txt footnote 40 reproduces the anecdote essentially verbatim, including the exact 'I made it up' quote; SSRN ID 4942046 confirmed via search to be the correct identifier for this exact paper. No caliber slippage found (no numerator/denominator swaps, no mean/median or asset/market-cap conflation issues applicable here since these are narrative/quote claims, not statistical ones). Only a very minor, non-material observation: the claim's framing of 'immediately followed by' compresses a few intervening sentences/paragraphs in the actual interview, and renders the 75% figure as a quoted phrase when the source presents it as journalistic paraphrase — neither rises to a substantive inaccuracy warranting a CORRECTED verdict.

itemVerdicts.item: Sept 2019 Bloomberg EMAIL interview — quote: "And now passive investing has removed price discovery from the equity markets... This is very much like the bubble in synthetic asset-backed CDOs before the Great Financial Crisis"
itemVerdicts.note: Both fragments exist verbatim in the Bloomberg original (Reed Stevenson, 2019-09-04), under the subhead 'Index Funds and Price Discovery': 'Central banks and Basel III have more or less removed price discovery from the credit markets, meaning risk does not have an accurate pricing mechanism in interest rates anymore. And now passive investing has removed price discovery from the equity markets. The simple theses and the models that get people into sectors, factors, indexes, or ETFs and mutual funds mimicking those strategies -- these do not require the security-level analysis that is required for true price discovery.' Then a SEPARATE quoted paragraph: 'This is very much like the bubble in synthetic asset-backed CDOs before the Great Financial Crisis in that price-setting in that market was not done by fundamental security-level analysis, but by massive capital flows based on Nobel-approved models of risk that proved to be untrue.' EMAIL is confirmed: 'One of his most provocative views from a lengthy email interview with Bloomberg News on Tuesday'. TWO CALIBER PROBLEMS. (1) WRONG: presenting the composite as flatly 'verbatim'. RIGHT: Bloomberg prints an explicit editorial note immediately before the quote blocks — 'Comments have been lightly edited and condensed.' It is verbatim-as-published, not verbatim-as-written by Burry. (2) WRONG: the draft's quote stops at 'Great Financial Crisis' with no closing ellipsis, cutting a sentence mid-clause. RIGHT: close with '...' or carry the clause through 'in that price-setting in that market was not done by fundamental security-level analysis, but by massive capital flows...'. Source read in full at /private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-cissychen-design/0f8bdcde-3464-42f4-af17-1552808c31d6/scratchpad/v3_37582b7cad4da385908d1fb6b2d9fcce.txt; independently cross-checked against the local Yahoo/GuruFocus copy burry_yahoo.txt.

itemVerdicts.item: Liquidity counts: 1,049 Russell 2000 stocks traded <$5m that day, 456 <$1m, 266 S&P 500 stocks <$150m
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers are exactly right. Bloomberg verbatim: 'In the Russell 2000 Index, for instance, the vast majority of stocks are lower volume, lower value-traded stocks. Today I counted 1,049 stocks that traded less than $5 million in value during the day. That is over half, and almost half of those -- 456 stocks -- traded less than $1 million during the day. ... The S&P 500 is no different -- the index contains the world's largest stocks, but still, 266 stocks -- over half -- traded under $150 million today.' Two structural facts the draft should not blur: the 456 are a SUBSET of the 1,049 ('almost half of those'), not a separate slice of the Russell 2000; and Burry glosses both 1,049/~1,960 and 266/500 as 'over half'. CORRECTION ON DATING: Bloomberg says the interview was conducted 'on Tuesday' and ran 2019-09-04 (Wednesday). Sept 2, 2019 was Labor Day, so Tuesday = 2019-09-03. WRONG: implying Burry's 'today I counted' tape is Sept 4. RIGHT: the counts are from the Sept 3, 2019 session (or leave undated); only the publication date is Sept 4.

itemVerdicts.item: "Like most bubbles, the longer it goes on, the worse the crash will be" — no date, trigger, or magnitude given
