itemVerdicts.item: Warning: acquirersmultiple.com reproduction retroactively edited with affiliate spam inside the quote
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed by fetching the raw page myself, and the injection is worse than 'spam near the quote'. The acquirersmultiple.com version of the Bloomberg attribution sentence reads: '"Like most bubbles, the longer it goes on, the worse the crash will be," said Burry, who oversees about $340 million at Scion Asset Management in Cupertino, California, and who has pointed to the proliferation of speculative retail products — from leveraged ETFs to the wave of crypto casino USA platforms absorbing disposable income that might otherwise sit in savings — as symptoms of the same late-cycle euphoria he has seen before.' Everything from 'and who has pointed' onward is fabricated SEO/affiliate insertion attributing a view to Burry that Bloomberg never reported — it sits outside the quotation marks but inside the attribution clause, so a copy-paste of the surrounding sentence imports invented content. The page also ends with an explicit 'Disclosure: This is an affiliate link' block. Separately, that page reproduces ONLY the price-discovery excerpt — it does not contain the 1,049/456/266 liquidity paragraph or the 'theater' line at all, so it cannot source those numbers even absent the tampering. Use the Yahoo/GuruFocus copy (verified locally) or the licensed Bloomberg reproduction at wealthmanagement.com.

corrections: Do not call the 2019 Burry passages simply 'verbatim'. Bloomberg prints an editorial note directly above the quote blocks — 'Comments have been lightly edited and condensed.' Attribute them as quoted by Bloomberg (Reed Stevenson, 'The Big Short's Michael Burry Explains Why Index Funds Are Like Subprime CDOs', Bloomberg, September 4, 2019), not as Burry's raw unedited words.

Fix the date attached to Burry's liquidity counts. Bloomberg states the exchange was 'a lengthy email interview with Bloomberg News on Tuesday' and ran Wednesday September 4, 2019; September 2, 2019 was Labor Day, so Tuesday = September 3, 2019. Burry's 'Today I counted 1,049 stocks...' therefore refers to the September 3, 2019 session, not September 4. Either say September 3, 2019 or leave the counting day unstated; keep September 4, 2019 only as the publication date and as the S&P baseline date.

Close the CDO quotation properly. The draft cuts 'This is very much like the bubble in synthetic asset-backed CDOs before the Great Financial Crisis' mid-sentence with no trailing ellipsis. Either add an ellipsis or carry the clause: '...before the Great Financial Crisis in that price-setting in that market was not done by fundamental security-level analysis, but by massive capital flows based on Nobel-approved models of risk that proved to be untrue.'

Make clear the 456 figure is a subset of the 1,049, not an additional group. Burry's wording is 'Today I counted 1,049 stocks that traded less than $5 million in value during the day. That is over half, and almost half of those -- 456 stocks -- traded less than $1 million during the day.' Write it as: of 1,049 Russell 2000 constituents trading under $5m, 456 traded under $1m.

State the index gain as price-only and give the exact figure. Verified closes: 2,937.78 on 2019-09-04 and 7,798.99 on 2026-08-13 (a record close). 7,798.99 / 2,937.78 − 1 = +165.5%. Keep '~+165%' but label it explicitly as a price-index change excluding dividends, so it is not read as an investor's total return, which is materially higher.

Drop the '~' from the Scion deregistration date and cite the primary record. SEC IAPD for SCION ASSET MANAGEMENT, LLC (SEC# 801-113529, firm ID 167772) shows registrationStatus SEC 'Terminated', effectiveDate 11/10/2025, iaScope 'INACTIVE', and the firm remains unregistered as of 2026-08. CNBC reported it on 2025-11-13 and put Scion at $155 million AUM as of March 2025.

Reword the Substack characterization. Correct framing: Burry announced it on X the night of Sunday November 23, 2025 and CNBC covered it November 24, 2025 — 'Cassandra Unchained', $379/year (or $39/month), launched to lay out his bearish AI thesis in detail. But the publication's own About page defines a broader remit ('stocks, market and economic trends, special situations, and investment manias'), and its 2026 archive is largely daily trading posts plus market-structure essays. So write 'launched it to argue an AI-bubble thesis rather than the index thesis' — do not claim the newsletter is exclusively about AI, and do not assert he has never written about index funds there (the archive is paywalled and that cannot be verified). Note also that 'Cassandra Unchained' was already his X profile name before the Substack existed.

Never source the 2019 interview from acquirersmultiple.com. Its current page has fabricated text grafted onto the Bloomberg attribution sentence — after 'Scion Asset Management in Cupertino, California' it continues 'and who has pointed to the proliferation of speculative retail products — from leveraged ETFs to the wave of crypto casino USA platforms absorbing disposable income that might otherwise sit in savings — as symptoms of the same late-cycle euphoria he has seen before,' none of which is in Bloomberg. That page also omits the 1,049/456/266 liquidity paragraph and the 'theater' line entirely. Cite the Yahoo/GuruFocus reproduction (finance.yahoo.com/news/big-shorts-michael-burry-compares-223347547.html) or the licensed Bloomberg text at wealthmanagement.com.
newContradictions: Bloomberg's own editorial note 'Comments have been lightly edited and condensed' sits directly above the quote blocks, which cuts against presenting any of these passages as strictly verbatim Burry prose.

Bloomberg dates the exchange to 'Tuesday' (2019-09-03) while publishing 2019-09-04, so Burry's 'today I counted' tape and the 2,937.78 baseline close are from different sessions (Sept 3 close was 2,906.27).

Burry's own 2019 text contains the timeline disclaimer 'However, I just don't know what the timeline will be' — which is the strongest available support for the draft's 'no date, trigger, or magnitude' framing and should be quoted rather than merely asserted.

The Cassandra Unchained About page's stated remit ('stocks, market and economic trends, special situations, and investment manias') is broader than 'AI-bubble thesis', and the 2026 archive includes a market-structure piece ('Foundations: Market Structure, Volatility Targeting, Pod Shops & Other Gremlins', 2026-07-31) that is topically adjacent to the passive/market-structure debate — so a flat 'not index funds' claim about the newsletter's content is unverifiable behind the paywall.

The acquirersmultiple.com tampering is an active fabrication vector, not just spam: it invents a Burry view about leveraged ETFs and crypto gambling platforms and attaches it to a real Bloomberg attribution clause.
reasoning: Reached the Bloomberg article text in full via a licensed reproduction (wealthmanagement.com, carrying the 'Reed Stevenson (Bloomberg) --' dateline and the complete section structure: Index Funds and Price Discovery / Liquidity Risk / It Won't End Well / Bank of Japan Cushion / Undervalued Japan Small-Caps / Cash Hoarding in Japan / Shareholder Activism), saved locally at /private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-cissychen-design/0f8bdcde-3464-42f4-af17-1552808c31d6/scratchpad/v3_37582b7cad4da385908d1fb6b2d9fcce.txt. Every string the draft quotes appears there character-for-character, and I cross-checked all of them against the independently-obtained local Yahoo/GuruFocus reproduction (burry_yahoo.txt) — they agree. The only substantive additions the primary makes are the 'lightly edited and condensed' note, the 'email interview ... on Tuesday' provenance, 'I just don't know what the timeline will be', 'it will be ugly', and Scion's then-AUM of about $340 million. I did not rely on any fetch summary for a quote: both the Bloomberg reproduction and the acquirersmultiple page were pulled as raw HTML with curl and stripped to text locally, so the quoted strings above are ones I read directly. Index levels were taken from the Yahoo chart JSON with the Unix timestamps decoded by hand (1567517400 = 2019-09-03 09:30 ET at 2906.27; 1567603800 = 2019-09-04 at 2937.78; 1786653303 = 2026-08-13 16:35 ET at 7798.99), then corroborated against Bloomberg/CNBC record-close coverage for 2026-08-13; the +165.47% was recomputed rather than accepted. Scion's deregistration was verified from the SEC's own IAPD API rather than from news: registrationStatus SEC 'Terminated', effectiveDate 11/10/2025, iaScope INACTIVE, all three isRegistered flags 'N' as of today. The acquirersmultiple warning was confirmed by direct comparison against the clean Bloomberg text, and the inserted clause is quoted exactly. What remains uncertain: I could not read paywalled Cassandra Unchained posts, so I cannot verify a negative about whether Burry has revisited the index/passive thesis there — the draft must not assert one. I also could not reach bloomberg.com itself (paywall), so the 'lightly edited and condensed' note and the 'Tuesday' provenance rest on a licensed republication plus a second independent republication rather than on Bloomberg's own server; both carry the identical wording, which I treat as strong but not absolute. Searches through 2026-08 turned up no correction, retraction, or credible challenge to Burry's 2019 liquidity counts, and no evidence he has recanted the index thesis — only low-quality SEO commentary, which I did not use.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Bogle WSJ op-ed (Nov 29, 2018), "Bogle Sounds a Warning on Index Funds": ownership-concentration/voting-control warning, zero price-discovery/bubble claims, numbers (4.5%→9%→>17%; Big Three 81% = Vanguard 51/BlackRock 21/SSGA 9), closes by quoting Coates and saying 'Amen'
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim against full extracted op-ed text (local file bogle_wsj.txt, sourced from shareholderforum.com mirror of the WSJ piece). Exact match: 'holdings doubling from 4.5% of total U.S. stock-market value in 2002 to 9% in 2009, and then almost doubling again to more than 17% in 2018.' Exact match: 'Three index fund managers dominate the field with a collective 81% share of index fund assets: Vanguard has a 51% share; BlackRock, 21%; and State Street Global, 9%.' Exact match: 'If historical trends continue, a handful of giant institutional investors will one day hold voting control of virtually every large U.S. corporation.' Confirmed zero mentions of price discovery, bubbles, mispricing, or market efficiency anywhere in the full op-ed text. Closing paragraph confirmed verbatim: Bogle quotes Coates — 'A ban on indexing would clearly not be a good idea.' — then writes 'I can only say, Amen to those words.' (the claim's quoted fragment 'I can only say, "Amen"' is an accurate partial excerpt of this exact sentence).

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Berkshire 2017 Yahoo Finance interview: 'chaos, catastrophe' quote, followed by 'It's zero' and 'not concerned about it,' plus 75% estimate not dangerous
itemVerdicts.note: Core quotes are verbatim-confirmed against the full extracted Yahoo Finance article (local file bogle_yahoo2.txt, May 6, 2017, by Myles Udland). Confirmed exact: '"If everybody indexed, the only word you could use is chaos, catastrophe," said Jack Bogle... at the Berkshire Hathaway annual meeting.' Confirmed exact: '"Now, what are the chances of everybody indexing? It's zero."' Confirmed exact (in quotation marks, genuinely Bogle's words): '...So, I'm not concerned about it. It's going to take a long, long time [for indexing to get] anywhere near 50% [of the market]...' TWO caliber slips: (1) the claim's framing 'IMMEDIATELY followed by... It's zero... and... I'm not concerned about it' compresses the actual sequence — 'It's zero' is indeed the next sentence after the chaos/catastrophe quote (only two short intervening sentences about 'no trading'), but 'I'm not concerned about it' comes ~100 words later, after an intervening passage about the 50% threshold, trading volume, and market efficiency getting 'a little less efficient' — it is NOT adjacent to 'It's zero,' though it is part of the same continuous interview answer. (2) The 75% clause is NOT a direct quotation of Bogle in the source: the article states in the reporter's own (unquoted) words, 'Bogle said he expects indexing could exceed 75% of the market and not have it become dangerous' — this is Myles Udland's paraphrase of Bogle's answer, not text inside quotation marks in the original article. The claim presents it with quote marks as if verbatim Bogle speech; it should be attributed as the journalist's paraphrase of Bogle's estimate, not a direct quote.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Asness SSRN 4942046 ('The Less-Efficient Market Hypothesis'), footnote 40: pressed Bogle on 75% figure, 'He said "I made it up."'
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in local file asness.txt, footnote 40 (correctly numbered — appears between footnotes 39 and 41): 'I once did a podcast hosting Jack Bogle (I'm doing this from memory) and asked him this question: how much of the market can be cap-weighted indexed before things break down? Jack absolutely acknowledged it can't be the entire market... I pushed him for a number, and he said something like "75%." I said "that's interesting Jack, where did you get that number from?" He said "I made it up." God I miss that man.' Title 'The Less-Efficient Market Hypothesis' confirmed on line 1 of the local file; SSRN abstract ID 4942046 independently confirmed via web search to correspond to this exact paper by Clifford Asness.

corrections: In the Berkshire 2017 Yahoo Finance item, do not present 'I'm not concerned about it' as immediately adjacent to 'It's zero' — roughly 100 words of intervening explanation (about the 50% threshold, trading volume, and markets getting 'a little less efficient') separate the two lines within the same interview answer. Accurate framing: '...followed shortly after by...' or 'later in the same answer,' not 'IMMEDIATELY followed by.'

In the Berkshire 2017 item, do not quote 'could exceed 75% of the market and not have it become dangerous' as Bogle's direct words. In the source (Yahoo Finance, Myles Udland, May 6 2017), this clause is the reporter's own paraphrase — 'Bogle said he expects indexing could exceed 75% of the market and not have it become dangerous' — with no quotation marks around it in the original. Attribute it as 'Bogle's reported estimate, per Yahoo Finance's paraphrase,' not as a direct quotation.
reasoning: Checked all three sub-claims against full primary-source text, not summaries. (a) WSJ op-ed: fetched via WebFetch and cross-checked against a pre-extracted local verbatim copy (bogle_wsj.txt, mirrored by shareholderforum.com from the original WSJ piece dated Nov 29, 2018, 'Bogle Sounds a Warning on Index Funds'). Every number (4.5%→9%→>17%; 81%/51%/21%/9%), the voting-control sentence, the complete absence of any price-discovery/bubble/efficiency language, and the closing Coates quote + 'Amen' were all confirmed character-for-character in the full op-ed text I read directly (not a summarizer's gloss). (b) Yahoo Finance interview: fetched the raw HTML/text (bogle_yahoo2.txt, 279KB, byte-level extraction) and located all four quoted fragments by direct string search with surrounding context, avoiding the fabrication trap flagged in the task (I did not trust any single summarized 'quote' — I pulled the actual passage and read the words around each fragment myself). Found that 'chaos, catastrophe' -> 'It's zero' is genuinely close/immediate (two short sentences between), but 'I'm not concerned about it' sits ~100 words downstream after an unrelated tangent on trading/efficiency, and the 75% figure is explicitly presented in the source as the reporter's paraphrase (no quotation marks), not Bogle's own words. These are caliber slips in attribution/adjacency, not fabrications of substance — the underlying facts (Bogle unworried, thinks 75%+ survivable, expects decades before even 50%) are accurate. (c) Asness footnote: grepped asness.txt directly, found footnote 40 (correctly numbered, sandwiched between fn 39 and fn 41) containing the exact 'I made it up' quote and matching context (podcast, pushed for a number, 75%). Independently confirmed via WebSearch that SSRN abstract_id=4942046 is indeed Asness's 'The Less-Efficient Market Hypothesis.' No web search for later corrections/retractions of these Bogle statements was needed since these are direct-quote/attribution checks against primary journalism/op-ed/working-paper text, not statistical findings subject to later revision — but I note no contradicting later source disputes these quotes exist. Net: (a) and (c) fully verbatim-hold; (b) is substantively accurate but has two real caliber slips (false adjacency claim, and treating a journalist's paraphrase as a direct quote), which is enough under the stated rules to move the overall group verdict from HOLDS to CORRECTED.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) 'equilibrium degree of disequilibrium' framing verbatim
itemVerdicts.note: Lines 39-40 of gs1980.txt: 'We propose here a model in which there is an equilibrium degree of disequilibrium: prices reflect the information of informed individuals (arbitrageurs) but only partially...' — exact verbatim match.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Conjecture 2 with two-channel mechanism; 'more passive → higher active returns' is the unstated contrapositive
itemVerdicts.note: Conjecture 2 (lines 162-164): 'The more individuals who are informed, the lower the ratio of expected utility of the informed to the uninformed.' Two channels given at lines 126-156: (a) price system becomes more informative as more traders become informed, eroding the informed's edge; (b) even without that, per-capita gains to informed traders fall as the informed/uninformed ratio rises. Confirmed that the paper never writes the contrapositive ('fewer informed/more passive → higher relative returns to being informed') explicitly — it is only inferable by the reader, exactly as the claim states.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Conjecture 3: equilibrium informed fraction pinned down by cost of information; λ is an output, not an exogenous indexing-migration shock
itemVerdicts.note: Conjecture 3 (lines 175-177): 'The higher the cost of information, the smaller will be the equilibrium percentage of individuals who are informed.' Text throughout (e.g. lines 167-174, 851ff 'C. The equilibrium percentage of informed...') treats the informed fraction (denoted X, OCR rendering of λ) as solved endogenously from cost/noise/signal-quality parameters — the model contains no mechanism for an exogenous preference-driven migration to indexing as a shock variable.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Conjecture 6 / Section IV nonexistence result driven by noise→0 (prices too informative), not by 'everyone indexes so nobody informed'
itemVerdicts.note: Theorem 5 (lines 951-967) and surrounding text (lines 862-999): nonexistence occurs '(a) if there is no noise (σ_x²=0)... (b) if information is perfect (σ_ε²=0)' — i.e. the informed fraction goes to zero BECAUSE noise/uncertainty vanishes, making prices too informative, not because of a mass shift to passive investing. Applying this to argue a 100%-passive-market breakdown misuses the mechanism, exactly as the claim warns.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Conjecture 7: thin markets at high-λ or low-λ corners — a volume claim, not mispricing
itemVerdicts.note: Lines 209-216: 'markets will be thinner under those conditions in which the percentage of individuals who are informed (X) is either near zero or near unity' — explicitly framed around market thinness/trade volume (further formalized at lines 1029-1049 via per-capita net trade calculations), with no mispricing claim attached.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) Authors state they could not obtain a general proof of the conjectures
itemVerdicts.note: Lines 219-221: 'Unfortunately, we have not been able to obtain a general proof of any of these propositions.' Exact verbatim match.

reasoning: Verified all six sub-claims directly against the local extraction of Grossman & Stiglitz (AER 1980), 'On the Impossibility of Informationally Efficient Markets' (gs1980.txt, 1797 lines, matches JSTOR stable URL 1805228, pp. 393-408). Located and read verbatim: the 'equilibrium degree of disequilibrium' sentence (lines 39-40); the full list of Conjectures 1-7 with surrounding derivation text (lines 126-221); Theorem 5 and its proof/discussion in the noise-goes-to-zero / perfect-information limiting cases (lines 850-999); the per-capita trade-volume analysis backing Conjecture 7's thin-markets claim (lines 1029-1049); and the authors' explicit admission of no general proof (lines 217-221). No numeric drift, no working-paper-vs-published-version discrepancy issues arise here since this is the single published AER 1980 article (no working paper predates it that would carry different numbers). The interpretive framings in the claim (that the 'more passive → higher active returns' inference is a reader's contrapositive not stated by the authors; that λ is model-endogenous so exogenous indexing-migration is outside the model's scope; that the nonexistence result is misapplied when stretched to a 100%-passive scenario) are all consistent with, and directly supported by, what the primary text actually contains and does not contain. The one caveat is that the paper's informed-fraction variable renders in this OCR extraction as 'X' rather than 'λ' — almost certainly a PDF/OCR artifact for the Greek letter, not a substantive discrepancy, and it does not affect any of the checked claims. All items confirmed with no caliber slippage found; verdict HOLDS.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Green claims a breaking point at ~83% passive, 'the market becomes so impossibly volatile... its closure', derived with co-author Hari Krishnan
itemVerdicts.note: Quotes verified verbatim in the Substack transcript. Green: 'that number of about 83% is actually a static number. That if you get to that level of passive effectively, the market becomes so impossibly volatile that it becomes an inevitable event that it will eventually cause its closure.' Assumptions verified verbatim: 'we are assuming that anyone who is not passive. Is fully active, effectively having a historical elasticity of about 0.75 to 0.8. Secondly, we are presuming no flows... So that doesn't include any redemptions. It doesn't include any contributions.' Outer-limit framing verified verbatim: 'If we make some assumptions about declines in elasticity for active managers... That number moves significantly lower. If we start incorporating components of flow into that, that number also begins to fall dramatically. And so we basically treat that 83% as an outer limit.' WRONG: 'co-author Hari Krishnan' (singular). RIGHT: there are TWO co-authors. Stephan Sturm's own WPI publications page lists item 20 as 'A Model for Passive That Breaks the Market, with M. Green and H.P. Krishnan (Preprint, 20 pages, 9 figures; Preprint available at SSRN)'. SSRN abstract_id=6438678 is Cloudflare-blocked to both curl and WebFetch, so I could not read the abstract itself, but the author's own homepage confirms the three-author lineup and that it remains an unpublished preprint as of 2026-08. Also WRONG: transcript date '2026-01-21'. RIGHT: the Substack page's JSON-LD reads datePublished 2026-01-20T21:49:53+00:00 and the visible byline reads 'Excess Returns Jan 20, 2026'.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-sub) The 83% result 'replicates an Andrew Lo-style result of 75-80%'
itemVerdicts.note: Green does say this verbatim: 'some of this work was actually replica is, is effectively a replication of work that was done by Andrew Lowe on a similar topic where he came to a very similar conclusion between 75 and 80% passive. The market would effectively cease functioning.' But I could NOT reach any Andrew Lo primary document containing a 75-80% passive threshold. I read the full 2017 Financial Sense interview 'MIT's Andrew Lo on Adaptive Markets, Passive Indexing, and Systemic Shocks' end to end; Lo's only passive-related passage is the crowded-theater/loss-of-diversity argument ('now that all of us are indexing... the potential for a systemic shock has actually increased') with NO numeric threshold. Repeated searches of alo.mit.edu and the literature returned nothing but restatements of Green's own claim. The article must present this as Green's attribution, not as an established Lo finding.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) 'we're about 54% passive by market share and we picked up about 4% last year' → 'five years out the world comes to an end'; denominator undefined
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim: 'my estimate is actually we're about 54% passive by market share and we picked up about 4% last year. So if that pace continues itself, we would be looking at somewhere in the neighborhood of five years out the world comes to an end.' I grepped the entire transcript for '54' — it appears exactly once and is never defined; no denominator, source, or asset universe is given anywhere in the episode. The ambiguity is material: ICI 2026 Investment Company Fact Book, ch.2, says index mutual funds plus index ETFs 'accounted for the majority (52%) of assets in long-term funds' at YE2025 (Figure 2.5), while 'index domestic equity mutual funds and ETFs remain relatively small investors in the US stock markets, holding 19% of the value of US stocks at year-end 2025' (Figure 2.6). Green's 54% sits just above the FUND-ASSET share and is roughly 2.8x the MARKET-CAP share — and his model's state variable is a market-cap concept.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Apple/CarMax arithmetic: Vanguard ~$350bn/yr inflows → Apple inflated ~23%/yr, 'more than Apple gained last year', rescued by fundamentals
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim: 'Vanguard's inflows last year were about $350 billion. The, that would suggest about a billion dollar order every day... Vanguard [sic — Apple] gets inflated by that order by 0.167%, right? CarMax gets inflated by 0.06%. If you scale that to an annual number, that works out to about a 6% increase in CarMax and about a 23% increase in Apple. By the way, that's actually more than Apple gained last year. So it, there are offsetting components to it among them, the fact that candidly, apple is not growing anymore.' I independently confirmed the over-prediction: AAPL monthly closes (stockanalysis.com history API) were 250.42 on 2024-12-31 and 271.86 on 2025-12-31, i.e. +8.6% price (+9.1% split/dividend-adjusted, 248.62→271.12) versus the model's ~23%. One framing caution for the article: Green does not say fundamentals ADDED return; he says deteriorating fundamentals are an 'offsetting component' that should have pushed Apple's multiple DOWN. Characterizing this as 'the model over-predicts and is rescued ad hoc' is defensible but should be carried alongside his actual words, not substituted for them.

itemVerdicts.item: (d)(i) The $1→$5 multiplier is Gabaix-Koijen's aggregate stocks-vs-bonds elasticity, point estimates 5.3/5.9/7.1/7.7/10.9, SEs ~1.9-2.3
itemVerdicts.note: Aggregate framing and all five point estimates CONFIRMED in the Cowles/SSRN May 12 2022 text. Abstract: 'investing $1 in the stock market increases the market's aggregate value by about $5.' Intro: 'when an investor sells $1 worth of bonds and buys $1 worth of stocks, what happens to the valuation of the aggregate stock market?' Flow-of-Funds section: 'We estimate a multiplier of M = 7.1... The corresponding standard error is 1.9... This lowers the multiplier estimate to M = 5.3' and 'The corresponding multipliers, M = 1/(zeta+zetaC), are M = 7.1 and M = 5.9.' Mutual-fund section: 'the multiplier estimate equals M = 10.9... the multiplier drops to M = 7.7 with a standard error of 2.3.' WRONG: 'SEs ~1.9-2.3'. RIGHT: the reported SEs span roughly 1.1 to 2.6 — Table 3 gives 7.08 (1.86) and 5.28 (1.10); Table 2 gives 10.93 (2.64) and 7.69 (2.32); the 5.9 is a derived quantity (1/(zeta+zetaC)) with no directly reported SE. Quoting '~1.9-2.3' understates the imprecision at the top (2.64) and overstates it at the 5.3 estimate (1.10). Separately, if the article quotes Green's on-air rendering of GK, note he says 'They estimated it was between five and eight' — GK's own text says 'our estimates are between $3 and $8, and we will use $5 for simplicity.' Also worth citing GK's Appendix: 'If we go beyond two principal components, the multiplier declines somewhat from 5.3 with two principal components to a range from 3.5 to 4.2 with three to five principal components.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d)(ii) GK contains essentially no analysis of passive indexing (one paraphrase of De Long 1990)
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed by exhaustive grep of the full text for 'passive', 'indexing', 'index fund', 'De Long', 'Basak', 'Goetzmann', 'Pavlova', 'Chinco', 'Sammon'. The only substantive occurrence is the literature-review sentence: 'We build on the insights of De Long et al. (1990)... They discuss a rich set of qualitative ideas, some of which we can formally analyze and quantify, such as the failure of the Modigliani-Miller theorem and the notion that if most market participants passively hold the market portfolio, prices react sharply to flows.' The only other 'passive' hit is an unrelated Appendix line about an agent who lets 'his equity share drift passively.' Two minor caveats the article should not be blindsided by: Table 1 Panel A lists index-inclusion event studies (Chang-Hong-Liskovich 2014; Pavlova-Sikorskaya 2020) as evidence that the MICRO multiplier is around 1, and the bibliography carries Goetzmann-Massa 'Index Funds and Stock Market Growth' and Haddad-Huebner-Loualiche. None of these amounts to analysis of the growth of passive indexing.

itemVerdicts.item: (d)(iii) NBER 28967 remains unpublished as of 2026-08; the companion GIV methods paper published in JPE 2024
itemVerdicts.note: nber.org/papers/w28967 (fetched 2026-08-14) shows Working Paper 28967, DOI 10.3386/w28967, Issue Date June 2021, with NO 'Published Versions' block anywhere in the page HTML (grep for 'published as' / 'Published Version' returns nothing). RePEc RePEc:nbr:nberwo:28967 lists the item only as 'NBER Working Papers 28967' with a single other version, 'CEPR Discussion Papers 16290' — no journal entry. Companion CONFIRMED published: RePEc:ucp:jpolec:doi:10.1086/728743 — 'Xavier Gabaix & Ralph S. J. Koijen, 2024. "Granular Instrumental Variables," Journal of Political Economy, University of Chicago Press, vol. 132(7), pages 2274-2303.'

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Green left Simplify in 2026 to launch Tier1 Alpha, an ETF/SMA firm trading passive-flow pressure
itemVerdicts.note: Substantively CONFIRMED from Green's OWN primary source — his Substack yesigiveafig.com, 'It's Time to Complicate,' dated Aug 09, 2026 (etfstream.com was indeed blocked, but this is better evidence). Verbatim: 'After five extraordinary years, I am leaving Simplify Asset Management to found Tier1 Alpha Asset Management, where I will serve as CEO and CIO.' Products verbatim: 'ETFs for RIAs and retail; SMAs and hedge funds for institutions. All built on the same underlying research.' Strategy verbatim: 'Our flagship implementation holds essentially the same securities as the leading U.S. large-cap benchmark, then tilts modestly and systematically toward the securities where our measurement suggests passive demand is strongest relative to available liquidity and away from — or underweights — those where the opposite is true.' Also verbatim: 'We seek to measure the smaller, continuous mechanical flow.' WRONG: 'launch Tier1 Alpha'. RIGHT: he founded Tier1 Alpha ASSET MANAGEMENT, a new arm; Tier1 Alpha, Inc. is a pre-existing market-structure research firm — its own About page lists Craig Peterson as 'CEO/ Co-founder', David Pegler as 'COO/ Co-founder', and Michael Green as 'Senior Executive Advisor' — and Green already referred to 'the team at Tier one Alpha' in the January 2026 podcast while still at Simplify ('I'm spending a lot of time working on the upside work with the team at Tier one Alpha').

itemVerdicts.item: (f) Green called Vanguard's Aug-2025 paper 'intentionally misleading' with a REIT/sector composition objection to the mid-cap ownership stat
itemVerdicts.note: CONFIRMED on both halves. The paper is 'Setting the record straight: The truths about index fund investing,' Vanguard research, August 2025, by James J. Rowley Jr. CFA, Stephen Lawrence Ph.D., and Ollie Ryder-Green (local extraction of the PDF). Its mid-cap claim reads verbatim: 'In practice, U.S. equity index funds' highest proportional ownership is in mid-cap stocks and not large-caps (Figure 5)... The largest stocks possess lower aggregate ownership amounts than mid-cap stocks.' Green's response verbatim: 'I think that there's a couple of things, and again, I think they're being intentionally misleading. So when they're describing index funds in this con, in this context, they're taking a slightly different approach. They're including index funds. That would be like the REIT index or nuclear power index... nobody in their 401k has the REIT ETF as their default investment vehicle. So almost everything that we're talking about, they're intentionally avoiding and obfuscating with this analysis.' Two caveats for the article: (1) Green uses 'intentionally misleading' TWICE and uses it FIRST about Vanguard's Figure 6 trading-volume chart, not the mid-cap chart — 'they are being intentionally misleading in this chart... I candidly think that Vanguard should be held liable for misleading people at this point.' The article should not imply the composition objection was the only or the first target. (2) The host mis-dates the paper on air as 'late last year'; it is August 2025.

corrections: Name both co-authors, not one: the model is Michael Green, Hari P. Krishnan AND Stephan Sturm (Worcester Polytechnic Institute), 'A Model for Passive That Breaks the Market'. Sturm's own WPI publications page lists it as preprint item 20 — 'Preprint, 20 pages, 9 figures; Preprint available at SSRN' (SSRN abstract_id 6438678). It is an unpublished, non-peer-reviewed preprint as of 2026-08; SSRN itself is Cloudflare-blocked to automated fetch, so do not quote its abstract without a human-verified read.

Fix the transcript date: the Excess Returns Substack post 'Full Transcript: Mike Green on the Passive Investing Breaking Point' carries datePublished 2026-01-20T21:49:53+00:00 and a visible byline of 'Jan 20, 2026', not 2026-01-21.

Do not present '75-80%' as an Andrew Lo result. It is solely Green's on-air attribution ('effectively a replication of work that was done by Andrew Lowe... between 75 and 80% passive'). No Lo primary document containing such a threshold could be reached; Lo's actual public passive commentary (2017 Financial Sense interview) is the qualitative crowded-theater/loss-of-diversity argument with no numeric threshold. Phrase it as 'Green says it replicates work by Andrew Lo' and flag that the underlying Lo result could not be located.

Fix the Gabaix-Koijen standard-error range: WRONG '~1.9-2.3'; RIGHT the reported SEs span roughly 1.1 to 2.6. Table 3 (Flow of Funds): M = 7.08 (SE 1.86) and M = 5.28 (SE 1.10). Table 2 (mutual fund flows): M = 10.93 (SE 2.64) and M = 7.69 (SE 2.32). The 5.9 figure is derived as 1/(zeta + zeta_C) and carries no directly reported standard error.

If quoting Green's rendering of Gabaix-Koijen, note he misstates their range: he says 'They estimated it was between five and eight'; GK's own text says 'our estimates are between $3 and $8, and we will use $5 for simplicity in the theory and discussion.' GK also report the multiplier falling to 3.5-4.2 with three to five principal components.

Fix the Tier1 Alpha description: WRONG 'left Simplify to launch Tier1 Alpha'; RIGHT he left Simplify to found Tier1 Alpha ASSET MANAGEMENT, where he is CEO and CIO (his own Substack 'It's Time to Complicate', Aug 09 2026). Tier1 Alpha, Inc. is a pre-existing market-structure research firm — Craig Peterson CEO/co-founder, David Pegler COO/co-founder, Green listed as 'Senior Executive Advisor' — and Green was already working with 'the team at Tier one Alpha' in January 2026 while still at Simplify.

When reporting the 'intentionally misleading' charge, note Green applies it twice and applies it FIRST to Vanguard's Figure 6 trading-volume chart ('they are being intentionally misleading in this chart'), then again to the mid-cap ownership chart with the REIT/nuclear-power-index composition objection. Do not imply the composition objection was his only or first use of the phrase.

Date the Vanguard paper correctly as August 2025 ('Setting the record straight: The truths about index fund investing', Rowley, Lawrence, Ryder-Green). If quoting the podcast, note the host mis-dates it on air as 'late last year'.

Ground the '54% by market share' denominator objection with a hard anchor: ICI 2026 Investment Company Fact Book reports index mutual funds plus index ETFs at 52% of long-term fund total net assets at YE2025 (Figure 2.5), while index domestic equity mutual funds and ETFs held 19% of US stock market capitalization at YE2025 (Figure 2.6). Green's 54% sits just above the fund-asset measure and roughly 2.8x the market-cap measure, and his model's state variable is a market-cap concept.
newContradictions: Green's own timeline does not reconcile with his own threshold. From 54% at +4 percentage points per year, reaching 83% takes about 7.25 years, not the 'somewhere in the neighborhood of five years' he states; five years at that pace reaches only 74%. He never says he is using a lower 'realistic' threshold for the five-year figure.

Green's Apple/CarMax daily-to-annual scaling does not reconcile internally. He states a 0.167% per-day impulse for Apple and 0.06% for CarMax, then annualizes to '23%' and '6%'. With ~250 trading days, 0.167%/day compounds to roughly 52% (42% simple) and 0.06%/day to roughly 16% (15% simple). Both stated annual figures are low by a factor of roughly 2.5 with no stated adjustment. The same gap appears later: he cites 13bp/day market-cap-weighted versus 9bp/day median (a 4bp/day spread, ~10%/yr) but calls it a 'six, 7%' annual differential.

Green's premise input appears overstated. He says 'Vanguard's inflows last year were about $350 billion'; Morningstar's December 2025 flows report states 'Vanguard's $240 billion inflow in 2025 was the second largest' behind iShares' $366 billion in US long-term funds. Substituting $240bn would cut his Apple figure from ~23% to roughly 16%.

Green's on-screen elasticity figures do not match the Haddad-Huebner-Loualiche paper he credits. He says 'the active managers themselves used to have elasticities in the range of 0.75 to 0.8. Today, that number is well below 50%.' HHL (March 2022 working paper, 'How Competitive is the Stock Market?') Figure 6 reports the average aggregate elasticity across stocks going 'from 0.46 to 0.31, a 40% drop' over 2000Q4-2020Q4, with the 90th percentile dropping from 0.64 to 0.53 and the 10th from 0.25 to 0.12; Table 3 Panel A gives an average of 0.489. No 0.75-0.8 baseline appears in HHL. If the article repeats the 0.75-0.8 figure, it must not attribute it to Haddad et al.

Independent check strengthens the (c) over-prediction: AAPL closed 2024-12-31 at $250.42 and 2025-12-31 at $271.86, a +8.6% price return (+9.1% adjusted, 248.62 to 271.12). Green's model implies ~23% from Vanguard flows alone — roughly 14 percentage points above what Apple actually delivered.
reasoning: I reached and read the primary documents directly rather than relying on summarizers. (1) The Excess Returns transcript: I curl'd the Substack page, stripped tags myself, and read the relevant passages in full — every quoted string in this report was seen verbatim in that extraction, including the 83% passage, the 0.75-0.8/zero-flow assumptions, the 'outer limit' framing, the 54%/4%/five-years passage, the Apple-CarMax arithmetic, the Tier1 Alpha mention, and both 'intentionally misleading' uses. Its JSON-LD datePublished is 2026-01-20T21:49:53+00:00. (2) Gabaix-Koijen: I read the local gk.txt (the May 12 2022 Cowles/SSRN version) and pulled Tables 2 and 3 raw, which is how I caught that the SE range is 1.10-2.64 rather than the stated ~1.9-2.3. I grepped the whole document for every passive/indexing term to confirm the single De Long paraphrase. (3) Publication status: NBER w28967's live page has no Published Versions block and RePEc lists no journal version; the GIV companion is confirmed at JPE 132(7):2274-2303, DOI 10.1086/728743. (4) Tier1 Alpha: rather than the blocked etfstream piece, I fetched Green's own announcement post at yesigiveafig.com (Aug 09 2026) and read it end to end, plus Tier1 Alpha's own About page for the pre-existing-firm distinction. (5) Vanguard: the August 2025 paper text was already extracted locally and I read the Figure 5 mid-cap passage and the Figure 6 cash-flow-adjusted-turnover note. (6) Corroborating numbers came from ICI's 2026 Fact Book chapter 2 (52% of long-term fund assets, 19% of US market cap), Morningstar's December 2025 flows report (Vanguard $240bn), HHL's own Figure 6 and Table 3, and AAPL month-end closes from stockanalysis.com's history API. What remains uncertain: I could not read the SSRN abstract for the Green/Krishnan/Sturm preprint (Cloudflare blocks both curl and WebFetch), so its internal thresholds are known to me only through Sturm's WPI listing and secondhand summaries I have deliberately not quoted; and I could not locate any Andrew Lo primary source containing a 75-80% passive threshold despite reading his one substantial public passive-investing interview in full, so that attribution stands unverified rather than refuted.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Green claims a breaking point at ~83% passive: market 'becomes so impossibly volatile... its closure'; assumptions = all non-passive money fully active at elasticity 0.75-0.8, zero net flows; 83% is an 'outer limit', realistic assumptions move it lower
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the transcript (local mg_transcript.txt, fetched from excessreturnspod.substack.com). 'that number of about 83% is actually a static number. That if you get to that level of passive effectively, the market becomes so impossibly volatile that it becomes an inevitable event that it will eventually cause its closure.' Assumptions: 'we are assuming that anyone who is not passive. Is fully active, effectively having a historical elasticity of about 0.75 to 0.8. Secondly, we are presuming no flows... So that doesn't include any redemptions. It doesn't include any contributions.' And 'we basically treat that 83% as an outer limit'; 'If we make some assumptions about declines in elasticity for active managers... That number moves significantly lower. If we start incorporating components of flow into that, that number also begins to fall dramatically.'

itemVerdicts.item: (a) 'derived with co-author Hari Krishnan'
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG (incomplete): two authors, Green + Hari Krishnan. RIGHT: the resulting paper has THREE authors — Michael Green, Hari Krishnan, and Stephan Sturm (WPI mathematician). Verified two ways: Crossref record for DOI 10.2139/ssrn.6438678 lists Green (first), Krishnan, Sturm (ORCID 0000-0002-7214-8843); and Sturm's own WPI homepage lists item 20: 'A Model for Passive That Breaks the Market, with M. Green and H.P. Krishnan (Preprint, 20 pages, 9 figures; Preprint available at SSRN)'. The transcript itself only says 'Hari' — the surname Krishnan never appears in it, so the article is inferring it (correctly, but from outside the transcript).

itemVerdicts.item: (a) 'replicating an Andrew Lo-style result of 75-80%'
itemVerdicts.note: Green's words are verbatim: 'effectively a replication of work that was done by Andrew Lowe [sic] on a similar topic where he came to a very similar conclusion between 75 and 80% passive.' I could NOT reach any primary Andrew W. Lo document containing a 75-80% passive threshold — searches of alo.mit.edu, his publication lists, and general search returned nothing with those numbers. The article's hedge ('Andrew Lo-style') is defensible as reporting, but the underlying attribution is unverified; do not restate it as an established Lo finding.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) 'we're about 54% passive by market share and we picked up about 4% last year' → 'five years out the world comes to an end'; the 54% denominator is undefined
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'my estimate is actually we're about 54% passive by market share and we picked up about 4% last year. So if that pace continues itself, we would be looking at somewhere in the neighborhood of five years out the world comes to an end.' Denominator genuinely undefined — he never says whether 54% is share of fund assets, share of US equity market cap, or share of some flow/ownership measure, and elsewhere in the same interview he uses at least two other, incompatible bases ('passive trading now makes up roughly 80% of market volume on a daily basis'; index-fund ownership percentages). NOTE the internal arithmetic gap: (83-54)/4 = 7.25 years, not five. Five years only works against a ~74% threshold, i.e. the Lo 75-80% band, not the 83% 'outer limit' he had just described.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Apple/CarMax arithmetic: Vanguard ~$350bn/yr inflows → Apple inflated ~23%/yr, 'that's actually more than Apple gained last year', explained away via fundamentals
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'Vanguard's inflows last year were about $350 billion. The, that would suggest about a billion dollar order every day... Vanguard [sic — he means Apple] gets inflated by that order by 0.167%, right? CarMax gets inflated by 0.06%. If you scale that to an annual number, that works out to about a 6% increase in CarMax and about a 23% increase in Apple. By the way, that's actually more than Apple gained last year.' He then supplies the fundamentals rescue: 'there are offsetting components to it among them, the fact that candidly, apple is not growing anymore... it should be trading at lower valuations.' The article's 'over-predicts and is rescued ad hoc' reading is supported by the text. Additional internal inconsistency worth noting: 0.167%/day × 252 = 42%, not 23%, and 0.06%/day × 252 = 15%, not 6% — the stated daily impulses do not produce the stated annual figures by any scaling he describes. Same problem later: 13bp vs 9bp/day → 10.1%/yr, but he says 'six, 7% differentials'.

itemVerdicts.item: (d)(i) Gabaix-Koijen estimate the AGGREGATE (stocks-vs-bonds) elasticity; point estimates 5.3/5.9/7.1/7.7/10.9 with SEs ~1.9-2.3
itemVerdicts.note: Aggregate/stocks-vs-bonds framing CONFIRMED verbatim: 'when an investor sells $1 worth of bonds and buys $1 worth of stocks, what happens to the valuation of the aggregate stock market?' All five point estimates CONFIRMED. But the SE range is WRONG. WRONG: 'SEs ~1.9-2.3'. RIGHT: Table 3 (Flow of Funds) M = 7.08 (SE 1.86) and M = 5.28 (SE 1.10); Table 2 (mutual-fund/13F) M = 10.93 (SE 2.64), 10.85 (2.78), 8.54 (2.18), 7.69 (2.32), 7.69 (2.34), 7.62 (1.92). So the reported SEs run 1.10 to 2.78, not 1.9-2.3. Also WRONG to attach an SE to 5.9: 5.9 is a DERIVED quantity, M = 1/(ζ+ζ_C) with two principal components, and the paper reports no standard error for it (the '5.99 (0.69)' adjacent in Table 3 is the GDP-growth coefficient, not a multiplier). Additional caliber points: the paper's own headline is '$5 (our estimates are between $3 and $8, and we will use $5 for simplicity)' and its robustness section says 'multiplier estimates ranging from 3.5 to 8'. Green in this transcript misstates that range — he says Gabaix-Koijen 'estimated it was between five and eight'; the paper says three to eight.

itemVerdicts.item: (d)(ii) Gabaix-Koijen contain essentially no analysis of passive indexing (one paraphrase of De Long 1990)
itemVerdicts.note: Grep of the full Cowles/SSRN-id3686935 text: the only substantive occurrence is the De Long paraphrase — 'They discuss a rich set of qualitative ideas, some of which we can formally analyze and quantify, such as the failure of the Modigliani-Miller theorem and the notion that if most market participants passively hold the market portfolio, prices react sharply to flows.' The words 'passive'/'index fund' otherwise appear only in bibliography entries (Goetzmann & Massa 'Index Funds and Stock Market Growth'; Haddad-Huebner-Loualiche; Chang-Hong-Liskovich index inclusion in Table 1) and once in an appendix in an unrelated sense ('an investor who would let his equity share drift passively'). No passive-share analysis, no threshold, no indexing mechanism.

itemVerdicts.item: (d)(iii) NBER 28967 has no 'published as'; the companion GIV methods paper DID publish in JPE 2024
itemVerdicts.note: Fetched both NBER pages with curl and grepped the raw HTML: w28967 (In Search of the Origins of Financial Fluctuations, Issue Date June 2021) contains ZERO occurrences of 'Published Version'. w28204 (Granular Instrumental Variables) contains exactly one 'Published Versions' block reading 'Journal of Political Economy, vol 132(7), pages 2274-2303.' Gabaix's own Harvard publications entry for the inelastic-markets paper is also filed with a '[Working Paper]' tag. Still unpublished as of 2026-08.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Green left Simplify in 2026 to launch Tier1 Alpha, an ETF/SMA firm whose strategy trades passive-flow pressure
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed from Green's OWN primary post, not the blocked etfstream piece: 'It's Time to Complicate', yesigiveafig.com, Aug 09, 2026 — 'After five extraordinary years, I am leaving Simplify Asset Management to found Tier1 Alpha Asset Management, where I will serve as CEO and CIO.' He joined Simplify April 2021 (~$200m AUM, now ~$14bn). Vehicle mix verbatim: 'ETFs for RIAs and retail; SMAs and hedge funds for institutions.' Strategy verbatim: 'We seek to measure the smaller, continuous mechanical flow' and 'Our flagship implementation holds essentially the same securities as the leading U.S. large-cap benchmark, then tilts modestly and systematically toward the securities where our measurement suggests passive demand is strongest relative to available liquidity.' Note timing: at the Jan-2026 podcast he was still Simplify CIS/PM and described Tier1 Alpha as a research arm ('I'm spending a lot of time working on the upside work with the team at Tier one Alpha').

itemVerdicts.item: (f) Green called Vanguard's Aug-2025 paper 'intentionally misleading' with a composition objection (REIT/sector index funds diluting the mid-cap ownership stat)
itemVerdicts.note: Vanguard paper identified and dated from the PDF itself: 'Vanguard research / August 2025 / Setting the record straight: The truths about index fund investing' by James J. Rowley Jr., Stephen Lawrence, Ollie Ryder-Green. Green uses 'intentionally misleading' TWICE. First on Figure 6 (trading volume): 'They are being intentionally misleading in this chart' — and his description is accurate, Vanguard's Figure 6 note reads 'The percentage of total trading volume is cash-flow adjusted turnover as a percentage of total U.S. exchange trading volume.' Second, on the mid-cap ownership point (Vanguard's Figure 5, index-mutual-fund ownership by Russell 3000 market-cap rank as of Dec 31 2024): 'I think that there's a couple of things, and again, I think they're being intentionally misleading. So when they're describing index funds in this context... They're including index funds. That would be like the REIT index or nuclear power index... but nobody in their 401k has the REIT ETF as their default investment vehicle.' So the pairing the article makes is correct; if the article implies the phrase was used only once, tighten it.

itemVerdicts.item: Transcript date given as 2026-01-21
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 2026-01-21. RIGHT: 2026-01-20. The Substack page carries datePublished '2026-01-20T21:49:53+00:00' and the visible byline reads 'Jan 20, 2026'. Canonical URL confirmed as https://excessreturnspod.substack.com/p/full-transcript-mike-green-on-the

corrections: Change the transcript date from 2026-01-21 to 2026-01-20 (Substack datePublished 2026-01-20T21:49:53Z; byline 'Jan 20, 2026').

The Green-Krishnan work is now a posted preprint with a THIRD author: Michael Green, Hari Krishnan and Stephan Sturm, 'A Model for Passive That Breaks the Market', SSRN, DOI 10.2139/ssrn.6438678, deposited 2026-03-27, still an unpublished 20-page preprint per Sturm's WPI page. Name Sturm as co-author.

MATERIAL: the actual preprint does NOT carry the 83% figure. Its abstract (verified verbatim via the Crossref deposit) states: 'Once the passive share reaches around 65%, index volatility may increase sharply. At 90% share, an increase in volatility at cubic speed is nearly inevitable, leading to exaggerated boom and bust cycles.' The article must present 83% as a January-2026 podcast-stage number that the authors' own March-2026 write-up replaced with a ~65% / 90% pair, and must not describe 83% as the paper's threshold.

Do not attach a standard error to the 5.9 estimate. It is a derived quantity, M = 1/(ζ+ζ_C) with two principal components, and the paper reports no SE for it. (The '5.99 (0.69)' printed nearby in Table 3 is the GDP-growth coefficient, not a multiplier.)

When stating GK's range, use their words: '$5' is the number they 'use for simplicity'; their stated estimate range is '$3 and $8', and robustness checks give 'multiplier estimates ranging from 3.5 to 8'. Green in this very transcript misreports it as 'between five and eight' — if the article renders his citation as '$1→$5' it is smoothing over an error he actually made; quote him as saying 'between five and eight' and note the paper says three to eight.

Add the internal-arithmetic gap in (b): at 54% rising 4 points a year, 83% is 7.25 years away, not the 'five years' Green states. Five years only reaches ~74%, i.e. the Lo 75-80% band, not the 83% 'outer limit'.

Add the internal-arithmetic gap in (c): the daily impulses Green states do not scale to his annual figures — 0.167%/day × 252 ≈ 42% (he says 23% for Apple) and 0.06%/day × 252 ≈ 15% (he says 6% for CarMax); likewise 13bp vs 9bp/day compounds to ~10%/yr, not the 'six, 7% differentials' he claims.

Do not present the Andrew Lo 75-80% result as an established finding. No primary Lo document containing that threshold could be located; attribute it strictly as Green's assertion ('Green says his result replicates work by Andrew Lo').

In (f), note that Green applies 'intentionally misleading' twice — once to Vanguard's Figure 6 (cash-flow-adjusted index-fund turnover, ~1.2% of 2024 volume) and once to the mid-cap ownership point (Figure 5, index-mutual-fund ownership across Russell 3000 market-cap ranks as of Dec 31, 2024). The REIT/nuclear-power-index composition objection attaches to the second, not the first. Identify the Vanguard paper precisely: 'Setting the record straight: The truths about index fund investing', Vanguard research, August 2025, Rowley, Lawrence and Ryder-Green.

For (e), cite Green's own announcement — 'It's Time to Complicate', yesigiveafig.com, Aug 9, 2026 — rather than the blocked etfstream article. It supports every element: leaving Simplify (joined April 2021, ~$200m → ~$14bn), founding Tier1 Alpha Asset Management as CEO/CIO, 'ETFs for RIAs and retail; SMAs and hedge funds for institutions', and a strategy that measures 'the smaller, continuous mechanical flow' into passive vehicles and tilts a benchmark-like portfolio toward names where passive demand is strongest relative to available liquidity.
newContradictions: Green, Krishnan and Sturm, 'A Model for Passive That Breaks the Market' (SSRN 6438678, deposited 2026-03-27) — the write-up of the very model Green describes in the podcast — reports thresholds of ~65% and 90%, and never states 83%. The abstract's operative sentences (verbatim from the Crossref deposit): 'Once the passive share reaches around 65%, index volatility may increase sharply. At 90% share, an increase in volatility at cubic speed is nearly inevitable, leading to exaggerated boom and bust cycles.' The abstract also makes no claim about market closure and does not mention Andrew Lo.
Green's own timeline does not follow from his own numbers: 54% today + 4 points/year reaches 83% in 7.25 years, not the 'five years' he asserts.

Green's Apple/CarMax daily impulses do not scale to his annual figures: 0.167%/day over 252 trading days is ~42% (not 23%) and 0.06%/day is ~15% (not 6%). His later median-vs-cap-weighted figures have the same problem (4bp/day → ~10%/yr, stated as 'six, 7%').

Green misstates the Gabaix-Koijen range in this transcript: he says they 'estimated it was between five and eight'; the paper says 'about $5 (our estimates are between $3 and $8)' and robustness 'ranging from 3.5 to 8'.

Green also says 'the regulatory framework changed radically in 2006... implemented in early 2008. That required 401Ks to default into passive vehicles and any selection of non-passive vehicles actually exposed the sponsor of the 401k to liability.' The PPA/QDIA rule does not require passive defaults — target-date, balanced and managed-account QDIAs qualify and many are actively managed. This is a separate, checkable overstatement in the same transcript that the article may be relying on; flag it if quoted.

'A Model for Passive That Breaks the Market' remains an unpublished preprint (Sturm's WPI page: 'Preprint, 20 pages, 9 figures'), so the 83%/65%/90% family of numbers has no peer-reviewed standing as of 2026-08.
reasoning: Primary documents reached verbatim: (1) the full Excess Returns transcript, local mg_transcript.txt/.html with the canonical URL and datePublished metadata — every quoted string in claims (a), (b), (c), (f) was matched character-for-character in it; (2) the Gabaix-Koijen Cowles/SSRN-id3686935 full text (gk.txt), including the abstract, the introduction's stocks-vs-bonds setup, Table 1, Table 2 and Table 3 with all point estimates and parenthesized standard errors, the De Long et al. (1990) paraphrase, and the robustness sentence; (3) the NBER landing pages for w28967 and w28204 fetched with curl and grepped in raw HTML for 'Published Version' (zero hits vs one hit citing JPE 132(7), 2274-2303); (4) Vanguard's August 2025 'Setting the record straight' PDF text, including the Figure 5 mid-cap ownership passage and the Figure 6 note confirming 'cash-flow adjusted turnover'; (5) Michael Green's own Substack announcement 'It's Time to Complicate' (yesigiveafig.com, Aug 9, 2026) confirming the Simplify departure and Tier1 Alpha's ETF/SMA structure and passive-flow strategy; (6) the Crossref record for DOI 10.2139/ssrn.6438678 (publisher-deposited JATS abstract) plus Stephan Sturm's WPI homepage, which together establish the three-author Green/Krishnan/Sturm preprint and its 65%/90% thresholds. Everything the article attributes to the transcript checks out verbatim; the corrections are (i) a one-day date error, (ii) an incorrect standard-error range and an SE wrongly implied for the derived 5.9 estimate, (iii) an incomplete author list, and (iv) a substantive omission: the authors' own written model, posted two months after the podcast, replaces 83% with ~65% and 90%. Remaining uncertain: I could not obtain the full text of SSRN 6438678 (Elsevier Cloudflare block on both WebFetch and curl; Semantic Scholar has no record), so I verified its abstract only via Crossref and could not check whether the paper itself cites Andrew Lo, discusses market closure, or reconciles 83% with 65%/90%. I could not locate any Andrew Lo primary document with a 75-80% passive threshold, so that attribution stays unverified rather than refuted. Green's '$350 billion' Vanguard inflow figure and his '54% passive by market share' were not independently checkable against a primary source within this pass and are reported as his claims only.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Interview dated "Dec 2025" EXPANSIÓN interview
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: "Dec 2025 EXPANSIÓN interview." RIGHT: the Expansión interview by Roberto Casado was published Monday, 3 November 2025 (original: https://www.expansion.com/mercados/2025/11/03/6904bb30e5fdea145f8b459b.html; Fundsmith's own reproduction, EN and ES, is datelined "Monday, 3 November 2025" / "lunes, 3 de noviembre de 2025", headline "Terry Smith: 'There could be a stock market bubble more extreme than the one in 2000'"). December 2025 is only the date of The Acquirer's Multiple repost (Johnny Hopkins, December 7, 2025), which is where the English wording in our sourcing came from.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Quote: "More than 50% of assets are now invested through index funds, which are not actually passive; they are a momentum strategy"
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in Fundsmith's own English rendering: "The effects are profound. More than 50% of assets are now invested through index funds, which are not actually passive; they are a momentum strategy [investing in assets with the best recent performance]." Spanish original: "Los efectos son profundos. Más del 50% de los activos están ahora invertidos a través de fondos indexados, que en realidad no son pasivos, son una estrategia de momentum..." Answering a question about how passive/index growth affects his strategy. No geography and no asset class stated — correctly noted in the claim.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Quote: "in 2000 less than 10% of funds were index funds, and now it's more than 50%" (denominator switches assets→funds)
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, and the denominator switch is genuinely in the original, not introduced by translation. Full sentence: "The effects are more extreme than in the dot-com bubble because in 2000 less than 10% of funds were index funds, and now it's more than 50%." Spanish: "...porque en 2000 menos del 10% de los fondos eran indexados y ahora son más del 50%." First answer says "activos"/assets; this one says "fondos"/funds. Neither specifies geography, asset class, or whether "funds" means fund count or fund assets. Quote the switch as evidence of loose sourcing, do not launder it into a single consistent statistic.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Letter quote: market "dominated by so-called passive or index funds (of which the majority are ETFs)" + AI
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim from the primary PDF (Fundsmith Equity Fund Semi-Annual Letter to Shareholders 2026, dated July 2026, p.2, https://www.fundsmith.co.uk/media/lfhpxi1x/fundsmith-equity-fund-semi-annual-letter-to-shareholders-2026.pdf): "The backdrop to this continues to be a market which is dominated by so-called passive or index funds (of which the majority are ETFs) and the boom surrounding AI which have combined to produce a market dominated by momentum rather than any fundamental factors like profitability, returns on capital and growth — in other words the factors we focus on." I downloaded and text-extracted the PDF myself; this is not a secondary reproduction.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Momentum's relative performance "at a 30 year high and more extreme than in late 1999"
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, p.4: "It is at a 30 year high and more extreme than in late 1999 just before the Dotcom bubble burst." Caliber note the article must carry: "it" refers to "the performance of momentum based investment... as this Bloomberg chart illustrates", and I extracted the chart image from the PDF — its title is "Momentum Is Showing Record Outperformance", series "MSCI US Momentum QoQ vs MSCI US QoQ", y-axis in percentage points, sample beginning 1995. So it is a quarter-over-quarter relative-return spread of a US momentum index vs the US market, and "30 year high" is the maximum over the entire plotted sample (the chart simply does not go back further). Latest bar ≈ +27-28pp (circled); the 1999-era spike ≈ +21pp, so "more extreme than in late 1999" is consistent with the chart as drawn.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) "I profess no insight into how or when this passive-led momentum market will end, other than to say badly."
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, p.7 of the primary letter, immediately after "We have no desire to hug the index." Continues: "It may be that a realisation that the humungous investment in AI cannot produce an adequate return or any clear winner(s) will derail it... But we do know that trees do not grow to the sky."

itemVerdicts.item: (c) H1 2026: -2.9% vs MSCI World +11.2%, ~14.1pp shortfall, T-class GBP
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed from the primary table (p.1). "Fundsmith Equity Fund1 -2.9 / Equities2 +11.2 / UK Bonds3 +0.7 / Cash4 +1.8" for 1st Jan to 30th June 2026. Footnote 1: "T Class Accumulation shares, net of fees priced at midday UK time, Inception, 1.11.2010, source: Bloomberg." Footnote 2: "MSCI World Index, £ Net, priced at close of business US time, source: www.msci.com." Body text: "Our Fund was down by 2.9% in the first six months of the year, 14.1 percentage points less than what is perhaps the most obvious comparator — the MSCI World Index (£ net)." So yes: T Class Accumulation, sterling, net of fees. Also on the table: "The Fund is not managed with reference to any benchmark; the above comparators are provided for information purposes only." Independently corroborated by interactive investor ("It lost 2.9%, versus a positive return of 11.2% from the MSCI World index"), though ii cites the I Acc share class.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) "~52% portfolio turnover in six months"
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: "~52%". RIGHT: 51.8%. Appendix 1: "Our portfolio turnover in the first half was 51.8%." Note the letter is internally inconsistent — the body (p.6) says "our portfolio turnover hit a high of 51% in the first half of this year". Use 51.8% and cite Appendix 1. Same appendix: voluntary dealing cost £11,404,962 (0.084%); OCF for T Class Acc 1.05%; Total Cost of Investment 1.12%. Context for how unusual this is: turnover was 12.7% for full-year 2025 and 3.2% for 2024 (interactive investor). Do NOT use valueandopportunity's "switched ~50% of the portfolio within 6 months" or its "previous years... on average less than 10%" — those are the blogger's characterisations, not the letter's.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Explicit process change to incorporate momentum
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, p.6: "We will take more account of momentum — both fundamental and share price — in our investment decisions. In particular, we will be much less willing to deploy the time-honoured technique of buying quality companies when they hit a glitch." Also p.6: "You should therefore expect that we will be more active in future." The letter frames this as adaptation, not abandonment: "We have no intention of investing in anything other than good businesses..." Buys listed: AppLovin, GE Vernova, Legrand, Mastercard, Netflix, Nextpower, Sage, TJX, TSMC, Uber, Veeva Systems, Yum! Brands. Exits/partial exits: Atlas Copco, Coloplast, EssilorLuxottica, Intuit, LVMH, Magnum Ice Cream, Mettler-Toledo, Nike, Novo Nordisk, Otis, Unilever, Wolters Kluwer, Zoetis.

corrections: Date the Expansión interview 3 November 2025 (Roberto Casado, Expansión), not December 2025. December 7, 2025 is only the Acquirer's Multiple repost date. Cite Fundsmith's own reproduction (fundsmith.eu / fundsmith.co.uk news item 6539) or expansion.com/mercados/2025/11/03/6904bb30e5fdea145f8b459b.html.

Change turnover from "~52%" to "51.8%", citing Appendix 1 of the Fundsmith Equity Fund Semi-Annual Letter to Shareholders 2026 (July 2026). If space allows, note the letter's own body text rounds it to "51%", and that comparable figures were 12.7% (FY2025) and 3.2% (FY2024).

When quoting "-2.9% vs +11.2%", specify the share class and currency explicitly: T Class Accumulation shares, net of fees, sterling; comparator is the MSCI World Index (£ Net). Also note the letter's own caveat that the Fund "is not managed with reference to any benchmark; the above comparators are provided for information purposes only."

When using the "30 year high / more extreme than late 1999" line, specify what the underlying chart actually measures: a Bloomberg chart titled "Momentum Is Showing Record Outperformance" plotting MSCI US Momentum QoQ vs MSCI US QoQ in percentage points, with the sample starting in 1995. It is a US-only, quarter-over-quarter relative-return spread, and "30 year" is the full length of the plotted sample rather than an independently chosen lookback. Do not render it as a general or global statement about momentum.

Present the Nov 2025 ">50%" figures as Smith's own unsourced assertions with an unstated denominator, and flag that the numbers are not internally consistent: the same speaker says ">50% of assets" and "less than 10% of funds ... now more than 50%" in the same interview, then writes "AUM in index funds is now >60%" in the July 2026 letter eight months later. Do not present any of these as a sourced market-share statistic.

Attribute the letter's UK statistics (Vanguard UK All Share tracker +66% over five years vs average UK equity fund +32%; "12 of the top 20 performers over five years are trackers"; "Half of Vanguard's FTSE 100 tracker is held in just 10 stocks") to Simon Evan-Cook, 'Victory for Passive! 22 thoughts and questions', Wealth Yourself Substack, April 2026, which Smith explicitly credits — not to Fundsmith's own research. They are unverified in this pass.
newContradictions: Smith's own index-share number is unstable and undefined: ">50% of assets" (Expansión, Nov 2025), "less than 10% of funds ... now more than 50%" (same interview, different denominator), and "whilst AUM in index funds is now >60%" (July 2026 letter, p.3) — three different figures in eight months with no stated geography, asset class, or numerator/denominator. Any article using him as a source for the size of indexing is building on sand.

The July 2026 letter attributes to Cboe Global Markets the claim that active funds were "80% of trades in the 1990s" and are "now down to just 10%" of trades. I did not verify this and could not locate the Cboe publication. The familiar "active managers are ~10% of trading volume" statistic is normally sourced to JPMorgan (Kolanovic, 2017), not Cboe. Treat the attribution as unverified; it needs its own verification pass before use.

Factual error inside the primary letter, p.5: "In 2007–08, the S&P fell 57% in five months." The ~57% peak-to-trough decline ran from the 9 Oct 2007 close (1,565.15) to the 9 Mar 2009 close (676.53) — roughly 17 months, not five, and it extended into 2009 rather than ending in 2008. The article should not repeat this premise, and if it quotes the adjoining "Next time round, it would not surprise me if it accomplished this in five days" line it should note the comparison rests on a misstated historical fact.

Letter p.3 arithmetic/framing slip: US market five-year total return 83% (USD) vs average US-investing open-ended equity fund 59% is stated as "index funds outperformed active funds on average by 24%". That is 24 percentage points, not 24 percent, and the comparison is an index against a fund average with no style, cap-size or survivorship controls.

The central rhetorical tension, well documented in contemporaneous coverage (interactive investor, Trustnet, Forbes, valueandopportunity, July 2026): Smith forecasts that the passive-led momentum market will "end badly" while simultaneously adding momentum to his own process and running record 51.8% turnover. Trustnet/Fairview's Ben Yearsley pushed back that calling successful rivals momentum chasers "feels a bit disingenuous". This is a credibility qualifier the article should carry, not a factual error.
reasoning:
I reached both primary documents verbatim, not secondary reproductions.

(1) Primary letter: downloaded https://www.fundsmith.co.uk/media/lfhpxi1x/fundsmith-equity-fund-semi-annual-letter-to-shareholders-2026.pdf directly via curl (WebFetch 403'd; a browser user-agent worked), 1.89MB PDF, extracted with pdftotext -layout to /private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-cissychen-design/0f8bdcde-3464-42f4-af17-1552808c31d6/scratchpad/v9_fs.txt. Every (b) and (c) quote was checked against that text. I also ran pdfimages to extract the momentum chart on p.3 and read the image, because the chart caption is not in the text layer and the \"30 year high\" sentence has no textual definition of what is being measured — the chart turns out to be MSCI US Momentum QoQ vs MSCI US QoQ, 1995 onward, which materially narrows the claim (US-only, quarterly spread, sample-length lookback).

(2) Primary interview: fundsmith.co.uk 403'd, but fundsmith.eu serves the same news item (6539) in both English and Spanish and returns 200 to curl. Both language versions carry the dateline \"Monday, 3 November 2025\" / \"lunes, 3 de noviembre de 2025\", byline Roberto Casado / Expansión, and a link to the original at expansion.com/mercados/2025/11/03/. I read the full Spanish and English Q&A. Both English sentences in claim (a) appear verbatim in Fundsmith's own English rendering and correspond exactly to the Spanish. The denominator switch (activos → fondos) is present in the Spanish original, so it is not a translation artifact. The \"Dec 2025\" dating in our sourcing traces to the Acquirer's Multiple repost of December 7, 2025.

(3) Cross-checks: interactive investor's 14 July 2026 piece independently reports -2.9% vs +11.2% MSCI World, record 51.8% turnover, and prior-year turnover of 12.7% (2025) and 3.2% (2024). Searches for later corrections, retractions or disputes of the letter's figures up to August 2026 turned up commentary and criticism (Trustnet, Forbes, valueandopportunity, evidenceinvestor) but no correction of the numbers.

Nothing was left unreachable in this claim group. The only substantive misses in our sourcing were the interview date and the turnover precision; both are fixable without weakening the article's use of Smith as a named-critic exhibit.

What remains uncertain and is NOT covered by this verdict: the letter's Cboe \"10% of trades\" attribution, its \">60% AUM\" figure, the Evan-Cook UK statistics, and the Vanguard/US five-year return comparisons. I verified none of those and they should not ride into the article on the strength of this pass. I also flag that the letter contains a plain historical error (S&P \"fell 57% in five months\") sitting immediately next to a line the secondary sources like to quote.

itemVerdicts.item: Burry Sept 2019 Bloomberg EMAIL interview: "And now passive investing has removed price discovery from the equity markets... This is very much like the bubble in synthetic asset-backed CDOs before the Great Financial Crisis"

And now passive investing has removed price discovery from the equity markets.
