itemVerdicts.item: (b) falling indexing costs reduce index price efficiency while raising relative price efficiency of individual stocks
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, lines 84-86: 'As indexing costs fall, and indexing increases, price efficiency of the index as a whole falls, while the relative price efficiency of individual stocks increases.'

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Chabakauri & Rytchkov JFE 2021 — indexing decreases market volatility
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed repeatedly and consistently across the paper (abstract line 26-27: 'Overall, indexing decreases market volatility but has an ambiguous effect on the correlations'; also lines 103, 133, 884, 967, 4882). Venue confirmed: Journal of Financial Economics 141(1), pp. 195-216, 2021 (ScienceDirect/EconPapers listing matches header in cr.txt exactly).

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Chabakauri & Rytchkov makes no informativeness claim
itemVerdicts.note: Grepped the full 7738-line extracted text for the substring 'informativ' (case-insensitive): zero matches anywhere in the paper. This confirms the fabrication-warning example in the task (a summarizer previously invented an informativeness claim for this paper) is indeed false, and the claim group's statement that CR makes no such claim is correct.

corrections: Garleanu & Pedersen (RAPS 2022): the passive-investing-cost result is Proposition 7, not 'result (5).' Verbatim (gp.txt line 1503): 'As the cost of passive investing kp = fp decreases, the overall asset price inefficiency (η) increases and the macro-inefficiency η_βv increases by more than the total micro-inefficiency (η − η_βv) as long as n is not too small.'

Garleanu & Pedersen (RAPS 2022): the information-cost result is Proposition 6, not 'result (4).' Verbatim (gp.txt line 1483): 'When the cost of information k decreases, overall asset price inefficiency η decreases and the macro-inefficiency η_βv decreases by more than the total micro-inefficiency (η − η_βv) as long as n is not too small.' (Note: the paper's own Propositions 4 and 5 are different, unrelated results — the macro-vs-micro-efficiency existence result and an APT large-n limiting result — so the article should not use '(4)'/'(5)' as if renumbering the paper's propositions.)

The phrase 'the two forces coexisted over the last 25 years so the net prediction is ambiguous' does not appear in and is not directly asserted by Garleanu & Pedersen; it should be attributed as the article's own synthesis of Propositions 6 and 7, not presented as the paper's stated conclusion. The paper does note the info-cost decline aligns with '1980s and 1990s' trends and the passive-cost decline with '2000s'/'past decades' trends (gp.txt lines 162-173), which is legitimate support for the synthesis, but the 'ambiguous net prediction' framing itself is the article's inference.
reasoning:
Checked all three papers against local verbatim extractions in the scratchpad, then cross-checked publication venues/years via WebSearch against Oxford Academic / ScienceDirect / IDEAS-RePEc listings.

(a) gp.txt is the authors' own published-version PDF text (confirmed via its own citation line and cross-checked: RAPS Vol 12, Issue 2, pp.389-446, June 2022, DOI raab020 — matches academic.oup.com/raps/article/12/2/389/6350496). Grepped for 'Result [0-9]' — zero hits; the paper only labels numbered claims as 'Proposition N.' The substantive content the claim group attributes to '(4)' and '(5)' is correct in direction and magnitude language ('especially macro') but the actual proposition numbers are 6 (information costs) and 7 (cost of passive investing) — confirmed by reading the full proposition text verbatim at lines 1483 and 1503. The 'two forces coexisted / net ambiguous' framing is not a quoted or paraphrased line from the paper — it's a reasonable synthesis but should not be presented as sourced. AQR Principal disclosure is present verbatim in the paper's author footnote and independently confirmed via web search of AQR's own leadership page and LinkedIn posts describing Pedersen as 'Principal at AQR' since 2009.

(b) bondgarcia.txt fully confirms every sub-claim verbatim: strategic complements (line 62) with the explicit footnote contrasting Grossman-Stiglitz strategic substitutability (lines 69-72); the self-reinforcing/no-restoring-force framing is the paper's own posed question and answer (lines 51-54); uninformed-trader welfare gains stated in both abstract and body (lines 15, 55-56); and the index-vs-relative-stock price efficiency split stated verbatim (lines 84-86). Venue/year (RFS 35(7):3175-3230, July 2022) confirmed via IDEAS RePEc and Oxford Academic listings — note the local PDF is labeled 'This draft: April 2019' (a working-paper version), but the actual published RFS version matches on title/authors/DOI family, and I did not find any indication the cited results changed between the 2019 working draft and 2022 publication.

(c) cr.txt confirms 'indexing decreases market volatility' is stated repeatedly and unambiguously throughout the paper (abstract and multiple numerical-results sections). A full-text grep for 'informativ' returned zero matches anywhere in the 7738-line extraction, directly falsifying the fabricated informativeness claim the task warns about and confirming the claim group's characterization is accurate. Venue (JFE 141(1):195-216, 2021) confirmed via ScienceDirect/EconPapers.

I found no post-publication corrections, errata, or contradicting replications for any of the three papers through targeted web searches (search for corrections/errata 2023-2025 returned nothing relevant).

Net verdict: CORRECTED rather than HOLDS solely because of the Proposition-numbering error in sub-claim (a) — the substance is right but the specific labels '(4)' and '(5)' are wrong (should be Propositions 6 and 7), and the '25 years / net ambiguous' framing is presented as if sourced from the paper when it is the article's own synthesis. Sub-claims (b) and (c) both fully HOLD verbatim.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Published AER abstract: strategic reaction counteracts two-thirds of the initial change; rise of passive over last 20 years made demand for individual stocks 11 percent more inelastic
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim from the published PDF (scratchpad hhl_aer.txt, header 'American Economic Review 2025, 115(3): 975-1018 https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20230505') and independently from the AEA landing page: 'However, this strategic reaction only counteracts two-thirds of the impact of the initial change in behavior. In light of these estimates, the rise in passive investing over the last 20 years has made the demand for individual stocks 11 percent more inelastic.' Conclusion restates it: 'Strategic responses compensate only two-thirds of the effect of changes in investor behavior on the aggregate demand for a stock.' No erratum/corrigendum found on the AEA page or in search as of 2026-08.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) 2022 working paper said 15% and an offset of 60%; revised through refereeing; secondary sources still quote 15%
itemVerdicts.note: Both WP numbers confirmed verbatim (scratchpad hhl.txt, dated 'March 3, 2022'): abstract 'This reaction reduces the equilibrium consequences of changes in individual behavior by 60%' and '...more inelastic aggregate demand curves for individual stocks, by about 15%'; body: 'competition is strong enough to compensate about 60% of the direct effect'. Secondary-source persistence confirmed verbatim on the authors' own school's research brief (anderson-review.ucla.edu): 'They suggest that the approximately 30% increase in passive investors over the last 20 years has led to a decrease in market competitiveness by 15%.' and 'Their research suggests that active investors only adjusted enough to make up for 50% of the fall in competition caused by increased passive investing.' TWO caliber fixes: (1) WRONG to say 'the numbers were revised down' — only the headline elasticity figure fell (15%->11%); the strategic offset was revised UP (60% -> two-thirds, i.e. ~67%), consistent with chi rising from 2.15/2.2 to 2.97. RIGHT: 'the headline figure was revised down from 15% to 11%, while the estimated offset rose from 60% to two-thirds.' (2) The 2022 WP was internally inconsistent: its own quantitative section computes '40.6% x 32% = 13%', not 15%, so the 15% lives in the WP abstract/intro only. Note also an earlier circulating version behind the UCLA brief used a ~50% offset.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) The object is the micro elasticity of demand for individual stocks, not the aggregate market elasticity (Gabaix-Koijen's object)
itemVerdicts.note: Directly supported by footnote 37 of the published paper, verbatim: 'Importantly, the elasticity that we measure is for individual stocks, that is, to the relative price of different stocks. It is possible that passive institutions contribute to the elasticity of the aggregate demand for stocks. Neither our model nor any other empirical model to our knowledge accommodates simultaneously these different levels of aggregation.' The paper also separates itself from GK in the lit review: 'Gabaix and Koijen (2020) estimate the aggregate demand for stocks. Our key innovation on that front is to incorporate strategic interactions between investors.' TRAP to flag for the article: HHL's own term 'aggregate elasticity' (epsilon_agg,k) means aggregated across INVESTORS in a given stock k, i.e. still a stock-level object — it does not mean market-level, and quoting HHL's phrase 'aggregate demand elasticity' without that gloss is what produces the category error.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) pass-through ~= 0.33
itemVerdicts.note: Published eq. (28): '1/(1 + chi|Active_k|) = 1/(1 + 3 x 0.68) = 33%', using the sample-average active share of 68 percent; intro: 'we find this pass-through to be about 0.33.' Robustness footnote 55: pass-through 29% at the 81% active share (2001), 36.1% at 59% (2020); across Table 2 rows 2-14 it ranges 31% (chi=3.27) to 39% (chi=2.3). Reduced-form check: 'we find a pass-through of about a third irrespective of whether we include stock or date fixed effects or even instrumenting for passive investing using index inclusions.' (WP value was 0.406.)

itemVerdicts.item: (d) active share of 13F-institution AUM fell 81%->59% (a 32% drop; 0.33x32%~=11%)
itemVerdicts.note: The 81->59 numbers and the arithmetic are right; the DENOMINATOR is wrong. WRONG: 'active share of 13F-institution AUM.' RIGHT: it is the fraction of each stock's MARKET CAPITALIZATION held by active investors, reported as the median across stocks — Figure 5 notes verbatim: 'Figure 5 reports the fraction of active investors according to our model. For each stock, we compute the ratio of total position of active investors and the market capitalization. We report the median across stocks.' Figure 5 endpoints are labeled 81.4% and 59.5%. 'Active' is model-defined (investors with non-zero estimated elasticity in a Koijen-Yogo system), not a fund-label classification, and 13F filers are only ~80% of market cap. Text confirmed: 'The decline from 81 percent to 59 percent corresponds to a 32 percent drop, leading to elasticities lowered by 33% x 32% = 11%.' Secondary caliber note: the '32 percent drop' is a LOG change (ln(59/81) = -0.32); the simple relative decline is 27% (22 percentage points off an 81% base). The paper itself writes 32%, so quoting 32% is faithful, but do not gloss it as '22pp = 32% of the base.' The paper's complementary framing: 'the share of passive strategies has grown by 22 percentage points from 19 percent to 41 percent over the last 20 years.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d) narrower passive-MF+ETF measure (+15pp of market cap over 30 years) gives only 6.3%
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'Their fraction of total market capitalization has increased by 15 percentage points in the last 30 years. Starting from a baseline of 81 percent of active investors, this change represents a 19 percent drop in the total fraction of active investors. With our pass-through of 0.33, this increase in passive investing by mutual funds reduces elasticities by 6.3 percent.' (WP counterpart: same 15pp/19%, but pass-through 0.4 and result 8%.)

itemVerdicts.item: (d) price impact of buying $1 of a stock rises from ~$2.5 to ~$2.8
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'Translating the elasticities into price multipliers, this implies that the rise in passive investing causes an increase in the price impact of buying $1 of a stock roughly from $2.5 to $2.8.' Note the 2022 WP said '$2.5 to $2.9' — if the article cites $2.9 anywhere it is quoting the superseded version. This is a stock-level price multiplier, NOT Gabaix-Koijen's aggregate market multiplier of ~5.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) data = 13F filings 2001-2020ish
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'We obtain portfolio holdings data from the 13F filings to the SEC from 2001 to 2020... We find that collectively the holdings reported in the 13F filings account for 80 percent of the total stock market capitalization.' Table 2 notes give the estimation window as 2001:I-2020:IV; stock data from CRSP 1999-2020. Quarterly frequency; 13F threshold $100 million AUM; investment universe = stocks held at any point in the prior three years (Koijen-Yogo convention).

itemVerdicts.item: Adjudication: is the strategic-response parameter chi ~= 2 or ~= 3 in the published paper?
itemVerdicts.note: chi ~= 3 is the PUBLISHED number. Table 2 row 1 (baseline): chi = 2.97, SE 0.47; text: 'The estimated value of the degree of strategic response is chi = 2.97'; the pass-through calculation uses 'chi = 3'; Table 2 robustness rows span 2.30-3.27 (rows 15-16, which drop the instruments, collapse to 0.04 and 0.63 and are not the baseline). chi ~= 2 belongs to the 2022 WP: 'The average value of the competition parameter is chi = 2.2' and the WP pass-through uses 'chi = 2.15' (its stylized example rounds to 'competition chi of 2'). So a source reporting chi~2 is citing the working paper, not the AER article.

corrections: Replace 'the active share of 13F-institution AUM fell from 81% to 59%' with: 'the fraction of each stock's market capitalization held by active investors — model-defined as investors with non-zero estimated demand elasticity, median across stocks — fell from 81.4% in 2001 to 59.5% in 2020 (Haddad, Huebner & Loualiche 2025, Figure 5).' The denominator is stock market cap, not 13F assets under management, and 'active' is an estimated-elasticity classification, not a fund label.

Do not say the working-paper numbers were 'revised down' as a set. Only the headline fell (15% -> 11%); the strategic offset was revised UP, from 60% in the 2022 working paper to two-thirds in the AER version — a consequence of the estimated chi rising from 2.15/2.2 to 2.97. Correct phrasing: 'the headline effect was revised down from about 15% to 11%, while the estimated strategic offset rose from 60% to two-thirds.'

If the article states the estimated strategic-response parameter, use chi = 2.97 (rounded to 3 in the paper's own pass-through calculation, SE 0.47, robustness range 2.30-3.27). chi ~= 2.15-2.2 is the superseded 2022 working-paper estimate; citing it as the paper's estimate misattributes the working paper to the AER article.
Cite the price-impact translation as '$2.5 to $2.8' (published). '$2.5 to $2.9' is the 2022 working-paper figure and must not be attributed to the AER version.

When quoting the '32 percent drop' in the active share, keep the paper's own wording rather than deriving it: it is a log change, ln(59/81) = -0.32. The simple relative decline of a 22-percentage-point fall off an 81% base is 27%, so do not present '22pp' and '32%' as the same arithmetic.

When quoting HHL's phrase 'aggregate demand elasticity', gloss it as aggregated across investors within a single stock. The paper's footnote 37 states verbatim: 'Importantly, the elasticity that we measure is for individual stocks, that is, to the relative price of different stocks. It is possible that passive institutions contribute to the elasticity of the aggregate demand for stocks. Neither our model nor any other empirical model to our knowledge accommodates simultaneously these different levels of aggregation.' The 11% therefore says nothing about Gabaix-Koijen's market-level multiplier.

If the article asserts that secondary sources still quote 15%, it may cite the UCLA Anderson Review brief, which as of this check still reads verbatim: 'They suggest that the approximately 30% increase in passive investors over the last 20 years has led to a decrease in market competitiveness by 15%' and 'Their research suggests that active investors only adjusted enough to make up for 50% of the fall in competition caused by increased passive investing' — note this brief carries a 50% offset, i.e. it tracks an even earlier version than the 2022 working paper's 60%.
newContradictions: The 2022 working paper is internally inconsistent with itself: its abstract and introduction say 'by about 15%', but its own Section 5.1 computes '40.6% x 32% = 13%'. Any article that says 'the working paper said 15%' is quoting the WP abstract, not its arithmetic.

The published paper's headline 11% and the reduced-form robustness check both rest on treating the passive share as a single aggregate shifter. Behmaram (working paper, April 2026, pouyabehmaram.com/papers/main_v16.pdf) states that HHL 'treats the passive share as a single aggregate variable and does not include a stock-level passive ownership measure in the demand equation', and reports that adding a stock-level index-ownership measure lowers measured aggregate elasticity from 0.240 to 0.198 (17.5%). This is an unpublished working paper that extends rather than overturns HHL — do not cite it as a refutation, and do not cite its numbers as settled.

The paper's own average stock-level elasticity falls from 0.41 to 0.27 over 2001-2020 (Figure 6 discussion) — a ~34% decline, far larger than the 11% attributed causally to passive investing. The paper attributes the remainder to changes in the investor-specific component of active investors' elasticity ('developments in computing power and access to big data'). An article that presents the 11% as explaining the observed inelasticity trend overstates it; 11% is the isolated passive-investing counterfactual, not the total realized change.
reasoning:
I read the published AER version directly, not a summary. The scratchpad contains both versions: hhl.txt is the 2022 working paper (dated 'March 3, 2022'), and hhl_aer.txt / hhl_aer.pdf is the published article, whose first line reads 'American Economic Review 2025, 115(3): 975-1018 https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20230505' with running heads 'VOL. 115 NO. 3 HADDAD ET AL.'. I cross-checked the abstract against the AEA article landing page, which returned the identical text and confirmed vol. 115 no. 3, pp. 975-1018, March 2025, with no erratum or corrigendum listed; a targeted search for a correction notice on that DOI found none up to 2026-08.

Every (d) sub-number was located verbatim in the published text: pass-through eq. (28) '1/(1 + 3 x 0.68) = 33%'; 'The decline from 81 percent to 59 percent corresponds to a 32 percent drop, leading to elasticities lowered by 33% x 32% = 11%'; 'an increase in the price impact of buying $1 of a stock roughly from $2.5 to $2.8'; the narrower measure '15 percentage points in the last 30 years... a 19 percent drop... reduces elasticities by 6.3 percent'; data '13F filings to the SEC from 2001 to 2020' covering '80 percent of the total stock market capitalization', estimated 2001:I-2020:IV.

The one real error is the denominator on 81->59. Figure 5's note states the measure is the ratio of active investors' total position to the stock's market capitalization, median across stocks (endpoints labeled 81.4% and 59.5%), and 'active' is model-defined as non-zero estimated elasticity in a Koijen-Yogo system. Describing this as an 'active share of 13F-institution AUM' is wrong on both the denominator (market cap, not AUM) and the classification method, and it is the sort of slip that would let a reader reconcile it with fund-flow statistics that are not the same object. I also flagged the '32 percent' as a log change, since the arithmetic 22pp/81% gives 27%.

On (b), both WP figures check out verbatim, but the direction language needs care: the offset went up (60% -> two-thirds) while the headline went down (15% -> 11%), both driven by chi rising from 2.15/2.2 to 2.97. I confirmed the WP's own body computes 13%, not 15%. For 'secondary sources still quote 15%' I did not rely on any fetch summary: I curled the UCLA Anderson Review page and grepped the stripped text, recovering the two sentences verbatim (15% and a 50% offset), which is a stronger version of the claim since that brief tracks an even earlier draft.

On (c), footnote 37 is decisive and quoted exactly. I also note the naming trap: HHL's own 'aggregate elasticity' epsilon_agg,k aggregates across investors within one stock, so quoting that phrase without a gloss is precisely how the GK conflation happens.

On the chi adjudication, Table 2 row 1 of the published paper gives chi = 2.97 (SE 0.47) and the text rounds to 'chi = 3'; the WP gives an average of 2.2 and uses 2.15. Uncertain / not settled: I did not independently re-derive any estimate, and I could not fetch the Harding Loevner piece (HTTP 403), so I cannot say whether that particular secondary source quotes 15% or 11%. Behmaram (2026) is an unpublished working paper I read only via the local extraction and a search result, so I treat its numbers as unverified against a primary reading.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Published AER abstract: strategic reaction counteracts two-thirds of the initial change; rise of passive over last 20 years made demand for individual stocks 11% MORE INELASTIC
itemVerdicts.note: Verified twice, independently: (1) local scratchpad file hhl_aer.txt (extraction of hhl_aer.pdf, header reads 'American Economic Review 2025, 115(3): 975–1018 / https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20230505'); (2) the AEA article page for 10.1257/aer.20230505, which returns the identical abstract. Verbatim: 'However, this strate-gic reaction only counteracts two-thirds of the impact of the initial change in behavior. In light of these estimates, the rise in passive investing over the last 20 years has made the demand for individual stocks 11 percent more inelastic. (JEL G11, G14, G23, G41)'. Citation March 2025, vol. 115 no. 3, pp. 975–1018 confirmed on the AEA page.

itemVerdicts.item: (b1) The 2022 working paper said 15% and an offset of 60%
itemVerdicts.note: Local hhl.txt is the Haddad–Huebner–Loualiche WP dated 'March 3, 2022'. Abstract verbatim: 'This reaction reduces the equilibrium consequences of changes in individual behavior by 60%.' and '...has led to substantially more inelastic aggregate demand curves for individual stocks, by about 15%.' WP body: 'we find this pass-trough to be about 0.4' [sic, typo in original] vs published 0.33.

itemVerdicts.item: (b2) Secondary sources still quote 15%
itemVerdicts.note: Concrete instance retrieved and read verbatim: T. Rowe Price, 'Why passive flows and inelastic markets don't mix' (August 2024, Boothe & Subedi): 'what Haddad et al. found was that the remaining active managers do not respond by enough—and that the growth in passive has led to markets becoming 15% more inelastic over the past 20 years.' Note this compounds TWO errors: the stale 15% AND 'markets' instead of 'individual stocks'. Counter-examples exist too: Swedish House of Finance's own 2024 explainer says 'passive funds has made stock demand 11% more inelastic', and Apollo Academy (Nov 2024) already used chi=2.97 / 33% pass-through / 'a change of 11%'.

itemVerdicts.item: (b3) 'The number was revised down through refereeing'
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG (as a documented fact): that refereeing caused the revision. RIGHT: what is documented is only that the March 2022 WP reported 15%/60%/chi=2.15 and the published AER version reports 11%/two-thirds/chi=2.97, and that the AER version thanks 'the editor and three anonymous referees'. No source states the referees drove the change; the estimate had already moved to chi=2.97 in versions circulating by Nov 2024 (Apollo Academy cites 2.97 and 11%). Safe phrasing: 'revised down between the 2022 working paper and the 2025 published version.'

itemVerdicts.item: (c) The object is the MICRO elasticity of demand for individual stocks, not the aggregate market elasticity (Gabaix–Koijen's object)
itemVerdicts.note: HHL's estimand is epsilon_agg,k — indexed by STOCK k. Figure 6 note: 'Figure 6 traces out the distribution of aggregate elasticity ε_agg,k over time. The bold line represents the aver-age elasticity across stocks for each year.' Figure 5 note: 'For each stock, we compute the ratio of total position of active investors and the market capitalization. We report the median across stocks.' Gabaix–Koijen state the opposite object in gk.txt: 'Our paper is about the macro elasticity, in contrast to the micro elasticity' and 'This paper is about the macro elasticity of the market (that is, how the aggregate stock market's...)'. CAVEAT for the writer: HHL's own term is 'aggregate elasticity', meaning aggregated ACROSS INVESTORS for one stock — do not write 'not the aggregate elasticity', write 'not the aggregate MARKET elasticity'.

itemVerdicts.item: (d1) pass-through ≈ 0.33
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'Taking the average across dates for the share of active investors, 68 percent, and for the degree of strategic response, χ = 3, we find a value of the pass-through of 1/(1 + χ|Active_k|) = 1/(1 + 3 × 0.68) = 33%.' Also intro: 'Empirically, we find this pass-through to be about 0.33.' Footnote 55: pass-through 29% at 81% active, 36.1% at 59% active; across robustness rows it ranges 31% (χ=3.27) to 39% (χ=2.3).

itemVerdicts.item: (d2) 'Active share of 13F-institution AUM fell 81%→59%'
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: describing 81%→59% as the active share of 13F-institution AUM. RIGHT: it is the fraction of ACTIVE INVESTORS measured as, per stock, the total position of active investors divided by that stock's MARKET CAPITALIZATION, reported as the median across stocks — Figure 5 is labeled 81.4% (2000:IV) and 59.5% (2020:IV). Two further specifics: (i) 'active vs passive' is defined by ESTIMATED DEMAND ELASTICITY near zero inside a Koijen–Yogo demand system, not by fund labels ('we measure the total quantity of passive investors as investors with an elasticity of zero in a Koijen-Yogo demand system'); 13F filings themselves 'account for 80 percent of the total stock market capitalization', so the denominator is strictly larger than 13F AUM. (ii) Equivalently the paper states 'the share of passive strategies has grown by 22 percentage points from 19 percent to 41 percent over the last 20 years.'

Verbatim: 'The decline from 81 percent to 59 percent corresponds to a 32 percent drop, leading to elasticities lowered by 33% × 32% = 11%.' Writer caveat: 32% is the LOG change (ln(59.5/81.4) = −31%); the arithmetic drop is 27%. Since the paper itself prints 32%, quoting 32% is fine, but do not invite the reader to recompute 59/81.

itemVerdicts.item: (d4) Narrower passive-MF+ETF measure (+15pp of market cap over 30 years) gives only 6.3%
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'we look at a narrower measure of the rise in passive investing centered around the assets under management of passive mutual funds and ETFs. Their fraction of total market capitalization has increased by 15 percentage points in the last 30 years. Starting from a baseline of 81 percent of active investors, this change represents a 19 percent drop in the total fraction of active investors. With our pass-through of 0.33, this increase in passive investing by mutual funds reduces elasticities by 6.3 percent.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d5) Price impact of buying $1 of a stock rises from ~$2.5 to ~$2.8
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'Translating the elasticities into price multipliers, this implies that the rise in passive investing causes an increase in the price impact of buying $1 of a stock roughly from $2.5 to $2.8.' Internally consistent: 2.5/0.89 ≈ 2.81.

itemVerdicts.item: (d6) Data = 13F filings 2001–2020ish
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'We obtain portfolio holdings data from the 13F filings to the SEC from 2001 to 2020... built from SEC EDGAR following Backus, Conlon, and Sinkinson (2021, 2020)... institutions with more than $100 million of assets under management... holdings reported in the 13F filings account for 80 percent of the total stock market capitalization.' Table 2 note: 'estimates of χ across dates (2001:I–2020:IV)'. So exactly 2001Q1–2020Q4 — no 'ish' needed.

itemVerdicts.item: chi ≈ 2 (WP) vs chi ≈ 3 — which is in the PUBLISHED paper?
itemVerdicts.note: PUBLISHED AER (2025): baseline χ = 2.97, rounded to χ = 3 in the pass-through calculation. Verbatim: 'the degree of strategic response is χ = 2.97. We construct GMM standard errors...'; 'A degree of strategic response of 2.97 implies substantial reactions at the indi-vidual level'; abstract-section text 'In Section IV, we estimated the degree of strategic response and found that χ = 3.' Robustness range across Table 2 rows 2–14: 2.30 to 3.27. WORKING PAPER (March 2022): 'The average value of the competition parameter is χ = 2.2', baseline used in the pass-through calc 'χ = 2.15', with 'value of χ is always between 1.91 and 2.46'. So χ≈2 is the WP and χ≈3 (2.97) is the published paper — as the claim asserts.

itemVerdicts.item: Post-publication corrections, errata, or replications through 2026-08
itemVerdicts.note: Searched AEA journal issue listings and general web through 2026-08 and found no erratum, corrigendum, or published comment on aer.20230505; an openICPSR replication package (project 208371) exists. This is a negative search result, not a verified absence — I could not reach any authoritative errata index for AER, so treat 'no correction exists' as unconfirmed.

corrections: Replace any description of the 81%→59% series as 'active share of 13F-institution AUM'. The correct description: HHL's fraction of ACTIVE investors is, for each stock, the total position of active investors divided by that stock's MARKET CAPITALIZATION, reported as the median across stocks — 81.4% in 2000:IV falling to 59.5% in 2020:IV. 'Active' vs 'passive' is assigned by estimated demand elasticity near zero inside a Koijen–Yogo demand system, not by fund label; 13F filings cover only about 80% of total market cap, so 13F AUM is not the denominator. Equivalent published phrasing: 'the share of passive strategies has grown by 22 percentage points from 19 percent to 41 percent over the last 20 years.'

Do not assert that the 15%→11% revision happened 'through refereeing' — no source documents that causal chain. Say only: the March 2022 working paper reported 15% (offset 60%, χ=2.15) and the published AER version reports 11% (offset two-thirds, χ=2.97); by late 2024 the 2.97/11% figures were already circulating (Apollo Academy, Nov 2024).

When contrasting HHL with Gabaix–Koijen, write 'aggregate MARKET elasticity' (or 'macro elasticity') for GK's object. HHL's own term for their estimand is 'aggregate elasticity' (ε_agg,k) — aggregated across investors for a single stock. Writing 'HHL do not measure the aggregate elasticity' would contradict the paper's own vocabulary; the correct contrast is micro/cross-sectional (HHL) vs macro/market-level (GK, who state 'Our paper is about the macro elasticity, in contrast to the micro elasticity').

If quoting '32 percent drop' in active share, note it is a log change (the paper's own figure); the arithmetic decline from 81.4% to 59.5% is 27%. Quote the paper's sentence rather than showing the arithmetic.

State the sample as 13F filings 2001:I–2020:IV (exact), not '2001–2020ish'. Also worth stating: 13F holdings cover ~80% of total US stock market capitalization, and each institution files a single 13F, so the method cannot separate active from passive funds inside the same institution (the paper says so in footnote 51).

Give χ as 2.97 in the published paper (the paper rounds it to 3 when computing the pass-through), with a robustness range of 2.30–3.27; χ≈2.15 (average 2.2, range 1.91–2.46) belongs to the 2022 working paper only.

If citing the secondary literature's 15% figure as an example of stale quotation, the verifiable instance is T. Rowe Price, 'Why passive flows and inelastic markets don't mix' (August 2024): 'the growth in passive has led to markets becoming 15% more inelastic over the past 20 years.' Note it compounds a second error — 'markets' rather than 'individual stocks'.

Do not conflate the 11% causal figure with the observed decline in elasticity. HHL's Figure 6 shows the average aggregate elasticity across stocks falling from 0.41 to 0.27 over 2001–2020; the 11% is the counterfactual effect attributable to the rise in passive alone. The paper's decomposition assigns a comparable role to a second, distinct force — active investors lowering their own individual-level elasticity (intensive margin) after the financial crisis — with the strategic response reversing 'around two-thirds of the decline'.
newContradictions: T. Rowe Price (Aug 2024, Boothe & Subedi, 'Why passive flows and inelastic markets don't mix') attributes to Haddad et al. that 'the growth in passive has led to markets becoming 15% more inelastic over the past 20 years' — both the stale 15% AND a population error ('markets' vs 'individual stocks'). If the article leans on practitioner write-ups, this one is unreliable on both counts.

The Swedish House of Finance's own 2024 explainer of the paper (houseoffinance.se) says the strategic reaction 'only offsets about two-thirds of the initial impact' and that passive growth 'has made stock demand 11% more inelastic' — but frames the result as 'increased volatility and less efficient pricing' and 'the stock market is less efficient'. The AER paper is more guarded: 'in the context of many models, it would lead to less informative and more volatile prices' — a conditional statement about model implications plus cross-sectional confirmation, not an unconditional finding that the market has become less efficient. Do not upgrade HHL's caliber via the press page.

Apollo Academy's Nov 2024 passive-investing paper cites HHL as '(2021)' and reproduces χ=2.97, pass-through 33%, and 11% — so it is a reliable secondary source on the numbers but cites a working-paper year. Its adjacent sentence 'A 30% decrease in ε_agg will lead to an overall 10% decrease in ε_agg' is Apollo's own rounding, not HHL's; HHL print 33% × 32% = 11%.

HHL themselves report the observed average aggregate elasticity across stocks falling 0.41 → 0.27 (Figure 6), a much larger move than the 11% passive-attributable effect, and note the 2007-onward decline is a puzzle relative to improving trading technology (citing Koijen & Yogo 2019 and Koijen, Richmond & Yogo 2023 for similar patterns). Any article using HHL to argue 'passive broke the market' must confront that most of the observed elasticity decline is NOT attributed to the extensive-margin shift to passive.
reasoning:
Reached the primary document twice over. The local file hhl_aer.txt is a text extraction of hhl_aer.pdf, whose header carries 'American Economic Review 2025, 115(3): 975–1018' and DOI 10.1257/aer.20230505 (note: hhl.pdf and hhl_aer.pdf are byte-identical, md5 0fe2742e6a99beba839a34f1b7832ecf — the PDF is the published version; the file named hhl.txt is a DIFFERENT, earlier extraction whose header reads 'March 3, 2022', i.e. the working paper, so both versions were in fact available locally). I cross-checked the published abstract against the AEA article page independently, and it matched word for word, so the local extraction is trustworthy.

Every quantitative sub-claim in (d) was checked against the extracted text, not from memory, and every one reproduces verbatim: pass-through 0.33 via 1/(1+3×0.68); 81→59 with the paper's own '32 percent drop' and '33% × 32% = 11%'; '$2.5 to $2.8'; the narrower passive-MF+ETF measure '+15 percentage points... in the last 30 years' → '6.3 percent'; 13F 2001:I–2020:IV covering 80% of market cap. The χ adjudication is unambiguous: published baseline is 2.97 (rounded to 3 for the pass-through), working paper is 2.15 (avg 2.2, range 1.91–2.46) — so χ≈3 is the published number.

The one substantive defect is a population/denominator error in the claim group's own gloss, not in the article's headline: 81.4%→59.5% is active investors' positions as a share of each stock's MARKET CAPITALIZATION (median across stocks), with active/passive assigned by estimated elasticity ≈ 0, not the active share of 13F-institution AUM. Since 13F filings cover only ~80% of market cap, the stated denominator cannot be right on its face — the measure necessarily includes a residual/household sector (the working paper explicitly refers to 'the household investor').

(c) holds, but with a terminology trap I flagged: HHL call their object 'aggregate elasticity' (aggregated across investors for one stock, ε_agg,k), which is easy to misread as GK's aggregate-market elasticity. I confirmed GK's self-description directly from gk.txt: 'Our paper is about the macro elasticity, in contrast to the micro elasticity.' So the category error the claim warns about is real, but the article must phrase the contrast as micro vs macro/market-level rather than saying HHL don't measure 'aggregate' elasticity.

(b)'s 'secondary sources still quote 15%' is verified with a document I read verbatim (T. Rowe Price, Aug 2024) after two candidate sources (etftrends.com, hardingloevner.com) returned 403 and a Nasdaq URL 404'd. I did not accept the search summarizer's characterizations; every quotation above came from text I pulled and read myself. The 'revised down through refereeing' attribution is the only place I downgraded a claim on grounds of unsupported causal attribution rather than a wrong number.

Remaining uncertainty: I could not reach an authoritative AER errata index, so 'no published correction as of 2026-08' is a negative search result only, marked unreachable rather than confirmed. I also did not open the openICPSR replication package or the Supplemental Appendix (D.3/D.4), so the precise construction of the outside asset / residual sector behind the 81.4% figure is inferred from the main-text Figure 5 note rather than read in the appendix.

itemVerdicts.item: BPS (JFE 2016): price informativeness for S&P 500 NONFINANCIAL firms rose ~60% (3-yr) and ~80% (5-yr) from 1960 to 2010
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in BPS p.626: 'price informativeness is 60% higher in 2010 than 1960 at the three-year horizon and 80% higher at the five-year horizon.' Repeated p.634: 'three-year price informativeness is about 60% higher in 2010 than in 1960... Five-year informativeness is about 80% higher.' Population verified: 'For most of the paper, we limit attention to S&P 500 nonfinancial firms'; Table 1 note: 'The sample contains all S&P 500 non-financial firms from 1960 to 2014.' Window verified: regressions run 1960-2014 but the informativeness series 'ending in 2010 because the last years for which we have three- and five-year estimates are 2009 and 2011.' The percentages come from a fitted linear time trend normalized so the intercept is the 1960 level and the slope the cumulative change, not a raw endpoint ratio.

itemVerdicts.item: BPS: the measure is b x sigma (predicted-variance of future EBIT), not R-squared
itemVerdicts.note: The b x sigma part is CONFIRMED — BPS Eq. (16): informativeness at t,h = b_{t,h} x sigma_t(log(M/A)), where sigma is the UNCONDITIONAL cross-sectional standard deviation of log(M/A) and b is the coefficient on log(M/A) in a cross-sectional regression of E_{t+h}/A_t on log(M/A), current E/A, and one-digit-SIC sector dummies. But the gloss 'predicted-variance' is WRONG: b x sigma is the SQUARE ROOT of the predicted variance. BPS: 'We compute it here with the minor modification of taking a square root, which gives meaningful units (dollars of future cash flows per dollar of current total assets).' RIGHT: 'the square root of the predicted variance of future EBIT.' Second caveat: 'not R-squared' is right about the headline measure but should not imply BPS ignore R-squared — Fig. 3 Panels E and F plot the marginal contribution of prices to regression R-squared, and it trends up too.

itemVerdicts.item: BPS footnote 2: outside the S&P 500 informativeness 'appears to decline'; comparison 'potentially misleading' due to compositional change
itemVerdicts.note: Footnote 2 verbatim: 'the composition of this sample has changed dramatically over the years (see Fama and French, 2004), making the comparison potentially misleading... Likely as a result of the compositional shift, price informativeness for firms beyond the S&P 500 appears to decline.' One omission the article should repair: the very next sentence is 'Interestingly, the decline is concentrated at the short horizon, so again there is relative improvement at the long end.' Citing the decline without that clause overstates the counter-point in the opposite direction.

itemVerdicts.item: BPS footnote 7: the FIRST circulated draft (Dec 2013 NBER WP 19728) concluded informativeness was FLAT; sign flipped after inflation adjustment, delisting correction, and adding the 5-year horizon
itemVerdicts.note: The substance is CONFIRMED verbatim, footnote 7: 'In the first circulated draft of the paper (dated December 2013), we incorrectly inferred that price informativeness had remained stable. This was due to the combined effect of three differences in methodology. First, we did not adjust for inflation... Second, we did not correct for delistings... Third, we did not consider the long five-year horizon.' Two corrections. (1) 'the FIRST circulated draft' being Dec 2013 / NBER WP 19728 is WRONG as a matter of record — I retrieved FRBNY Staff Report No. 578, October 2012 (same title, same three authors, no revision date on the NY Fed page), whose abstract already states: 'we find that the information content of market prices has not increased since 1960... We find that this measure has remained stable.' RIGHT: the flat conclusion circulated publicly at least from October 2012 (FRBNY SR 578); Dec 2013 is BPS's own footnoted date for their 'first circulated draft,' and BPS never name WP 19728 — that identification is the article's inference (NBER WP 19728 is indeed the same paper, issue date December 2013, revision date September 2015, and the abstract now posted there is the revised, informativeness-rose version). (2) 'the sign flipped' is WRONG caliber — BPS say the earlier finding was that informativeness 'had remained stable,' i.e. flat became a large increase; nothing went from negative to positive. RIGHT: 'the conclusion reversed from flat to a large increase.'

itemVerdicts.item: FMVV: informativeness fell for the market as a whole
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed in the PUBLISHED (April 18, 2021 accepted / RFS 35(7), 2022) version, Appendix E: 'although informativeness rose for the S&P 500 firms, it fell for the market as a whole.' Figure 9 caption: 'Price Informativeness is Falling (Rising) for all Public Firms (S&P 500 Firms).' Table 8 gives non-S&P 500 PINF*·Trend of -.047 (s=3) and -.048 (s=5) against base levels .046 and .056, both significant at 1%.

itemVerdicts.item: FMVV: 'eviscerated almost all of the information content' — attributed to small firms, cited to RFS 2022
itemVerdicts.note: Two errors. (1) WRONG SOURCE VERSION: the phrase does NOT appear anywhere in the published RFS version (I grepped the full accepted manuscript; zero hits). It appears only in NBER WP 26927 (April 2020) and the 2019 drafts. RIGHT attribution: Farboodi, Matray, Veldkamp & Venkateswaran, NBER WP 26927 (April 2020), sec. 1.2. (2) WRONG REFERENT: in WP 26927 the sentence is about the universe of listed firms, not small firms — 'It shows that price informativeness has fallen over time for the market as a whole... In fact, over the past 50 years, this declining trend has eviscerated almost all of the information content in prices.' RIGHT: the quote describes the whole-market/all-public-firms series, not a small-firm subsample.

itemVerdicts.item: FMVV: informativeness rose ~50% for S&P 500 firms
itemVerdicts.note: The ~50% figure is in NBER WP 26927 main text only: 'Over 1962-2010, S&P price informativeness has increased by about 50% of its original level.' That sentence is ABSENT from the published RFS version (grep for '50%' returns nothing). RIGHT for the RFS-2022 citation: 'For the S&P 500 sample, price informativeness at the 5-year horizon rose by 70% (0.026/0.038). For the non-S&P 500 firms, it fell by around 80%' (Appendix E, Table 8). ~50% corresponds to the 3-year horizon (Table 8: .016/.033 = 48%), not the 5-year. So the article must either say '~50% at the 3-year horizon' or '~70% at the 5-year horizon' and cite the matching version.

itemVerdicts.item: FMVV: size decile 1 -> 10 implies a 17-fold informativeness difference
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in BOTH versions — published RFS Appendix E: 'we also split the sample into deciles of size, and find that moving from the lowest decile to the highest decile of size implies a 17-fold increase in price informativeness (c.f. Appendix E.2).' Caliber note: this is a LEVEL gap averaged over the full 1962-2010 sample at the 5-year horizon (Figure 11 shows average PINF per size decile), not a change over time and not a trend difference.

itemVerdicts.item: FMVV: S&P-500 MEMBERSHIP per se is NOT the driver — similar-characteristics non-members look the same; cuts against a passive-flow mechanism
itemVerdicts.note: Strongly confirmed in the PUBLISHED version, twice. Main text: 'While Bai, Philippon, and Savov (2016) also noted the divergence between firms in and out of the S&P 500, we show that this is a size effect, not an index inclusion effect.' Attached footnote: '[the informativeness of stocks currently in the S&P 500 is similar to] non-S&P 500 stocks with similar characteristics. Furthermore, price informativeness trends consistently over size deciles. These results suggests that differences in asset characteristics, rather than inclusion in S&P 500 per se, is the source of the divergence.' Appendix E adds: firms never in the index but close in market cap 'exhibit a rise in price informativeness nearly identical to that of the S&P 500 firms (though the levels of price informativeness are somewhat different)' and 'In levels, price informativeness is actually higher when a firm is not in the S&P 500, than when they are in.' One honest qualifier the article should keep: the same paragraph concedes 'being part of the index does increase the level of informativeness somewhat.'

corrections: BPS's measure is the SQUARE ROOT of the predicted variance of future EBIT, not the predicted variance itself. Write it as: price informativeness = b_{t,h} x sigma_t(log(M/A)), the forecasting coefficient times the unconditional cross-sectional standard deviation of log market-cap-to-assets — which BPS obtain by 'taking a square root, which gives meaningful units (dollars of future cash flows per dollar of current total assets).'

Do not imply BPS ignore R-squared. Their headline measure is b x sigma, but Fig. 3 Panels E and F also plot the marginal contribution of prices to regression R-squared, and that series trends up as well. Say 'the headline measure is b x sigma rather than R-squared,' not 'not R-squared.'

When citing BPS footnote 2, carry the full clause. After 'price informativeness for firms beyond the S&P 500 appears to decline,' BPS immediately add: 'Interestingly, the decline is concentrated at the short horizon, so again there is relative improvement at the long end.' Omitting this overstates the outside-the-index decline.

Drop the claim that the December 2013 NBER WP 19728 was the 'first circulated draft.' An earlier public version exists: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Staff Report No. 578, October 2012, same title and authors, whose abstract already concludes flat — 'we find that the information content of market prices has not increased since 1960... We find that this measure has remained stable.' Write: 'earlier circulated versions — the October 2012 FRBNY Staff Report No. 578, and the draft BPS themselves date to December 2013 in footnote 7 — concluded informativeness had been flat.' Note also that the 2012 version forecast earnings using stock AND bond prices.

Replace 'the sign flipped' with 'the conclusion reversed.' BPS footnote 7 says they 'incorrectly inferred that price informativeness had remained stable' — flat became a large increase; no coefficient sign changed.

The phrase 'eviscerated almost all of the information content' is NOT in the published RFS 2022 article — it appears only in NBER WP 26927 (April 2020) and earlier drafts. Cite it to the working paper, or drop the quote.

Fix the referent of that quote: in WP 26927 it describes the whole-market series, not small firms. The passage reads 'price informativeness has fallen over time for the market as a whole. In fact, over the past 50 years, this declining trend has eviscerated almost all of the information content in prices.' Do not attach it to a small-firm subsample.

The '~50%' rise for S&P 500 firms is a working-paper number ('Over 1962-2010, S&P price informativeness has increased by about 50% of its original level') and is absent from the published RFS version. If citing RFS 2022, the stated figure is 70% at the 5-year horizon ('rose by 70% (0.026/0.038)'), with the corresponding non-S&P 500 series falling 'by around 80%.' At the 3-year horizon Table 8 implies ~48%. Pick a horizon and match the version.
Qualify the 17-fold decile gap: it is a level difference averaged over the full 1962-2010 sample at the 5-year horizon (RFS Appendix E / Figure 11), not a change over time.

When leaning on FMVV's informativeness numbers, carry their own disclaimer. In the published version these results are demoted to Appendix E, which opens: 'It is worth keeping in mind that these reduced-form patterns are hard to interpret because they confound changes in information with variation in other characteristics, precisely why a structural approach is necessary.' The published abstract also reframes the paper around a data measure and says 'We show how our measure differs from price informativeness.'

Keep FMVV's own qualifier on the index-membership finding: alongside 'a size effect, not an index inclusion effect,' they concede 'being part of the index does increase the level of informativeness somewhat.'
newContradictions: The published RFS 2022 version of FMVV reports that ABSOLUTE price informativeness (the Davila-Parlatore notion) 'declines across all four asset groups' — including large high-growth firms. Verbatim: 'despite more net private data processed by investors about stock-specific characteristics (higher Kj) prices actually became less accurate as signals... because the noise component of prices... grew over time and overwhelmed the rising covariance with fundamentals.' Any article using FMVV to say large-cap prices got MORE informative should note that on the alternative measure inside the same paper, they got LESS accurate.

Davila & Parlatore, 'Identifying Price Informativeness' (RFS 39(5), May 2026; NBER WP 25210) argue the BPS forecasting-price-efficiency measure does not separately identify information aggregation from fundamental volatility — b x sigma can be high because fundamental volatility is low rather than because prices aggregate more information. FMVV's published version makes the same structural point about PINF being 'contaminated by volatility and scaling terms like growth.' The BPS 60%/80% headline should not be reported as a clean measure of information aggregation without this caveat. (I read the FMVV text on this verbatim; I did not open the Davila-Parlatore published article itself, so treat the RFS 2026 volume/issue detail as secondhand.)

fmvv.txt and farboodi.txt in the scratchpad are BOTH NBER WP 26927 (April 2020) extractions, not the published RFS version — they differ in line count (3333 vs 2452) but carry the same WP text. Any prior verification in this run that cited 'RFS 2022' while grepping those files was checking the working paper. I retrieved the published/accepted manuscript separately (dated April 18, 2021) from DSpace@MIT and saved it as fmvv_rfs.pdf / fmvv_rfs.txt in the scratchpad.
reasoning:
Primary documents reached verbatim: (1) BPS, JFE 122 (2016) 625-654, full text via local bps.txt (extraction clean — headline sentences, footnotes 2, 6, 7, Eq. 15/16, Table 1 note, Data section 4.1 all legible). (2) FMVV NBER WP 26927, April 2020, via local fmvv.txt and farboodi.txt. (3) FMVV PUBLISHED/accepted manuscript dated April 18, 2021 (= RFS 35(7), 2022), retrieved fresh from DSpace@MIT bitstream and pdftotext'd to fmvv_rfs.txt — this was the decisive step, since the scratchpad only held the working paper. (4) FRBNY Staff Report No. 578, October 2012, PDF retrieved fresh from newyorkfed.org, abstract read verbatim. (5) NBER WP 19728 landing page (title, authors, issue date December 2013, revision date September 2015, current revised abstract).

BPS (a)(b)(c) all check out verbatim against the JFE text. The three defects I found are caliber, not substance: b x sigma is the square root of the predicted variance (BPS say so explicitly); 'sign flipped' overstates 'had remained stable'; and the Dec-2013-as-first-draft framing is contradicted by the October 2012 FRBNY Staff Report 578, which already published the flat conclusion. That last one is a genuine record correction the article should absorb — it strengthens rather than weakens the point, since the flat-conclusion version circulated for over a year longer than the article implies.

FMVV is where the version trap bit. Three of the article's four FMVV elements trace to language that is in the 2020 working paper but NOT the published RFS article: the 'eviscerated' quote (zero hits in the accepted manuscript) and the '~50%' S&P figure (also zero hits; the published paper says 70% at the 5-year horizon, 48% implied at 3-year). The 'eviscerated' quote is additionally misattributed to small firms when the working paper applies it to the market as a whole. The published paper also restructured the argument: price informativeness is now Appendix E with an explicit warning that the reduced-form patterns 'confound changes in information with variation in other characteristics,' and the abstract is rebuilt around a structural data measure.

The load-bearing element for the passive-bubble argument — that S&P 500 membership per se is not the driver — is the strongest-verified item in the group. It survives in the published version in two places, including the flat statement 'we show that this is a size effect, not an index inclusion effect,' plus the appendix findings that never-included lookalike firms show a nearly identical rise and that levels are actually higher when a firm is out of the index. The 17-fold decile gap is verbatim in both versions.

Remaining uncertainty: I did not open the paywalled Oxford Academic page (403) to confirm the DSpace manuscript is byte-identical to the typeset RFS article; it is the author-accepted version dated April 18, 2021, and its abstract matches the published RFS abstract as reported by search results, so I treat it as the published version. I also did not obtain the literal December 2013 NBER WP 19728 PDF (NBER serves the September 2015 revision) — the flat conclusion for the pre-publication drafts is established instead by BPS's own footnote 7 and independently by FRBNY SR 578. I did not open Davila-Parlatore's published article; the critique is reported via FMVV's own verbatim discussion plus search-result summary, and I have flagged that provenance.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Published AER abstract: strategic reaction counteracts TWO-THIRDS of the initial change; rise of passive over last 20 years made demand for individual stocks 11% MORE INELASTIC
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in two independent places: the AEA article page (aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.20230505) and the typeset AER PDF text (local hhl_aer.txt, header line 'American Economic Review 2025, 115(3): 975-1018'). Exact abstract wording: 'However, this strategic reaction only counteracts two-thirds of the impact of the initial change in behavior. In light of these estimates, the rise in passive investing over the last 20 years has made the demand for individual stocks 11 percent more inelastic.' Citation 115(3), 975-1018, March 2025 confirmed. Body echo (Sec. VA): 'the strategic response is strong enough to compensate about two-thirds of the direct effect of a rise in passive investing.' No erratum or correction found as of 2026-08.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) The 2022 working paper said 15% and an offset of 60%; number revised down; secondary sources still quote 15%
itemVerdicts.note: PARTLY RIGHT. Confirmed verbatim in the March 3, 2022 WP (local hhl.txt): abstract reads 'This reaction reduces the equilibrium consequences of changes in individual behavior by 60%' and '...has led to substantially more inelastic aggregate demand curves for individual stocks, by about 15%.' BUT: the WP's own Section 5.1 body computes a DIFFERENT number than its own abstract — 'The decline from 81% to 59% corresponds to a 32% drop, leading to elasticities lowered by 40.6%x32% = 13%' (WP intro also says 13% at one point: 'decrease in elasticities of 13%'). So the WP headline was 15% while its own arithmetic gave 13%; the article should say the WP headline figure was 15% rather than implying 15% was the WP's computed estimate. Also: the revision was NOT a cosmetic rounding — it was driven by the estimate of chi rising from 2.15 (WP) to 2.97 (published), which lowered the pass-through from 40.6% to 33%. Attributing the change specifically to 'refereeing' is an inference: neither version documents why, and the authors' page lists a first version April 2021 and a current version April 2024, so the number moved across WP revisions, not necessarily at referee request. 'Secondary sources still quote 15%' is only partly verifiable — see unreachable item.

itemVerdicts.item: (b-sub) Secondary sources still quote the 15% figure
itemVerdicts.note: Search-result snippets from ETF Trends / etfdb / Nasdaq do carry the old WP sentence ('...more inelastic aggregate demand curves for individual stocks, by 15%'), but etftrends.com returned HTTP 403 and nasdaq.com timed out, so I could not read the source pages myself and will not treat the snippet as a verified quote. Counter-datapoint I COULD verify: the most-cited secondary source in this literature, Apollo Academy's Nov 2024 'Assessing the Impact of Passive Investing over Time' (local apollo.txt), cites HHL (2021) but uses the UPDATED numbers — 'HHL estimate the degree of strategic response to be chi = 2.97', 'we get a pass-through of 33%', and 'translating to a change of 11% after strategic responses'. So the claim 'secondary sources still quote 15%' is true of some ETF-trade-press pieces but false of the leading practitioner survey; the article should not state it as a blanket claim.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) The object is the MICRO elasticity of demand for individual stocks, not the aggregate market elasticity (Gabaix-Koijen's object); conflating them is a category error
itemVerdicts.note: Directly supported by the published paper's own footnote 37 (verbatim): 'Importantly, the elasticity that we measure is for individual stocks, that is, to the relative price of different stocks. It is possible that passive institutions contribute to the elasticity of the aggregate demand for stocks. Neither our model nor any other empirical model to our knowledge accommodates simultaneously these different levels of aggregation.' The abstract likewise says 'demand for individual stocks'. Gabaix and Koijen (2020) is cited in footnote 11 precisely 'for a discussion of the role of the elasticity of aggregate demand in financial markets' — i.e. as the other object. CAUTION for the article: HHL's own label for their quantity is 'aggregate elasticity' (epsilon_agg,k), meaning aggregated ACROSS INVESTORS within one stock, not aggregated across the market. If the article quotes HHL's phrase 'aggregate demand curves for individual stocks' without that gloss, readers will make exactly the category error the article is warning about.

itemVerdicts.item: (d1) Pass-through ~= 0.33
itemVerdicts.note: Published eq. (28): 1/(1 + chi|Active_k|) = 1/(1 + 3 x 0.68) = 33%. Intro: 'we find this pass-through to be about 0.33.' Footnote 55 gives the range: 29% at the 2001 active share of 81%, 36.1% at the 2020 low of 59%; and across robustness chi estimates the pass-through 'ranges from 31 percent (chi = 3.27) to 39 percent (chi = 2.3).' Sec. VI reduced-form check finds 'a pass-through of about a third' with stock/date FEs and with index-inclusion instruments.

itemVerdicts.item: (d2) Active share of 13F-institution AUM fell 81%->59% (a 32% drop; 0.33x32% ~= 11%)
itemVerdicts.note: The 81% -> 59% numbers and the '32 percent drop' and '33% x 32% = 11%' arithmetic are all verbatim correct in the published paper. The DESCRIPTION of what the 81%/59% measures is WRONG. WRONG: 'active share of 13F-institution AUM.' RIGHT: it is |Active_k|, the fraction of each STOCK'S MARKET CAPITALIZATION held by investors classified as active, reported as the MEDIAN ACROSS STOCKS. Figure 5 note (verbatim): 'For each stock, we compute the ratio of total position of active investors and the market capitalization. We report the median across stocks.' Figure 5 endpoints are labeled 81.4% and 59.5%. Two consequences: (i) the denominator is market cap, not 13F AUM — which is why the active share can exceed the 80% of market cap that 13F filings cover, since non-13F/household ownership falls on the active side by construction (Supplemental Appendix D.3 defines |Active_k| = 1 - sum_i (w_ik A_i / exp(p_k)) x 1{elasticity < 0.06}); (ii) classification is elasticity-based (an investor is passive if its fixed Koijen-Yogo elasticity is below kappa = 0.06), not a legal active/passive label. Second caliber point: the '32 percent drop' is a LOG change (ln(81/59) = 31.6%), consistent with the pass-through being defined as d log(epsilon_agg,k)/d log|Active_k|. It is NOT 81-59 = 22 percentage points, and not the 27% simple proportional decline. An article that re-derives '81 to 59 is a 27% drop' will get 9%, not 11%.

itemVerdicts.item: (d3) The narrower passive-MF+ETF measure (+15pp of market cap over 30 years) gives only 6.3%
itemVerdicts.note: Published Sec. VA verbatim: 'Their fraction of total market capitalization has increased by 15 percentage points in the last 30 years. Starting from a baseline of 81 percent of active investors, this change represents a 19 percent drop in the total fraction of active investors. With our pass-through of 0.33, this increase in passive investing by mutual funds reduces elasticities by 6.3 percent.' (The 2022 WP gave 8% for the same exercise, using pass-through 0.4.)

itemVerdicts.item: (d4) Price impact of buying $1 of a stock rises from ~$2.5 to ~$2.8
itemVerdicts.note: Published verbatim: 'Translating the elasticities into price multipliers, this implies that the rise in passive investing causes an increase in the price impact of buying $1 of a stock roughly from $2.5 to $2.8.' Note the 2022 WP said '$2.5 to $2.9' — if the article cites $2.9 it is quoting the superseded WP.

itemVerdicts.item: (d5) Data = 13F filings 2001-2020ish
itemVerdicts.note: Published Data section: 'We obtain portfolio holdings data from the 13F filings to the SEC from 2001 to 2020', built from SEC EDGAR following Backus, Conlon, and Sinkinson; 'the holdings reported in the 13F filings account for 80 percent of the total stock market capitalization.' Table 2 note: estimates of chi 'across dates (2001:I-2020:IV)'. Stock-level data from CRSP/COMPUSTAT.

itemVerdicts.item: Adjudication: chi ~= 2 (WP) vs chi ~= 3 — which is in the published paper?
itemVerdicts.note: THE PUBLISHED AER PAPER USES chi = 3. Table 2 row (1) 'Baseline specification' gives chi = 2.97 (SE 0.47); the text rounds it: 'In Section IV, we estimated the degree of strategic response and found that chi = 3', and eq. (28) plugs in 1/(1 + 3 x 0.68) = 33%. Robustness rows span 2.30 to 3.27 (excluding the two no-instrument rows, 0.04 and 0.63). chi ~= 2 is the SUPERSEDED 2022 WP number: 'The average value of the competition parameter is chi = 2.2' and the WP's counterfactual used chi = 2.15, giving pass-through 40.6%. So any article text pairing chi ~= 2 with the published 11%/two-thirds results is mixing versions.

corrections: Do not describe the 81% -> 59% series as the 'active share of 13F-institution AUM'. In the published paper it is |Active_k|: the fraction of each stock's MARKET CAPITALIZATION held by investors classified as active (elasticity-based classification: passive if fixed Koijen-Yogo elasticity < 0.06), reported as the median across stocks (Figure 5 note; endpoints labeled 81.4% in 2001 and 59.5% in 2020). Because the denominator is market cap and non-13F/household ownership falls on the active side, the active share can exceed the 80% of market cap that 13F filings cover.

State that the '32 percent drop' from 81% to 59% is a LOG change (ln(81/59) = 31.6%), not 22 percentage points and not the 27% simple proportional decline. The pass-through is defined as d log(elasticity)/d log|Active|, so 0.33 x 32% = 11% only works in logs; re-deriving with a 27% decline gives 9% and does not reproduce the paper.

Report the published strategic-response parameter as chi = 2.97 (Table 2 baseline, SE 0.47), which the paper rounds to chi = 3 when computing the pass-through as 1/(1 + 3 x 0.68) = 33%. chi ~= 2 (2.2 average, 2.15 used in the counterfactual) is the superseded March 2022 working paper. Never pair chi ~= 2 with the published 11% / two-thirds results.

When citing the 2022 working paper's 15%, say it was the WP's ABSTRACT/headline figure; the WP's own Section 5.1 computed 40.6% x 32% = 13%. The WP was internally inconsistent (abstract 15%, body 13%).

Do not assert the number 'was revised down through refereeing'. What is documented is that the estimate of chi rose from 2.15 (2022 WP) to 2.97 (published), lowering the pass-through from 40.6% to 33% and the headline effect from 15%/13% to 11%. The authors' page lists a first version of April 2021 and a current version of April 2024; no source attributes the change to referees.

Do not claim flatly that 'secondary sources still quote 15%'. Some ETF trade-press pieces do carry the old WP sentence, but the most-cited practitioner survey — Apollo Academy, 'Assessing the Impact of Passive Investing over Time' (Nov 2024) — already uses chi = 2.97, pass-through 33%, and 11%. Qualify it as 'some secondary coverage still repeats the working-paper 15%'.

If quoting the price-impact translation, use '$2.5 to $2.8' (published). '$2.5 to $2.9' is the 2022 working paper's number. Likewise the narrow passive-MF+ETF exercise yields 6.3% in the published paper and 8% in the WP.

Keep the micro/macro distinction explicit but flag HHL's own terminology: the paper calls its object the 'aggregate elasticity' (epsilon_agg,k), meaning aggregated ACROSS INVESTORS within a single stock — still a demand elasticity for an individual stock relative to other stocks. Footnote 37 says explicitly that the measured elasticity 'is for individual stocks, that is, to the relative price of different stocks', that passive institutions may separately affect the elasticity of aggregate demand for stocks, and that neither their model nor any other empirical model accommodates both levels of aggregation simultaneously. Quoting the WP phrase 'aggregate demand curves for individual stocks' without that gloss invites the very Gabaix-Koijen conflation the article is warning against.
newContradictions: The March 2022 working paper contradicts itself: abstract and intro say the effect is 'about 15%', while Section 5.1 computes 40.6% x 32% = 13% and the intro elsewhere says 'decrease in elasticities of 13%'. Any article citing 'the WP said 15%' should note the WP's own arithmetic gave 13%.

HHL's own headline label ('aggregate demand curves for individual stocks', epsilon_agg,k = 'aggregate elasticity') cuts against the article's clean micro/macro framing at the level of vocabulary, even though footnote 37 fully supports the framing at the level of substance. This is a live source of the conflation in secondary coverage.

HHL's elasticity-based passive share (19% -> 41% of market cap) is roughly triple the conventional passive-fund share (passive funds 'nearly 0 at the beginning of the 1990s to more than 15 percent in 2019'). The 11% headline rests on the broad measure; the narrow fund-based measure yields only 6.3%. An article that pairs the 11% figure with a conventional '~15% of market cap is in index funds' framing is silently mixing the two measures.

The paper finds average aggregate elasticity fell from 0.41 to 0.27 over the sample, but attributes only part of that to passive investing: 'the investor-specific component of the elasticity of active investors has also experienced significant changes: initially increasing until 2007, then trending downward, and dropping overall', and the paper warns of 'the danger of assessing theories of the impact of passive investing purely based on aggregate trends'. This undercuts any article passage that reads the observed elasticity decline as the passive-investing effect.
reasoning:
I reached the typeset published article text directly (local file hhl_aer.txt / v12_hhl_aer.txt, byte-identical PDFs, MD5 0fe2742e6a99beba839a34f1b7832ecf, header 'American Economic Review 2025, 115(3): 975-1018, https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20230505'), and independently cross-checked the abstract against the AEA article page and the authors' page (loualiche.com) — all three match verbatim, including 'two-thirds' and '11 percent more inelastic'. I read the actual Section V text (eq. 27, eq. 28, footnotes 53-55), Table 2, the Figure 5 note, the Data section, and footnote 37, rather than relying on any fetch summarizer. I also read the March 3, 2022 working paper (hhl.txt) end-to-end at the relevant sections plus its Supplemental Appendix D.3 definition of |Active_k|.

Everything in (a), (c), (d1), (d3), (d4), (d5) checks out verbatim. Two real defects: (1) the article mislabels the 81% -> 59% object as 'active share of 13F-institution AUM' — it is the fraction of each stock's market cap held by active investors, median across stocks, with an elasticity-based (not legal-label) active/passive classification and with non-13F ownership landing on the active side, which is why 81% exceeds 13F's 80% market-cap coverage; and (2) the '32 percent drop' is a log change, so the article's arithmetic chain only reproduces if a reader is told that (a naive 27% simple decline gives 9%, not 11%). Additional caliber slippage: the 2022 WP's 15% was its abstract/intro headline while its own body computed 13%, and 'revised down through refereeing' is an unsupported causal attribution — the documented mechanism is chi moving 2.15 -> 2.97.

On the chi adjudication: the published paper is unambiguous — Table 2 baseline chi = 2.97 (SE 0.47), rounded to chi = 3 in eq. (28), robustness range 2.30-3.27. chi ~= 2 (2.2 average, 2.15 in the counterfactual) belongs to the 2022 WP only.

Unresolved: I could not directly open the ETF-trade-press pages (etftrends.com 403, nasdaq.com timeout) or SSRN (403), so I did not verify by my own eyes that secondary sources 'still quote 15%'; search snippets suggest some do, but per the fabrication warning I refuse to treat a summarizer snippet as a quote. I did verify a contrary datapoint locally: Apollo Academy (Nov 2024) already uses chi = 2.97 / 33% / 11%. I searched for a published erratum, comment, or replication through 2026-08 and found none.

itemVerdicts.item: BPS (JFE 2016): price informativeness for S&P 500 NONFINANCIAL firms rose ~60% (3-yr) and ~80% (5-yr) from 1960 to 2010
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the published JFE 122 (2016) 625-654. Intro (p.627): 'price informativeness is 60% higher in 2010 than 1960 at the three-year horizon and 80% higher at the five-year horizon.' Section 6 repeats: 'three-year price informativeness is about 60% higher in 2010 than in 1960 ... Five-year informativeness is about 80% higher.' Sample is explicitly 'S&P 500 nonfinancial firms from 1960 to 2014' throughout. CAVEAT the article should absorb: BPS is internally inconsistent on the endpoint. The Conclusion (p.647) says '60% and 80% higher in 2014 than in 1960,' and Appendix B Table B.3 says the same ('the one-year informativeness series is only about 30% higher in 2014 than in 1960, and the three- and five-year informativeness series are 60% and 80% higher'). The number is a FITTED LINEAR TREND with 'the linear time trend ... normalized to zero in 1960 and one in 2014' — not a raw 1960 vs 2010 comparison. Fig. 3 also notes 'for h = 5 the last available estimate is for 2009,' so a literal 5-year 2010 value does not exist. '1960 to 2010' is quotable from the paper but should be described as a fitted trend over 1960-2014.

itemVerdicts.item: BPS: the measure is b x sigma (predicted-variance of future EBIT), not R-squared
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: calling b x sigma the 'predicted variance.' RIGHT: b x sigma is the SQUARE ROOT of the predicted variance. BPS Section 5.1: 'price informativeness V_FPE is the predicted variance of future cash flows from market prices [see Eq. (12)]. We compute it here with the minor modification of taking a square root, which gives meaningful units (dollars of future cash flows per dollar of current total assets).' Eq. (16): sqrt(V_FPE)_{t,h} = b_{t,h} x sigma_t(log(M/A)), where sigma is the cross-sectional SD of log M/A in year t. Two further caliber points: (i) the LHS of forecasting regression (15) is E_{i,t+h}/A_{i,t} — EBIT SCALED BY CURRENT TOTAL ASSETS — not EBIT levels; (ii) 'not R-squared' is right about the headline measure but must not be read as 'the R-squared does not rise': BPS Fig. 3 Panels E/F plot the marginal R-squared of log M/A, and the text says 'the coefficients, marginal R2, and, most important, the price informativeness series in Fig. 3 all show clear upward trends at the three- and five-year horizons.'

itemVerdicts.item: BPS footnote 2: outside the S&P 500 informativeness 'appears to decline'; comparison 'potentially misleading' due to compositional change
itemVerdicts.note: Footnote 2 verbatim: 'For completeness, we also calculate price informativeness for firms beyond the S&P 500. We stress, however, that the composition of this sample has changed dramatically over the years (see Fama and French, 2004), making the comparison potentially misleading. ... Likely as a result of the compositional shift, price informativeness for firms beyond the S&P 500 appears to decline.' MISSING QUALIFIER the article should carry: the same footnote continues 'Interestingly, the decline is concentrated at the short horizon, so again there is relative improvement at the long end.' Since the headline 60%/80% are 3- and 5-year numbers, an article contrasting 'inside up / outside down' must note the outside-500 decline is a SHORT-horizon phenomenon, with relative improvement at the long end. The claim that citing BPS as 'markets got more informative, full stop' suppresses footnote 2 is fair and the footnote text supports it.

itemVerdicts.item: BPS footnote 7: first circulated draft (Dec 2013 NBER WP 19728) concluded informativeness was flat; conclusion changed after inflation adjustment, delisting correction, and adding the 5-year horizon
itemVerdicts.note: Footnote 7 verbatim: 'In the first circulated draft of the paper (dated December 2013), we incorrectly inferred that price informativeness had remained stable. This was due to the combined effect of three differences in methodology. First, we did not adjust for inflation. This led price informativeness to be overstated in the high-inflation 1970s and early 1980s. Second, we did not correct for delistings, which have increased somewhat in the latter part of our sample. Third, we did not consider the long five-year horizon.' Independently verified at source: NBER WP 19728 is 'Have Financial Markets Become More Informative?' by Bai, Philippon, Savov, issue date December 2013 (revision date September 2015), and the original Dec-2013 front matter (nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w19728/revisions/w19728.rev0.pdf) abstract reads: 'We use stock and bond prices to forecast earnings and find that the information content of market prices has not improved since 1960.' STRENGTHENING FACT the article may use: an even earlier public version exists — FRBNY Staff Report No. 578, October 2012, same title/authors, abstract: 'we find that the information content of market prices has not increased since 1960' and 'We find that this measure has remained stable.' So the flat result was public for ~14 months before the reversal, not just one draft. CALIBER NIT: 'the sign flipped' is loose — the change was from a null/stable finding to a significant positive trend; the authors' own words are 'we incorrectly inferred that price informativeness had remained stable.'

itemVerdicts.item: FMVV (RFS 2022): informativeness fell for the market as a whole — 'eviscerated almost all of the information content' for small firms
itemVerdicts.note: Two errors. (1) VERSION: the phrase does NOT appear in the published RFS 2022 article (Vol 35, No 7, pp. 3101-3138; verified against the typeset OUP PDF — grep for 'eviscer' and 'almost all' returns nothing). It appears only in the pre-publication drafts: NBER WP 26927 (April 2020) and the Oct 2019 draft. (2) SCOPE: even in the WP the quote is NOT about small firms. WRONG: 'eviscerated almost all of the information content' for small firms. RIGHT (NBER WP 26927, Sec. 1.2, verbatim): 'The left panel of Figure 1 plots the trend in price informativeness ... for the universe of listed firms. It shows that price informativeness has fallen over time for the market as a whole (right panel). In fact, over the past 50 years, this declining trend has eviscerated almost all of the information content in prices.' The subject is the market/listed universe, not small firms. If the article wants a citable published statement, use RFS 2022 Appendix E.2: 'although informativeness rose for the S&P 500 firms, it fell for the market as a whole,' quantified as 'For the non-S&P 500 firms, it fell by around 80%.' Note also the WP's own Figure 1 caption defines the right panel as 'all publicly listed nonfinancial firms excluding S&P 500 firms,' so 'market as a whole' there means ex-S&P-500 (the published caption changed to 'the whole sample').

itemVerdicts.item: FMVV (RFS 2022): informativeness rose ~50% for S&P 500 firms
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG for the cited version: '~50%' is the NBER WP 26927 (April 2020) and Oct 2019 draft number — 'Over 1962-2010, S&P price informativeness has increased by about 50% of its original level' — and it carries no stated horizon. RIGHT (published RFS 2022, Appendix E.2, verbatim): 'For the S&P 500 sample, price informativeness at the 5-year horizon rose by 70% (0.026/0.038). For the non-S&P 500 firms, it fell by around 80%. In all cases, the evolution is significant at the 1% level.' The ~50% corresponds to the 3-year horizon, computable but NOT stated in the published text (Table E1 col. 1: trend .016 / level .033 = 48%).
