So: cite '~70% at the 5-year horizon' if attributing to RFS 2022, or '~50%' only if attributing to NBER WP 26927. Minor internal wrinkle in the published paper: the text computes 0.026/0.038 while Table E1 col. (2) prints .027 for that trend coefficient.

itemVerdicts.item: FMVV: size decile 1 -> 10 implies a 17-fold informativeness difference
itemVerdicts.note: Survives into the published version verbatim. RFS 2022, Appendix E.1: 'These patterns are robust to alternative criterion for size: we also split the sample into deciles of size, and find that moving from the lowest decile to the highest decile of size implies a 17 fold increase in price informativeness (cf. Appendix E.3).' Identical wording (hyphenated '17-fold') in NBER WP 26927 and the Oct 2019 draft. CALIBER: this is a pooled CROSS-SECTIONAL LEVEL difference across size deciles (all firm-year observations pooled), not a change over time — do not let the article present it as a widening trend.

itemVerdicts.item: FMVV: S&P 500 MEMBERSHIP per se is NOT the driver — similar-characteristics non-members look the same
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed in the PUBLISHED RFS 2022 version, in two places. Footnote 17 (p.3119): 'Appendix E.2 shows that the informativeness of stocks currently in the S&P 500 is similar to non-S&P 500 stocks with similar characteristics. Furthermore, price informativeness trends consistently over size deciles. These results suggest that differences in asset characteristics, rather than inclusion in S&P 500 per se, is the source of the divergence.' Appendix E.2: 'we look at firms that have never been included in the S&P 500 but are relatively close in terms of market capitalization and size. These firms exhibit a rise in price informativeness nearly identical to that of the S&P 500 firms (though the levels of price informativeness are somewhat different). This suggests that the rising trend in price informativeness has more to do with firm characteristics (like size) rather than inclusion in the S&P 500 per se (though being part of the index does increase the level of informativeness somewhat).' A SECOND test in the same appendix goes further and cuts the other way on levels: 'among the sample of firms that are in the S&P 500 at some point in their life, the trend in price informativeness is similar for firms currently in and out of the S&P 500. In levels, price informativeness is actually higher when a firm is not in the S&P 500, than when they are in.' The claim that this cuts against a passive-flow/index-membership mechanism is well supported — but the article must carry the parenthetical about levels, since FMVV say membership does lift the LEVEL somewhat even though it does not drive the TREND.

corrections: BPS measure: change 'b x sigma (predicted-variance of future EBIT)' to 'b x sigma — the SQUARE ROOT of the predicted variance of future EBIT-over-assets.' BPS Eq. (16) is sqrt(V_FPE) = b_{t,h} x sigma_t(log M/A); the paper states it 'compute[s] it here with the minor modification of taking a square root, which gives meaningful units (dollars of future cash flows per dollar of current total assets).' The forecast target is E_{i,t+h}/A_{i,t}, EBIT scaled by current assets, not EBIT levels.

BPS 'not R-squared': do not let this imply the R-squared fails to rise. BPS Fig. 3 Panels E/F report the marginal R-squared of log M/A and the text says 'the coefficients, marginal R2, and, most important, the price informativeness series in Fig. 3 all show clear upward trends at the three- and five-year horizons.' Phrase it as 'the headline measure is b x sigma, not R-squared' and stop there.

BPS endpoint: describe the 60%/80% as a fitted linear trend over the 1960-2014 sample, not a raw 1960-to-2010 comparison. BPS's Conclusion and Appendix B Table B.3 both state '60% and 80% higher in 2014 than in 1960'; the trend is 'normalized to zero in 1960 and one in 2014'; and Fig. 3 notes 'for h = 5 the last available estimate is for 2009,' so no literal 2010 five-year value exists.

BPS footnote 2: add the horizon qualifier the footnote itself supplies — 'Interestingly, the decline is concentrated at the short horizon, so again there is relative improvement at the long end.' Comparing the outside-500 decline to the inside-500 3-/5-year rise without this is a like-for-unlike comparison.

BPS footnote 7: replace 'the sign flipped' with the authors' own caliber — the first draft 'incorrectly inferred that price informativeness had remained stable,' and the finding changed to a significant positive trend after inflation adjustment, delisting correction, and adding the five-year horizon. Optionally strengthen with the fact that an even earlier public version, FRBNY Staff Report No. 578 (October 2012), already reported 'the information content of market prices has not increased since 1960' — the flat result circulated for over a year, not just one draft.

FMVV '~50%' rise for S&P 500 firms: WRONG as attributed to RFS 2022. The published RFS 2022 (Appendix E.2) states 'For the S&P 500 sample, price informativeness at the 5-year horizon rose by 70% (0.026/0.038). For the non-S&P 500 firms, it fell by around 80%.' The '~50%' figure ('increased by about 50% of its original level') is from NBER WP 26927 (April 2020) and the Oct 2019 draft. Either cite ~70% at the 5-year horizon to RFS 2022, or cite ~50% to NBER WP 26927 — do not pair the WP number with the RFS citation.

FMVV 'eviscerated almost all of the information content': WRONG on both version and scope. The phrase does not appear in the published RFS 2022 article at all — it is from NBER WP 26927 (April 2020) / Oct 2019 draft — and there it describes the trend for 'the universe of listed firms' / 'the market as a whole', NOT small firms. If the article wants a published statement, use RFS 2022 Appendix E.2: 'although informativeness rose for the S&P 500 firms, it fell for the market as a whole,' with the magnitude 'For the non-S&P 500 firms, it fell by around 80%.'
FMVV 17-fold: label it as a pooled cross-sectional LEVEL gap between the lowest and highest size deciles, not a trend or a widening over time.

FMVV membership-per-se: keep the authors' parenthetical. They say the TREND is driven by firm characteristics 'rather than inclusion in the S&P 500 per se (though being part of the index does increase the level of informativeness somewhat).' The trend result is the one that cuts against a passive-flow mechanism; the level result does not.

Attribution/framing: in the published RFS 2022 version the S&P-500-versus-market price-informativeness comparison was DEMOTED from Section 1.2 of the working paper to Appendix E; the paper's main contribution is a structural 'data' measure that the authors say is 'conceptually different from our data measure' of price informativeness. Do not present the S&P-vs-market informativeness split as the headline finding of the published paper.
newContradictions: Dávila and Parlatore, 'Identifying Price Informativeness' (verified verbatim in the October 2018 NBER WP 25210 version; now published in the Review of Financial Studies, advance article doi 10.1093/rfs/hhaf051, 2025) directly attacks the BPS measure: 'the measure they use to make inferences about price informativeness (forecasting price efficiency, V_FPE) does not allow to separately identify the role of financial markets aggregating dispersed information from the volatility of the fundamental. While their measure V_FPE is relevant to infer whether the allocation of capital in financial markets has improved or worsened, our results show that it is not the right measure to understand whether financial markets have become better at aggregating information. Forecasting price efficiency, V_FPE, can be high due to a low volatility of the fundamental or due to a high level of price informativeness.' They also object that BPS 'estimate V_FPE by running cross-sectional regressions, which implicitly assumes that the fundamental and noise are distributed identically across all of the stocks in their sample.' Any article using BPS as evidence that 'markets got more informative' should note this measurement critique. (I verified these sentences in the Oct 2018 PDF; the published RFS wording may differ and should be re-checked before quoting as RFS 2025.)

FMVV's own published Section 3.2.3 cuts against a simple 'big firms got more informative' reading: 'As Figure 2 shows, absolute price informativeness declines across all four asset groups. Thus, despite more net private data processed by investors about stock-specific characteristics (higher K_j) prices actually became less accurate as signals (the Davila-Parlatore notion of price informativeness).' They add that this reverses with raw prices and earnings: 'If we redo their exercise with raw prices and earnings, price information does show a rising trend.' So on the Davila-Parlatore metric, even large/high-growth stocks got LESS informative — the direction of the FMVV result is metric-dependent.

FMVV published Figure 3 (main text) reports the BPS-style measure across four quadrants and finds 'informativeness has increased for the Large/High-growth group, but declined for the others' — i.e. the rise is confined to large AND high-growth firms, not to large firms generally. Appendix E.1 confirms: 'price informativeness declines for both high-growth and low-growth firms' overall, and the rise shows up only in the large/high-growth cell. An article summarizing FMVV as 'big firms up, small firms down' loses the growth interaction that the authors say does the work.

The BPS non-S&P-500 versus FMVV whole-market results are not independent corroboration of each other in the way an 'index bubble' narrative might use them: BPS footnote 2 explicitly attributes the outside-500 decline to compositional change in the listed universe ('Likely as a result of the compositional shift'), and FMVV's structural answer is also compositional/characteristic-based (size and growth), with an explicit finding that index membership per se is not the driver. Neither paper offers a passive-flow mechanism, and FMVV's membership test is evidence against one.

Read Eq. (15)/(16) and surrounding definition text, the intro magnitude sentence, Section 6 results, the Conclusion, footnote 2, footnote 7, Fig. 3 caption, and Appendix B Table B.3 caption/text. (2) NBER WP 19728 front matter, December 2013 issue date, retrieved from nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w19728/revisions/w19728.rev0.pdf — abstract read verbatim, confirming the flat conclusion. NBER landing page confirms issue date December 2013, revision date September 2015. (3) FRBNY Staff Report No. 578, October 2012 — an even earlier public version with the same flat conclusion, abstract read verbatim. (4) Farboodi, Matray, Veldkamp, Venkateswaran, NBER WP 26927, April 2020 (local farboodi.txt / fmvv.txt, byte-identical content). (5) The October 2019 Wharton-hosted draft. (6) CRITICALLY, the PUBLISHED typeset RFS version (Review of Financial Studies 35(7):3101-3138, RFS-OP-REVF210119.tex, with the OUP download watermark), obtained from chenzi-xu.com/files/Matray_papers/Published_papers/bigdata_rfs.pdf — this is what exposed the version drift. Key discriminating checks performed: horizon (3- vs 5-year), population (S&P 500 nonfinancial vs largest-500 by market cap vs all listed vs ex-S&P-500), level vs trend, cross-sectional level gap vs time trend, square root vs variance, fitted trend vs raw endpoint values, and working-paper vs published version. The version check is what produced the two corrections: the '~50%' S&P 500 figure and the 'eviscerated almost all of the information content' quote are both artifacts of the pre-publication FMVV drafts and are absent from the RFS 2022 article the article cites; the published numbers are 70% (5-year, S&P 500) and 'fell by around 80%' (non-S&P 500). The 'eviscerated' quote is additionally mis-scoped to small firms when the source sentence is about the listed universe.

Remaining uncertainty: (a) I could not retrieve the Wayback snapshot of the December 2013 NBER landing page (HTTP 429 rate limit), so my evidence for the first draft's conclusion is the Dec-2013 NBER front-matter PDF abstract plus the Oct-2012 FRBNY abstract, plus BPS's own footnote 7 — three independent confirmations, which I consider sufficient. (b) I did not read the full body of the December 2013 draft (the rev0 file is only 7 pages of front matter); the flat conclusion is established from its abstract and the authors' footnote. (c) The Dávila-Parlatore quotes are verified in the October 2018 working-paper PDF, not the RFS 2025 published version; wording may have changed and should be re-verified before quoting with the RFS citation. (d) I could not access the OUP full text directly (the abstract page returns navigation chrome only), so the RFS 2022 verification rests on the typeset PDF bearing the OUP article URL, pagination 3101-3138, and the production tex stamp — I regard that as the published version of record, but it is a third-party-hosted copy.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Koijen, Richmond & Yogo, "Which Investors Matter for Equity Valuations and Expected Returns?", Review of Economic Studies 2024, 91(4), 2387-2424 — active-to-passive transition had a LARGE effect on prices but a SMALL effect on price informativeness because capital did not on average flow from more-informed to less-informed investors
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim from two primary sources. NBER WP 27402 landing page (issue date June 2020, revision date September 2023) abstract: "The transition from active to passive investment management had a large impact on equity prices but a small impact on price informativeness because capital did not flow from more to less informed investors on average." Crossref's publisher-deposited abstract for DOI 10.1093/restud/rdad083 carries the identical sentence, and Crossref metadata confirms Review of Economic Studies, volume 91, issue 4, pages 2387-2424, published-print 2024-07-05 (online 2023-08-21), authors Koijen (first), Richmond, Yogo. OUP's own URL path (/restud/article/91/4/2387/7246738) independently corroborates volume/issue/first page. The OUP article page itself is behind Cloudflare and was not readable, but the Crossref-deposited abstract is publisher-supplied. Koijen is indeed a co-author of Gabaix & Koijen, "In Search of the Origins of Financial Fluctuations: The Inelastic Markets Hypothesis" — verified from the local gk.txt title page — so the "same author" observation is correct.

itemVerdicts.item: (b-i) van der Beck, "Short versus Long-run Demand Elasticities in Asset Pricing" (HBS WP 26-070, July 2025): price impacts are ~3x larger at quarterly horizons than in long-run equilibrium
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the primary document. I re-downloaded the HBS PDF fresh (hbs.edu/ris/Publication Files/26-070_4d9218f6-e1d0-439b-a233-d91503eba0f6.pdf) and it matches local vdb.txt exactly. Cover: "Working Paper 26-070", "Copyright © 2025 and 2026 by Philippe van der Beck"; paper dated "July 1, 2025". Abstract: "The estimates imply that price impacts are three times larger at quarterly horizons than in the long-run equilibrium." The same sentence appears in the Crossref-deposited abstract for SSRN 4111329. Body (Section 6): "The average short-run multiplier across stocks is 3 and strongly declines over time to around 1." Separately, elasticities (not multipliers) rise ~4x: AUM-weighted short-run elasticity 0.37 vs long-run 1.45; average weight on the quarterly buy-and-hold portfolio 0.82, i.e. quarterly adjustment speed 0.18.

itemVerdicts.item: (b-ii) "...implying a quarterly M≈5-7 maps to long-run M≈2"
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as an attribution to van der Beck: the paper never maps 5-7 to 2. RIGHT: van der Beck's own estimated multipliers are short-run (quarterly) M≈3 declining to long-run M≈1 ("The average short-run multiplier across stocks is 3 and strongly declines over time to around 1"). Two further caliber problems with the 5-7→2 arithmetic. (1) Object mismatch: van der Beck's 3→1 are STOCK-LEVEL (micro) multipliers from a Koijen-Yogo cross-sectional demand system; M≈5 (range $3-$8; Table 3 point estimates 7.1 with one PC, 5.3 with two PCs) is Gabaix-Koijen's AGGREGATE/MACRO multiplier. GK explicitly separate the two — gk.txt: "the existing evidence in the literature suggests a micro multiplier around 1 ... and a factor or macro multiplier that is well above 1." Applying vdB's micro-level 3x decay ratio to GK's macro multiplier is an extrapolation the paper does not license. (2) Even taken as pure arithmetic, 5/3=1.7 and 7/3=2.3, so "≈2" is a rounding of the article's own division, not a published estimate. If the article wants the sentence, it must be framed as its own inference and must first report vdB's actual 3→1 numbers.

itemVerdicts.item: (b-iii) Publication status: cited as "HBS WP 26-070, July 2025"
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG (stale as of 2026-08): citing it as an unpublished HBS working paper. RIGHT: the paper is now published — Philippe van der Beck, "Short versus long-run demand elasticities in asset pricing", Journal of Financial Economics, vol. 184, article 104337, DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2026.104337, published-print date 2026-10 (Crossref). The HBS WP 26-070 (July 1, 2025 draft) remains the openly readable version and its abstract carries the "three times larger at quarterly horizons" sentence; I could NOT read the JFE version's full text (ScienceDirect returns 403), so I cannot confirm the final published numbers are unchanged from the WP. Cite the JFE article and flag that the 3x figure is verified from the WP/SSRN-deposited abstract.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Hartley & Gerding, "The Elastic Markets Hypothesis" (SSRN 5205817, 2025): finds multipliers neither as large nor as permanent, decaying rapidly
itemVerdicts.note: I DID reach the actual paper's front matter (not a snippet): the author posted a full-resolution image of the paper's title page and abstract (pbs.twimg.com/media/GtGY0k3bMAMfiJA.jpg, attached to Jon Hartley's own tweet of 2025-06-10, text retrieved verbatim via the fxtwitter/vxtwitter APIs). The full PDF body remains unreachable (SSRN 403s to curl, WebFetch, r.jina.ai and an allorigins proxy; no copy on jonhartley.net, jonathanhartley.net, Gerding's site, Hoover, NBER, OpenAlex or Semantic Scholar). What the title page says: title "The Elastic Markets Hypothesis"; byline "Felix Gerding and Jonathan S. Hartley" (Gerding FIRST on the paper, though SSRN/Crossref metadata for DOI 10.2139/ssrn.5205817 lists Hartley first — so "Hartley & Gerding" matches the SSRN record but not the PDF byline); paper dated "October 2024" (SSRN record created 2025-05-06, issued 2025). Abstract verbatim: "This paper presents new evidence on the response of macro asset prices to exogenous changes in quantities. In contrast to Gabaix and Koijen (2021), we show evidence that the demand for stocks can be inelastic in the short-run, but remains elastic in the long-run (the price elasticity of the aggregate stock market with respect to quantities are less than one or that $1 of flows leads to less than a $1 in price increases). We also present a model of sticky portfolio adjustments with fixed rebalancing periods and quadratic rebalancing adjustment costs showing how the model is consistent with our empirical evidence." Author's own summary (verbatim tweet): "Using country index additions/subtractions, we find multipliers (of flows on stock market prices) are not as high or permanent as recent lit. Stock market demand may be inelastic in short-run but is elastic in long-run". So "neither as large nor as permanent" is right (author's words); "decaying rapidly" is NOT the paper's language and is unverified; and the article UNDERSTATES the paper's actual long-run claim, which is that the long-run aggregate multiplier is below 1 ($1 of flows → less than $1 of market value). Also: this is a standalone unrefereed working paper with no publication venue as of 2026-08 (Hartley's own site lists it as a working paper with no journal), and it is one paper against Gabaix-Koijen — the article must not present it as settled.

itemVerdicts.item: Framing: all three papers as "the 2024-2026 turn in the flow-multiplier literature toward 'large but transitory'"
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: grouping Koijen-Richmond-Yogo into a 2024-2026 "large but transitory" turn. RIGHT on two counts. (1) KRY is not a transitory-multiplier paper at all — its price effect is a permanent level/cross-sectional repricing effect; the paper's contribution is the informativeness channel being weak. Only van der Beck and Gerding-Hartley speak to transitoriness. (2) It is not a 2024-2026 result: the RESTUD publication is 2024 but the paper first circulated March 2019, was NBER WP 27402 in June 2020, and the active-to-passive counterfactual is unchanged from the July 2022 draft. Dating the finding to the recent "turn" is a chronology error.

corrections: Replace any claim that van der Beck implies 'quarterly M≈5-7 maps to long-run M≈2' as a finding of the paper. The paper's own estimates are: average short-run (quarterly) stock-level multiplier ≈3, declining to ≈1 in the long run ('The average short-run multiplier across stocks is 3 and strongly declines over time to around 1'). If the article wants a 5-7→~2 mapping it must be labelled explicitly as the article's own arithmetic (divide by 3), and it must first state vdB's actual 3→1 numbers.

Do not apply van der Beck's 3x decay ratio to Gabaix-Koijen's aggregate multiplier without flagging the object mismatch. Van der Beck's multipliers are stock-level (micro) multipliers from a Koijen-Yogo demand system; Gabaix-Koijen's M≈5 ($3-$8 range; Table 3 point estimates 7.1 and 5.3) is the macro multiplier, and GK explicitly note the literature's micro multiplier is ≈1 while the macro multiplier is 'well above 1'.

Update the van der Beck citation: it is now published as Philippe van der Beck, 'Short versus long-run demand elasticities in asset pricing', Journal of Financial Economics 184 (2026), article 104337, DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2026.104337. HBS Working Paper 26-070 (draft dated July 1, 2025) is the openly readable version and is the source for the verified 'three times larger at quarterly horizons than in the long-run equilibrium' sentence.

Correct the Gerding-Hartley description. Do not write 'decaying rapidly' — that phrase is not in the paper. Its abstract says demand for stocks 'can be inelastic in the short-run, but remains elastic in the long-run (the price elasticity of the aggregate stock market with respect to quantities are less than one or that $1 of flows leads to less than a $1 in price increases)', and its model is 'a model of sticky portfolio adjustments with fixed rebalancing periods and quadratic rebalancing adjustment costs'. Identification is from country equity index additions/deletions.

Fix the Gerding-Hartley citation details: the paper's own title page reads 'Felix Gerding and Jonathan S. Hartley', dated October 2024; the SSRN/Crossref record (DOI 10.2139/ssrn.5205817) lists Hartley first and was created 2025-05-06. Cite it as an unrefereed working paper with no journal venue as of August 2026, and note it is a single paper contesting Gabaix-Koijen rather than a settled result.

Remove Koijen-Richmond-Yogo from the '2024-2026 turn toward large but transitory'. KRY says nothing about transitory multipliers, and the finding is not new to 2024: the paper first circulated in March 2019 and appeared as NBER WP 27402 in June 2020; the active-to-passive counterfactual is unchanged from the July 2022 draft. Present it instead as the informativeness-channel result (large price effect, negligible informativeness effect), published in RESTUD 91(4): 2387-2424 (2024).

When describing KRY's 'large impact on equity prices', state what the magnitude actually is: the counterfactual resets the 2016 institutional AUM size distribution back to its 2007 value and yields total repricing of 14%, where repricing is defined as the sum of the absolute value of changes in firms' market capitalization divided by total market capitalization in 2016. That is a cross-sectional repricing/dispersion measure over 2007-2016, not a 14% move in the aggregate market level. Do not let 'large impact on prices' read as an index-level valuation effect.

If the article uses the 'transitory' framing to characterize the aggregate multiplier, note the countervailing primary evidence in Gabaix-Koijen themselves: their Figure 4 estimates the aggregate multiplier by horizon out to four quarters and they write that 'the cumulative impact is fairly stable over time', adding that 'the confidence interval widens quite rapidly with the horizon, which limits what we can say about the long-run multiplier.' The horizon question is unresolved rather than decided against GK.
newContradictions: Gabaix & Koijen's own horizon analysis cuts against a clean 'transitory' narrative at the aggregate level: gk.txt, Figure 4 and surrounding text, estimates p_{t+h}-p_{t-1} = a_h + M_h Z_t + ... for h=0..4 quarters and reports 'We find that the cumulative impact is fairly stable over time... consistent with the theory, persistent flow shocks lead to persistent deviations in prices. ... Unfortunately, however, the confidence interval widens quite rapidly with the horizon, which limits what we can say about the long-run multiplier.' So GK find no measurable reversal within four quarters (though imprecisely estimated); the transitory claim rests on van der Beck's structural extrapolation and on Gerding-Hartley's country-index event studies, not on a direct refutation of GK's own horizon evidence.

Micro vs macro multiplier conflation risk: GK report the literature's micro multiplier is 'around 1', factor-level 'closer to 5', and their macro estimate ~5 (robustness range 3.5 to 8; Table 3 gives 7.1 with one principal component and 5.3 with two). Van der Beck's 3→1 decay is a micro/stock-level object. Any article sentence that treats these as the same M is wrong regardless of which paper it cites.

KRY's 'large price impact' is a 14% total repricing statistic over 2007-2016 from resetting the institutional AUM size distribution — a sum-of-absolute-changes cross-sectional measure, concentrated in smaller firms ('substantial repricing, especially among smaller firms'). This is easily misread as an aggregate market-level effect.

The July 2022 KRY draft used weaker language than the published version: its abstract says 'a nontrivial impact on valuations, yet a small impact on price informativeness', versus the final 'a large impact on equity prices but a small impact on price informativeness'. If the article quotes 'large', it must quote the 2023-revision/RESTUD wording, not the earlier draft.

FABRICATION ALERT (third incident this run): a WebSearch summarizer produced a fictitious description of the Gerding-Hartley model — 'trades reveal information about a transient latent state while imposing inventory pressure on intermediaries with finite balance sheet capacity' — and also asserted the paper 'was published on October 1, 2024' on SSRN. The real abstract describes 'a model of sticky portfolio adjustments with fixed rebalancing periods and quadratic rebalancing adjustment costs', and the SSRN/Crossref record was created 2025-05-06 (October 2024 is the date printed on the draft, not the posting date). Do not let any of that invented model language reach the article.

Publication-status drift found: van der Beck is now in print (JFE 184, 104337, 2026); Gerding-Hartley is still an unrefereed working paper with no venue as of 2026-08 (confirmed against Hartley's own research page, which lists it under working papers with only an SSRN link and a Marginal Revolution mention).
reasoning: Approach: refute-first, primary documents only. (a) I read the NBER WP 27402 landing page HTML (local kry_nber.html, de-tagged) and pulled the publisher-deposited abstract for DOI 10.1093/restud/rdad083 from the Crossref API; both carry the sentence verbatim, and Crossref confirms RESTUD 91(4):2387-2424, published-print 2024-07-05. OUP's own page is Cloudflare-blocked (local kry_oup.html is a challenge page), but the URL path /restud/article/91/4/2387/ corroborates the pagination. I also downloaded the NYU Stern July 2022 draft to check version drift and found the earlier abstract said 'nontrivial impact on valuations' where the final says 'large impact on equity prices', and I located the actual magnitude behind 'large': 14% total repricing (sum of |change in firm market cap| / total 2016 market cap) from resetting the 2016 AUM size distribution to 2007. (b) I re-downloaded the HBS PDF fresh rather than trusting the local extraction; it matches vdb.txt. Abstract verbatim confirms '3x larger at quarterly horizons than in the long-run equilibrium'; Section 6 gives the paper's own multipliers as 3 → ~1, and the intro gives elasticities 0.37 → 1.45 with inertia 0.82. Crossref shows the paper is now JFE 184:104337 (2026); ScienceDirect 403s so I could not read the final text — the 3x sentence is verified from the WP and the SSRN-deposited abstract only. The article's '5-7 → 2' mapping appears nowhere in the paper and mixes micro with macro multipliers; I cross-checked GK (local gk.txt) for the micro/macro distinction and the M=5 ($3-$8), 7.1/5.3 point estimates. (c) SSRN is hard-blocked (403 to curl with browser headers, WebFetch, r.jina.ai, allorigins; Semantic Scholar has no record; Chrome MCP is not connected). I reached the paper's actual title page and full abstract via the full-resolution image the author attached to his own announcement tweet, retrieved through the fxtwitter/vxtwitter APIs and read directly — that is the paper's own front matter, not a snippet. It confirms author order (Gerding first on the PDF, Hartley first in SSRN metadata), date October 2024, and an abstract whose long-run claim is stronger than the article's ('$1 of flows leads to less than a $1 in price increases'), with a sticky-portfolio-adjustment model rather than the intermediary-inventory model a search summarizer invented. Remaining uncertainty: the Gerding-Hartley body, tables, event-study windows and decay speeds are unread, so any specific number or the phrase 'decaying rapidly' cannot be sourced; and the final JFE text of van der Beck is unread, so I cannot rule out revised point estimates between the July 2025 draft and the published version.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Koijen, Richmond & Yogo, "Which Investors Matter for Equity Valuations and Expected Returns?", Review of Economic Studies 2024, 91(4), 2387-2424; NBER WP 27402 — active-to-passive transition had a LARGE effect on prices but a SMALL effect on price informativeness because capital did not on average flow from more-informed to less-informed investors
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in two independent primary sources. NBER WP 27402 PDF (cover: 'June 2020, Revised September 2023'), abstract: 'The transition from active to passive investment management had a large impact on equity prices but a small impact on price informativeness because capital did not flow from more to less informed investors on average.' Crossref record for DOI 10.1093/restud/rdad083 returns the identical abstract sentence and confirms Review of Economic Studies, volume 91, issue 4, pages 2387-2424, published-print 2024-07-05. Body text (Section 6.4) repeats: 'There is little correlation between the two variables, which implies that capital did not flow from more to less informed investors on average. Thus, the transition from active to passive investment management did not reduce price informativeness, despite the large effect that it had on equity prices.' Characterization and citation are accurate.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-cont.) Koijen co-authored the inelastic-markets paper, so this is the same author finding the informativeness channel weak
itemVerdicts.note: Verified from the local Gabaix-Koijen text (gk.txt), 'In Search of the Origins of Financial Fluctuations: The Inelastic Markets Hypothesis', Xavier Gabaix and Ralph S.J. Koijen, May 12, 2022: 'we find that investing $1 in the stock market increases the market's aggregate value by about $5.' Same Koijen. But the article must not imply Koijen is walking back inelasticity: KRY finds the price effect LARGE (consistent with inelastic demand); what he finds weak is only the price-INFORMATIVENESS channel.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-scope) KRY as evidence in a "2024-2026 turn toward large but transitory" multipliers
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: treating KRY as part of a 2024-2026 turn toward 'large but transitory' price impacts. RIGHT: KRY makes no transitory/decay claim anywhere — its counterfactual is a static comparison of two equilibria (2016.Q4 prices with the 2007.Q4 institutional wealth distribution), and its message is 'large but not informativeness-destroying', not 'large but transitory'. Also the timing is wrong: the finding first circulated as NBER WP 27402 in June 2020 (revised September 2023); only the journal publication falls in 2024.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-magnitude) What "large impact on equity prices" means in KRY
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG (if the article leaves it unquantified or reads it as a market-level price-level effect). RIGHT: KRY define 'equity repricing' as the value-weighted absolute percent change in prices between actual 2016.Q4 and the counterfactual, and report: 'We find an economically significant estimate of 14%.' That is a cross-sectional repricing magnitude over 2007.Q4-2016.Q4 among US 13F institutions, not a 14% rise in the market level. Prices 'change substantially, especially among smaller stocks.'

itemVerdicts.item: (a-qualifier) KRY's informativeness result is measure-specific
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG (if stated as 'passive did not reduce price informativeness' full stop). RIGHT: KRY measure informativeness only with the Bai, Philippon & Savov (2016) regression of future profitability on log market-equity-to-book-assets (standardized coefficient 0.049, s.e. 0.003 in 2016.Q4). They explicitly write that 'the definition of price informativeness depends on the motivating theory and econometric specification', cite Dávila-Parlatore (2022) and Sammon (2022) as alternative measures, and state: 'We leave the implementation to these other measures for future research.'

itemVerdicts.item: (b) van der Beck, "Short versus Long-run Demand Elasticities in Asset Pricing", HBS WP 26-070, July 2025: price impacts ~3x larger at quarterly horizons than in long-run equilibrium
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the HBS-hosted PDF (https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/26-070_4d9218f6-e1d0-439b-a233-d91503eba0f6.pdf), cover 'Working Paper 26-070', title page dated July 1, 2025, abstract: 'The estimates imply that price impacts are three times larger at quarterly horizons than in the long-run equilibrium.' Crossref for SSRN id 4111329 carries the identical abstract sentence. Caveat to carry: the paper's own introduction says the opposite rounding — 'investors' long-run elasticities are four times larger than their quarterly short-run elasticities. This implies that the impact of counterfactual experiments is four times larger at a quarterly horizon than in the long-term equilibrium' — and Section C/E say 'roughly 3 to 4 times'. Safest phrasing is 'three to four times', or attribute 'three times' specifically to the abstract/structural multiplier estimate.

itemVerdicts.item: (b-status) Publication status and vintage of van der Beck (2025)
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: citing it only as a July 2025 HBS working paper, as if it were a fresh 2025 result. RIGHT: it is now published — Journal of Financial Economics, vol. 184, article 104337, DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2026.104337, publication date 2026-10-01 (confirmed via Crossref and Semantic Scholar). And it is not new work: an SSRN version (id 4111329) dates to 2022, and the paper's own acknowledgments list AFA 2023 and EFA 2024 presentations, and note it supersedes 'On the Estimation of Demand-based Asset Pricing Models'.

itemVerdicts.item: (b-inference) "implying a quarterly M≈5-7 maps to long-run M≈2"
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: presenting 'quarterly M≈5-7 → long-run M≈2' as an implication of van der Beck. RIGHT: van der Beck never makes this mapping and his own estimated multipliers are far smaller: 'The average short-run multiplier across stocks is 3 and strongly declines over time to around 1. This suggests that the impact of counterfactual experiments is 3 times larger in the short run than over long horizons.' His M is explicitly cross-sectional/stock-level — 'M is the cross-sectional pendant to the scalar multiplier in Gabaix and Koijen (2023)' — estimated on US 13F institutional trades with a mandate-based instrument. The 5 in 'M≈5-7' is Gabaix-Koijen's AGGREGATE (macro) multiplier; applying a micro/cross-sectional horizon ratio to it is the article's own extrapolation, not the paper's, and it is precisely the macro-vs-micro conflation Hartley flags publicly. The '7' has no source in van der Beck at all (his 7 is the long-run ELASTICITY of large value investors, not a multiplier). Underlying estimates to cite instead: AUM-weighted average short-run elasticity 0.37 vs long-run 1.45; quarterly portfolio adjustment speed 0.18.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Hartley & Gerding, "The Elastic Markets Hypothesis" (SSRN 5205817, 2025): multipliers neither as large nor as permanent, decaying rapidly
itemVerdicts.note: COULD NOT REACH THE PAPER. SSRN 403s behind a Cloudflare managed challenge on every route tried: plain curl, the Delivery.cfm PDF endpoint, r.jina.ai proxy, and a real headless browser (page never resolves past 'Just a moment...'; I did not attempt to defeat the bot check). Not indexed in OpenAlex, CORE, scholar.archive.org, or RePEc; no PDF on either author's page (Felix Gerding's research page does not list it at all); not in Hoover's economics working paper listing; web.archive.org returned 429 on every attempt. What IS verified: (1) Jon Hartley's own website lists '"The Elastic Markets Hypothesis", with Felix Gerding' hyperlinked to papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5205817 — so the SSRN ID in the citation is correct; (2) the author's own X post of 6:15 PM, Jun 10, 2025, reads verbatim: '"The Elastic Markets Hypothesis" new paper w Felix Gerding. Using country index additions/subtractions, we find multipliers (of flows on stock market prices) are not as high or permanent as recent lit. Stock market demand may be inelastic in short-run but is elastic in long-run'. That supports 'neither as large nor as permanent' as an author self-description and supports the 2025 dating, but it is a tweet, not the paper. NOT VERIFIED: 'decaying rapidly', any decay speed or half-life, any multiplier point estimate, any model description, the SSRN posting date, and the sample. Search-engine summaries offered a fluent abstract-like paraphrase (transient latent state, intermediary inventory pressure, finite balance-sheet capacity); I could not confirm a single word of it against the document and am treating it as unverified per the fabrication warning.

itemVerdicts.item: (c-scope) Hartley & Gerding identification is macro (country index additions/deletions), not stock-level
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG (if the article uses H-G to rebut stock-level/micro multipliers). RIGHT: per Hartley's own thread, the identification is country additions/deletions to indices such as the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, measuring the MACRO multiplier, and he explicitly distinguishes: Gabaix and Koijen 'argue that multipliers are as high as 5 & are permanently high. To be clear these are macro not micro mutlipliers.' Since the paper text is unreachable, the article should attribute this framing to the authors' public description, not to a document anyone has read.

corrections: Do not present Koijen-Richmond-Yogo as evidence for a '2024-2026 turn toward large but transitory' multipliers. KRY make no transitory or decay claim; their counterfactual is a static comparison of two equilibria. Their contribution is 'large price effect, small informativeness effect'. Also note the finding is not new to 2024: NBER WP 27402 circulated June 2020 and was revised September 2023; only the Review of Economic Studies publication (2024, 91(4), 2387-2424) is 2024.

When citing KRY's 'large impact on equity prices', quantify it correctly: a 14% value-weighted absolute repricing (their 'equity repricing' statistic) in the counterfactual that restores the 2007.Q4 institutional wealth distribution in 2016.Q4 — a cross-sectional repricing among US 13F institutions, not a 14% change in the market level.

Qualify KRY's informativeness result as measure-specific: it uses the Bai-Philippon-Savov (2016) regression of three-year-ahead profitability on log market equity to book assets (standardized coefficient 0.049, s.e. 0.003 in 2016.Q4). KRY themselves write that the definition of price informativeness depends on the motivating theory and specification, cite Dávila-Parlatore (2022) and Sammon (2022) as alternatives, and leave those measures to future research.

If the article implies Koijen is retracting the inelastic-markets result, remove that. KRY finds the price effect LARGE, which is consistent with inelastic demand; what KRY finds weak is only the price-informativeness channel.

Update van der Beck's citation: it is no longer only HBS Working Paper 26-070 (July 1, 2025). It is published as 'Short versus long-run demand elasticities in asset pricing', Journal of Financial Economics, vol. 184, article 104337 (DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2026.104337, 2026). Also drop any framing of it as brand-new 2025 evidence: an SSRN version (id 4111329) dates to 2022 and it was presented at AFA 2023 and EFA 2024.

Fix the van der Beck number's caliber. The abstract says price impacts are 'three times larger at quarterly horizons than in the long-run equilibrium', but the paper's own introduction and conclusion say four times and the reduced-form section says 'roughly 3 to 4 times'. Write 'three to four times' or attribute 'three times' specifically to the abstract/structural multiplier estimate.

Delete or re-source the claim that van der Beck implies 'a quarterly M≈5-7 maps to long-run M≈2'. He makes no such mapping. His own multipliers are an average short-run stock-level multiplier of 3 declining to about 1, and his M is explicitly the 'cross-sectional pendant to the scalar multiplier in Gabaix and Koijen (2023)' — a micro object estimated on US 13F institutional trades, not the aggregate multiplier. The '5' is Gabaix-Koijen's macro multiplier and the '7' appears nowhere as a multiplier (van der Beck's 7 is the long-run ELASTICITY of large value investors). If the article wants a decayed aggregate multiplier, it must flag it as its own arithmetic and note the macro-vs-micro conflation.

If citing van der Beck's magnitudes, use the ones actually in the paper: AUM-weighted average short-run elasticity 0.37 versus long-run 1.45; average quarterly portfolio adjustment speed 0.18 (weight 0.82 on the quarterly buy-and-hold portfolio); reduced-form average elasticity rising from 0.58 at one quarter to 1.68 at four years.

Do not characterize the contents of Hartley & Gerding, 'The Elastic Markets Hypothesis' (SSRN 5205817). Three independent verifier attempts could not reach the document (SSRN Cloudflare 403; no mirror on any author page, Hoover, NBER, RePEc, OpenAlex, CORE, or the Wayback Machine). In particular, drop 'decaying rapidly' and any multiplier magnitude — those are unverified. The only defensible statement is attributed to the authors' own public description: in a June 10, 2025 post announcing the paper, Hartley writes that using country index additions/subtractions they 'find multipliers (of flows on stock market prices) are not as high or permanent as recent lit' and that 'Stock market demand may be inelastic in short-run but is elastic in long-run.' Label it as an author summary of an unpublished, non-peer-reviewed working paper the article has not read.

Note that Hartley & Gerding identify MACRO multipliers from country-level index additions and deletions (e.g. MSCI Emerging Markets). Hartley explicitly distinguishes these from micro multipliers when describing Gabaix-Koijen's M=5. Do not use H-G to rebut stock-level index-inclusion multipliers.
newContradictions: The three papers do not form one coherent 'large but transitory' turn. KRY is a static equilibrium comparison with no time dimension and no decay claim; van der Beck is about horizon-dependent CROSS-SECTIONAL elasticities among US institutions; Hartley-Gerding is about AGGREGATE/macro multipliers from country index events. Bundling them into a single narrative silently mixes micro and macro multipliers — the exact distinction Hartley draws when characterizing Gabaix-Koijen's M=5.

Chronology problem for the '2024-2026' framing: KRY's result dates to NBER WP 27402 (June 2020, revised September 2023), and van der Beck's SSRN version dates to 2022 with AFA 2023/EFA 2024 presentations. Only the journal publication dates (RES 2024; JFE 2026) sit inside the claimed window.

van der Beck's own structural estimates cut against the article's implied long-run M≈2: he reports average short-run stock-level multiplier 3 falling to about 1, i.e. essentially elastic long-run cross-sectional demand — a stronger deflation of the multiplier story than the article states, but on a different (micro) object than Gabaix-Koijen's M=5.

van der Beck notes his structural decay is faster than his own reduced-form evidence implies: 'the decay of price impact in the structural model is somewhat faster than suggested by the reduced-form regressions' and that the functional form for inertia 'remains restrictive'. He also warns that 'the overall magnitude of counterfactual price changes likely depends on the instrument with which elasticities are identified'. Any headline decay ratio inherits that instrument dependence.

Hartley's own thread cites Fuchs, Fukuda & Neuhann (2025) that 'knife-edge symmetry conditions can give biased and unstable results and produce estimated elasticities that are very low' — a live methodological critique aimed at the demand-system estimates underlying both KRY and van der Beck. If the article leans on demand-system counterfactuals, this critique belongs in the text.

Hartley is a named critic of the very literature the article uses him to summarize (he is publicly skeptical that quarterly holdings data can identify investor-type elasticities at all). Citing an unread, unrefereed working paper by an interested party as the capstone of a literature 'turn' is weak footing; at minimum flag its status.
reasoning: I reached three primary documents verbatim and failed on one. (a) I read NBER WP 27402 in full text (locally cached PDF, re-extracted with pdftotext -layout to 217KB) and independently pulled the Review of Economic Studies record from the Crossref API for DOI 10.1093/restud/rdad083, which returned volume 91, issue 4, pages 2387-2424, published-print 2024-07-05, and an abstract identical to the working paper's. The sentence the article relies on is verbatim correct. Reading the body surfaced three caliber issues the abstract hides: the 'large' price effect is a 14% value-weighted absolute repricing statistic, not a market-level move; the informativeness null is specific to the Bai-Philippon-Savov measure, with alternatives explicitly deferred; and the exercise is a static two-equilibrium comparison over 2007.Q4-2016.Q4 that says nothing about transience, so KRY does not belong in a 'large but transitory' bucket. (b) I re-downloaded the HBS PDF fresh from hbs.edu/ris (1.0MB, WP 26-070, dated July 1, 2025) rather than trusting the cached vdb.txt, and confirmed the abstract's 'three times larger at quarterly horizons than in the long-run equilibrium' verbatim, cross-checked against the Crossref abstract for SSRN 4111329. Two things the article gets wrong: the paper is now published in the Journal of Financial Economics (vol. 184, art. 104337, DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2026.104337, confirmed via Crossref and Semantic Scholar) and dates back to a 2022 SSRN version; and the 'quarterly M≈5-7 maps to long-run M≈2' inference is not his — his estimated stock-level multiplier runs 3 to about 1, his M is explicitly the cross-sectional analogue of Gabaix-Koijen's scalar, and the '7' in the article corresponds to nothing but a long-run elasticity of large value investors. I verified Gabaix-Koijen's $1 to $5 aggregate multiplier from the local gk.txt to pin down where '5' comes from and confirm the macro/micro mismatch. (c) Hartley-Gerding is genuinely unreachable. SSRN blocks curl, the Delivery.cfm PDF path, an r.jina.ai proxy, and a real headless browser (Cloudflare managed challenge that never resolves; I did not try to defeat it). The paper is absent from OpenAlex, CORE, scholar.archive.org, RePEc, Hoover's working paper listing, and both authors' pages, and the Wayback Machine returned 429 on every request. Two search summarizers produced a fluent abstract-like paraphrase about transient latent states and intermediary inventory pressure; I could not confirm one word of it and am reporting it as unverified. What I could verify is only the SSRN ID (from the href on Hartley's own site) and the authors' own one-sentence public description from the June 10, 2025 X post, whose text I read directly out of the saved page's og:description and title tag. Remaining uncertain: the published JFE version of van der Beck (ScienceDirect 403s and Crossref/S2 carry no abstract for it), so I cannot rule out that a number moved between the July 2025 working paper and the 2026 journal version; and everything about the Hartley-Gerding paper's actual contents, magnitudes, sample, and decay speed.

itemVerdicts.item: BPS (JFE 2016): price informativeness for S&P 500 NONFINANCIAL firms rose ~60% (3-yr) and ~80% (5-yr) from 1960 to 2010
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the published JFE version (bps.txt, p.627): 'price informativeness is 60% higher in 2010 than 1960 at the three-year horizon and 80% higher at the five-year horizon.' Repeated in Section 5.2: 'three-year price informativeness is about 60% higher in 2010 than in 1960... Five-year informativeness is about 80% higher.' Nonfinancial restriction confirmed: 'For most of the paper, we limit attention to S&P 500 nonfinancial firms' (Section 4.1), and every relevant figure/table note reads 'The sample contains S&P 500 nonfinancial firms from 1960 to 2014.' CAVEAT the article should not trip on: the SAME 60/80% figures are stated with a DIFFERENT endpoint elsewhere in the paper — Section 5.3 trend regression: 'the one-year informativeness series is only about 30% higher in 2014 than in 1960, and the three- and five-year informativeness series are 60% and 80% higher, respectively,' and the Conclusion repeats 'is 60% and 80% higher in 2014 than in 1960.' So the paper says both 'vs 2010' and 'vs 2014' for the same numbers. Writing '1960 to 2010' is defensible (it is the intro's own wording) but 'over the 1960-2014 sample' is safer.

itemVerdicts.item: BPS measure is b×sigma (predicted-variance of future EBIT), not R²
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as phrased on two counts. (1) It is NOT the predicted VARIANCE — BPS explicitly take the square root: 'aggregate efficiency... can be quantified by the predicted variance of future cash flows... Our price informativeness measure is its square root,' and Section 5.1: 'We compute it here with the minor modification of taking a square root, which gives meaningful units (dollars of future cash flows per dollar of current total assets).' RIGHT: the predicted VARIATION (standard deviation) of future cash flows from prices. (2) The sigma is NOT a sigma of EBIT. Eq. (16): VFPE_{t,h} = b_{t,h} × sigma_t(log(M/A)), where b_{t,h} is the forecasting coefficient on log M/A in a regression of E(t+h)/A on current log M/A plus controls, and 'sigma_t(log(M/A))' is 'the cross-sectional standard deviation of the forecasting variable log M/A in year t' — i.e. the dispersion of the PRICE ratio, not of earnings. (3) 'not R²' is right about the headline measure but must not be spun as BPS avoiding R²: Fig. 3 Panels E and F plot 'the marginal contribution of market prices to the regression R²,' and BPS state 'the coefficients, marginal R², and, most important, the price informativeness series in Fig. 3 all show clear upward trends at the three- and five-year horizons.' The marginal R² trends UP too.

itemVerdicts.item: BPS footnote 2: outside the S&P 500 informativeness 'appears to decline,' comparison 'potentially misleading' due to compositional change
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, footnote 2 of the JFE version: 'For completeness, we also calculate price informativeness for firms beyond the S&P 500. We stress, however, that the composition of this sample has changed dramatically over the years (see Fama and French, 2004), making the comparison potentially misleading... Likely as a result of the compositional shift, price informativeness for firms beyond the S&P 500 appears to decline. Interestingly, the decline is concentrated at the short horizon, so again there is relative improvement at the long end. Above all, we view these results as motivating our focus on S&P 500 firms.' Section 5.3 and the Conclusion repeat it: 'for all firms it appears to have declined. The decline occurs...' and 'The apparent decline is more pronounced at the short [horizon].' So yes — citing BPS as 'markets got more informative, full stop' suppresses an authors' caveat that is in the paper three times. Note the authors themselves attribute the outside-500 decline to composition, not to a market-structure mechanism.

itemVerdicts.item: BPS footnote 7: the first circulated draft (Dec 2013, NBER WP 19728) concluded informativeness was FLAT; sign flipped after inflation adjustment, delisting correction, and adding the 5-year horizon
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, footnote 7: 'In the first circulated draft of the paper (dated December 2013), we incorrectly inferred that price informativeness had remained stable. This was due to the combined effect of three differences in methodology. First, we did not adjust for inflation. This led price informativeness to be overstated in the high-inflation 1970s and early 1980s. Second, we did not correct for delistings, which have increased somewhat in the latter part of our sample. Third, we did not consider the long five-year horizon.' NBER WP 19728 identity independently confirmed from nber.org meta tags: citation_title 'Have Financial Markets Become More Informative?', citation_author Bai / Philippon / Savov, citation_publication_date 2013/12/12. One caliber note: the footnote says 'remained stable,' not 'flat' — 'flat' is a fair paraphrase, but the sentence to quote is 'incorrectly inferred that price informativeness had remained stable.' Also note the inflation fix worked by REMOVING an upward bias in the 1970s-80s (lowering the early-period level), not by raising the late period.

itemVerdicts.item: FMVV: 'eviscerated almost all of the information content' for small firms, per RFS 2022
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG twice. (1) VERSION: the phrase does NOT appear anywhere in the published RFS 2022 article (RFS 35(7):3101-3138, doi 10.1093/rfs/hhab110). Zero hits in the published text and zero in the April 2021 revision. It appears ONLY in the working papers: Oct 4 2019 Wharton draft ('over the past 50 years, this declining trend has eviscerated almost all of the information content in prices') and NBER WP 26927, April 2020 (same sentence). RIGHT attribution if the article wants the quote: Farboodi, Matray, Veldkamp & Venkateswaran, NBER WP 26927 (April 2020) / Oct 2019 draft — not RFS 2022. (2) POPULATION: even in the drafts the sentence is about the MARKET AS A WHOLE, not small firms. Context: 'The left panel of Figure 1 plots the trend in price informativeness... for the universe of listed firms. It shows that price informativeness has fallen over time for the market as a whole. In fact, over the past 50 years, this declining trend has eviscerated almost all of the information content in prices.' RIGHT: the quote describes the universe of listed firms. What the PUBLISHED version says instead, in Appendix E.2.1: 'The figures show that although informativeness rose for the S&P 500 firms, it fell for the market as a whole.' That sentence is safe to cite to RFS 2022; 'eviscerated' is not.

itemVerdicts.item: FMVV: informativeness rose ~50% for S&P 500 firms
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG for the published version. '50%' has ZERO occurrences in the published RFS 2022 article and zero in the April 2021 revision. The ~50% figure is working-paper-only main text: 'Over 1962-2010, S&P price informativeness has increased by about 50% of its original level' (NBER WP 26927 / Oct 2019 draft, Section 1.2, read off the fitted trend in their Figure 1). RIGHT figure for RFS 2022, Appendix E.2 (the only magnitude the published paper gives): 'For the S&P 500 sample, price informativeness at the 5-year horizon rose by 70% (0.026/0.038). For the non-S&P 500 firms, it fell by around 80%. In all cases, the evolution is significant at the 1% level.' So: 70% up for S&P 500 (5-yr horizon), ~80% down for non-S&P 500. Note both numbers already coexisted in the working papers (50% from the figure trend, 70% from the Table 5 coefficient ratio); the published paper dropped the 50% sentence and kept only 70%.

itemVerdicts.item: FMVV: size decile 1→10 implies a 17-fold informativeness difference
itemVerdicts.note: Survives into the published RFS 2022, Appendix E.1: 'These patterns are robust to alternative criterion for size: we also split the sample into deciles of size, and find that moving from the lowest decile to the highest decile of size implies a 17 fold increase in price informativeness (cf. Appendix E.3).' Method per Appendix E.3: 'we pool all firm-year observations and construct deciles of firm size (defined as market value in 2009 dollars). We then run the cross-sectional regression (E.1) within each bin.' Figure E4 note: 'the regression in (E.1) for each year t = 1962,...,2010 with horizon s = 5 for each size decile. The sample contains publicly listed nonfinancial firms from 1962 to 2010.' CALIBER: this is a POOLED CROSS-SECTIONAL LEVEL difference across size bins at the 5-year horizon, averaged over the whole 1962-2010 sample — it is NOT a change over time, and it is not a within-year 2010 snapshot. Write it as 'big firms' prices are ~17x more informative than the smallest firms' (pooled 1962-2010, 5-year horizon)', never as 'informativeness rose 17-fold.'

itemVerdicts.item: FMVV: S&P 500 MEMBERSHIP per se is NOT the driver — similar-characteristics non-members look the same
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed in the published RFS 2022 MAIN TEXT, Section 3.2.1: 'While Bai, Philippon, and Savov (2016) also note the divergence between firms in and out of the S&P 500, we show that this is a size effect, not an index inclusion effect.' Footnote 17: 'Appendix E.2 shows that the informativeness of stocks currently in the S&P 500 is similar to non-S&P 500 stocks with similar characteristics. Furthermore, price informativeness trends consistently over size deciles. These results suggest that differences in asset characteristics, rather than inclusion in S&P 500 per se, is the source of the divergence.' Two tests in Appendix E.2: (i) never-in-index firms close in market cap 'exhibit a rise in price informativeness nearly identical to that of the S&P 500 firms (though the levels of price informativeness are somewhat different)... rather than inclusion in the S&P 500 per se (though being part of the index does increase the level of informativeness somewhat)'; (ii) within-firm switchers: 'the trend in price informativeness is similar for firms currently in and out of the S&P 500. In levels, price informativeness is actually higher when a firm is not in the S&P 500, than when they are in.' The TREND claim is clean; the LEVEL effect is small and the two tests point in OPPOSITE directions, so the article must not say 'membership has no effect at all' — say 'the trend is a size effect, not an index-inclusion effect; level effects are small and inconsistently signed across their two tests.'

corrections: Do NOT attribute 'eviscerated almost all of the information content' to Farboodi-Matray-Veldkamp-Venkateswaran, RFS 2022. That phrase has zero occurrences in the published RFS article. Cite it to NBER Working Paper 26927 (April 2020) or the October 2019 draft, or replace it with the published sentence from RFS 2022 Appendix E.2.1: 'although informativeness rose for the S&P 500 firms, it fell for the market as a whole.'

The 'eviscerated' sentence is about the UNIVERSE OF LISTED FIRMS / the market as a whole, not about small firms. WRONG: "eviscerated almost all of the information content" for small firms. RIGHT: the drafts say the declining trend for the market as a whole 'has eviscerated almost all of the information content in prices.' The small-firm result is a separate finding (small firms 'started from roughly the same levels as that of largest firms in 1962, fell sharply over this time period').

FMVV's S&P 500 rise: WRONG '~50%' if attributed to RFS 2022. RIGHT for the published version: 'price informativeness at the 5-year horizon rose by 70% (0.026/0.038)' for the S&P 500 sample, and 'For the non-S&P 500 firms, it fell by around 80%' (RFS 2022, Appendix E.2, Table E3). The ~50% figure is working-paper-only ('Over 1962-2010, S&P price informativeness has increased by about 50% of its original level', NBER WP 26927 / Oct 2019 draft) and was deleted before publication. If the article wants a number tied to RFS 2022, it must be 70% up / 80% down, and it must state the horizon (5-year) and window (1962-2010).

BPS measure: WRONG 'predicted-variance of future EBIT'. RIGHT: BPS's plotted measure is the SQUARE ROOT of the predicted variance — the predicted VARIATION (standard deviation) of future cash flows from prices, in units of dollars of future cash flows per dollar of current total assets. BPS: 'Our price informativeness measure is its square root.'

BPS measure: WRONG to describe the sigma in 'b x sigma' as a sigma of EBIT. RIGHT: Eq. (16) is VFPE_{t,h} = b_{t,h} x sigma_t(log(M/A)), where sigma_t(log(M/A)) is 'the cross-sectional standard deviation of the forecasting variable log M/A in year t' — the dispersion of the market-cap-to-assets ratio (the right-hand-side price variable), not of earnings. b_{t,h} is the coefficient on log M/A in a regression whose dependent variable is E(t+h)/A.

Do not imply BPS shunned R². They report a marginal R² alongside the b x sigma series and it moves the same way: 'the coefficients, marginal R², and, most important, the price informativeness series in Fig. 3 all show clear upward trends at the three- and five-year horizons.' The correct statement is that the HEADLINE, welfare-based measure is b x sigma rather than R² — not that R² was avoided or would show something different.

BPS endpoint: the paper states the same 60%/80% figures against two different endpoints — 'higher in 2010 than 1960' (Introduction and Section 5.2) and 'higher in 2014 than in 1960' (Section 5.3 trend regression and Conclusion). '1960 to 2010' is verbatim-supported, but if the article cites the trend-regression table it must say 2014. Safest phrasing: '60% (3-year) and 80% (5-year) higher over the 1960-2014 sample.'

BPS footnote 7: quote the actual wording. The draft did not say 'flat'; it says the authors 'incorrectly inferred that price informativeness had remained stable.' Also note the inflation fix operated by removing an UPWARD bias in the high-inflation 1970s-early 1980s (lowering the early-period level), not by lifting the modern period.

FMVV's index-membership result must carry its own caveats. The clean finding is about TRENDS: 'we show that this is a size effect, not an index inclusion effect.' On LEVELS the paper is mixed and must not be flattened into 'membership does nothing': Appendix E.2 says matched non-members' rise is 'nearly identical... (though being part of the index does increase the level of informativeness somewhat),' while the within-firm switcher test says 'In levels, price informativeness is actually higher when a firm is not in the S&P 500, than when they are in.'

State FMVV's sample window whenever the paper is used to adjudicate a passive-flow mechanism: price informativeness is estimated for t = 1962,...,2010 ('Since our last price data is from mid-2016... our last annual price informativeness estimate is 2010'). The evidence therefore ENDS BEFORE the bulk of the passive shift in US equity fund assets. FMVV cannot be cited as evidence for or against what passive ownership did to price informativeness after 2010.

Do not treat FMVV's PINF as identical to BPS's. RFS 2022 Section 3.2.1 lists the differences: FMVV 'remove aggregate/common components from both cash flows and prices, while Bai, Philippon, and Savov (2016) work with unadjusted cash flows'; FMVV use MktVal/Assets 'in levels, rather than logs'; and BPS scale 'by the unconditional standard deviation of prices, while our structural framework suggests scaling by the standard deviation of prices conditional on the controls.' The authors say these 'affect magnitudes but... do not significantly change the overall trends.'

BPS's outside-the-500 decline is attributed BY THE AUTHORS to sample composition, not to market structure: 'the composition of this sample has changed dramatically over the years (see Fama and French, 2004), making the comparison potentially misleading... Likely as a result of the compositional shift, price informativeness for firms beyond the S&P 500 appears to decline.' The article may use footnote 2 to block a 'markets got more informative, full stop' reading of BPS, but must not present it as BPS endorsing a market-wide informativeness decline.
newContradictions: The published RFS 2022 explicitly frames price informativeness as an INADEQUATE measure of data/information — it argues PINF 'is also affected by growth and volatility effects in addition to data' and that its own data measure is the contribution. An article that leans on FMVV's PINF numbers as a clean informativeness verdict is using the part of the paper the authors themselves de-emphasized in publication.

FMVV's evidence window ends in 2010 (last price informativeness estimate = 2010; price data through mid-2016). The passive share of US equity fund assets roughly doubled after 2010. FMVV's 'size effect, not index inclusion effect' finding therefore cannot rule out (or support) a passive-flow mechanism operating in the 2010s-2020s. Any article using it to close the question is overreaching on the time window.

BPS themselves report the outside-S&P-500 decline (footnote 2, Section 5.3, Conclusion) and attribute it to compositional change, while FMVV report the same divergence and attribute it to firm SIZE. Neither attributes it to indexing. Both papers are therefore weak evidence for a passive-flow story in either direction, and citing 'BPS says markets got more informative' vs 'FMVV says they got less informative' as opposing camps misreads two papers that agree on the fact pattern and differ only on which composition variable explains it.

BPS's own headline numbers are stated against inconsistent endpoints within the published paper (2010 in the Introduction and Section 5.2; 2014 in Section 5.3 and the Conclusion, with identical 60%/80% values). This is a latent citation trap: any secondary source quoting '60% since 1960' without an endpoint is ambiguous.

FMVV's two index-membership tests disagree on the sign of the LEVEL effect (Appendix E.2: index membership 'does increase the level of informativeness somewhat'; within-firm switcher test: 'price informativeness is actually higher when a firm is not in the S&P 500'). Only the TREND result is robust across both.
reasoning:
I verified against primary documents held locally and re-checked identity/metadata online where the local extraction could not settle it.

BPS (JFE 2016): read the published Journal of Financial Economics 122 (2016) 625-654 text (bps.txt, 4,335 lines, extraction clean). Reached verbatim: the abstract; the Introduction sentence carrying '60% higher in 2010 than 1960... 80% higher at the five-year horizon'; Section 4.1 restricting to 'S&P 500 nonfinancial firms'; Eq. (16) VFPE = b x sigma_t(log(M/A)) with the definition of sigma as the cross-sectional SD of the FORECASTING VARIABLE log M/A; the 'Our price informativeness measure is its square root' sentence; footnote 2 in full; footnote 7 in full; Section 5.3 and the Conclusion (which restate 60%/80% against 2014 rather than 2010). NBER WP 19728 identity confirmed independently by curling nber.org and reading the citation_title / citation_author / citation_publication_date meta tags directly (2013/12/12, Bai-Philippon-Savov) rather than trusting a fetch summary.

FMVV: this is where the claim group breaks, and it is a version-drift failure of exactly the kind flagged. I had four versions locally and diffed them: the October 4 2019 Wharton draft, NBER WP 26927 (April 2020), the April 18 2021 revision, and the PUBLISHED RFS 35(7):3101-3138 (v2_fmvv_rfs.txt, carrying the RFS-OP-REVF210119.tex page furniture and doi 10.1093/rfs/hhab110, advance access October 17 2021). Grep counts across all four: 'eviscerat' appears in the two working papers and ZERO times in the April 2021 revision or the published article. '50%' / 'original level' appears in the two working papers and ZERO times in the published article. '70%' appears in all four, always in the appendix table discussion. So both of the claim's headline FMVV facts are drawn from a superseded draft: the 'eviscerated' quote was deleted before publication, and the '~50%' main-text sentence was deleted and replaced by the appendix's 70% (5-year horizon) / -80% (non-S&P 500) pair. Additionally, in the drafts the 'eviscerated' sentence describes the universe of listed firms, not small firms, so the claim also mis-assigns its population.

The two FMVV items that DO survive into the published RFS: the 17-fold size-decile figure (Appendix E.1, cross-referencing E.3, pooled firm-years, 5-year horizon, 1962-2010) and the index-membership result, which is in the published MAIN text at Section 3.2.1 ('we show that this is a size effect, not an index inclusion effect') plus footnote 17 and Appendix E.2. On membership I found material the claim omits and that cuts both ways: E.2 concedes 'being part of the index does increase the level of informativeness somewhat,' while the within-firm switcher test in the same appendix finds levels are 'actually higher when a firm is not in the S&P 500.' The trend result is robust; the level result is not, and the article should not flatten it.

I also confirmed FMVV's estimation window ends in 2010, which materially limits the 'cuts against a passive-flow mechanism' inference the claim draws — that inference is the article's, not the authors', and it rests on evidence that stops before most of the passive shift.

Searched for post-publication corrections, replications, or comments on either paper up to 2026-08 and found none; the hits were the papers themselves plus downstream citing work (e.g. a RESTUD manuscript on market power and price informativeness), no replication or erratum. I did not fetch or quote from those; the search results were summaries and I treated them as leads only, not evidence.

Remaining uncertainty: I did not independently verify the two working-paper PDFs against their hosting URLs (fnce.wharton.upenn.edu draft, nber.org/papers/w26927) since the local extractions were internally consistent, well-formed, and mutually corroborating on the disputed sentences. The RFS published text carried its own typesetting headers and DOI, which is strong evidence the extraction is of the journal version and not a preprint. No number in any passage I quoted looked garbled, so I did not need to re-fetch.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Russell first stage: switching indexes moves passive ownership ~1.5pp of market cap (~15% of a ~10% baseline)
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the paper (Section on first-stage ownership effects): 'The average change in passive ownership for stocks that switch indexes is approximately 1.5% of the stock's total market capitalization. The average level of ownership by passive funds prior to treatment is approximately 10% of market cap (see Table I). Thus, the change represents roughly 15% of the baseline level of ownership by passive funds.' Table II backs it: FundOwnPassive +1.81pp*** (lower band, t=7.4) and -1.16pp*** (upper band, t=-5.5); Table I mean FundOwnPassive = 10.51 (lower band). Elsewhere the paper writes the range as 'a 1.5 to 1.7 percentage point change'. Unit is percentage points OF MARKET CAP (correct in the claim), and it is passive-FUND ownership from fund holdings data, not total index-linked ownership.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Into-R2000 panel: EDGAR page requests -24.8 log points (205->159/day, -22%); analyst reports -10.8 (p<0.10). Out-of-R2000 panel: EDGAR +20.3, analyst reports +14.3, better powered
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers all confirmed verbatim. Text: 'Google SVI falls by 3.8 log points, EDGAR page requests fall by 24.8 log points, and the number of analyst reports falls by 10.8 log points... the 24.8 log point decrease relative to the baseline average of 5.32 (in logs) corresponds to moving from 205 to 159 EDGAR page requests per day (a decrease of 22%)'; Panel B: 'a 4.4 log point increase in Google SVI, a 20.3 log point increase in EDGAR page views, and a 14.3 log point increase in the number of analyst reports', with 'nearly twice as many stocks in this subsample'. WRONG in the claim: attaching 'weak significance, p<0.10' only to analyst reports. RIGHT: in the into-R2000 (lower-band) panel BOTH are weak — Table IV Panel A shows log(EDGAR) -0.248* (t=-1.9) and log(AnalystReports) -0.108* (t=-1.8), and the text says 'the estimates on EDGAR page views and analyst reports are statistically significant at p < 0.10'. In Panel B: EDGAR +0.203** (t=2.5), analyst reports +0.143*** (t=2.8). Also omitted: Google SVI, the third of the three measures named in the abstract, is statistically INSIGNIFICANT in both panels (-0.038, t=-1.0; +0.044, t=1.5) — the paper's own text concedes 'the result on Google SVI is statistically insignificant'. The claim's note is correct that the popular '-14.1% EDGAR' quote is wrong: 14.3 is the analyst-report coefficient in Panel B (out-of-R2000), and EDGAR in that panel is 20.3.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Price-efficiency outcomes are precisely-estimated zeros: 4/8-day AVR (effect -0.017 vs SD 0.413; MDES +/-0.068), anomaly-mispricing score, PEAD
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed verbatim: 'the estimated treatment effect from index assignment is a change of -0.017 to the 4-day absolute variance ratio... the standard deviation of the 4-day AVR in the lower-band sample is 0.413... the minimum detectable effect size (MDES) for the AVR in this estimate is +/-0.068... Yet we find no effect - precisely estimated.' Table V Panel A: AbsVarRatio4 -0.017 (t=-0.7), AbsVarRatio8 -0.027 (t=-0.4), Misprice 0.001 (t=0.0), BetaPEAD -0.034 (t=-1.0); Panel B: 0.011, 0.004, 0.005, -0.014, all insignificant. Minor precision point: the three quoted figures (-0.017 / 0.413 / +/-0.068) are the 4-DAY, LOWER-BAND cell only; the 8-day lower-band figures are -0.027, SD 1.353, MDES +/-0.221. Mispricing is Stambaugh-Yu-Yuan (2015) 11-anomaly composite; sample mean 0.501 vs 0.503 for the CRSP universe.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Same paper finds significant positives: idiosyncratic volatility, comovement with both indexes, market beta, trading volume +12.1%, short interest +1.9% (Section D)
itemVerdicts.note: Section D is indeed titled 'D. Effects on Underlying Asset Markets' and does report these. Table III Panel A (into R2000): LogTurn +0.121*** (t=2.8), ShortInt +0.019*** (t=3.2), LogVlt +0.064* (t=1.7), rho_R1000 +0.046*** (t=2.9), rho_R2000 +0.069*** (t=4.5), MarketBeta +0.300*** (t=4.5). Panel B mirrors with opposite signs (-0.093***, -0.015***, -0.049**, -0.035***, -0.053***, -0.175***). WRONG: calling idiosyncratic volatility flatly 'SIGNIFICANT'. RIGHT: the volatility effect is the weakest of the six — only p<0.10 in the into-R2000 panel (+0.064*, t=1.7) and p<0.05 in the out panel (-0.049**, t=-2.1). Two further caliber notes: (i) Table III's own note defines column 3 as 'LogVlt is the log of daily return volatility' (total daily return volatility), while the body text calls it 'idiosyncratic volatility' — the paper is internally loose here, so do not lean hard on the word 'idiosyncratic'; (ii) units — 'trading volume +12.1%' is really TURNOVER ('LogTurn is the log of monthly volume divided by shares outstanding'), and 'short interest +1.9%' is +1.9 percentage points of shares outstanding (ShortInt = short interest / shares outstanding; sample SD 0.081), not a 1.9% relative increase. Both phrasings are the paper's own, so quote them as the paper does rather than as independent facts.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Figure 5: Russell 3000 index ownership 2%->11% of market cap 2007-2016 while the 4-day variance ratio improved from 1.16 to 1.10
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed verbatim: 'Figure 5 plots the yearly average levels of passive ownership and inverse price efficiency (measured by the 4-day variance ratio) across all Russell 3000 stocks during our sample period from 2007 to 2016. In this ten year period, index fund ownership quintupled from 2% to 11% of market capitalization on average. Yet over the same period, the average variance ratio fell slightly from 1.16 to 1.10, reflecting a slight improvement in price efficiency. The conclusions are similar when we weight the averages by market capitalization.' WRONG: the phrase 'Russell 3000 index ownership'. RIGHT: it is average passive index-FUND ownership as a share of market cap, averaged across Russell 3000 stocks — a fund-holdings measure, materially narrower than broader passive-share estimates (e.g. Chinco-Sammon's 33.5%), so it must not be read as 'the passive share of the market'. Also note Figure 5 plots the raw 4-day variance ratio, not the absolute (centered) variance ratio used in the regressions, and the caption shows both equal-weighted (dashed) and value-weighted (solid) lines.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) Authors' external-validity caveat: LATE on mid-cap slices; 'not clear whether our estimates generalize to larger changes or higher levels of index investing'
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'Empirically, we caution that the external validity of our results remains unknown. The difference-in-differences methodology we employ estimates the local average treatment effect (LATE) of index assignment around the upper and lower Russell bands both narrow slices of mid-cap U.S. stocks. As such, it is not clear whether our estimates generalize to larger changes or higher levels of index investing.' Note for balance: the authors partly walk this back on the next page — 'our model's theoretical predictions hold for any feasible level of passive investing, which suggests our estimates would hold for larger or smaller changes in index investing.' They also flag a second confound: 'if index switching causes other changes that are not due to changes in ownership, this could confound our inferences.'

itemVerdicts.item: Version control: which document contains these results, and does the published JFE 145(3) text match
