itemVerdicts.note: WRONG (a real trap here): the local scratchpad copy chr.pdf/chr.txt is the OCTOBER 20, 2017 draft (47 pp), and so is the GWU-hosted copy at business.gwu.edu/.../Paper%20Ringgenberg.pdf. That 2017 draft contains NO EDGAR/analyst/Google analysis and reaches the OPPOSITE price-efficiency conclusion: 'index investing introduces noise into stock prices'; 'a change in investor composition, from active investors to passive investors, leads to a degradation in weak-form price efficiency'; 'stocks experience an increase in their variance ratios of approximately 30%'. RIGHT: every claim above is verified against the JANUARY 18, 2022 draft (61 pp, pdfTeX creation date 2022-01-18), which is what the cited URL https://r.jordan.im/download/investing/coles2017.pdf actually serves despite its filename. Its abstract matches the published JFE 145(3) abstract word-for-word except 'but the remaining mix of investors adjusts' (draft) vs 'but the mix of investors adjusts' (published, per EconPapers/JFE), indicating this is the accepted manuscript. Lead-article status confirmed: 'On index investing' is first in the JFE volume 145 issue 3 (2022) listing, pp. 665-683.

corrections: In the into-R2000 (lower-band) panel, do NOT single out analyst reports as the weak result: Table IV Panel A shows log(EDGAR) -0.248* (t=-1.9) and log(AnalystReports) -0.108* (t=-1.8), and the paper states 'the estimates on EDGAR page views and analyst reports are statistically significant at p < 0.10'. BOTH are p<0.10. The precisely-estimated results are in Panel B (out-of-R2000): EDGAR +0.203** (t=2.5), analyst reports +0.143*** (t=2.8).

Add the third information-production measure the article currently drops: Google Search Volume Index is -3.8 log points (t=-1.0) into R2000 and +4.4 (t=1.5) out of R2000 — statistically INSIGNIFICANT in both panels, even though the abstract lists 'Google searches' among the three measures showing lower information production. The paper concedes 'the result on Google SVI is statistically insignificant.'

Downgrade 'idiosyncratic volatility' from a flat 'significant positive': it is the weakest of the six Table III outcomes — +0.064* (t=1.7, p<0.10) into R2000 and -0.049** (t=-2.1) out. Also note Table III's own note defines that column as 'LogVlt is the log of daily return volatility' (total daily return volatility) while the body text calls it idiosyncratic volatility.

Fix the units on the two Section D headline numbers. 'Trading volume +12.1%' is TURNOVER: 'LogTurn is the log of monthly volume divided by shares outstanding' (coefficient 0.121***). 'Short interest +1.9%' is +1.9 percentage points of shares outstanding (ShortInt = short interest / shares outstanding, coefficient 0.019***, sample SD 0.081), not a 1.9% relative increase. If quoting '12.1%' and '1.9%', attribute them as the paper's own phrasing.

Rewrite the Figure 5 description: it is average passive index-FUND ownership as a share of market cap across Russell 3000 stocks rising 2% -> 11% (2007-2016), not 'Russell 3000 index ownership'. This is a fund-holdings measure and must not be presented as the passive share of the market (contrast Chinco-Sammon's 33.5%). Figure 5 plots the raw 4-day variance ratio (1.16 -> 1.10), not the absolute/centered variance ratio used in Table V, and shows both equal- and value-weighted lines.

When quoting the AVR numbers, say they are the 4-DAY, LOWER-BAND (into-R2000) cell: effect -0.017, sample SD 0.413, MDES +/-0.068. The 8-day lower-band figures are -0.027, SD 1.353, MDES +/-0.221. Do not present '-0.017 / 0.413 / 0.068' as covering both horizons and both bands.

CITATION HAZARD — verify which PDF is being read. The 2017 working-paper version (October 20, 2017, 47 pp; still served at business.gwu.edu/.../Paper%20Ringgenberg.pdf and cached locally as chr.pdf) has NO EDGAR/analyst/Google tests and concludes the OPPOSITE: 'index investing introduces noise into stock prices', 'a degradation in weak-form price efficiency', 'an increase in their variance ratios of approximately 30%'. Bond & Garcia cite exactly that 2017 version. All claims in this group are true only of the January 2022 accepted version (61 pp), which is what r.jordan.im/download/investing/coles2017.pdf actually serves. Cite the paper as Coles, Heath & Ringgenberg (2022), JFE 145(3), 665-683, and never mix in 2017-draft findings.

If the article quotes the external-validity caveat, note the authors immediately counterweight it: 'our model's theoretical predictions hold for any feasible level of passive investing, which suggests our estimates would hold for larger or smaller changes in index investing.' They also flag a second confound: 'if index switching causes other changes that are not due to changes in ownership, this could confound our inferences.'
newContradictions: The paper's abstract ('lower information production as measured by Google searches, EDGAR views, and analyst reports') is stronger than its own Table IV: the Google SVI coefficient is insignificant in BOTH panels (t=-1.0 and t=1.5), and in the into-R2000 panel the EDGAR and analyst coefficients clear only p<0.10. The clean information-production result rests on the out-of-R2000 (upper-band) panel alone.

The October 2017 working-paper version of this same paper concluded the reverse on price efficiency — 'a degradation in weak-form price efficiency' and 'an increase in their variance ratios of approximately 30%' following addition to the Russell 2000 — versus the 2022 published version's precisely-estimated zero. Anyone citing 'Coles, Heath & Ringgenberg' from a pre-2019 draft (as Bond & Garcia do, citing 'Coles, Heath, and Ringgenberg (2017)') is citing a conclusion the authors themselves abandoned. This flip is itself a fact worth reporting.

The paper's own Section D results (higher volatility, higher comovement with BOTH the small- and large-cap indexes, higher market beta, more short interest, more turnover) are the empirical core of the index-bubble critics' case, and the authors flag beta specifically as economically consequential: 'this increase in beta is economically important as it may generate real economic effects - changes to beta will affect a firm's cost of capital, thereby affecting corporate investment decisions.' Citing this paper as a clean 'passive is harmless' verdict misrepresents it.
reasoning:
I first checked the local scratchpad and found chr.pdf/chr.txt is the STALE October 20, 2017 draft (47 pp) — it contains no EDGAR/analyst/Google analysis at all and reaches the opposite price-efficiency conclusion, so it could not be used to verify these claims. I then downloaded the cited URL (https://r.jordan.im/download/investing/coles2017.pdf) directly with curl and ran pdftotext -layout on it: despite the filename, it is the January 18, 2022 draft (61 pp, pdfTeX CreationDate 2022-01-18), i.e. the accepted manuscript of JFE 145(3). I read the relevant sections and Tables I-V verbatim from that extraction, not from any fetch summary. I also downloaded the GWU-hosted copy, which turned out to be the 2017 draft again — confirming the version hazard is live on the open web.

Verified verbatim from the January 2022 text: the 1.5%-of-market-cap / ~10% baseline / ~15%-of-baseline first stage (plus Table II: +1.81pp*** lower band, -1.16pp*** upper band; Table I mean 10.51); the information-production sentence with -3.8 / -24.8 / -10.8 log points and the 205->159 (-22%) EDGAR arithmetic off a 5.32 log baseline; the Panel B +4.4 / +20.3 / +14.3; the AVR passage with -0.017, SD 0.413, MDES +/-0.068 and 'Yet we find no effect - precisely estimated'; Table V's four insignificant columns in both panels; Table III's six coefficients including +0.121***, +0.019***, +0.064*, +0.046***, +0.069***, +0.300***; the Figure 5 passage (2%->11%, 1.16->1.10) and its caption; and the LATE/external-validity caveat with its verbatim 'not clear whether our estimates generalize to larger changes or higher levels of index investing'.

Three caliber slips justify CORRECTED rather than HOLDS: (1) the claim implies EDGAR is a firmer into-R2000 result than analyst reports, when the paper's own text and Table IV Panel A put BOTH at p<0.10; (2) idiosyncratic volatility is called 'significant' when it is only p<0.10 in the into-panel, and the table note actually defines the variable as total daily return volatility; (3) 'Russell 3000 index ownership 2%->11%' misdescribes what is passive index-FUND ownership. Secondary unit issues on 'trading volume' (really turnover) and 'short interest +1.9%' (percentage points of shares outstanding) come from the paper's own loose text and should be attributed as such.

Residual uncertainty: I could not obtain the typeset ScienceDirect PDF of JFE 145(3) 665-683 (paywalled; ResearchGate and corpgov.law.harvard.edu both blocked by Cloudflare). I cross-checked the published abstract via EconPapers/RePEc, which matches the January 2022 draft abstract word-for-word except for the deletion of 'remaining' in one clause — consistent with a light copyedit, so I judge the numbers unchanged, but I have not read the typeset version's tables with my own eyes. Lead-article status confirmed from the JFE issue listing (first article) plus RePEc pages 665-683. I searched for later corrections, replications, or contradicting sources up to 2026-08 and found no erratum; search-summarizer text about Russell-banding critiques (Appel-Gormley-Keim, Gormley 2025 'Do Index Funds Monitor? Revisited') is untrusted and I did not read those primary documents, so I make no claim about them here.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Koijen, Richmond & Yogo (RES 2024, 91(4) 2387-2424; NBER WP 27402): active-to-passive transition had a LARGE effect on prices but a SMALL effect on price informativeness because capital did not on average flow from more-informed to less-informed investors
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the primary document (NBER WP 27402, June 2020 rev. September 2023, extracted locally to v13_kry_full.txt via pdftotext, 217KB). Abstract, line-for-line: 'The transition from active to passive investment management had a large impact on equity prices but a small impact on price informativeness because capital did not flow from more to less informed investors on average.' Body (Section 6.4, p.29): 'There is little correlation between the two variables, which implies that capital did not flow from more to less informed investors on average. Thus, the transition from active to passive investment management did not reduce price informativeness, despite the large effect that it had on equity prices.' Publication data confirmed independently via Crossref DOI 10.1093/restud/rdad083: Review of Economic Studies, vol 91, issue 4, pages 2387-2424, published online 2023-08-21, print issue 2024-07-05 — so '2024, 91(4), 2387-2424' is exactly right; the OUP URL path /restud/article/91/4/2387/7246738 corroborates (OUP page itself is Cloudflare-blocked). The published Crossref abstract is word-identical to the WP abstract, so no version drift on this sentence. Author identity confirmed: 'Ralph S. J. Koijen' on the KRY cover page, the same Ralph S.J. Koijen who co-authored Gabaix & Koijen, 'In Search of the Origins of Financial Fluctuations: The Inelastic Markets Hypothesis' (local gk.txt cover page) — the 'same author' framing holds. CALIBER NOTES the article must not slide past: (i) 'large impact on prices' in KRY means CROSS-SECTIONAL repricing, not an aggregate market-level rise — 'The value-weighted absolute percent change in equity prices, which we call equity repricing throughout the paper, is quite large at 14%' for the 2007.Q4→2016.Q4 counterfactual; (ii) population is US firms on NYSE/AMEX/Nasdaq with FactSet institutional holdings, not global (an earlier draft was titled 'Which Investors Matter for GLOBAL Equity Valuations'); (iii) the informativeness null is measured with ONE metric, Bai-Philippon-Savov (2016), standardized coefficient 0.049 (s.e. 0.003) in 2016.Q4, and KRY explicitly flag that 'the definition of price informativeness depends on the motivating theory and econometric specification', citing Davila-Parlatore (2022) and Sammon (2022) as alternatives they do not implement — Sammon's measure is the one that finds passive ownership reduces informativeness; (iv) the aggregate active share numbers behind it are 38.9% (2007.Q4) → 32.8% (2016.Q4).

itemVerdicts.item: (b) van der Beck, 'Short versus Long-run Demand Elasticities in Asset Pricing' (HBS WP 26-070, July 2025): price impacts ~3x larger at quarterly horizons than in long-run equilibrium — implying quarterly M≈5-7 maps to long-run M≈2
itemVerdicts.note: The 3x statement is CONFIRMED verbatim; the citation status and the M≈5-7→M≈2 mapping are WRONG. Confirmed part: local vdb.txt and a fresh download of the HBS PDF (https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/26-070_4d9218f6-e1d0-439b-a233-d91503eba0f6.pdf, saved as v13_vdb_hbs.pdf/.txt) both show 'Working Paper 26-070', 'Philippe van der Beck, Harvard Business School', dated 'July 1, 2025', abstract: 'The estimates imply that price impacts are three times larger at quarterly horizons than in the long-run equilibrium.' WRONG #1 — publication status: the article cites it as a 2025 HBS working paper. RIGHT: it is now PUBLISHED — Journal of Financial Economics, Vol. 184 (October 2026), article 104337, DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2026.104337, Crossref record created 2026-07-18 (also confirmed in OpenAlex, publication_date 2026-07-18). I could not read the JFE version's abstract verbatim (ScienceDirect serves a CAPTCHA), so I cannot rule out wording drift between WP and VoR. WRONG #2 — the multiplier mapping: van der Beck's own estimated multiplier LEVELS are not 5-7 and not 2. Section 6, verbatim: 'The average short-run multiplier across stocks is 3 and strongly declines over time to around 1. This suggests that the impact of counterfactual experiments is 3 times larger in the short run than over long horizons.' His underlying elasticities are AUM-weighted 0.37 short-run vs 1.45 long-run. So on his own numbers the mapping is M≈3 (quarterly) → M≈1 (long run), not 5-7 → 2. WRONG #3 — object mismatch: van der Beck's M is a stock-level CROSS-SECTIONAL multiplier matrix estimated from 13F institutional holdings; he states explicitly 'M is the cross-sectional pendant to the scalar multiplier in Gabaix and Koijen (2023)'. Gabaix-Koijen's M≈5 (and M=7.1 in their GIV specification) is an AGGREGATE/macro market multiplier. Dividing GK's macro M by van der Beck's cross-sectional decay factor is the article's own extrapolation, not a result in the paper — van der Beck never applies his ratio to GK's macro multiplier. He does support using the ratio rather than the level ('while the overall magnitude of counterfactual price changes likely depends on the instrument with which elasticities are identified, Figure 2 suggests that there are important differences in the relative impact over time'), so the qualitative move is defensible; the specific numbers are not his. WRONG #4 — the '~3x' is the abstract's number but the paper is internally inconsistent: the introduction says 'This implies that the impact of counterfactual experiments is four times larger at a quarterly horizon than in the long-term equilibrium', and Section 5 says 'long-term elasticities are 3 to 4 times larger than quarterly elasticities.' Safest caliber is '3-4x (abstract: three times).'

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Hartley & Gerding, 'The Elastic Markets Hypothesis' (SSRN 5205817, 2025): multipliers neither as large nor as permanent, decaying rapidly
itemVerdicts.note: I could NOT reach the paper and am not characterizing it from snippets. Attempts, all failed: direct curl of papers.ssrn.com abstract page and of the Delivery.cfm PDF (HTTP 403 Cloudflare); WebFetch of the SSRN page (403); r.jina.ai proxy (returns 'Just a moment... security verification'); two CORS proxies (allorigins, codetabs — 522); the built-in browser pane (stuck on the Cloudflare interstitial through repeated waits — I did not attempt to solve the challenge); Wayback Machine (no capture of the abstract URL exists; web/2025id_ returns 404 and the CDX API rate-limited); Semantic Scholar (no record by title or by DOI); OpenAlex (record exists but abstract_inverted_index is null); no NBER, Hoover, arXiv, or author-site mirror — jonathanhartley.net/research links only to the SSRN page and hosts no PDF. WHAT I DID VERIFY from primary metadata: Crossref DOI 10.2139/ssrn.5205817, title 'The Elastic Markets Hypothesis', authors Jonathan Hartley (first) and Felix Gerding, SSRN posting created 2025-05-06, reference-count 40, is-referenced-by-count 0, type posted-content, no abstract deposited. Jon Hartley's own research page (fetched, 78KB) lists it under working papers with NO journal, NO NBER/Hoover number, and no revision — so it remains an unrefereed SSRN working paper as of 2026-08. The only author-sourced description I actually read verbatim is his X thread of 10 Jun 2025 (locally cached page): 'The Elastic Markets Hypothesis new paper w Felix Gerding. Using country index additions/subtractions, we find multipliers (of flows on stock market prices) are not as high or permanent as recent lit. Stock market demand may be inelastic in short-run but is elastic in long-run' and 'Gabaix and Koijen (2021) ... argue that multipliers are as high as 5 & are permanently high. To be clear these are macro not micro mutlipliers.' That is an author tweet, not the paper. FABRICATION FLAG: every search summarizer I invoked returned a fuller, suspiciously identical 'abstract' containing phrases like 'trades reveal information about a transient latent state while imposing inventory pressure on intermediaries with finite balance sheet capacity' and 'temporary frictions in intermediation and information processing rather than permanently downward-sloping demand curves', plus a date 'October 2024' that CONTRADICTS the Crossref SSRN posting date of 2025-05-06. None of that is verified — do not quote any of it.

corrections: Replace the van der Beck citation: he is no longer only a working paper. Cite Philippe van der Beck, 'Short versus long-run demand elasticities in asset pricing', Journal of Financial Economics, Vol. 184 (October 2026), article 104337, DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2026.104337 (online 2026-07-18); the HBS Working Paper 26-070 dated July 1, 2025 may be cited as the working-paper version, not as the current status.

Delete or rewrite the sentence 'implying a quarterly M≈5-7 maps to long-run M≈2.' Van der Beck reports no such mapping. WRONG: 'quarterly M≈5-7 maps to long-run M≈2.' RIGHT: van der Beck's own estimates are 'The average short-run multiplier across stocks is 3 and strongly declines over time to around 1' (underlying AUM-weighted elasticities 0.37 short-run vs 1.45 long-run). If the article wants to apply his decay factor to Gabaix-Koijen's M, it must say so explicitly as its own arithmetic and flag the object mismatch.

Add the object-mismatch caveat wherever van der Beck's 3x is used against Gabaix-Koijen: van der Beck's multiplier is a stock-level CROSS-SECTIONAL matrix estimated from 13F institutional holdings — he writes 'M is the cross-sectional pendant to the scalar multiplier in Gabaix and Koijen (2023)' — whereas GK's ~$5 (and M=7.1) is an AGGREGATE macro market multiplier. Van der Beck never applies his horizon ratio to GK's macro multiplier.

Fix the multiple '~3x': the paper's abstract says 'three times', but its introduction says 'the impact of counterfactual experiments is four times larger at a quarterly horizon than in the long-term equilibrium' and Section 5 says 'long-term elasticities are 3 to 4 times larger than quarterly elasticities.' WRONG: a bare '~3x'. RIGHT: '3-4x (the abstract states three times; the introduction states four).'

Do not describe Koijen-Richmond-Yogo as part of a '2024-2026 turn'. WRONG: dating the KRY finding to 2024-2026. RIGHT: NBER WP 27402 first circulated June 2020, revised September 2023, published online at Review of Economic Studies 2023-08-21 with the print issue 91(4) dated July 2024 — the finding predates the alleged turn by three to four years.

Qualify KRY's 'large effect on prices': it is cross-sectional repricing, not an aggregate market-level effect. Verbatim: 'The value-weighted absolute percent change in equity prices, which we call equity repricing throughout the paper, is quite large at 14%', computed for a 2007.Q4 → 2016.Q4 counterfactual on a sample of US NYSE/AMEX/Nasdaq common stocks with FactSet institutional holdings.

Qualify KRY's informativeness null as measure-specific. It uses only the Bai-Philippon-Savov (2016) regression (standardized coefficient 0.049, s.e. 0.003, in 2016.Q4), and KRY themselves write that 'the definition of price informativeness depends on the motivating theory and econometric specification', citing Davila-Parlatore (2022) and Sammon (2022) as alternative measures they leave 'for future research'. Sammon's measure is the one that finds passive ownership reduces informativeness, so KRY is not a refutation of him.

Do not quote or paraphrase any abstract text for Hartley & Gerding beyond what the authors themselves published publicly. The SSRN paper is unreachable (persistent 403). The only verifiable author statement is Jon Hartley's post of 10 June 2025: 'we find multipliers (of flows on stock market prices) are not as high or permanent as recent lit. Stock market demand may be inelastic in short-run but is elastic in long-run.' Phrases circulating in search results such as 'transient latent state', 'inventory pressure on intermediaries with finite balance sheet capacity', and a date of 'October 2024' are unverified and the date contradicts the Crossref SSRN posting date of 2025-05-06.

Label Hartley & Gerding's evidentiary weight honestly: it is an unrefereed SSRN working paper (DOI 10.2139/ssrn.5205817, posted 2025-05-06, Crossref is-referenced-by-count 0), listed on the author's own research page with no journal, no NBER or Hoover number, and no revision as of August 2026. It should not be presented as peer-reviewed evidence on a par with the Review of Economic Studies and Journal of Financial Economics papers in the same passage.
newContradictions: Van der Beck's paper is internally inconsistent about the decay factor: abstract 'three times', introduction 'four times larger at a quarterly horizon than in the long-term equilibrium', Section 5 '3 to 4 times'. Any single-number citation is cherry-picking one of the paper's own two figures.

Van der Beck's own multiplier LEVELS (short-run ~3, long-run ~1) are far below Gabaix-Koijen's macro M≈5-7 even in the SHORT run. If the article uses van der Beck to shrink GK's multiplier, it should note that his short-run estimate already undercuts GK's headline number — the disagreement is about level as well as persistence, and van der Beck explicitly warns the level 'likely depends on the instrument with which elasticities are identified'.

Hartley & Gerding's identification (country-level MSCI EM index additions/deletions) is a macro multiplier design, van der Beck's is a cross-sectional 13F design, and Koijen-Richmond-Yogo's is a cross-sectional demand-system counterfactual. Bundling all three as one 'large but transitory' turn conflates macro and micro multipliers — a distinction Hartley himself insists on ('To be clear these are macro not micro mutlipliers').

Koijen-Richmond-Yogo do NOT find flow multipliers transitory; they find price effects large and say nothing about decay. Their contribution to the group is the informativeness null, not a 'transitory' finding. Using them as evidence for transitoriness would be a misattribution.

Koijen-Richmond-Yogo's informativeness null is a coauthored-by-Koijen result but it does not weaken the inelastic-markets multiplier at all — KRY's own price effect is 14% repricing, i.e. it corroborates large price impacts. Presenting it as 'the same author finding the channel weak' is true only for the INFORMATIVENESS channel, and the article must not let that bleed into the price-impact channel.
reasoning: I reached two of the three primary documents in full and read the relevant sentences myself. (a) KRY: extracted the full NBER WP 27402 PDF locally with pdftotext (v13_kry_full.txt, 217KB) and read the abstract, the introduction's summary of the active-to-passive exercise, and Sections 6.3-6.4 verbatim; the characterization in the article matches the paper word for word. Publication data was verified independently through the Crossref API on DOI 10.1093/restud/rdad083 (RES 91(4) 2387-2424, online 2023-08-21, print 2024-07-05), and the published Crossref abstract is identical to the WP abstract, ruling out version drift on the load-bearing sentence. Koijen's identity as the GK coauthor was checked against the local gk.txt cover page. (b) van der Beck: I re-downloaded the HBS PDF myself from hbs.edu rather than trusting the pre-extracted vdb.txt, extracted it, and confirmed the two agree on every number I checked (0.37/1.45 elasticities, the '3 to 4 times' language, the 'average short-run multiplier across stocks is 3 ... declines to around 1' passage). Searching for a later version turned up the published JFE article (Crossref 10.1016/j.jfineco.2026.104337, Vol. 184, art. 104337, Oct 2026 issue, record created 2026-07-18; corroborated in OpenAlex) — the article's working-paper citation is now stale. The JFE abstract itself I could NOT read verbatim (ScienceDirect CAPTCHA), so I flag possible VoR wording drift as an open uncertainty. The article's '3x' is verbatim from the abstract, but the mapping 'quarterly M≈5-7 → long-run M≈2' appears nowhere in the paper and contradicts van der Beck's own levels of ~3 → ~1; it also crosses object types, since his M is explicitly the 'cross-sectional pendant' to GK's scalar macro multiplier. (c) Hartley & Gerding: unreachable. I exhausted curl (direct page and Delivery.cfm PDF), WebFetch, r.jina.ai, two CORS proxies, the built-in browser pane, the Wayback Machine (no capture exists), Semantic Scholar (no record), and OpenAlex (no abstract), and looked for mirrors on the author's own site, NBER, Hoover and arXiv — none. I deliberately did not attempt to defeat the Cloudflare/CAPTCHA challenge. I verified only metadata (Crossref: DOI 10.2139/ssrn.5205817, Hartley & Gerding, SSRN created 2025-05-06, 40 references, zero citations, still unpublished per the author's own research page) plus the authors' own X thread, which I read as a locally cached page and which corroborates the direction of the claim but is not the paper. Every richer 'abstract' returned by search summarizers is unverified and one of its details (an October 2024 date) contradicts the Crossref posting date, so I treat all of it as unreliable. Remaining uncertainty: the JFE version's exact abstract wording for (b), and the entire text of (c).

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Russell first stage: switching indexes moves passive ownership ~1.5pp of market cap, ~15% of a ~10% baseline
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the paper (Section IV.C, p.24 of the Jan-2022 accepted draft): 'The average change in passive ownership for stocks that switch indexes is approximately 1.5% of the stock's total market capitalization. The average level of ownership by passive funds prior to treatment is approximately 10% of market cap (see Table I). Thus, the change represents roughly 15% of the baseline level of ownership by passive funds.' Table I corroborates the baseline: FundOwnPassive mean 10.51 (lower band, N=319) and 10.14 (upper band, N=564). Table II gives the underlying coefficients: +1.81*** (t=26.5) lower band, -1.16*** (t=-5.5) upper band. Caveat worth knowing but not an error: the paper elsewhere (Section IV.E) writes 'a 1.5 to 1.7 percentage point change', and the authors' own Harvard Law School Forum post on the published paper (15 Aug 2022) says 'ownership by passive funds increases by approximately 2% of its market capitalization' for the R1000->R2000 switch. All three are the same estimates described differently; ~1.5pp is the paper's own average figure, so the claim as written is fine.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Information production: into-R2000 EDGAR -24.8 log points (205->159/day, -22%), analyst reports -10.8 (p<0.10); out-of-R2000 EDGAR +20.3, analyst reports +14.3 (better powered). NOTE that '-14.1% EDGAR' is a misquote of the -14.3 analyst figure.
itemVerdicts.note: The magnitudes are right; the significance attribution and the NOTE are wrong. (1) SIGNIFICANCE — WRONG: 'analyst reports -10.8 (weak significance, p<0.10)' implies EDGAR -24.8 is more strongly significant. RIGHT: Table IV Panel A shows log(EDGAR) -0.248* (t=-1.9) and log(AnalystReports) -0.108* (t=-1.8) — BOTH carry a single star, i.e. both are significant only at p<0.10; log(SVI) -0.038 (t=-1.0) is insignificant. The paper's own text: 'the result on Google SVI is statistically insignificant while the estimates on EDGAR page views and analyst reports are statistically significant at p < 0.10.' (2) THE NOTE IS WRONG: '-14.1% EDGAR' is NOT a popular misquote of -14.3. It is the paper's own introduction, verbatim: 'Following an exogenous increase in index fund ownership, Google search volume falls by 3.8%, EDGAR page views fall by 14.1%, and the number of analyst reports falls by 10.8%.' The authors repeat it verbatim in their Harvard Law School Forum summary of the published JFE paper (15 Aug 2022). The 14.1% figure is irreconcilable with any coefficient in the paper (exp(-0.141)-1 = -13.2%, implying 205->178, not 205->159) — it is an internal inconsistency in the paper's own introduction, not a misquote by third parties. (3) The rest checks out: Section IV.E, 'Google SVI falls by 3.8 log points, EDGAR page requests fall by 24.8 log points, and the number of analyst reports falls by 10.8 log points... the 24.8 log point decrease relative to the baseline average of 5.32 (in logs) corresponds to moving from 205 to 159 EDGAR page requests per day (a decrease of 22%)' — arithmetic verified (exp(5.32)=204.4; exp(5.072)=159.5; exp(-0.248)-1=-22.0%). Panel B: log(EDGAR) +0.203** (t=2.5), log(AnalystReports) +0.143*** (t=2.8), log(SVI) +0.044 (t=1.5, insignificant); paper: 'some of the coefficients are more precisely estimated because we have nearly twice as many stocks in this subsample' (N=11,844 vs 6,699 monthly; 3,384 vs 1,914 quarterly). 14.3 IS correctly the out-of-index analyst-report figure — that half of the NOTE is right.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Price-efficiency outcomes are precisely-estimated zeros: 4/8-day absolute variance ratios (effect -0.017 vs SD 0.413; MDES ±0.068), anomaly mispricing, PEAD
itemVerdicts.note: Table V Panel A (lower band): AbsVarRatio4 -0.017 (t=-0.7), MDES ±0.068, Sample St.Dev. 0.413; AbsVarRatio8 -0.027 (t=-0.4), MDES ±0.221, SD 1.353; Misprice 0.001 (t=0.0), MDES ±0.048, SD 0.137; beta_PEAD -0.034 (t=-1.0), MDES ±0.099, SD 0.102. All insignificant. Paper text verbatim: 'the minimum detectable effect size (MDES) for the AVR in this estimate is +/-0.068, so our research design has the ability to reliably detect a treatment effect on the order of (0.068 / 0.413) = one-sixth of one standard deviation. Yet we find no effect – precisely estimated.' (0.068/0.413=0.165, checks out.) Panel B (upper band) likewise all insignificant: 0.011, 0.004, 0.005, -0.014. Misprice is the Stambaugh-Yu-Yuan (2015) 11-anomaly combined ranking; beta_PEAD is the SUE-loading over t+3 to t+63.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Same paper finds significant positives: idiosyncratic volatility, comovement with both indexes, market beta, trading volume +12.1%, short interest +1.9% (Section D)
itemVerdicts.note: Substantially right, one significance overstatement plus two unit/label nuances. (1) VOLATILITY — WRONG to call it flatly 'SIGNIFICANT': Table III Panel A LogVlt is +0.064* (t=1.7), i.e. p<0.10 only, the weakest result in the table; Panel B is -0.049** (t=-2.1). RIGHT: 'volatility rises, weakly significant (p<0.10) in the into-index panel, p<0.05 in the out-of-index panel.' (2) LABEL: the paper's text says index investing 'raises the idiosyncratic volatility of the individual stock', but Table III defines LogVlt as 'the log of daily return volatility' — total, not residual, volatility. (3) Everything else confirmed, Panel A / Panel B: LogTurn +0.121*** (t=2.8) / -0.093*** — paper text 'a 12.1% increase in monthly trading volume'; ShortInt +0.019*** (t=3.2) / -0.015*** — paper text '1.9% increase (1.5% decrease) in short interest', but the variable is short interest divided by shares outstanding with a sample mean of 0.10, so +0.019 is +1.9 percentage points of shares outstanding, roughly a 19% relative rise; rho_R1000 +0.046*** and rho_R2000 +0.069*** (comovement with BOTH indexes rises — confirmed); MarketBeta +0.300*** (t=4.5) / -0.175***. The section letter is right: these are in Section IV.D, 'Effects on Underlying Asset Markets'. The 'suppression' point stands — the paper explicitly frames the volatility result as 'an out-of-sample validation' of Ben-David, Franzoni and Moussawi (2018), and footnote 23 cites Wurgler (2011) that the beta increase 'may generate real economic effects'.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Figure 5: Russell 3000 index ownership 2%->11% of market cap 2007-2016 while the 4-day variance ratio improved from 1.16 to 1.10
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim (Section V): 'Figure 5 plots the yearly average levels of passive ownership and inverse price efficiency (measured by the 4-day variance ratio) across all Russell 3000 stocks during our sample period from 2007 to 2016. In this ten year period, index fund ownership quintupled from 2% to 11% of market capitalization on average. Yet over the same period, the average variance ratio fell slightly from 1.16 to 1.10, reflecting a slight improvement in price efficiency. The conclusions are similar when we weight the averages by market capitalization.' Figure 5 caption confirms it plots both equal-weighted (dashed) and value-weighted (solid) averages. One nuance for the article: the authors' own HLS Forum post describes the same figure as the variance ratio being 'unchanged', which is a weaker framing than 'improved' — the paper itself says 'fell slightly... a slight improvement', so the claim tracks the paper. Note the direction convention: the variance ratio here is INVERSE price efficiency, so a fall is an improvement.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) Authors' external-validity caveat: LATE on mid-cap slices; 'not clear whether our estimates generalize to larger changes or higher levels of index investing'
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim (Section V, p.33): 'Empirically, we caution that the external validity of our results remains unknown. The difference-in-differences methodology we employ estimates the local average treatment effect (LATE) of index assignment around the upper and lower Russell bands both narrow slices of mid-cap U.S. stocks. As such, it is not clear whether our estimates generalize to larger changes or higher levels of index investing.' They also concede a confound: 'stocks at the bottom of the R1000 may be less important in their index, since they have a lower weight, which could lead to lower attention and/or lower turnover.' IMPORTANT CONTEXT the article should not omit: the authors immediately push back on their own caveat on the next page — 'our model's theoretical predictions hold for any feasible level of passive investing, which suggests our estimates would hold for larger or smaller changes in index investing.' Presenting the caveat as the authors' final word would be one-sided. Sample scale: mean market cap $1.63bn (lower band) and $3.02bn (upper band), i.e. genuinely mid-cap.

corrections: Sub-claim (b), significance: do NOT write that the analyst-report result is the weak one. In Table IV Panel A (into-R2000), BOTH the EDGAR coefficient (-0.248, t=-1.9) and the analyst-report coefficient (-0.108, t=-1.8) carry a single star and are significant only at p<0.10; Google SVI (-0.038, t=-1.0) is insignificant. The paper's own sentence: 'the result on Google SVI is statistically insignificant while the estimates on EDGAR page views and analyst reports are statistically significant at p < 0.10.' The into-index information-production panel as a whole is only marginally significant; the strong results (+0.203**, +0.143***) are all in the out-of-index panel.

Sub-claim (b), the NOTE: DELETE the assertion that the '-14.1% EDGAR' figure is a misquote of the -14.3 analyst-report number. WRONG: '-14.1% EDGAR is wrong; -14.3 is the analyst-report figure.' RIGHT: -14.1% is the paper's OWN introduction, verbatim — 'Following an exogenous increase in index fund ownership, Google search volume falls by 3.8%, EDGAR page views fall by 14.1%, and the number of analyst reports falls by 10.8%' — and the authors repeat it verbatim in their Harvard Law School Forum post on the published paper (15 Aug 2022). It contradicts the paper's own Table IV and Section IV.E (-0.248 = -24.8 log points, 205->159 requests/day, -22%), and cannot be derived from any coefficient in the paper (exp(-0.141)-1 = -13.2%, i.e. 205->178). The accurate framing is: the paper is internally inconsistent on the EDGAR magnitude, with the introduction reporting -14.1% and the results section reporting -24.8 log points / -22%. Separately, +14.3 log points IS correctly the out-of-R2000 analyst-report coefficient (+0.143***).

Sub-claim (d), volatility: soften 'significant'. WRONG: listing idiosyncratic volatility among the flatly 'SIGNIFICANT positives.' RIGHT: LogVlt is +0.064 with t=1.7 (p<0.10, single star) in the into-index panel and -0.049 with t=-2.1 (p<0.05) in the out-of-index panel. Also note the table defines LogVlt as 'the log of daily return volatility' (total volatility) even though the body text calls it idiosyncratic volatility.

Sub-claim (d), short interest units: '+1.9%' reproduces the paper's own wording, but ShortInt is short interest divided by shares outstanding with a sample mean of 0.10, so the coefficient +0.019 is +1.9 PERCENTAGE POINTS of shares outstanding — roughly a 19% relative increase. Say 'percentage points of shares outstanding' to avoid implying a 1.9% relative change.

Source/version hygiene: the URL https://r.jordan.im/download/investing/coles2017.pdf serves the JANUARY 2022 draft despite the '2017' filename — cite it as Coles, Heath & Ringgenberg (2022), never as '(2017)'. This matters because the genuine October 2017 SSRN draft of the same paper reaches the OPPOSITE empirical conclusion and must not be cited or quoted: it states 'increased index investing is associated with prices that significantly deviate from a random walk model. Following their addition to the Russell 2000 index, stocks experience an increase in their variance ratios of approximately 30%', and its first stage is +0.4% of market cap (1993-2006) / +0.8% (2007-2016), not 1.5pp. Any number resembling '+30% variance ratios' or '0.4%/0.8% of market cap' attributed to this paper is from the superseded draft.

Publication details verified and safe to state: Journal of Financial Economics 145(3), September 2022, pp. 665-683, DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2022.05.007; it is the lead article of the issue (first article listed on the JFE issue page, and Ringgenberg's own CV labels it 'Lead Article').

Sub-claim (f): if the article quotes the LATE caveat, note that the authors immediately qualify it — 'our model's theoretical predictions hold for any feasible level of passive investing, which suggests our estimates would hold for larger or smaller changes in index investing.' Quoting only the caveat misrepresents the authors' stated position.
newContradictions: The paper contradicts itself on the headline EDGAR magnitude: the Introduction (and the authors' own Harvard Law School Forum summary of the published version) says EDGAR page views fall by 14.1%, while Section IV.E and Table IV Panel A report -0.248, i.e. -24.8 log points, 205->159 page requests per day, a 22% decline. The 14.1% figure matches no coefficient in the paper. Any article citing this paper must pick one and flag the discrepancy rather than assert the other is a third-party misquote.

Version reversal: the October 2017 SSRN draft of this exact paper concluded that index investing DEGRADES weak-form price efficiency ('stocks experience an increase in their variance ratios of approximately 30%') using a 1993-2006 RDD plus 2007-2016 sample, and reported a first stage of ~0.4%/~0.8% of market cap. The published 2022 version reverses this to precisely-estimated zeros and reports a 1.5pp first stage. Any secondary source citing 'Coles, Heath and Ringgenberg (2017)' for a pro-index-bubble finding is citing a superseded draft.

First-stage magnitude varies by framing across the authors' own outputs: paper body 'approximately 1.5%' (average across both directions), 'a 1.5 to 1.7 percentage point change' (Section IV.E), Table II 1.81 (lower band) / -1.16 (upper band), and the authors' HLS Forum post 'approximately 2% of its market capitalization' for the R1000->R2000 switch. Not an error, but pick one and label the direction.

Identification caveat from outside sources (not verified to primary here, flagged only): the post-2007 Russell banding design used in this paper has been contested in the methodological literature (Appel, Gormley and Keim; Wei and Young), including on whether cohort-year fixed effects rather than year fixed effects are required for stacked difference-in-differences. Hoefler and Schlag's 'Passive Investing and Market Quality' cites Coles-Heath-Ringgenberg as the leading 'no detrimental effect' paper, indicating the finding is contested in the literature rather than settled.
reasoning:
I verified against the actual PDF at the cited URL, downloaded fresh with curl and extracted with pdftotext -layout (897KB, 140,708 chars of text). Critically, that file is NOT a 2017 draft despite the filename 'coles2017.pdf' — its title page reads 'First Draft: March 2017 / This Draft: January 2022', i.e. it is the accepted version of the JFE 145(3) 2022 article, SSRN 3055324. I read Section IV.C (first stage), Section IV.D (asset-market effects), Section IV.E (information production), Section IV.F (price informativeness), Section V (Figure 5 and caveats), and Tables I through V directly, and re-derived the arithmetic (exp(5.32)=204.4; exp(5.32-0.248)=159.5; exp(-0.248)-1=-22.0%; 0.068/0.413=0.165).

I separately confirmed that the scratchpad file chr.txt is the genuine October 2017 draft of the same paper, and it reaches the opposite conclusion on price efficiency (+30% variance ratios) with a different first stage (0.4%/0.8% of market cap) and no EDGAR analysis at all. This is the version-change trap the task warned about.

Primary documents reached verbatim: (1) the January 2022 accepted draft PDF; (2) the October 2017 SSRN draft; (3) the authors' own Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance post of 15 August 2022, which I fetched as raw HTML with curl and stripped with a local Python script rather than trusting any fetch summarizer — it reproduces the introduction's numbers ('Google search volume about the stock falls by 3.8%, EDGAR page views fall by 14.1%, and the number of analyst reports about the stock falls by 10.8%') and gives the first stage as 'approximately 2% of its market capitalization'; (4) Ringgenberg's own research page, fetched raw, which labels the paper 'Journal of Financial Economics, September 2022 - Lead Article'; (5) Crossref and OpenAlex metadata confirming DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2022.05.007, volume 145 issue 3, pages 665-683, September 2022.

What remains uncertain: the Elsevier typeset PUBLISHED version is closed access (OpenAlex: oa_status 'closed', no repository full text; no OA PDF found on the authors' sites or GWU, whose hosted PDF is the older October 2017 draft). So I could not confirm that the typeset Table IV coefficient is identical to the January 2022 draft's -0.248. Two things make me confident it is: the -24.8 log point figure is internally consistent with the paper's own baseline (logEDGAR mean 5.32 -> 205 requests) and its stated 205->159 conversion, whereas -0.141 would imply 205->178; and the authors' post about the published paper reproduces the introduction sentence containing 14.1% unchanged, indicating the introduction/results inconsistency survived into print rather than being resolved. I have NOT independently verified the methodological critiques of the post-2007 Russell banding design (Appel-Gormley-Keim, Wei-Young) to primary text — those appear in newContradictions as flags only, not as verified findings. I also did not verify Table A-level online-appendix balance tests beyond noting they exist.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) All four pre-earnings informativeness measures deteriorated 1990-2019: |Ret| 2%→4%; |Ret|/SD ~1→3.5; price-jump ratio 0.2→0.5; IV-difference 0.02→0.05
itemVerdicts.note: The four number pairs are verbatim correct (Sammon, Oct 2023 version, p.4): 'In 1990, average |Ret| was roughly 2% while by 2019 this average had grown to 4%'; '|Ret|/SD, which increased from just over 1 in 1990 to 3.5 by 2019'; 'P J also increased on average over my sample, going from 0.2 to 0.5'; 'average IV D increased from 0.02 to 0.05'. WRONG: applying the window '1990-2019' to all four. RIGHT: IVD cannot start in 1990 — Sammon states on p.12 'The sample for IV D is shorter than for the other three measures of pre-earnings announcement price informativeness because OptionMetrics coverage begins in 1996,' and the appendix confirms 'Implied volatility is computed by OptionMetrics and runs from 1996 until the end of my sample.' So IVD is 1996-2019; only |Ret|, |Ret|/SD and PJ span 1990-2019. Second, minor terminology: Sammon calls PJ the 'price jump measure' of Weller (2018), not a 'ratio'. Note also Figure 1 plots value-weighted averages alongside equal-weighted; the intro numbers are the cross-sectional averages, not a single weighting scheme the article should assert.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) 90th-vs-10th percentile of passive ownership in 2019 (27% vs 3% of shares) → 152bp higher |Ret| (~1/3 of the 476bp mean)
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, Sammon p.17: 'The point estimate implies that a firm in the 90th percentile of passive ownership in 2019 (27%) has a 152 basis point higher |Ret| than a firm in the 10th percentile of passive ownership in 2019 (3%). For reference, 152 basis points is roughly 1/3rd of |Ret|'s whole sample mean of 476 basis points and 1/4th of its whole sample standard deviation of 621 basis points.' Table 2 col.1 coefficient 0.0635*** (SE 0.007), N=441,238, equal-weighted, firm + year-quarter fixed effects, controls, SEs double-clustered by firm and year-quarter. One caliber caution for the article: this is a regression coefficient rescaled by the 2019 cross-sectional spread in passive ownership (24pp), NOT an observed 2019 difference between two groups of stocks. Value-weighting shrinks the coefficient (col.5: 0.0572***, and the VW mean of |Ret| is 306bp, not 476bp).

itemVerdicts.item: (c) IV estimates (same Russell design as CHR + S&P 500 additions; first-stage F>200) are 2.5-4x the OLS; published '15% increase → 1/4 of mean' headline is the conservative OLS average; reduced form 'not always significant'
itemVerdicts.note: Three parts confirmed, two need fixing. CONFIRMED: 'across all four measures, the IV estimates are 2.5-4 times as large as the OLS estimates' (p.5, verbatim). CONFIRMED: first-stage F = 222.7 (Russell Panel A) and 242 (S&P Panel B), and Appendix D.4 says 'the first stage is very strong (F > 200 for both experiments).' CONFIRMED: the 1/4 headline is OLS-derived — p.19: 'Based on the OLS regressions in Table 2, a 15% higher level of passive ownership is correlated with a 95 basis point higher |Ret|, a 0.66 higher |Ret|/SD, a 0.037 higher P J and a 0.0167 higher IV D... An equal weighted average of these effects relative to variables' means is 0.23 (roughly 1/4th), while an equal weighted average of these effects relative to variables' standard deviations is 0.16 (roughly 1/6th).' (Caveat: the published abstract itself attributes the figure to 'estimates across several research designs,' not explicitly to OLS.) WRONG #1: characterising the reduced form merely as 'not always significant.' That is Sammon's main-text phrase, but Table D3 shows only 1 of 8 interaction coefficients (Post × Treated × Passive Gap) is significant — Russell IVD 0.93*** — while Russell |Ret| 0.18, |Ret|/SD 1.61, PJ −0.31 and S&P |Ret| 0.053, |Ret|/SD 1.513, PJ 0.779, IVD −0.138 are all insignificant, two of them negatively signed. RIGHT: Sammon's own Appendix D.4 says the coefficient 'is almost always insignificant' (1 of 8 significant). WRONG #2: 'same Russell design as CHR.' RIGHT: Sammon follows Coles-Heath-Ringgenberg (2022) only for constructing treated/control cohorts around post-2007 Russell reconstitution; his estimator is 2SLS, whereas CHR explicitly decline an IV — 'IV approaches crucially require an untestable only-through condition... Our approach is more flexible, as it compares treated and control firms before and after index reconstitution.' Same sample construction, different estimator and different identifying assumption. Minor: the ratio band 2.5-4x is Sammon's own summary; the actual Table 3 ratios are Russell 2.5x/2.6x/3.6x/3.2x and S&P 3.5x/3.3x/6.3x/3.7x — the S&P PJ ratio (1.568 vs OLS 0.248) is ~6.3x, above the stated band.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Sammon's own reconciliation with CHR: different TIMING — CHR show information is fully impounded within ~2 days after announcements with no exploitable drift; Sammon shows less was in prices BEFORE
itemVerdicts.note: The CHR half is false. WRONG: 'CHR show information is fully impounded within ~2 days after announcements with no exploitable drift.' RIGHT: CHR report large, statistically significant average PEAD. Coles-Heath-Ringgenberg, 'On Index Investing' (Jan 2022 draft, the version published in JFE 2022), p.31: 'The mean BetaPEAD in our sample is 4.3%; in other words, a 1% standard deviation positive surprise in the stock's earnings announcement is followed by a predictable post-announcement return drift of 4.3%. The sample mean has a standard error of 0.6% and so the mean is strongly different from zero; that is, in our sample of mid-cap stocks, there is significant PEAD on average.' The '~2 days / no drift' sentence the claim relies on is CHR's DEFINITION of the null benchmark, not their finding: 'A value of BetaPEAD = 0 corresponds to no post-earnings-announcement drift i.e. the stock incorporates all the information contained in the earnings announcement, on average, within 2 trading days after the announcement.' What CHR actually find is a precisely-estimated ZERO TREATMENT EFFECT of Russell index assignment on PEAD ('Table V Column 4 shows that passive investing is not associated with any change in the speed of incorporation of new information into stock prices'). Separately, the ATTRIBUTION is a version error. The reconciliation paragraph exists only in the MARCH 2023 HBS working-paper version (hbs.edu/ris/Publication Files/sammon_passive march 23...pdf, p.7): 'Another possible reason for a small PEAD, however, is that the earnings information was incorporated into prices before the announcement itself. Therefore, the Coles et al. (2022) result that PEADs are small is consistent with the idea that prices were uninformative before earnings announcements but information is rapidly incorporated after earnings announcements.' The October 2023 PDF at the cited URL (marcosammon.com/images/sammon_passive.pdf), whose abstract matches the published Management Science abstract verbatim, contains ZERO occurrences of 'PEAD' or 'drift'; its only treatment of Coles et al. is that they document 'no relationship' plus the footnote that 'with one exception, none of these papers are focused on the effect of passive ownership on pre-earnings announcement price informativeness.' Also note Sammon's own gloss 'the Coles et al. (2022) result that PEADs are small' is itself a loose reading of a paper reporting significant average PEAD.

itemVerdicts.item: (d-supplement) Whether the timing reconciliation survives into the published Management Science (2025) text
itemVerdicts.note: Could not reach the published article body. Management Science 71(6):4582-4598, published online 17 Sep 2024, in print June 2025, DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2023.00836 — pubsonline.informs.org full text is paywalled; OpenAlex reports oa_status 'closed', no repository full text; SSRN 3243910 returns 403. Confirmed from the INFORMS landing page that the published abstract is verbatim identical to the October 2023 version's abstract ('...approximately one-fourth of its whole-sample mean and one-sixth of its whole-sample standard deviation'), which is evidence the published text descends from the Oct 2023 revision that dropped the PEAD paragraph — but not proof. Do not cite the Oct 2023 PDF or the published article for the reconciliation without seeing the published text.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Sammon's passive denominator: <1% → ~15% of US market cap 1990-2019, nowhere near 50%
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, p.1: 'From 1990 to 2019, the share of U.S. equities held by passive investors rose from less than 1% to almost 15%.' And p.19: 'As shown in Figure 1, value weighted average passive ownership increased by 15% between 1990 and 2019.' Definition (p.12): 'passive ownership, which I define as the fraction of a stock's shares outstanding which are held by passive funds. Following Appel et al. (2016), I identify passive funds using the CRSP mutual fund database, selecting all index funds, all ETFs and all funds with names that identify them as index funds,' matched to Thomson S12 holdings. So it is share of shares outstanding / market cap, not share of fund assets — the article's framing is right. Required caveat: Sammon himself flags this as a lower bound in footnote 16 — his measure 'only captures funds that are explicitly passive, and misses e.g., shadow index funds (Mauboussin, 2019), as well as institutions that do index replication internally.' The ~15% therefore cannot be used to refute higher figures built on a broader index-tracking definition or on a fund-assets denominator; it refutes only claims that index FUNDS own half the US market cap.

corrections: Item (a): restrict the window on the fourth measure. Say '|Ret|, |Ret|/SD and PJ over 1990-2019; the implied-volatility difference over 1996-2019' — Sammon states 'The sample for IV D is shorter than for the other three measures... because OptionMetrics coverage begins in 1996.' Do not present all four as 1990-2019 series.
Item (a): call PJ the 'price jump measure' of Weller (2018), not the 'price-jump ratio'.

Item (b): do not describe the 152bp as an observed 2019 gap. It is a Table 2 OLS coefficient (0.0635***, equal-weighted, firm + year-quarter FE, N=441,238) rescaled by the 24-percentage-point 2019 spread in passive ownership. Value-weighting shrinks it (0.0572***) and the value-weighted mean of |Ret| is 306bp, not 476bp.

Item (c): replace 'the reduced form is not always significant' with the accurate magnitude. In Appendix Table D3, only 1 of 8 Post x Treated x Passive Gap coefficients is significant (Russell IVD, 0.93***); the other seven — Russell |Ret| 0.18, |Ret|/SD 1.61, PJ -0.31; S&P |Ret| 0.053, |Ret|/SD 1.513, PJ 0.779, IVD -0.138 — are insignificant, and two are negatively signed. Sammon's own Appendix D.4 wording is 'almost always insignificant'. This is a larger soft spot than the article currently concedes.

Item (c): replace 'same Russell design as CHR' with 'follows Coles-Heath-Ringgenberg's treated/control cohort construction around post-2007 Russell reconstitution, but estimates by 2SLS'. CHR explicitly decline an IV: 'IV approaches crucially require an untestable only-through condition... Our approach is more flexible, as it compares treated and control firms before and after index reconstitution.'

Item (c) optional precision: '2.5-4x the OLS' is Sammon's own summary sentence, not the full table. Actual ratios are Russell 2.5x/2.6x/3.6x/3.2x and S&P 3.5x/3.3x/6.3x/3.7x; the S&P price-jump ratio (1.568 vs OLS 0.248) is about 6.3x, outside the stated band. Either quote the band as his characterisation or give the table range.

Item (d), MANDATORY: strike 'CHR show information is fully impounded within ~2 days after announcements with no exploitable drift.' This is false — it restates CHR's definition of the null benchmark as if it were their result. Replace with: CHR report a mean BetaPEAD of 4.3% with a standard error of 0.6%, 'strongly different from zero; that is, in our sample of mid-cap stocks, there is significant PEAD on average.' What CHR find to be zero is the TREATMENT EFFECT of Russell index assignment on PEAD, precisely estimated.

Item (d), MANDATORY: fix the attribution. The timing reconciliation with Coles et al. appears in Sammon's MARCH 2023 HBS working paper, p.7, not in the October 2023 PDF at marcosammon.com/images/sammon_passive.pdf, which contains no occurrence of 'PEAD' or 'drift' and whose abstract matches the published Management Science abstract verbatim. Either cite the March 2023 working paper explicitly and date it, or drop the 'Sammon's own reconciliation' framing. Do not cite the linked PDF or the published article for it.

Item (d): if the March 2023 passage is quoted, note that Sammon's phrase 'the Coles et al. (2022) result that PEADs are small' is his gloss and does not match CHR's own reported significant average PEAD.

Item (e): add the lower-bound caveat Sammon gives in footnote 16 — his measure 'only captures funds that are explicitly passive, and misses e.g., shadow index funds (Mauboussin, 2019), as well as institutions that do index replication internally.' The ~15% therefore rebuts only 'index funds own half the market cap'; it does not rebut figures using a broader index-tracking definition or a share-of-fund-assets denominator.

Citation hygiene: cite the published article as Management Science 71(6):4582-4598, published online 17 September 2024, in print June 2025, DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2023.00836 — and note that the marcosammon.com PDF is the October 2023 working-paper version, which is where every number in this claim group was verified.
reasoning:
Primary documents reached verbatim: (1) Sammon, "Passive Ownership and Price Informativeness," October 2023, downloaded fresh from https://marcosammon.com/images/sammon_passive.pdf (84pp, pdfTeX CreationDate 2023-10-20), text and layout-mode extraction including Table 2, Table 3 and Appendix Table D3; (2) Sammon, same title, March 2023, HBS Publication Files PDF; (3) Coles, Heath, Ringgenberg, "On Index Investing," January 2022 draft (SSRN 3055324, the version published in JFE 2022) plus the October 2017 first draft, both locally extracted; (4) the INFORMS landing page for DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2023.00836 for the published abstract, volume/issue/pages and dates; (5) Crossref and OpenAlex metadata.

What checks out verbatim: all four time-series number pairs in (a); the entire cross-sectional sentence in (b) including 27%, 3%, 152bp and the 476bp mean; the "IV estimates are 2.5-4 times as large as the OLS estimates" sentence; first-stage F of 222.7 and 242 with the appendix's "F > 200 for both experiments"; the explicit OLS derivation of the 1/4-of-mean headline ("Based on the OLS regressions in Table 2... An equal weighted average of these effects relative to variables' means is 0.23 (roughly 1/4th)"); and the "<1% to almost 15%" aggregate passive share with its shares-outstanding definition.

Second, item (d)'s attribution is a version error: the reconciliation paragraph exists only in the March 2023 draft and was removed by October 2023. Third, item (c) understates the reduced-form weakness — 7 of 8 interaction coefficients in Table D3 are insignificant, two negatively signed, and Sammon's own appendix says "almost always insignificant." Fourth, item (a) misapplies the 1990 start to the IVD series, which begins in 1996 with OptionMetrics coverage. The published abstract is verbatim identical to the October 2023 version's abstract, which is strong circumstantial evidence that the published text descends from the revision that dropped the Coles/PEAD paragraph, but I did not confirm it directly and have marked that as unreachable rather than guessing. itemVerdicts.item: (a) All four pre-earnings informativeness measures deteriorated 1990-2019: |Ret| 2%→4%; |Ret|/SD ~1→3.5; price-jump ratio 0.2→0.5; IV-difference 0.02→0.05
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in Sammon (Oct 2023 = published MS version), Introduction pp.4: 'In 1990, average |Ret| was roughly 2% while by 2019 this average had grown to 4%'; '|Ret|/SD, which increased from just over 1 in 1990 to 3.5 by 2019'; 'P J also increased on average over my sample, going from 0.2 to 0.5'; 'average IV D increased from 0.02 to 0.05'. Section 2.3 repeats each ('just above 1 in 1990 to about 3.5 in 2019'; 'from 0.2 to over 0.5'; 'from about 0.02 to 0.05'). Direction correct: higher values = LESS information in prices before the announcement. Minor context worth carrying: these are equal-weighted cross-sectional averages (the whole-sample EW mean of |Ret| is 476bp; the value-weighted mean is only 306bp), and Sammon flags that the |Ret| series spikes in the dot-com and GFC years because those were high-volatility periods.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) 90th-vs-10th percentile of passive ownership in 2019 (27% vs 3% of shares) → 152bp higher |Ret|, ~1/3 of the 476bp mean
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, Section 3.1: 'a firm in the 90th percentile of passive ownership in 2019 (27%) has a 152 basis point higher |Ret| than a firm in the 10th percentile of passive ownership in 2019 (3%). For reference, 152 basis points is roughly 1/3rd of |Ret|'s whole sample mean of 476 basis points and 1/4th of its whole sample standard deviation of 621 basis points.' Arithmetic reproduces exactly from Table 2 col.1 (OLS coef 0.0635 × 0.24 = 0.01524 = 152bp). Note this is the EQUAL-WEIGHTED OLS estimate; Sammon's own footnote 7 says value-weighting shrinks the coefficient (VW mean |Ret| = 306bp, VW SD = 353bp).

itemVerdicts.item: (c) IV estimates 2.5-4x OLS (Russell design following CHR + S&P 500 additions, first-stage F>200); the 1/4-of-mean headline is the conservative OLS average; reduced form 'not always significant'
itemVerdicts.note: Substance confirmed, one attribution imprecise. Verbatim: 'across all four measures, the IV estimates are 2.5-4 times as large as the OLS estimates' (Intro); 'the first stage is very strong (F > 200 for both experiments)' (Appendix D.4 and D.5); 'the coefficient on Passive Gap_{i,t} × Treated_{i,t} × Post_{i,t} is not always significant' (Section 4, verbatim — the article's phrasing is the paper's own). Conclusion confirms the OLS attribution: 'taking the average of the point estimates from the OLS regressions implies that a 15% increase in passive ownership decreases pre-earnings announcement price informativeness by 1/4th of its whole sample mean and 1/6th of its whole sample standard deviation' (I reproduced the average: 0.20, 0.33, 0.10, 0.29 → 0.23). WRONG in the article: 'same Russell design as CHR.' RIGHT: Sammon follows Coles-Heath-Ringgenberg's May market-capitalization proxy and ±100-rank treated/control cohort construction, but implements a difference-in-differences IV, not CHR's regression discontinuity design. Also worth noting: the PUBLISHED abstract attributes the one-fourth figure to 'estimates across several research designs,' not to OLS specifically — only the paper's conclusion pins it to the OLS average. And the appendix states the soft spot more harshly than the main text: 'the reduced form coefficient on the interaction term between Post, Treated and Passive Gap is almost always insignificant' (D.4) and 'a consistently insignificant coefficient on one of the two instruments' (D.5).

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Sammon's own reconciliation with CHR is about TIMING: CHR show information is fully impounded within ~2 days after announcements with no exploitable drift; Sammon shows less was in prices BEFORE
itemVerdicts.note: Both halves fail. (i) The words 'drift,' 'PEAD,' 'post-earnings' and 'semi-strong' appear ZERO times anywhere in Sammon's paper (verified by grep on both plain and -layout pdftotext extractions of the live marcosammon.com PDF, which is byte-identical to the published-version working paper). Sammon offers no reconciliation with CHR at all: he lists Coles et al. (2022) among papers finding a 'non-existent link' and attributes the literature's disagreement to two other things — 'the papers differ in how they measure price informativeness' and 'passive investors collect different types of information.' The timing reconciliation he does make is with a DIFFERENT pair of papers: 'The findings in Figure 1 seem striking, as previous literature (e.g., Bai et al. (2016), Dávila and Parlatore (2018)) have shown a time series trend toward increased price informativeness. My analysis focuses on a different question, namely when information is incorporated into prices.' (ii) WRONG: 'CHR show information is fully impounded within ~2 days after announcements with no exploitable drift.' RIGHT: CHR find the OPPOSITE about the level of drift — 'The mean BetaSUE in our sample is 4.3%... The sample mean has a standard error of 0.6% and so the mean is strongly different from zero; that is, in our sample of mid-cap stocks, there is significant PEAD on average.' The '2 trading days' sentence is a DEFINITION, not a finding: 'A value of BetaSUE = 0 corresponds to no post-earnings-announcement drift i.e. the stock incorporates all the information contained in the earnings announcement, on average, within 2 trading days after the announcement.' CHR's actual result is a precisely-estimated ZERO TREATMENT EFFECT of Russell 2000 assignment on PEAD ('We find a zero treatment effect, which is precisely estimated'); the published JFE version summarizes it as 'a stock switching indexes is accompanied by zero change in price efficiency.' The article's underlying editorial point — that Sammon and CHR measure different objects and so are not a head-on contradiction — is defensible as the article's OWN synthesis, but it cannot be attributed to Sammon, and it cannot be built on the false premise that CHR found no drift.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Sammon's passive denominator: <1% → ~15% of US market cap 1990-2019, nowhere near 50%
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, Intro: 'From 1990 to 2019, the share of U.S. equities held by passive investors rose from less than 1% to almost 15%.' Conclusion: 'Relative to total institutional ownership, passive ownership is still small, owning only about 15% of the US stock market.' Section 3.1: 'value weighted average passive ownership increased by 15% between 1990 and 2019.' Denominator is market cap, not fund assets — so the contrast with '50%' (a share-of-fund-assets statistic) is legitimate. Two caveats the article should carry: Sammon uses the Appel-Gormley-Keim (2016) CRSP-mutual-fund definition (all index funds, all ETFs, and funds whose names identify them as index funds), so the 15% is a LOWER bound; Sammon says so himself in footnote 16 — his measure 'only captures funds that are explicitly passive, and misses e.g., shadow index funds (Mauboussin, 2019), as well as institutions that do index replication internally.' The series also ends in 2019 and is not a 2026 figure.

corrections: Item (d) must be cut or rewritten. Sammon's paper never mentions post-earnings-announcement drift — the words 'drift,' 'PEAD,' and 'semi-strong' appear zero times in it — so there is no 'Sammon's own reconciliation with CHR.' Delete the attribution to Sammon.

Correct the description of Coles-Heath-Ringgenberg. WRONG: 'CHR show information is fully impounded within ~2 days after announcements with no exploitable drift.' RIGHT: CHR report that PEAD is significantly positive on average in their sample (mean BetaSUE = 4.3%, standard error 0.6%, 'strongly different from zero'); the '2 trading days' phrasing is their definition of what BetaSUE = 0 would mean, not a result. Their finding is that Russell 2000 index assignment has a precisely-estimated ZERO effect on PEAD — index investing does not change semi-strong-form efficiency.

If the article keeps the timing argument, present it as the article's own synthesis and state it correctly: Sammon measures how much earnings information is in prices BEFORE the announcement, while CHR measure whether index assignment CHANGES how fast information is impounded AFTER it — different objects, so not a head-on contradiction. Do not claim CHR found zero drift.

Fix 'same Russell design as CHR.' WRONG: implies Sammon replicates CHR's regression discontinuity. RIGHT: Sammon follows Coles et al. (2022)'s May market-capitalization proxy and ±100-rank treated/control cohort construction (724 treated, 618 control firms), but runs a difference-in-differences instrumental-variables specification, not an RDD.

Cite the published version, not only the working paper. The URL used (marcosammon.com/images/sammon_passive.pdf) is the October 2023 working paper — I confirmed it is byte-identical to the file still live at that address. The published citation is Management Science 71(6):4582-4598, June 2025 (online September 17, 2024), DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2023.00836, accepted by Will Cong. Crossref shows no corrections or retractions. Note that earlier drafts differ materially: the March 2023 draft's headline was a decline of 'roughly 16%,' and the November 2021 draft had only three measures — so any number quoted must come from the October 2023/published version.

On item (c), note that the abstract of the published paper attributes the one-fourth figure to 'estimates across several research designs,' and only the conclusion pins it explicitly to 'the average of the point estimates from the OLS regressions.' The 'conservative OLS' framing is defensible but should cite the conclusion, not the abstract.

On item (c), the paper's appendix states the reduced-form weakness more bluntly than the main text: 'the reduced form coefficient on the interaction term between Post, Treated and Passive Gap is almost always insignificant' (Appendix D.4). If the article calls this a real soft spot, quoting the appendix is more honest than the main text's 'not always significant.'

On item (b), add that 152bp is the equal-weighted OLS estimate; Sammon's own footnote 7 notes value-weighting shrinks the coefficient, and the value-weighted mean of |Ret| is 306bp (versus the 476bp equal-weighted mean used in the '~1/3' comparison).

On item (e), add Sammon's own caveat (footnote 16) that his ~15% is a lower bound: it captures only explicitly passive funds and 'misses e.g., shadow index funds (Mauboussin, 2019), as well as institutions that do index replication internally.' Also date-stamp it: the series ends in 2019.
newContradictions: The article's own framing of item (d) attributes to Sammon a reconciliation he never wrote, while item (c) simultaneously and correctly notes Sammon uses CHR's Russell setup. Sammon in fact classifies Coles et al. (2022) among papers finding a 'non-existent link' between passive ownership and price informativeness — i.e., Sammon himself treats CHR as being in tension with his result, not as a complementary timing study.

Sammon's IV estimates being 2.5-4x the OLS is presented as strengthening the result, but Sammon notes that under the reverse-causality story he raises, OLS should have been biased UPWARD; IV coming in larger is used by him only to rule out that specific bias, not as evidence the true effect is 2.5-4x the headline. The article should not silently promote the IV magnitudes into the headline.

CHR's finding that index assignment does NOT change PEAD sits directly against the article's larger thesis and should be reported as a live contrary primary result, not neutralized by the false 'no exploitable drift' gloss.

Sammon's ~15% passive share of market cap (1990-2019, explicit index funds and ETFs only) is not commensurable with the 50%+ figures circulating elsewhere, which are share of US-equity FUND assets. If the article uses Sammon's 15% to rebut '50%', it must name both denominators explicitly or it commits the same category error in reverse.
