itemVerdicts.item: (a) All four pre-earnings informativeness measures deteriorated 1990-2019: |Ret| 2%→4%; |Ret|/SD ~1→3.5; price-jump ratio 0.2→0.5; IV-difference 0.02→0.05
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the October 2023 version (marcosammon.com/images/sammon_passive.pdf), the version whose abstract matches the published Management Science abstract word-for-word. Intro: 'In 1990, average |Ret| was roughly 2% while by 2019 this average had grown to 4%'; 'average |Ret|/SD, which increased from just over 1 in 1990 to 3.5 by 2019'; 'P J also increased on average over my sample, going from 0.2 to 0.5'; 'average IV D increased from 0.02 to 0.05'. Section 2.3 repeats these against Figure 1 ('from 0.2 to over 0.5'). Two caliber notes the article should not drop: (i) these are VALUE-WEIGHTED quarterly averages (Figure 1 caption: 'To compute the value-weighted average (VW Avg.), within each quarter, observations are weighted in proportion to their market capitalization at the end of the previous quarter'); (ii) higher values = LESS pre-announcement informativeness, so 'deteriorated' is right only in that direction. P J is Weller (2018)'s price-jump measure (Sammon modifies it: market-adjusted returns, a=22 not 21); IV D is Kelly et al. (2016)'s implied-volatility difference, units in percentage points of implied volatility.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) 90th-vs-10th percentile of passive ownership in 2019 (27% vs 3%) → 152bp higher |Ret|, ~1/3 of the 476bp mean
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim, Section 3.1: 'a firm in the 90th percentile of passive ownership in 2019 (27%) has a 152 basis point higher |Ret| than a firm in the 10th percentile of passive ownership in 2019 (3%). For reference, 152 basis points is roughly 1/3rd of |Ret|'s whole sample mean of 476 basis points and 1/4th of its whole sample standard deviation of 621 basis points.' Arithmetic checks against Table 2 col 1: coefficient 0.0635 × 24pp = 0.01524. Unstated caveats: this is the EQUAL-weighted panel spec with firm + year-quarter FE; the value-weighted spec (col 5) has a smaller coefficient (0.0572) and a smaller VW mean |Ret| of 306bp. Sammon's own 'preferred' headline in the intro is the |Ret|/SD version (1.06 higher, ~1/2 of its 2.00 mean), which is a bigger number than 1/3 — so the article picked the more conservative of his two framings.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) IV estimates 2.5-4x OLS, first-stage F>200; published 'a 15% increase in passive ownership decreases pre-announcement informativeness by 1/4 of its mean' headline is the conservative OLS average; reduced form 'not always significant'
itemVerdicts.note: All three parts verified. Intro: 'across all four measures, the IV estimates are 2.5-4 times as large as the OLS estimates.' Appendix D.4/D.5: 'the first stage is very strong (F > 200 for both experiments)' — Table 3 reports F-statistics of 222.7 and 242. Conclusion, verbatim: 'taking the average of the point estimates from the OLS regressions implies that a 15% increase in passive ownership decreases pre-earnings announcement price informativeness by 1/4th of its whole sample mean and 1/6th of its whole sample standard deviation' — so the headline IS the OLS average, and it is conservative relative to the IV. Main text on the reduced form: 'the coefficient on Passive Gap × Treated × Post is not always significant.' TWO CALIBER FLAGS: (1) the appendix states it more harshly than the main text — D.4 says the interaction coefficient is 'almost always insignificant' and D.5 says the reduced form shows 'a consistently insignificant coefficient on one of the two instruments.' If the article calls this the 'real soft spot' it should use the appendix wording, not the main-text euphemism. (2) The article names only one soft spot; Appendix E is a second, arguably larger one: extending the sample to 1990-2022 shrinks the |Ret| OLS coefficient 'by a little more than a 1/3rd', 'nearly cut[s] in half' the |Ret|/SD and P J coefficients, and in the 2020-2022 subsample alone 'the coefficient on IV D switches sign'; in Table E10 the IV for IV D in the S&P experiment loses significance (0.093, s.e. 0.141). Sammon attributes this to COVID volatility, but it is an unresolved robustness weakness. Also note Panel B (S&P) PJ IV/OLS ratio is 1.568/0.248 ≈ 6.3x, above the stated 2.5-4x band — the band is the paper's own summary, not a tight bound.

itemVerdicts.item: (d-i) Sammon himself reconciles with Coles-Heath-Ringgenberg on TIMING (CHR = after, Sammon = before)
itemVerdicts.note: The reconciliation is real but is NOT in the cited PDF. WRONG: attributing it to https://marcosammon.com/images/sammon_passive.pdf or to the published Management Science (2025) paper. I grepped the October 2023 text for 'PEAD', 'post-earnings', 'drift', 'rapidly' — ZERO hits; that version mentions Coles et al. (2022) only in a list of papers finding a 'non-existent link', adding 'with one exception, none of these papers are focused on the effect of passive ownership on pre-earnings announcement price informativeness' (the exception is Kacperczyk et al., not CHR). RIGHT: the explicit timing reconciliation appears in the SUPERSEDED March 2023 HBS draft (hbs.edu/ris/Publication Files/sammon_passive march 23_886aa010-2cb8-476a-b698-7dfd03301561.pdf), verbatim: 'Another possible reason for a small PEAD, however, is that the earnings information was incorporated into prices before the announcement itself. Therefore, the Coles et al. (2022) result that PEADs are small is consistent with the idea that prices were uninformative before earnings announcements but information is rapidly incorporated after earnings announcements. In other words, passive ownership may be reducing price informativeness without meaningfully changing PEADs.' That March 2023 draft also has a DIFFERENT headline (decline of 'roughly 16%') and different measures (jump, DM, QVS — not the four in claim (a)), so the article must not blend the two versions.

itemVerdicts.item: (d-ii) 'CHR show information is fully impounded within ~2 days after announcements with no exploitable drift'
itemVerdicts.note: CHR do not show this. WRONG: 'information is fully impounded within ~2 days after announcements with no exploitable drift.' RIGHT: the '2 trading days' is the DEFINITION of a zero coefficient, not a finding — CHR (Jan 2022 draft, SSRN 3055324) write 'A value of Beta_PEAD = 0 corresponds to no post-earnings-announcement drift i.e. the stock incorporates all the information contained in the earnings announcement, on average, within 2 trading days after the announcement.' Their actual estimate is the opposite: 'The mean Beta_PEAD in our sample is 4.3%... The sample mean has a standard error of 0.6% and so the mean is strongly different from zero; that is, in our sample of mid-cap stocks, there is significant PEAD on average.' Their finding is that index investing does not CHANGE PEAD ('passive investing is not associated with any change in the speed of incorporation of new information into stock prices'), in a narrow population of Russell 1000/2000 cutoff mid-cap stocks. The 4.3% mean and the zero-treatment-effect result are identical in the 2017 draft, so this is not a version artifact. Sammon's own gloss 'the Coles et al. (2022) result that PEADs are small' is itself loose and should not be quoted as CHR's result.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Sammon's passive denominator: <1% → ~15% of US market cap 1990-2019, nowhere near 50%
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim three times. Intro: 'From 1990 to 2019, the share of U.S. equities held by passive investors rose from less than 1% to almost 15%.' Section 2.3: 'From 1990 to 2019, average passive ownership went from nearly zero to owning almost 15% of the US stock market. These numbers closely mirror those in the ICI factbook.' Conclusion: 'Relative to total institutional ownership, passive ownership is still small, owning only about 15% of the US stock market.' Definition (Figure 1 caption): 'the fraction of a stock's shares which are held by all index funds, all ETFs and all mutual funds with names that identify them as index funds' — so it is share of MARKET CAP held by explicitly-labelled index vehicles, not share of fund assets and not share of trading. MANDATORY CAVEAT the article must carry: Sammon's own footnote 16 concedes the measure 'only captures funds that are explicitly passive, and misses e.g., shadow index funds (Mauboussin, 2019), as well as institutions that do index replication internally,' and his own later coauthored paper (Chinco & Sammon, 'The passive ownership share is double what you think it is,' JFE 157 (2024) 103860) puts the true figure at more than double: 'While index funds held 16% of the US stock market in 2021, we put the overall passive ownership share at 33.5%.' So '~15%, nowhere near 50%' is correct for THIS paper's measure but would be a misuse of Sammon if deployed as a general rebuttal to high passive-share claims.

corrections: Do not write that CHR 'show information is fully impounded within ~2 days after announcements with no exploitable drift.' Coles, Heath & Ringgenberg report a mean Beta_PEAD of 4.3% with a standard error of 0.6%, i.e. 'in our sample of mid-cap stocks, there is significant PEAD on average.' The '2 trading days' phrase is only their definition of what a zero coefficient would mean. Their actual result is that index investing produces NO CHANGE in PEAD (a precisely-estimated null on the treatment effect), in a narrow Russell 1000/2000-cutoff mid-cap population — not that drift is absent.

Do not attribute the Sammon-vs-CHR timing reconciliation to https://marcosammon.com/images/sammon_passive.pdf or to Management Science (2025). The October 2023 version — the one whose abstract matches the published paper verbatim — contains no mention of PEAD, drift, or any timing reconciliation with Coles et al.; it lists them only among papers finding a 'non-existent link.' The reconciliation passage exists in the superseded March 2023 HBS draft. Either cite the March 2023 draft explicitly and label it as an earlier version, or drop 'Sammon's own reconciliation' and present the timing distinction as the article's own inference from the two papers' designs.

Do not import any other numbers from the March 2023 draft. That version reports a decline of 'roughly 16%' and uses three different measures (jump, DM, QVS); the published version reports ~1/4 of the whole-sample mean and 1/6 of the whole-sample standard deviation using four measures (|Ret|, |Ret|/SD, PJ, IVD). The April 2020 draft ('Earnings Announcements and the Rise of Passive Ownership') is different again. Cite Management Science 71(6), June 2025, pp. 4582-4598, DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2023.00836.

State the reduced-form weakness at the paper's own appendix caliber, not its main-text caliber. Main text says the interaction coefficient is 'not always significant'; Appendix D.4 says it is 'almost always insignificant' and D.5 says the reduced form shows 'a consistently insignificant coefficient on one of the two instruments.' Use the stronger wording if the article is flagging this as the soft spot.

Add the second, larger soft spot the claim omits: Appendix E shows that extending the sample to 1990-2022 shrinks the |Ret| OLS coefficient by more than a third, 'nearly cut[s] in half' the |Ret|/SD and PJ coefficients, and in the 2020-2022 subsample alone the IVD coefficient 'switches sign'; in the IV Table E10 the IVD estimate for the S&P experiment loses significance (0.093, s.e. 0.141). Sammon attributes this to COVID-era volatility making the learning problem harder — that is an explanation, not a resolution.
Label the 1990-2019 trend figures as VALUE-WEIGHTED quarterly averages (Figure 1's 'VW Avg.' series), not simple sample means, and note that rising values mean LESS pre-announcement informativeness.

When citing the 152bp cross-sectional effect, note it comes from the equal-weighted panel spec (Table 2, col 1); value-weighting shrinks the coefficient to 0.0572 against a value-weighted |Ret| mean of 306bp. Also note that Sammon's own 'preferred' intro framing uses |Ret|/SD, where the 90th-vs-10th gap is ~1/2 the whole-sample mean, i.e. larger than the 1/3 the article quotes.

If the article uses Sammon's ~15% figure to argue passive is 'nowhere near 50%', it must carry Sammon's own footnote 16 (the measure misses shadow indexing and internal index replication) and his own later result with Chinco (JFE 157, 2024, 103860): 'While index funds held 16% of the US stock market in 2021, we put the overall passive ownership share at 33.5%.' Otherwise the article cites Sammon against Sammon.

Optional precision: Sammon follows Coles et al. (2022) for Russell index-membership prediction and treated/control cohort construction, but his design is a Passive-Gap × Treated × Post IV/DiD, not CHR's own reduced-form treatment specification (and CHR explicitly note that post-2007 Russell methodology changes render 'traditional regression discontinuity designs infeasible'). 'Same Russell design as CHR' is defensible shorthand but 'follows CHR's Russell cohort construction' is exact. Also note his stated IV/OLS ratio band of 2.5-4x is the paper's summary, not a bound: the S&P panel's PJ ratio is ~6.3x.

And the 'Sammon's own reconciliation' half is misattributed: grepping the October 2023 / published text for PEAD, post-earnings, drift and rapidly returns zero hits, and Coles et al. appear there only inside a list of null-result papers. The reconciliation exists only in the superseded March 2023 draft, which carries different headline numbers — exactly the version-blending hazard flagged in the brief.

Remaining uncertainty: I could not open the typeset Management Science article itself (INFORMS is behind a Cloudflare JS challenge; SSRN blocked the request; the HBS faculty page returned 403). My inference that the published text contains no PEAD/CHR reconciliation rests on the October 2023 draft's abstract matching the Crossref-published abstract verbatim, which is strong but not conclusive — if anyone can open the typeset article, the single thing worth re-checking is whether a Coles/PEAD timing paragraph was reinstated in the literature review. I also searched for post-publication replications, comments or corrections through August 2026 and found none; search-result summaries repeatedly regurgitated superseded draft numbers (16%, 1990-2018, pre-earnings volume declines), which I discarded rather than relied on.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) One-SD PassiveFlow_SP500 (mean 0.05%, SD 0.09% quarterly, 1996-2020, 99 quarters) raises quarterly excess returns: top-10 +0.687% (t=2.46), top-50 +0.528% (t=3.66), top-100 +0.303%, top-150 +0.208%, top-200 +0.145% (t=1.64, insignificant)
itemVerdicts.note: CONFIRMED verbatim in both the LSE final PDF (Table 6.2 Panel B) and the published RFS typeset version (Table 5.2 Panel B, p.3490). Coefficients read exactly: 0.00687 (2.46), 0.00528 (3.66), 0.00303 (3.02), 0.00208 (2.28), 0.00145 (1.64); N=99 in every column; Controls=Y; Adj R2 0.049/0.125/0.105/0.124/0.125. Text: 'A one-standard-deviation increase in PassiveFlow_SP500 is associated with an increase in the quarterly excess return on the value-weighted portfolio of the top 200 firms by 0.145%, the top 150 firms by 0.208%, the top 100 firms by 0.303%, the top 50 firms by 0.528%, and the top 10 firms by 0.687%.' Descriptives: 'the mean and standard deviation of PassiveFlow_SP500 are 0.05% and 0.09%, respectively' and 'Since our sample comprises 99 quarters'. Sample stated as 'Our S&P500 sample begins in the second quarter of 1996 and ends in the fourth quarter of 2020' (=99 quarters exactly). Two caliber notes for the writer: (i) the dependent variables are returns IN EXCESS OF THE INDEX RETURN, not raw returns; (ii) the t=3.66 pairing for top-50 is the value-weighted-with-controls spec; Panel A shows the top-50 coefficient ranges 0.528%-0.557% with t from 3.65 to 4.19 across four specs, so 'the' top-50 estimate is spec-dependent within a narrow band.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) The 29% cumulative figure is the authors' own linear extrapolation (0.528% x (0.05/0.09) x 99 = 29.04%); the calibrated model predicts only 0-4% for the same object; authors say the estimate 'is larger than in our calibration' and can partly mean-revert
itemVerdicts.note: CONFIRMED verbatim. Published text (p.3491): 'the cumulative effect of PassiveFlow_SP500 on the excess return on the value-weighted top-50 firm portfolio is 0.528% x 0.05%/0.09% x 99 = 29.04%. According to this estimate, the rise in passive investing over the past 25 years caused a firm that was in the top 50 of the S&P500 index during the entire period to rise by 29% more than the index.' Next paragraph: 'The estimated 29% effect of passive flows in Table 5.2 is larger than in our calibration. For example, the difference between the return on size group 5 and the average return on size groups 3, 4, and 5 in Tables 4.2-4.5 ranges from zero (Table 4.2, switch from active to passive, all firms in index) to 4% (Table 4.5, switch from active to passive, size groups 3-5 in index).' And: 'Second, the 30% estimate concerns a contemporaneous effect of passive flows, which can partly mean-revert.' So 0-4% calibration range, the 'larger than in our calibration' quote, and the mean-reversion caveat are all exact. Note the paper's own back-reference says '30% estimate' where the computed figure is 29.04% - an internal rounding slip in the source; do not present '30%' as a distinct estimate.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) The mechanism is explicitly NOT informational ('information in our model is symmetric'); using JVZ as 'passive breaks price discovery' evidence misreads it; it is a relative-price (top-50 vs index) distortion claim
itemVerdicts.note: CONFIRMED verbatim. Introduction, published p.3462: 'These effects are generated by a different mechanism than in the REE and index-addition literatures because information in our model is symmetric and the effects arise even when indices include all firms.' The preceding sentences attribute the 'prices less informative' channel to OTHER work (Grossman 1976; Grossman and Stiglitz 1980), not to themselves. A full-text grep for 'informativ' finds only that one attribution sentence - JVZ make no price-informativeness or price-discovery finding of their own. The 29% object is indeed relative: every left-hand-side variable in Table 5.2 is a large-stock portfolio return 'in excess of the index return'. CAVEAT the article must not overshoot: JVZ do ALSO make an aggregate-level claim - 'the effects on the largest firms can be sufficiently strong to cause the aggregate market to rise even when the growth of passive funds comes entirely from investors switching from active funds... Passive investing thus biases the stock market toward overvaluation.' So 'not informational' and 'the 29% is relative' are both correct, but 'JVZ is only a relative-price claim with no aggregate implication' would be wrong.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Placebo: no significant effect for large stocks in the S&P600
itemVerdicts.note: CONFIRMED. Published Table 5.4 (p.3493): PassiveFlow_S&P600 coefficients are -0.00541 (-1.26), -0.00540 (-1.04), -0.00397 (-0.94), -0.00392 (-0.75); N=77, 77, 76, 76. Text: 'Consistent with our model, the relationship between passive flows and excess returns on large stocks in the S&P600 is statistically insignificant.' Two precision notes: the S&P600 portfolio is the top 60 firms (the top size decile counterpart of the S&P500 top 50), and the S&P600 sample is a DIFFERENT, shorter window - 'Our S&P600 sample begins in the fourth quarter of 2001 and ends in the fourth quarter of 2020' - so this is not a same-sample placebo. Also, point estimates are negative, not merely near zero.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Idiosyncratic volatility: top-50 differential significant (t=2.53) but non-top-50 main effect NOT (t=1.21)
itemVerdicts.note: CONFIRMED. Published Table 5.3: L.PassiveFlow_SP500 x Top50 = 19.32 (t=2.53) in the firm-FE column and 18.46 (t=2.45) in the firm+time-FE column; L.PassiveFlow_SP500 = 20.63 (t=1.21), present only in the first column (dropped when time FE are added). N=45,737; SEs double-clustered by firm and time. Text: 'Moreover, the incremental effect for large firms is statistically significant, while the effect for other firms is not.' Magnitudes: 1.86% (=20.63 x 0.09%) for non-top-50 and 3.60% (=(19.32+20.63) x 0.09%) for top-50. Note the regressor is ONE-QUARTER-LAGGED passive flow, and the dependent variable is log idiosyncratic volatility (quarterly SD of daily FF3 residual returns).

corrections: Cite the PUBLISHED version and its table numbers, not the preprint's. In RFS 38(12) 2025, pp. 3461-3496 the empirical section is Section 5: the return regression is Table 5.2 (not 6.2), idiosyncratic volatility is Table 5.3 (not 6.3), the S&P600 placebo is Table 5.4 (not 6.4), and the calibration tables the 0-4% range comes from are Tables 4.2-4.5 (not 5.2-5.5). The preprint at personal.lse.ac.uk/vayanos/Papers/PIRMF_RFSf.pdf uses the 6.x/5.x numbering; the printed journal does not.

State that the left-hand-side variable is the large-stock portfolio return IN EXCESS OF THE S&P500 INDEX RETURN. The 29% is explicitly 'rise by 29% more than the index' - a relative-price wedge between mega-caps and the rest of the index, NOT a claim that the index or the market is 29% overvalued.

Do not write that JVZ show passive investing has no aggregate price effect. Alongside the relative result they argue the opposite at the market level: 'the effects on the largest firms can be sufficiently strong to cause the aggregate market to rise even when the growth of passive funds comes entirely from investors switching from active funds... Passive investing thus biases the stock market toward overvaluation.' The correct framing is: the ESTIMATED 29% is relative; the aggregate claim is a model result, not a reduced-form estimate.

If the article quotes the mean-reversion caveat, quote it as the paper writes it: 'the 30% estimate concerns a contemporaneous effect of passive flows, which can partly mean-revert.' The paper says 30% there while the computed figure two sentences earlier is 29.04% - this is an internal rounding slip in JVZ, not a second estimate. Do not present 29% and 30% as two different findings.

The S&P600 placebo runs on a different and shorter sample (2001Q4-2020Q4, N=76-77) than the main S&P500 test (1996Q2-2020Q4, N=99), and it uses the top 60 S&P600 firms (the top size decile). Do not describe it as a same-sample, same-portfolio placebo. Its point estimates are negative (-0.0054 to -0.0039), not approximately zero.

Do not cite NBER w28253 (Dec 2020, rev. Sept 2022) for these numbers. That version reports a different headline - 'a one-standard-deviation increase in PassiveFlow is associated with an increase in the quarterly excess returns of large stocks by 0.55%' - and contains no 29.04% cumulative extrapolation and no top-10/100/150/200 ladder. The ladder and the 29% figure appear only in the 2024+/RFS version.

For (e), specify that the flow regressor is one-quarter LAGGED and the dependent variable is log idiosyncratic volatility (quarterly SD of daily Fama-French 3-factor residual returns). Also note the insignificant 20.63 main effect exists only in the firm-FE specification; it is dropped in the firm+time-FE specification, so 'passive flows raise volatility for non-mega-caps too' has no significant support in either column.
newContradictions: JVZ's calibrated model produces a 0-4% relative effect while their own reduced-form estimate is 29% - roughly an order of magnitude gap that the authors flag but do not resolve. Any article using the 29% figure as the headline quantification of index-driven mega-cap distortion is using the number the paper's own structural model does not reproduce.

JVZ explicitly place themselves OUTSIDE the Grossman-Stiglitz informational channel ('information in our model is symmetric'). If the article elsewhere leans on Grossman-Stiglitz / price-informativeness framing for the index-bubble thesis, JVZ cannot be stacked as corroborating evidence for that channel - it is an independent, non-informational mechanism (idiosyncratic risk of large high-demand firms deterring arbitrage).

JVZ cite Haddad-Huebner-Loualiche (2025, Figure 3) approvingly for smaller demand elasticities among large firms. HHL is often deployed in the opposite direction in this debate (active investors' aggregate elasticity has not fallen / demand has adapted). The article should not use HHL and JVZ as if they point the same way without stating which specific HHL result each claim rests on.

JVZ's own S&P600 placebo showing negative and insignificant coefficients means the mechanism is size-in-the-ECONOMY specific, not indexing-specific. Passive flows into a small-cap index do not distort that index's large stocks. This cuts against any generic 'passive flows distort whatever they buy' framing.

PassiveFlow S P500  20.63 (1.21)'; N=45,737, firm FE, double-clustered by firm and time. corrections: Do not describe JVZ as purely a relative-price claim. Its empirical estimates are relative (top-N returns in excess of the S&P500 index return), but the model additionally claims market-level overvaluation: verbatim 'Passive investing thus biases the stock market toward overvaluation', with a pure active-to-passive switch raising the aggregate market by 0.09% (Table 4.4) and 1.47%/1.68% (Table 4.5) in calibration.

Qualify the top-200 result as 'not significant at the 5% level' rather than flatly 'insignificant'. The paper prints no significance stars; t=1.64 (Newey-West, 3 lags, N=99) is roughly p=0.10, and the paper never itself labels this coefficient insignificant.

State that Table 5.2 is a CONTEMPORANEOUS same-quarter regression of excess returns on passive flows, with controls only for the S&P500 return, its one-quarter lag, and VIX. The authors themselves flag this: 'the 30% estimate concerns a contemporaneous effect of passive flows, which can partly mean-revert.' Only the idiosyncratic-volatility regression (Table 5.3) uses lagged flows. The abstract's word 'following' overstates the timing for returns.

Do not call the S&P600 result a 'placebo'. The paper presents it as a directional test of its second model prediction (the effect appears only when the index's largest firms are also the economy's largest). Give the correct details: portfolio is the top 60 S&P600 firms, sample 2001Q4-2020Q4 (N=77/76, not 99), and coefficients are negative (-0.00541 to -0.00392, t between -1.26 and -0.75).

If quoting the calibration comparison, note the authors write both '29%' and 'the 30% estimate' in adjacent sentences, and that the 0-4% model benchmark is specifically 'the difference between the return on size group 5 and the average return on size groups 3, 4, and 5 in Tables 4.2-4.5' - an analogue of, not literally identical to, the empirical top-50-minus-index object.

The top-50 coefficient of 0.528% is the value-weighted, with-controls specification; the paper's own reported range across the four Panel A specifications is 0.528%-0.557% with t from 3.65 to 4.19. Use the range if the article implies robustness.

Specify the flow variable's construction if the article characterizes it: PassiveFlow_SP500 is the quarterly CHANGE in the ratio of S&P500 index-fund (mutual fund plus three plain-vanilla ETFs) net assets to S&P500 market capitalization - i.e. a change in passive ownership share, not a dollar flow - and it is standardized to mean 0, SD 1 in the regressions.
newContradictions: The paper's own abstract and headline ('prices ... rise the most FOLLOWING flows into that index') is in tension with the return regressions being contemporaneous rather than predictive; the authors concede this in the mean-reversion caveat. Any article leaning on JVZ for a causal 'passive flows caused the mega-cap run' story must carry this caveat.

JVZ's reduced-form 29% is roughly 7x-to-infinite the range its own structural calibration produces (0%-4%). The authors offer two reconciliations (fewer truly active investors than calibrated; contemporaneous effect that partly mean-reverts) but do not resolve it. Citing 29% without the calibration gap is the single largest caliber risk in this group.

JVZ's aggregate-market claim ('biases the stock market toward overvaluation') is a MODEL result only - the calibrated magnitudes are 0.09%-1.68%, i.e. small - and is not separately tested empirically. Do not present the 29% empirical number as an estimate of aggregate market overvaluation; it is a top-50-versus-index differential.
reasoning:
I worked from the published RFS text, not a summary. Primary document reached verbatim: the LSE Research Online copy of the OUP typeset published version (local extraction jvz_published_v1.txt in the scratchpad), whose cover page states 'Review of Financial Studies, 38(12), 3461 - 3496, https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhaf085' and whose running heads read 'The Review of Financial Studies / v 38 n 12 2025' with the relevant pages numbered 3489-3493 — so the citation in the claim group (RFS 38(12) 2025, 3461-3496) is correct. I also cross-read the June 19, 2025 accepted manuscript (jvz.txt), which carries identical coefficients (0.00687, 0.00528, 29.04%, t=2.53/1.21/1.64) at its Table 6.2/6.3 numbering, and the September 2022 NBER revision (jvz_nber.txt), which is materially DIFFERENT: its Table 8 reports 0.00549/0.00550/0.00523/0.00525 with t of 3.60/3.67/4.14/3.64, has no top-10/100/150/200 decomposition, and contains NO 29% cumulative extrapolation. So the version-drift risk this literature carries is real here, and the article's numbers are correctly drawn from the published version, not the working paper.

Every number in (a), (b), (d), and (e) matched the published tables and body text exactly — I read Tables 5.1, 5.2 (Panels A and B), 5.3, 5.4, 4.1, 4.2, 4.4, 4.5 and the surrounding prose. I independently re-derived the calibration benchmark from Table 4.5 (group-5 minus average of groups 3-5 gives 3.63pp constant-bn, 3.37pp varying-bn) rather than taking the authors' '4%' on faith, and confirmed Table 4.2's switch-to-passive column is literally all zeros. I confirmed the 'information in our model is symmetric' clause and the 'Passive investing thus biases the stock market toward overvaluation' sentence by exact string match against the whitespace-normalized full text, not by any fetch summarizer.

The verdict is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS on two qualifier grounds, both in the article's framing rather than its arithmetic. First, (c)'s claim that JVZ 'is a relative-price (top-50 vs index) distortion claim' is true of the empirics but understates the paper: the model explicitly claims aggregate-market overvaluation (calibrated at 0.09%, 1.47%, 1.68%). An article that says JVZ makes no market-level claim would be wrong. Second, (d)'s 'placebo' label is the article's, not the paper's — the paper frames the S&P600 result as a positive directional test of its second prediction, on a different sample (2001Q4-2020Q4, N=77/76) and a different portfolio (top 60), with negative point estimates. I also flag that the paper prints no significance stars, so 'insignificant' for t=1.64 is an inference at the 5% level (p roughly 0.10), and that Table 5.2 is contemporaneous while Table 5.3 uses lagged flows — a distinction the article should preserve.

Remaining uncertainty: I searched for a post-publication erratum, comment, or replication up to 2026-08 and found none indexed. Two web-search summarizers returned unreliable output in the process — one asserted the paper was published in March 2025 (the DOI issue is 38(12), 2025, received July 4 2024, editorial decision June 28 2025), and another conflated the 29% cumulative extrapolation with a 29.71% CAPM R-squared from the calibration section. I discarded both and relied only on the PDF text. I did not independently verify the Internet Appendix E.3 robustness tests (index-concentration regressions, beginning-of-month dummy, idiosyncratic-beta earnings-announcement test) — the main text describes them but I did not reach the appendix file, so any article claim resting on those specific appendix numbers is outside what I checked.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) One-SD increase in PassiveFlow_SP500 (mean 0.05%, SD 0.09% quarterly, 1996-2020, 99 quarters) raises quarterly excess returns: top-10 +0.687% (t=2.46), top-50 +0.528% (t=3.66), top-100 +0.303%, top-150 +0.208%, top-200 +0.145% (t=1.64, insignificant)
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in Table 6.2 Panel B of the accepted version (= Table 5.2 in RFS published version, p.3490). Coefficients 0.00687 (2.46), 0.00528 (3.66), 0.00303 (3.02), 0.00208 (2.28), 0.00145 (1.64); N=99, controls Y, Adj-R2 0.049/0.125/0.105/0.124/0.125. Table 6.1 (=5.1): PassiveFlow_SP500 mean 0.05, SD 0.09, N=99. Text: 'A one-standard-deviation increase in PassiveFlow_SP500 is associated with an increase in the quarterly excess return on the value-weighted portfolio of the top 200 firms by 0.145%, the top 150 firms by 0.208%, the top 100 firms by 0.303%, the top 50 firms by 0.528%, and the top 10 firms by 0.687%.' Sample is 1996Q2-2020Q4 = 99 quarters. TWO PRECISION CAVEATS the article must carry: (i) 'excess return' here means IN EXCESS OF THE S&P 500 INDEX RETURN, not over the risk-free rate ('quarterly returns on portfolios of large stocks in the S&P500 index in excess of the index return'); the top-N portfolios have NEGATIVE unconditional means (-0.02 to -0.19 per quarter). (ii) the regression is CONTEMPORANEOUS quarterly OLS with Newey-West(3) errors and controls (S&P500 return, lagged S&P500 return, VIX), not an identified causal design; the paper itself calls it 'a contemporaneous effect.' Also note the omitted middle t-stats are all significant (top-100 t=3.02, top-150 t=2.28), so the ladder is not monotone in significance the way a 'only the very top matters' reading would suggest. 'Insignificant' for t=1.64 is correct at the 5% level and (barely) at 10%.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) The '29%' cumulative claim is the authors' own linear extrapolation (0.528% x (0.05/0.09) x 99 = 29.04%); the calibrated model predicts only 0-4% for the same object; authors say the estimate 'is larger than in our calibration' and can partly mean-revert
itemVerdicts.note: The extrapolation and the 0-4% range are verbatim; the phrase 'for the same object' is WRONG as stated. RIGHT: the paper's own text is 'the cumulative effect of PassiveFlow_SP500 on the excess return on the value-weighted top-50 firm portfolio is 0.528% x (0.05%/0.09%) x 99 = 29.04%. According to this estimate, the rise in passive investing over the past 25 years caused a firm that was in the top 50 of the S&P500 index during the entire period to rise by 29% more than the index.' Then: 'The estimated 29% effect of passive flows in Table 5.2 is larger than in our calibration.' The calibration benchmark is NOT 'the same object': it is 'the difference between the return on size group 5 and the average return on size groups 3, 4, and 5 in Tables 4.2-4.5' which 'ranges from zero (Table 4.2, switch from active to passive, all firms in index) to 4% (Table 4.5, switch from active to passive, size groups 3-5 in index)' - i.e. the model's largest-size-group vs large-stock-average differential, not top-50 vs the whole index. Mean-reversion caveat verbatim: 'Second, the 30% estimate concerns a contemporaneous effect of passive flows, which can partly mean-revert.' Note the paper is internally inconsistent in rounding: it computes 29.04%, says '29%', then one sentence later calls it 'the 30% estimate' (this is where press/secondary coverage's '30%' comes from; neither 29% nor 30% appears in the abstract).

itemVerdicts.item: (c) The mechanism is explicitly NOT informational ('information in our model is symmetric'); using JVZ as 'passive breaks price discovery' evidence misreads it; it is a relative-price (top-50 vs index) distortion claim
itemVerdicts.note: The quote is verbatim and the core point holds, but the second half needs a qualifier. VERBATIM (intro, both versions): 'These effects are generated by a different mechanism than in the REE and index-addition literatures because information in our model is symmetric and the effects arise even when indices include all firms.' The paper explicitly contrasts itself with the Grossman-Stiglitz price-discovery channel, so citing JVZ as evidence that passive degrades informational efficiency IS a misreading. WRONG as stated: 'it is a relative-price (top-50 vs index) distortion claim' full stop. RIGHT: the EMPIRICS are relative-price (top-N vs index), but the MODEL also makes an aggregate-level overvaluation claim - 'the aggregate market can rise even when flows are entirely due to investors switching from active to passive funds... Passive investing thus biases the stock market toward overvaluation.' And 'symmetric information' does not mean 'no mispricing': the paper states 'A switch from active to passive exacerbates noise-trader mispricing in our model as well. Our main results, however, concern how the effects of passive flows depend on stock size, and hold even in the absence of noise traders.' The stated mechanism is idiosyncratic-risk-based: passive flows raise the idiosyncratic risk of large high-demand firms, which deters arbitrageurs from correcting the price effect.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Placebo: no significant effect for large stocks in the S&P 600
itemVerdicts.note: Verified in Table 6.4 (=Table 5.4 published, p.3494). PassiveFlow_SP600 coefficients on the top-60 S&P600 portfolio: -0.00541 (-1.26), -0.00540 (-1.04), -0.00397 (-0.94), -0.00392 (-0.75); N=77 (76 with controls). Text: 'Consistent with our model, the relationship between passive flows and excess returns on large stocks in the S&P600 is statistically insignificant.' Precision notes: the authors do not use the word 'placebo' - they frame it as a test of the model's second prediction, that flows raise an index's largest firms only when those firms are also the largest in the ECONOMY. The test regresses S&P600 top-60 excess returns on S&P600 (not S&P500) passive flows over a shorter sample (2001Q4-2020Q4, 77 quarters), and all point estimates are negative. Low power is a live alternative reading of the null.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Idiosyncratic volatility: the top-50 differential is significant (t=2.53) but the non-top-50 main effect is NOT (t=1.21)
itemVerdicts.note: Verified in Table 6.3 (=Table 5.3 published). L.PassiveFlow_SP500 x Top50 = 19.32 (t=2.53) with firm FE, 18.46 (t=2.45) with firm+time FE; L.PassiveFlow_SP500 main effect = 20.63 (t=1.21), dropped in the time-FE column. N=45,737, double-clustered by firm and time. The paper's own sentence: 'the incremental effect for large firms is statistically significant while the effect for other firms is not.' Worth carrying: the insignificant main effect is nonetheless economically large - the paper reads it as +1.86% idio vol per SD for non-top-50 firms, 'approximately doubl[ing]' to 3.60% for the top 50 - so this is not evidence that passive flows leave smaller firms' volatility alone, only that the level effect is imprecisely estimated.

corrections: Do not write that JVZ's calibrated model predicts 0-4% 'for the same object' as the 29% reduced-form estimate. The calibration benchmark is a different construct: the model's difference between the return on size group 5 and the average return on size groups 3, 4 and 5 (Tables 4.2-4.5 published / 5.2-5.5 accepted version), which 'ranges from zero ... to 4%' depending on index breadth. Phrase it as: the reduced-form 29% is roughly an order of magnitude larger than the closest analogue the authors' own calibration produces.

Define 'excess return' every time this result is cited: the dependent variable is the top-N portfolio return IN EXCESS OF THE S&P 500 INDEX RETURN, not in excess of the risk-free rate. The '29%' therefore means a top-50 firm rose 29% MORE THAN THE INDEX over 25 years - it is not a claim that passive flows added 29% to the market. The unconditional quarterly means of these excess-return series are negative (-0.02% to -0.19%).

Do not describe JVZ as showing that passive investing is a relative-price distortion only. The model additionally claims that the largest-firm effect is strong enough that the aggregate market rises even under a pure active-to-passive switch - 'Passive investing thus biases the stock market toward overvaluation.' Conversely, do not describe the model as having no mispricing: it states 'A switch from active to passive exacerbates noise-trader mispricing in our model as well,' while the size-dependent main results 'hold even in the absence of noise traders.'

Attribute causal language carefully. The estimates come from contemporaneous quarterly OLS (Newey-West, 3 lags) with S&P500 return, lagged S&P500 return and VIX as controls - not from an identified shock. The authors themselves flag that 'the 30% estimate concerns a contemporaneous effect of passive flows, which can partly mean-revert.'

If the article says 'insignificant' for the top-200 result, specify the level: t=1.64 is insignificant at 5% and marginal at 10%. Do not present the size ladder as 'only the top 10/50 matter' - top-100 (t=3.02) and top-150 (t=2.28) are also significant; what declines monotonically is the magnitude, not significance across the whole ladder.

Cite the RFS 2025 version, not NBER w28253. The NBER working paper (Dec 2020, rev. Sept 2022) reports a single 'large stocks' regression with coefficients 0.549/0.550/0.523/0.525 (t = 3.60/3.67/4.14/3.64) and contains NO top-10/50/100/150/200 ladder and NO 29% cumulative extrapolation. Those are additions in the published version.

If quoting the cumulative figure, use 29% (the paper's computed 29.04%) and note that the paper itself back-refers to it as 'the 30% estimate' one sentence later. Secondary coverage citing '30%' is echoing that loose sentence, not a separate result; neither number appears in the abstract.
newContradictions: The paper is internally inconsistent on the headline number: it computes 0.528% x (0.05%/0.09%) x 99 = 29.04% and says '29% more than the index', then in the very next paragraph refers to 'the 30% estimate'. Secondary sources (e.g. press coverage) circulate '30%' as if it were the paper's figure. Both trace to the same single regression coefficient.

The paper cites Ben-David, Franzoni and Moussawi (2018) and Haddad, Huebner and Loualiche (2025) as corroborating that large firms are less elastic - but BDFM (2018) is also the paper JVZ cite in footnote 5 as finding that ETFs LOWER informational efficiency for underlying stocks. Anyone using JVZ's own citation chain to argue an informational-efficiency story is borrowing from BDFM, not from JVZ, whose model has symmetric information.

The idiosyncratic-volatility result (Table 6.3/5.3) points in the OPPOSITE direction from Chabakauri-Rytchkov, whose abstract says indexing DECREASES market volatility. These are different objects (firm-level idiosyncratic vol vs. market vol) and should not be presented as a consistent body of evidence without saying so.
reasoning:
Primary documents reached verbatim, two independent copies. (1) I re-downloaded the cited URL https://personal.lse.ac.uk/vayanos/Papers/PIRMF_RFSf.pdf myself with curl; MD5 23b7e1e108cad33ce876f38403cf1582 matched the pre-existing local jvz.pdf, so the local extraction is trustworthy. I re-ran pdftotext -layout on my own download and read Tables 6.1, 6.2, 6.3, 6.4 and surrounding text directly (accepted version, dated June 19, 2025). (2) I cross-checked every figure against the OUP published version (LSE Research Online copy of the RFS typeset PDF, download stamp academic.oup.com/rfs/article/38/12/3461/8280528), confirming RFS 38 (2025) 3461-3496, DOI 10.1093/rfs/hhaf085, Advance Access 10 Oct 2025, and that all coefficients, t-stats, N and the 29.04% arithmetic are IDENTICAL between accepted and published versions. Note table renumbering: accepted Tables 6.1-6.4 = published Tables 5.1-5.4; accepted Tables 5.2-5.5 = published 4.2-4.5.

Version-drift check (the prompt warned about it, and it is real here): the NBER w28253 version (Dec 2020, revised Sept 2022) reports only a single pooled 'large stocks' regression (0.00549/0.00550/0.00523/0.00525, t 3.60/3.67/4.14/3.64), with no size ladder and no cumulative extrapolation. The 29% figure and the top-10/50/100/150/200 breakdown exist only in the 2025 published/accepted version. The claim group is therefore correctly sourced.

Every number in sub-claims (a), (d) and (e) reproduces verbatim; I read them off the tables rather than the narrative. The 29.04% arithmetic checks (0.528 x 0.5556 x 99 = 29.04). The 'information in our model is symmetric' quote is verbatim in both versions.

Two caliber problems drive the CORRECTED verdict rather than HOLDS. First, (b)'s phrase 'for the same object' is not accurate: the calibration's 0-4% range refers to the model's size-group-5 minus average-of-size-groups-3-to-5 differential, an analogue the authors chose, not literally top-50 vs the index. Second, (c) understates the paper by reducing it to a relative-price claim - the model's headline result includes an aggregate overvaluation claim, and the paper does say a switch to passive exacerbates noise-trader mispricing (just not via an information channel). Separately, 'excess return' throughout means excess over the INDEX return, a distinction that will mislead readers if the article does not spell it out; I flagged it as a required qualifier though it is not an error in the claim as written.

I actively searched for post-publication corrections, errata, comments and replications through 2026-08 and found none: no erratum indexed at OUP/RePEc/LSE RO, no comment paper, no replication. Absence of a correction is the finding; I did not verify OUP's errata page directly beyond search indexing, so a very recent erratum cannot be fully excluded.

No fabrication risk incurred: every quoted string was read from pdftotext output of a file I hashed myself, not from a WebFetch summary. The only web tool used was WebSearch, and I used it solely to look for corrections/critiques - I discarded its assertion that 'the main paper shows ... 30%' as an unverified summarizer gloss, then traced the real source of that number to the paper's own line 'the 30% estimate concerns a contemporaneous effect'.

Remaining uncertainty: I did not independently verify the Internet Appendix E.3 robustness tests (index-concentration regressions, beginning-of-month dummy, idiosyncratic betas) - they are referenced in the main text but live in supplementary material I did not open. None of the five sub-claims depend on them.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) The "16%" is, in the paper's own text, "a 20 bps increase in daily volatility, which represents 16% of a standard deviation of the dependent variable"
itemVerdicts.note: The sentence is verbatim CORRECT — but in the NBER WORKING PAPER, not verifiably in the published JF article. I re-downloaded https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w20071/w20071.pdf (md5 2b7eb3e0916cc04a9d135a01eca69614, identical to local bdfm2.pdf) and read Section 4.3: "In Column (1), a one standard deviation increase in stock ownership for S&P 500 stocks (1.44%) is associated with a 20 bps increase in daily volatility, which represents 16% of a standard deviation of the dependent variable." Footnote 15 gives the arithmetic: "(0.146 * 1.440) / 1.290 = 0.1630." CAUTION on the exact wording: the NBER *revision* file (w20071/revisions/w20071.rev0.pdf, md5 84d60da3...) renders the same sentence as "16% of THE standard deviation". WRONG: attributing this quote to "Ben-David, Franzoni & Moussawi, Journal of Finance 73(6), 2018." RIGHT: attribute to NBER Working Paper No. 20071 (April 2014, rev. June 2014), Section 4.3 / Table 4, Column (1). The published JF text is paywalled with no OA accepted version (Unpaywall/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar all point only back to the NBER WP), so I could not confirm the sentence survived into the published article — and the published version is materially revised (sample extended to Dec 2015, RDD on index membership foregrounded, a new risk-premium result added).

itemVerdicts.item: (a) It is a one-SD (1.44% of market cap) increase in ETF ownership, S&P 500 STOCKS ONLY
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim "(1.44%)" in the sentence above, and confirmed against Table 1 Panel B (monthly frequency, S&P 500): "ETF ownership (%; average within the month)" Mean 2.110, Std Dev 1.440 — so the SD is 1.44 percentage points of stock market cap. Population is correct: "In Columns (1) to (3), we limit the sample to S&P 500 stocks, and in Columns (4) to (6), we extend it to Russell 3000 stocks." The dependent variable is "Daily stock volatility (%)", the SD of daily returns within a month; for S&P 500 stocks its Mean is 2.080 and Std Dev 1.290, which is the 1.290 denominator in footnote 15.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Extended to smaller stocks the effect is ~5% of a SD
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: "Extending the universe to smaller stocks (Column (4)), the effect is diluted, amounting to about 5% of a standard deviation." Footnote 16: "(0.044 * 1.730) / 1.490 = 0.0511." One precision note: Column (4) is the Russell 3000 universe (which contains the large stocks too), not a small-stock-only subsample — the paper's own phrase is "extending the universe to smaller stocks", so the article's wording tracks the source.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Quoting it as "16% higher volatility" is a caliber error
itemVerdicts.note: The substance is RIGHT — 16% of a standard deviation is not 16% higher volatility; against the S&P 500 mean daily volatility of 2.080%, the 20 bps coefficient is about 9.6% higher volatility, not 16%. But the article must not pin the error solely on secondary popularizers. WRONG: implying the loose reading is purely third-party sloppiness. RIGHT: the NBER WP's OWN ABSTRACT says "an increase of one standard deviation in ETF ownership is associated with an increase of 16% in daily stock volatility" — the ambiguity originates with the authors' working-paper abstract. The WP's own introduction states it correctly: "the effect of a one standard deviation increase in ETF ownership is about 16% of a standard deviation of daily volatility."

itemVerdicts.item: (b) CRITICAL: does the PUBLISHED JF abstract contain the "16%" phrasing?
itemVerdicts.note: SETTLED — NO. The published JF abstract does NOT contain "16%" anywhere. Verified against three independent primary/publisher sources that agree word for word: (1) Wiley's own Crossref JATS deposit for 10.1111/jofi.12727 (fetched live from api.crossref.org); (2) the American Finance Association's own journal issue page, https://afajof.org/issue/volume-73-issue-6/, which prints the abstract inline under "Do ETFs Increase Volatility? | Pages: 2471-2535"; (3) RePEc/EconPapers/IDEAS (series maintained by "Wiley Content Delivery"). The real published abstract reads: "Due to their low trading costs, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are a potential catalyst for short-horizon liquidity traders. The liquidity shocks can propagate to the underlying securities through the arbitrage channel, and ETFs may increase the nonfundamental volatility of the securities in their baskets. We exploit exogenous changes in index membership and find that stocks with higher ETF ownership display significantly higher volatility. ETF ownership increases the negative autocorrelation in stock prices. The increase in volatility appears to introduce undiversifiable risk in prices because stocks with high ETF ownership earn a significant risk premium of up to 56 basis points monthly." So the RePEc "56 basis points" headline is the CORRECT published abstract; the "16%" abstract belongs to NBER WP w20071 only. Note the contamination vector: Semantic Scholar's record for DOI 10.1111/JOFI.12727 serves the NBER WP abstract (with the 16% sentence) under the published DOI — that is how the wrong abstract propagates.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) ETF ownership raises negative autocorrelation
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed, and it is specifically a PUBLISHED-version claim. Verbatim in the JF abstract: "ETF ownership increases the negative autocorrelation in stock prices." The 2014 NBER WP never uses the phrase "negative autocorrelation" for this result (grep returns nothing); it says ETFs "add a mean-reverting component to stock prices both intraday (Table 5) and at the daily frequency (Table 6)." So this phrasing should be cited to JF 2018, not to the WP.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) ~45% of flow-driven price shocks revert within 20 days (so ~55% permanent)
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as a description of the published paper. RIGHT for the 2014 WP only. WP verbatim: "after twenty days, about 45% of the initial shock has reverted. Extending the horizon farther out to forty days does not increase the magnitude of reversals (not reported), which suggests that on average flows convey fundamental and non-fundamental shocks in roughly equal shares." But the PUBLISHED version's own Internet Appendix (authors' site, https://people.lu.usi.ch/franzonf/ETF%20internet%20appendix.pdf — carries Moussawi's Villanova affiliation and samples running to Dec 2015, i.e. the final version) states: "our evidence on the price impact of ETF flows, which we have updated through 2015 and reported in Table VII, suggests that, following ETF flows, the half-life to convergence of prices to the initial level is about 10 days." A ~10-day half-life to FULL convergence is not a 45%-reverts/55%-permanent split. The article should either drop the "~55% permanent" inference or explicitly flag it as the 2014 working-paper result superseded by the published Table VII.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) The efficiency deterioration is at 15-SECOND horizons (microstructure), not allocative informativeness
itemVerdicts.note: The "not allocative informativeness" qualifier STANDS — neither version measures price informativeness about fundamentals; the measure is a random-walk-deviation variance ratio. But the "15-second" horizon is WP-only. WP verbatim: "price efficiency deteriorates for stocks with higher ETF ownership at the fifteen second frequency", with the variance ratio built as 15-second return variance over 3x the 5-second variance, chosen "on the observation that information about NAV is disseminated by ETF sponsors at fifteen second" intervals. In the PUBLISHED version, the Internet Appendix's variable table (I.A. Table AI) defines the headline measure as "Variance ratio 5 [days]: The ratio of 5-day return variance divided by 5 times the 1-day return variance minus 1. The numerator and denominator are computed using daily and 5-day returns within a quarter" — a daily-to-weekly horizon, matching the published abstract's "negative autocorrelation in stock prices." The intraday variance ratio survives only in an IA robustness table (I.A. Table AXVI, Panel B). RIGHT: say the WP documented the deviation at a 15-second horizon, while the published paper documents it at daily-to-weekly horizons (5-day vs 1-day variance ratio) — in both cases a random-walk/noise measure, not allocative informativeness.

itemVerdicts.item: Published JF main text (pp. 2471-2535) body verification
itemVerdicts.note: Could not reach. Wiley returns HTTP 403 to both WebFetch and curl for /doi/abs/ and /doi/full/; SSRN (abstract_id 1967599 and 2430066, the links the authors themselves post on their OSU page) is behind Cloudflare and returns 403; ResearchGate is "Request PDF" only; Unpaywall/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar/fatcat list the NBER WP as the only OA copy; the NBER revision endpoints rev1-rev3 are 404 and rev0 is still the April 2014 / rev. June 2014 text; the Jacobs Levy Center copy (jacobslevycenter.wharton.upenn.edu/.../Moussawi_Paper.pdf) is also the April 2014 version. I therefore cannot confirm verbatim whether the "20 bps / 16% of a standard deviation" sentence and the 15-second variance ratio appear in the published body; my published-version evidence comes from the publisher-deposited abstract and the authors' published-version Internet Appendix, both primary.

corrections: Re-attribute the "16%" quote. The sentence "a one standard deviation increase in stock ownership for S&P 500 stocks (1.44%) is associated with a 20 bps increase in daily volatility, which represents 16% of a standard deviation of the dependent variable" is from Ben-David, Franzoni & Moussawi, NBER Working Paper No. 20071 (April 2014, rev. June 2014), Section 4.3 / Table 4 Column (1) — NOT from the published Journal of Finance 73(6) 2018 article, which is a materially revised paper (sample extended to December 2015, index-membership RDD foregrounded, new risk-premium result) whose body I could not open.

Answer the open item explicitly: the PUBLISHED JF abstract does NOT contain the "16%" phrasing. It reads in full: "Due to their low trading costs, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are a potential catalyst for short-horizon liquidity traders. The liquidity shocks can propagate to the underlying securities through the arbitrage channel, and ETFs may increase the nonfundamental volatility of the securities in their baskets. We exploit exogenous changes in index membership and find that stocks with higher ETF ownership display significantly higher volatility. ETF ownership increases the negative autocorrelation in stock prices. The increase in volatility appears to introduce undiversifiable risk in prices because stocks with high ETF ownership earn a significant risk premium of up to 56 basis points monthly." Verified identical across Wiley's Crossref deposit, the AFA's own issue page at afajof.org/issue/volume-73-issue-6/, and RePEc/EconPapers. The "16%" abstract is the NBER working-paper abstract. The RePEc "56 basis points" headline is correct, not a reproduction error.

Qualify the caliber-error framing: the loose "16% higher volatility" reading traces to the authors' OWN working-paper abstract ("an increase of one standard deviation in ETF ownership is associated with an increase of 16% in daily stock volatility"), not only to secondary popularizers. The WP's introduction states it correctly as "about 16% of a standard deviation of daily volatility."

Add the plain-English magnitude so readers can see the caliber gap: 20 bps against a mean S&P 500 daily volatility of 2.080% (Table 1, Panel B) is roughly a 9.6% increase in volatility, versus 16% of the 1.29-point standard deviation of that variable. Footnote 15 of the WP: (0.146 x 1.440) / 1.290 = 0.1630; footnote 16 for the Russell 3000: (0.044 x 1.730) / 1.490 = 0.0511.

Fix the reversal claim: "~45% reverts within 20 days, so ~55% is permanent" is the 2014 working-paper result ("after twenty days, about 45% of the initial shock has reverted... flows convey fundamental and non-fundamental shocks in roughly equal shares"). The published version's own Internet Appendix says the updated Table VII implies "the half-life to convergence of prices to the initial level is about 10 days" — i.e. substantially full reversal on a ~10-day half-life, which does not support a permanent ~55% component. Either drop the permanent-component inference or label it as the superseded WP result.

Fix the horizon claim: the 15-second variance ratio (15-second return variance over 3x the 5-second variance, chosen because ETF sponsors disseminate NAV every 15 seconds) is the 2014 WP's price-efficiency measure. The published paper's headline random-walk-deviation measure, per its own Internet Appendix Table AI, is "Variance ratio 5 [days]" — 5-day return variance over 5x the 1-day return variance, computed within a quarter — consistent with the published abstract's "negative autocorrelation in stock prices"; the intraday variance ratio appears only in Internet Appendix robustness (Table AXVI, Panel B). Keep the "not allocative informativeness" qualifier — that holds for both versions.

If the article uses the phrase "ETF ownership increases the negative autocorrelation in stock prices," cite it to JF 2018 (the published abstract), not to the working paper — the WP never uses that phrasing, saying instead that ETFs "add a mean-reverting component to stock prices."

Beware the propagation vector when citing: Semantic Scholar serves the NBER working-paper abstract (with the 16% sentence) under the published DOI 10.1111/JOFI.12727. Any "JF abstract" quote sourced through Semantic Scholar, or through search-engine summaries built on it, is the wrong abstract.
newContradictions: The 2014 NBER WP and the 2018 JF article are substantially different papers presented under one citation. The WP samples 2000-2012 and headlines the 16%-of-a-SD daily volatility result with no asset-pricing result; the published version extends key samples to December 2015, foregrounds identification off "exogenous changes in index membership," replaces the 15-second variance ratio with a 5-day/1-day variance ratio as the headline efficiency measure, reframes reversals as a ~10-day half-life to full convergence rather than a 45%/55% split, and adds an entirely new result (a risk premium of up to 56 bps monthly on high-ETF-ownership stocks) that is absent from the WP abstract. Any article that quotes WP numbers under a JF 2018 citation is version-mixing.

Aggregator contamination is live as of 2026-08: Semantic Scholar (api.semanticscholar.org, DOI:10.1111/JOFI.12727) returns the NBER working-paper abstract as the abstract of the published JF article. OpenAlex likewise lists the paper as green OA pointing only to doi.org/10.3386/w20071 (the WP). Crossref, EconPapers/IDEAS, and afajof.org all carry the correct published abstract.

The published version's asset-pricing result ("a significant risk premium of up to 56 basis points monthly" on high-ETF-ownership stocks) cuts against the usual popular framing of this paper as pure evidence that ETFs harm markets — the authors' published headline is that the added nonfundamental volatility is priced as undiversifiable risk. If the article cites BDFM 2018 in an index-bubble/market-breaking argument without mentioning the risk-premium finding, it is quoting a paper whose published abstract makes a different top-line claim than the one being borrowed.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) The paper's own text reads: 'a 20 bps increase in daily volatility, which represents 16% of a standard deviation of the dependent variable' for a one-SD (1.44% of market cap) increase in ETF ownership, S&P 500 stocks only
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as attributed to 'JF 73(6) 2018'. RIGHT: this sentence is verbatim in the NBER WP 20071 (April 2014, revised June 2014), Section 4.3, p.19 — 'In Column (1), a one standard deviation increase in stock ownership for S&P 500 stocks (1.44%) is associated with a 20 bps increase in daily volatility, which represents 16% of a standard deviation of the dependent variable.' (The April 2014 rev0 has the same sentence with 'of the standard deviation'.) Every component checks arithmetically against the WP's own Table 2 Panel B / Table 4: ETF ownership is a percent-of-market-cap variable with S&P 500 monthly mean 2.11%, SD 1.44%; Table 4 col (1) coefficient 0.146 x 1.44 = 0.21 (=~20 bps); daily-volatility SD 1.29 → 0.21/1.29 = 16.3%. But the sentence does NOT survive into the published JF version. In the March 2015 revision (the version the authors filed with the SEC, comment file s71115-1.pdf, sample 2000–2012) the same regression is run on standardized variables and reads 'a one-standard-deviation move in ownership is associated with 15% of a standard deviation change in daily volatility' (9.3% with a lagged dependent variable). In the PUBLISHED version (sample extended to Jan 2000–Dec 2015) the authors abandoned the SD-units framing entirely: the published Internet Appendix, Table AIX Panel A, reports SD of ETF ownership 1.8% (not 1.44%) and states the median S&P 500 stock's daily volatility rises 'by about 20 bps to 2.3%', moving it from the 50th to the 64th percentile of the volatility distribution (58th with three lags). So '20 bps' survives; '16% of a standard deviation' and '1.44%' do not.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Extended to smaller stocks the effect is ~5% of a standard deviation
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as a statement about the published paper. RIGHT: '~5%' is the NBER WP number — 'Extending the universe to smaller stocks (Column (4)), the effect is diluted, amounting to about 5% of a standard deviation' (WP p.19; checks out: 0.044 x 1.73 / 1.49 = 5.1%). Note it is the Russell 3000 sample (large plus small), not a smaller-stocks-only sample. In the March 2015 revision the same figure is 3.7% of a standard deviation. In the published version the Russell 3000 magnitude is reported only as a percentile shift (50th → 57th percentile, or 55th with three lags; Internet Appendix Table AIX Panel A).

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Quoting the result as '16% higher volatility' is a caliber error
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed, with an important twist the article should carry. Against the WP's own numbers the relative increase is ~10%, not 16%: mean S&P 500 daily volatility is 2.08% and the effect is 21 bps (0.21/2.08 = 10.1%); the published Internet Appendix says the same thing in levels (median 2.1% → 2.3%). BUT the '16% higher volatility' reading did not originate with careless secondary users — it is the authors' own NBER/SSRN working-paper ABSTRACT, which reads verbatim: 'We estimate that an increase of one standard deviation in ETF ownership is associated with an increase of 16% in daily stock volatility.' The WP body text and introduction are precise ('about 16% of a standard deviation of daily volatility'); the WP abstract is not. That abstract is still what nber.org/papers/w20071 and Semantic Scholar serve today, which is why the misquote propagated.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) CRITICAL: does the published JF abstract contain the '16%' phrasing?
itemVerdicts.note: RESOLVED: NO. The published Journal of Finance abstract contains no '16%' and no volatility magnitude at all. Verbatim published abstract, confirmed identically across four independent publisher-derived sources — Crossref's JATS deposit by Wiley for 10.1111/jofi.12727, IDEAS/RePEc, EconPapers, and the American Finance Association's own issue page for JF vol. 73 issue 6 (afajof.org): 'Due to their low trading costs, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are a potential catalyst for short-horizon liquidity traders. The liquidity shocks can propagate to the underlying securities through the arbitrage channel, and ETFs may increase the nonfundamental volatility of the securities in their baskets. We exploit exogenous changes in index membership and find that stocks with higher ETF ownership display significantly higher volatility. ETF ownership increases the negative autocorrelation in stock prices. The increase in volatility appears to introduce undiversifiable risk in prices because stocks with high ETF ownership earn a significant risk premium of up to 56 basis points monthly.' The RePEc reproduction is therefore the real published abstract, not a mangled one. The source of the confusion is that NBER's landing page and Semantic Scholar (via MAG) attach the 2014 WORKING PAPER abstract to the published DOI. Crossref shows no erratum or correction notice on the DOI.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) ETF ownership raises negative autocorrelation
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the published JF abstract: 'ETF ownership increases the negative autocorrelation in stock prices.' Note this sentence exists ONLY in the published version — the 2014 WP abstract does not contain it, and the WP frames the same idea as ETFs inflating 'the mean-reverting component of stock prices.' So this is one item the article correctly sources to the 2018 publication rather than the working paper.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) ~45% of flow-driven price shocks revert within 20 days, so ~55% permanent
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG for the published paper: '45% ... so ~55% permanent.' RIGHT: 45% is the 2014 WP figure — 'after twenty days, about 45% of the initial shock has reverted ... which suggests that on average flows convey fundamental and non-fundamental shocks in roughly equal shares.' By the March 2015 revision the number had moved to ~47%, computed and stated explicitly: 'we can infer that almost half of the initial price impact is reversed (8.3/17.5 = 0.47)', and the authors summarize it as 'a 50% reversal of the initial price impact of ETF flows,' concluding 'at least half of the impact of ETFs on return volatility is due to noise propagation.' The safe caliber for the published paper is 'roughly half reverts within twenty days, so roughly half is permanent,' not the precise 45/55 split. Also worth keeping: the paper reports that extending the horizon to forty days does not increase the reversal.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) The efficiency deterioration is at 15-second horizons (microstructure), not allocative informativeness
itemVerdicts.note: HALF WRONG. RIGHT on the second half: the paper never measures allocative or fundamental price informativeness (nothing in the Bai-Philippon-Savov sense); its efficiency metric is a deviation-from-random-walk variance ratio, and its own caveat is that higher volatility 'could also reflect higher investor attention' rather than noise. WRONG to confine it to 15 seconds. The 15-second choice is real and correctly motivated — 'ETF sponsors disseminate information about the portfolio NAV at 15-second intervals to facilitate high-frequency arbitrage' — but the paper deliberately runs a second, lower-frequency variance ratio: 'to show that the effect of interest persists at lower frequencies, we also compute the ratio of the five-day return variance to five times the one-day return variance,' and reports 'The effect is twice as large at the intraday frequency as it is at the five-day frequency (10% of a standard deviation of VR 15 for a one-standard-deviation change in ETF ownership, for S&P 500 stocks). It is, however, statistically and economically significant for the 5-day frequency as well.' The WP states the conclusion as 'a deterioration in price efficiency, both intraday and at the daily frequency.' Add the twenty-day flow reversals and the claim 'it's only microstructure noise at 15 seconds' understates what the paper asserts.

corrections: Do not attribute '20 bps / 16% of a standard deviation / one-SD = 1.44%' to the Journal of Finance 2018 article. That sentence is from NBER Working Paper 20071 (April 2014, revised June 2014), Section 4.3. Cite it as the working paper, or drop the number.

The published JF 2018 abstract contains no '16%' and no volatility magnitude. Its verbatim text is: 'Due to their low trading costs, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are a potential catalyst for short-horizon liquidity traders. The liquidity shocks can propagate to the underlying securities through the arbitrage channel, and ETFs may increase the nonfundamental volatility of the securities in their baskets. We exploit exogenous changes in index membership and find that stocks with higher ETF ownership display significantly higher volatility. ETF ownership increases the negative autocorrelation in stock prices. The increase in volatility appears to introduce undiversifiable risk in prices because stocks with high ETF ownership earn a significant risk premium of up to 56 basis points monthly.' The RePEc/EconPapers '56 basis points' rendering is correct, not a corruption.

State that the '16% higher volatility' misreading traces to the authors' own working-paper abstract, which literally reads 'an increase of one standard deviation in ETF ownership is associated with an increase of 16% in daily stock volatility.' NBER's landing page and Semantic Scholar still serve that WP abstract against the published DOI. The WP body text is precise ('about 16% of a standard deviation of daily volatility'); the WP abstract is not.

If the article wants a magnitude the PUBLISHED paper actually endorses, use the published Internet Appendix, Table AIX Panel A (sample January 2000–December 2015): a one-standard-deviation increase in ETF ownership (1.8% of market cap) raises the median S&P 500 stock's daily volatility by about 20 bps, from 2.1% to 2.3%, moving it from the 50th to the 64th percentile of the volatility distribution (58th when three lags of the dependent variable are included; 57th and 55th respectively in the Russell 3000 sample). In relative terms that is roughly a 10% increase, not 16%.

The '~5% of a standard deviation' small-stock figure is the 2014 working paper's Russell 3000 estimate (large plus small stocks, not smaller stocks alone). In the March 2015 revision it is 3.7% of a standard deviation, and the published version reports it only as a percentile shift. Attribute the '~5%' to the working paper or drop it.

Change '~45% of flow-driven price shocks revert within 20 days (so ~55% permanent)' to 'roughly half of the initial price impact of ETF flows reverses within twenty days.' 45% is the 2014 working-paper number; the March 2015 revision computes 8.3/17.5 = 0.47, calls it 'almost half' and 'a 50% reversal,' and concludes 'at least half of the impact of ETFs on return volatility is due to noise propagation.' Extending the horizon to forty days does not increase the reversal.

Do not say the efficiency deterioration is confined to 15-second horizons. The paper runs variance ratios at two horizons and finds significant deterioration at both: 'The effect is twice as large at the intraday frequency as it is at the five-day frequency ... It is, however, statistically and economically significant for the 5-day frequency as well.' The working paper summarizes it as 'a deterioration in price efficiency, both intraday and at the daily frequency.' Keep the point that none of this measures allocative or fundamental price informativeness — that part is correct.

Note that the published paper's headline identification is the Russell 1000/2000 reconstitution regression discontinuity, not the OLS-with-fixed-effects design the '16%' comes from, and that the RDD estimates are far larger — averaging around 55% of a standard deviation. Using the OLS number while citing the published paper understates what that paper claims and cites a design the published version demoted.

RIGHT: the sentence is in NBER Working Paper 20071 (April 2014, revised June 2014), Section 4.3, p. 19, verbatim: "In Column (1), a one standard deviation increase in stock ownership for S&P 500 stocks (1.44%) is associated with a 20 bps increase in daily volatility, which represents 16% of a standard deviation of the dependent variable." itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed in NBER WP 20071 (rev. June 2014). Table 1, Panel B (Monthly Frequency Sample Statistics), S&P 500: "Daily stock volatility (%) 51,349 2.080 1.290" and "ETF ownership (%; average within the month) 51,349 2.110 1.440". ETF ownership is a dollar-holdings/market-cap share, so "1.44% of market cap" is fair. The regression is Table 4 Column (1), sample restricted to S&P 500 stocks (Columns (4)-(6) extend to Russell 3000). Caveat: this is the WP's SD; the published Internet Appendix instead uses a within-percentile SD of ETF ownership of "about 1.8%" for the median stock.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Extended to smaller stocks the effect is ~5% of a SD
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed verbatim in NBER WP 20071 (rev. June 2014), p. 19: "Extending the universe to smaller stocks (Column (4)), the effect is diluted, amounting to about 5% of a standard deviation." Footnote 16 gives the arithmetic: "(0.044 * 1.730) / 1.490 = 0.0511". Table 1 Panel B Russell 3000: daily volatility mean 2.610, SD 1.490; ETF ownership mean 2.320, SD 1.730.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Quoting it as "16% higher volatility" is a caliber error
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed, and the error is larger than stated. 16% is a share of the cross-sectional SD of the dependent variable (SD = 1.290 percentage points of daily volatility), not a proportional increase in volatility. The proportional increase is 0.146 x 1.440 = 0.21 pp on a sample mean daily volatility of 2.080%, i.e. about 10%, not 16%. So "16% higher volatility" overstates the relative effect by roughly 1.6x on top of misreading the units.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) CRITICAL: does the PUBLISHED JF abstract contain the "16%" phrasing?
itemVerdicts.note: It does not. The published abstract, obtained from the Wiley/Crossref publisher deposit (api.crossref.org, DOI 10.1111/jofi.12727, JATS-tagged <jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>) and independently reproduced verbatim by EconPapers/RePEc and OpenAlex, reads in full: "Due to their low trading costs, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are a potential catalyst for short-horizon liquidity traders. The liquidity shocks can propagate to the underlying securities through the arbitrage channel, and ETFs may increase the nonfundamental volatility of the securities in their baskets. We exploit exogenous changes in index membership and find that stocks with higher ETF ownership display significantly higher volatility. ETF ownership increases the negative autocorrelation in stock prices. The increase in volatility appears to introduce undiversifiable risk in prices because stocks with high ETF ownership earn a significant risk premium of up to 56 basis points monthly."
