itemVerdicts.item: (c) ETF ownership raises negative autocorrelation
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed verbatim in the published JF abstract: "ETF ownership increases the negative autocorrelation in stock prices." This result is NOT in the 2014 NBER WP (the word autocorrelation appears there only in the standard-error clustering discussion), so it must be cited to the 2018 published version, not the working paper.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) ~45% of flow-driven price shocks revert within 20 days, so ~55% permanent
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as a statement about the published 2018 paper, and the "55% permanent" gloss is the article's, not the authors'. RIGHT: the 45%/20-day number is NBER WP 20071 (rev. June 2014), Table 6 discussion, p. 22: "In terms of magnitude, after twenty days, about 45% of the initial shock has reverted. Extending the horizon farther out to forty days does not increase the magnitude of reversals (not reported), which suggests that on average flows convey fundamental and non-fundamental shocks in roughly equal shares." The authors say "roughly equal shares" of fundamental vs non-fundamental, never "55% permanent". The March 2015 revision gives 47%: "we can infer that almost half of the initial price impact is reversed (8.3/17.5 = 0.47)". The PUBLISHED version's data were extended: its Internet Appendix says "our evidence on the price impact of ETF flows, which we have updated through 2015 and reported in Table VII, suggests that, following ETF flows, the half-life to convergence of prices to the initial level is about 10 days" — a ~10-day half-life implies materially MORE than 45% reversion by day 20 and describes convergence to the initial level, which does not support a "55% permanent" reading. I could not open published Table VII itself, so treat the exact published reversion fraction as unverified; do not print 45%/55% against the 2018 citation.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) The efficiency deterioration is at 15-SECOND horizons (microstructure), not allocative informativeness
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as a statement about the published 2018 paper. RIGHT: 15-second-only is true of the 2014 NBER WP, which used a single variance ratio — "we measure single-period returns from transaction prices at five-second intervals and choose k = 3, so that multi-period returns are measured over fifteen-second intervals" — justified because "information about NAV is disseminated by ETF sponsors at fifteen second intervals". From the March 2015 revision onward the paper uses TWO horizons: "In our application, we construct the variance ratio using two different horizons... Second, to show that the effect of interest persists at lower frequencies, we also compute the ratio of the five-day return variance to five times the one-day return variance... using all the returns within a quarter" (VR 15 monthly, VR 5 quarterly; "The effect is twice as large at the intraday frequency as it is at the five-day frequency (10% of a standard deviation of VR 15...)"). The published version keeps both: its Internet Appendix Table AI defines "Variance ratio 5 days — The ratio of 5-day return variance divided by 5 times the 1-day return variance... computed using daily and 5-day returns within a quarter" (source CRSP), and IA Table AXVI Panel B uses "the intraday variance ratio". The SECOND half of the claim survives: neither version measures allocative or fundamental price informativeness (no earnings-predictability, no price-informativeness-about-cash-flows measure anywhere in the paper); the efficiency evidence is random-walk deviation plus 20-day return reversals. Rephrase as: the price-efficiency evidence is random-walk deviation at intraday (15-second) AND 5-day horizons plus multi-day flow reversals, not allocative informativeness.

itemVerdicts.item: Identification strategy attributed to the paper
itemVerdicts.note: Not in the stated claim group but load-bearing if the article describes the design. WRONG (WP-era): "identification strategies based on the mechanical variation in ETF ownership" (NBER WP abstract). RIGHT (published): "We exploit exogenous changes in index membership" — the Russell 1000/2000 June reconstitution, used as a fuzzy RDD/IV. If the article cites JF 2018, describe the design as Russell index-reconstitution-based.

itemVerdicts.item: Later corrections / replications up to 2026-08
itemVerdicts.note: One formal author-issued follow-up exists and should be cited if the article leans on the causal magnitude: Ben-David, Franzoni & Moussawi, 2019, "A Note to 'Do ETFs Increase Volatility?': An Improved Method to Predict Assignment of Stocks into Russell Indexes," Journal of Finance Replications and Corrigenda (web-only, https://afajof.org/comments-and-rejoinders/, PDF at https://afajof.org/wp-content/uploads/20191016-Note-for-JF.pdf, dated October 2019). It re-runs the fuzzy RDD with a better predictor of Russell assignment: "we find that volatility increases significantly with ETF ownership, by 21% to 76% (depending on the bandwidth and polynomial degree) of a standard deviation for a one-standard-deviation change in ETF ownership. Restricting attention to the bandwidths above 50 for comparability, the magnitude of the median estimate is about 31%, which is almost identical to the result presented in our 2018 paper of about 31% of a standard deviation." So the result is reinforced, not overturned — but at ~31% of a SD (IV/LATE), a different number from the 16% OLS figure, and the authors' Internet Appendix warns the LATE estimates are "not necessarily generalizable to the entire sample." I found no comment, corrigendum, or retraction contesting the paper's findings through 2026-08.

The published JF 2018 abstract contains no "16%" and no one-standard-deviation volatility magnitude. Its full text is: "Due to their low trading costs, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are a potential catalyst for short-horizon liquidity traders. The liquidity shocks can propagate to the underlying securities through the arbitrage channel, and ETFs may increase the nonfundamental volatility of the securities in their baskets. We exploit exogenous changes in index membership and find that stocks with higher ETF ownership display significantly higher volatility. ETF ownership increases the negative autocorrelation in stock prices. The increase in volatility appears to introduce undiversifiable risk in prices because stocks with high ETF ownership earn a significant risk premium of up to 56 basis points monthly." The RePEc/EconPapers "risk premium of up to 56 basis points monthly" headline is the genuine published abstract, not a reproduction artifact.

Never render the finding as "16% higher volatility." It is 16% of one cross-sectional standard deviation of the dependent variable (SD = 1.290 percentage points of daily volatility). The proportional increase is 0.146 x 1.440 = 0.21 percentage points on a sample mean daily volatility of 2.080%, i.e. about 10%.

State the population and window: the 16%-of-a-SD figure is Table 4 Column (1) of the 2014 working paper, S&P 500 stocks only, monthly panel, ETF ownership SD 1.44% of market cap. The same regression extended to Russell 3000 gives about 5% of a standard deviation (working paper footnote 16: (0.044 * 1.730) / 1.490 = 0.0511).

If the article cites the 2018 published paper's magnitude, use the authors' own characterization from their 2019 Journal of Finance Replications and Corrigenda note: the 2018 paper's instrumented estimate is "about 31% of a standard deviation" for a one-standard-deviation change in ETF ownership, and the improved-instrument re-estimation spans 21% to 76% with a median of about 31%. Note that these are local-average-treatment-effect estimates on Russell 1000/2000 index switchers, which the authors' own Internet Appendix says are "not necessarily generalizable to the entire sample."

If the article prefers the published paper's OLS framing, use the percentile language from its Internet Appendix rather than a percent: a one-standard-deviation shock to ETF ownership moves the median stock's daily volatility to roughly the 58th-64th percentile of the volatility distribution (S&P 500), and the authors' overall conclusion is "a normal shock to ETF ownership causes the median stock volatility to shift to between the 55th and 65th percentiles of the volatility distribution." They add that this is "comparable to that of a well-known determinant of volatility" (the prior-month return).

Do not print "~45% of flow-driven price shocks revert within 20 days, so ~55% is permanent" against the 2018 citation. The 45% figure is the 2014 working paper (Table 6, p. 22); the March 2015 revision gives 47% (8.3/17.5); and the published version's Internet Appendix says the updated Table VII implies "the half-life to convergence of prices to the initial level is about 10 days," which implies substantially more than 45% reversion by day 20. The authors never say "permanent" — they say flows "convey fundamental and non-fundamental shocks in roughly equal shares."

Do not say the paper's efficiency deterioration is at 15-second horizons only. That is true of the 2014 working paper. From the March 2015 revision onward, including the published version, the variance-ratio evidence runs at two horizons: an intraday variance ratio (15-second returns vs 3x 5-second returns) and a 5-day variance ratio (5-day return variance / 5x 1-day return variance, estimated within a quarter). The correct caliber point to keep is that none of this measures allocative or fundamental price informativeness — there is no cash-flow-informativeness or earnings-predictability test anywhere in the paper.

If the article describes the paper's identification, use the published design: exogenous changes in Russell 1000/2000 index membership at the June reconstitution (fuzzy RDD / IV). "Identification strategies based on the mechanical variation in ETF ownership" is the 2014 working paper's language.
newContradictions: The article's three headline BDFM numbers (16% of a SD, 45% reversion in 20 days, 15-second efficiency horizon) are all from the 2014 NBER working paper, while the citation given is the 2018 Journal of Finance article. The paper changed materially across versions — identification switched from mechanical ETF-ownership variation to Russell index reconstitution, the risk-premium and negative-autocorrelation results were added, and the sample was extended through 2015 — so mixing WP numbers with the JF citation is a version error, not a rounding quibble.

Authors' 2019 JF Replications and Corrigenda note (https://afajof.org/wp-content/uploads/20191016-Note-for-JF.pdf): "the magnitude of the median estimate is about 31%, which is almost identical to the result presented in our 2018 paper of about 31% of a standard deviation." This is roughly double the 16% figure the article uses and comes from a different estimator (fuzzy RDD/IV on Russell switchers, a LATE) than the 16% (panel OLS on S&P 500 stocks). Whichever is used, the estimator and population must be named.

Published Internet Appendix, Table AIX discussion: "Although the economic magnitudes appear significant, they do not seem excessively large" and the effect of ETF ownership on volatility is "comparable to that of a well-known determinant of volatility" (the prior-month return, per French, Schwert & Stambaugh 1987). Any framing of this paper as evidence that ETFs are destabilizing markets at scale runs against the authors' own stated calibration.

Published Internet Appendix: "following ETF flows, the half-life to convergence of prices to the initial level is about 10 days," based on Table VII updated through 2015. This cuts against the "~55% of the shock is permanent" reading the article draws from the working paper's 45%/20-day number.

Semantic Scholar (and, in this session, two independent web-search summarizers) attach the NBER working paper's 16% abstract to DOI 10.1111/jofi.12727. Anyone who checks the "published" abstract via those aggregators will be told the 16% is in the JF article. It is not. Only the Crossref publisher deposit, RePEc/EconPapers, and OpenAlex carry the real published abstract.
reasoning:
Primary documents I reached and read verbatim: (1) NBER WP 20071 rev. June 2014, full text, local files bdfm.txt and bdfm2.txt — confirmed the abstract's "increase of 16% in daily stock volatility", the Section 4.3 sentence "a one standard deviation increase in stock ownership for S&P 500 stocks (1.44%) is associated with a 20 bps increase in daily volatility, which represents 16% of a standard deviation of the dependent variable", footnote 15 "(0.146 * 1.440) / 1.290 = 0.1630", the "about 5% of a standard deviation" extension with footnote 16 "(0.044 * 1.730) / 1.490 = 0.0511", Table 1 Panel B summary stats (S&P 500 daily volatility mean 2.080 SD 1.290; ETF ownership mean 2.110 SD 1.440; Russell 3000 2.610/1.490 and 2.320/1.730), the 15-second/5-second variance ratio construction, and "after twenty days, about 45% of the initial shock has reverted... flows convey fundamental and non-fundamental shocks in roughly equal shares." (2) NBER w20071.rev0.pdf, freshly downloaded — the April 2014 original, same 16% abstract. (3) A March 2015 revision of the paper (local sec_bdfm.txt, the version circulated to the SEC) — abstract already rewritten to index-membership identification with no 16%; text reads "between 9% and 15% of a standard deviation" and "15% of a standard deviation change in daily volatility"; reversal is 8.3/17.5 = 0.47; variance ratios now at TWO horizons, VR 15 (intraday) and VR 5 (quarterly). (4) The PUBLISHED version's Internet Appendix, downloaded fresh from the corresponding author's own page, https://people.lu.usi.ch/franzonf/ETF%20internet%20appendix.pdf — Table AI variable definitions (including "Variance ratio 5 days"), the Table AIX magnitude discussion (SD of ETF ownership "about 1.8%", "increase by about 20 bps to 2.3%", "64th percentile", conclusion "between the 55th and 65th percentiles"), and the Table AXI note that the updated Table VII implies "the half-life to convergence of prices to the initial level is about 10 days". (5) The authors' 2019 Journal of Finance Replications and Corrigenda note, downloaded fresh from afajof.org — "about 31%, which is almost identical to the result presented in our 2018 paper of about 31% of a standard deviation." (6) The published abstract via the Wiley/Crossref publisher deposit, cross-checked against EconPapers/RePEc HTML and the OpenAlex inverted index; all three are character-identical and contain no "16%".

Settling item (b): the published JF abstract does NOT contain the 16% phrasing. The RePEc "risk premium of up to 56 basis points monthly" headline is the real publisher abstract. The 16% abstract is the NBER working paper's.

What remains uncertain: I could not open the published JF main text. Wiley returned 403 to direct requests and a CAPTCHA wall through a text proxy; SSRN returned 403; Unpaywall/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar/CORE register no open-access copy of the published version (only the NBER WP), and NBER hosts no post-2014 revision. So I cannot state with document-in-hand certainty that the string "16%" is absent from the published main text — only that the abstract lacks it, that the intermediate 2015 version had already replaced it with 9%-15%, that the published Internet Appendix uses percentile framing instead, and that the authors themselves describe the 2018 paper's headline as ~31% of a standard deviation. That is strong but circumstantial; the safe editorial move is to attribute the 16% to the working paper. I also could not extract the local Glosten-Nallareddy-Zou PDFs (both were failed downloads), so I make no claim about contrary informational-efficiency evidence; the only formal follow-up I verified is the authors' own 2019 note, which reinforces rather than overturns the result.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Barberis-Shleifer-Wurgler JFE 2005: S&P daily beta increase 0.067 (1976-87) vs 0.214 (1988-2000); 0.326/-0.319 is the bivariate spec
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers all confirmed verbatim in BSW (JFE 75 (2005) 283-317), Table 1 Panel A (daily returns) and pp.286. Text: 'stocks added to the S&P during 1976-1987 experience an average increase in daily S&P beta of 0.067 after inclusion, the average increase in the 1988-2000 period is 0.214' (univariate, N=196 and N=259). And: 'S&P betas increase by 0.326 on average over the 1976-2000 period, while non-S&P betas fall by an average of 0.319' (bivariate). MISSING QUALIFIER: 0.326/-0.319 is not only the BIVARIATE spec, it is also the FULL 1976-2000 sample, whereas 0.067/0.214 are UNIVARIATE SUBPERIOD figures. The like-for-like bivariate subperiod values are 0.286/-0.301 (1976-87) and 0.357/-0.332 (1988-2000); the like-for-like univariate full-sample value is 0.151. WRONG if written as '0.067 rose to 0.214, and in the bivariate spec to 0.326' — that silently swaps both the spec AND the window. RIGHT: 'univariate daily: 0.067 (1976-87) -> 0.214 (1988-2000), 0.151 full sample; bivariate daily full sample 1976-2000: S&P beta +0.326, non-S&P beta -0.319.' Also note all figures are daily-frequency; weekly additions are 0.110 univariate / 0.174 bivariate (1976-2000).

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Chen-Singal-Whitelaw JFE 2016: bivariate spec uninformative; univariate diff-of-diff +0.020 (t=0.76), +0.199 (t=4.94), -0.004 (t=-0.14)
itemVerdicts.note: All four numbers confirmed verbatim in CSW (JFE 121 (2016) 624-644) Table 1 Panel A, 'Diff. of diff.' column (beta2 - beta1): 1976-1987 N=197, 0.020, t=0.763; 1988-2000 N=269, 0.199, t=4.938; 2001-2012 N=214, -0.004, t=-0.137; 1976-2012 N=680, 0.083, t=4.080. The abstract confirms the bivariate critique verbatim: 'We show that the bivariate regressions in this literature provide little information about the economic magnitude of excess comovement, with coefficients that are sensitive to unrelated factors.' CALIBER SLIPPAGE: 'the effect is statistically ZERO in the decade passive grew fastest' is true ONLY of the difference-of-differences. In the SAME Table 1 row, the raw univariate S&P beta change for 2001-2012 is still +0.071 with t=2.439 — i.e. the BSW-style headline number is positive and significant in 2001-2012. WRONG: 'CSW find no beta increase after 2001.' RIGHT: 'CSW find the S&P beta still rises (+0.071, t=2.44) but so does the non-S&P beta (+0.075, t=2.50), so the excess-comovement diff-of-diff is -0.004 (t=-0.14).' The effect vanishes outright only in Table 6, after the Dimson non-synchronous-trading adjustment AND a momentum-matched control: sample-minus-match 2001-2012 delta-beta2 = -0.014 (t=-0.247), diff-of-diff -0.009 (t=-0.458). That Table 6 result actually strengthens the article's point and is the cleaner citation. One more Table 6 fact worth carrying: the Dimson adjustment alone cuts the 1988-2000 S&P beta change from 0.214 to 0.078.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Kasch-Sarkar FRBNY Staff Report 484: no permanent value/comovement effect after pre-inclusion momentum; declines bivariate spec because regressors correlate >93%
itemVerdicts.note: Both halves confirmed in the primary PDF (sr484, February 2011; revised November 2012). Abstract: 'Contrary to the consensus in the literature, our results indicate that - after accounting for the firms' extraordinary preinclusion performance - index inclusion has no permanent effect on value and comovement.' Footnote 25: 'we ... documented that the correlation between S&P 500 and non-S&P 500 stock returns exceeds 93%. The concern regarding a multiple regression with highly correlated regressors is that its parameter estimates are likely to be regression artifacts, rendering their interpretation difficult. Therefore, we do not consider specifications which include both of these highly correlated indices in one regression.' THREE CORRECTIONS. (i) WRONG: 'pre-inclusion momentum.' RIGHT: 'pre-inclusion performance' — the abstract specifies three things, 'large increases in earnings, appreciation in market value, and positive price momentum'; momentum alone is one leg. (ii) Their own Table VII carries an exception the article must not suppress: 'the daily change in the S&P 500 beta delta-beta-sp remains statistically significant in the multi-factor regressions, although the magnitude of the effect is reduced' — the null is at weekly frequency ('the sample average weekly delta-beta-sp is 0.022 with t = 0.66'). So it is 'no PERMANENT effect; the residual comovement is a high-frequency daily effect only.' (iii) Publication status: this is still an unpublished Fed staff report — searches to 2026-08 turn up only FRBNY SR 484 / SSRN 2171235 / EconPapers, no journal version. Do not describe it as peer-reviewed.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) BIS March 2018: correlation 0.45 -> 0.52 on inclusion, 462 stocks, 2000-2017, raw before/after with no matched control
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed in BIS Quarterly Review, March 2018, p.119, Sushko & Turner, 'The implications of passive investing for securities markets', Graph 3 left panel: data labels 0.45 ('Before joining, from t-200 to t-1') and 0.52 ('After joining, from t+1 to t+200'). Footnote 1: 'Sample based on 462 stocks joining the S&P 500 between January 2000 and September 2017. Stocks subject to mergers and acquisitions, stocks with poor data availability and those that have left the index during the first 30 days after the inclusion date are excluded.' Footnote 2: 'Correlation of daily returns with the S&P 500 index.' No control sample, no momentum match, no Dimson/non-synchronous-trading adjustment is mentioned anywhere — so the article's methodological gloss is fair. Two free adversarial points the article can use: (1) the window is +/-200 trading days around the inclusion date, not CSW's pre-announcement/post-effective one-year windows; (2) the SAME Graph 3 shows daily trading volume jumping (~1.0 -> ~2.2x) and bid-ask spreads narrowing (~0.144% -> ~0.096%) on inclusion — which mechanically raises a measured daily-return correlation by reducing non-synchronous trading, i.e. the confound is visible inside BIS's own exhibit. Also, this is a descriptive graph in a Quarterly Review special feature, not a regression result.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) ECB FSR Nov 2024 box: +0.005 correlation per 1pp passive ownership, euro area, stock+time FE, index-inclusion IV, base correlation 0.50
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers confirmed verbatim in the ECB box (Dieckelmann, Siciliano, Sowinski, FSR November 2024): 'Between the first quarter of 2010 and the first quarter of 2024, a 1 percentage point increase in the passive ownership share of a euro area stock was associated with an increase of around 0.005 in the correlation coefficient with the EURO STOXX index.' Base rate confirmed in footnote 4: 'the average return correlation coefficient of a euro area stock with the EURO STOXX index between the first quarter of 2010 and the first quarter of 2024 is 0.50.' SPEC MISDESCRIBED. WRONG: 'stock+time FE, index-inclusion IV' as if one specification produced 0.005. RIGHT, per the Chart B panel a notes verbatim: 'a panel regression with stock and time fixed effects that regress correlation with the EURO STOXX index on the passive ownership share of constituent stocks, controlling for market capitalisation, liquidity, valuation and 1 autoregressive lag of the correlation coefficient' — and separately, 'The results also hold in a two-step regression set-up, using index inclusion as an instrumental variable for passive ownership share', i.e. the IV is a ROBUSTNESS CHECK, not the headline spec. Two further caveats: the omitted AR(1) lag of the dependent variable makes 0.005 a short-run/partial coefficient, so a straight x10 to '+0.05' is the article's own linear extrapolation and is not made by the ECB (a dynamic-panel long-run multiplier would be larger); and the ECB's own verb throughout is 'associated with', never 'causes'. Window Q1 2010-Q1 2024 should be stated.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) Anadu et al. Table 4: 'For equities, comovement effects have declined significantly since 2001'
itemVerdicts.note: Quote confirmed verbatim as a Table 4 cell. WRONG framing: 'Table 4 verdict.' RIGHT: it is the entry in the column headed 'Evidence that active-to-passive shift has exacerbated?' for the row 'Comovement of returns', in Table 4 ('Impact of active-to-passive shift on index-inclusion effects and financial stability'), FEDS working paper 2018-060r1 (first draft Aug 27 2018, this draft May 15 2020). CONTEXT THE ARTICLE MUST NOT DROP: the very next row of the same table says the opposite for liquidity — 'Systematic liquidity associated with index investing has increased in recent years' — and the paper's own abstract concludes 'evidence is mixed on the links between indexing and comovement of asset returns and liquidity.' So Table 4 is not a clean acquittal on comovement; it is an acquittal on EQUITY RETURN comovement specifically, alongside a conviction on liquidity comovement. Also, the basis for the cell is CSW itself: 'Chen, Singal, and Whitelaw (2016) ... do not find evidence of an upward trend in recent years. They report that adding a stock to the index had a smaller effect on its beta during the period from 2001 to 2012 than in the previous decade' — so (b) and (f) are one piece of evidence, not two independent ones. ATTRIBUTION: cite as FEDS 2018-060r1; the published version is Financial Analysts Journal 76(4), 2020, pp. 23-39, titled without 'Potential' ('The Shift from Active to Passive Investing: Risks to Financial Stability?'), and I could not verify that the table number is still 4 there.

corrections: BSW: the 0.326 / -0.319 pair is the bivariate spec AND the full 1976-2000 sample. Do not juxtapose it with the univariate subperiod figures 0.067/0.214 without saying both things changed. Like-for-like: univariate full sample = 0.151; bivariate subperiods = 0.286/-0.301 (1976-87) and 0.357/-0.332 (1988-2000). All figures are daily-frequency (BSW Table 1 Panel A).

CSW: the 2001-2012 zero is the DIFFERENCE-OF-DIFFERENCES (-0.004, t=-0.14). In the same Table 1 row the raw univariate S&P beta change is still +0.071 with t=2.439 — statistically significant. Never write 'CSW find no beta increase after 2001'; write 'the S&P beta still rises, but so does the non-S&P beta, so the excess-comovement differential is zero.'

CSW: the stronger and cleaner 2001-2012 citation is Table 6 (Dimson adjustment plus momentum-matched control), where sample-minus-match delta-beta_S&P = -0.014 (t=-0.247) and diff-of-diff = -0.009 (t=-0.458). Also usable: the Dimson adjustment alone cuts the 1988-2000 S&P beta change from 0.214 to 0.078.
Kasch-Sarkar: change 'pre-inclusion momentum' to 'pre-inclusion performance' — the paper's abstract specifies 'large increases in earnings, appreciation in market value, and positive price momentum.'

Kasch-Sarkar: state the frequency caveat. Their Table VII finds the DAILY change in S&P 500 beta 'remains statistically significant in the multi-factor regressions, although the magnitude of the effect is reduced'; the null is weekly (delta-beta_sp = 0.022, t = 0.66). The claim is 'no PERMANENT effect', not 'no effect at any horizon.'

Kasch-Sarkar: label it an unpublished Federal Reserve Bank of New York staff report (no. 484, February 2011, revised November 2012). As of August 2026 no journal-published version exists. Do not imply peer review.

ECB Nov 2024 box: correct the specification. The headline 0.005 comes from a panel regression with stock and time fixed effects controlling for market capitalisation, liquidity, valuation and one autoregressive lag of the correlation coefficient. Index inclusion as an instrumental variable is a separate two-step robustness check ('the results also hold'), not part of the headline spec.

ECB Nov 2024 box: the '10pp -> +0.05' arithmetic is the article's own linear extrapolation, not the ECB's, and the AR(1) lag in the specification means 0.005 is a short-run/partial coefficient. Attribute the multiplication to the article, and state the window (Q1 2010-Q1 2024) and the ECB's own non-causal verb ('associated with').

Anadu et al.: the quoted line is a cell in the column 'Evidence that active-to-passive shift has exacerbated?', row 'Comovement of returns', Table 4 of FEDS working paper 2018-060r1 (draft of 15 May 2020) — not a prose verdict. Cite the FEDS working paper for the table number; the published version is Financial Analysts Journal 76(4), 2020, pp. 23-39, with 'Potential' dropped from the title.

Anadu et al.: do not present Table 4 as a blanket acquittal. The adjacent row reads 'Systematic liquidity associated with index investing has increased in recent years', and the paper's abstract says 'evidence is mixed on the links between indexing and comovement of asset returns and liquidity.'

Anadu et al. and CSW are not independent evidence: Anadu's equity-comovement cell rests on CSW ('Chen, Singal, and Whitelaw (2016) ... do not find evidence of an upward trend in recent years'). Present them as one finding plus a regulator endorsing it, not as two corroborating studies.

BIS March 2018: attribute to Sushko and Turner, BIS Quarterly Review, March 2018, Graph 3 — a descriptive exhibit, not a regression. Strengthen the critique by noting that the same Graph 3 shows trading volume jumping and bid-ask spreads narrowing on inclusion, which mechanically inflates a measured daily-return correlation via reduced non-synchronous trading; the confound is visible inside BIS's own chart.
reasoning:
I reached every primary document except the paywalled Financial Analysts Journal version of Anadu et al.

Documents read verbatim: (1) Barberis-Shleifer-Wurgler, "Comovement", JFE 75 (2005) 283-317 — read the introduction passage on p.286 and Table 1 Panel A in full, confirming univariate daily deltas 0.067 (1976-87, N=196), 0.214 (1988-2000, N=259), 0.151 (1976-2000, N=455) and bivariate 0.326 / -0.319 for the full 1976-2000 window, with subperiod bivariate values 0.286/-0.301 and 0.357/-0.332. (2) Chen-Singal-Whitelaw, "Comovement revisited", JFE 121 (2016) 624-644 — read the abstract, Table 1 Panel A in full, and Table 6 (Dimson plus momentum match) in full. All four claimed numbers match to the digit including t-statistics (0.763, 4.938, -0.137). (3) Kasch-Sarkar, FRBNY Staff Report 484 (Feb 2011, rev. Nov 2012) — read the abstract, the Section 4.1 passage on the S&P 500 specification, footnote 25 with the ">93%" refusal, and the full Section 6 conclusions. (4) BIS Quarterly Review March 2018, Sushko-Turner special feature — read Graph 3 and both footnotes plus surrounding prose. (5) ECB FSR November 2024 box (Dieckelmann/Siciliano/Sowinski) — read the full box text including the Chart B panel a notes and footnote 4. (6) Anadu-Kruttli-McCabe-Osambela, FEDS 2018-060r1 — read the abstract, Table 4 in full, and the "Effects on comovement" section.

Nothing in the group is fabricated or overturned; the comovement trail is real and every stated figure survives verbatim checking. The verdict is CORRECTED because of caliber problems rather than factual errors: (i) the BSW pair 0.326/-0.319 changes both spec and time window relative to 0.067/0.214, and the article risks reading as if only the spec changed; (ii) the CSW "zero" is the difference-of-differences only — the raw univariate S&P beta change for 2001-2012 is +0.071 with t=2.44, significant, and an article that says "no beta increase after 2001" would be wrong; (iii) Kasch-Sarkar say "preinclusion performance" (earnings, market value, momentum), not "momentum", and their own Table VII keeps a significant daily S&P beta change in multifactor specs, with the null at weekly frequency; (iv) the ECB's 0.005 comes from a dynamic panel with an AR(1) lag and three controls, with index-inclusion IV as a robustness check rather than the headline spec, and the x10 extrapolation is the article's own; (v) the Anadu quote is a table cell in a column asking whether the shift "exacerbated" the effect, sits next to an opposite-signed liquidity row, and rests on CSW itself, so it is not independent corroboration.

Remaining uncertainty: I could not open the paywalled FAJ 76(4) published version of Anadu et al. to confirm the table retains the number 4 and the identical cell wording there — the article should cite the FEDS working paper for the table reference. I also could not find any post-2016 replication, correction, or erratum to Chen-Singal-Whitelaw, and no journal publication of Kasch-Sarkar as of August 2026; searches returned only the FRBNY/SSRN/EconPapers listings of the same November 2012 revision.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) BSW JFE 2005: S&P daily beta increase on inclusion 0.067 (1976-87) vs 0.214 (1988-2000); 0.326/-0.319 is the bivariate spec
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in bsw.txt (JFE 75 (2005) 283-317). Text p.286: 'While stocks added to the S&P during 1976-1987 experience an average increase in daily S&P beta of 0.067 after inclusion, the average increase in the 1988-2000 period is 0.214.' Table (Panel A, daily returns) confirms univariate Db: 1976-2000 = 0.151*** (s.e. 0.021), 1976-1987 = 0.067*** (0.023), 1988-2000 = 0.214*** (0.032). Bivariate columns for 1976-2000: DbSP500 = 0.326*** (0.027), DbnonSP500 = -0.319*** (0.033); text: 'S&P betas increase by 0.326 on average over the 1976-2000 period, while non-S&P betas fall by an average of 0.319.' So the 0.326/-0.319 pair is indeed the BIVARIATE spec, daily frequency, FULL 1976-2000 sample (not a subperiod) — the bivariate subperiod values are 0.286/-0.301 and 0.357/-0.332. N = 196 and 259 for the two subperiods. Pre/post windows [-12,-1] and [+1,+12] months for daily.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) CSW JFE 2016: bivariate uninformative; univariate diff-of-diff +0.020 (t=0.76) 1976-87, +0.199 (t=4.94) 1988-2000, -0.004 (t=-0.14) 2001-2012 — zero in the decade passive grew fastest
itemVerdicts.note: NUMBERS ALL CONFIRMED VERBATIM (local csw.txt and an independent fresh fetch of the Stern PDF agree). Table 1 Panel A, 'Diff. of diff.' column (b2-b1): 1976-1987, nobs 197, 0.020, t = 0.763; 1988-2000, nobs 269, 0.199, t = 4.938; 2001-2012, nobs 214, -0.004, t = -0.137. TWO CALIBER ERRORS. (i) 'the bivariate spec is uninformative' is too flat. WRONG: uninformative. RIGHT: CSW's abstract says the bivariate regressions 'provide little information about the economic magnitude of excess comovement, with coefficients that are sensitive to unrelated factors'; body: 'the bivariate results are unreliable in terms of assessing the economic magnitude of any excess comovement.' The claim is about MAGNITUDE. This matters because CSW's own Panel B bivariate diff-of-diff for 2001-2012 is +0.607 (t = 5.41) — LARGER than the 1976-87 value of +0.537 — i.e. the bivariate spec, if believed, would say comovement got stronger, which is precisely why they discard it. (ii) 'the decade passive grew fastest' is false — see corrections. Also note the 2001-2012 zero is a NET: the raw univariate S&P beta change is still +0.071 (t = 2.439) and the non-S&P beta change +0.075 (t = 2.496); they cancel. CSW: 'it is not that stocks are moving more with S&P500 returns after they join the index, but simply that they are moving more with all stocks.' Event windows are one year pre (ending the month before announcement) and one year post (starting the month after the effective date).

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Kasch-Sarkar NY Fed SR 484: no permanent value or comovement effect after accounting for pre-inclusion momentum; declines the bivariate spec because regressors correlate >93%
itemVerdicts.note: Both halves verified in the SR 484 PDF (Feb 2011, revised Nov 2012). Footnote 25 verbatim: '...documented that the correlation between S&P 500 and non-S&P 500 stock returns exceeds 93%. The concern regarding a multiple regression with highly correlated regressors is that its parameter estimates are likely to be regression artifacts, rendering their interpretation difficult. Therefore, we do not consider specifications which include both of these highly correlated indices in one regression.' Conclusion verbatim: 'This paper demonstrates that the S&P 500 index inclusion has no permanent effect on market value and return comovement of the index-included firms.' CORRECTION on the conditioning variable. WRONG: 'after accounting for pre-inclusion momentum.' RIGHT: after accounting for extraordinary pre-inclusion PERFORMANCE, which the abstract defines as 'large increases in earnings, appreciation in market value, and positive price momentum' — momentum is one of three ingredients, and the size increase does most of the work on the market/S&P beta. Second qualifier the article omits: KS do NOT find a clean zero at daily frequency — 'index inclusion tends to contribute to an increase in synchronicity of comovement of the index-included stocks with the larger stocks in the market, as reflected in decline of the daily SMB betas. This is a high-frequency effect consistent with transitory price pressures of index trading. At the lower weekly frequency, index membership has no independent effect on comovement.' Also, in the multi-factor specs using the S&P return, 'delta-beta-sp remains statistically significant... although the magnitude of the effect is reduced.' Publication status: never journal-published; it remains a NY Fed staff report (previously circulated as 'Are Comovements Excessive?' and 'Comovement Revisited').

itemVerdicts.item: (d) BIS March 2018: correlation 0.45 -> 0.52 on inclusion, 462 stocks, 2000-2017, raw before/after with no matched control
itemVerdicts.note: Verified in local bis2018.txt AND in an independent fresh fetch of https://www.bis.org/publ/qtrpdf/r_qt1803j.pdf. Sushko & Turner, 'The implications of passive investing for securities markets,' BIS Quarterly Review, March 2018, Graph 3 left panel 'Correlation with the S&P 500 index': 0.45 'Before joining (from t-200 to t-1)' vs 0.52 'After joining (from t+1 to t+200)'. Footnote 1: 'Sample based on 462 stocks joining the S&P 500 between January 2000 and September 2017. Stocks subject to mergers and acquisitions, stocks with poor data availability and those that have left the index during the first 30 days after the inclusion date are excluded.' Footnote 2: 'Correlation of daily returns with the S&P 500 index.' The characterisation as an uncontrolled before/after is accurate — the only listed sample restrictions are those exclusions; no matched or control sample appears anywhere in the graph, its notes, or the text. Note the windows are +/-200 TRADING days, and this is a descriptive chart in a policy-review feature, not a regression.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) ECB FSR Nov 2024 box: +0.005 correlation per 1pp passive ownership share, euro area, stock+time FE, index-inclusion IV, base correlation 0.50; 10pp -> +0.05
itemVerdicts.note: Core number CONFIRMED verbatim from two independent local extractions of the ECB page (Dieckelmann, Siciliano, Sowinski, FSR November 2024): 'Between the first quarter of 2010 and the first quarter of 2024, a 1 percentage point increase in the passive ownership share of a euro area stock was associated with an increase of around 0.005 in the correlation coefficient with the EURO STOXX index.' Base rate confirmed in footnote 4: 'the average return correlation coefficient of a euro area stock with the EURO STOXX index between the first quarter of 2010 and the first quarter of 2024 is 0.50.' TWO CALIBER ERRORS. (i) The IV is not part of the headline spec. WRONG: presenting '+0.005 (stock+time FE, index-inclusion IV)' as one estimate. RIGHT: the estimate comes from 'a panel regression with stock and time fixed effects that regress correlation with the EURO STOXX index on the passive ownership share of constituent stocks, controlling for market capitalisation, liquidity, valuation and 1 autoregressive lag of the correlation coefficient'; index inclusion appears only as a robustness check — 'The results also hold in a two-step regression set-up, using index inclusion as an instrumental variable for passive ownership share.' No IV coefficient magnitude is reported. (ii) 'a 10pp passive rise maps to +0.05' is the article's own linear extrapolation, not the ECB's — the box never scales the coefficient. It is also mis-specified as stated: with an autoregressive lag of the dependent variable in the regression, 0.005 is a within-period (short-run) effect, so the implied long-run effect is LARGER than a 10x scaling, not equal to it. The ECB also reports only a 95% confidence interval in a chart, no point standard error in text.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) Anadu et al. Table 4 verdict: 'For equities, comovement effects have declined significantly since 2001.'
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in two independent local extractions (anadu.txt, fed2018060r1.txt). Table 4, 'Comovement of returns' row, rightmost column headed 'Evidence that active-to-passive shift has exacerbated?': 'For equities, comovement effects have declined significantly since 2001'. Source is Anadu, Kruttli, McCabe & Osambela, 'The Shift from Active to Passive Investing: Potential Risks to Financial Stability?', FEDS Working Paper 2018-060r1, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (Aug 2018, revised June 2020) — the Fed BOARD, not a regional reserve bank paper. Two context points: this cell is a literature-summary verdict, not the authors' own estimate, and it rests entirely on CSW ('Chen, Singal, and Whitelaw (2016), who look more specifically at index-inclusion effects on return betas, do not find evidence of an upward trend in recent years'). The adjacent 'Comovement of liquidity' row cuts the other way: 'Systematic liquidity associated with index investing has increased in recent years.' Quoting only the returns row without the liquidity row is selective.

corrections: Item (b): DELETE the phrase 'the decade passive grew fastest' for 2001-2012. It is false. Per ICI Fact Book Figure 5, index mutual funds plus index ETFs were 19% of US long-term fund total net assets at year-end 2010, 28% at 2015, 40% at 2020 and 52% at 2025 — passive grew far faster AFTER 2012 than during 2001-2012, and the post-2012 acceleration lies entirely outside CSW's sample (their additions sample ends in 2012). Replace with CSW's own wording: their 2001-2012 subperiod is one 'when indexing gained even more importance' than in 1988-2000, or Anadu et al.'s 'even as indexing had become more common.' Add explicitly that CSW's evidence says nothing about 2013-2026.

Item (b): Restate what CSW call uninformative. WRONG: 'the bivariate spec is uninformative.' RIGHT: CSW say the bivariate regressions 'provide little information about the economic MAGNITUDE of excess comovement, with coefficients that are sensitive to unrelated factors.' Sharpen the point by reporting CSW's own bivariate diff-of-diff numbers: +0.537 (t=5.38) for 1976-87, +0.750 (t=7.37) for 1988-2000 and +0.607 (t=5.41) for 2001-2012 — the bivariate spec shows a LARGER effect in the last subperiod than in the first, which is exactly the artifact CSW are diagnosing.

Item (b): Add the netting mechanism so 'statistically zero' is not misread as 'the added stock's index beta does not rise.' In CSW Table 1 Panel A for 2001-2012 the univariate S&P500 beta change is +0.071 (t = 2.439) and the non-S&P500 beta change is +0.075 (t = 2.496); the diff-of-diff of -0.004 (t = -0.137) is what nets to zero. CSW's own gloss: 'it is not that stocks are moving more with S&P500 returns after they join the index, but simply that they are moving more with all stocks.'

Item (b): State CSW's event window — one-year pre-event window ending the month before announcement, one-year post-event window starting the month after the effective date. This is load-bearing given the 2025 long-horizon rebuttal (see new contradictions).

Item (c): Fix the conditioning variable. WRONG: 'after accounting for pre-inclusion momentum.' RIGHT: after accounting for the firms' extraordinary PRE-INCLUSION PERFORMANCE — which Kasch-Sarkar's abstract defines as 'large increases in earnings, appreciation in market value, and positive price momentum.' The pre-inclusion increase in market size, not momentum, is what they show explains the rise in CAPM/S&P beta.

Item (c): Add Kasch-Sarkar's own residual caveat rather than presenting a clean null. They write that 'index inclusion tends to contribute to an increase in synchronicity of comovement of the index-included stocks with the larger stocks in the market, as reflected in decline of the daily SMB betas. This is a high-frequency effect consistent with transitory price pressures of index trading. At the lower weekly frequency, index membership has no independent effect on comovement.' Their claim is about PERMANENT effects, not the absence of any effect. Also note SR 484 (Feb 2011, revised Nov 2012) was never published in a journal.

Item (d): Specify the BIS windows and provenance: the 0.45 is the correlation of daily returns with the S&P 500 over t-200 to t-1 TRADING days and the 0.52 over t+1 to t+200, from Graph 3 of Sushko & Turner, 'The implications of passive investing for securities markets,' BIS Quarterly Review, March 2018. The only sample restrictions the note states are exclusion of M&A stocks, stocks with poor data availability, and stocks leaving the index within 30 days of inclusion — confirming there is no matched control.

Item (e): Correct the specification attribution. WRONG: '+0.005 ... stock+time FE, index-inclusion IV' as a single estimate. RIGHT: the +0.005 is from a panel regression with stock and time fixed effects controlling for market capitalisation, liquidity, valuation AND one autoregressive lag of the correlation coefficient; the ECB reports index inclusion as an instrument only as a robustness check — 'The results also hold in a two-step regression set-up, using index inclusion as an instrumental variable for passive ownership share' — with no IV coefficient given.

Item (e): Label the '10pp -> +0.05' as the article's own arithmetic, not the ECB's, and drop it or caveat it. The box never scales the coefficient, and because the regression includes an autoregressive lag of the dependent variable, 0.005 is a within-period effect, so a straight 10x scaling understates the implied long-run effect rather than reproducing it. Also state the estimation window (Q1 2010 to Q1 2024) and that the 0.50 base is the AVERAGE correlation of a euro area stock with the EURO STOXX over that same window.

Item (f): Attribute correctly and stop calling it a 'verdict.' It is the literature-summary cell in Table 4 of Anadu, Kruttli, McCabe & Osambela, FEDS Working Paper 2018-060r1, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (Aug 2018, revised June 2020), and it rests entirely on CSW. If the returns row is quoted, quote the adjacent liquidity row too — 'Systematic liquidity associated with index investing has increased in recent years' — otherwise the citation is selective.
newContradictions: PUBLISHED 2025 REBUTTAL OF CSW THAT THE ARTICLE MUST ADDRESS: DeCoste, Joseph (2025), 'Comovement and S&P 500 membership,' Global Finance Journal, vol. 65(C), DOI 10.1016/j.gfj.2025.101110. Abstract (retrieved verbatim from the RePEc/IDEAS record, handle RePEc:eee:glofin:v:65:y:2025:i:c:s1044028325000377; the ScienceDirect page returned HTTP 403 so I could not read the full text): 'This paper tests the existence of excessive comovement among firms in the S&P 500. Using a fuzzy regression discontinuity approach I show that membership in the S&P 500 leads to significant positive excess comovement in the long term. I evaluate a traditional, liquidity based explanation and a friction based explanation, and find no evidence that liquidity is driving excess comovement in the sample. I show that the previous lack of evidence for excess comovement shown in Chen, Singal, Whitelaw (2016) is due to heterogeneous effects on firms who are newly included versus those that are established members. One potential explanation is that immediately after inclusion, investors take time to rebalance and fully integrate the new stock into the group, reducing observed increases in comovement in the short term.' This directly attacks the load-bearing pillar of this claim group: it argues CSW's null is an artifact of their short (one-year) post-inclusion window and of pooling new entrants with established members. It does not dispute any of CSW's reported numbers, but the article cannot present CSW as the settled last word without disclosing DeCoste (2025).

Anadu et al.'s own Table 4 companion row cuts against the comovement-is-fading narrative: 'Systematic liquidity associated with index investing has increased in recent years,' and their body text cites Kamara-Lou-Sadka (2008, 2010), Bolla-Kohler-Wittig (2017) and Agarwal-Hanouna-Moussawi-Stahel (2018) for rising liquidity commonality. Their overall summary is 'the evidence is mixed on whether return comovement has increased more broadly with the growth of passive investing' — not that comovement effects are dead.

Anadu et al. also cite Da & Shive (2018, European Financial Management 24(1), 136-168) for the finding that ETF ownership of stocks boosts return comovement, and the ECB Nov 2024 box cites the same paper. The article's trail runs BSW -> CSW -> null, but both the Fed and the ECB place Da & Shive on the other side of the ledger, post-dating CSW's 2012 sample end.
reasoning:
I reached and read all six primary documents. Local extractions used: bsw.txt (BSW JFE 2005 full text incl. Table 1 Panel A), csw.txt (CSW JFE 2016 full text incl. Table 1 Panels A and B), v20_sr484.txt (NY Fed SR 484), bis2018.txt (BIS QR March 2018), ecb_box2.txt and ecb.txt (two independent extractions of the ECB FSR Nov 2024 box), anadu.txt and fed2018060r1.txt (two independent extractions of FEDS 2018-060r1). Because charts and tables extract unreliably, I re-fetched two documents fresh and re-extracted with pdftotext -layout: the BIS Quarterly Review PDF from bis.org (Graph 3 confirmed 0.45 before / 0.52 after, 462 stocks, Jan 2000-Sep 2017, +/-200 trading days) and the CSW PDF from pages.stern.nyu.edu (Table 1 Panel A confirmed 0.020/t=0.763, 0.199/t=4.938, -0.004/t=-0.137, nobs 197/269/214). Every headline number in the claim group survives verbatim; I found no fabricated figure.

What fails is caliber, in four places. (1) The claim that 2001-2012 is 'the decade passive grew fastest' is false and I falsified it against ICI Fact Book Figure 5 (index share of US long-term fund assets 19% in 2010, 28% in 2015, 40% in 2020, 52% in 2025) — the fastest passive growth is post-2012, outside CSW's sample entirely. (2) CSW call the bivariate spec uninformative about economic MAGNITUDE, not uninformative full stop, and their own bivariate estimates for 2001-2012 (+0.607, t=5.41) are larger than for 1976-87, which the article should use rather than suppress. (3) Kasch-Sarkar condition on 'extraordinary preinclusion performance' (earnings, market value, momentum), not momentum alone, and they report a surviving daily-frequency SMB-beta effect they interpret as transitory price pressure — their null is about PERMANENT effects. (4) The ECB's +0.005 comes from a stock-and-time-FE panel with an AR(1) lag of the dependent variable; the index-inclusion IV is only a stated robustness check with no reported coefficient, and the '10pp -> +0.05' scaling is the article's own and is mis-specified given the lagged dependent variable.

The most important adversarial find is a later published contradiction: DeCoste (2025), Global Finance Journal 65, uses a fuzzy RD design and reports significant positive excess comovement from S&P 500 membership in the long term, explicitly attributing CSW's null to heterogeneous effects between newly included and established members. I verified its title, author, journal, volume and abstract through the RePEc/IDEAS record; ScienceDirect returned 403, so I could not read the full text and cannot independently assess its identification strategy or magnitudes. That limitation is the main remaining uncertainty. I also could not check whether the Financial Analysts Journal 2020 version of Anadu et al. reproduces Table 4 verbatim; I verified only the FEDS 2018-060r1 version, which is what the claim cites.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Published JF abstract: additions 7.4% (1990s) → less than 1% over the past decade; deletions large negative (1990s) → +0.1% average 2010-2020; JF 80(2), April 2025, 657-698
itemVerdicts.note: Crossref DOI 10.1111/jofi.13410 (local cr.json) gives verbatim: 'has fallen from an average of 7.4% in the 1990s to less than 1% over the past decade... A similar pattern has occurred for index deletions, with large negative abnormal returns during the 1990s but an average return of only 0.1% between 2010 and 2020.' Metadata confirmed: volume 80, issue 2, pages 657-698, published-print 2025-04, authors GREENWOOD and SAMMON. TWO CAVEATS. (i) The abstract says 'over the past decade' for additions, not '2010-2020'; only the deletions sentence is dated 2010-2020. (ii) The published paper's own BODY contradicts its abstract on deletions: the accepted manuscript (Harvard DASH, March 2024) says at p.~12 'The deletion effect fell in magnitude to -12.4% in the 2000s and disappeared in the 2010s, with an average abnormal return of -0.6%', and published Table 2 column (3) reports 2010-2020 deletions = -0.62 (ns). The abstract's +0.1% is most likely the effective-date (not total) abnormal return (+0.127% in the WP table). So the '+0.1%' is quotable from the abstract but should not be presented as the paper's estimate of the 2010-2020 deletion effect.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-note) Version drift: Dec-2022 NBER WP says 3.4% (1980s)/7.6% (1990s)/0.8% (2010s), deletions -0.6%
itemVerdicts.note: NBER w30748 abstract verbatim (local gs.txt): 'has fallen from an average of 3.4% in the 1980s and 7.6% in the 1990s to 0.8% over the past decade... but only -0.6% between 2010 and 2020.' BUT the two-version framing is INCOMPLETE — there are at least four public abstracts: (1) NBER w30748 / HBS WP 23-025, Dec 2022: 3.4/7.6/0.8, deletions -0.6%; (2) the June-2023 revision, which is what marcosammon.com/images/greenwood_sammon.pdf currently serves: same abstract numbers but 'over the past two decades'; (3) HBS WP 23-025 revised Nov 2023: 'from an average of 7.4% in the 1990s to 0.3% over the past decade... deletions... only 0.1%'; (4) JF/DASH March 2024: 7.4% → 'less than 1%', deletions 0.1%. So the marcosammon.com PDF listed as a source for this group is NOT the 7.4%/<1% version — it is the June-2023 draft. Citing it for the published figures would be a mis-citation. The 0.3% figure circulating on the web (alphaarchitect, some search summaries) is the Nov-2023 draft, not the published paper.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) WP Table 2: additions 1980s 3.42%, 1990s 7.25%, 2000s 5.14%, 2010-20 0.804% (ns); deletions 1990s -16.1%, 2010-20 -0.62% (ns); deletion decade cells 39-87 events
itemVerdicts.note: NUMBERS CORRECT BUT ATTRIBUTED TO THE WRONG WORKING PAPER. These match ONLY the June-2023 revision (the live marcosammon.com PDF), Table 2 'Addition and deletion abnormal returns by decade': Panel A Total = 0.0411*** (All) / 0.0342*** / 0.0725*** / 0.0514*** / 0.00804 (no stars) / -0.043***; Panel B Total = -0.0820*** / -0.0464** / -0.161*** / -0.124*** / -0.0062 (no stars) / 0.118***; Panel B N = 267 / 39 / 56 / 85 / 87. So 'ns' and '39-87 events' both check out. WRONG: the Dec-2022 NBER WP w30748 Table 2 Panel A gives 0.0417 / 0.0342 / 0.0759 / 0.0521 / 0.00799 — i.e. 7.59% and 5.21%, not 7.25% and 5.14%. ALSO WRONG if cited to the published article: the JF paper has no such table (its Table 2 is 'Cumulative abnormal returns, controlling for characteristics'), and its decade-dummy estimates without controls are additions 3.654*** / 7.414*** / 4.950*** / 0.782 (ns), N=610, and deletions -2.184 (ns) / -15.20*** / -12.71*** / -0.62 (ns), N=237.

itemVerdicts.item: (c1) S&P-500-tracking funds grew ~0 → 7% of market cap
itemVerdicts.note: CONFLATES TWO DIFFERENT QUANTITIES. The ~0→6-8% series in the paper is net trading by trackers as a percentage of THE ADDED/DELETED STOCK'S SHARES OUTSTANDING, not the tracking industry's share of market cap. Published text: 'in the early 1990s, net buying by trackers of additions was close to 0% of shares outstanding, while now it is over 6%. This pattern is mirrored for deletions, going from approximately 0% to almost 8% of shares outstanding' (Figure 1). The industry's AUM share of index capitalization appears only implicitly, in the MidCap comparison: published version says MidCap trackers reached 'about 6% of capitalization, slightly more than that of the S&P 500, which we showed earlier' — i.e. S&P 500 trackers just UNDER ~6% of S&P 500 market cap. The '7%' reading comes from the June-2023 draft, whose same sentence read 'nearly 8% of capitalization, slightly more than that of the S&P 500' (implying ~7%); it was revised down to ~6% in the published version.

itemVerdicts.item: (c2) Trackers buy 7-8% of shares outstanding on addition yet total institutional ownership barely moves; active investors provide the liquidity
itemVerdicts.note: Published intro verbatim: 'although index trackers now buy about 7-8% upon index addition, total institutional ownership barely moves around index changes. We interpret this as professional active investors providing liquidity to passive buyers and sellers.' Body/Table 7 quantifies it: 'for the average addition in 2020, index trackers buy 7.53% of shares outstanding. However, institutional ownership only increases by 0.65% of shares outstanding... in 2020, index trackers sell an average of 8.45% of shares outstanding upon deletion, but institutional ownership overall falls by only 1.42%.' ONE NUANCE the article must not blur: the paper explicitly rules out active MUTUAL FUNDS as the providers — 'The "Active" column shows that active mutual funds are not the group providing liquidity, as their average net demand is roughly zero. This implies that non-S12 filing institutions (e.g., hedge...)'. So 'active investors' means non-mutual-fund institutions such as hedge funds, not active managers generally.

itemVerdicts.item: (c3) Migrations (simultaneous S&P MidCap 400 exit) rose from ~40% to >80% of additions
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG for the published paper. Published JF/DASH text: 'From the 1990s to the present day, migrations went from about 50% of additions to over 70%.' Body: 'In the 1990s, migrations accounted for about 69% of additions and less than 10% of deletions. In recent years, they both make up over 70% of index changes.' The 40%→80% pair exists only in the Dec-2022 NBER WP ('migrations went from about 40% of additions to over 80%'), which is itself internally inconsistent — its own body says 'In the mid-1990s, migrations were about 40% of additions and 0% of drops. In recent years, they both make up over 60% of index changes.' The June-2023 draft says '50% ... to over 70%' in the intro and '60% ... over 70%' in the body. Note the published body's 69% 1990s starting point makes the 'rise in migrations' story much weaker than 40%→80% implies. Definition confirmed: 'a migration [is] any stock which is added to (dropped from) the S&P 500 and dropped from (added to) the S&P MidCap within 5 calendar days.'

itemVerdicts.item: (c4) Direct additions still earned +5.3% in the 2010s, Tesla-driven; ex-Tesla the 2020 average inclusion effect was -3bp
itemVerdicts.note: 5.3% is the June-2023 draft figure ('for direct additions, the index inclusion effect was 10.5% in the late 90s, 8.6% in the 2000s, and 5.3% in the 2010s'). The PUBLISHED version says 5.4%: 'for direct additions, the index inclusion effect was 10.2% in the late 90s, 8.8% in the 2000s, and 5.4% in the 2010s. The large positive return in the last period is driven by Tesla, which... had a massive return of 53.35% between its announcement and effective dates.' Published Table 3 shows Direct additions 1995-1999 10.23%, 2000-2009 8.80%, 2010-2020 5.40%; migrations 6.65% / 2.72% / -1.82%; Diff -3.58% / -6.07% / -7.22% (SE 2.12% / 1.34% / 0.99%). The '-3 basis points' quote is real — 'Excluding Tesla, the average inclusion effect in 2020 was -3 basis points' — but it is the 2020 average across ALL additions, NOT the ex-Tesla direct-addition average for the 2010s; the article must not present it as the ex-Tesla version of the 5.3/5.4% number. Additional caution: Table 3's caption says 'Standard error from two-sided t-test reported below the means', and 8.38% sits under the 5.40%; read literally, the direct-addition 2010s mean is statistically insignificant, and the only significant quantity is the direct-minus-migration difference.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Authors frame the decay as arbitrage/anomaly decay (McLean-Pontiff), not as evidence passive is harmless; Bennett-Stulz-Wang documented the decline first (1997-2017 additions)
itemVerdicts.note: Published text verbatim: '...the decline of the index effect is much like the evidence for other anomalies: they decline once they are well recognized by the market (McLean and Pontiff, 2016).' Conclusion: 'when demand shocks become regular and repeated, competitive markets adapt over time to minimize price impact, in the spirit of Lo's (2004) adaptive markets hypothesis' — the scope is price impact around index changes, with no claim that passive investing is benign generally; they leave open why adaptation took until the 2010s. Priority verbatim: 'Most closely related to our paper is Bennett et al. (2020), who first noted the decline in the index inclusion effect among additions between 1997 and 2017' (also 'consistent with Bennett et al. (2020)' in the intro and 'as originally highlighted by Bennett et al. (2020)' in Section 3). Reference list: 'Bennett, Benjamin, Rene Stulz, and Zexi Wang, 2020, Does Joining the S&P 500 Index Hurt Firms?' — NBER w27593, sample 1997-2017, 659 additions.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) NEW-WINDOW CHECK: Coinbase jumped ~24% on its May 12, 2025 S&P 500 inclusion announcement
itemVerdicts.note: Announcement verified at the primary source: S&P Dow Jones Indices press release, NEW YORK, May 12, 2025 — 'Coinbase Global Inc. (NASD: COIN) will replace Discover Financial Services (NYSE: DFS) in the S&P 500 effective prior to the opening of trading on Monday, May 19.' Released after the close (contemporaneous coverage reported an ~8% post-market pop). Market data (daily closes): COIN 207.22 on 2025-05-12 → 256.90 on 2025-05-13 = +23.97%; SPY same day +0.66%, so the market-adjusted announcement-day move is ~+23.3%. On the paper's own event window (last close before announcement 5/9 = 199.32 → first close after implementation 5/20 = 261.38) COIN returned +31.1% vs SPY +5.05%, a CAR of about +26.1%. NOT AN ISOLATED CASE: after the S&P DJI announcement of 2025-09-05 (also after the close), Robinhood closed +15.8% and AppLovin +11.6% on 2025-09-08. Caveats to carry: these are single events, not an abnormal-return estimate; I did not screen the 5/9-5/20 window for other COIN-specific news; and the peer-reviewed sample ends in 2020, so any 2021-2025 revival is outside what Greenwood-Sammon tested.

corrections: Do not cite marcosammon.com/images/greenwood_sammon.pdf for the published figures. That file is the June-2023 revision, whose abstract still reads '3.4% in the 1980s and 7.6% in the 1990s to 0.8%... deletions... only -0.6%'. For the published numbers cite the Journal of Finance article, DOI 10.1111/jofi.13410, 80(2), April 2025, 657-698, or the Harvard DASH accepted manuscript (March 2024).

There are at least FOUR public abstracts, not two. Dec-2022 NBER w30748 / HBS WP 23-025: additions 3.4% (1980s) / 7.6% (1990s) / 0.8% (2010s), deletions -0.6%. June-2023 revision (live on marcosammon.com): same numbers, 'past two decades'. HBS WP 23-025 revised Nov-2023: additions 7.4% (1990s) → 0.3%, deletions 0.1%. Published JF: additions 7.4% (1990s) → 'less than 1%', deletions 0.1%. Any '0.3%' figure seen online is the Nov-2023 draft and must not be attributed to the JF article.

If quoting the published deletion figure of +0.1%, attribute it to the abstract only and note that the paper's own body and Table 2 report the 2010-2020 deletion effect as -0.6% (Table 2 col. 3: -0.62, statistically insignificant). Wrong: 'Greenwood and Sammon find deletions earned +0.1% in 2010-2020.' Right: 'the published abstract states 0.1%, while the paper's text and tables report -0.6%, insignificantly different from zero.'

The decade table numbers 3.42% / 7.25% / 5.14% / 0.804% (additions) and -16.1% / -0.62% (deletions), with deletion cell counts of 39/56/85/87, are Table 2 of the JUNE-2023 working-paper revision. Wrong: attributing them to the Dec-2022 NBER working paper, whose Table 2 gives 3.42% / 7.59% / 5.21% / 0.799%. Also wrong: attributing them to 'Table 2' of the published article — the JF Table 2 is a characteristics-controlled regression whose decade-dummy estimates (col. 1) are 3.654% / 7.414% / 4.950% / 0.782% for additions (N=610) and -2.184% / -15.20% / -12.71% / -0.62% for deletions (N=237).

Fix the tracking-industry statistic. Wrong: 'S&P-500-tracking funds grew from ~0 to 7% of market cap.' Right: net buying by S&P 500 trackers grew from close to 0% to over 6% of the ADDED STOCK's shares outstanding (and to almost 8% of shares outstanding sold on deletions); separately, the published paper implies S&P 500 tracker AUM is a bit under ~6% of S&P 500 market capitalization ('dollars tracking the MidCap... reaching about 6% of capitalization, slightly more than that of the S&P 500'). The ~7-8% figure is the event-time demand shock, not the industry's ownership share.

Fix the migrations figures. Wrong: 'migrations rose from ~40% to more than 80% of additions.' Right (published): 'migrations went from about 50% of additions to over 70%', and the body states migrations were already about 69% of additions in the 1990s and are now over 70% of index changes (deletions went from less than 10% to over 70%). The 40%→80% pair appears only in the Dec-2022 NBER draft, which even there conflicts with its own body text (40%→over 60%).

Fix the direct-addition figure and the Tesla adjustment. Wrong: 'direct additions still earned +5.3% in the 2010s; ex-Tesla that was -3bp.' Right: the published paper reports 5.4% for direct additions in 2010-2020 (5.3% only in the June-2023 draft), attributes the level to Tesla's 53.35% announcement-to-effective return, and separately reports that 'excluding Tesla, the average inclusion effect in 2020 was -3 basis points' — a 2020 all-additions statistic, not an ex-Tesla direct-addition average for the decade. If the article leans on 5.4%, add that published Table 3 lists 8.38% beneath it, labelled a standard error, so the level is not statistically distinguishable from zero; what is significant is the direct-minus-migration gap of -7.22% (SE 0.99%).

When describing who absorbs the tracker demand, do not say 'active managers' or 'active funds'. The paper's intro says 'professional active investors providing liquidity', but its body states that active MUTUAL FUNDS are not the providers ('their average net demand is roughly zero') and points to non-S12-filing institutions such as hedge funds.

State the Coinbase event precisely and date the announcement to the close of May 12, 2025. S&P DJI announced on 2025-05-12 that COIN replaces Discover Financial Services effective before the open on Monday, 2025-05-19. COIN's next-session move was +23.97% (207.22 → 256.90) against SPY +0.66%, an abnormal move of about +23.3%; on Greenwood-Sammon's own window (5/9 close to 5/20 close) the market-adjusted CAR is about +26.1%. Do not write 'jumped 24% on May 12' without noting the announcement was after the close and the move occurred on May 13.

If the article treats 2025 as a possible revival, note that Coinbase was not unique: after the after-close announcement of 2025-09-05, Robinhood closed +15.8% and AppLovin +11.6% on 2025-09-08. Also state explicitly that Greenwood-Sammon's sample ends in 2020, so nothing in the peer-reviewed paper speaks to 2021-2025, and that individual events are not abnormal-return estimates.
newContradictions: The published JF abstract (Crossref 10.1111/jofi.13410 and the DASH accepted manuscript) says the 2010-2020 deletion effect averaged 0.1%, while the same paper's body text says '-0.6%' and its Table 2 column (3) reports -0.62. The abstract figure appears to correspond to the effective-date abnormal return (+0.127% in the working-paper table), not the total CAR. Any article quoting '+0.1%' as the deletion effect is repeating an internal inconsistency in the paper.

The Dec-2022 NBER working paper is internally inconsistent on migrations: its introduction says migrations went 'from about 40% of additions to over 80%', while its own body says 'In the mid-1990s, migrations were about 40% of additions and 0% of drops. In recent years, they both make up over 60% of index changes.'

The migrations statistic moved substantially across versions (40%→80%, then 50%→70%, and in the published body 69%→over 70%), which materially weakens the 'migrations explain the decline' magnitude relative to what the widely circulated working-paper numbers imply.

Post-2020 market data contradict a flat 'the index effect has disappeared' framing: COIN +24.0% (abnormal ~+23.3%) on 2025-05-13, HOOD +15.8% and APP +11.6% on 2025-09-08. All three fall entirely outside the paper's 1980-2020 sample.
reasoning: I read five distinct primary texts of the paper end to end from local extractions plus a live Crossref record, and treated each as a separate document rather than assuming version equivalence. (1) Crossref record for DOI 10.1111/jofi.13410 (local cr.json) gave the publisher-deposited abstract verbatim along with volume 80, issue 2, pp. 657-698, published-print April 2025 — this confirms sub-claim (a) word for word. (2) NBER w30748 (Dec 2022) full text confirmed the 3.4/7.6/0.8/-0.6 abstract AND revealed its Table 2 values are 0.0342/0.0759/0.0521/0.00799, which do NOT match the numbers in sub-claim (b). (3) The June-2023 revision — which is what marcosammon.com currently serves, byte-identical to a fresh fetch made during this run — has Table 2 values 0.0342/0.0725/0.0514/0.00804 with deletions -0.161/-0.0062 and Panel B N = 267/39/56/85/87, matching sub-claim (b) exactly. So (b)'s numbers are real but belong to a specific draft. (4) The HBS WP 23-025 Nov-2023 revision surfaced a third abstract ('0.3%', deletions '0.1%'), which the claim's two-version framing misses and which is what several web summaries are echoing. (5) The Harvard DASH accepted manuscript (March 2024, matching the published abstract) showed the decade panel table was dropped in publication and replaced by a characteristics-controlled Table 2 whose decade dummies are 3.654/7.414/4.950/0.782 and -2.184/-15.20/-12.71/-0.62. Mechanism items were checked against verbatim sentences in the published manuscript: the 7-8%/institutional-ownership-barely-moves claim and the 'professional active investors providing liquidity' interpretation are exact, but the migrations figures (published: 50%→over 70%, body 69%→over 70%) refute the claimed 40%→80%, the direct-addition figure is 5.4% not 5.3%, and the '~0→7% of market cap' conflates net event buying as a share of the added stock's shares outstanding with the tracking industry's AUM share (published text implies just under 6%). Attribution and McLean-Pontiff/adaptive-markets framing checked verbatim, as did the Bennett-Stulz-Wang priority sentence and BSW's 1997-2017 / 659-addition sample. For the new-window check I verified the S&P DJI press release directly (dated May 12, 2025, effective May 19) and computed COIN's move from daily closes (207.22→256.90 = +23.97%) with SPY as the market benchmark (+0.66%), giving ~+23.3% abnormal, and ~+26.1% on the paper's own announcement-to-implementation window; I additionally checked HOOD and APP around the Sept 5, 2025 announcement, both of which popped double digits. Remaining uncertainty: I could not open the Wiley version-of-record HTML (Cloudflare challenge), so I cannot rule out that the VOR body text differs from the March-2024 accepted manuscript on the deletion figure — but the VOR abstract deposited to Crossref matches the accepted manuscript's abstract exactly, and the accepted manuscript's body says -0.6%. I also did not independently screen COIN for firm-specific news inside the 5/9-5/20 window, so the +26.1% window CAR should not be read as a clean inclusion effect.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Published JF abstract: additions fell from 7.4% average in the 1990s to less than 1% over 2010-2020; deletions from large negative to +0.1% average 2010-2020; JF 80(2), April 2025, 657-698
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim from two independent primary records. Crossref deposit for 10.1111/jofi.13410 (local cr.json, indexed 2026-08-14) and RePEc/IDEAS JSON-LD both give: "The abnormal return associated with a stock being added to the S&P 500 has fallen from an average of 7.4% in the 1990s to less than 1% over the past decade. ... A similar pattern has occurred for index deletions, with large negative abnormal returns during the 1990s but an average return of only 0.1% between 2010 and 2020." Crossref: published-print 2025-04, issue 2, page 657-698; RePEc confirms vol. 80. Note the abstract says "over the past decade," not "2010-2020," for the additions figure (the paper's sample is 1980-2020, so the two coincide). CAVEAT that must travel with this number: the +0.1% deletions figure appears NOWHERE in the paper's own tables. Published Table 1 reports 2010s deletion total CAR = -0.62% (statistically insignificant), and the published body text (p.11 of the accepted MS) says the deletion effect "disappeared in the 2010s, with an average abnormal return of -0.6%." The only +0.1-ish cell is the 2010s deletion EFFECTIVE-window CAR of +0.13%.

itemVerdicts.item: NOTE on version drift: Dec-2022 NBER WP says 3.4%/7.6%/0.8% and deletions -0.6%; the deletions figure FLIPPED SIGN between versions
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as stated: nothing flipped sign in the DATA. RIGHT: the NBER w30748 abstract is confirmed verbatim (local gs.txt lines 34-39: "...from an average of 3.4% in the 1980s and 7.6% in the 1990s to 0.8% over the past decade... but only -0.6% between 2010 and 2020"). But the underlying decade estimate for 2010-2020 deletions is -0.603% (Dec-2022 Table 2), -0.62% (June-2023 Table 2), and -0.62% (published Table 1) — identical across all three. Only the ABSTRACT wording changed. Also WRONG: there are FOUR abstract variants, not two. HBS Working Paper 23-025 (revised November 2023, local v19c_hbs.txt line 33) reads "from an average of 7.4% in the 1990s to 0.3% over the past decade... but only 0.1% between 2010 and 2020" — so a third additions figure (0.3%) is circulating, and the 0.1% deletions wording was introduced in Nov 2023, not at publication.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) WP Table 2: additions 1980s 3.42%, 1990s 7.25%, 2000s 5.14%, 2010-20 0.804% (ns); deletions 1990s -16.1%, 2010-20 -0.62% (ns); deletion decade cells rest on 39-87 events
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers verified EXACTLY, but against the wrong document if labelled generically as "the WP." RIGHT attribution: these are Table 2 of the JUNE 2023 revision (marcosammon.com/images/greenwood_sammon.pdf; local gs2.txt/gs_final.txt lines 1936-1948): additions Total 0.0342 / 0.0725 / 0.0514 / 0.00804 (SE 0.005, ns); deletions Total -0.0464 / -0.161 / -0.124 / -0.0062 (SE 0.011, ns); deletion N = 267 all, 39 / 56 / 85 / 87 by decade. WRONG if cited to the Dec-2022 NBER w30748, whose Table 2 reads additions 0.0342 / 0.0759 / 0.0521 / 0.00799 and deletions -0.0464 / -0.166 / -0.123 / -0.00603, with addition N 196/128/210/150. ALSO WRONG for the published paper: in the JF version the decade breakdown is TABLE 1 ("S&P 500 Addition and deletion cumulative abnormal returns by year"), not Table 2, and reads additions 3.42%*** / 7.39%*** / 5.16%*** / 0.83% (ns) with N 196/134/211/153, deletions -4.64%** / -16.11%*** / -12.39%*** / -0.62% (ns) with N 39/56/85/87. The 39-87 deletion-event range is correct in every version.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) S&P-500-tracking funds grew ~0 to 7% of market cap
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the published/accepted text: "We estimate that funds tracking the S&P 500 in the form of mutual funds or ETFs have grown from essentially zero in the 1980s to approximately 7 percent of market capitalization in recent years." The paper immediately adds that other estimates (Chinco and Sammon 2022, or sell-side research) "suggest even higher levels of investor indexation to the S&P 500 today" — worth carrying, since 7% is the authors' explicit lower bound, not a ceiling.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Trackers buy 7-8% of shares outstanding on addition yet total institutional ownership barely moves (active investors provide the liquidity)
itemVerdicts.note: Magnitudes RIGHT, attribution of the seller WRONG. Verbatim: "for the average addition in 2020, index trackers buy 7.53% of shares outstanding. However, institutional ownership only increases by 0.65% of shares outstanding... in 2020, index trackers sell an average of 8.45% of shares outstanding upon deletion, but institutional ownership overall falls by only 1.42%." Published Table 7 gives trackers 7.43%/7.57%/7.53% for 2018/2019/2020 additions, so "7-8%" is fair for the late 2010s. Two caliber fixes: (1) Table 7 reports the MEDIAN by year, not the mean, despite the body calling it "the average addition"; (2) the paper says liquidity "is provided, on average, by other institutions exiting their positions, rather than accommodation by other parties such as retail investors" — it does NOT say active funds. Table 7's "Active" mutual-fund column for 2020 additions is +2.40% (active funds were net BUYERS). Write "other 13F institutions," not "active investors."

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Migrations (simultaneous S&P400 exit) rose from ~40% to >80% of additions
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: ~40% to >80% is the Dec-2022 NBER w30748 wording only (gs.txt lines 127-128 and 492). RIGHT (published/accepted and June-2023 versions): "From the 1990s to the present day, migrations went from about 50% of additions to over 70%. The trend toward more migrations is even stronger among S&P 500 index deletions." And in the body: "In the 1990s, migrations accounted for about 69% of additions and less than 10% of deletions. In recent years, they both make up over 70% of index changes." This reverses the story: in the published paper the migration share of ADDITIONS barely moved (~69% to ~70%); the dramatic rise is in DELETIONS (<10% to >70%).

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Direct additions still earned +5.3% in the 2010s, Tesla-driven; ex-Tesla the 2020 average inclusion effect was -3bp
itemVerdicts.note: Tesla claim CONFIRMED verbatim: "Excluding Tesla, the average inclusion effect in 2020 was -3 basis points." Direct-addition figure WRONG for the published paper: 5.3% (5.337%) is Table 4 of the June-2023 WP. RIGHT: published Table 3 gives direct additions CAR of 10.23% (1995-99), 8.80% (2000-09), 5.40% (2010-20); migrations 6.65% / 2.72% / -1.82%. Body: "for direct additions, the index inclusion effect was 10.2% in the late 90s, 8.8% in the 2000s, and 5.4% in the 2010s. The large positive return in the last period is driven by Tesla, which... had a massive return of 53.35% between its announcement and effective dates." Note the published direct-addition means carry an SE of 8.38% for 2010-2020, i.e. the 5.4% is not distinguishable from zero on its own.
