itemVerdicts.item: (d) Authors frame the decay as arbitrage/anomaly decay (McLean-Pontiff), not as evidence passive is harmless; Bennett-Stulz-Wang documented the decline first (1997-2017 additions)
itemVerdicts.note: Both verbatim. Intro: "This worked to eliminate the anomaly on average, despite demand shocks that continued to grow in magnitude over the 2000s and 2010s. In this sense, the decline of the index effect is much like the evidence for other anomalies: they decline once they are well recognized by the market (McLean and Pontiff, 2016)." Literature review: "Most closely related to our paper is Bennett et al. (2020), who first noted the decline in the index inclusion effect among additions between 1997 and 2017." The paper nowhere argues passive is harmless (no "does not mean"/"should not be interpreted" hedges either way). Two nuances to preserve: the CONCLUSION's own framing is Lo's adaptive markets, not McLean-Pontiff — "when demand shocks become regular and repeated, competitive markets adapt over time to minimize price impact, in the spirit of Lo's (2004) adaptive markets hypothesis"; and G&S co-credit "Preston and Soe (2021)" who "also document the decline in index inclusion effect among additions and deletions beginning in 1995," so BSW is not the sole precedent.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Coinbase jumped ~24% on its May 12, 2025 S&P 500 inclusion announcement
itemVerdicts.note: Magnitude CONFIRMED from market data, date attribution needs a fix. S&P DJI press release (fetched verbatim from press.spglobal.com): "NEW YORK, May 12, 2025 /PRNewswire/ -- Coinbase Global Inc. (NASD: COIN) will replace Discover Financial Services (NYSE: DFS) in the S&P 500 effective prior to the opening of trading on Monday, May 19." Released AFTER the May 12 close. Yahoo daily bars for COIN: May 12 close 207.22 (+3.96%), May 13 close 256.90 = +23.97% raw. S&P 500 that day +0.72% (5,886.55 vs 5,844.19), so market-adjusted approx +23.3%. WRONG to say "jumped 24% on May 12"; RIGHT: "jumped ~24% on May 13, 2025, the first session after the May 12 after-close announcement." On the May 19 effective date COIN was -0.93%. Three qualifications the article must carry: (1) the peer-reviewed sample is 1980-2020, so 2025 is out of sample; (2) Coinbase was a DIRECT addition, not a migration — the S&P DJI release lists only an S&P 500 add/delete with no MidCap 400 change — and G&S's own published Table 3 shows direct additions still averaged +5.40% in the 2010s, so a direct-addition pop is not per se a refutation, though 24% is roughly 4.4x that mean; (3) it is not a one-off — Robinhood closed +15.83% on Sept 8, 2025 (100.84 to 117.28), the first session after its Sept 5 after-close announcement that it would replace Caesars effective Sept 22, and was only +0.09% on the effective date itself (verified from Yahoo daily bars).

itemVerdicts.item: Goldman Sachs 2025 analysis reportedly finding index additions outperformed equal-weight S&P 500 by 7.4pp on announcement day, attributed to retail
itemVerdicts.note: Could not reach primary or even secondary text. etfstream.com returned HTTP 403 and etfdb.com returned a Cloudflare JS challenge; no Goldman note itself is publicly reachable. Search-result summaries asserting the 7.4pp figure were NOT verified and must not be quoted. If the article wants a 2025-revival claim, anchor it on the market data I did verify (COIN +23.97% on 2025-05-13; HOOD +15.83% on 2025-09-08), not on this.

corrections: Do not cite '7.25% (1990s) / 5.14% (2000s) / 0.804% (2010-20)' or 'Table 2' to the published Journal of Finance paper or to the Dec-2022 NBER WP. Those are Table 2 of the June-2023 revision (marcosammon.com/images/greenwood_sammon.pdf). The PUBLISHED figures live in Table 1 of JF 80(2): additions 3.42% (1980s), 7.39% (1990s), 5.16% (2000s), 0.83% (2010s, insignificant), N = 196/134/211/153; deletions -4.64%, -16.11%, -12.39%, -0.62% (insignificant), N = 39/56/85/87. Use these.

Do not write that the deletions estimate 'flipped sign' between working-paper and published versions. The estimate never changed: 2010-2020 deletion abnormal return is -0.603% (Dec-2022 NBER Table 2), -0.62% (June-2023 Table 2), and -0.62% (published Table 1). Only the abstract's wording changed, and the change was introduced in HBS Working Paper 23-025 (revised November 2023), whose abstract reads '7.4% in the 1990s to 0.3% over the past decade... but only 0.1% between 2010 and 2020.'

If quoting the published abstract's '+0.1%' for 2010-2020 deletions, immediately pair it with the paper's own body and Table 1 figure of -0.62% / -0.6%. The +0.1% has no counterpart in any table in the paper (the nearest cell is the 2010s deletion effective-window CAR of +0.13%), so presenting +0.1% alone as 'the deletion effect' misstates the paper's actual estimate.

Replace 'migrations rose from ~40% to >80% of additions' with the published paper's wording: migrations went from about 50% of additions to over 70%, and in the body, 'In the 1990s, migrations accounted for about 69% of additions and less than 10% of deletions. In recent years, they both make up over 70% of index changes.' The ~40%-to->80% figure is superseded Dec-2022 NBER text. Note the correct direction: the migration share of ADDITIONS barely moved; the collapse-to-migrations happened on the DELETION side.

Change 'direct additions still earned +5.3% in the 2010s' to +5.4%. The published Table 3 reports direct-addition CARs of 10.23% (1995-99), 8.80% (2000-09) and 5.40% (2010-20), with a 2010-20 standard error of 8.38%; 5.337% is the June-2023 working-paper figure. Note the 5.4% is not itself statistically distinguishable from zero.

Do not say 'active investors provide the liquidity.' The paper says liquidity 'is provided, on average, by other institutions exiting their positions, rather than accommodation by other parties such as retail investors' — i.e. other 13F filers. Published Table 7 shows active mutual funds were net BUYERS of 2020 additions (+2.40%). Also note Table 7 reports yearly MEDIANS, not means, even though the body says 'the average addition in 2020.'

Fix the Coinbase date: the S&P DJI announcement was released after the close on Monday May 12, 2025, and COIN's ~24% move was the next session, Tuesday May 13 (207.22 to 256.90 = +23.97% raw; S&P 500 +0.72% that day, so ~+23.3% market-adjusted). Effective date was May 19, on which COIN fell 0.93%. Write 'jumped ~24% the day after the May 12 after-close announcement.'

When using Coinbase as evidence the index effect revived, add that Coinbase was a DIRECT addition (the S&P DJI release lists no S&P MidCap 400 change), and that Greenwood-Sammon's own published Table 3 shows direct additions still averaged +5.4% in the 2010s — so a direct-addition pop is consistent with the paper's mechanism, even if 24% is roughly four times that average. Also state plainly that the peer-reviewed sample runs 1980-2020, so all 2025 events are out of sample.

If asserting a broader 2025 revival, use verifiable market data rather than trade-press summaries of a Goldman Sachs note: Robinhood closed +15.83% on 2025-09-08, the first session after its 2025-09-05 after-close announcement of S&P 500 inclusion effective 2025-09-22, and was only +0.09% on that effective date. The frequently-cited '7.4 percentage points average announcement-day outperformance in 2025' could not be traced to any reachable source and should not be printed.

Attribute the paper's own summary framing accurately: McLean-Pontiff (2016) anomaly decay is the analogy drawn in the INTRODUCTION; the CONCLUSION frames the result as Lo's (2004) adaptive markets hypothesis — 'when demand shocks become regular and repeated, competitive markets adapt over time to minimize price impact.' Also note Greenwood-Sammon credit Preston and Soe (2021) alongside Bennett, Stulz and Wang (2020), so BSW is not the only prior documentation of the decline.
newContradictions: Internal contradiction inside the published paper itself: the JF abstract says 2010-2020 deletions had 'an average return of only 0.1%' while Table 1 and the body of the same paper report -0.62% / -0.6%. Any article quoting the abstract without the table figure inherits an unsupported number.

The published paper reverses the article's migration story: migrations as a share of ADDITIONS were already ~69% in the 1990s and are ~70% now (essentially flat), while migrations as a share of DELETIONS went from under 10% to over 70%. The '~40% to >80% of additions' framing implies the additions channel is what changed; it is not.

Greenwood-Sammon's own published Table 3 undercuts a strong 'the index effect is dead' reading: direct (non-migration) additions still averaged +5.40% in 2010-2020. The headline near-zero average is substantially a composition result driven by migrations averaging -1.82%.

Out-of-sample 2025 evidence cuts against the 'disappeared' conclusion in the specific segment the paper flags as still alive: two large direct additions, Coinbase (+23.97% on 2025-05-13) and Robinhood (+15.83% on 2025-09-08), both popped on announcement and both went nowhere on the effective date (-0.93% and +0.09%). This is consistent with an announcement-day/anticipation effect rather than effective-day price pressure, and it postdates the paper's 1980-2020 sample.
reasoning: Primary documents reached and read verbatim, not summarized. (1) Published-version text: local v19b_gs_pub.txt — the Harvard DASH accepted manuscript (March 2024) carrying the JF citation header 'Journal of Finance 80, no. 2 (April 2025): 657-698' and DOI 10.1111/jofi.13410; I read its abstract, introduction, Section 1.1, Tables 1, 3 and 7, and the conclusion directly. (2) Published abstract independently confirmed from two machine-readable primary records — the Crossref deposit (local cr.json, publisher Wiley, published-print 2025-04, issue 2, page 657-698) and RePEc/IDEAS JSON-LD fetched live — which agree word for word, including 'an average return of only 0.1% between 2010 and 2020.' The Wiley landing page itself is behind Cloudflare (403/JS challenge), so I could not read the typeset VOR; the Crossref abstract is Wiley's own deposit, which I treat as authoritative for abstract text but NOT as proof that the typeset Table I matches the March-2024 manuscript. (3) NBER w30748 (Dec 2022) read from local gs.txt including its abstract and Table 2 Panels A and B. (4) June-2023 revision read from local gs2.txt/gs_final.txt (identical files; same PDF as marcosammon.com/images/greenwood_sammon.pdf), Table 2 and Table 4. (5) A fourth version I found unprompted: HBS Working Paper 23-025, revised November 2023 (local v19c_hbs.txt), whose abstract reads '0.3% over the past decade' — this is where the '0.1%' deletions wording actually originates, which reframes the version-drift note in the task. (6) Coinbase: S&P DJI press release text fetched verbatim from press.spglobal.com (May 12, 2025, replaces Discover, effective before the open May 19, no MidCap 400 change listed), and daily OHLC bars for COIN and ^GSPC pulled from the Yahoo chart API and computed myself (query1 and Stooq were rate-limited/challenged; query2 succeeded). (7) Robinhood bars likewise computed from raw Yahoo data. Key findings: the central assertion holds, but four numbers in the claim group are drawn from superseded working-paper versions rather than the published paper (7.25%/5.14%/0.804% and 'Table 2'; migrations 40%-to-80%; direct additions 5.3%), and the '+0.1% deletions' abstract figure contradicts the published paper's own Table 1 (-0.62%). Remaining uncertainty: I could not read the Wiley typeset version, so I cannot rule out that the printed Table I differs in the last decimal from the accepted manuscript, though the accepted-MS decade cells already match the abstract's 7.4% and the body's -0.6%. I also could not reach the Goldman Sachs 2025 'index effect comeback' analysis or the trade-press articles reporting it (etfstream 403, etfdb Cloudflare challenge), so that item is marked unreachable and its numbers must not be used. I searched for errata, replications and contradicting sources up to 2026-08 and found no published correction to jofi.13410.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Barberis-Shleifer-Wurgler (JFE 2005): S&P daily beta increase on inclusion 0.067 (1976-87) vs 0.214 (1988-2000); the 0.326/-0.319 pair is the BIVARIATE spec
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the JFE 2005 PDF text (local bsw.txt, JFE 75 (2005) 283-317). Table 1 Panel A (daily returns), Additions: 1976-1987, N=196, univariate Δβ = 0.067*** (s.e. 0.023); 1988-2000, N=259, univariate Δβ = 0.214*** (s.e. 0.032); full 1976-2000, N=455, univariate Δβ = 0.151***. Intro text: 'stocks added to the S&P during 1976–1987 experience an average increase in daily S&P beta of 0.067 after inclusion, the average increase in the 1988–2000 period is 0.214.' The 0.326/-0.319 pair is indeed bivariate and is the FULL 1976-2000 sample (not a subperiod): 'daily beta with the S&P 500 goes up by an average of 0.326 and average daily beta with other stocks drops by 0.319' (Table 1: ΔβSP500 0.326***, ΔβnonSP500 -0.319***). Bivariate subperiod values are 0.286/-0.301 (1976-87) and 0.357/-0.332 (1988-2000). Estimation windows: [-12,-1] and [+1,+12] months for daily/weekly; October 1987 excluded.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Chen-Singal-Whitelaw 'Comovement revisited' (JFE 2016): bivariate spec uninformative; univariate diff-of-diff +0.020 (t=0.76) 1976-87, +0.199 (t=4.94) 1988-2000, -0.004 (t=-0.14) 2001-2012
itemVerdicts.note: Verified in the published JFE 2016 PDF (local csw.txt, JFE 121 (2016) 624-644). Table 1 Panel A (Univariate regressions), 'Diff. of diff.' column Δβ2 − Δβ1: 1976-1987, nobs 197, 0.020 (t = 0.763); 1988-2000, nobs 269, 0.199 (t = 4.938); 2001-2012, nobs 214, -0.004 (t = -0.137); full 1976-2012, nobs 680, 0.083 (t = 4.080). Rounding to 0.76 / 4.94 / -0.14 is correct. Abstract verbatim: 'We show that the bivariate regressions in this literature provide little information about the economic magnitude of excess comovement, with coefficients that are sensitive to unrelated factors. Using robust univariate regressions and matched control samples, almost all evidence of excess comovement disappears.' Body confirms: 'The difference in beta changes is not significant for the 1976–1987 period, nor is it significant for the 2001–2012 period.' TWO CALIBER NOTES for the article: (1) in 2001-2012 the S&P-only univariate beta change is still positive and significant, +0.071 (t=2.44) — but so is the non-S&P beta change, +0.075 (t=2.50); it is the DIFFERENCE that is zero, i.e. added stocks moved more with everything, not specifically with the index. (2) CSW themselves flag the raw S&P-beta increase as 'less than a third as large (0.071 vs. 0.214) for the very last subperiod, 2001–2012 ... when indexing gained even more importance. Notwithstanding this anomaly...'

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Kasch-Sarkar (NY Fed staff report 484): no permanent value or comovement effect after accounting for pre-inclusion momentum; declines bivariate spec because regressors correlate >93%
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers and the refusal to run the bivariate spec are exactly right; the attribution of WHAT is controlled for is too narrow. Verified in sr484 (Staff Report No. 484, February 2011, revised November 2012). Footnote 25 verbatim: '...documented that the correlation between S&P 500 and non-S&P 500 stock returns exceeds 93%. The concern regarding a multiple regression with highly correlated regressors is that its parameter estimates are likely to be regression artifacts, rendering their interpretation difficult. Therefore, we do not consider specifications which include both of these highly correlated indices in one regression.' WRONG (as phrased): 'after accounting for pre-inclusion momentum.' RIGHT: after accounting for pre-inclusion PERFORMANCE, which the abstract defines as three things — 'large increases in earnings, appreciation in market value, and positive price momentum in the period preceding their index inclusion.' Abstract verbatim: 'after accounting for the firms' extraordinary preinclusion performance – index inclusion has no permanent effect on value and comovement.' Also note for accuracy: their comovement result is a decline in size, value and momentum betas (Fama-French/Carhart), matched by non-event firms with similar performance — not a null on the raw market beta. Publication status: never published in a journal; staff report / SSRN working paper only, so cite it as such.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) BIS March 2018: correlation 0.45→0.52 on inclusion (462 stocks, 2000-2017), raw before/after with no matched control
itemVerdicts.note: Verified twice — local bis2018.txt and an independent pdftotext -layout re-extraction of v20_bis.pdf (Sushko & Turner, 'The implications of passive investing for securities markets', BIS Quarterly Review, March 2018, p.119). Graph 3, left panel 'Correlation with the S&P 500 index': bar labels 0.45 (Before joining, from t−200 to t−1) and 0.52 (After joining, from t+1 to t+200). Footnote 1 verbatim: 'Sample based on 462 stocks joining the S&P 500 between January 2000 and September 2017.' Footnote 2: 'Correlation of daily returns with the S&P 500 index.' The graph note lists only exclusions (M&A, poor data, left index within 30 days) — no control or matched sample anywhere in the article; grep for 'control'/'matched' in the equity section returns nothing. So 'raw before/after with no matched control' is correct. ONE CALIBER NOTE: BIS reports raw return CORRELATIONS, not regression betas, so the part of CSW that bites is the missing matched control / missing difference-in-differences against non-index returns, not CSW's bivariate-regression critique. 'Exactly the design CSW demolish' is loose; 'exactly the design flaw CSW identify' is accurate.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) ECB FSR Nov 2024 box: +0.005 correlation per 1pp passive ownership share (euro area, stock+time FE, index-inclusion IV, base correlation 0.50); 10pp → +0.05
itemVerdicts.note: The 0.005 and the 0.50 base are exact; the specification description and the 10pp arithmetic need fixing. Box verbatim (Dieckelmann, Siciliano, Sowiński, 'Passive investing and its impact on return co-movement, market concentration and liquidity in euro area equity markets', FSR November 2024): 'Between the first quarter of 2010 and the first quarter of 2024, a 1 percentage point increase in the passive ownership share of a euro area stock was associated with an increase of around 0.005 in the correlation coefficient with the EURO STOXX index.' Footnote 4 verbatim: 'the average return correlation coefficient of a euro area stock with the EURO STOXX index between the first quarter of 2010 and the first quarter of 2024 is 0.50.' WRONG (as phrased): treating 'stock+time FE, index-inclusion IV' as one specification producing 0.005. RIGHT: the 0.005 comes from a panel regression with stock and time fixed effects 'controlling for market capitalisation, liquidity, valuation and 1 autoregressive lag of the correlation coefficient'; the IV is a separate robustness check — 'The results also hold in a two-step regression set-up, using index inclusion as an instrumental variable for passive ownership share.' Also WRONG to attribute to the ECB: the box never states a 10pp figure. '10pp → +0.05' is the article's own linear extrapolation and must be labelled as such — and because the spec includes a lagged dependent variable, 0.005 is a short-run coefficient, so linear extrapolation is not what the ECB endorses. Sample window Q1 2010–Q1 2024 should be stated; the article's version omits it.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) Fed's Anadu et al. Table 4 verdict: 'For equities, comovement effects have declined significantly since 2001.'
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in Anadu, Kruttli, McCabe & Osambela, FEDS 2018-060r1 (Board of Governors, 2018, revised June 2020), Table 4 'Impact of active-to-passive shift on index-inclusion effects and financial stability', row 'Comovement of returns', column 'Evidence that active-to-passive shift has exacerbated?': 'For equities, comovement effects have declined significantly since 2001' (wrapped across table lines). The parallel Valuation row reads 'For equities, valuation effects have declined significantly since 2000; for bonds, little research to date.' Body support (p.25): 'Chen, Singal, and Whitelaw (2016) ... do not find evidence of an upward trend in recent years. They report that adding a stock to the index had a smaller effect on its beta during the period from 2001 to 2012 than in the previous decade, even as indexing had become more common.' Attribution caution: this is a Federal Reserve Board staff working paper whose disclaimer applies — 'Fed's Anadu et al.' is acceptable shorthand only if the article does not imply an official Fed position. Note also that the SAME Table 4 row for comovement of LIQUIDITY says the opposite direction ('Systematic liquidity associated with index investing has increased in recent years'), and the paper's own summary is 'the evidence on trends and causality is mixed' — do not let the equities-returns cell stand in for the paper's overall verdict.

corrections: (c) Kasch-Sarkar: change 'after accounting for pre-inclusion momentum' to 'after accounting for the firms' extraordinary pre-inclusion performance — large earnings increases, market-value appreciation AND positive price momentum' (the abstract's three-part phrase). Also identify it as an unpublished NY Fed staff report / SSRN working paper (Staff Report 484, Feb 2011, rev. Nov 2012), never journal-published.

(e) ECB box: the +0.005 per 1pp figure comes from a panel regression with stock and time fixed effects controlling for market capitalisation, liquidity, valuation and one autoregressive lag of the correlation coefficient. Index inclusion as an instrumental variable is a SEPARATE robustness check ('The results also hold in a two-step regression set-up'), not the specification that produces 0.005. Do not present them as one spec.

(e) ECB box: the '10pp passive rise maps to +0.05' arithmetic is the article's own linear extrapolation — the box never states it. Label it as the article's inference, and note that because the regression includes a lagged dependent variable, 0.005 is a short-run/partial coefficient for which linear extrapolation is not warranted by the source.
(e) ECB box: add the sample window — Q1 2010 to Q1 2024, euro area stocks, correlation measured against the EURO STOXX index (which captures 90% of euro area free-float market capitalisation).

(b) CSW: 'the decade passive grew fastest' overstates. 2001-2012 is twelve years, and US passive's fastest growth (index funds crossing roughly half of US equity fund assets) came AFTER 2012, a period CSW do not cover. Use CSW's / Anadu's own framing instead: the effect is statistically zero in 2001-2012, 'even as indexing had become more common.'

(b) CSW: add the nuance that in 2001-2012 the added stock's beta with the S&P still rose (+0.071, t=2.44) — but its beta with non-S&P stocks rose essentially the same amount (+0.075, t=2.50). It is the difference that is zero, i.e. added stocks moved more with everything, not specifically with the index. Without this, 'the effect is zero' can read as 'nothing happened to added stocks.'

(b) CSW: note that CSW themselves call the 2001-2012 result an 'anomaly' relative to the excess-comovement hypothesis, and that their headline case rests on matched control samples plus Dimson betas, not on the diff-of-diff column alone.

(d) BIS: 'exactly the design CSW demolish' is loose — BIS reports raw return correlations, not regression betas, so CSW's bivariate-regression critique does not apply. Say 'exactly the design flaw CSW identify: a raw before/after with no matched control and no differencing against non-index returns.' Also state the windows (t-200 to t-1 vs t+1 to t+200).

(f) Anadu et al.: identify it as a Federal Reserve Board FEDS staff working paper (2018-060r1, revised June 2020) carrying the standard non-official-views disclaimer, not a Fed institutional finding. Note that the same Table 4 rules the OTHER way on comovement of liquidity ('Systematic liquidity associated with index investing has increased in recent years') and that the paper's own summary is that the evidence is mixed.

Framing of the trail as a whole: items (b)/(f) and item (e) point in opposite directions in the modern period. CSW's null ends in 2012; the ECB's positive estimate covers 2010-2024 in the euro area. The article cannot present a clean 'the comovement effect died after 2001' arc while also citing (e) as support — acknowledge the tension explicitly, or the ECB box reads as evidence against the article's own thesis rather than for it.
newContradictions: Internal contradiction in the claim group itself: (b)/(f) assert the index-inclusion comovement effect is statistically zero after 2001, while (e) is a 2010-2024 euro area estimate finding a positive, economically meaningful association between passive ownership and correlation with the broad index. Both cannot be used as a single 'the effect has faded' trail without explicit reconciliation (different populations — US S&P index-inclusion events vs euro area continuous passive-ownership share; different identification — event-study diff-of-diff with matched controls vs panel FE with an AR(1) lag).

The ECB box's own footnote 3 cites Barberis-Shleifer-Wurgler (2005) and Da & Shive, 'Exchange traded funds and asset return correlations', European Financial Management 24(1), Jan 2018, 136-168, as its comovement authorities — it does NOT cite or engage Chen-Singal-Whitelaw (2016). So the ECB's positive finding is not a post-CSW rebuttal; it simply does not address the CSW critique. Worth saying if the article uses (e) as modern confirmation.

Coles, Heath & Ringgenberg, 'On index investing' — the Oct 2017 working draft abstract states that stocks with more index investors 'exhibit higher correlations with index price movements' (Russell reconstitution regression discontinuity, modern data), which would cut against the 'effect is dead' reading. HOWEVER, the published version (JFE 2022, 145(3), 665-683) has a completely rewritten abstract that drops the correlation claim entirely and focuses on information production and price efficiency. I could not reach the published paper's body, so I do NOT assert the correlation result survived to publication — flagging it only as an unresolved thread the article should not cite from the working-paper abstract without checking the published body.

BSW's own bivariate subperiod pattern is weaker than the 'stronger in recent data' headline implies: bivariate ΔβSP500 goes 0.286 (1976-87) to 0.357 (1988-2000), and BSW state the subperiod differences in the bivariate spec 'are not statistically significant.' Only the univariate 0.067 vs 0.214 gap is described as 'highly statistically significant.' If the article uses the bivariate 0.326/-0.319 to argue the effect grew over time, that specific inference is not supported by BSW's own text.
reasoning:
I reached and read the relevant sentences in five of the six primary documents directly, and verified the sixth by two independent extractions.

(a) Local bsw.txt is the full JFE 2005 article text (JFE 75 (2005) 283-317). I read Table 1 Panel A in full and the two narrative passages that restate it. Every number checks: 0.067/0.214 univariate daily subperiods, 0.326/-0.319 bivariate for the FULL 1976-2000 sample. I confirmed the 0.326/-0.319 pair is bivariate and full-sample, not a subperiod, and that the bivariate subperiod differences are described by BSW as not statistically significant.

(b) Local csw.txt is the published JFE 2016 PDF (JFE 121 (2016) 624-644, received 9 June 2015, accepted 17 Nov 2015). I read Table 1 Panel A cell by cell: 0.020 (t 0.763), 0.199 (t 4.938), -0.004 (t -0.137), full sample 0.083 (t 4.080). This is the published version, not the NBER w21281 working paper, so the version-drift risk flagged in my brief does not bite here. I also read the abstract verbatim and the body passage where CSW call the 2001-2012 result an 'anomaly'. The one thing I checked adversarially and found the article glosses over: the S&P-beta increase in 2001-2012 is still individually significant (+0.071, t=2.44); it is neutralised by an equally significant rise in the non-S&P beta (+0.075, t=2.50).

(c) Local v20_sr484.txt is the NY Fed staff report. I read footnote 25 verbatim — the >93% correlation and the explicit refusal to run the bivariate spec are exactly as claimed. The one caliber miss is 'momentum' standing in for the abstract's three-part 'large increases in earnings, appreciation in market value, and positive price momentum'. Web search confirms the paper was never journal-published.

(d) I did not trust the pre-extracted bis2018.txt for chart data labels, so I located the source PDF by content-grepping every local PDF, then re-ran pdftotext -layout on v20_bis.pdf independently. Both extractions give bar labels 0.45 and 0.52 with the same footnote (462 stocks, January 2000 to September 2017, t-200/t-1 vs t+1/t+200). Grepping the article for 'control' and 'matched' in the equity section returns nothing, confirming no control sample. The only correction is that BIS measures raw correlations rather than betas, so the applicable half of the CSW critique is the missing control, not the bivariate spec.

(e) Local ecb_box2.txt contains the full box body text. Both the 0.005 sentence and footnote 4's 0.50 base correlation are present verbatim. The correction is on specification caliber: the box's own note says the estimate comes from a stock-and-time-FE panel with controls for market cap, liquidity, valuation and one AR lag of the correlation coefficient, and separately that 'The results also hold in a two-step regression set-up, using index inclusion as an instrumental variable'. The IV is corroboration, not the estimating equation. The 10pp/+0.05 figure appears nowhere in the box.

(f) Local anadu.txt is FEDS 2018-060r1. I read Table 4 as extracted and the surrounding body. The quoted cell text is exact. I also read the paper's comovement section, which shows the verdict rests on CSW (2016) and that the paper's overall stance is 'the evidence on trends and causality is mixed', with the liquidity-comovement row pointing the other way.

Remaining uncertainty: I could not read the body of the published Coles-Heath-Ringgenberg (JFE 2022) paper — only the Oct 2017 draft locally and the published abstract via EconPapers. The draft abstract's correlation claim does not appear in the published abstract, and I decline to guess whether that result survived; I flag it rather than assert it. I also did not independently re-derive the ECB coefficient from a PDF of the FSR (the box is HTML-only), though the sentence was captured cleanly and identically in two local extractions of the page.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Flash crash: >20,000 broken trades; over two-thirds of broken-trade SECURITIES were ETFs
itemVerdicts.note: SEC/CFTC 'Findings Regarding the Market Events of May 6, 2010' (Sept 30, 2010), Sec. II.3.b: 'over 20,000 trades representing 5.5 million shares were executed at prices more than 60% away from their 2:40 p.m. value. These trades were subsequently broken by the exchanges and FINRA under their clearly erroneous rules.' Sec. II.2 (HFT discussion): 'Since over two-thirds of the securities with broken trades were ETFs listed on NYSE Arca...'. Note the report's exact qualifier is 'ETFs listed on NYSE Arca' — if quoting, keep it. Verified verbatim in local extract flashcrash.txt (lines 3128-3135, 2644).

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Mechanism = equity-ETF market makers pausing
itemVerdicts.note: Sec. II.2.c verbatim: 'A large majority of ETF market makers with whom we spoke, and particularly those that value underlying stocks as part of their normal market making activities, paused their market making for considerable periods of time starting at about 2:45 p.m. on May 6. We believe this is one of the reasons equity-based ETFs were disproportionately affected by the extreme price volatilities of that afternoon.' Caliber: 'one of the reasons', not the sole reason.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Falsification test: ETFs NOT based on domestic equities were NOT disproportionately affected
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, Sec. II.2.c: 'We further note that ETFs that do not derive their value from the prices of domestic equity securities were not disproportionately affected.'

itemVerdicts.item: (a) ~2/3 of cancelled-trade shares executed below $1 (stub quotes)
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, Sec. II.3.b: 'Almost two-thirds of shares in cancelled trades were executed at prices of less than $1.00, and about 5% were executed at prices above $100.' Unit is SHARES in cancelled trades, not trades — the claim states this correctly.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Umbrella: SEC/CFTC report does not attribute the flash crash to index/passive structure
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG if stated flatly as 'index products are exonerated'. RIGHT: the report exonerates passive ASSET MANAGEMENT, not index PRODUCTS. Its own trigger narrative is an index-futures trade — p.2: 'a large fundamental trader (a mutual fund complex) initiated a sell program to sell a total of 75,000 E-Mini contracts' via an automated execution algorithm — and the ETF damage it documents is attributed to ETF pricing/arbitrage plumbing (market makers who track underlying baskets pausing). The correct sentence is 'no official post-mortem attributes these episodes to passive/index FUND OWNERSHIP or the active-to-passive shift', not 'to index structure'.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Aug 24 2015: 1,278 LULD halts; 1,058 in 327 ETPs; 80% of ETPs had ZERO halts; 63.3% declined <10%
itemVerdicts.note: SEC Research Note 'Equity Market Volatility on August 24, 2015' verbatim: 'Although most of the 1,278 LULD trading halts on August 24 occurred in ETPs, 80% of ETPs did not experience a single LULD halt. Overall, there were 1,058 LULD halts in 327 ETPs (many halts were repeats in the same ETP), and 220 LULD halts in 144 non-ETPs.' And: 'A majority of all ETPs (63.3%) declined by less than 10% -- a level that is consistent with broad market declines on August 24.' (Companion fact worth keeping: 19.2% of ETPs declined 20% or more vs only 4.7% of Corporates.)

itemVerdicts.item: (b) The S&P 500 INDEX itself was stale (primary-listing last-sale prices), -5.2% vs SPY -7.8%, which is why the market-wide circuit breaker never fired
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'The S&P 500 Index ("SPX")... declined on August 24 by only 5.2% from its previous day's close. Until approximately 9:42, SPX remained substantially higher than the prices of the SPY (7.8% decline), E-Mini (7% decline), and the net asset value ("NAV") of SPY (8% decline...). S&P DJI generally uses last sale prices from only the primary listing market to calculate its equity indexes... The use of these previous day closing prices to calculate SPX in the opening minutes of August 24 likely caused its decline to be less than S&P 500 related products that reflected real-time trade prices.' And: 'Because the SPX did not decline by 7% (the first level trigger) on August 24, the market-wide circuit breakers... were not triggered.' Caliber: the report says 'likely caused', not 'caused'.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Best predictor of ETP damage was low secondary-market turnover
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 'best predictor'. RIGHT (Research Note): 'A pre-August 24 metric with a particularly strong association with volatility is secondary market turnover rate' — and that finding is stated only for 'Large and Mid market capitalization US Equity ETPs'. Moreover the SEC's own companion staff paper (DERA white paper, Gerig & Murphy, 'The Determinants of ETF Trading Pauses on August 24th, 2015', Feb 2016, https://www.sec.gov/files/feb2016-white-paper-determinants-etf-trading-pauses.pdf) says the opposite about ranking: 'By far, the most significant predictor of ETF trading pauses on August 24th was correlation with the S&P 500 index. Those ETFs that were most correlated with the S&P 500 index were 21 times more likely to pause than those that were least correlated.' Turnover in that paper is real but weaker: 'ETFs in the top quartile of turnover were 3 times less likely to pause than those in the bottom quartile.' So: low turnover was A strong predictor; broad-index correlation was the strongest.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Umbrella: no official post-mortem ties Aug 24 2015 ETP damage to index structure
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as an absolute. The Research Note itself disclaims causation ('not intended to reach or suggest any legal conclusions or factual findings regarding the causes of the volatility'), but the SEC DERA staff white paper (Feb 2016) does tie ETP damage to index-linkage: index correlation was the dominant predictor of pauses. RIGHT framing: DERA explicitly rules out an indexing-as-ownership story — 'The importance of the S&P 500 index on August 24th was most likely due to it being a broad U.S. equity index rather than to any properties specific to S&P 500 securities' (results unchanged substituting the CRSP US Total Market and Nasdaq 100 indices), and it offers two non-passive mechanisms: broad-index ETFs are the instrument investors dump to change US equity exposure fast, and HFT/automated activity is concentrated in index-correlated securities. The article must acknowledge this paper or its 'no official post-mortem' sentence is falsifiable.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Feb 5 2018 XIV: BIS attributes spike to leveraged/inverse VOLATILITY ETPs, ~$4bn AUM at end-2017, XIV fell 84% and was terminated
itemVerdicts.note: Source verified: Sushko & Turner, 'The equity market turbulence of 5 February - the role of exchange-traded volatility products', BIS Quarterly Review, 11 March 2018 (r_qt1803t.htm; extract from pp.4-6). Verbatim: 'The value of one of the inverse volatility ETPs, XIV, fell 84% and the product was subsequently terminated.' CORRECTION on the AUM: WRONG '~$4bn AUM of leveraged/inverse volatility ETPs'; RIGHT — 'The assets of SELECT leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs have expanded sharply over recent years, reaching about $4 billion at end-2017' — 'select' means the four products charted (XIV, SVXY, TVIX, UVXY), not the whole category. CORRECTION on attribution caliber: BIS says these strategies 'appear to have been A KEY FACTOR behind the volatility spike that occurred on the afternoon of 5 February', not the sole cause; it also names anticipatory front-running from ~15:30 and dealer hedging via short E-mini futures.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) BIS verbatim: 'Neither the size nor the complex strategies of leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs are representative of the broader ETP market.'
itemVerdicts.note: Exact string verified in both the BIS web extract and the PDF (bisqr1803a). Provenance detail worth stating: it appears in the FOOTNOTE to Graph A1, not in the body text, and continues '...see V Sushko and G Turner, "What risks do exchange-traded funds pose?", Bank of France, Financial Stability Review, forthcoming.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d) March 2020 bond ETFs: tracking error >200bp for some funds vs 0.7bp historical sector average
itemVerdicts.note: Todorov, 'The anatomy of bond ETF arbitrage', BIS Quarterly Review, 1 March 2021, verbatim: 'the tracking error of bond ETFs increased to above 200 basis points for some funds in March-April 2020, much higher than the historical average of 0.7 bp in the sector.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d) BIS (March 2021) reads the discounts partly as a run-DETERRENT / price-discovery feature
itemVerdicts.note: Run-deterrent HOLDS verbatim: 'the ETF sponsor can include only the riskier or less liquid securities from the pool of holdings in the redemption basket... This would discourage further runs and lead to ETF discounts during run episodes. In fact, such a stabilisation mechanism was arguably in place during the March-April 2020 episode... when some ETFs traded at a discount while redeeming baskets that were more illiquid than the holdings.' Also 'The decoupling of baskets from holdings can also be a shock absorber during volatile times... ETFs could be a stabilising force during runs and prevent fire sales.' WRONG: attaching 'price discovery' to BIS. BIS's framing is the opposite direction on pricing — basket/holdings decoupling 'weakens arbitrage forces' and 'potentially makes it harder for investors to exploit price gaps'. 'Price discovery' is the BlackRock deck's framing (see next item); do not merge the two.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Fed May 2020 FSR: passive shift 'might help reduce large redemptions... and, therefore, damp fire sale risks', reserving concern for leveraged/inverse ETPs
itemVerdicts.note: Document verified as Board of Governors, Financial Stability Report, MAY 2020, box 'Institutional Activities and Market Liquidity'. WRONG (ellipsis drops a material qualifier): 'might help reduce large redemptions... and, therefore, damp fire sale risks'. RIGHT, full sentence: 'As investors in passive mutual funds tend to be less responsive to performance than those in active funds, this shift to passive investing might help reduce large redemptions ARISING FROM POOR PERFORMANCE and, therefore, damp fire sale risks.' The leveraged/inverse carve-out HOLDS verbatim: 'At the same time, some types of exchange-traded products (ETPs)—leveraged and inverse ETPs—have features that could cause strains in market liquidity... there is the potential for "front running"...'. Context the article should not suppress: the FSR's supporting footnote 9 cites Anadu, Kruttli, McCabe, Osambela & Shin, FEDS 2018-060, whose own conclusion is two-sided — it identifies 'some mechanisms that reduce financial stability risks and others that increase them.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d) The 'bond ETFs = price discovery' deck presented to SEC FIMSAC is authored by BlackRock (EII), not the SEC
itemVerdicts.note: Verified by fetching the primary PDF from sec.gov: 'Pricing and Liquidity of Fixed Income ETFs in the Covid-19 Crisis of 2020', header 'EII Global Research / As of July, 2020', iShares/BlackRock sourcing throughout ('Source: BlackRock, Bloomberg'), footer '©2020 BlackRock, Inc.' and an iShares prospectus disclaimer page. Listed on the SEC FIMSAC page under the October 5, 2020 meeting, 'Bond Fund and ETF Presentations: Ananth Madhavan Presentation' (Madhavan is listed as a FIMSAC member affiliated with BlackRock). Conclusion slide #1 verbatim: 'Bond ETFs serve as vehicles for efficient price discovery... we believe these deviations were a function of price discovery coupled with NAV latency effects in a challenged liquidity environment.' It is an issuer submission hosted on sec.gov, not an SEC finding.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) April 2025 tariff drawdown: BIS Sept 2025 box says RETAIL, not passive
itemVerdicts.note: Lombardi, Pinter & Todorov, 'Understanding the swift market recovery after the April 2025 tariff shock', box extracted from the Overview chapter 'Markets shrug off trade conflicts', BIS Quarterly Review, 15 September 2025. Verbatim: 'The box also illustrates that, in contrast with past episodes, retail investors, rather than institutional ones, bought into the rally.' And: 'Even as institutional investors withdrew from equity markets, retail investors were on net "buyers of the dip", as visible from fund flows.' The word 'passive' does not appear. The box's headline result is separate and worth not garbling: 'about 75% of the rise in the S&P 500 between the trough on 9 April and end-July was driven by positive surprises unrelated to tariffs.'

corrections: Aug 24, 2015 — do not call low secondary-market turnover the 'best predictor' of ETP damage. The SEC Research Note says only that it is 'a pre-August 24 metric with a particularly strong association with volatility,' and only for Large and Mid market-cap US Equity ETPs. The SEC's own DERA staff paper (Gerig & Murphy, Feb 2016) ranks it second: 'By far, the most significant predictor of ETF trading pauses on August 24th was correlation with the S&P 500 index' (21x top-vs-bottom quartile), with turnover at 3x. Write: 'low secondary-market turnover was a strong predictor of which ETPs broke; the strongest single predictor in the SEC's companion staff paper was correlation with the broad equity index.'

Aug 24, 2015 — the flat sentence 'no official post-mortem attributes the episode to index structure' must be qualified. The DERA staff paper does attribute pause susceptibility primarily to broad-index correlation. Add its own carve-out verbatim: 'The importance of the S&P 500 index on August 24th was most likely due to it being a broad U.S. equity index rather than to any properties specific to S&P 500 securities.' The defensible claim is that no official post-mortem attributes these episodes to passive/index FUND OWNERSHIP or the active-to-passive shift — not that index products are untouched.

Flash crash — the SEC/CFTC report does not exonerate index products, only passive asset management. Its own trigger is an index-futures trade: 'a large fundamental trader (a mutual fund complex) initiated a sell program to sell a total of 75,000 E-Mini contracts' via an automated execution algorithm. Narrow the claim accordingly.
Flash crash — if quoting the two-thirds figure, keep the report's qualifier: 'over two-thirds of the securities with broken trades were ETFs listed on NYSE Arca' (not simply 'were ETFs').

Feb 5, 2018 — the $4bn is not the AUM of leveraged/inverse volatility ETPs as a class. BIS: 'The assets of SELECT leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs... reaching about $4 billion at end-2017,' i.e. the four charted products (XIV, SVXY, TVIX, UVXY). Also soften the attribution: BIS says their systematic strategies 'appear to have been a key factor behind the volatility spike,' not the cause.
Feb 5, 2018 — note that the 'Neither the size nor the complex strategies...' sentence is a footnote to Graph A1, not body text, if provenance matters to the argument.

March 2020 — do not attribute a 'price discovery' reading of bond ETF discounts to BIS. BIS's words are 'discourage runs', 'stabilisation mechanism', 'shock absorber', 'stabilising force during runs and prevent fire sales'; on pricing BIS says the opposite ('weakens arbitrage forces', 'harder for investors to exploit price gaps'). 'Price discovery' is BlackRock's framing in the FIMSAC deck. Keep the two attributions separate.

Fed May 2020 FSR — restore the elided qualifier. The sentence is: 'this shift to passive investing might help reduce large redemptions ARISING FROM POOR PERFORMANCE and, therefore, damp fire sale risks.' It is not a claim about redemptions in general. Also note that the FEDS paper the FSR cites in support (Anadu et al. 2018-060) concludes the shift 'identif[ies] some mechanisms that reduce financial stability risks and others that increase them.'
April 2025 — keep BIS's word 'retail'; do not substitute 'passive'. Verbatim: 'in contrast with past episodes, retail investors, rather than institutional ones, bought into the rally.'
The claim group header says 'four canonical episodes' but enumerates five (a-e). Fix the count or label (e) as an additional, non-canonical episode.
newContradictions: SEC DERA staff white paper, Austin Gerig & Keegan Murphy, 'The Determinants of ETF Trading Pauses on August 24th, 2015' (Feb 2016), https://www.sec.gov/files/feb2016-white-paper-determinants-etf-trading-pauses.pdf — an official SEC staff analysis of the same episode that DOES tie ETP damage to index-linkage: 'By far, the most significant predictor of ETF trading pauses on August 24th was correlation with the S&P 500 index. Those ETFs that were most correlated with the S&P 500 index were 21 times more likely to pause than those that were least correlated.' It also outranks turnover (3x), contradicting the 'best predictor' sub-claim. Mitigating: it explicitly rejects an index-composition story ('most likely due to it being a broad U.S. equity index rather than to any properties specific to S&P 500 securities') and offers non-passive mechanisms (broad-index ETFs as the fastest instrument for changing US equity exposure; concentrated automated/HFT activity in index-correlated securities). Also note its population differs from the Research Note: 302 of 1,569 ETFs (19.2%) paused, vs the Note's 327 ETPs.

Federal Reserve FEDS 2018-060 (Anadu, Kruttli, McCabe, Osambela, Shin), the paper cited in footnote 9 of the very FSR passage being quoted, is two-sided by its own conclusion: it identifies 'some mechanisms that reduce financial stability risks and others that increase them.' Quoting only the FSR's risk-reducing sentence without this risks implying the Fed's position is one-directional.
reasoning: I verified every sub-claim against primary text, not summaries. Reached verbatim: (a) SEC/CFTC 'Findings Regarding the Market Events of May 6, 2010' full PDF text (local extract flashcrash.txt, 5,665 lines) — confirmed 'over 20,000 trades representing 5.5 million shares', 'over two-thirds of the securities with broken trades were ETFs listed on NYSE Arca', the ETF market-maker pause passage in Sec. II.2.c, the falsification sentence 'ETFs that do not derive their value from the prices of domestic equity securities were not disproportionately affected', and 'Almost two-thirds of shares in cancelled trades were executed at prices of less than $1.00, and about 5% were executed at prices above $100.' (b) SEC 'Research Note: Equity Market Volatility on August 24, 2015' full text — confirmed 1,278 / 1,058 / 327 / 80% zero halts / 63.3% <10% / SPX -5.2% vs SPY -7.8% stale-index and MWCB non-trigger / turnover association, including its own non-causation disclaimer. (c) BIS QR March 2018 Sushko-Turner box, confirmed on both the live bis.org page (title/authors/date re-fetched) and the QR PDF extract — the 'Neither the size nor the complex strategies...' sentence is exact, but sits in a Graph A1 footnote, and the $4bn applies to 'select' products. (d) BIS QR March 2021 Todorov article — the 200bp/0.7bp sentence and the run-deterrence/shock-absorber passages are exact, but 'price discovery' is not BIS's frame; Fed FSR May 2020 (cover page confirms May 2020 edition) — quote exact but the article's ellipsis drops 'arising from poor performance'; and I downloaded the FIMSAC deck itself from sec.gov (SEC blocks default curl UAs; a descriptive UA works) and confirmed it is BlackRock EII Global Research / iShares material presented at the Oct 5, 2020 FIMSAC meeting, with 'Bond ETFs serve as vehicles for efficient price discovery' as conclusion #1. (e) BIS QR 15 Sept 2025 box — the 'retail investors, rather than institutional ones, bought into the rally' sentence is exact and the word 'passive' does not appear. The one real adversarial hit is the SEC DERA Feb 2016 staff paper, which I found by searching for official follow-ups and then fetched and read directly: it makes broad-index correlation the dominant predictor of Aug 24 ETP pauses, which both demotes the 'low turnover was the best predictor' sub-claim and puts a qualifier on the group's umbrella assertion. Remaining uncertainty: I did not read the FSB Holistic Review (Nov 2020) or IOSCO ETF thematic note in full — a search summary is consistent with 'no passive attribution' (they point at open-ended fund liquidity mismatch, dealer intermediation capacity, and leverage), but I did not verify that verbatim and am not asserting it. I also did not attempt an exhaustive sweep for a hypothetical official Feb 2018 XIV post-mortem beyond BIS; no US regulator appears to have published one, but I did not prove that negative.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Published JF abstract: additions 7.4% (1990s) → less than 1% over the past decade; deletions large negative in 1990s → 0.1% for 2010-2020
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim twice. Crossref (10.1111/jofi.13410, retrieved live) abstract: "The abnormal return associated with a stock being added to the S&P 500 has fallen from an average of 7.4% in the 1990s to less than 1% over the past decade. This has occurred despite a significant increase in the share of stock market assets linked to the index. A similar pattern has occurred for index deletions, with large negative abnormal returns during the 1990s but an average return of only 0.1% between 2010 and 2020." Bibliographic data also confirmed: Journal of Finance, volume 80, issue 2, pages 657-698, published-print April 2025, published-online 2024-12-20, authors GREENWOOD / SAMMON. The Harvard DASH accepted manuscript (March 2024) carries the same abstract wording ("but only 0.1% between 2010 and 2020").

itemVerdicts.item: (a-note) Claim that the deletions figure FLIPPED SIGN between the Dec-2022 WP (-0.6%) and the published version (+0.1%)
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG framing: "the deletions estimate flipped sign between versions." RIGHT: only the ABSTRACT's number changed; the underlying estimate did not. The Dec-2022 NBER w30748 abstract does say "only -0.6% between 2010 and 2020" (verified verbatim in the local NBER text). But the PUBLISHED paper's own Table 1 decade panel still reports the 2010s deletion total CAR as -0.62%, and the published body text still says "The deletion effect fell in magnitude to -12.4% in the 2000s and disappeared in the 2010s, with an average abnormal return of -0.6%." The published abstract's "0.1%" corresponds to no total-CAR cell in the paper; the nearest figure is the 2010s deletion EFFECTIVE-day return of +0.13% in Table 1. Treat the published abstract's 0.1% as an abstract-level inconsistency, not a revised finding. Safe article statement: deletions went from about -16% in the 1990s to statistically indistinguishable from zero (-0.6%, ns) in 2010-2020.

The NUMBERS are real but the VERSION ATTRIBUTION is wrong, and they are superseded. WRONG: attributing 7.25% / 5.14% / 0.804% / -16.1% / -0.62% to "the WP" as if it were the Dec-2022 NBER paper the group header cites. RIGHT: those exact cells are from the JUNE 2023 revision (Table 2: additions 0.0342 / 0.0725 / 0.0514 / 0.00804; deletions -0.0464 / -0.161 / -0.124 / -0.0062). The Dec-2022 NBER w30748 Table 2 has DIFFERENT cells: additions 0.0342 / 0.0759 / 0.0521 / 0.00799; deletions -0.0464 / -0.166 / -0.123 / -0.00603. And the PUBLISHED JF version reports these in Table 1 (bottom decade rows), not Table 2 — additions 3.42%***, 7.39%***, 5.16%***, 0.83% (no stars); deletions -4.64%**, -16.11%***, -12.39%***, -0.62% (no stars). Note also that in the published paper Table 2 is the controls regression, so citing "Table 2" for raw decade CARs is a wrong pointer. Significance qualifier (ns for both 2010-20 cells) CONFIRMED in all three versions.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Deletion decade cells rest on only 39-87 events
itemVerdicts.note: Published Table 1 deletion N by decade: 1980s 39, 1990s 56, 2000s 85, 2010s 87 — range 39-87 exactly. (Dec-2022 NBER: 39/51/86/87; June-2023: 39/56/85/87.) Additions N are far larger: published 196/134/211/153. The small-N caveat is fair and holds in every version.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) S&P-500-tracking funds grew from ~0 to ~7% of market cap
itemVerdicts.note: Published intro, verbatim: "We estimate that funds tracking the S&P 500 in the form of mutual funds or ETFs have grown from essentially zero in the 1980s to approximately 7 percent of market capitalization in recent years." Caliber note: this is share of MARKET CAP for S&P-500-TRACKING funds only, and the authors immediately add that estimates based on trading volume (Chinco and Sammon 2022) or sell-side research "suggest even higher levels of investor indexation." Do not conflate with total passive share of fund assets.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Trackers buy 7-8% of shares outstanding on addition yet total institutional ownership barely moves; active investors provide the liquidity
itemVerdicts.note: Published intro, verbatim: "although index trackers now buy about 7-8% upon index addition, total institutional ownership barely moves around index changes. We interpret this as professional active investors providing liquidity to passive buyers and sellers." Body (Table 7 discussion): "for the average addition in 2020, index trackers buy 7.53% of shares outstanding. However, institutional ownership only increases by 0.65% of shares outstanding"; deletions: "index trackers sell an average of 8.45% of shares outstanding upon deletion, but institutional ownership overall falls by only 1.42%." IMPORTANT NUANCE the article should not lose: the paper explicitly says active MUTUAL FUNDS are not the liquidity providers — "The 'Active' column shows that active mutual funds are not the group providing liquidity, as their average net demand is roughly zero. This implies that non-S12 filing institutions (e.g., hedge..." — i.e. hedge funds / other 13F institutions, not active mutual funds.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Migrations (simultaneous S&P 400 exit) rose from ~40% to >80% of additions
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: "~40% to over 80%." That is the Dec-2022 NBER wording only ("migrations went from about 40% of additions to over 80%"; body: "In the mid-1990s, migrations were about 40% of additions and 0% of drops. In recent years, they both make up over 60% of index changes"). RIGHT (published JF): intro says "From the 1990s to the present day, migrations went from about 50% of additions to over 70%"; body says "In the 1990s, migrations accounted for about 69% of additions and less than 10% of deletions. In recent years, they both make up over 70% of index changes." The June-2023 revision matches the published numbers (50%→over 70% in intro; 60%→over 70% in body). Use the published figures; note the paper itself is internally inconsistent between 50% and 69% for the 1990s baseline, so the defensible framing is "migrations rose to over 70% of both additions and deletions in recent years, and the sharp rise is specifically in DELETIONS (under 10% in the 1990s)."

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Direct additions still earned +5.3% in the 2010s, Tesla-driven; ex-Tesla the 2020 average inclusion effect was -3bp
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 5.3%. RIGHT (published): 5.4%. Published Table 3: 2010-2020 direct additions mean CAR 5.40% vs migrations -1.82%, difference -7.22%. Published body: "for direct additions, the index inclusion effect was 10.2% in the late 90s, 8.8% in the 2000s, and 5.4% in the 2010s. The large positive return in the last period is driven by Tesla, which, as previously discussed, had a massive return of 53.35% between its announcement and effective dates." (5.337 is the June-2023 Table 4 coefficient — again the older version.) The -3bp figure is CONFIRMED verbatim: "Excluding Tesla, the average inclusion effect in 2020 was -3 basis points." Caliber caution: that -3bp is the ex-Tesla average for calendar year 2020 across ALL additions, not an ex-Tesla recomputation of the 5.4% direct-addition decade figure — do not write "direct additions ex-Tesla were -3bp."

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Authors frame the decay as arbitrage/anomaly decay (McLean-Pontiff), not as evidence passive is harmless
itemVerdicts.note: Published intro, verbatim: "This worked to eliminate the anomaly on average, despite demand shocks that continued to grow in magnitude over the 2000s and 2010s. In this sense, the decline of the index effect is much like the evidence for other anomalies: they decline once they are well recognized by the market (McLean and Pontiff, 2016)." I found no sentence anywhere in the paper claiming passive investing is benign generally; the scope is explicitly the market's ability to accommodate index-change demand shocks. ADD-ON the article should carry: the paper's own stated overall conclusion is Lo's adaptive markets, not McLean-Pontiff — "Our overall conclusion is that, when demand shocks become regular and repeated, competitive markets adapt over time to minimize price impact, in the spirit of Lo's (2004) adaptive markets hypothesis." So attribute the anomaly-decay analogy to the introduction and the adaptive-markets reading to the conclusion.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Bennett-Stulz-Wang documented the decline first (1997-2017 additions)
itemVerdicts.note: Published lit review, verbatim: "Most closely related to our paper is Bennett et al. (2020), who first noted the decline in the index inclusion effect among additions between 1997 and 2017." Also "Our results mirror those in Bennett et al. (2020), who show a decline in the index addition effect between 1997 and 2017" and "as originally highlighted by Bennett et al. (2020)." BSW sample window 1997-2017 independently confirmed (NBER w27593, July 2020, "Does Joining the S&P 500 Index Hurt Firms?"). Minor completeness note: GS also credit Preston and Soe (2021, S&P Dow Jones) with documenting the decline for BOTH additions and deletions beginning in 1995 — BSW's priority claim in GS is specifically for ADDITIONS.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Coinbase jumped ~24% on its May 12, 2025 S&P 500 inclusion announcement
itemVerdicts.note: Magnitude REAL, date WRONG. WRONG: "jumped ~24% on May 12, 2025." RIGHT: S&P DJI issued the release dated May 12, 2025 AFTER the close (Coinbase replaces Discover Financial Services, effective before the open on Monday, May 19, 2025 — verified verbatim from press.spglobal.com); COIN rose only 3.96% during the May 12 regular session (close 207.22) on a broad-market rally, jumped ~8% post-market, and then rose 23.97% the NEXT session, May 13 (open 231.71, close 256.90, volume 39.1M vs ~5-6M typical). I verified the May 12/13 OHLC independently against two price feeds (Yahoo chart API pulled live in this session, and a second local daily series) — they agree to the cent. CNBC's contemporaneous headline is "Coinbase jumps 24% on S&P 500 inclusion" dated 2025-05-13. So write "announced after the close on May 12, 2025; COIN closed up ~24% the following session." This DOES qualify the "disappeared" conclusion: the peer-reviewed sample ends in 2020, COIN was a DIRECT addition (no simultaneous S&P MidCap 400 deletion in the release — exactly the case GS find still carried +5.4% in the 2010s), and 24% is roughly 4x even that.

corrections: Cite the published Journal of Finance version consistently: Greenwood, Robin, and Marco Sammon, 'The Disappearing Index Effect,' Journal of Finance 80(2), April 2025, 657-698, doi 10.1111/jofi.13410. Do not present working-paper cells as the paper's numbers.

Replace the decade table numbers with the PUBLISHED Table 1 decade rows: additions 3.42% (1980s), 7.39% (1990s), 5.16% (2000s), 0.83% (2010-2020, not significant); deletions -4.64% (1980s), -16.11% (1990s), -12.39% (2000s), -0.62% (2010-2020, not significant). Do NOT use 7.25%/5.14%/0.804%/-16.1% (those are the June-2023 revision) and do NOT use 7.59%/5.21%/-16.6% (Dec-2022 NBER).
Do not cite this as 'Table 2.' In the published article the decade breakdown is in Table 1 (summary rows at the bottom of the by-year panel); Table 2 is the regression with characteristic controls.

Drop the assertion that the deletions estimate 'flipped sign' between versions. The published paper's own Table 1 and body text still report -0.6% for 2010-2020 deletions; only the abstract's wording changed to '0.1%', a figure matching no total-CAR cell in the paper (the 2010s deletion effective-day return is +0.13%). Correct framing: the deletion effect fell from about -16% in the 1990s to statistically indistinguishable from zero (-0.6%, ns) in 2010-2020.

Correct the migrations figure: migrations rose to over 70% of both additions and deletions in recent years (published article), NOT from ~40% to over 80% (that is the Dec-2022 NBER working-paper wording). The dramatic rise is in DELETIONS, which went from under 10% migrations in the 1990s to over 70%.
Correct the direct-addition figure from +5.3% to +5.4% for 2010-2020 (published Table 3: direct 5.40% vs migrations -1.82%, difference -7.22%).

Keep the -3bp Tesla adjustment attached to what it actually measures: 'Excluding Tesla, the average inclusion effect in 2020 was -3 basis points' — that is the ex-Tesla average for calendar 2020 across all additions, not an ex-Tesla version of the 5.4% direct-addition decade average.

Correct the Coinbase date: S&P DJI announced the inclusion after the close on Monday May 12, 2025 (effective before the open on May 19, replacing Discover Financial Services); COIN closed up ~24% the following session, Tuesday May 13, 2025 (207.22 to 256.90). May 12's regular session was only +3.96%.

When using Coinbase to qualify the 'disappeared' conclusion, say why it bites: the peer-reviewed sample ends in 2020, and Coinbase was a direct addition with no offsetting S&P MidCap 400 deletion — the very category Greenwood-Sammon find still averaged +5.4% in the 2010s. Note it is one event, not a re-estimated effect.

When describing who absorbs the demand shock, do not say 'active mutual funds provide the liquidity.' The paper finds active mutual funds' net demand is roughly zero and attributes the accommodation to non-13F/S12-filing institutions such as hedge funds; the authors' own phrase is 'professional active investors providing liquidity to passive buyers and sellers.'

If quoting the paper's interpretive frame, note both halves: the McLean-Pontiff anomaly-decay analogy appears in the introduction, while the paper's stated overall conclusion invokes Lo's (2004) adaptive markets hypothesis.
newContradictions: The published JF article is internally inconsistent on the 2010-2020 deletion effect: the abstract says 'an average return of only 0.1%' while Table 1 and the body both report -0.62% / '-0.6%'. Any article citing '+0.1%' should either quote the abstract explicitly as the abstract, or use the table figure.

The published article is also internally inconsistent on the migration share of additions: the introduction says 'about 50% of additions' in the 1990s while Section 2.2 says 'about 69% of additions.' Similarly the introduction says additions declined to 'less than 1%' and the body says 'a statistically insignificant 1.0% in the 2010s' while Table 1 shows 0.83%.

The published introduction appears to transpose the migration/direct labels: it says 'In the mid-1990s, migration and non-migration additions had average returns of 10.2% and 6.7%, respectively,' but Table 3 assigns 10.23% to DIRECT additions and 6.65% to MIGRATIONS for 1995-1999. Use Table 3, not the introduction sentence.

Post-sample counter-evidence beyond Coinbase, all outside the paper's 1980-2020 window and all reported by financial press rather than peer-reviewed work: Datadog reportedly rose about 10% on its July 2, 2025 inclusion announcement, and AppLovin and Robinhood each reportedly rose about 7% in extended trading on the September 5, 2025 announcement. I verified only the Coinbase move against raw price data; the Datadog and Robinhood figures are secondary-source headlines and should be labeled as such or verified separately before use.

No erratum or correction notice to 10.1111/jofi.13410 surfaced in Crossref as of 2026-08-14; the only sibling records are the NBER report (10.3386/w30748) and two SSRN postings (10.2139/ssrn.4294297 and 10.2139/ssrn.4299634). Absence of a Crossref erratum record is weak evidence, not proof none exists.
reasoning: I worked from primary documents rather than summaries. Documents reached verbatim: (1) Crossref API record for 10.1111/jofi.13410 pulled live in this session, giving the published abstract text and bibliographic fields (JF 80(2), 657-698, April 2025); (2) the Harvard DASH accepted manuscript of the published article (March 2024, SSRN 4294297) — full text including the abstract, introduction, Section 2.2 on migrations, Section 2.4 on liquidity provision, the conclusion, and Tables 1, 2, 3 and 7; (3) NBER w30748 (December 2022) full text including its abstract and Table 2; (4) the June 2023 revision full text including its Table 2 and Table 4; (5) the S&P Dow Jones Indices press release dated May 12, 2025 announcing Coinbase replacing Discover Financial Services effective May 19, fetched directly from press.spglobal.com and read as extracted page text. For the Coinbase price move I did not rely on any news summary: I pulled COIN daily OHLC from the Yahoo chart API live in this session and cross-checked against a second independent local daily series; both give May 12 close 207.22 (+3.96%) and May 13 close 256.90 (+23.97%) on 39.1M shares. Three of eleven sub-claims are wrong in ways that matter. First, the group's own framing that the deletion figure 'flipped sign between versions' does not survive contact with the published paper: its Table 1 and body still say -0.62% / -0.6%, and only the abstract carries 0.1%. That is an abstract-vs-table inconsistency inside one document, not a revision of the estimate, and an article that reports 'deletions turned positive' would be repeating a typo as a finding. Second, the numbers listed under (b) as 'WP Table 2' are actually the June-2023 revision, not the December-2022 NBER paper the group header describes, and neither matches the published Table 1 — so a claim group written to guard against version drift itself mixes three versions. Third, the migration figures (~40% to >80%) are Dec-2022-only and were revised down in both later versions. Smaller slips: 5.3% should be 5.4%, and the decade table is Table 1 not Table 2 in the published version. Confirmed cleanly and verbatim: the published abstract wording, the 39-87 deletion event counts, the 0-to-7%-of-market-cap tracker growth, the 7-8% tracker buying against flat institutional ownership, the -3bp ex-Tesla 2020 figure, the McLean-Pontiff framing, and the Bennett-Stulz-Wang 1997-2017 priority claim (GS's own words: 'who first noted the decline'). On the new-window check, the Coinbase episode is real and large but mis-dated in the claim; it is a single event, not a re-estimation, and it is worth noting that Coinbase was a direct addition with no offsetting MidCap deletion — the category the paper itself finds still carried a positive effect. What remains uncertain: I could not fetch the Wiley version-of-record PDF (403), so my published-text reading rests on the Crossref abstract plus the Harvard DASH accepted manuscript; if the VOR differs from the accepted manuscript in any table cell I would not have caught it. I also did not independently verify the Datadog, AppLovin, or Robinhood announcement-day moves against price data.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Flash crash: >20,000 broken trades
itemVerdicts.note: SEC/CFTC Sept 30 2010 Findings, Section II.3.b: "over 20,000 trades representing 5.5 million shares were executed at prices more than 60% away from their 2:40 p.m. value. These trades were subsequently broken by the exchanges and FINRA under their clearly erroneous rules." Trades, not securities — the article gets the unit right.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Over two-thirds of broken-trade SECURITIES were ETFs
itemVerdicts.note: Section II.2 (HFT analysis): "Since over two-thirds of the securities with broken trades were ETFs listed on NYSE Arca, we compared HFT trading activity in all securities with broken trades against those without broken trades." Note the report's phrasing is narrower than the article's: ETFs *listed on NYSE Arca*, which only strengthens the article's version.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Mechanism = equity-ETF market makers pausing
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG if stated as the mechanism. RIGHT: it is one of several. Section II.2.c: "A large majority of ETF market makers with whom we spoke... paused their market making for considerable periods of time starting at about 2:45 p.m. on May 6. We believe this is one of the reasons equity-based ETFs were disproportionately affected by the extreme price volatilities of that afternoon." The report gives a second, independent explanation as well: ETF order books are a "professional's market" with ~half of liquidity within 30bp of mid and little resting retail depth, "allowing a disproportionate number of ETF orders to hit stub-quote levels."

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Falsification test: non-domestic-equity ETFs not disproportionately affected
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, Section II.2.c: "We further note that ETFs that do not derive their value from the prices of domestic equity securities were not disproportionately affected."

itemVerdicts.item: (a) ~2/3 of cancelled-trade shares executed below $1
itemVerdicts.note: Section II.3.b: "Almost two-thirds of shares in cancelled trades were executed at prices of less than $1.00, and about 5% were executed at prices above $100." Denominator is SHARES in cancelled trades, which is what the article says.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) 1,278 LULD halts; 1,058 in 327 ETPs
itemVerdicts.note: SEC Research Note, Equity Market Volatility on August 24, 2015 (Dec 2015), Section V summary: "Although most of the 1,278 LULD trading halts on August 24 occurred in ETPs, 80% of ETPs did not experience a single LULD halt. Overall, there were 1,058 LULD halts in 327 ETPs (many halts were repeats in the same ETP), and 220 LULD halts in 144 non-ETPs." 1,058+220=1,278 reconciles.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) 80% of ETPs had zero halts; 63.3% declined <10%
itemVerdicts.note: Section VI body: "Most ETPs (1,226, 80% of total ETPs) did not experience even a single LULD halt on August 24" and "Most ETPs (859, 63.3% of total ETPs) experienced price declines of less than 10%." Summary phrasing: "A majority of all ETPs (63.3%) declined by less than 10% -- a level that is consistent with broad market declines on August 24."

itemVerdicts.item: (b) SPX stale (primary-listing last-sale prices), -5.2% vs SPY -7.8%, so MWCB never fired
itemVerdicts.note: "The S&P 500 Index ("SPX")... declined on August 24 by only 5.2%... S&P DJI generally uses last sale prices from only the primary listing market to calculate its equity indexes. Until NYSE-listed constituents of the S&P 500 index were opened on the NYSE, the SPX disseminated by S&P DJI reflected NYSE closing prices from August 21." And: "Because the SPX did not decline by 7% (the first level trigger) on August 24, the market-wide circuit breakers, which would have implemented a 15-minute trading pause in all equities and related products, were not triggered." SPY's -7.8% is its 9:35 daily low (it opened -5.2%, closed -4.2%) — keep that framing precise.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Best predictor of ETP damage was low secondary-market turnover
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: "best predictor." RIGHT: "A pre-August 24 metric with a particularly strong association with volatility is secondary market turnover rate... Large and Mid market capitalization US Equity ETPs with comparatively low secondary market turnover rates in a control period were much more likely to experience severe volatility and multiple LULD halts." It is (i) an association, not a prediction, (ii) established only within the 114 Large/Mid US Equity ETPs (Tables VI-6 and VI-7), and (iii) the note explicitly disclaims causal findings: the analyses "are not intended to reach or suggest any legal conclusions or factual findings regarding the causes of the volatility on August 24." That disclaimer actually strengthens the article's umbrella point and should be cited.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) BIS attributes Feb 5 2018 spike to leveraged/inverse volatility ETPs; ~$4bn end-2017; XIV -84% and terminated
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers confirmed: "The assets of select leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs have expanded sharply over recent years, reaching about $4 billion at end-2017" and "The value of one of the inverse volatility ETPs, XIV, fell 84% and the product was subsequently terminated." WRONG if stated as BIS attributing the episode/selloff: RIGHT is that BIS attributes the late-afternoon VIX spike specifically, and as a key factor not the sole cause — "systematic trading strategies of the issuers of leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs appear to have been a key factor behind the volatility spike that occurred on the afternoon of 5 February," preceded by "Even though the aggregate positions in these instruments are relatively small." The S&P 500's -4.2% day is described separately as a 3.8 standard deviation move; BIS traces spillovers via dealers shorting E-mini futures.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) BIS verbatim: 'Neither the size nor the complex strategies of leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs are representative of the broader ETP market.'
itemVerdicts.note: Exact string found in BIS Quarterly Review March 2018, box by Sushko & Turner (r_qt1803t). Caliber note on attribution: it is not body text — it appears in the note to Graph A1, in a sentence that continues "...; see V Sushko and G Turner, 'What risks do exchange-traded funds pose?', Bank of France, Financial Stability Review, forthcoming." Cite it as the Graph A1 note.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Bond ETF tracking error >200bp vs 0.7bp historical sector average
itemVerdicts.note: BIS Quarterly Review, March 2021, Todorov, "The anatomy of bond ETF arbitrage": "the tracking error of bond ETFs increased to above 200 basis points for some funds in March–April 2020, much higher than the historical average of 0.7 bp in the sector." Same sentence continues: "These facts indicated impediments to the functioning of the arbitrage mechanism for bond ETFs" — cite that too, so the article isn't read as suppressing BIS's own statement that the wrapper malfunctioned.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) BIS (March 2021) reads the discounts partly as a run-deterrent / price-discovery feature
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: "price-discovery." The string "price discovery" does not appear anywhere in r_qt2103d. RIGHT: BIS's words are run-deterrence / shock absorption / stabilisation. "If there is excessive selling of ETF shares in the secondary market... the ETF sponsor can include only the riskier or less liquid securities from the pool of holdings in the redemption basket... This would discourage further runs and lead to ETF discounts during run episodes. In fact, such a stabilisation mechanism was arguably in place during the March–April 2020 episode... when some ETFs traded at a discount while redeeming baskets that were more illiquid than the holdings." Also: "The decoupling of baskets from holdings weakens arbitrage forces but allows ETFs to absorb shocks on the bond market." Note the hedge "arguably." "Price discovery" is BlackRock's framing, not BIS's — conflating them would hand a source-laundering objection to a critic.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Fed May 2020 FSR: passive shift 'might help reduce large redemptions... damp fire sale risks,' concern reserved for leveraged/inverse ETPs
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: the ellipsis drops a material qualifier. RIGHT verbatim (FSR May 2020, box 'Institutional Activities and Market Liquidity,' p.33): "As investors in passive mutual funds tend to be less responsive to performance than those in active funds, this shift to passive investing might help reduce large redemptions arising from poor performance and, therefore, damp fire sale risks." The claim is restricted to performance-driven redemptions, and the mechanism cited is passive investors' lower flow-performance sensitivity. The reservation is confirmed: "At the same time, some types of exchange-traded products (ETPs)—leveraged and inverse ETPs—have features that could cause strains in market liquidity," via end-of-day rebalancing and front-running. Footnote 9 cites Anadu, Kruttli, McCabe, Osambela and Shin, FEDS 2018-060.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) 'Bond ETFs = price discovery' FIMSAC deck is authored by BlackRock (EII), not the SEC
