itemVerdicts.note: Deck cover reads "EII Global Research / As of July, 2020 / Pricing and Liquidity of Fixed Income ETFs in the Covid-19 Crisis of 2020"; bullet: "Market participants turned to fixed income ETFs for price discovery"; every chart sourced "Source: BlackRock, Bloomberg"; closing pages carry the iShares prospectus disclaimer and "©2020 BlackRock, Inc." PDF metadata: Title "Evaluating the Performance of Flagship iShares Fixed Income ETFs", Author "Rui, Fang", created 2020-10-02. Hosted at sec.gov/spotlight/fixed-income-advisory-committee/100520-sec-conference-bond-etf-behavior-during-covid-volatility.pdf, i.e. the 5 Oct 2020 FIMSAC meeting (SEC press release 2020-243 confirms that meeting covered the bond fund and ETF market). SEC hosting is not SEC authorship — the article's point stands.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) BIS Sept 2025 box: 'retail investors, rather than institutional ones, bought into the rally'
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, BIS Quarterly Review 15 September 2025, box by Lombardi, Pinter and Todorov: "The box also illustrates that, in contrast with past episodes, retail investors, rather than institutional ones, bought into the rally." Supporting text: "Even as institutional investors withdrew from equity markets, retail investors were on net 'buyers of the dip', as visible from fund flows." I grepped the full box for passive/index/ETF: ZERO hits. The do-not-conflate warning is correct and well founded.

itemVerdicts.item: Umbrella: no official post-mortem attributes any of these episodes to index/passive structure
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as flatly stated. RIGHT: no official post-mortem attributes these episodes to the GROWTH OF INDEX/PASSIVE OWNERSHIP or to index-fund flows. Two of them do explicitly attribute disproportionate damage to the ETF wrapper's own machinery — SEC/CFTC 2010: "equity-based ETFs were disproportionately affected," traced to market makers who value underlying components pausing; BIS 2021: the tracking-error blowout "indicated impediments to the functioning of the arbitrage mechanism for bond ETFs." An adversarial reader will call the flat version false. Separately, I grepped both SEC documents for passive/index-fund attribution: the SEC/CFTC 2010 report's only uses of "passive" refer to passive ORDER EXECUTION (liquidity provision), not passive investing; the Aug 24 2015 note contains no instance of "passive", "index fund", or "indexing" at all. I found no later official document (FSB Holistic Review Nov 2020, Fed FSRs, BIS) attributing any of these five episodes to passive/index ownership.

itemVerdicts.item: Counting: 'four canonical episodes' followed by five enumerated items (a)-(e)
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: "four canonical episodes" with (a) 2010, (b) 2015, (c) 2018, (d) 2020, (e) 2025 listed. RIGHT: either say five, or say "four canonical episodes" for (a)-(d) and introduce April 2025 separately as a fifth, more recent case. As written the sentence miscounts its own list.

corrections: Change "the mechanism = equity-ETF market makers pausing" to "one of the reasons the SEC/CFTC report gives": the report says "We believe this is one of the reasons equity-based ETFs were disproportionately affected," and offers a second explanation — ETF order books concentrate ~half of liquidity within 30bp of mid with little resting retail depth far from mid, "allowing a disproportionate number of ETF orders to hit stub-quote levels."

Change "best predictor of ETP damage was low secondary-market turnover" to the report's own caliber: "A pre-August 24 metric with a particularly strong association with volatility is secondary market turnover rate." Add that the finding is established only within the 114 Large/Mid-cap US Equity ETPs, and that the note disclaims causal findings entirely ("not intended to reach or suggest any legal conclusions or factual findings regarding the causes of the volatility on August 24") — a disclaimer that supports the article's thesis and should be quoted.

Narrow the Feb 2018 attribution: BIS says leveraged/inverse volatility ETP issuers' rebalancing "appear to have been a key factor behind the volatility spike that occurred on the afternoon of 5 February" — a key factor in the afternoon VIX spike, not the cause of the day's equity selloff, and prefaced by "Even though the aggregate positions in these instruments are relatively small." Also keep BIS's word "select" in "select leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs... about $4 billion at end-2017."
Attribute the "Neither the size nor the complex strategies..." sentence to the note to Graph A1 in the BIS March 2018 box, not to the box's body text.

Delete "price discovery" from the BIS March 2021 attribution. The phrase does not appear in the article. BIS's framing is run-deterrence and shock absorption: sponsors tilting redemption baskets toward less liquid bonds "would discourage further runs and lead to ETF discounts during run episodes," and "such a stabilisation mechanism was arguably in place during the March–April 2020 episode." "Price discovery" is BlackRock's language and should stay attached to the BlackRock deck only.

Restore the dropped qualifier in the Fed May 2020 FSR quote: "this shift to passive investing might help reduce large redemptions arising from poor performance and, therefore, damp fire sale risks." The Fed's claim is limited to performance-driven redemptions and rests on passive investors' lower flow-performance sensitivity.

Add BIS's own adverse sentence when citing the >200bp tracking error, so the article is not read as cherry-picking: "These facts indicated impediments to the functioning of the arbitrage mechanism for bond ETFs."

Reword the umbrella claim from "no official post-mortem attributes any of these episodes to index/passive structure" to "no official post-mortem attributes any of these episodes to the growth of index/passive ownership or to index-fund flows." Two of the documents do attribute disproportionate damage to ETF wrapper mechanics (SEC/CFTC 2010: "equity-based ETFs were disproportionately affected"; BIS 2021 on impeded bond-ETF arbitrage), and the flat version is refutable on its face.

Fix the count: the sentence says "four canonical episodes" but enumerates five ((a) 2010, (b) 2015, (c) 2018, (d) 2020, (e) April 2025). Either say five, or scope "four canonical" to (a)-(d) and present April 2025 separately.

Optional strengthener for the Aug 24 2015 item: state that the SEC research note contains no instance of "passive," "index fund," or "indexing," and that the SEC/CFTC 2010 report's only uses of "passive" denote passive order execution (liquidity provision), not passive investing. This is a verifiable negative that makes the umbrella claim harder to attack.
newContradictions: The article's own umbrella sentence ("no official post-mortem attributes... to index/passive structure") sits in tension with the material it then quotes: the SEC/CFTC 2010 report affirmatively finds "equity-based ETFs were disproportionately affected" and explains it by the ETF valuation/market-making mechanism, and BIS 2021 says bond-ETF arbitrage was impeded. The distinction the article needs is ownership share vs wrapper plumbing, and it must be made explicitly or the sentence is refutable.

The BIS March 2021 stabilisation reading is hedged ("arguably in place") and is a conditional mechanism about redemption-basket composition, not a measured decomposition of the March 2020 discounts. Presenting it as BIS's finding that the discounts WERE a run deterrent overstates it; "reads the discounts partly as" is acceptable only if the hedge survives into the article.

The BIS Sept 2025 box also credits the rebound mainly to "backtracking from the initial tariff shock" and, from mid-May, to "news unrelated to tariffs"; retail buying is described as possibly amplifying ("They may have also been amplified by retail investors"). If the article uses this box for anything beyond the retail-vs-institutional contrast, that hierarchy of causes should be preserved.

The SPY figures need care: -5.2% is the OPEN, -7.8% is the 9:35 daily low, and the close was -4.2%. The clean comparison to SPX's -5.2% index decline is SPY's -7.8% low (the report's own pairing), but the article should not let "SPY fell 7.8%" read as a closing move.
reasoning: I reached all six primary documents in full text and grepped them verbatim rather than relying on summaries. (1) SEC/CFTC "Findings Regarding the Market Events of May 6, 2010" (Sept 30, 2010) — read Sections II.2.b, II.2.c and II.3.b in full; confirmed the >20,000 broken trades / 5.5m shares sentence, the "over two-thirds of the securities with broken trades were ETFs listed on NYSE Arca" sentence, the "Almost two-thirds of shares in cancelled trades were executed at prices of less than $1.00" sentence, and the falsification sentence "ETFs that do not derive their value from the prices of domestic equity securities were not disproportionately affected." The only slippage is caliber: the market-maker pause is "one of the reasons," and the report gives a second order-book-depth explanation. (2) SEC OAR/TM Research Note "Equity Market Volatility on August 24, 2015" (Dec 2015) — confirmed 1,278 / 1,058 / 327 / 220 / 144 (arithmetic reconciles), 80% zero-halt (1,226 ETPs), 63.3% (859 ETPs) declining <10%, the SPX staleness mechanism and the -5.2% vs -7.8% pairing, and the MWCB non-trigger. Read Tables VI-6 and VI-7 directly: the turnover finding is an association within 114 Large/Mid US Equity ETPs, and the note carries an explicit no-causal-findings disclaimer, so "best predictor" is overclaimed. (3) BIS QR March 2018 box (Sushko & Turner, r_qt1803t) — confirmed $4bn end-2017 for "select" ETPs, XIV -84% and termination, and located the "Neither the size nor the complex strategies..." sentence exactly, but it lives in the note to Graph A1, and BIS's causal language is "a key factor behind the volatility spike that occurred on the afternoon of 5 February," qualified by the small aggregate positions. (4) BIS QR March 2021 (Todorov, "The anatomy of bond ETF arbitrage") — confirmed the >200bp / 0.7bp sentence verbatim; confirmed the run-deterrence/shock-absorber reading including "such a stabilisation mechanism was arguably in place during the March–April 2020 episode"; but grep for "price discovery" returned ZERO hits, so that half of the attribution is wrong and must be dropped. (5) Fed FSR May 2020 — confirmed the passage on p.33 and found the article's ellipsis silently drops "arising from poor performance"; the leveraged/inverse ETP reservation is confirmed verbatim. (6) BIS QR Sept 2025 box (Lombardi, Pinter, Todorov) — confirmed the retail-not-institutional sentence verbatim, and grep for passive/index/ETF in the box returned zero hits, so the no-conflation warning is sound. Provenance of the FIMSAC deck required one live check: PDF metadata (Author "Rui, Fang", title "Evaluating the Performance of Flagship iShares Fixed Income ETFs"), the EII Global Research cover, BlackRock chart sourcing and iShares disclaimers all establish BlackRock authorship, and the sec.gov path plus SEC press release 2020-243 place it at the 5 Oct 2020 FIMSAC meeting. I also searched for later official documents (FSB Holistic Review Nov 2020 and subsequent) attributing any of these episodes to passive/index investing and found none; the FSB review attributes March 2020 to the demand-for-liquidity imbalance, dealer capacity, and leveraged non-bank Treasury selling. Remaining uncertainty: I did not read the full FSB Holistic Review text, only its published summary framing, so a buried passive reference there is not fully excluded; and I did not verify the SPY -4.2% close against an independent price source, though it is stated in the SEC note itself. The core thesis survives, but the umbrella sentence needs the ownership-vs-plumbing distinction, the "price discovery" attribution to BIS must be removed, the Fed quote must be restored in full, and the four-vs-five count must be fixed.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Flash crash: >20,000 broken trades; over two-thirds of broken-trade SECURITIES were ETFs
itemVerdicts.note: SEC/CFTC 'Findings Regarding the Market Events of May 6, 2010' read verbatim from local extraction of the full report. p.1: 'Over 20,000 trades across more than 300 securities were executed at prices more than 60% away from their values just moments before.' Section II.2 (HFT analysis): 'Since over two-thirds of the securities with broken trades were ETFs listed on NYSE Arca, we compared HFT trading activity in all securities with broken trades against those without broken trades.' Note the report's own wording adds 'listed on NYSE Arca' — the count is securities, not trades or dollar volume, which the claim states correctly.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Mechanism = equity-ETF market makers pausing
itemVerdicts.note: Section II.2.c 'ETFs AND MAY 6', verbatim: 'A large majority of ETF market makers with whom we spoke, and particularly those that value underlying stocks as part of their normal market making activities, paused their market making for considerable periods of time starting at about 2:45 p.m. on May 6. We believe this is one of the reasons equity-based ETFs were disproportionately affected by the extreme price volatilities of that afternoon.' Caliber note: the report says 'one of the reasons', not the reason.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Falsification test: ETFs NOT based on domestic equities were NOT disproportionately affected
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, immediately following the market-maker-pause sentence: 'We further note that ETFs that do not derive their value from the prices of domestic equity securities were not disproportionately affected.' Exact wording is 'do not derive their value from the prices of domestic equity securities' — quote it that way rather than 'not based on domestic equities'.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) ~2/3 of cancelled-trade shares executed below $1 (stub quotes)
itemVerdicts.note: Section II.3.a/b verbatim: 'over 20,000 trades representing 5.5 million shares were executed at prices more than 60% away from their 2:40 p.m. value... Almost two-thirds of shares in cancelled trades were executed at prices of less than $1.00, and about 5% were executed at prices above $100.' Denominator is SHARES in cancelled trades (5.5m shares), not number of trades — the claim states this correctly.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Aug 24 2015: 1,278 LULD halts, 1,058 in 327 ETPs, 80% of ETPs zero halts, 63.3% declined <10%
itemVerdicts.note: SEC OAR/TM Research Note 'Equity Market Volatility on August 24, 2015' (December 2015), Section V summary, verbatim: 'Although most of the 1,278 LULD trading halts on August 24 occurred in ETPs, 80% of ETPs did not experience a single LULD halt. Overall, there were 1,058 LULD halts in 327 ETPs (many halts were repeats in the same ETP), and 220 LULD halts in 144 non-ETPs.' Section VI: 'A majority of all ETPs (63.3%) declined by less than 10% -- a level that is consistent with broad market declines on August 24.' Body text (p.~85) gives the count: '859, 63.3% of total ETPs'. Note total halts were in 471 securities.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) The S&P 500 INDEX itself was stale (primary-listing last-sale prices), -5.2% vs SPY -7.8%, which is why the market-wide circuit breaker never fired
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'The S&P 500 Index ("SPX"), as calculated and disseminated by S&P Dow Jones Indices LLP ("S&P DJI"), declined on August 24 by only 5.2% from its previous day's close. Until approximately 9:42, SPX remained substantially higher than the prices of the SPY (7.8% decline), E-Mini (7% decline), and the net asset value ("NAV") of SPY (8% decline...). S&P DJI generally uses last sale prices from only the primary listing market to calculate its equity indexes. Until NYSE-listed constituents of the S&P 500 index were opened on the NYSE, the SPX disseminated by S&P DJI reflected NYSE closing prices from August 21.' And: 'Because the SPX did not decline by 7% (the first level trigger) on August 24, the market-wide circuit breakers, which would have implemented a 15-minute trading pause in all equities and related products, were not triggered on August 24.' All four numbers exact. Watch a coincidence trap: 5.2% is BOTH the SPX max decline and SPY's OPENING gap; SPY's 7.8% is its 9:35 daily low.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Best predictor of ETP damage was low secondary-market turnover
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG (as stated): 'best predictor'. RIGHT: the note calls it a strong ex-ante association, not a ranked best predictor. Verbatim: 'A pre-August 24 metric with a particularly strong association with volatility is secondary market turnover rate – the ratio of average daily volume in the secondary market for an ETP to its shares outstanding. Large and Mid market capitalization US Equity ETPs with comparatively low secondary market turnover rates in a control period were much more likely to experience severe volatility and multiple LULD halts on August 24...' Section VI adds that the other correlates (volume increase, depth-of-book, imbalances) are '"after-the-fact" metrics based on August 24 trading. ADV Turnover Rate, in contrast, is based solely on control period trading volume' — i.e. it is the strongest EX-ANTE metric among those examined, and applies to Large/Mid US Equity ETPs, not all ETPs. Also: the note explicitly disclaims causation — 'not intended to reach or suggest any legal conclusions or factual findings regarding the causes of the volatility on August 24'. That disclaimer strengthens the article's umbrella claim and is worth quoting.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Feb 5 2018: BIS attributes spike to leveraged/inverse volatility ETPs (~$4bn AUM end-2017); XIV fell 84% and was terminated
itemVerdicts.note: BIS Quarterly Review March 2018 box, Sushko & Turner, 'The equity market turbulence of 5 February - the role of exchange-traded volatility products' (r_qt1803t.htm), read verbatim from local file and re-fetched live. 'The assets of select leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs have expanded sharply over recent years, reaching about $4 billion at end-2017'. Note the qualifier 'select' — it is the four products shown in Graph A1, not all such ETPs. 'The value of one of the inverse volatility ETPs, XIV, fell 84% and the product was subsequently terminated.' Attribution caliber: BIS says 'systematic trading strategies of the issuers of leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs appear to have been a key factor behind the volatility spike that occurred on the afternoon of 5 February' — A key factor, not the cause.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) BIS verbatim: 'Neither the size nor the complex strategies of leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs are representative of the broader ETP market.'
itemVerdicts.note: Exact string match in both the local extraction and a live re-fetch of https://www.bis.org/publ/qtrpdf/r_qt1803t.htm. Attribution nuance: this sentence sits in the note accompanying Graph A1, not the running body text, and continues '...; see V Sushko and G Turner, "What risks do exchange-traded funds pose?", Bank of France, Financial Stability Review, forthcoming.' Cite it as the Graph A1 note if precision matters.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) March 2020 bond ETFs: tracking error >200bp for some funds vs 0.7bp historical sector average
itemVerdicts.note: BIS Quarterly Review March 2021, Todorov, 'The anatomy of bond ETF arbitrage' (r_qt2103d), verbatim: 'In addition, the tracking error of bond ETFs increased to above 200 basis points for some funds in March–April 2020, much higher than the historical average of 0.7 bp in the sector.' Both numbers exact; note it is 'for some funds', not the sector, and the 0.7bp is the sector historical average.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) BIS (March 2021) reads the discounts partly as a run-DETERRENT / price-discovery feature
itemVerdicts.note: HALF WRONG. RIGHT (run-deterrent): verbatim — 'the ETF sponsor can include only the riskier or less liquid securities from the pool of holdings in the redemption basket. The lower-quality bonds that APs obtain after redeeming ETF shares would in turn reassure non-running investors that their shares are now backed with holdings of higher average quality. This would discourage further runs and lead to ETF discounts during run episodes. In fact, such a stabilisation mechanism was arguably in place during the March–April 2020 episode... when some ETFs traded at a discount while redeeming baskets that were more illiquid than the holdings.' Also: 'ETFs could be a stabilising force during runs and prevent fire sales.' WRONG (price discovery): the phrase 'price discovery' does NOT appear anywhere in the BIS March 2021 article (grep, case-insensitive, zero hits). BIS frames it as run-prevention / shock absorption / stabilisation only. The 'price discovery' framing belongs to the BlackRock FIMSAC deck ('Market participants turned to fixed income ETFs for price discovery'), so attaching it to BIS silently launders an issuer's framing into a central-bank source.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Fed May 2020 FSR: passive shift 'might help reduce large redemptions... and, therefore, damp fire sale risks'; concern reserved for leveraged/inverse ETPs
itemVerdicts.note: Substance confirmed, quotation caliber off. Federal Reserve Financial Stability Report, May 2020, box 'Institutional Activities and Market Liquidity', verbatim: 'As investors in passive mutual funds tend to be less responsive to performance than those in active funds, this shift to passive investing might help reduce large redemptions arising from poor performance and, therefore, damp fire sale risks.' WRONG: the article's ellipsis elides 'arising from poor performance' — a material scope limiter (the Fed is not claiming passive damps redemptions generally, only performance-chasing ones), and the premise is specifically about PASSIVE MUTUAL FUND investors' lower performance-sensitivity. RIGHT: quote the qualifier in full. The leveraged/inverse reservation is the immediately following paragraph, verbatim: 'At the same time, some types of exchange-traded products (ETPs)—leveraged and inverse ETPs—have features that could cause strains in market liquidity.' Footnote 9 cites Anadu, Kruttli, McCabe, Osambela & Shin, FEDS 2018-060.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) The 'bond ETFs = price discovery' deck presented to SEC FIMSAC is authored by BlackRock (EII), not the SEC
itemVerdicts.note: Deck read in full locally. Cover: 'EII Global Research / As of July, 2020 / Pricing and Liquidity of Fixed Income ETFs in the Covid-19 Crisis of 2020'; every chart sourced 'BlackRock, Bloomberg'; compliance code ICRMH0920U-1319728-1/13 through -13/13; back matter '©2020 BlackRock, Inc. iSHARES and BLACKROCK are trademarks of BlackRock, Inc.' and 'The iShares Funds are distributed by BlackRock Investments, LLC'. Slide 2 verbatim: 'Market participants turned to fixed income ETFs for price discovery.' Venue confirmed on the live SEC FIMSAC spotlight page (retrieved via text proxy; sec.gov blocks direct fetch): under 'October 5, 2020 ... Bond Fund and ETF Presentations: Ananth Madhavan Presentation' linking to /spotlight/fixed-income-advisory-committee/100520-sec-conference-bond-etf-behavior-during-covid-volatility.pdf. Madhavan was BlackRock's head of EII research. So: a BlackRock presentation TO the committee, hosted on an sec.gov path whose filename ('sec-conference-...') invites misreading it as an SEC document. Do not cite it as 'the SEC found'.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) April 2025: BIS Sept 2025 box says 'retail investors, rather than institutional ones, bought into the rally' — retail, not passive
itemVerdicts.note: BIS Quarterly Review, 15 September 2025, box by Lombardi, Pinter & Todorov, 'Understanding the swift market recovery after the April 2025 tariff shock' (r_qt2509w), verbatim: 'The box also illustrates that, in contrast with past episodes, retail investors, rather than institutional ones, bought into the rally.' Supporting body text: 'Even as institutional investors withdrew from equity markets, retail investors were on net "buyers of the dip", as visible from fund flows (Graph A2.C). These dynamics were somewhat unusual compared with past stress episodes (eg the GFC), when retail investors were net sellers and institutional investors were net buyers.' The word 'passive' does not appear in the box. The box's headline finding is separate and should not be conflated either: 'about 75% of the rise in the S&P 500 between the trough on 9 April and end-July was driven by positive surprises unrelated to tariffs.'

itemVerdicts.item: Umbrella framing: 'No official post-mortem attributes any of the four canonical episodes to index/passive structure'
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG on two counts. (1) COUNT: the claim says 'four canonical' episodes but enumerates five, (a) through (e). Either drop (e) from the canonical set or say five. (2) CALIBER on 'index': BIS DOES attribute 5 Feb 2018 to leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs, which are exchange-traded INDEX-linked products (they track VIX-futures indices) — the claim survives only because BIS's own Graph A1 note says they 'are not representative of the broader ETP market'. Likewise, the SEC/CFTC flash-crash report's proximate trigger is an automated sell program in an INDEX futures product: 'a large fundamental trader (a mutual fund complex) initiated a sell program to sell a total of 75,000 E-Mini contracts' executed by an algorithm that did not take price into account — an active manager hedging via an index instrument. RIGHT: scope the sentence to plain-vanilla index-fund / passive OWNERSHIP structure (i.e. cap-weighted index funds and their flows), not to 'index products' generally, or a hostile reader overturns it in one line.

corrections: Delete 'price discovery' from the BIS March 2021 attribution. The phrase does not appear anywhere in Todorov, 'The anatomy of bond ETF arbitrage' (BIS QR March 2021). BIS reads the March–April 2020 discounts strictly as a run-deterrent / stabilisation mechanism: 'This would discourage further runs and lead to ETF discounts during run episodes. In fact, such a stabilisation mechanism was arguably in place during the March–April 2020 episode.' The 'price discovery' framing is BlackRock's, from the FIMSAC deck ('Market participants turned to fixed income ETFs for price discovery') — attributing it to BIS launders an issuer's framing into a central-bank source.

Restore the elided qualifier in the Fed FSR quote. WRONG: 'might help reduce large redemptions... and, therefore, damp fire sale risks.' RIGHT (Federal Reserve Financial Stability Report, May 2020): 'As investors in passive mutual funds tend to be less responsive to performance than those in active funds, this shift to passive investing might help reduce large redemptions arising from poor performance and, therefore, damp fire sale risks.' The Fed is claiming passive damps PERFORMANCE-CHASING redemptions specifically, and reasons from passive MUTUAL FUND investors' lower performance-sensitivity.

Soften 'best predictor of ETP damage was low secondary-market turnover.' RIGHT (SEC Research Note, Dec 2015): 'A pre-August 24 metric with a particularly strong association with volatility is secondary market turnover rate.' It is the strongest EX-ANTE metric examined — the note contrasts it with volume-increase, depth-of-book and imbalance, which it calls '"after-the-fact" metrics based on August 24 trading' — and the finding is stated for Large and Mid market-capitalization US Equity ETPs, not all ETPs.

Fix the episode count: the claim says 'four canonical' episodes but lists five, (a) May 2010, (b) Aug 2015, (c) Feb 2018, (d) March 2020, (e) April 2025. Say five, or exclude April 2025 from the canonical set explicitly.

Narrow the umbrella claim from 'index/passive structure' to 'plain-vanilla index-fund / passive ownership structure'. As written it is falsifiable in one line: BIS attributes 5 Feb 2018 to leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs, which ARE index-linked exchange-traded products, and the SEC/CFTC flash-crash report's trigger is 'a large fundamental trader (a mutual fund complex) initiated a sell program to sell a total of 75,000 E-Mini contracts' — an active manager selling an INDEX futures product via a price-insensitive algorithm.

In (a), keep the report's own hedges: it says the market-maker pause 'is one of the reasons equity-based ETFs were disproportionately affected' (not the reason), and the two-thirds figure is 'over two-thirds of the securities with broken trades were ETFs listed on NYSE Arca'. Also state the denominator explicitly for the stub-quote figure: 'Almost two-thirds of SHARES in cancelled trades were executed at prices of less than $1.00' (out of 5.5 million shares), not two-thirds of trades.

In (c), attribute the 'not representative' sentence precisely: it appears in the note to Graph A1 of the BIS March 2018 box, not the body text, and BIS's causal wording is that issuers' systematic strategies 'appear to have been a key factor behind the volatility spike' — a key factor, not the cause. The ~$4bn is for 'select' leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs (the four products in Graph A1), not the whole category.

In (b), add the SEC's own causal disclaimer, which strengthens the argument: the Research Note's data 'are not intended to reach or suggest any legal conclusions or factual findings regarding the causes of the volatility on August 24'. And avoid the 5.2% collision — 5.2% is both SPX's maximum decline and SPY's opening gap; SPY's 7.8% is its 9:35 daily low.

In (d), label the FIMSAC deck unambiguously as third-party industry material: 'Ananth Madhavan (BlackRock, EII Global Research), Pricing and Liquidity of Fixed Income ETFs in the Covid-19 Crisis of 2020, presented at the SEC FIMSAC meeting of October 5, 2020.' The sec.gov filename ('100520-sec-conference-bond-etf-behavior-during-covid-volatility.pdf') invites misreading it as an SEC staff finding; it is not.
newContradictions: BIS March 2021 (Todorov, 'The anatomy of bond ETF arbitrage') contains zero instances of 'price discovery' or 'informative'. Its stabilisation argument is about run prevention and shock absorption via in-kind redemption baskets ('ETFs could be a stabilising force during runs and prevent fire sales'), a mechanism it explicitly says 'is not available to other investment vehicles with cash redemptions such as mutual funds'. Any article sentence pairing BIS with 'price discovery' is unsupported.

BIS March 2021 also notes the opposite-signed risk the article should not omit: basket/holdings decoupling 'weakens arbitrage forces', and the stabilisation strategy 'can backfire in the long run... If investors perceive an ETF as redeeming only low-quality bonds in stress times, they may withdraw from the ETF altogether.' Citing only the benign half is selective.

The SEC/CFTC flash-crash narrative was materially supplemented by later official action: the DOJ/CFTC 2015 case against Navinder Sarao attributed spoofing in E-Mini futures a role in the 6 May 2010 conditions. This does not touch the ETF/passive question, but an article leaning on the 2010 report's trigger account (the 75,000-contract mutual-fund sell program) should not present it as the last official word. I did not fetch the CFTC complaint in this pass — flagging as an open thread, not a verified finding.

Item (e) has a second BIS finding the article may be tempted to over-read: 'about 75% of the rise in the S&P 500 between the trough on 9 April and end-July was driven by positive surprises unrelated to tariffs.' That is a VAR decomposition of tariff vs non-tariff news, not a statement about investor type or flows; do not merge it with the retail-vs-institutional sentence.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) 21% of active strategies survived and beat their passive composite over the 10 years through 2025
itemVerdicts.note: Key Takeaways, p.3, verbatim in the live PDF: "Just 21% of active strategies survived and beat their passive counterparts over the 10 years through 2025." Note Morningstar's own wording here is "passive counterparts," not "asset-weighted passive composite" — the asset-weighted framing comes from the 1-year bullet and the Appendix B Success Rate definition, so applying it to the 10-year number is an inference (a safe one, since it is the same success-rate metric).

itemVerdicts.item: (a) 1-year 2025: 38% all funds, 37% US stock-pickers
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: "Just 38% survived and beat their asset-weighted average passive composite, down 4 percentage points from a year earlier" and "US stock-pickers also trended slightly lower with a 37% success rate for 2025, a 1-percentage-point drop from 2024." Caution: 37% is ALL US stock-pickers. The report's US large-cap section separately says "Active US large-cap managers... Their 36% success rate marked a 1-percentage-point decrease from 2024," while the Key Takeaways bullet says "mid- and large-cap managers (37%)" — Morningstar is internally inconsistent by 1pp on large caps. Do not write "37% of US large-cap managers."

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Exhibit 1 10-year success rates: Large Blend 8.1, Large Growth 3.6, Large Value 20.3, Small Growth 37.0, Foreign Large Blend 22.8, Diversified EM 29.1, Intermediate Core Bond 41.7, Corporate Bond 52.2, High-Yield 39.1
itemVerdicts.note: All nine match Exhibit 1 exactly, verified twice: in the local extract and in a fresh download of the source PDF (pdftotext -layout, pages 3-4). The Corporate Bond pairing is the one worth flagging in prose: 52.2% over 10 years but only 4.4% in 2025 alone.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Universe ~9,248 funds ≈ USD 26T ≈ 67% of the US fund market
itemVerdicts.note: Executive Summary, p.2, verbatim: "The US Active/Passive Barometer spans nearly 9,248 unique funds that accounted for approximately USD 26 trillion in assets, or about 67% of the US fund market, at the end of 2025." This is a share of the US FUND market (open-end + ETF, excluding funds of funds and money market funds), not of US market cap and not of trading.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Methodology: success = survived AND beat the ASSET-WEIGHTED average of actual passive funds in the category, net of fees, magnitude ignored
itemVerdicts.note: Net-of-fees and magnitude-ignored are exact. The ASSET-WEIGHTED part is NOT unambiguous in the source — Morningstar contradicts itself. RIGHT (Appendix B, Success Rate): "...survive and generate a return in excess of the asset-weighted average passive fund return over the period... We do not consider magnitude of outperformance in defining success." But the very next paragraph of Appendix B says they "count the number that rank higher than the equal weighted average return for the passive funds in the category," and Appendix C repeats it: "count the number of funds with returns exceeding the equal-weighted average of the passive funds in the category." So the report states the hurdle as asset-weighted once and equal-weighted twice. This matters: in US Large Blend the 10-yr passive asset-weighted return is 14.5% vs equal-weighted 13.9% — a 0.6pp difference in the hurdle. The article should not present ASSET-WEIGHTED as a settled, load-bearing methodological fact; say Morningstar benchmarks against a composite of the actual net-of-fee passive funds in the category (its own text describes that composite as asset-weighted in one place and equal-weighted in two others).

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Morningstar 'fixes SPIVA's costless-benchmark objection'
itemVerdicts.note: Morningstar never mentions SPIVA or S&P Dow Jones anywhere in the 31-page report (grep: zero hits). RIGHT: Appendix C makes a generic argument — its approach "differs from the convention of using a single, representative index," because "One cannot directly invest in indexes. Their performance does not account for the real costs associated with replicating their performance and packaging and distributing them in an investable format," and it also claims to "mitigate the effects that might stem from cherry-picking a single index." Attributing the fix specifically to SPIVA is the article's inference and must be framed as such.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Harsher answer for US large cap: 8.1% vs SPIVA's ~14% success
itemVerdicts.note: Two defects. (1) WINDOW: ~14% is not a year-end-2025 SPIVA figure I could verify. It matches SPIVA U.S. Scorecard MID-YEAR 2025, Report 1a, All Large-Cap Funds vs S&P 500, 10-year = 85.98% underperforming → 14.02% success, data as of June 30, 2025. SPIVA Year-End 2024 was 84.34% → 15.66% success. The SPIVA Year-End 2025 scorecard (the true match for Morningstar's Dec-31-2025 data) is behind an Akamai 403 and I could not read it — see unreachable item. (2) POPULATION: the comparison is not like-for-like. Morningstar's 8.1% is the US Large BLEND category; SPIVA's ~14% is ALL Large-Cap (core + growth + value, each vs a different S&P benchmark). SPIVA's actual blend analog is Large-Cap CORE vs S&P 500: 96.57% underperforming at 10 years (MY2025) and 96.62% (YE2024) → ~3.4% success — i.e. SPIVA is HARSHER than Morningstar's 8.1% on the matched row, which reverses the twist. If the article wants a Morningstar-vs-SPIVA aggregate contrast it should compare like to like (Morningstar's three US large-cap rows are 8.1 blend / 3.6 growth / 20.3 value).

itemVerdicts.item: (d) '...partly because passive funds survive better (80.4% vs 62.4% at 10 years in Large Blend)'
itemVerdicts.note: The two numbers are exact — Exhibit 5, US Large Blend, 10-Year row: 383 active funds at start, 62.4% survivorship; 138 passive funds at start, 80.4% survivorship; active success rate 8.1%. But the CAUSAL clause is unsupported and points the wrong way. Morningstar nowhere attributes its success rates to differential survivorship. Mechanically it cannot explain a Morningstar-vs-SPIVA gap: SPIVA uses the same construction (Appendix B glossary: "we use the opportunity set available at the beginning of the period as the denominator. We determine the count of funds that have survived and beat the index"), and SPIVA's hurdle is an index with no fund mortality at all — a 100%-surviving benchmark — so benchmark survivorship would make SPIVA harsher, not gentler. Also, Morningstar's hurdle is net of fees, which makes it a LOWER bar than a costless index, again pushing the wrong way. The real drivers of the 8.1-vs-14 gap are category taxonomy (see previous item) and which passive funds sit in the Morningstar large-blend composite. If the article wants a survivorship point, the defensible one is internal to Morningstar and about the benchmark, not the comparison: "When a passive fund becomes obsolete, its starting weight is subsumed by the passive composite using their pro rata starting weights" — i.e. the passive composite itself is survivor-reweighted.

reasoning:
I read the primary document twice: the local extract mstar_apb_h12026.txt and a fresh download of the source PDF (3.19 MB, HTTP 200, from the exact URL given), re-extracting pages 1-4 with pdftotext -layout to guard against extraction error. Every number in claims (a), (b) and the universe part of (c) matches verbatim in both copies: Exhibit 1's nine 10-year success rates (Large Blend 8.1, Large Value 20.3, Large Growth 3.6, Small Growth 37.0, Foreign Large Blend 22.8, Diversified EM 29.1, Intermediate Core Bond 41.7, Corporate Bond 52.2, High-Yield 39.1); the 21% / 38% / 37% headline figures; and 'nearly 9,248 unique funds... approximately USD 26 trillion... about 67% of the US fund market.' Exhibit 5's US Large Blend 10-year row confirms 383 active funds at 62.4% survivorship, 138 passive at 80.4%, success 8.1%, with passive asset-weighted return 14.5% vs active 13.2%.

Three problems survived scrutiny. First, Morningstar's methodology is internally inconsistent on the hurdle: Appendix B's Success Rate definition says 'asset-weighted average passive fund return,' but the immediately following paragraph and Appendix C both say the count is of funds exceeding the EQUAL-weighted average of the category's passive funds. The article states asset-weighted as a settled methodological fact, which overstates the source. Second, Morningstar never mentions SPIVA (zero grep hits for SPIVA or S&P Dow Jones across 31 pages); the costless-benchmark argument in Appendix C is generic. Third, and most serious, the '8.1% vs SPIVA's ~14%' contrast fails on both window and population. I traced ~14% to SPIVA Mid-Year 2025 Report 1a (All Large-Cap vs S&P 500, 10-year, 85.98% underperforming = 14.02% success, as of June 30 2025) from the local spiva-my2025.txt, and cross-checked SPIVA Year-End 2024 (84.34% → 15.66%) from the reproduced tables in Cremers-Fulkerson-Riley's May 2026 draft in iaa_spiva.txt. Neither is a Dec-31-2025 figure. More damaging, SPIVA's matched row — Large-Cap Core vs S&P 500 — is 96.57% underperforming at 10 years (96.62% at YE2024), i.e. ~3.4% success, harsher than Morningstar's 8.1%, so the direction of the 'twist' depends entirely on pairing Morningstar's Large Blend against SPIVA's broader All Large-Cap aggregate.

I also checked the causal gloss and found it backwards. SPIVA's Appendix B glossary uses the same survive-and-beat construction on a beginning-of-period denominator, and its benchmark is a costless index with no fund mortality; Morningstar's hurdle is net of fees, hence a lower bar. Neither channel can make Morningstar the harsher measure via passive-fund survivorship. The defensible survivorship point is internal to Morningstar — its passive composite redistributes dead passive funds' starting weight pro rata to survivors.

Remaining uncertainty: I could not reach the SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Year-End 2025 PDF. spglobal.com returns Akamai 403 to curl with plain and full browser headers, to WebFetch, and to r.jina.ai; the four local 'ye2025' files in the scratchpad are 2,011-byte 403 HTML pages masquerading as PDFs, so they will silently yield nothing to anyone grepping them. Only the 1-year YE2025 figure is corroborated by secondary reporting (79% of large-cap funds underperformed in 2025, up from 65%, fourth-worst in 25 years). Search-tool summaries offered 10-year figures of '83-84%', 'fewer than one in six', and '89.93%' — mutually inconsistent and unsourced; I discarded all three rather than pass along an unverified number. I did not verify Exhibit 1 rows outside the nine claimed, nor the fee-quintile 31%/17% figures, as they were not part of this claim group.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Report 2 survivorship: 49.95% of large-cap funds survived 15 years; 88.29% decomposes into ~50pp dead + ~38pp survived-and-lost
itemVerdicts.note: Report 2 (p.13), 15-Year block, 'All Large-Cap Funds': Number of Funds at Start 1033, Survivorship 49.95%, Style Consistency 54.70%. Decomposition is methodologically valid: Appendix B glossary states 'we use the opportunity set available at the beginning of the period as the denominator. We determine the count of funds that have survived and beat the index. We then report the index outperformance percentage.' So underperform% = 100 − (survived AND beat)/start, i.e. every non-surviving fund is counted as underperforming. 100 − 49.95 = 50.05pp died; 88.29 − 50.05 = 38.24pp survived and lost; 11.71pp survived and won. Two cautions the article must respect: (i) the decomposition assumes Report 1a and Report 2 share the same 15-yr starting universe (both are the 1033-fund opportunity set — consistent, but SPIVA does not print the Report 1a denominator explicitly); (ii) 'dead' ≠ 'underperformed before dying' — funds also merge for business reasons, which is precisely the first of three methodological objections in Cremers, Fulkerson & Riley (draft 4 May 2026).

Use the benchmark's full name 'S&P Composite 1500' (not 'S&P 1500') for the 93.81% 20-year All Domestic Funds figure.

Label the Report 3/4 returns as ANNUALIZED (the report footnote reads 'Returns shown are annualized for periods greater than one year'), and label the 10.85 vs 12.46 pair explicitly as equal-weighted vs asset-weighted average ACTIVE FUND returns, not fund-count shares.

Attribute the Year-End 2025 79% / 'fourth-worst' figures secondhand (InvestmentNews, S&P's own Indexology commentary as reproduced by marketsgroup.org, tker.co) — the spglobal.com PDF is Akamai-403 and could not be opened; do not cite it as if read directly.

Keep the vendor flag on all SPIVA numbers, and add the counterweight: Cremers, Fulkerson & Riley, 'How the SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Understates the Performance of Actively Managed Mutual Funds' (draft 4 May 2026, funded by the Investment Adviser Association's Active Managers Council) replicates SPIVA closely (they get 92.04% vs SPIVA's reported 92.66% for the average 20-year U.S. equity category) but argues three choices bias it: counting every exiting fund as an underperformer regardless of pre-exit performance, equal-weighting funds, and benchmarking to hypothetical indices rather than actual passive fund returns. Their restated figure is 55% of active U.S. equity fund ASSETS underperforming over 20 years, and they reverse the sign for fixed income. That paper is itself trade-association-funded and is a working paper, so flag both sides.

When using the survivorship decomposition, do not write or imply that ~50% of large-cap funds 'died from underperformance'. RIGHT: 50.05pp of the 1033-fund starting universe did not survive the 15 years and are counted as underperformers by SPIVA's construction, 38.24pp survived and lost, 11.71pp survived and won. Whether the dead funds actually trailed before exit is exactly the contested point.
newContradictions: Cremers, Fulkerson & Riley (draft 4 May 2026, IAA Active Managers Council funding), local file iaa_spiva.txt: replicating SPIVA's own method they get 92.04% of active funds underperforming in the average 20-year U.S. equity category vs SPIVA's 92.66%; after (i) crediting exiting funds with their actual pre-exit performance, (ii) asset-weighting, and (iii) benchmarking to actual passive fund returns rather than indices, only 55% of active U.S. equity fund ASSETS underperformed over 20 years, and only 37% of fixed income (vs SPIVA's 71% over 10 years) — a sign reversal for bonds. This directly attacks the survivorship decomposition in sub-claim (b) and the equal-weighted framing behind the headline percentages.

Two web-search summarizers in this session gave mutually contradictory numbers for the 2025 S&P 500 return quoted from the same YE2025 PDF ('gaining 18% and logging 39 record highs' vs 'up 35% in 2025'). Neither is verifiable and neither should be used. Treat all summarizer output on the blocked spglobal PDF as unreliable.

The SPIVA MY2025 headline (54% of large-cap funds underperforming in H1 2025, 'on track for the best year since 2022') is directly reversed by the YE2025 result (79%, fourth-worst in 25 years). Any article passage citing the H1 2025 improvement as evidence of anything must not be left standing without the full-year outcome.
reasoning:

itemVerdicts.item: (a) 21% of active strategies survived and beat their asset-weighted passive composite over the 10 years through 2025; 1-yr 2025: 38% all-funds, 37% US stock-pickers
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the Key Takeaways of Morningstar's US Active/Passive Barometer Year-End 2025 (local mstar_apb_h12026.txt, byte-identical to mstar_h12026.txt; source URL returns HTTP 200 application/pdf). Exact text: 'Just 38% survived and beat their asset-weighted average passive composite, down 4 percentage points from a year earlier.'; 'US stock-pickers also trended slightly lower with a 37% success rate for 2025, a 1-percentage-point drop from 2024.'; 'Just 21% of active strategies survived and beat their passive counterparts over the 10 years through 2025.' Note the 10-yr bullet says 'their passive counterparts', not 'asset-weighted passive composite' — the asset-weighted gloss is correct per Appendix B but is the article's wording, not the bullet's.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Exhibit 1 10-yr success rates: US Large Blend 8.1, Large Growth 3.6, Large Value 20.3, Small Growth 37.0, Foreign Large Blend 22.8, Diversified EM 29.1, Intermediate Core Bond 41.7, Corporate Bond 52.2, High-Yield 39.1
itemVerdicts.note: All nine values confirmed. I re-extracted Exhibit 1 independently with `pdftotext -layout -f 3 -l 3 mstar_h12026.pdf` to guard against a bad prior extraction; the 10-Year column reads 8.1 / 20.3 / 3.6 (Large Blend/Value/Growth), 37.0 (US Small Growth), 22.8 (Foreign Large Blend), 29.1 (Diversified Emerging Markets), 41.7 (Intermediate Core Bond), 52.2 (Corporate Bond), 39.1 (High-Yield Bond). Source line: 'Data and Calculations as of Dec. 31, 2025.' These are fund-count-based success rates over the trailing 10 years, denominator = funds existing at the start of the period.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Methodology: success = survived AND beat the asset-weighted average of actual passive funds in the category (net of fees), magnitude ignored; universe ~9,248 funds ≈ $26T ≈ 67% of the US fund market
itemVerdicts.note: Executive Summary: 'spans nearly 9,248 unique funds that accounted for approximately USD 26 trillion in assets, or about 67% of the US fund market, at the end of 2025', and 'the "benchmark" reflects the actual, net-of-fees performance of investable passive funds.' Appendix B, Success Rate: 'what percentage of funds that started the sample period went on to survive and generate a return in excess of the asset-weighted average passive fund return over the period... We do not consider magnitude of outperformance in defining success: A fund that just barely beat the passive alternative counts as much as a fund that significantly outperformed.' CAVEAT (not a defect in the claim): Appendix B is internally inconsistent — the paragraph immediately following says 'count the number that rank higher than the equal weighted average return for the passive funds in the category'. The same contradictory boilerplate appears verbatim in the Midyear 2025 edition (mstar_h22025.txt line 2190ff), so it is legacy text. The article should not assert the report is unambiguous on asset- vs equal-weighting of the passive composite.

itemVerdicts.item: (d-i) Morningstar 'fixes' SPIVA's costless-benchmark objection by benchmarking to net-of-fee actual passive funds
itemVerdicts.note: Morningstar: benchmark 'reflects the actual, net-of-fees performance of investable passive funds' and 'differs from the convention of using a single, representative index to gauge success.' SPIVA by contrast compares to indices; SPIVA MY2025 methodology confirms fund returns are 'net of fees, excluding loads' but the comparison index is costless. So the mechanical description is right. The word 'fixes' is doing editorial work — Morningstar never mentions SPIVA anywhere in the report (grep for 'SPIVA', 'S&P Dow', 'costless' returns zero hits); the framing is the article's, not Morningstar's.

itemVerdicts.item: (d-ii) Morningstar gets a HARSHER answer for US large cap: 8.1% vs SPIVA's ~14% success
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as framed: it pits Morningstar's US Large Blend (8.1%), a single style-box category, against SPIVA's 'All Large-Cap Funds' aggregate (~14%). RIGHT: (1) Morningstar's own US large-cap aggregate is 10%, stated verbatim on p.6: 'Just 10% of them survived and beat their average passive rival over the decade through 2025.' (Fund-count check: 383x8.1 + 350x20.3 + 417x3.6 over 1,150 funds = 10.2%.) (2) The '~14%' traces to SPIVA U.S. Mid-Year 2025, Report 1a, All Large-Cap Funds vs S&P 500, 10-Year = 85.98% underperforming → 14.02% success, data as of June 30, 2025 — a different measurement date from Morningstar's Dec 31, 2025. (3) The sign REVERSES on the matched category: SPIVA MY2025 'Large-Cap Core Funds vs S&P 500' 10-Year = 96.57% underperforming → ~3.4% success, i.e. SPIVA is far harsher than Morningstar's 8.1% Large Blend. So 'Morningstar is harsher' is an artifact of which SPIVA row is chosen, not a robust finding.

itemVerdicts.item: (d-iii) ...partly because passive funds survive better (80.4% vs 62.4% at 10 years in Large Blend)
itemVerdicts.note: The two NUMBERS are verbatim correct — Exhibit 5, US Large Blend, 10-Year row: active funds 383 at beginning / 62.4% survivorship; passive funds 138 at beginning / 80.4% survivorship. But the CAUSAL claim is refuted. WRONG: passive funds' higher survivorship makes Morningstar harsher than SPIVA. RIGHT: it cannot, for two reasons. (1) SPIVA is itself survivorship-bias-corrected — 'SPIVA Scorecards account for the entire opportunity set—not just the survivors' — so active-fund mortality is penalized in both studies (SPIVA MY2025 All Large-Cap 10-yr survivorship 65.52%, close to Morningstar's 62.4%). (2) Passive-fund survivorship enters nowhere in Morningstar's active success rate: the denominator is active funds at the start, and per Appendix B 'when a passive fund becomes obsolete, its starting weight is subsumed by the passive composite using their pro rata starting weights.' The 80.4/62.4 pair is a Morningstar-internal active-vs-passive mortality contrast, a legitimate point on its own, but it is not the mechanism for any Morningstar-vs-SPIVA gap.

itemVerdicts.item: (d-iv) Direction of the costless-benchmark fix
itemVerdicts.note: The article's logic runs backwards. Cremers, Fulkerson & Riley, 'How the SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Understates the Performance of Actively Managed Mutual Funds' (draft May 4, 2026, supported by the IAA Active Managers Council; local iaa_spiva.txt) isolate exactly this change and find it LOWERS measured underperformance: 'the Scorecard method indicates that, over the 3-year period of 2022 through 2024, 81% of large-cap core funds underperform... comparing against equivalent passive funds decreases it to 73%'; for fixed income at a 10-year horizon 'the underperformance rate decreases by an across-category average of 11%.' Consistent with this, Morningstar's Large Blend 10-yr asset-weighted PASSIVE composite return is 14.5% (Exhibit 5) versus an S&P 500 10-yr annualized total return of roughly 14.8% through Dec 2025 (secondary sources only — I could not reach a primary index factsheet), i.e. Morningstar's bar is at or slightly BELOW the costless index, not above it. Whatever makes Morningstar look harsher on the All-Large-Cap comparison comes from category definitions and universe construction (Morningstar uses unique fund IDs across all share classes and includes ETFs and institutional classes; SPIVA uses the largest share class only and different style mappings), not from replacing the index with net-of-fee passive funds. Extra counterexample: for calendar 2025, SPIVA Year-End 2025 reports '79% of all active large-cap U.S. equity funds underperformed the S&P 500' (21% success) while Morningstar reports a 36% one-year success rate for active US large-cap — here the 'fixed' benchmark yields a much MILDER verdict.

itemVerdicts.item: SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Year-End 2025, 10-year All Large-Cap underperformance rate (the edition-matched comparator)
itemVerdicts.note: Could not reach the primary document. https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/documents/spiva/spiva-us-year-end-2025.pdf returns HTTP 403 to curl with full browser headers, to WebFetch, and through r.jina.ai (Akamai 'Access Denied'); the spglobal SPIVA article page is likewise 403; the cloudfront mirror pattern that works for Mid-Year 2025 (d1e00ek4ebabms.cloudfront.net/production/uploaded-files/spiva-us-mid-year-2025-<uuid>.pdf) has no discoverable Year-End 2025 UUID; the local spiva-ye2025.pdf / spiva_ye2025.pdf are 2,011-byte HTML error pages, not PDFs. Only the 1-year figure (79% underperforming) is available, quoted verbatim in secondary coverage (InvestmentNews). A search summarizer volunteered 'approximately 83%' for the 10-year figure — that is an inference, not a quote, and I am not treating it as evidence. Do not print a Year-End 2025 10-year SPIVA number without opening the PDF.

corrections: Item (b), (a), (c): no changes needed — every number checks out verbatim against the PDF, re-extracted independently.

Do not compare Morningstar's 8.1% (US Large Blend, one style-box category) to SPIVA's 'All Large-Cap Funds' aggregate. Use Morningstar's own like-for-like aggregate, stated verbatim on p.6: 'Just 10% of them survived and beat their average passive rival over the decade through 2025.'

State the SPIVA edition and date. The '~14%' figure is SPIVA U.S. Mid-Year 2025, Report 1a, All Large-Cap Funds vs S&P 500, 10-Year = 85.98% underperforming (14.02% success), data as of June 30, 2025 — six months earlier than Morningstar's Dec. 31, 2025 cut. Either match editions or say the dates differ. I could not reach SPIVA U.S. Year-End 2025 (403 everywhere); do not print its 10-year figure unverified.

Add the counter-comparison or drop the 'harsher' claim: on the matched category, SPIVA is harsher, not milder. SPIVA MY2025 'Large-Cap Core Funds vs S&P 500' 10-Year = 96.57% underperforming, i.e. ~3.4% success, versus Morningstar Large Blend's 8.1%. The direction of the Morningstar-vs-SPIVA gap depends entirely on which SPIVA row is picked.

Delete the causal clause 'partly because passive funds survive better.' The 80.4% vs 62.4% figures are correct (Exhibit 5, US Large Blend, 10-Year: passive survivorship 80.4%, active 62.4%) but they cannot explain a Morningstar-vs-SPIVA gap: SPIVA is also survivorship-bias-corrected on the active side ('account for the entire opportunity set—not just the survivors'), and passive-fund survivorship never enters Morningstar's active success rate — obsolete passive funds' starting weight is 'subsumed by the passive composite using their pro rata starting weights.' Keep 80.4/62.4 only as a standalone active-vs-passive mortality fact.

Reverse the stated mechanism. Replacing a costless index with net-of-fee passive funds makes the bar EASIER, not harder. Cremers-Fulkerson-Riley (May 2026) isolate the change: large-cap core 3-year underperformance falls from 81% to 73%, and fixed-income 10-year underperformance falls by an average of 11 percentage points. Morningstar's own Large Blend 10-yr passive composite returned 14.5% asset-weighted, at or below the S&P 500's roughly 14.8%. If the article keeps a 'harsher' narrative, attribute it to universe and category-mapping differences (Morningstar: unique fund IDs, all share classes, ETFs included, 20 Morningstar Categories; SPIVA: largest share class only, CRSP-based style mappings), not to the benchmark fix.

If the article wants a fair 'the fix cuts both ways' line, the honest one is: for calendar 2025 Morningstar's net-of-fee passive benchmark is far MILDER than SPIVA's index — 36% success for active US large-cap versus SPIVA Year-End 2025's '79% of all active large-cap U.S. equity funds underperformed the S&P 500' (21% success).

Add a one-line caveat on methodology: Morningstar's Appendix B contradicts itself, defining success against 'the asset-weighted average passive fund return' and then, one paragraph later, against 'the equal weighted average return for the passive funds in the category.' The same boilerplate appears in the Midyear 2025 edition. Cite the asset-weighted definition (it matches the Key Takeaways and the exhibits) but do not claim the report is unambiguous.

Attribution hygiene: Morningstar never mentions SPIVA in this report (zero hits for 'SPIVA', 'S&P Dow', 'costless'). Present the SPIVA contrast as the article's own analysis, not as something Morningstar argues.
newContradictions: Cremers, Fulkerson & Riley, 'How the SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Understates the Performance of Actively Managed Mutual Funds' (draft May 4, 2026, IAA Active Managers Council; local file iaa_spiva.txt) directly contradicts the article's causal story: the costless-benchmark fix reduces measured underperformance (large-cap core 3-year 81%→73%; fixed income 10-year −11pp average), and their combined-adjustment headline is that only 56% of active U.S. equity fund ASSETS underperformed equivalent passive funds in 2024, with active fixed income tending to OUTPERFORM over both short and long horizons. If the article cites Morningstar as the rigorous fix to SPIVA, it owes readers this paper, which applies the same fix plus asset-weighting and non-survivor handling and lands in the opposite place. Note the metric difference: CFR report share of ASSETS, Morningstar reports share of FUNDS — do not compare 56% to 21% as if they were the same quantity.

SPIVA MY2025 Large-Cap Core Funds 10-year underperformance of 96.57% (≈3.4% success) is a direct counterexample to 'Morningstar is harsher for US large cap.' On the matched category the index-based scorecard is the more damning one.

SPIVA Year-End 2025's calendar-2025 large-cap result (79% underperformed, i.e. 21% success) versus Morningstar's 36% one-year US large-cap success rate is a second counterexample, at the short horizon, in the same direction.

Morningstar's Large Blend 10-yr asset-weighted passive composite return of 14.5% sitting at or below the S&P 500's ~14.8% means Morningstar's 'investable' bar is not a tougher bar than the index — undercutting any claim that harsher results follow from making the benchmark investable.
reasoning: Primary document reached in full: Morningstar's US Active/Passive Barometer Year-End 2025, both via the local extraction (/private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-cissychen-design/0f8bdcde-3464-42f4-af17-1552808c31d6/scratchpad/mstar_apb_h12026.txt, byte-identical to mstar_h12026.txt) and by independently re-running pdftotext -layout on mstar_h12026.pdf for the Exhibit 1 page and the Exhibit 5 (US Large Blend) page, so the numbers are not resting on a single possibly-garbled extraction. The stated source URL returns HTTP 200 application/pdf. itemVerdicts.item: (a) SPIVA MY2025 Report 1a: All Large-Cap vs S&P 500 — 1-yr 72.61%, 5-yr 86.91%, 10-yr 85.98%, 15-yr 88.29%, 20-yr 91.03%; All Domestic vs S&P 1500 20-yr 93.81%; Report 1b risk-adjusted 10-yr 94.39%
itemVerdicts.note: All seven figures read verbatim off the primary PDF (spiva-my2025.pdf, 48pp, 'Data as of June 30, 2025'), re-extracted myself with pdftotext -layout rather than trusting the pre-existing .txt. Report 1a row 'All Large-Cap Funds / S&P 500': YTD 54.31, 1-Year 72.61, 3-Year 64.87, 5-Year 86.91, 10-Year 85.98, 15-Year 88.29, 20-Year 91.03. Row 'All Domestic Funds / S&P Composite 1500': 20-Year 93.81. Report 1b ('Based on Risk-Adjusted Return') row 'All Large-Cap Funds / S&P 500': 10-Year 94.39 (also 3-yr 75.64, 5-yr 90.50, 15-yr 98.16, 20-yr 96.17). No slippage. Two unused-but-relevant guards: the article must not conflate the Report 1a 1-yr 72.61% (12 months to 2025-06-30) with the report's headline 54% (which is YTD H1 2025 only), and Report 1b is a different population statistic (risk-adjusted), not a stronger version of the same one.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Report 2 survivorship: only 49.95% of large-cap funds survived 15 years; 88% 15-yr figure = ~50pp dead + ~38pp survived-and-lost
itemVerdicts.note: Report 2, 15-Year panel, 'All Large-Cap Funds': Number of Funds at Start 1033, Survivorship (%) 49.95, Style Consistency (%) 54.70. Same opportunity set underlies Report 1a's 88.29%, so the decomposition is exact: 100 − 49.95 = 50.05pp non-survivors, 88.29 − 50.05 = 38.24pp survived-and-underperformed, leaving 11.71pp survived-and-beat (i.e. 23.4% of survivors beat). Appendix B confirms the mechanism verbatim: 'To correct for survivorship bias, we use the opportunity set available at the beginning of the period as the denominator. We determine the count of funds that have survived and beat the index.' One caveat the article must keep: SPIVA does not claim the ~50pp of dead funds underperformed while alive — they are simply excluded from the 'survived and beat' numerator. Stating it as '~50pp dead' (not '~50pp that lost') is the correct phrasing and the claim gets this right.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) 25-year annual series (Exhibit 1): majority beat in only three years — 2005 (49), 2007 (45), 2009 (48); worst 2014 (87), 2021 (85), 2011 (82); no clean secular trend
itemVerdicts.note: The numbers are right; the label '25-year annual series' applied to the MY2025 Exhibit 1 is wrong. I recovered every bar label by x-coordinate (pdftotext -bbox) rather than reading the jumbled linear text dump, which mis-orders the labels. MY2025 Exhibit 1 = 2001:65, 2002:68, 2003:75, 2004:69, 2005:49, 2006:68, 2007:45, 2008:56, 2009:48, 2010:66, 2011:82, 2012:63, 2013:55, 2014:87, 2015:65, 2016:66, 2017:63, 2018:65, 2019:71, 2020:60, 2021:85, 2022:51, 2023:60, 2024:65, then an H1 2025 stub at 54. WRONG: describing that as a '25-year annual series'. RIGHT: it is 24 full calendar years (2001–2024) plus a half-year stub (H1 2025 = 54%); a genuine 25-calendar-year series (2001–2025) requires the Year-End 2025 vintage, which appends 2025 = 79%. Substance survives either way: sub-50 years are exactly {2005, 2007, 2009} in both framings, and the three worst are 2014/2021/2011 at 87/85/82 (2025's 79 slots in fourth, consistent with SPIVA's own 'fourth-worst' language). I cross-checked the whole series against an independent vintage — SPIVA Year-End 2024, reached via mirror requisitecm.com/pdf/SPIVA-US-Scorecard-Year-End-2024.pdf, 44pp — and all 24 values match to the digit, so these are not one-vintage artifacts. Two caveats to carry: (i) 2005 (49) and 2009 (48) are rounded chart labels, so 'majority beat' in those years is a 1–2pp margin inside rounding — only 2007 (45) is a comfortable win; (ii) 'no clean secular trend' is quantitatively defensible but should be stated with the number, not as a flat 'no trend': OLS on 2001–2025 gives slope +0.235 pp/yr, r = 0.157, r² = 0.025, while the half-sample means do drift 62.8% (2001–2012) to 67.1% (2013–2025) against a series SD of ~12pp.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Year-End 2025: 79% of large-cap funds underperformed in CY2025, 'fourth-worst showing in the 25-year history'
itemVerdicts.note: Figure confirmed; the quoted phrasing is misattributed. spglobal.com returns 403 to every route I tried (direct, ?force_download, ?amp=, referer-spoofed, Wayback, jina). I reached S&P DJI's own Year-End 2025 Scorecard commentary through a sponsored verbatim republication at marketsgroup.org/strategic-insights/spiva-u-s-scorecard (published May 19, 2026, 'Sponsored By S&P Dow Jones Indices', charts sourced 'Data as of Dec. 31, 2025'), fetched as raw HTML and de-tagged locally — not via a summarizer. Its exact sentence: 'In our largest and most closely watched comparison, 79% of all active large-cap U.S. equity funds underperformed the S&P 500, worse than the 65% rate observed in 2024 and the fourth-worst year for active large-cap managers over the 25-year history of our SPIVA Scorecards.' WRONG: presenting 'fourth-worst showing in the 25-year history' as a SPIVA quote. RIGHT: SPIVA's words are 'the fourth-worst year for active large-cap managers over the 25-year history of our SPIVA Scorecards'; 'fourth-worst showing' is InvestmentNews's paraphrase — in that article (Leo Almazora, Mar 04 2026, raw HTML pulled and read directly) the quotation marks enclose only '79% of all active large-cap U.S. equity funds underperformed the S&P 500', with 'up from 65% in 2024 and the fourth-worst showing for large-cap managers in the 25-year history of the study' outside them. Two further independent reproductions of the 79%: WealthManagement.com, May 12 2026 ('in 2025, the study found that 79% of all active large cap U.S. equity funds underperformed the S&P 500'), and the Cremers-Fulkerson-Riley critique. Corroborating YE2025 detail from the same S&P DJI text: 55% of mid-cap and 41% of small-cap funds underperformed; 63% international, 76% global; bond cross-category average 70% vs 62% for equities; S&P 500 +18% with 39 record closing highs. Full Report 1a/1b/2 tables for YE2025 remain unreachable — do not quote YE2025 long-horizon or survivorship numbers.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) EW vs AW gap (MY2025): 10-yr S&P 500 13.65% vs large-cap funds EW 10.85% / AW 12.46%; 20-yr gap EW −1.96pp vs AW −1.25pp
itemVerdicts.note: Report 3 (Equal-Weighted): 'S&P 500' 10-Year 13.65, 20-Year 10.73; 'All Large-Cap Funds' 10-Year 10.85, 20-Year 8.77. Report 4 (Asset-Weighted): 'All Large-Cap Funds' 10-Year 12.46, 20-Year 9.48. Arithmetic: 20-yr EW gap 8.77 − 10.73 = −1.96pp exactly; AW gap 9.48 − 10.73 = −1.25pp exactly. 10-yr gaps, if the article wants them, are −2.80pp EW and −1.19pp AW. Returns are annualized, net of fees excluding loads (Appendix B: 'The fund returns used are net of fees, excluding loads.'). The EW/AW spread is the article's own best internal evidence that SPIVA's headline fund-count percentages overstate the dollar-weighted investor experience — which is exactly the axis the Cremers-Fulkerson-Riley critique attacks.

corrections: MY2025's Exhibit 1 is not a '25-year annual series.' Describe it as 24 full calendar years (2001–2024) plus an H1 2025 stub of 54%, OR cite the Year-End 2025 vintage for a true 25-calendar-year series (2001–2025, which appends 2025 = 79%). The sub-50 count is three either way.

Do not present 'fourth-worst showing in the 25-year history' as an S&P DJI quote — that is InvestmentNews's paraphrase. S&P DJI's own Year-End 2025 wording is: 'the fourth-worst year for active large-cap managers over the 25-year history of our SPIVA Scorecards.' The only clause InvestmentNews puts inside quotation marks is '79% of all active large-cap U.S. equity funds underperformed the S&P 500.'

Replace the flat assertion 'no clean secular trend' with the statistic. OLS on the full 2001–2025 series gives slope +0.235 pp/yr, r = 0.157, r² = 0.025 — negligible — but the half-sample means do rise from 62.8% (2001–2012) to 67.1% (2013–2025), so 'no trend' overstates it. Say the trend explains ~2.5% of the variance against a ~12pp year-to-year SD.

Flag that 2005 (49%) and 2009 (48%) are rounded chart labels, so 'a majority beat the index' in those two years rests on a 1–2pp margin inside rounding; only 2007 (45%) is a comfortable majority-beat year.

Do not quote any Year-End 2025 long-horizon (5/10/15/20-yr) or survivorship figures. Only the CY2025 headline rates were reachable; the YE2025 Report 1a/1b/2 tables are behind a 403 and were not verified.

Date-stamp the window whenever the 54% figure appears. SPIVA's Mid-Year 2025 headline was 54% underperforming with the industry 'on track for the best year since 2022'; the same calendar year closed at 79%, the fourth-worst on record. Quoting 54% without the H1-only qualifier inverts the year's actual result.

When stating claim (b), keep the phrasing '~50pp dead,' not '~50pp that lost.' SPIVA does not assert non-survivors underperformed while alive; they are merely absent from the 'survived and beat' numerator. Exact decomposition: 88.29% = 50.05pp non-survivors + 38.24pp survived-and-underperformed, leaving 11.71pp survived-and-beat (23.4% of the 49.95% that survived).

Attach the vendor flag symmetrically and cite the live methodological challenge: Cremers, Fulkerson & Riley (Notre Dame / Dayton / Arkansas), 'How the SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Understates the Performance of Actively Managed Mutual Funds,' draft May 4, 2026, funded by the Investment Adviser Association's Active Managers Council — an unpublished working paper from the active-management trade body, mirroring S&P DJI's index-vendor interest. They replicate SPIVA closely (92.04% vs SPIVA's reported 92.66% for the 20-yr U.S. equity category average), then show three changes cut it to 55% of assets.

SPIVA is evidence about active managers' net-of-fee returns, not about index-driven price distortion. It cannot carry weight for the index bubble thesis, and S&P DJI's own Year-End 2025 text attributes the 79% to large-cap dominance and breadth, never to passive indexing.
newContradictions: Cremers-Fulkerson-Riley (May 4, 2026 draft, IAA Active Managers Council-sponsored; local file iaa_spiva.txt, 44pp) directly attacks the statistic the article is leaning on. Their worked example, verbatim: over 2022–2024, 'the Scorecard method indicates that ... 81% of large-cap core funds underperform. Not automatically counting exiting funds as underperformers decreases that percentage to 77%. Likewise, weighting by assets decreases the underperformance to 71% and comparing against equivalent passive funds decreases it to 73%. Making all three changes simultaneously decreases the percentage to 46%.' At the 20-year horizon, averaging across cap-valuation U.S. equity categories, SPIVA's 92% becomes 55% of assets after their three adjustments, 'with half of the categories having an underperformance rate for their assets below 50%.' Note the sponsorship flag runs both ways, and this is a working paper, not published.

The survivorship convention that claim (b) decomposes is itself contested on cited grounds, not just rhetorically. CFR invoke Bessembinder, Cooper & Zhang (2023) — that a significant portion of exiting funds did not underperform — and Linnainmaa (2013) on reverse survivorship bias, i.e. that survivorship corrections can themselves understate active performance. The article's ~50pp/~38pp split is arithmetically right but should be presented as an artifact of SPIVA's counting rule, which is exactly what the literature disputes.

S&P DJI's own Year-End 2025 causal narrative undercuts any index-bubble reading of the 79%. In the same text, S&P DJI reports the top five stocks' contribution to S&P 500 return 'weakened in a linear fashion from 78% in Q1 2025 ... to 11% in Q4' — concentration of return contribution fell sharply in the very year active managers posted their fourth-worst result. S&P DJI attributes the underperformance instead to S&P 500 Equal Weight lagging and to breadth ('only 30% of stocks outperformed overall in 2025'), and notes dispersion was 'the highest since 2009' — high dispersion being the condition that should favor stock pickers. Using SPIVA as evidence that passive flows distort prices runs against the vendor's own stated mechanism.

Tone-inversion trap within one calendar year: MY2025 (data to 2025-06-30) reports 54% and says the industry was 'on track for the best year since 2022'; YE2025 reports 79% and the fourth-worst year on record. S&P DJI's YE2025 text explicitly reconciles this — 'The more fruitful grounds for active managers in the early innings of last year may also help explain the relatively benign H1 2025 large-cap underperformance rate of 54%.' Any article mixing MY2025 tables with the YE2025 headline must not let the 54% stand as a 2025 result.

MY2025's own Report 3/4 contradict the headline's implied severity: the asset-weighted 20-yr shortfall for large-cap funds is −1.25pp vs the equal-weighted −1.96pp, i.e. the dollars investors actually hold did materially better than the fund-count statistic implies. This is the article's internal evidence for the same asset-weighting objection CFR raise, and it should be surfaced rather than buried under the 91.03%.

Unreachable, so bounded: the Year-End 2025 primary PDF is 403 on spglobal.com via every route attempted, and only the narrative summary (via S&P DJI's sponsored republication at marketsgroup.org, plus InvestmentNews and WealthManagement reproductions) was verified. The YE2025 Report 1a/1b/2 tables — including any updated 15-yr survivorship or 20-yr underperformance figures — remain unverified and must not be cited.
reasoning:
Worked primarily from the local primary PDF rather than the pre-extracted text, because the linear text dump of Exhibit 1 mis-orders the bar labels (it reads them by vertical band, producing a plausible-looking but wrong year mapping — e.g. it appears to put 68 on 2005 and 49 on 2006). I re-extracted with pdftotext -bbox and reassigned every label by x-coordinate against the axis tick positions, which yields the correct series. I then cross-checked the entire 2001–2024 series against an independent vintage, SPIVA Year-End 2024 (44pp, reached through the requisitecm.com mirror after spglobal.com 403'd), using the same coordinate method: all 24 values match to the digit, so the annual series is stable across vintages and not a rounding artifact of one chart.

Verbatim reads from spiva-my2025.pdf (48pp, 'Data as of June 30, 2025'): Report 1a and 1b rows, the four Report 2 survivorship panels, Reports 3 and 4 return tables, and Appendix B's glossary — which supplies the methodology sentence that makes the (b) decomposition legitimate ('we use the opportunity set available at the beginning of the period as the denominator ... funds that have survived and beat the index'). Every number in (a), (b) and (e) checks out exactly, and the 20-yr EW/AW gaps recompute to −1.96pp and −1.25pp on the nose.

For the Year-End 2025 items I treated both summarizer outputs as unverified per the fabrication warning and re-fetched raw HTML with curl, stripping tags locally, for both InvestmentNews and marketsgroup.org. The marketsgroup page turned out to be a full sponsored republication of S&P DJI's own YE2025 Scorecard commentary (dated May 19, 2026, exhibits sourced 'Data as of Dec. 31, 2025'), which is as close to the primary narrative as I could get and confirms the 79% and the 'fourth-worst' framing in S&P DJI's own words — though phrased differently from the article's version, hence the attribution correction. The YE2025 tables themselves stay unreachable.

The two substantive caliber problems are the '25-year annual series' label on a chart that is 24 years plus a half-year stub, and the quotation-mark attribution on 'fourth-worst showing.' Beyond those, the adversarial findings that matter most are external: the Cremers-Fulkerson-Riley paper (already sitting in the scratchpad as iaa_spiva.txt) attacks precisely the survivorship convention that claim (b) trades on and the fund-count weighting that claim (e) already half-concedes, taking 92% to 55% of assets at 20 years; and S&P DJI's own YE2025 mechanism — mega-cap return contribution collapsing from 78% to 11% across the year while active had its fourth-worst showing, with dispersion at a post-2009 high — points away from, not toward, an indexing explanation. Remaining uncertainty: the CFR paper is an unpublished trade-body-funded draft whose numbers could move between versions, and I could not verify any YE2025 long-horizon or survivorship table.
