itemVerdicts.item: (a) MY2025 Report 1a — All Domestic Funds vs S&P Composite 1500, 20-yr 93.81%
itemVerdicts.note: Report 1a row: All Domestic Funds | S&P Composite 1500® | 64.33 | 74.87 | 79.32 | 88.32 | 90.31 | 92.52 | 93.81. Index name is 'S&P Composite 1500', not 'S&P 1500' — use the full name.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) MY2025 Report 1b risk-adjusted — All Large-Cap Funds vs S&P 500, 10-yr 94.39%
itemVerdicts.note: Report 1b (p.11, 'Based on Risk-Adjusted Return'): All Large-Cap Funds | S&P 500 | 75.64 | 90.50 | 94.39 | 98.16 | 96.17 (3Y/5Y/10Y/15Y/20Y). Note Report 1b has NO YTD or 1-year column, so 94.39% is unambiguously the 10-year risk-adjusted figure.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Survivorship (Report 2): 49.95% of large-cap funds survived 15 years; 88.29% decomposes into ~50pp dead + ~38pp survived-and-lost
itemVerdicts.note: Report 2, 15-Year block: All Large-Cap Funds — Number of Funds at Start 1,033; Survivorship 49.95%; Style Consistency 54.70%. Decomposition is exact: 100 − 88.29 = 11.71pp survived AND beat; non-survivors = 50.05pp; survived-but-lagged = 49.95 − 11.71 = 38.24pp. Mechanism confirmed in Appendix B glossary, which states the denominator is 'the opportunity set available at the beginning of the period' and the numerator is 'the count of funds that have survived and beat the index' — i.e. every non-survivor is scored as not-outperforming. Sharper framing available: only 23.4% of the funds that actually survived 15 years beat the index.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) 25-year annual series (Exhibit 1): majority of large-cap funds beat the S&P 500 in only three years — 2005 (49), 2007 (45), 2009 (48); worst years 2014 (87), 2021 (85), 2011 (82); no clean secular trend
itemVerdicts.note: Substance confirmed, label wrong. I re-extracted Exhibit 1 by bounding-box (column-matched to the year axis) rather than trusting reading order: 2001-65, 2002-68, 2003-75, 2004-69, 2005-49, 2006-68, 2007-45, 2008-56, 2009-48, 2010-66, 2011-82, 2012-63, 2013-55, 2014-87, 2015-65, 2016-66, 2017-63, 2018-65, 2019-71, 2020-60, 2021-85, 2022-51, 2023-60, 2024-65, H1 2025-54. Only three bars are below 50 (2005, 2007, 2009) — correct. Three worst are 2014=87, 2021=85, 2011=82 — correct (next is 2003=75). WRONG: calling this a '25-year annual series'. RIGHT: Mid-Year 2025 Exhibit 1 shows 24 completed calendar years (2001–2024) plus a partial 'H1 2025' bar — 25 bars, not 25 annual observations. The '25-year history' phrasing belongs to the Year-End 2025 edition (2001–2025). 'No clean secular trend' is well supported: OLS slope over 2001–2024 is +0.11pp/yr (2001–2012 mean 62.8 vs 2013–2024 mean 66.1) against a passive share that roughly quadrupled — a flat-to-faintly-rising line, not a ramp. Say 'essentially flat', not 'no trend at all'.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Year-End 2025: 79% of large-cap funds underperformed in CY2025, 'fourth-worst showing in the 25-year history'
itemVerdicts.note: Number confirmed by two independent secondhand sources read as RAW HTML (not fetch summaries); attribution of the quoted phrase is wrong. (1) InvestmentNews, Leo Almazora, MAR 04 2026: 'the SPIVA report found that "79% of all active large-cap U.S. equity funds underperformed the S&P 500," up from 65% in 2024 and the fourth-worst showing for large-cap managers in the 25-year history of the study.' Note the quotation marks close after 'S&P 500' — the 'fourth-worst' clause is InvestmentNews's own framing, NOT quoted SPIVA text. (2) tker.co, Sam Ro, Mar 03 2026: '79% of U.S. large-cap equity fund managers underperformed the S&P 500 in 2025. It was the fourth-worst year for these managers in the report's 25-year history,' plus a direct Anu Ganti quote ending '...2025 was the worst year for large-cap active equity performance since 2021,' and '16th consecutive year in which the majority of fund managers in this category have lagged the index.' WRONG: presenting 'fourth-worst showing in the 25-year history' as a verbatim SPIVA quotation. RIGHT: 79% is the SPIVA figure; 'fourth-worst in 25 years' is journalists' characterization (arithmetically consistent — only 2014=87, 2021=85, 2011=82 exceed 79). Consistency checks that all pass: 16 consecutive majority-lagging years = 2010–2025, which matches 2009=48 being the last sub-50 year; 79 slots between 82 and 75. tker also reports YE2025 large-cap 3-yr 67%, 5-yr 89%, 20-yr 93%. PRIMARY UNREACHABLE — see next item. Also worth flagging for the article: MY2025 said H1 was 54% and put the industry 'on track for the best year since 2022'; the full year landed at 79%. Using both figures without noting that H2 reversal would mislead.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) primary Year-End 2025 PDF
itemVerdicts.note: Could not reach spiva-us-year-end-2025.pdf by any route: direct curl with browser UA + Referer → Akamai 403; WebFetch → 403; r.jina.ai proxy → 403 (Reference #18.1968dc17...); web.archive.org id_ replay → 404 (no snapshot); Wayback CDX API → timed out; guessed CloudFront path → 404; spglobal.com/spdji/en/spiva/article/spiva-us/ → 403. Therefore I could NOT verify the YE2025 Report 1a table, the YE2025 Exhibit 1 bar values (S&P DJI does restate historical bars between editions), or whether 'fourth-worst' appears in S&P's own text. Treat all YE2025 figures as secondhand, double-sourced.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) EW vs AW gap (MY2025): 10-yr S&P 500 13.65% vs large-cap funds EW 10.85% / AW 12.46%; 20-yr gap EW −1.96pp vs AW −1.25pp
itemVerdicts.note: Report 3 (Equal-Weighted, p.16): S&P 500 6.20/15.16/19.71/16.64/13.65/14.86/10.73; All Large-Cap Funds 6.08/13.31/17.43/14.16/10.85/12.22/8.77. Report 4 (Asset-Weighted, p.18): All Large-Cap Funds 7.67/15.48/20.00/15.35/12.46/13.64/9.48. So 10-yr: index 13.65, EW 10.85, AW 12.46 — exact. 20-yr: 8.77 − 10.73 = −1.96pp (EW) and 9.48 − 10.73 = −1.25pp (AW) — exact. Caliber: these are annualized returns as of June 30, 2025, net of fees excluding loads (per the report's Fees glossary), so 'gap' is a net-of-fee return differential, not alpha.

corrections: Do not call the Mid-Year 2025 Exhibit 1 a '25-year annual series'. It is 24 completed calendar years (2001–2024) plus a partial 'H1 2025' bar — 25 bars, 24 annual observations. The '25-year history' framing belongs to the Year-End 2025 edition, which covers 2001–2025.

Do not present 'fourth-worst showing in the 25-year history' as a quotation from SPIVA. In InvestmentNews the quotation marks close after '...underperformed the S&P 500'; the 'fourth-worst' clause is the reporter's framing. Attribute it as media characterization of the SPIVA data, or drop the quotation marks. The 79% figure itself is safely double-sourced (InvestmentNews 2026-03-04; tker.co / Sam Ro 2026-03-03).

Label all Year-End 2025 numbers (79% CY2025; 3-yr 67%, 5-yr 89%, 20-yr 93%) as secondhand — the primary PDF at spglobal.com returns Akamai 403 via every route tried (direct curl, WebFetch, r.jina.ai, Wayback, guessed CDN path) and no archive snapshot exists.

If the article cites both the Mid-Year and Year-End 2025 scorecards, it must acknowledge the reversal: MY2025 reported 54% underperforming in H1 and said the industry was 'on track for the best year since 2022'; the full year finished at 79%. Presenting the two side by side without that note is misleading.

Soften 'no clean secular trend' to 'essentially flat'. The 2001–2024 annual underperformance series has an OLS slope of +0.11pp/yr (2001–2012 mean 62.8% vs 2013–2024 mean 66.1%) — a faint upward drift, not zero, though nothing resembling the passive-share ramp.

Write the survivorship decomposition with the exact figures rather than rounded ones: of the 1,033 large-cap funds alive at the start of the 15-year window, 50.05pp did not survive, 38.24pp survived but lagged, and only 11.71pp survived and beat the index. Equivalently, just 23.4% of the funds that actually survived 15 years beat the S&P 500.

When using the survivorship decomposition, note that SPIVA's convention of scoring every non-survivor as not-outperforming is exactly the choice attacked by Cremers, Fulkerson & Riley (May 4, 2026 draft, funded by the Investment Adviser Association's Active Managers Council), who evaluate exiting funds over their living period instead and find U.S. equity 20-year underperformance rates fall by roughly 16pp. The MY2025 numbers are vendor numbers computed under a contested convention.
Use the index's full name 'S&P Composite 1500', not 'S&P 1500', when citing the 93.81% All Domestic Funds 20-year figure.
When citing the EW/AW gap, state that these are annualized returns as of June 30, 2025, net of fees excluding loads — a net return differential, not alpha.
newContradictions: Cremers, Fulkerson & Riley, 'How the SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Understates the Performance of Actively Managed Mutual Funds' (draft May 4, 2026; supported by the Investment Adviser Association's Active Managers Council) replicates SPIVA closely (they get 92.04% vs SPIVA's reported 92.66% for the 20-year average U.S. equity category) but argues three methodology choices bias it: counting all exiting funds as underperformers, equal-weighting funds regardless of AUM, and benchmarking against indices rather than investable passive funds. Adjusted, they report only 56% of ASSETS in active U.S. equity funds underperformed equivalent passive funds in 2024 (vs SPIVA's 79% of FUNDS vs the S&P Composite 1500) — a fund-count vs asset-share distinction the article must not blur. Local file: iaa_spiva.txt.

SPIVA's own MY2025 data cuts against a simple 'indexing is eating alpha' story in the smaller-cap segments: only 25.34% of All Mid-Cap and 22.33% of All Small-Cap funds underperformed YTD H1 2025, and the report notes the 2024 small-cap underperformance rate of 30% was 'the lowest annual underperformance rate across more than two decades' of SPIVA scorecards. Report 1a also shows Large-Cap Value at just 16.06% YTD and Small-Cap Value at 4.08%.

The Mid-Year and Year-End 2025 editions point in opposite directions within the same calendar year (54% at H1, 79% for the full year), which is itself evidence that these rates are driven by mega-cap concentration episodes rather than by a monotone passive-share effect.
reasoning: I verified (a), (b), (c) and (e) directly against the primary PDF, and confirmed the local copy's provenance by SHA-256 against S&P's own CloudFront-hosted file (identical, 931,922 bytes) — so no extraction-source risk. For Report 1a/1b/2/3/4 I read pdftotext -layout output where the column alignment was unambiguous. For Exhibit 1, whose reading-order text extraction scrambles the bars across vertical bands, I did NOT trust the flat text: I re-extracted word bounding boxes with pdftotext -bbox and matched each two-digit label's x-centre to the x-centre of the year-axis labels (every match within 1.1pt), producing the full 2001–2024 + H1 2025 series. That is how I confirmed exactly three sub-50 years and the three worst years, and computed the trend slope myself. The only defect found in (a)/(b)/(e) was nomenclature ('S&P 1500'); the defect in (c) is the '25-year annual series' label, which the Mid-Year edition does not support. The Year-End 2025 primary is genuinely unreachable — Akamai 403 on the spglobal path via direct curl with browser headers, via WebFetch, and via the r.jina.ai proxy; Wayback has no snapshot (404 on id_ replay) and the CDX API timed out; the CloudFront path pattern that works for Mid-Year 2025 404s for Year-End. I therefore refused to accept the WebFetch summary's quotes at face value and instead pulled the raw HTML of two independent outlets with curl and read the surrounding text myself. Both give 79% and both use 'fourth-worst ... 25-year history', but reading the raw InvestmentNews sentence shows the quotation marks close before 'fourth-worst', which is why I downgraded that phrase from SPIVA quote to media framing. Three internal consistency checks on 79% all pass (it slots fourth behind 87/85/82; 'worst since 2021' fits 2021=85; '16th consecutive year' fits 2009=48 being the last sub-50 year), which is strong circumstantial support but is not the primary document. What remains uncertain: the Year-End 2025 Report 1a table, whether S&P restated any 2001–2024 Exhibit 1 bars in that edition, and whether 'fourth-worst' appears in S&P's own prose.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Exhibit 1 10-year success rates: Large Blend 8.1, Large Growth 3.6, Large Value 20.3, Small Growth 37.0, Foreign Large Blend 22.8, Diversified EM 29.1, Intermediate Core Bond 41.7, Corporate Bond 52.2, High-Yield 39.1

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Methodology: success = survived AND beat the asset-weighted average of actual passive funds in the category, net of fees, magnitude ignored
itemVerdicts.note: Appendix, "Success Rate": "The success rate indicates what percentage of funds that started the sample period went on to survive and generate a return in excess of the asset-weighted average passive fund return over the period... We do not consider magnitude of outperformance in defining success: A fund that just barely beat the passive alternative counts as much as a fund that significantly outperformed." Net-of-fees is verbatim on page 1: the benchmark "reflects the actual, net-of-fees performance of investable passive funds." CAVEAT the article should know: the SAME report contradicts itself twice — the next paragraph says success counts funds ranking "higher than the equal weighted average return for the passive funds in the category," and Appendix C says "count the number of funds with returns exceeding the equal-weighted average of the passive funds in the category." This is longstanding boilerplate (identical contradiction in the H2-2025 edition, mstar_h22025.txt lines 2192 and 2266). Safe to say "asset-weighted" (that is the report's own Success Rate definition and headline language), but do not present the methodology as unambiguous.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Universe ~9,248 funds, ~$26T, ~67% of the US fund market
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim page 1: "spans nearly 9,248 unique funds that accounted for approximately USD 26 trillion in assets, or about 67% of the US fund market, at the end of 2025." ("nearly 9,248" is Morningstar's own odd phrasing; the figure is a count of unique funds, not share classes.) Note 67% is share of US FUND assets, not of US market cap.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Passive funds survive better: 80.4% vs 62.4% at 10 years in US Large Blend
itemVerdicts.note: Exhibit 5 (US Large Blend), 10-Year row: active # at beginning 383, active survivorship 62.4%; passive # at beginning 138, passive survivorship 80.4%; active success rate 8.1%. Numbers are exactly right.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Morningstar fixes SPIVA's costless-benchmark objection
itemVerdicts.note: Supported, though Morningstar never names SPIVA anywhere in the report (grep: zero hits for "SPIVA" or "S&P Dow Jones"). Appendix C: "We believe this is a better benchmark because it reflects the performance of actual investable options and not an index. One cannot directly invest in indexes. Their performance does not account for the real costs associated with replicating their performance and packaging and distributing them in an investable format." Attribute as Morningstar's stated rationale versus "the convention of using a single, representative index," not as an explicit rebuttal of SPIVA.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Harsher answer for US large cap: 8.1% vs SPIVA's ~14%
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as framed: it pairs Morningstar's NARROW US Large Blend category (8.1%) against SPIVA's BROAD All Large-Cap aggregate (~14%), which bundles growth, core and value. The matched comparison reverses the sign. SPIVA's Large-Cap CORE row is the analog of Morningstar Large Blend, and there SPIVA is far HARSHER: Mid-Year 2025 Report 1a shows Large-Cap Core Funds vs S&P 500, 10-year underperformance 96.57% (= 3.43% success) — verified from a freshly downloaded PDF, not just the local extract; SPIVA Year-End 2024 shows 96.62% (= 3.38% success), as reproduced in Cremers-Fulkerson-Riley (2026). RIGHT framing: compare aggregate to aggregate. Morningstar's three US large-cap categories, weighted by starting fund counts, give 10-year success of about 10.2% (383 funds x 8.1% + 350 x 20.3% + 417 x 3.6%, all from Exhibits 5/8/11 = 11,708.5/1,150 = 10.18%), against SPIVA All Large-Cap 10-year success of 14.02% (Mid-Year 2025) or 15.66% (Year-End 2024). So Morningstar IS somewhat harsher at the aggregate level, but the gap is roughly 4pp, not the ~6pp implied, and the 8.1%-vs-14% pairing is not like-for-like. Also note the two studies use different fund universes (Morningstar Categories vs Lipper/CRSP classifications) and different hurdles (Large Blend's passive composite includes total-market funds like VTSMX, not only S&P 500 trackers), so a direct head-to-head needs a hedge in any case.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) '...partly because passive funds survive better (80.4% vs 62.4%)' as the explanation for the harsher answer
itemVerdicts.note: The causal clause is unsupported and mechanically wrong. Morningstar makes no such attribution anywhere in the report. Differential survivorship cannot explain a Morningstar-vs-SPIVA gap because SPIVA applies the identical convention — SPIVA Appendix B glossary, verbatim: "To correct for survivorship bias, we use the opportunity set available at the beginning of the period as the denominator. We determine the count of funds that have survived and beat the index." Both studies already count dead active funds as failures. Separately, the operative fact for the LEVEL of 8.1% is that ACTIVE funds survive poorly (62.4%, so 37.6% are automatic failures), not that passive funds survive well; passive survivorship (80.4%) only affects the passive composite's return, and only marginally (dead passive funds' starting weights are subsumed pro rata by survivors). Either drop the causal clause or rewrite it as the active-attrition point.

itemVerdicts.item: SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Year-End 2025 exact 10-year All Large-Cap underperformance rate
itemVerdicts.note: Could not reach the primary document. spglobal.com is blocked at the Akamai edge from this environment (HTTP 403 on the PDF and on the SPIVA article page, via curl with browser headers, WebFetch, r.jina.ai, three CORS proxies, and the Chrome browser tool); there is no Wayback capture of spiva-us-year-end-2025.pdf; the S&P CloudFront mirror (which works for Mid-Year 2025) requires a per-file UUID I could not discover. Two web-SEARCH SUMMARIZERS returned conflicting/unverifiable 10-year figures ("fewer than one in six" and "89.93%") — per the fabrication warning I am treating both as unverified and NOT reporting either as fact. What I could verify from primary text: SPIVA Mid-Year 2025 (data as of June 30, 2025) All Large-Cap 10-year underperformance 85.98% (= 14.02% success), and SPIVA Year-End 2024 All Large-Cap 10-year 84.34% (= 15.66% success). If the article's "~14%" is meant to be the Year-End 2025 figure covering the same 2016-2025 window as Morningstar's 8.1%, it is currently sourced to the wrong vintage and must be re-checked against the Year-End 2025 PDF before publication.

corrections: Do not write "8.1% vs SPIVA's ~14%" as a like-for-like large-cap comparison. Morningstar's US Large Blend is the analog of SPIVA's Large-Cap Core, where SPIVA is far harsher: 10-year underperformance 96.57% (= 3.43% success) in SPIVA Mid-Year 2025, and 96.62% (= 3.38%) in SPIVA Year-End 2024. Compare aggregate to aggregate instead: Morningstar's three US large-cap categories, weighted by starting fund counts (383 Large Blend at 8.1%, 350 Large Value at 20.3%, 417 Large Growth at 3.6%), give about 10.2% 10-year success, versus SPIVA All Large-Cap 14.0% (Mid-Year 2025) / 15.7% (Year-End 2024).

Delete or rewrite the clause "partly because passive funds survive better (80.4% vs 62.4%)." Morningstar makes no such causal claim, and it cannot explain a gap versus SPIVA because SPIVA uses the same survivorship convention (SPIVA Appendix B: "we use the opportunity set available at the beginning of the period as the denominator. We determine the count of funds that have survived and beat the index"). If the point is worth keeping, state it as: the 8.1% is capped by active attrition — only 62.4% of the 383 US large-blend active funds that existed at the start of 2016 were still alive at the end of 2025, and every one of the other 37.6% counts as a failure by construction (passive funds in the same category survived at 80.4%).

Re-source the SPIVA comparison figure. The "~14%" matches SPIVA Mid-Year 2025 (data as of June 30, 2025), not a year-end-2025 window. If the article compares to Morningstar's "10 years through 2025," pull the corresponding row from SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Year-End 2025 (data as of Dec. 31, 2025) and state which SPIVA edition and which row (All Large-Cap vs Large-Cap Core) is being used.

When stating the Morningstar methodology, note that the hurdle is described inconsistently within the report itself: the "Success Rate" definition and the key takeaways say the ASSET-WEIGHTED average passive fund return, while the following paragraph and Appendix C both say the EQUAL-WEIGHTED average of the passive funds in the category (the same contradiction appears in the H2-2025 edition). Say "asset-weighted average passive composite, per Morningstar's stated definition" rather than asserting it as settled.

Say Morningstar rejects "the convention of using a single, representative index" and never names SPIVA — do not write that Morningstar is answering or rebutting SPIVA. The report contains zero mentions of SPIVA or S&P Dow Jones Indices.
Make the units explicit for the universe figures: ~9,248 unique funds, ~USD 26 trillion, and about 67% of the US FUND market (share of fund assets), not 67% of US market capitalization.
newContradictions: Cremers, Fulkerson & Riley, "How the SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Understates the Performance of Actively Managed Mutual Funds" (draft dated May 4, 2026; local file iaa_spiva.txt) argues in the opposite direction from the article's twist: it claims SPIVA's methodological choices "systematically understate the performance of active funds," and that after adjustment "only 56% of assets invested in active U.S. equity funds in 2024 underperformed equivalent passive funds," with the sign reversing for fixed income. Sponsorship must be disclosed if cited: "This research was supported by the Investment Adviser Association's Active Managers Council," and Cremers is an independent director at Ariel Investments. Note that this paper's central fix — benchmarking against equivalent passive FUNDS rather than an index — is exactly what Morningstar already does, so citing it alongside the Morningstar 8.1% needs care.

Morningstar's own report contains a partial counterweight the article should not omit: "Over the past 10 years, the average dollar invested in active funds outperformed the average active fund in 17 of the 20 categories examined," and "31% of active funds in the cheapest quintile of their respective categories beat their average passive peer, compared with 17% for the priciest funds" (Exhibit 1 shows US Large Blend lowest-cost quintile at 17.1% versus 8.1% overall). The 8.1% headline is an equal-weighted count across all funds regardless of size or fee; the asset-weighted return gap in US Large Blend over 10 years is 13.2% active vs 14.5% passive, i.e. 1.3pp/yr, not a wipeout.

The report's fixed-income results are volatile enough to undercut any single-year narrative: Corporate Bond had a 52.2% 10-year success rate but only 4.4% in 2025 (a 62.9pp year-over-year drop, the largest in Exhibit 2), and US Real Estate fell 51.0pp and Global Real Estate 57.9pp. If the article uses the 10-year bond numbers as evidence of anything structural, it should flag this instability.
reasoning:
Primary document reached in full: I verified the Morningstar PDF at the exact cited URL is byte-identical to the local extract (HTTP 200, content-length 3,192,094 = local mstar_h12026.pdf size; content-disposition filename US-Active-Passive-Barometer-H12026.pdf; PDF metadata CreationDate Feb 15 2026, 37 pages). I re-extracted pages 1-4 and the appendix independently with pdftotext -layout rather than relying on the pre-made .txt, so none of the numbers below rest on a possibly-garbled extraction. Local file mstar_apb_h12026.txt and mstar_h12026.txt are the same file (identical md5).

(a) and (b) check out verbatim, every figure, with no caliber slippage. The universe line in (c) is verbatim. The methodology description in (c) matches the report's "Success Rate" appendix section word for word — but I found that the SAME appendix contradicts itself two paragraphs later and again in Appendix C, both times saying the hurdle is the EQUAL-weighted passive average. I confirmed this is longstanding boilerplate, not an extraction artifact, by finding the identical contradiction in the prior H2-2025 edition. The article's "asset-weighted" claim is defensible but should not be stated as unambiguous.

(d) is where the group breaks. The survivorship numbers (80.4% passive vs 62.4% active, US Large Blend 10-year) are exactly right, from Exhibit 5. Morningstar's costless-benchmark rationale is verbatim in Appendix C, though the report never mentions SPIVA. But the two analytical moves in (d) both fail. First, the 8.1%-vs-~14% pairing is category-mismatched: I pulled SPIVA Mid-Year 2025 Report 1a from a freshly downloaded S&P CloudFront PDF (not just the local extract) and the Large-Cap Core row — the true analog of Morningstar's Large Blend — shows 96.57% 10-year underperformance, i.e. 3.43% success, which makes SPIVA much harsher than Morningstar, reversing the article's twist at the matched-category level. The same reversal holds in SPIVA Year-End 2024 (96.62% / 3.38%), which I read in the Cremers-Fulkerson-Riley reproduction. The claim survives only as an aggregate-to-aggregate comparison, where I computed Morningstar's fund-count-weighted large-cap success from Exhibits 5, 8 and 11 at about 10.2% against SPIVA's 14.0-15.7%. Second, the "partly because passive funds survive better" clause is unsupported by Morningstar and cannot explain a gap versus SPIVA, because SPIVA's Appendix B glossary — which I read verbatim — uses the identical opportunity-set denominator and the identical survived-and-beat numerator.

Remaining uncertainty: I could not reach SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Year-End 2025, the vintage that actually matches Morningstar's 10-years-through-2025 window. spglobal.com is blocked at the Akamai edge from this environment across every route I tried (curl with full browser headers on www and bare domain and a Spanish-locale path, WebFetch, r.jina.ai, three CORS proxies, and the Chrome browser tool, which returned the same Access Denied page); there is no Wayback capture; the CloudFront mirror needs a per-file UUID I could not discover, though I confirmed the mirror works by successfully downloading the Mid-Year 2025 file. Two web-search summarizers volunteered 10-year figures for Year-End 2025 that I could not corroborate against any document text, so per the fabrication warning I am discarding both rather than repeating them. This means the specific "~14%" is verified as a real SPIVA number for Mid-Year 2025 but is NOT verified for the year-end window the article implies, and that sub-item stays open.

itemVerdicts.item: Cremers, Fulkerson & Riley paper metadata: working paper dated May 4, 2026; supported by IAA Active Managers Council; Cremers disclosures (Ariel director, Touchstone advisor) on title page
itemVerdicts.note: Downloaded the PDF fresh (the claimed local iaa_spiva.txt did not exist — the scratchpad was empty). Title page reads 'This Draft: May 4, 2026'. Footnote verbatim: 'This research was supported by the Investment Adviser Association's Active Managers Council. Martijn Cremers serves as an independent director at Ariel Investments and as an independent academic advisor to Touchstone Investments.' Note the word 'independent' appears in BOTH roles — do not drop it. Still a working paper (SSRN 6710358 + IAA-hosted PDF, 40pp); no journal publication found as of Aug 2026.

itemVerdicts.item: Replication matches SPIVA: 92.04% vs reported 92.66% for 20-yr US equity
itemVerdicts.note: Exec summary p.3 verbatim: 'we find that 92.04% of active funds in the average U.S. equity category underperformed over the last 20 years. The Scorecard reports 92.66%.' I independently re-derived both: averaging the twelve cap-valuation categories' 20-yr column in Table 2 gives exactly 92.66 and in Table 3 exactly 92.04. QUALIFIER REQUIRED: these are equal-weighted averages ACROSS twelve style-box categories, not a single headline number. SPIVA's own 'All Domestic Funds' 20-yr line is 94.11% reported vs 94.05% replicated.

itemVerdicts.item: After three adjustments (credit dead funds' actual performance, asset-weight, benchmark = actual passive funds) the 20-yr US equity figure falls to 55.31% of assets underperforming
itemVerdicts.note: Table I Panel B, U.S. Equity Funds, 20-Year = 55.31. I re-derived it: average of the twelve cap-valuation categories in Table 7 Panel A 20-yr column = 55.31 exactly. QUALIFIER REQUIRED: it is an average of twelve category percentages (each asset-weighted internally, categories equal-weighted), not an aggregate. In the same Table 7 the broadest single row, 'All Domestic Funds' 20-yr, is still 77.56% of assets underperforming. The 55.31 average is also pulled down hard by two implausible outliers — Mid-Cap Growth 9.93% and Mid-Cap Value 13.98% — i.e. categories where one or two giant funds dominate the asset weight.

itemVerdicts.item: Fixed income reverses: 10-yr 71.34% → 37.09%
itemVerdicts.note: Table I Panel A Fixed Income 10-Year = 71.34; Panel B = 37.09. Exec summary states '71% ... drops to only 37%'. Note the table caption: 'Results are only displayed when full category coverage for both panels is available' — so this averages a subset of the 16 fixed-income categories (the raw 16-category average of Table 2's 10-yr column is 76.0, not 71.34).

itemVerdicts.item: Abstract quote: 'only 56% of assets invested in active U.S. equity funds in 2024 underperformed equivalent passive funds'
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the abstract, immediately after 'stating, for example, that 79% of active U.S. equity funds in 2024 underperformed the S&P Composite 1500.' CALIBER WARNING: this 56% is the ONE-YEAR (2024) figure for the 'All Domestic Funds' row (56.49% in Table 7 Panel A), NOT the 20-year 55.31%. The two numbers are nearly identical and are easy to conflate; they measure different horizons and different populations.

itemVerdicts.item: Ptak, Morningstar, June 8, 2026, 'Have We Been Too Hard on Active Funds?'
itemVerdicts.note: WebFetch returned 403; I curled the page directly and parsed the HTML. Byline 'Jeffrey Ptak, CFA', dateline 'Jun 8, 2026'. Verbatim conclusion: 'I just didn't find the argument persuasive.'

itemVerdicts.item: Nearly one-fifth of the 37pp FIXED-INCOME improvement stems from replication errors
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as framed: it is not the fixed-income asset class. RIGHT: Ptak writes 'nearly one-fifth of the 37-percentage-point improvement of active investment-grade intermediate bond funds stemmed from replication errors—that is, the authors not being able to exactly reproduce SPIVA's findings.' I traced every number in the paper: SPIVA reports 61.33% for Investment-Grade Intermediate at 10 years (Table 2); the authors' replication reaches only 54.34% (Table 3 — Ptak: 'couldn't get closer than a 54% failure rate'); fully adjusted it is 23.91% (Table 7 — Ptak: 'around 24%'). 61.33 − 23.91 = 37.4pp, and the 6.99pp replication gap is 18.7% of it — 'nearly one-fifth' checks out for THAT CATEGORY ONLY. The fixed-income aggregate improvement is 71.34 → 37.09 = 34.25pp, a different number.

itemVerdicts.item: Only two of three adjustments individually improved results; the benchmark adjustment and the interaction made results worse in that category
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'only two of those adjustments—crediting dead funds and asset-weighting—actually improved the results. The others—the benchmark adjustment and the interaction effect of applying all three adjustments together—made the results worse.' I verified against the paper's own tables for Investment-Grade Intermediate 10-yr: replication 54.34 → survivorship-only 40.46 (Table 4, better), asset-weight-only 28.21 (Table 5, better), benchmark-only 56.07 (Table 6, WORSE than 54.34), all three 23.91 (Table 7). Additive decomposition predicts 16.06 vs actual 23.91, so the interaction adds ~+7.9pp of underperformance. Ptak's claim is arithmetically sound. Keep the 'in that category' scoping — it is essential.

itemVerdicts.item: High-yield census: of 150 HY funds at Dec-2004, 78 died over 20 years
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'the 150 funds (largest share class of each fund) that were assigned to the high-yield bond Morningstar Category as of Dec. 31, 2004. Seventy-two of those funds survived the ensuing 20 years. Of the 78 funds that died, the average lifespan was 8.3 years.' CAVEAT: Morningstar's own chart source-notes on that page contradict the body text — they say 'as of Dec. 31, 2014' and 'All share classes of all funds' where the body says Dec. 31, 2004 and largest share class only. The body text and the 20-year framing (returns measured from Jan. 1, 2005) make clear 2004 is correct and the chart notes carry a typo; cite the body, not the chart note.

itemVerdicts.item: Dead outperformers lived 2,844 fund-months in aggregate vs 4,518 for laggards — dead funds skew losers
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'the dead funds that outperformed survived 2,844 months in aggregate, while those that lagged lived nearly twice as long: 4,518 months in total.' Also verbatim: 'Thirty-two of the 78 dead funds outperformed the index.' CAVEAT the article must not swallow: 4,518/2,844 = 1.59x, so Ptak's 'nearly twice as long' is a stretch even in aggregate, and the gap is driven mostly by COUNT (46 laggards vs 32 outperformers), not by duration — per-fund mean lifespans are 88.9 vs 98.2 months, a ~10% difference. Do not restate 'nearly twice as long' as a per-fund claim. Separately, Ptak's own figures do not fully reconcile: 78 funds × 8.3 years = 7,769 fund-months, but 2,844 + 4,518 = 7,362.

itemVerdicts.item: COI: IAA = active-management trade body
itemVerdicts.note: IAA hosts the PDF on its own site under /active-managers-council/, issued a GlobeNewswire release on 2026-05-05 headlined 'Active Management Performs Much Better Than SPIVA U.S. Scorecard States,' and ran an advocacy post 'Time to Rethink the SPIVA Scorecard's View of Active Management.' Financial Planning describes the Active Managers Council as having 'commissioned and released' the study.

itemVerdicts.item: COI: Ptak defends a convention his own Morningstar Barometer shares
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG if stated flatly across all three conventions. RIGHT: it holds for two of the three and explicitly fails for the third. Ptak writes verbatim: 'The one adjustment I concurred with was the authors' modification of the benchmark using the asset-weighted average net return of passive funds in lieu of a costless index. This is a practice my colleagues employ as part of the Active/Passive Barometer.' So on the benchmark question the Barometer already sides WITH Cremers et al. and Ptak concedes the point. He does defend dead-funds-are-failures ('failures in my book') and he notes 'My colleagues who publish the Active/Passive Barometer report don't asset-weight when tallying success rates.' Also: he DISCLOSES the Barometer in the article's second paragraph, so do not imply a hidden conflict.

itemVerdicts.item: Cremers' earlier pro-active paper (CFMS 2016) was runner-up for S&P DJI's own SPIVA award
itemVerdicts.note: The award is CONFIRMED from two primary sources: the JFE version's own acknowledgment footnote reads 'We also thank the sponsors of the S&P Dow Jones Indices' SPIVA award (runner up)', and S&P's press release of May 22, 2014 names Cremers, Ferreira, Matos and Starks as second prize ($15,000). Two corrections: (1) the award was granted in 2014 under the earlier working-paper title 'The Mutual Fund Industry Worldwide: Explicit and Closet Indexing, Fees, and Performance'; the JFE publication is 2016. (2) Calling it a 'pro-active paper' is WRONG. Its abstract concludes: 'Overall, our evidence suggests that explicit indexing improves competition in the mutual fund industry.' That is a pro-INDEXING finding — which is precisely why S&P DJI honored it. The irony the article wants (S&P once rewarded Cremers) survives; the adjective 'pro-active' does not.

corrections: Ptak's 'nearly one-fifth from replication errors' applies to the INVESTMENT-GRADE INTERMEDIATE BOND category, not to fixed income as a class. Correct statement: SPIVA reported 61.33% underperformance for investment-grade intermediate bond funds over 10 years; Cremers et al. fully adjusted reach 23.91%, a 37.4pp improvement — but their own replication only got to 54.34%, so ~7pp (about 19%) of the 'improvement' is unreproduced SPIVA data rather than any methodological adjustment. Do NOT attach the 37pp figure to the fixed-income headline (71.34% → 37.09% is a 34.25pp move, a different number).

Do not describe Cremers, Ferreira, Matos & Starks (2016) as a 'pro-active' paper. Its stated conclusion is 'explicit indexing improves competition in the mutual fund industry' — a pro-indexing finding, which is why S&P DJI awarded it. Also, the SPIVA award was second prize announced May 22, 2014, for the earlier working-paper title 'The Mutual Fund Industry Worldwide: Explicit and Closet Indexing, Fees, and Performance'; the Journal of Financial Economics publication is 2016. The acknowledgment survives in the published paper's footnote: 'We also thank the sponsors of the S&P Dow Jones Indices' SPIVA award (runner up).'

Do not say Ptak 'defends a convention his own Morningstar Barometer shares' without splitting the three adjustments. He defends the dead-funds-are-failures convention and the equal-weighted success-rate convention (both shared with the Barometer), but he EXPLICITLY CONCEDES the benchmark adjustment: 'The one adjustment I concurred with was the authors' modification of the benchmark using the asset-weighted average net return of passive funds in lieu of a costless index. This is a practice my colleagues employ as part of the Active/Passive Barometer.' He also discloses the Barometer in the article, so avoid implying a concealed conflict.

Qualify the 92.04%/92.66% and 55.31% figures: all three are equal-weighted averages ACROSS twelve cap-valuation (style-box) categories, not aggregate rates. The paper's broadest single row, 'All Domestic Funds' at 20 years, moves only from 94.11% (SPIVA reported) / 94.05% (replicated) to 77.56% after all three adjustments — a far less dramatic result than 92% → 55%. The 55.31 average is also driven by two implausible category outliers (Mid-Cap Growth 9.93%, Mid-Cap Value 13.98%).

Keep the abstract's '56%' distinct from the '55.31%'. The 56% is the ONE-YEAR 2024 figure for All Domestic Funds (56.49% in Table 7), paired in the abstract with SPIVA's 79% one-year figure. The 55.31% is the 20-year twelve-category average. Conflating them is the single easiest error to make with this paper.

When quoting Ptak's high-yield lifespan statistic, state it as an aggregate and do not repeat his phrase 'nearly twice as long' as if it were per-fund. 2,844 vs 4,518 fund-months is a 1.59x ratio, and the gap comes mostly from there being 46 laggards vs 32 outperformers; mean per-fund lifespans are ~89 vs ~98 months.

Cite Cremers' disclosure with the word 'independent' intact: 'independent director at Ariel Investments' and 'independent academic advisor to Touchstone Investments'; and the funding as 'supported by' / commissioned by the Investment Adviser Association's Active Managers Council. The paper remains an unpublished working paper (SSRN 6710358, draft May 4, 2026) as of August 2026 — label it as such, not as a peer-reviewed study.
reasoning:
The claimed local extracts did not exist — the scratchpad directory named in my instructions contained only two unrelated subdirectories and no .txt files, so I obtained every primary document myself rather than relying on any summary.

Primary documents reached verbatim: (1) the full 40-page Cremers/Fulkerson/Riley PDF from investmentadviser.org, extracted with pdftotext -layout, giving me the title page disclosures, abstract, executive summary, and Tables 1-10 as raw numbers; (2) the raw HTML of Ptak's Morningstar article (WebFetch returned 403; curl succeeded), from which I extracted the full body text and confirmed every quoted string character-by-character; (3) the JFE-forthcoming Cremers-Ferreira-Matos-Starks PDF hosted at Darden, whose acknowledgment footnote contains the SPIVA award line and whose abstract contains the pro-indexing conclusion; (4) S&P Global's May 22, 2014 press release naming the second-prize recipients.

Rather than trust the paper's stated summary figures, I re-derived them arithmetically from its own tables: averaging the twelve cap-valuation categories' 20-year column reproduced 92.66 (Table 2), 92.04 (Table 3) and 55.31 (Table 7) to the penny. That is what let me establish the population qualifier — these headline numbers are equal-weighted averages of twelve style-box categories, and the paper's own broadest row ('All Domestic Funds') only moves 94.05% → 77.56%. I also fully decomposed the investment-grade intermediate bond case (61.33 reported → 54.34 replicated → 40.46 / 28.21 / 56.07 per single adjustment → 23.91 combined), which both confirmed Ptak's arithmetic and exposed the group's one genuine caliber error: the 37pp figure is a single bond category, not the fixed-income class.

Two claims came back corrected on characterization rather than number: CFMS 2016 is a pro-indexing paper, not a pro-active one (its abstract says explicit indexing improves competition), and Ptak's conflict is real for two of three conventions but explicitly inverted on the third, since he concedes the benchmark adjustment because Morningstar's Barometer already makes it.

Remaining uncertainty: I could not open the SSRN landing page (403), so publication status rests on the PDF's own 'This Draft: May 4, 2026' plus the absence of any journal placement in searches through August 2026 — I am confident it is still a working paper but did not see an SSRN version history. S&P DJI's rebuttal quote I have only through Financial Planning's reporting, not from an S&P-issued document, so it should be attributed to that coverage. I did not attempt to audit SPIVA's underlying data, which neither Cremers et al. nor Ptak had access to either — a limitation both sides acknowledge and the article should too.

Martijn Cremers serves as an independent director at Ariel Investments and as an independent academic advisor to Touchstone Investments.' Note the paper says 'supported by', not 'funded by' — prefer the paper's own word. Still an unpublished working paper as of 2026-08; no revised version located.

itemVerdicts.item: Their replication matches SPIVA: 92.04% vs reported 92.66% for 20-yr US equity
itemVerdicts.note: Executive Summary p.2: 'following the Scorecard, we find that 92.04% of active funds in the average U.S. equity category underperformed over the last 20 years. The Scorecard reports 92.66%.' I re-derived both from the tables: 92.66 is the simple mean of the twelve cap-valuation cells in Table 2 Panel A 20-Year, and 92.04 the mean of the same twelve cells in Table 3. CAVEAT the article must not drop: these are averages ACROSS twelve style categories, not SPIVA's headline broad-market number. SPIVA's own 'All Domestic Funds' 20-year figure is 94.11% (Table 2), which CFR replicate at 94.05% (Table 3).

itemVerdicts.item: After three adjustments the 20-yr US equity figure falls to 55.31% OF ASSETS underperforming
itemVerdicts.note: Table I Panel B, U.S. Equity Funds, 20-Year = 55.31 (and Table 7 Panel A supplies the components). Panel B is post-adjustment and asset-weighted, so 'of assets' is right. CAVEAT the article must carry: 55.31 is the equal-weighted mean of twelve style categories' asset-weighted rates — I verified the arithmetic (76.17+78.29+41.73+9.93+91.68+13.98+44.56+72.00+44.34+82.21+69.22+39.60)/12 = 55.31. The single broadest category, 'All Domestic Funds', is 77.56% post-adjustment over 20 years (Table 7 Panel A). So the 'coin flip' headline depends on giving Mid-Cap Growth (9.93%) and Mid-Cap Value (13.98%) the same weight as Large-Cap Core. Presenting 55% as 'the' post-adjustment US equity number without that qualifier is caliber slippage.

itemVerdicts.item: Fixed income reverses: 10-yr 71.34% → 37.09%
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG if 71.34 is attributed to SPIVA. RIGHT: 71.34 is CFR's own REPLICATION (Table I Panel A is headed 'SPIVA Replication'; I re-derived 71.34 as the mean of the sixteen Table 3 Panel C 10-Year cells). SPIVA as actually reported (Table 2 Panel C) averages 76.00% over the same sixteen categories. 37.09 is confirmed as the mean of the sixteen Table 7 Panel C 10-Year cells. So the correct sentence is 'their replication of SPIVA, 71.34%, falls to 37.09%' — SPIVA itself printed ~76%, and the ~4.7pp replication gap is exactly what Ptak attacks.

itemVerdicts.item: Abstract: 'only 56% of assets invested in active U.S. equity funds in 2024 underperformed equivalent passive funds'
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the abstract, p.2. Worth knowing: the 56% traces to the Table 7 Panel A 'All Domestic Funds' 1-Year cell (56.49), whereas Table I Panel B's 1-Year US-equity figure is 57.87 (the twelve-category average). The paper therefore switches denominators between its abstract and its own summary table — quote the abstract as the abstract, not as Table I.

itemVerdicts.item: Ptak, Morningstar, June 8 2026, 'Have We Been Too Hard on Active Funds?'
itemVerdicts.note: Byline 'Jeffrey Ptak, CFA', dateline 'Jun 8, 2026' on morningstar.com/funds/have-we-been-too-hard-active-funds. WebFetch returns 403 on this URL; I retrieved it with curl and a browser UA and read the raw text.

itemVerdicts.item: Nearly one-fifth of the 37pp FIXED-INCOME improvement stems from replication errors
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: '37pp fixed-income improvement'. RIGHT: Ptak's sentence is about one category — 'nearly one-fifth of the 37-percentage-point improvement of active investment-grade intermediate bond funds stemmed from replication errors—that is, the authors not being able to exactly reproduce SPIVA's findings. (The authors couldn't get closer than a 54% failure rate...)'. The fixed-income CLASS improvement is 71.34→37.09 = 34.25pp (or 76.00→37.09 = 38.9pp measured off SPIVA-as-printed), not 37pp. The 37pp is investment-grade intermediate 10-yr: 61.33 (Table 2) → 23.91 (Table 7). I verified Ptak's fraction against the paper: the replication step is 61.33→54.34 = 6.99pp of 37.42pp = 18.7%, i.e. 'nearly one-fifth'. His arithmetic is sound; only the article's scope label is wrong.

itemVerdicts.item: Only two of three adjustments individually improved results; benchmark adjustment and the interaction made results worse in that category
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'And only two of those adjustments—crediting dead funds and asset-weighting—actually improved the results. The others—the benchmark adjustment and the interaction effect of applying all three adjustments together—made the results worse.' Independently verified against the paper for IG-intermediate 10-yr: replication base 54.34 (T3); survivorship-only 40.46 (T4); assets-only 28.21 (T5); benchmark-only 56.07 (T6, i.e. WORSE by 1.73pp); all three together 23.91 (T7), versus ~16.1 if the three were additive — so the interaction is worse by ~7.9pp. Keep 'in that category' (investment-grade intermediate); the decomposition is not claimed for fixed income generally.

itemVerdicts.item: High-yield census: 150 HY funds at Dec-2004, 78 died over 20 years
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'focusing on the 150 funds (largest share class of each fund) that were assigned to the high-yield bond Morningstar Category as of Dec. 31, 2004. Seventy-two of those funds survived the ensuing 20 years. Of the 78 funds that died, the average lifespan was 8.3 years, or less than half the 20-year horizon.' Caveat for accuracy, not a correction to the article: two of Ptak's own exhibit source lines say the cohort is 'as of Dec. 31, 2014' — an internal inconsistency in Morningstar's chart notes. The prose (2004) is the version consistent with a 20-year window to Dec 2024; cite the prose.

itemVerdicts.item: Dead outperformers lived 2,844 fund-months in aggregate vs 4,518 for laggards — dead funds skew losers
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'Thirty-two of the 78 dead funds outperformed the index... All told, the dead funds that outperformed survived 2,844 months in aggregate, while those that lagged lived nearly twice as long: 4,518 months in total.' Caliber caveat: these are AGGREGATE fund-months over unequal counts (32 outperformers vs 46 laggards). Per fund it is 88.9 vs 98.2 months — a ~10% gap, not 2x. Do not restate 'nearly twice as long' as a per-fund lifespan claim; the aggregate ratio is partly just headcount.

itemVerdicts.item: COI: IAA = active-management trade body
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 'IAA = active-management trade body'. RIGHT: the IAA is the trade association for SEC-registered investment advisers generally; the funder is its Active Managers Council, whose own page states verbatim: 'The Active Managers Council is the premier industry voice for active investment management. Its mission is to advocate for a more balanced narrative on active and passive management and to provide education about the benefits of active management...' Attribute the interest to the Council, which is if anything a sharper COI than the parent body.

itemVerdicts.item: COI: Ptak defends a convention his own Morningstar Barometer shares
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG if stated as a bare or undisclosed conflict. RIGHT, with two qualifiers. (i) The shared convention is only the survivorship one — the Barometer's success rate counts funds that 'survived and beat the average passive fund in their Morningstar Category', confirmed in the Morningstar US Active/Passive Barometer PDF, which is precisely the convention Ptak defends hardest ('Dead Funds Are Failures, Period'). (ii) The Barometer does NOT share the other two conventions: it already benchmarks against actual investable passive-fund composites and reports asset-weighted alongside equal-weighted results (its tables carry 'Asset-Weighted' and 'Equal-Weighted' columns). So Morningstar already implements two of CFR's three adjustments — which is why Ptak ranks the benchmark critique as most persuasive and cost-free to concede. (iii) Ptak discloses in the piece: 'We have our own version of SPIVA called the Morningstar Active/Passive Barometer. It's an excellent report. But since the authors focused on SPIVA, that explains why I address that study and not our own barometer report here.'

itemVerdicts.item: COI: Cremers' earlier pro-active paper (CFMS 2016) was runner-up for S&P DJI's own SPIVA award
itemVerdicts.note: The award is CONFIRMED from the primary document — the CFMS working paper's own acknowledgment footnote reads 'We also thank the sponsors of the S&P Dow Jones Indices' SPIVA award (runner up)', and the PR Newswire release for the third annual SPIVA Awards names Cremers, Ferreira, Matos and Starks as second-prize winners ($15,000) for 'The Mutual Fund Industry Worldwide: Explicitly and Closet Indexing, Fee, and Performance'. But 'pro-active paper' is WRONG. RIGHT: the paper's own abstract concludes 'Overall, our evidence suggests that explicit indexing improves competition in the mutual fund industry' — active funds 'are more active and charge lower fees when they face more competitive pressure from low-cost explicitly indexed funds'. That is a pro-INDEXING finding, which is why an index provider honored it. Also the award was announced in 2014 under the earlier working-paper title, two years before the JFE 2016 publication as 'Indexing and Active Fund Management: International Evidence'.

corrections: Do not call 71.34% 'SPIVA's fixed-income figure'. It is Cremers-Fulkerson-Riley's own REPLICATION of SPIVA (their Table I Panel A is headed 'SPIVA Replication'). SPIVA as printed averages 76.00% across the same sixteen fixed-income categories over 10 years. Write: 'their replication of SPIVA's 10-year fixed-income rate, 71.34%, falls to 37.09% after the three adjustments — while SPIVA itself printed about 76%.'

Replace 'nearly one-fifth of the 37pp fixed-income improvement' with the category-specific version. Ptak's sentence reads: 'nearly one-fifth of the 37-percentage-point improvement of active investment-grade intermediate bond funds stemmed from replication errors.' The 37pp is investment-grade intermediate bonds only (61.33% per SPIVA to 23.91% post-adjustment). The fixed-income class improvement is 34.25pp (71.34 to 37.09), not 37pp.

Qualify the 55.31% figure. It is the equal-weighted average of twelve style categories' asset-weighted underperformance rates, not a single asset-weighted number for US equity. The paper's own broadest US-equity row, 'All Domestic Funds', is 77.56% post-adjustment over 20 years (Table 7 Panel A). Add: 'the coin-flip headline comes from averaging twelve style boxes equally, so Mid-Cap Growth at 9.93% counts as much as Large-Cap Core; the paper's own all-domestic-equity row still shows 77.56% of assets lagging over 20 years.'

Qualify the 92.04% vs 92.66% replication match the same way — both are means across the twelve cap-valuation categories, described by the paper as 'the average U.S. equity category'. SPIVA's headline 'All Domestic Funds' 20-year figure is 94.11%, replicated at 94.05%.

Change 'funded by the Investment Adviser Association's Active Managers Council' to the paper's own wording, 'supported by', and change 'IAA = active-management trade body' to 'the IAA's Active Managers Council, whose stated mission is to advocate for a more balanced narrative on active and passive management'. The IAA itself is the trade association for SEC-registered investment advisers generally; the Council is the active-management advocacy arm.

Fix the CFMS 2016 characterization. It is not a 'pro-active paper'. Its abstract concludes that 'explicit indexing improves competition in the mutual fund industry' — a pro-indexing finding, which is why an index provider awarded it. The SPIVA award itself is confirmed (runner-up, third annual SPIVA Awards, announced 2014, under the earlier title 'The Mutual Fund Industry Worldwide: Explicitly and Closet Indexing, Fee, and Performance'; acknowledged in the paper's own footnote). Say 'Cremers has been on the other side of this too: an earlier paper of his finding that indexing improves competition took S&P DJI's own SPIVA award runner-up prize in 2014.'

Narrow the Ptak conflict claim. The convention his Barometer shares is only the survivorship one (its success rate counts funds that 'survived and beat the average passive fund'). The Barometer already uses actual passive-fund composites as the benchmark and already publishes asset-weighted results — i.e. Morningstar already does two of CFR's three adjustments, which is why Ptak concedes the benchmark point and fights only on dead funds. Also note he discloses the Barometer in the piece rather than hiding it.

Do not restate '2,844 vs 4,518 fund-months' as dead outperformers living half as long per fund. Those are aggregates over 32 outperformers and 46 laggards; per fund it is 88.9 vs 98.2 months. Ptak's 'nearly twice as long' is an aggregate figure driven partly by headcount.

Add S&P DJI's on-record reply, which the group omits. Quoted in WealthManagement.com's coverage: 'It is important to note that SPIVA measures the proportion of funds that underperform, rather than the proportion of assets... The fundamental claim of active management is the ability to "beat the market"—not to outperform a basket of index funds.' That is the crux — CFR change the question from funds to assets and from index to index-fund, and say so openly ('Collectively, these changes reframe the question').
Label the CFR paper as an unpublished, non-peer-reviewed working paper. No revised version or journal publication was found as of August 2026.
newContradictions: The paper's own Table 7 Panel A reports 'All Domestic Funds' at 77.56% underperforming over 20 years post-adjustment — against the 55.31% twelve-category average the paper headlines. Any article using 55% as 'the' answer is using the more favorable of two numbers the paper itself prints.

The abstract's '56% ... in 2024' does not match Table I Panel B's 1-year US equity figure of 57.87%. The 56% is the 'All Domestic Funds' cell (56.49); Table I averages twelve categories. The paper mixes denominators between abstract and summary table.

SPIVA-as-reported for fixed income over 10 years averages 76.00% (Table 2 Panel C), but CFR's replication is 71.34% (Table 3 Panel C) — a 4.66pp gap before any adjustment. Ptak's 'replication errors' critique therefore applies to the fixed-income headline as a whole, not just to investment-grade intermediate.

S&P DJI's substantive defense is a scope argument, not a methodology concession: SPIVA deliberately measures the proportion of FUNDS against a market benchmark, because the claim being tested is 'beat the market', not 'beat a basket of index funds'. CFR concede the reframing in their own Executive Summary. The two sides are measuring different things, so 'SPIVA understates' is contestable as a category error rather than an error of execution.
Ptak's own exhibit source notes date the high-yield cohort 'as of Dec. 31, 2014' while his prose says Dec. 31, 2004. Cite the prose; flag if quoting the exhibit.
reasoning:
The scratchpad extracts named in my brief (iaa_spiva.txt and ~200 others) do not exist in this session's scratchpad — that directory contains only an unrelated venv — so I fetched every primary document myself rather than relying on any prior extraction.

Documents reached verbatim: (1) the Cremers-Fulkerson-Riley PDF from investmentadviser.org, downloaded by curl and converted with pdftotext -layout to 1,424 lines, and read directly (title page, abstract, executive summary, Table I, and Tables 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 in full). (2) The Ptak Morningstar article — WebFetch returns HTTP 403, so I pulled it with curl under a browser UA and stripped the HTML to text, reading the full body rather than any summary. (3) The CFMS working paper PDF (dynamic.ca reprint) for the abstract and the SPIVA-award acknowledgment footnote. (4) The PR Newswire third-annual-SPIVA-Awards release. (5) The Morningstar US Active/Passive Barometer PDF for the survivorship and weighting conventions. (6) The IAA Active Managers Council page for its self-description. (7) WealthManagement.com's coverage for S&P DJI's quoted reply.

I did not accept any figure on the strength of a fetch summary. Every number in the group was re-derived from the paper's own tables where derivation was possible: 92.66 and 92.04 as means of the twelve cap-valuation cells in Tables 2 and 3; 55.31 as the mean of the twelve Table 7 Panel A 20-year cells; 71.34 and 37.09 as means of the sixteen Table 3 and Table 7 Panel C 10-year cells. I also independently checked Ptak's arithmetic against the paper and it holds: investment-grade intermediate 10-year runs 61.33 (SPIVA) to 54.34 (replication) to 40.46 (survivorship only) to 28.21 (assets only) to 56.07 (benchmark only, worse) to 23.91 (all three), so the replication step is 6.99 of 37.42 percentage points, 18.7 percent — 'nearly one-fifth' — and the benchmark adjustment plus the interaction do move against the authors.

Two substantive failures found. First, the group attaches Ptak's 37-percentage-point figure to fixed income as a class; his sentence attaches it to investment-grade intermediate bond funds specifically, and the class-level improvement is 34.25 points. Second, CFMS 2016 is described as a 'pro-active paper' when its abstract concludes that explicit indexing improves competition — a pro-indexing result, which is the natural reason an index provider awarded it; the award itself is confirmed from the paper's own footnote. Three lesser slippages: 71.34 is a replication rather than SPIVA's printed 76.00; the IAA is a general adviser trade body whose Active Managers Council is the active-management advocacy arm; and the Ptak-conflict claim is true only of the survivorship convention, since the Barometer already benchmarks against real passive funds and already publishes asset-weighted results.

The largest unflagged risk is not in the group as written but in how the 55.31% will read: it is an equal-weighted average of twelve style categories, and the paper's own broadest US-equity row is 77.56%. An article that quotes 55% as the asset-weighted answer for US equity is quoting the friendlier of two numbers the same table prints.

Remaining uncertainty: I could not open the SSRN landing page (403) to check posting and revision dates, so 'no revised version since May 4, 2026' rests on search coverage plus the absence of any later draft in trade or academic sources, not on SSRN's own version history. S&P DJI's reply is verified as a direct quotation inside reported trade coverage, not from an S&P-issued document.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) YE2024 Report 2: of Dec-2020 top-quartile domestic funds, 5.27% remained top-quartile after one year, 0.00% by years 2-4
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the primary PDF (SPIVA U.S. Persistence Scorecard Year-End 2024, Report 2, p.5, 'Performance Persistence of Domestic Equity Funds over Five Consecutive 12-Month Periods'). Row 'All Domestic Funds', Fund Count at Start (December 2020) = 512; Dec 2021 = 5.27; Dec 2022 = 0.00; Dec 2023 = 0.00; Dec 2024 = 0.00. Summary p.1 states verbatim: 'Among top-quartile funds within all reported active domestic equity categories as of December 2020, not a single fund remained in the top quartile over the next four years (see Report 2).' Note for completeness: All Small-Cap Funds was NOT zero in year 2 (2.36 in Dec 2021, 0.79 in Dec 2022, then 0.00) — the 'zero throughout years 2-4' pattern is exact for All Domestic, but a blanket 'every category was zero from year 2 on' would be wrong. Percentages are count-based (equal-weighted fund counts), not asset-weighted.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-cont.) Arithmetic: pure chance predicts 0.25^4 = 0.39% (~2 of 512 funds), so 'zero' is 0.39pp below random, not orders of magnitude
itemVerdicts.note: Arithmetic checks out exactly: 0.25^4 = 0.00390625 = 0.3906%; 512 x 0.00390625 = 2.00 funds exactly; gap from observed 0.00% is 0.39pp. I independently strengthened this: under pure chance with n=512, P(zero survivors) = (1-0.00390625)^512 = 0.135, i.e. observing zero is a ~13.5% outcome — entirely unremarkable, not significant at even the 10% level. IMPORTANT: SPIVA itself never states a 0.39% expectation anywhere in the document; the only random benchmarks printed are 6.25% (footnote 1, for the top-HALF five-year test) and 6.25%/25% in the Report 1 highlights. So 0.39% must be presented as the article's own derivation, not attributed to S&P.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-cont.) Honest test is top-half persistence: 4.21% (all domestic) and 2.42% (large-cap) stayed top-half five consecutive years vs 6.25% random
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim, YE2024 Report 2, Top Half panel: All Domestic Funds, Fund Count at Start (Dec 2020) = 1021, Dec 2024 = 4.21; All Large-Cap Funds, count 330, Dec 2024 = 2.42. The 6.25% random benchmark is S&P's own, footnote 1 p.1 verbatim: 'The odds of a top-half fund in one year randomly staying in the top half over the next four years are 50%*50%*50%*50% = 6.25%, or 1/16.' Exhibit 1 shows the same figures rounded (All Domestic 4.2, All Large-Cap 2.4) under the headline 'Only 2% of All Large-Cap Equity Funds Remained in the Top Half Over a Five-Year Period.' In fund counts: All Domestic expected 63.8, observed ~43; large-cap expected 20.6, observed ~8 — below random but the same order of magnitude, which is exactly the article's point.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Mortality asymmetry: 25% of fourth-quartile funds (2014-19 performance) merged/liquidated within five years vs 7% of top-quartile
itemVerdicts.note: Verified twice. Report Highlights p.2 verbatim: 'For example, 25% of all fourth-quartile domestic U.S. equity funds (based on 2014-2019 performance) were either merged or liquidated within the subsequent five years; the comparable figure for top-quartile funds was only 7%. There were similar results among both active equity and active fixed income funds (see Reports 5 and 11).' Underlying table Report 5 (p.8), All Domestic Funds, ranking window December 2014-December 2019, outcome window December 2019-December 2024: 4th Quartile Merged/Liquidated = 24.89 (n=470); 1st Quartile = 6.81 (n=470). The 25%/7% rounding is S&P's own. CITATION CALIBER: the specific 25%/7% numbers come from Report 5 ONLY (domestic equity). Report 11 is the fixed-income analogue and contains no such figures — it shows the same directional asymmetry (e.g. Investment-Grade Intermediate 4th quartile 30.00% merged/liquidated vs 1st quartile 10.00%; Global Income 45.00% vs 15.00%). Cite 'Report 5' for the numbers, 'Reports 5 and 11' only for the general pattern.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) YE2025: 0.46% of 2021 top-quartile domestic equity funds remained top-quartile through Dec 2025
itemVerdicts.note: Could NOT reach the primary. spglobal.com returns HTTP 403 to every automated request — the YE2024 PDF at the same host also 403s, confirming a blanket bot block rather than a missing document; Wayback holds only a capture of the 403 error page itself; requisitecm.com has no YE2025 mirror; browser tooling was unavailable this session. The 0.46% figure appears verbatim in exactly ONE reachable secondary source, VettaFi/ETFTrends (8 May 2026): 'The S&P Persistence Scorecard highlights that of the domestic equity funds in the top quartile in 2021, only 0.46% managed to stay there through December 2025.' That sentence sits inside an auto-generated-looking FAQ block whose neighbouring sentence ('This statistic is particularly striking because it encompasses the entire U.S. fund universe, regardless of vehicle wrapper') reads as machine paraphrase, so I do not treat it as a reliable transcription of a table cell. A second, independent secondary source that demonstrably read the YE2025 tables (genuineimpact.substack.com, 'What Persists Is Failure') does NOT contain the string '0.46' anywhere, and reports the cohort differently: 'Of the 164 large-cap funds that started in the top quartile, 20.1% held it through 2022. Through 2023, the figure was zero, and it stayed at zero through 2024 and 2025. Across every reported active domestic equity category except small-cap, not one top-quartile fund from 2021 was still top-quartile at the end of 2025' and 'Of the 124 small-cap funds in the top quartile at the end of 2021, 2.4% were still there at the end of 2025.' A nonzero All-Domestic figure is reconcilable with that only if 'All Domestic Funds' is read as a separately-ranked aggregate row rather than a 'category' — plausible, but I did not confirm it. Per the task's own instruction, do not print 0.46% as unverified.

corrections: Attribute the 0.39% random-chance benchmark to the article's own arithmetic, NOT to S&P. WRONG: implying SPIVA reports a 0.39% expected persistence rate. RIGHT: SPIVA prints only 6.25% (footnote 1, for the top-half four-subsequent-year test) and 6.25%/25% in the Report 1 highlights; 0.25^4 = 0.3906% is a derivation the article performs itself.

Do not extend the 'zero is only 0.39pp below random' critique to SPIVA's headline persistence findings generally. The critique is valid ONLY for Report 2's four-subsequent-year top-quartile test. SPIVA's own Report Highlights bullet uses Report 1's TWO-year test, where the benchmark is 0.25^2 = 6.25%: 'None of the top-quartile large-cap funds from 2022 maintained their position in the top quartile for the subsequent two years, compared to an expected 6.25% based on random chance.' There n=176, expected 11 funds, observed 0, and P(zero | pure chance) = 1.2e-5. That zero IS far below chance. Conflating the two tests would make the article's critique wrong.

Cite Report 5, not 'Reports 5/11', for the 25%/7% mortality figures. WRONG: '25% vs 7% (Reports 5/11)'. RIGHT: the 25%/7% domestic-equity figures are Report 5 alone (exact values 24.89% and 6.81%, n=470 per quartile); Report 11 is the fixed-income analogue showing the same direction (e.g. Investment-Grade Intermediate 30.00% vs 10.00%) with different numbers.

Date the mortality statistic to the YE2024 vintage and state both windows. WRONG: an undated '25% of fourth-quartile funds merged or liquidated within five years'. RIGHT: 'ranked on December 2014-December 2019 performance, then observed over December 2019-December 2024 (SPIVA U.S. Persistence Scorecard, Year-End 2024, Report 5)'. The figure is vintage-specific: a secondary source reading the YE2025 edition reports 23.1% vs 9.8% for the corresponding 2015-2020 to 2020-2025 windows.

When citing the mortality asymmetry as validating SPIVA's dead=underperformer convention, note that merged/liquidated is not the only exit. Report 5 has a separate 'Style Changed' column that is large and NOT skewed toward losers (All Domestic: 25.11% for 1st quartile vs 28.72% for 4th). Total attrition therefore far exceeds the merged/liquidated column, and the convention still misclassifies the 6.81% of top-quartile funds that died — 'partially validates' is the right caliber; 'validates' would be too strong.

Do NOT print the YE2025 '0.46%' figure. It is unverified against the primary document, appears in only one reachable secondary source (VettaFi/ETFTrends) inside an apparently machine-generated FAQ block, and is absent from a second independent secondary source that demonstrably read the YE2025 tables. If a YE2025 datapoint is wanted, either obtain the primary PDF by hand or attribute explicitly, e.g. 'VettaFi, reporting on the Year-End 2025 scorecard, puts the figure at 0.46%' — never 'S&P reports 0.46%'.

If the article states that no top-quartile 2020 fund survived in ANY category, qualify it. WRONG: 'every category hit zero from year two onward'. RIGHT: All Small-Cap Funds was 2.36% in Dec 2021 and still 0.79% in Dec 2022 before reaching 0.00%; only the four-year endpoint is zero across all reported categories.

Specify that Report 2 percentages are counts of funds (equal-weighted), not asset-weighted, and that the denominators are the Dec-2020 top-quartile/top-half cohorts (512 and 1021 for All Domestic; 162 and 330 for Large-Cap) — not the full fund universe.
newContradictions: VettaFi/ETFTrends (8 May 2026) states 0.46% of 2021 top-quartile domestic equity funds stayed top-quartile through Dec 2025, while genuineimpact.substack.com, reading the same YE2025 report, writes 'Across every reported active domestic equity category except small-cap, not one top-quartile fund from 2021 was still top-quartile at the end of 2025' and never uses the figure 0.46. The two are reconcilable only if 'All Domestic Funds' is treated as a separately-ranked aggregate row rather than a category, which I could not confirm against the primary.

The mortality asymmetry is not stable across scorecard vintages. YE2024 Report 5 (verified primary): 24.89% of 4th-quartile vs 6.81% of 1st-quartile domestic equity funds merged/liquidated. A secondary source reading YE2025 Report 5 reports 23.1% of 459 vs 9.8% of 458 — the ratio compresses from ~3.7x to ~2.4x. Any 'more than three times as likely' phrasing is YE2024-specific.

SPIVA's YE2024 Report 5 shows large-cap 1st-quartile persistence that cuts against a blanket no-persistence reading: 54.76% of top-quartile large-cap funds (Dec 2014-Dec 2019) were still 1st quartile in Dec 2019-Dec 2024, versus 25% under chance, and only 0.60% fell to 4th quartile. Over non-overlapping five-year blocks rather than consecutive single years, large-cap persistence looks strong. The article should not cite Report 2's consecutive-year zeros without acknowledging Report 5's very different picture for the same asset class.

A May 2026 working paper directly attacking the SPIVA methodology is in circulation and was already downloaded into this run's scratchpad: Cremers (Notre Dame), Fulkerson (Dayton) and Riley (Arkansas), 'How the SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Understates the Performance of Actively Managed Mutual Funds', draft 4 May 2026, 40pp. It targets the SPIVA Scorecard rather than the Persistence Scorecard, but any article leaning on SPIVA conventions (including the dead=underperformer convention that item (b) partially validates) should engage it or at least note it is contested and unpublished.
