I extended the check: P(zero | pure chance) = 0.135, so the Report 2 zero is not merely unimpressive, it is the modal-ish outcome under randomness. That materially strengthens the article's point.

The single biggest risk I found is a conflation hazard rather than a factual error. SPIVA's own marquee persistence claim is not the Report 2 four-year zero; it is the Report 1 two-year zero (large-cap, n=176, 0.00% vs 6.25% expected), where P(zero | chance) = 1.2e-5. The article's debunk is correct for Report 2 and would be flatly wrong if applied to Report 1. I flagged this as a required correction because the sub-claim as written ("not orders of magnitude") invites exactly that overreach.

(b) Confirmed at two levels — the Report Highlights sentence verbatim and the underlying Report 5 cells (24.89 vs 6.81, n=470 each, ranking Dec 2014-Dec 2019, outcome Dec 2019-Dec 2024). Two caliber issues: the numbers are Report 5 only (Report 11 is fixed income, different numbers, same direction), and Report 5's separate Style Changed column (25.11% Q1 / 28.72% Q4) means merged/liquidated understates total attrition and is not the whole exit story.

(c) UNREACHABLE at the primary level, and I am declining to bless it. spglobal.com blanket-403s (verified with the YE2024 file as a control, so this is a bot block, not a missing document); Wayback archived only the 403 page; no mirror exists; browser tooling was down. The 0.46% string exists in exactly one document I could actually read — a VettaFi/ETFTrends FAQ block with machine-generated characteristics — and is absent from an independent secondary that clearly worked from the YE2025 tables and reports adjacent figures (164 large-cap funds, 20.1% through 2022 then zero; 124 small-cap funds, 2.4% surviving to end-2025). Per the fabrication warnings in my brief, I treated the repeated appearance of 0.46% in search-summarizer prose as worthless corroboration; the summarizers also demonstrably misattributed YE2023 language ("top-quartile large-cap funds from 2021... subsequent two years") to the YE2025 report in two separate searches, which is precisely the failure mode I was warned about.

REMAINING UNCERTAINTY: whether SPIVA's YE2025 Report 2 "All Domestic Funds" row is 0.46 is genuinely open. It is arithmetically plausible (3 survivors on a cohort of ~650) and consistent with small-cap being the sole source of survivors, but plausibility is not verification. Someone with browser access should pull https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/documents/spiva/persistence-scorecard-year-end-2025.pdf by hand and read the Report 2 Top Quartile panel, December 2025 column.

Separately, I noticed a 40-page May 2026 Cremers/Fulkerson/Riley draft attacking SPIVA methodology sitting in the scratchpad; it targets the SPIVA Scorecard rather than the Persistence Scorecard, but it bears on the dead=underperformer convention that item (b) is used to defend, so I logged it as a contradiction to address rather than leaving it for another verifier to find.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) PST (JFE 2015): +1pp active-industry share of market cap -> gross fund performance falls ~40bp/yr; extended sample ~20bp
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in NBER w19891 PDF: 'consider a one percentage point increase in IndustrySize... In our main sample, this increase in IndustrySize is associated with a sizable decrease in fund performance: 0.0326% per month, or almost 40 bp per year. In the extended sample, the magnitude of the same effect is smaller but still substantial, about 20 bp per year.' Table 3: -0.0326 (t=-3.60) Panel A Main Sample March 1993-December 2011; -0.0164 (t=-4.34) Panel B Extended Sample January 1979-December 2011. Table 3 header defines IndustrySize as 'the total AUM of all active equity mutual funds divided by the total market cap of all stocks in CRSP' and GrossR as 'the fund's benchmark-adjusted gross return'. Flags: these are the OLS-fund-fixed-effects estimates; the no-FE OLS gives -0.0169 (t=-1.93) main and -0.00671 (t=-1.92) extended, i.e. ~20bp and ~8bp, only marginally significant. Sample ENDS Dec 2011, so the post-2010 inference is the article's, not PST's. IndustrySize 'starts at 2.4% in January 1979, peaks at 18.6% in July 2008, and finishes at 16.8% in December 2011.' Robustness: Adams-Hayunga-Mansi called the scale relation an outlier artifact; Pastor-Stambaugh-Taylor-Zhu, 'Diseconomies of Scale in Active Management: Robust Evidence' (CFR 11(3-4) 2022), reply verbatim: 'When we apply robust regression methods, we confirm both studies' inferences about scale diseconomies at the fund and industry levels.' So (a) survives.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-attribution) PST framed as 'the G-S prediction'
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: presenting PST's industry-size result as a Grossman-Stiglitz informational-equilibrium test. RIGHT: PST cite Berk and Green (2004) and frame the finding as returns to scale / capacity; grep of the full paper finds no mention of Grossman or Stiglitz anywhere. The direction coincides with G-S but the mechanism and citation do not.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) CFMS (JFE 2016): average alpha higher where explicit indexing is bigger, but interaction shows marginal return to being active is lower there
itemVerdicts.note: Both halves verbatim in the published-version PDF. Abstract: 'the average alpha generated by active management is higher in countries with more explicit indexing and lower in countries with more closet indexing.' Body: 'the coefficient on the interaction between active share and the market share of explicitly indexed funds is negative and significant (in Panel B)... We thus conclude that the marginal returns to active management are lower in markets with more prevalent and cheaper explicitly indexed funds.' Table 7 Panel B (by country of sale): Explicit indexing (%TNA) +0.1196 (t=4.16); Active share x Explicit indexing -0.1753 (t=-4.21). CRITICAL QUALIFIER: in Panel A (by country of domicile) BOTH are insignificant - main effect 0.0106 (t=0.43), interaction -0.0351 (t=-0.95). Dependent variable is a four-factor alpha built from fund NET returns, so this is an after-fee/competition result, not gross alpha. Sample 2002-2010.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Fama-French 2010: aggregate gross VW three-factor alpha +0.13%/yr (t=0.40) on 1984-2006; 'alpha = minus fees'
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the JF Vol LXV No. 5 October 2010 PDF: 'The intercepts in (1) for VW gross returns are quite close to zero, 0.13% per year (t = 0.40) for the three-factor version of (1), and -0.05% per year (t = -0.15) for the four-factor model.' Table II VW gross three-factor row: 0.13, t 0.40. Net VW three-factor is -0.81% (t=-2.50); FF: 'The three-factor and four-factor (annualized) intercepts for EW and VW net returns are negative, ranging from -0.81% to -1.00% per year, with t-statistics from -2.05 to -3.02.' Precise window is January 1984 through September 2006 (state it as 1984-2006 only if the 'through September' is acceptable).

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Harvey & Liu (JF 2022): FF bootstrap 'has little or no power to detect the truly outperforming funds'
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG (as an unqualified claim about FF's results): quoting it as a blanket verdict on Fama-French 2010. RIGHT: the sentence is 'Given these results, it is perhaps unsurprising that the FF technique has little or no power to detect the truly outperforming funds in our simulation.' (JF Vol LXXVII No. 3, June 2022). Two scope corrections: (i) the words 'in our simulation' belong in the quote; (ii) the critique targets the CROSS-SECTIONAL BOOTSTRAP used to identify individual outperforming funds via an undersampling problem concentrated in short-lived funds - it says nothing about, and does not disturb, the aggregate VW time-series alpha of +0.13%. Harvey and Liu also do NOT discard FF: 'our general recommendation is to use FF's technique that captures cross-sectional correlations, but to implement it in a way that is consistent with KTWW's approach in which the minimum number of observations is increased.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Berk-van Binsbergen (JFE 2015): AUM-weighted mean value added $3.2m/yr (t=5.74), median negative, 57.01% of funds below zero
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 'AUM-weighted mean'. RIGHT: the $3.2m/yr figure is the TIME-WEIGHTED (duration-weighted) mean - Table 3's note states the weighted mean is 'computed by weighting by the number of periods the fund exists, that is, they are the statistical properties of S-bar-W defined by (9).' The body reads: 'The average fund added an economically significant $270,000 per month, or $3.2 million annually (in Y2000 dollars).' Numbers otherwise check out: Table 3 Vanguard Benchmark column, Cross-Sectional Weighted Mean 0.27 ($m/month), SE 0.05, t-Statistic 5.74; 50th Percentile -0.02 (i.e. the median fund lost ~$20,000/month); Percent with less than zero 57.01% (FFC-benchmark column is 59.70%). Also add: the units are Y2000 dollars, and the UNWEIGHTED cross-sectional mean is also positive and significant at 0.14/month (t=4.57), so 'both sides quote the same table' is fair. Table 3 is byte-identical in the NBER w18184 draft and the 2014 Wharton draft, and the published JFE 2015 abstract confirms '$3.2 million per year'; note the earlier 2012 NBER abstract said about $2 million per year, so cite the JFE/2014 figure only.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Unterberg SSRN 6902444: net 4-factor alpha -0.72%/yr (1984-2009) -> -1.82%/yr (2010-24); VW gross alpha ~0 -> -0.66%/yr post-2010; industry-level passive-share vs active-minus-passive spread flipped sign after 2010
itemVerdicts.note: Could NOT reach the primary paper. papers.ssrn.com returns a Cloudflare 'Performing security verification' interstitial to both WebFetch (403) and a real browser session, and then bounces to an spglobal 'Access Denied' page; I did not attempt to defeat the bot check. ResearchGate 403s. The author's own site (hannahunterberg.com) hosts no PDF and only links back to SSRN. Semantic Scholar has no record. WHAT I DID REACH FIRST-HAND: the publisher-deposited abstract via the Crossref API for DOI 10.2139/ssrn.6902444 (posted 2026, deposit created 2026-06-19T16:50:23Z; OpenAlex confirms Hannah Unterberg, University of California Irvine, Paul Merage School of Business). Verbatim: 'Using U.S. equity fund data (1984-2024), I document a decline in active fund performance after 2010, with average annual four-factor alpha falling by around one percentage point and the previously positive relation between Active Share and performance reversing. These patterns contrast with theories predicting improved performance as the active sector shrinks.' That corroborates the SAMPLE (1984-2024), the ~1pp decline (-0.72 to -1.82 is 1.10pp), and the article's overall 'runs the wrong way' framing. It does NOT contain -0.72, -1.82, -0.66, the gross/value-weighted split, or the industry-level spread flip. Those four specifics are traceable only to Swedroe's Morningstar piece (Aug 12, 2026), which I read verbatim in-browser and which does state them: 'average net alpha for active funds fell from negative 0.72% annually (1984-2009) to negative 1.82% annually (2010-24)'; 'After 2010, the value-weighted portfolio earns a four-factor gross alpha of negative 0.66% per year'; and finding 6, 'Historically, a larger passive share of the industry predicted a wider active-minus-passive return spread... After 2010, a larger passive share predicts a narrower spread.' So the article reproduces its secondhand source faithfully - but these remain unverified against the paper.

corrections: Berk-van Binsbergen: change 'AUM-weighted mean value added $3.2m/yr' to 'duration-weighted mean value added $3.2m/yr (in Y2000 dollars)'. Table 3's note says the weighted mean is computed 'by weighting by the number of periods the fund exists' - not by assets. Keep t=5.74, median -$20,000/month, and 57.01% below zero, all of which are correct (57.01% is the Vanguard-benchmark column; the FFC column is 59.70%).

Do not present Pastor-Stambaugh-Taylor's industry-size result as a test of Grossman-Stiglitz. PST cite Berk and Green (2004) and frame it as decreasing returns to scale; Grossman and Stiglitz appear nowhere in the paper. Say the direction of PST's result coincides with what G-S would imply, and attribute the G-S prediction separately.

Do not let 'shrinking active share' slide between two different denominators. PST's IndustrySize is active equity mutual fund AUM divided by TOTAL STOCK MARKET CAP (2.4% in Jan 1979, peaking at 18.6% in Jul 2008, 16.8% in Dec 2011) - not the passive-vs-active split of FUND assets that Swedroe describes going 'from about 19% to over 50% of equity fund assets since 2010'. A fall in passive-vs-active fund share does not mechanically imply a fall in PST's variable; if the article converts a decline into a predicted alpha gain, it must use the market-cap-denominated series and say so.
State that PST's sample ends December 2011, so the claim that post-2010 shrinkage 'should have raised gross alpha' is the article's own extrapolation, not a PST finding.

When citing PST's ~40bp/20bp, note these are the OLS specifications WITH fund fixed effects (t = -3.60 and -4.34). Without fund fixed effects the coefficients are roughly half and only marginally significant: -0.0169 (t=-1.93, ~20bp/yr) main sample and -0.00671 (t=-1.92, ~8bp/yr) extended sample.

Cremers-Ferreira-Matos-Starks: qualify that the positive explicit-indexing main effect and the negative Active-share x Explicit-indexing interaction are significant only in Panel B (by country of sale): +0.1196 (t=4.16) and -0.1753 (t=-4.21). In Panel A (by country of domicile) both are insignificant: 0.0106 (t=0.43) and -0.0351 (t=-0.95). Also state that the dependent variable is a four-factor alpha built from fund NET returns over 2002-2010, so this is an after-fee competition result, not a gross-alpha result.

Harvey & Liu: quote the sentence in full - 'the FF technique has little or no power to detect the truly outperforming funds in our simulation' - and confine the critique to the cross-sectional bootstrap used to identify individual outperforming funds. It does not bear on Fama-French's aggregate value-weighted gross alpha of +0.13% (t=0.40), which is a plain time-series regression. Add that Harvey and Liu recommend keeping FF's method with a higher minimum-observations requirement rather than discarding it.

Fama-French 2010: the window is January 1984 through September 2006. Net value-weighted three-factor alpha is -0.81%/yr (t=-2.50) and four-factor -1.00%/yr (t=-3.02), which is what supports 'alpha = minus fees'; give those alongside the +0.13% gross figure.

Unterberg: attribute -0.72%/yr, -1.82%/yr, the ~0 to -0.66%/yr value-weighted gross alpha, and the industry-level passive-share sign flip to Swedroe's Morningstar write-up (Aug 12, 2026), not to the paper itself - the SSRN full text was not reachable. What CAN be sourced to the paper is its own abstract: U.S. equity fund data 1984-2024, 'average annual four-factor alpha falling by around one percentage point and the previously positive relation between Active Share and performance reversing', and 'These patterns contrast with theories predicting improved performance as the active sector shrinks.'

Note that the paper's own abstract highlights the reversal of the ACTIVE-SHARE-to-performance relation at the fund level; the separate industry-level 'passive share vs active-minus-passive spread' sign flip appears only in the Morningstar summary's finding 6 and is not in the abstract. Keep the two distinct rather than merging them into one claim.
Label the Unterberg paper as an unpublished 2026 SSRN working paper (presented at WFA 2026), not a peer-reviewed result, and say so wherever its numbers carry weight in the argument.
newContradictions: Adams, Hayunga & Mansi (Critical Finance Review) argue the negative scale-performance relation in active management is an artifact of extreme observations; Pastor, Stambaugh, Taylor & Zhu reply in CFR 11(3-4), 593-611 (2022) that robust regression 'confirm[s] both studies' inferences about scale diseconomies at the fund and industry levels' and that they 'reject constant returns to scale even after dropping 25% of the most extreme return observations.' The article should be aware the PST industry-size coefficient has been publicly contested and defended, even though it survives.

Reuter & Zitzewitz, Review of Finance 25(5), 1395-1432 (2021), find via regression discontinuity that FUND size has a negligible causal effect on returns. This does not touch PST's INDUSTRY-size coefficient, but if the article leans on fund-level diseconomies anywhere it conflicts with this paper.

Fama-French 2010's aggregate result and Berk-van Binsbergen 2015's positive value added are not in tension the way an 'evidence runs the wrong way' framing might suggest: FF measure a value-weighted alpha in percent, BvB measure a dollar quantity (alpha times AUM) against Vanguard index-fund benchmarks. If the article stacks them as opposing camps quoting 'the same table', that is only true within BvB's own Table 3, not across FF and BvB.
reasoning:
The scratchpad files named in the task (pst.txt, bvb.txt, cfms2016.txt, ff2010real.txt, etc.) DO NOT EXIST — the session scratchpad contains only v15_oii and v15venv directories, and a filesystem-wide search for pst.txt/bvb.txt/cfms2016.txt returned nothing. Every check below was therefore done against documents I downloaded and extracted myself with curl + pdftotext, or read in a browser.

PRIMARY DOCUMENTS REACHED VERBATIM: (1) Pastor-Stambaugh-Taylor, NBER w19891 PDF plus a second Aug-2013 draft — I read the 40bp/20bp sentence, Table 3 (coefficients -0.0326/t=-3.60 and -0.0164/t=-4.34, with the no-fixed-effects columns -0.0169 and -0.00671), the IndustrySize definition, and the 2.4%/18.6%/16.8% time path. (2) Cremers-Ferreira-Matos-Starks, the Darden-hosted published-version PDF — abstract, the interaction paragraph, and Table 7 Panels A and B in full. (3) Fama-French, the Journal of Finance Oct 2010 typeset PDF — the 0.13%/t=0.40 sentence and Table II. (4) Harvey & Liu, the Journal of Finance June 2022 typeset PDF — the 'little or no power' sentence in context plus their recommendation. (5) Berk-van Binsbergen, both the 2012 NBER w18184 and the 2014 Wharton Rodney White drafts — Table 3 including the note that fixes the weighting scheme, cross-checked against the published JFE abstract via EconPapers. (6) Pastor-Stambaugh-Taylor-Zhu's robustness reply PDF.

FOUR OF FIVE SUB-CLAIMS SURVIVE ESSENTIALLY INTACT. The one real numeric/descriptor error is in (d): the $3.2m/yr is duration-weighted (weighted by the number of periods a fund exists), not AUM-weighted. Everything else I flag is caliber slippage rather than falsity: the CFMS results hold only in Panel B; the PST magnitudes are the fixed-effects variants and stop at 2011; the Harvey-Liu quote is missing 'in our simulation' and is about the cross-sectional bootstrap rather than the aggregate alpha; and calling PST a Grossman-Stiglitz test misattributes the mechanism.

WHAT REMAINS UNCERTAIN: the Unterberg paper itself. SSRN sits behind a Cloudflare bot check that blocked WebFetch, curl, and a live browser session (which then redirected to an spglobal 'Access Denied' page); I did not try to defeat it. ResearchGate 403s, Semantic Scholar has no record, and the author's website hosts no PDF. I did recover the publisher-deposited abstract verbatim through the Crossref API for DOI 10.2139/ssrn.6902444, which independently confirms the 1984-2024 sample, the ~1pp alpha decline, the Active-Share relation reversing, and the 'contrast with theories predicting improved performance as the active sector shrinks' framing. It does not contain -0.72, -1.82, or -0.66, nor any gross/value-weighted split, nor the industry-level spread flip. Those four figures trace only to Swedroe's Morningstar article, which I read verbatim in-browser and which does state them accurately as the article renders them. Per instructions I mark the item unreachable rather than promoting secondhand numbers.

One structural caution I could not resolve empirically and flag as the biggest live risk in this claim group: the article's inferential step from PST to 'post-2010 shrinkage should have raised gross alpha' silently swaps denominators. PST's regressor is active fund AUM over TOTAL MARKET CAP; the widely cited collapse in 'active share' is active over TOTAL FUND ASSETS. Those are different series and the second falling does not establish the first fell.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Russell first stage: switching indexes moves passive ownership ~1.5pp of market cap, ~15% of a ~10% baseline
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the cited PDF (p.24): "The average change in passive ownership for stocks that switch indexes is approximately 1.5% of the stock's total market capitalization. The average level of ownership by passive funds prior to treatment is approximately 10% of market cap (see Table I). Thus, the change represents roughly 15% of the baseline level of ownership by passive funds." Table I confirms baseline FundOwnPassive mean = 10.51 (lower band) and 10.14 (upper band). CALIBER NOTE, not an error: 1.5 is the average of the two asymmetric first-stage coefficients in Table II — FundOwnPassive is +1.81*** into the R2000 (lower band) and -1.16*** out of it (upper band); elsewhere the paper says "a 1.5 to 1.7 percentage point change." The paper's own Introduction (p.2-3) instead says passive ownership "increases by approximately 2% of its market capitalization," as does the authors' Harvard Law School Forum summary. If the article quotes ~1.5pp it should attribute it to the results section, not the abstract/intro.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Into-R2000 panel: EDGAR page requests -24.8 log points (205→159/day, -22%); analyst reports -10.8
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim (p.27): "Google SVI falls by 3.8 log points, EDGAR page requests fall by 24.8 log points, and the number of analyst reports falls by 10.8 log points... the 24.8 log point decrease relative to the baseline average of 5.32 (in logs) corresponds to moving from 205 to 159 EDGAR page requests per day (a decrease of 22%)." Arithmetic checks: exp(5.32)=204.4; exp(5.32-0.248)=159.5.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Analyst reports -10.8 described as the weakly-significant one (p<0.10)
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as stated: the qualifier is attached only to analyst reports, implying the EDGAR result is more strongly significant. RIGHT: in Table IV Panel A BOTH are weakly significant — log(EDGAR) = -0.248* (t = -1.9) and log(AnalystReports) = -0.108* (t = -1.8), single star = p<0.1; log(SVI) = -0.038 (t = -1.0) is insignificant. The paper's own text: "the result on Google SVI is statistically insignificant while the estimates on EDGAR page views and analyst reports are statistically significant at p < 0.10." So the headline -24.8 EDGAR figure is itself only p<0.10.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Out-of-R2000 panel: EDGAR +20.3, analyst reports +14.3, better powered
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim (p.28): "a lower level of index investing upon crossing the upper band is followed by a 4.4 log point increase in Google SVI, a 20.3 log point increase in EDGAR page views, and a 14.3 log point increase in the number of analyst reports." Table IV Panel B: log(EDGAR) +0.203** (t=2.5), log(AnalystReports) +0.143*** (t=2.8), log(SVI) +0.044 (t=1.5, insignificant). "Better powered" is supported: paper says "nearly twice as many stocks in this subsample"; MDES falls from ±0.374 to ±0.229 (EDGAR) and ±0.166 to ±0.144 (analyst reports).

itemVerdicts.item: (b) NOTE: 'the popular -14.1% EDGAR quote is wrong; -14.3 is the ANALYST-REPORT figure'
itemVerdicts.note: This note is itself false on both halves. WRONG: that -14.1% for EDGAR is a misquote. RIGHT: 14.1% is the paper's OWN headline figure, on p.3 of the exact PDF the article cites: "Following an exogenous increase in index fund ownership, Google search volume falls by 3.8%, EDGAR page views fall by 14.1%, and the number of analyst reports falls by 10.8%." The authors repeat it verbatim in their own Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance summary (15 Aug 2022): "Google search volume about the stock falls by 3.8%, EDGAR page views fall by 14.1%, and the number of analyst reports about the stock falls by 10.8%." The real problem is an INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY in the paper: the introduction's 14.1% is irreconcilable with the body/Table IV coefficient of -0.248 log points, which the paper itself converts to -22% (205→159). WRONG: '-14.3 is the analyst-report figure.' RIGHT: the analyst-report DECREASE is -10.8 log points; +14.3 log points is the analyst-report INCREASE in the opposite (upper-band, out-of-R2000) panel. There is no -14.3 anywhere in the paper.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Price-efficiency outcomes are precisely-estimated zeros: 4/8-day absolute variance ratios (effect -0.017 vs SD 0.413; MDES ±0.068), anomaly mispricing, PEAD
itemVerdicts.note: Table V Panel A: AbsVarRatio4 = -0.017 (t=-0.7), MDES ±0.068, Sample St.Dev. 0.413; AbsVarRatio8 = -0.027 (MDES ±0.221, SD 1.353); Misprice = 0.001 (MDES ±0.048, SD 0.137); betaPEAD = -0.034 (MDES ±0.099, SD 0.102). Panel B all insignificant too (+0.011, +0.004, +0.005, -0.014). Text p.29-30 verbatim: "the estimated effect is less than one-twentieth of one standard deviation... the minimum detectable effect size (MDES) for the AVR in this estimate is +/-0.068, so our research design has the ability to reliably detect a treatment effect on the order of (0.068 / 0.413) = one-sixth of one standard deviation. Yet we find no effect – precisely estimated." Note the -0.017/0.413/±0.068 triple is the 4-day figure specifically; the 8-day estimate is -0.027.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Same paper finds significant positives: idiosyncratic volatility, comovement with both indexes, market beta, trading volume +12.1%, short interest +1.9% (Section D)
itemVerdicts.note: Section label and existence CONFIRMED — Section D 'Effects on Underlying Asset Markets' is real and does report these. Table III Panel A (into R2000): LogTurn +0.121***, ShortInt +0.019***, LogVlt +0.064*, rho_R1000 +0.046***, rho_R2000 +0.069***, MarketBeta +0.300***; Panel B symmetric negatives. Three caliber corrections: (i) VOLATILITY — WRONG to list it as a flat 'significant positive' equal to the others: in the into-index panel LogVlt is only p<0.10 (0.064*, t=1.7); it reaches p<0.05 only in the out-of-index panel (-0.049**). Also the variable is defined in Table III as 'the log of daily return volatility' (total), though the paper's prose on p.26 does loosely call it 'idiosyncratic volatility.' (ii) SHORT INTEREST — WRONG to read '+1.9%' as a 1.9% relative increase. RIGHT: ShortInt is 'the mid-month short interest divided by shares outstanding,' baseline mean 0.10 (Table I), so the +0.019 coefficient is +1.9 percentage points of shares outstanding, i.e. roughly a 19% relative increase in short interest — an order of magnitude larger than a naive '+1.9%' reading. (iii) TRADING VOLUME — the +12.1% is on LogTurn, 'the log of monthly volume divided by shares outstanding,' i.e. turnover; the paper's own intro calls it 'higher share turnover.'

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Figure 5: Russell 3000 index ownership 2%→11% of market cap 2007-2016 while 4-day variance ratio improved from 1.16 to 1.10
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim p.33-34: "index fund ownership quintupled from 2% to 11% of market capitalization on average. Yet over the same period, the average variance ratio fell slightly from 1.16 to 1.10, reflecting a slight improvement in price efficiency. The conclusions are similar when we weight the averages by market capitalization." Figure 5 caption confirms it plots "the average 4-day return variance ratio and average passive fund ownership across all stocks in the Russell 3000, yearly during our sample period from 2007-2016," with dashed = equal-weighted and solid = value-weighted. Note the direction convention: a LOWER variance ratio is BETTER here (the paper calls it 'inverse price efficiency'), so 1.16→1.10 is indeed an improvement; also note 2→11 is 5.5x, which the paper calls 'quintupled.' This is descriptive time-series, not the identified estimate.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) External-validity caveat: LATE on mid-cap slices; 'not clear whether our estimates generalize to larger changes or higher levels of index investing'
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim p.33: "Empirically, we caution that the external validity of our results remains unknown. The difference-in-differences methodology we employ estimates the local average treatment effect (LATE) of index assignment around the upper and lower Russell bands both narrow slices of mid-cap U.S. stocks. As such, it is not clear whether our estimates generalize to larger changes or higher levels of index investing." CONTEXT the article must not omit: two paragraphs later the authors partially walk it back — "our model's theoretical predictions hold for any feasible level of passive investing, which suggests our estimates would hold for larger or smaller changes in index investing." They also flag a separate confound: "stocks at the bottom of the R1000 may be less important in their index... which could lead to lower attention and/or lower turnover." Quoting the caveat alone, without the walk-back, is a mild cherry-pick in the skeptics' direction; quoting the walk-back alone is the reverse.

itemVerdicts.item: Publication metadata: JFE 145(3) 2022, lead article; SSRN 3055324; S0304405X22001143
itemVerdicts.note: Crossref on DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2022.05.007 returns 'On index investing,' JFE vol 145, issue 3, pp. 665-683, published print September 2022. The JFE's own issue table of contents (jfe-journal.org/volume-145-issue-3-2022/) lists it as item 1 of 14 — lead article confirmed. RePEc/EconPapers confirms pages 665-683 and the ScienceDirect PII S0304405X22001143.

itemVerdicts.item: Identity of the cited PDF (r.jordan.im/download/investing/coles2017.pdf)
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG implication of the filename: it is not the 2017 working paper. RIGHT: I downloaded it (md5 6198892764e4b45afcc0e12ec1ab8e18) and it is byte-identical to the January 2022 SSRN draft — title page reads 'First Draft: March 2017 / This Draft: January 2022', copyright 'c 2017-2022', and it thanks 'an anonymous referee'. This is effectively the accepted manuscript (JFE acceptance date 25 Feb 2022). The genuine October 2017 draft is a materially different paper — I pulled it from GWU (business.gwu.edu/.../Paper%20Ringgenberg.pdf, identical to the local chr.pdf) and it contains NO EDGAR analysis at all. Any article citing 'coles2017' as a 2017 working paper is misdating its own source; cite it as Coles, Heath & Ringgenberg (2022).

itemVerdicts.item: Typeset published JFE version — whether its intro numbers differ from the accepted manuscript
itemVerdicts.note: Could not reach the typeset JFE 145(3) text. ScienceDirect is paywalled (OpenAlex: oa_status 'closed', no repository full text); SSRN is Cloudflare-blocked to scripted access; Semantic Scholar has no record for the DOI; the JFE's own site posts no PDF. This matters because two independent search summarizers reported the published version as '24.6%' EDGAR and '10.7%' analyst reports rather than 14.1%/10.8% — I did NOT verify that and am flagging it as unverified summarizer output, not fact. Countervailing evidence that 14.1% survived into print: the authors' own post-publication Harvard Law School Forum summary (15 Aug 2022) still says 14.1%. Recommendation: the article should quote the log-point/Table IV figures (-24.8, -10.8, +20.3, +14.3), which are stable and internally consistent, rather than the intro's percent restatements.

corrections: Delete the assertion that the '-14.1% EDGAR' figure is a misquote. It is the paper's own headline number, stated on p.3 of the exact PDF cited: 'Google search volume falls by 3.8%, EDGAR page views fall by 14.1%, and the number of analyst reports falls by 10.8%' — and repeated verbatim by the authors in their Harvard Law School Forum summary of 15 Aug 2022. If the article wants to make a point here, the correct point is that the paper is internally inconsistent: the introduction's 14.1% cannot be reconciled with the body's Table IV coefficient of -24.8 log points, which the paper itself converts to -22% (205→159 page requests/day).

Delete the assertion that '-14.3 is the analyst-report figure.' There is no -14.3 in the paper. The analyst-report DECREASE (into the R2000) is -10.8 log points; +14.3 log points is the analyst-report INCREASE in the opposite panel (out of the R2000, upper band).

Do not attach the weak-significance qualifier only to analyst reports. In Table IV Panel A both the EDGAR coefficient (-0.248, t = -1.9) and the analyst-report coefficient (-0.108, t = -1.8) carry a single star, p<0.10. The headline '-24.8 log point' EDGAR result is itself only marginally significant. Google SVI (-0.038, t = -1.0) is insignificant.

Do not present the short-interest result as '+1.9%' without units. ShortInt is defined as short interest divided by shares outstanding, with a baseline mean of 0.10, so the +0.019 coefficient is +1.9 PERCENTAGE POINTS of shares outstanding — roughly a 19% relative increase in short interest, not a 1.9% one. Placing '+1.9%' next to '+12.1%' (a log-point figure that does read as ~12%) makes the short-interest effect look an order of magnitude smaller than it is.

Qualify the volatility item in the Section D list. In the into-R2000 panel LogVlt is +0.064 with only a single star (p<0.10, t = 1.7); it reaches p<0.05 only in the out-of-R2000 panel (-0.049**). It should not be listed flatly alongside the p<0.01 results (turnover, short interest, both comovement coefficients, market beta). Also note the outcome variable is defined in Table III as 'the log of daily return volatility' (total volatility), even though the paper's prose calls it idiosyncratic volatility.

Note that '+12.1% trading volume' is measured on LogTurn, defined as 'the log of monthly volume divided by shares outstanding' — i.e. turnover. The paper's own introduction calls it 'higher share turnover.'

Cite the paper as Coles, Heath & Ringgenberg (2022), JFE 145(3), 665-683. The file at r.jordan.im/download/investing/coles2017.pdf is misleadingly named: it is byte-identical to the January 2022 SSRN draft ('This Draft: January 2022', thanks an anonymous referee), effectively the accepted manuscript. The genuine October 2017 draft is a different paper containing no EDGAR analysis whatsoever, so do not describe the cited PDF as a 2017 working paper.

When quoting the external-validity caveat, either also quote the authors' partial walk-back on the next page — 'our model's theoretical predictions hold for any feasible level of passive investing, which suggests our estimates would hold for larger or smaller changes in index investing' — or drop the pretense that the authors themselves treat the LATE limitation as decisive. Quoting only the caveat is a cherry-pick in the same class as quoting only the 'passive is harmless' conclusion.

Prefer the log-point figures from Table IV (-24.8 and -10.8 into the index; +20.3 and +14.3 out of it) over the introduction's percent restatements. The log-point numbers are stable across the accepted manuscript and internally consistent with the tables; the introduction's percentages are not, and I could not reach the typeset JFE version to confirm whether they were corrected in proofs.

Note that '~1.5pp' is the average across two asymmetric first-stage coefficients (+1.81pp into the R2000, -1.16pp out of it, Table II), and that the paper's own introduction gives the figure as 'approximately 2% of its market capitalization.' Attribute the 1.5pp figure to the results section, not the abstract.
newContradictions: Internal contradiction within the paper itself: the introduction (p.3) says EDGAR page views fall by 14.1%, while Section E and Table IV give -24.8 log points, which the same paper converts to a 22% decline (205→159 requests/day). The two cannot both be right. Any article quoting a percent EDGAR figure inherits this defect; quote the log points instead.

Höfler & Schlag, 'Passive Investing and Market Quality' (AEA 2025 program; local hofler.txt), explicitly classifies CHR (2022) among papers documenting 'no detrimental effects' and reports the opposite for ETF passive ownership: higher PO 'decreases the importance of firm-specific information while simultaneously increasing the importance of return noise,' plus lower liquidity and higher tail risk, over a June 1997–December 2021 sample of 872 US equity ETFs. Different identification (ETF ownership, longer sample) and different outcome variables, so it is not a direct refutation of CHR's variance-ratio nulls, but it is a live contradicting primary source the article should not omit.

Haddad, Huebner & Loualiche (local hhl.txt) cite CHR as showing 'that an increase in passive investing does not affect price informativeness IN THIS BASELINE MODEL' — i.e. they read the CHR non-result as a property of the baseline Grossman-Stiglitz competitive setup, and their own paper's contribution is that relaxing competition/elasticity assumptions overturns it. The article should not present CHR's null as model-free empirics when a leading citing paper frames it as model-conditional.

Ringgenberg's own Congressional testimony of 25 June 2026 (local ring_test.txt) restates the finding without retraction — 'greater passive ownership is associated with a reduction in information production, however... overall price efficiency has not significantly changed in recent years because active investors continue to gather information whenever it is profitable' — but he immediately adds 'none of this means that passive investing is harmful to society in net' AND that 'active investors provide a public service... including passive investors who free-ride on the price discovery that active managers provide.' So as of 2026 the lead author himself frames the paper as neither a clean exoneration of passive nor a warning; an article using it for either pole is misusing it.

Ringgenberg's website lists 'A note on Russell-based methodologies - Paper coming soon' (surfaced in search, not independently verified). If that appears before publication it may bear directly on the validity of the very research design underpinning this claim group — worth a pre-publication recheck.
reasoning:
I verified every sub-claim against the primary document rather than against summaries. The cited URL (r.jordan.im/download/investing/coles2017.pdf) was downloaded fresh and hashes to md5 6198892764e4b45afcc0e12ec1ab8e18, byte-identical to the local v15_chr2022.pdf / v15_coles.pdf / v15_coles2017.pdf (all the same file), which is the January 2022 SSRN draft — the accepted manuscript, not the 2017 working paper the filename implies. I separately pulled the genuine October 2017 draft from GWU (identical to local chr.pdf) and confirmed it contains no EDGAR analysis at all, which explains where the version drift comes from.

Read verbatim from the cited PDF: the first-stage passage on p.24 (1.5% of market cap, ~10% baseline, ~15% of baseline), Table I summary stats (FundOwnPassive means 10.51 and 10.14; logEDGAR mean 5.32; ShortInt mean 0.10), Table II first stage (+1.81*** / -1.16*** on FundOwnPassive), Table III asset-market outcomes with all stars and MDES rows, Table IV information production with all stars, Table V price informativeness with all four columns and both panels, the Section E and F narrative text, the Figure 5 caption and the p.33-34 aggregate-trend passage, and the external-validity caveat plus its walk-back. Arithmetic independently checked: exp(5.32)=204.4 and exp(5.072)=159.5, so the 205→159 / -22% conversion of -0.248 log points is correct.

Four things the claim group gets wrong or under-calibrates. First and most serious, the NOTE instructing that '-14.1% EDGAR' is a misquote is itself false — 14.1% is on p.3 of the very PDF cited, and the authors repeat it verbatim in their own Harvard Law School Forum post of 15 Aug 2022 (I fetched that page and read the paragraph in raw HTML, not via a summarizer). The real defect is that the paper's introduction and its own Table IV disagree. And 14.3 is not a decrease figure at all; it is the +14.3 log-point analyst-report INCREASE in the upper-band panel. Second, the weak-significance qualifier is placed only on analyst reports when Table IV Panel A shows EDGAR is equally p<0.10 (t = -1.9 vs -1.8). Third, '+1.9% short interest' is a units trap: ShortInt is a fraction of shares outstanding with mean 0.10, so +0.019 is +1.9pp, about a 19% relative rise. Fourth, volatility is only p<0.10 in the into-index panel, so listing it flatly among the significant positives overstates it.

Confirmed without qualification: the 1.5pp/10%/15% first stage, the -24.8/205→159/-22% EDGAR figure, the +20.3/+14.3 upper-band figures and their better power (MDES ±0.374→±0.229), the -0.017 / SD 0.413 / MDES ±0.068 variance-ratio null and the mispricing and PEAD nulls, the Figure 5 2%→11% and 1.16→1.10 series, the LATE caveat verbatim, and lead-article status (Crossref: pp. 665-683; the JFE's own issue TOC lists it as item 1 of 14).

Remaining uncertainty, stated plainly: I could not reach the typeset published version. ScienceDirect is paywalled, OpenAlex reports oa_status 'closed' with no repository full text, SSRN returned a Cloudflare content-block to scripted access, Semantic Scholar has no record for the DOI, and the JFE site hosts no PDF. Two search summarizers volunteered that the published version reads '24.6%' and '10.7%' rather than 14.1% and 10.8%; per the fabrication warning I treat that as unverified and did not act on it, but I flag it because if true it means the introduction's percentages were repaired in proofs — which is a further reason to quote the log-point figures instead. The authors' own post-publication summary still says 14.1%, which cuts the other way.

itemVerdicts.item: Cremers, Fulkerson & Riley, "How the SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Understates the Performance of Actively Managed Mutual Funds," working paper dated May 4, 2026
itemVerdicts.note: Downloaded the IAA-hosted PDF (SSRN 6710358, 40pp) and extracted text. Title page line 19 reads verbatim "This Draft: May 4, 2026". Authors: K.J. Martijn Cremers (Notre Dame), Jon Fulkerson (Dayton), Timothy Riley (Arkansas, corresponding). Still an unpublished working paper as of 2026-08; no journal version found. SSRN's own page is Cloudflare-403 to automated fetch, so I could not independently confirm SSRN revision history — but the IAA-hosted copy is unambiguous.

itemVerdicts.item: Funded by the Investment Adviser Association's Active Managers Council; Cremers is a director at Ariel Investments and advisor to Touchstone
itemVerdicts.note: Substance confirmed on the title page (footnote *), but wording is off. WRONG: "funded by ... ; Cremers is a director at Ariel Investments and advisor to Touchstone." RIGHT (verbatim, iaa_spiva.txt lines 25-27): "This research was supported by the Investment Adviser Association's Active Managers Council. Martijn Cremers serves as an independent director at Ariel Investments and as an independent academic advisor to Touchstone Investments." The paper says "supported by," not "funded by"; and the roles are "independent director" and "independent academic advisor" — dropping "independent" overstates the COI in a way the source does not support.

itemVerdicts.item: Their replication matches SPIVA: 92.04% vs reported 92.66% for 20-yr US equity
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, lines 56-58: "following the Scorecard, we find that 92.04% of active funds in the average U.S. equity category underperformed over the last 20 years. The Scorecard reports 92.66%." One caliber note: 92.04 is the ACROSS-CATEGORY AVERAGE of the twelve cap-valuation categories (Table I note, lines 110-114), not a single "US equity" aggregate. The single "All Domestic Funds" 20-yr numbers are 94.11 (SPIVA reported, Table 2) vs 94.05 (replication, Table 3).

itemVerdicts.item: After three adjustments the 20-yr US equity figure falls to 55.31% of ASSETS underperforming
itemVerdicts.note: Table I Panel B (line 126): U.S. Equity Funds 20-Year = 55.31. I recomputed it from Table 7 Panel A (line ~1195 block): the twelve cap-valuation 20-yr cells (76.17, 78.29, 41.73, 9.93, 91.68, 13.98, 44.56, 72.00, 44.34, 82.21, 69.22, 39.60) sum to 663.71, /12 = 55.31 exactly. It is a share of assets because adjustment 2 is asset-weighting; exec summary line 82: "we find that 55% of assets underperformed." Note 6 of the 12 categories fall below 50%, matching the paper's "half of the investment categories."

itemVerdicts.item: Fixed income reverses: 10-yr 71.34% → 37.09%
itemVerdicts.note: Table I (lines 122, 128): Fixed Income Funds 10-Year, Panel A (SPIVA replication) = 71.34, Panel B (post-adjustments) = 37.09. Exec summary lines 88-97 confirms the "reverse the Scorecard's conclusion" framing. Caveat: 71.34 is the authors' REPLICATION, not SPIVA's own published figure, and it is a category average across all fixed-income categories.

itemVerdicts.item: Abstract: "only 56% of assets invested in active U.S. equity funds in 2024 underperformed equivalent passive funds."
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, abstract lines 37-38. Traced to source: this is the ALL DOMESTIC FUNDS 1-year (2024) cell in Table 7 Panel A = 56.49 (line 1181), versus SPIVA's reported 78.65 for the same cell (Table 2, line 866) — matching the abstract's "79% ... underperformed the S&P Composite 1500." Important: this 56% is a ONE-YEAR (2024) figure for the single broad category, NOT the 55.31% twenty-year cap-valuation average. An article that runs the two together will be wrong.

itemVerdicts.item: Ptak, Morningstar, June 8, 2026, "Have We Been Too Hard on Active Funds?"
itemVerdicts.note: Fetched the page and extracted text. <title> = "Have We Been Too Hard on Active Funds? | Morningstar"; byline "Jeffrey Ptak, CFA"; meta datePublished content="2026-06-08T12:00:00Z", displayed as "Jun 8, 2026".

itemVerdicts.item: Nearly one-fifth of the 37pp FIXED-INCOME improvement stems from replication errors
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: attributing the 37pp to fixed income as a class. RIGHT (Ptak verbatim): "nearly one-fifth of the 37-percentage-point improvement of active investment-grade intermediate bond funds stemmed from replication errors—that is, the authors not being able to exactly reproduce SPIVA's findings. (The authors couldn't get closer than a 54% failure rate...)" This is ONE category, not the fixed-income class. The class-level fixed-income 10-yr improvement is 71.34→37.09 = 34.25pp, a different number. I reconciled Ptak's arithmetic against the paper: IG-Intermediate 10-yr = 61.33 (Table 2, SPIVA reported, line 902) → 54.34 (Table 3, replication, line 964) → 23.91 (Table 7, all adjustments, line 1217). Improvement 61.33−23.91 = 37.42pp; replication gap 61.33−54.34 = 6.99pp = 18.7% of it — "nearly one-fifth" checks out exactly.

itemVerdicts.item: Only two of three adjustments individually improved results; the benchmark adjustment and the interaction made results worse in that category
itemVerdicts.note: Ptak verbatim: "only two of those adjustments—crediting dead funds and asset-weighting—actually improved the results. The others—the benchmark adjustment and the interaction effect of applying all three adjustments together—made the results worse." Verified against the paper for IG-Intermediate 10-yr from the 54.34 replication baseline: survivorship 40.46 (Table 4, line 1028, −13.88), asset-weighting 28.21 (Table 5, line 1091, −26.13), benchmark 56.07 (Table 6, line 1154, +1.73 = worse). Sum of individual effects would give 16.06; actual combined is 23.91, so the interaction adds +7.85 (worse). Ptak's arithmetic is sound.

itemVerdicts.item: HY census: of 150 HY funds at Dec-2004, 78 died over 20 years; dead outperformers lived 2,844 fund-months vs 4,518 for laggards
itemVerdicts.note: Ptak verbatim: "focusing on the 150 funds (largest share class of each fund) that were assigned to the high-yield bond Morningstar Category as of Dec. 31, 2004. Seventy-two of those funds survived the ensuing 20 years. Of the 78 funds that died, the average lifespan was 8.3 years" and "the dead funds that outperformed survived 2,844 months in aggregate, while those that lagged lived nearly twice as long: 4,518 months in total." CAUTIONS the article must not gloss over: (i) 32 of the 78 dead funds (41%) DID outperform while alive — that cuts toward CFR, not against them; (ii) the 2,844-vs-4,518 gap is mainly a HEADCOUNT effect (32 vs 46 funds), not a lifespan effect — per fund it is 88.9 vs 98.2 months, ~10% apart, so "lived nearly twice as long" is true only in aggregate; (iii) Morningstar's own chart source notes under this section say "as of Dec. 31, 2014" while the body text says Dec. 31, 2004 — the body text is the consistent one (72+78=150), the footnote is a Morningstar typo.

itemVerdicts.item: Ptak defends a convention his own Morningstar Active/Passive Barometer shares
itemVerdicts.note: Partly right, and needs splitting by adjustment. CONFIRMED for two of the three: on equal-weighting, Ptak himself writes "My colleagues who publish the Active/Passive Barometer report don't asset-weight when tallying success rates like the authors did"; on dead funds, Morningstar's Barometer commentary repeatedly defines success as survival plus outperformance — e.g. verbatim from morningstar.com/funds/measuring-performance-active-funds-against-their-passive-peers: "Just 7% of them survived and beat their average passive rival over the decade through December 2024." WRONG if stated as blanket agreement: on CFR's THIRD adjustment the Barometer already does what CFR demand — it benchmarks against the "average passive peer," i.e. actual passive funds, not a costless index. Ptak also explicitly discloses the Barometer in the piece ("We have our own version of SPIVA called the 'Morningstar Active/Passive Barometer.'"), which the article should acknowledge rather than framing it as an undisclosed conflict.

itemVerdicts.item: Cremers' earlier pro-active paper (CFMS 2016) was runner-up for S&P DJI's own SPIVA award
itemVerdicts.note: The award is real but three details are wrong. Primary source is S&P DJI's press release of May 22, 2014 (Third Annual SPIVA Awards), verbatim: "Honorable mention (second prize) was awarded to Martijn Cremers of the University of Notre Dame, Miguel Ferreira of Nova School of Business and Economics, Pedro Matos of the University of Virginia – Darden School of Business, and Laura Starks of the University of Texas at Austin for their research paper entitled, 'The Mutual Fund Industry Worldwide: Explicitly and Closet Indexing, Fee, and Performance'." (1) WRONG: "CFMS 2016." RIGHT: the award went in 2014 to the working paper under its earlier title; the JFE 2016 article "Indexing and active fund management: International evidence" is the later published version. (2) WRONG: "runner-up" unqualified. RIGHT: honorable mention / second prize, USD $15,000 (first prize, $30,000, went to Ferri & Benke's "A Case of Index Fund Portfolios"). (3) WRONG and the most serious: calling it a "pro-active paper." S&P DJI's own summary of it reads "The findings suggest that the growth of explicitly indexed funds worldwide improves the efficiency of the asset management industry" — a pro-INDEXING result, which is precisely why S&P DJI awarded it. The mirror-COI point that actually survives is narrower and sharper: Cremers has previously taken $15,000 in prize money from S&P DJI, the very firm whose scorecard he now attacks under trade-body sponsorship.

itemVerdicts.item: IAA = active-management trade body
itemVerdicts.note: Loose. The Investment Adviser Association is the trade association for SEC-registered investment advisers generally (per its own site: policy/advocacy, compliance, IAA PAC, membership across the adviser industry); the Active Managers Council is the IAA's active-management advocacy arm, and it is the Council specifically — not the IAA at large — that the paper names as its supporter. RIGHT framing: "the active-management advocacy arm (Active Managers Council) of the investment-adviser trade association."

itemVerdicts.item: Later corrections/rejoinders through 2026-08
itemVerdicts.note: I could not reach two items. (1) SSRN abstract page 6710358 returns Cloudflare 403 to both curl and WebFetch, so I could not confirm whether a revision later than the May 4, 2026 draft has been posted; the IAA-hosted PDF is the May 4 draft and no journal publication surfaced in searches. (2) Advisor Perspectives, 2026-06-29, "The SPIVA Scorecard Does Not Capture the Actual Experience of Investors" — 403 to both curl and WebFetch; this may be a Cremers-side rejoinder post-dating Ptak and should be checked before the article claims Ptak had the last word. I also saw S&P DJI quoted in trade press as saying SPIVA "measures the proportion of funds that underperform, rather than the proportion of assets," but that quote came only from a search summarizer, not from a document I read, so I am NOT vouching for it.

corrections: The 37-percentage-point improvement Ptak attributes partly to replication error is for ACTIVE INVESTMENT-GRADE INTERMEDIATE BOND FUNDS specifically (SPIVA-reported 61.33% -> 23.91% after all adjustments), not for fixed income as a class. Do not write "the 37pp fixed-income improvement." The class-level fixed-income 10-year figure is a 34.25pp move (71.34% -> 37.09%), a different number.

Do not run the 56% and the 55.31% together. The abstract's "only 56% of assets" is the ONE-YEAR (2024) figure for the single broad "All Domestic Funds" category (56.49%, vs SPIVA's 78.65% for the same cell). The 55.31% is the TWENTY-YEAR average across the twelve cap-valuation categories.

Note that 92.04% vs 92.66% is an across-category average of the twelve cap-valuation US equity categories, not a single aggregate. (The single "All Domestic Funds" 20-year pair is 94.11% reported vs 94.05% replicated.)

Change "funded by" to "supported by," and restore the word "independent": the title page says Cremers "serves as an independent director at Ariel Investments and as an independent academic advisor to Touchstone Investments." Dropping "independent" overstates what the disclosure says.

Fix the SPIVA award attribution: it was an honorable mention / second prize (USD $15,000) in S&P DJI's THIRD ANNUAL SPIVA Awards, announced May 22, 2014, for the working paper "The Mutual Fund Industry Worldwide: Explicitly and Closet Indexing, Fee, and Performance" — later published as Cremers, Ferreira, Matos & Starks (JFE 2016). First prize went to Ferri & Benke.

Stop calling the CFMS paper "pro-active." S&P DJI's own citation says its findings suggest "the growth of explicitly indexed funds worldwide improves the efficiency of the asset management industry" — a pro-indexing result. The usable COI point is that Cremers previously accepted $15,000 in prize money from S&P DJI, the firm whose scorecard he now attacks under trade-body sponsorship.

Split the Ptak COI claim by adjustment. Morningstar's Active/Passive Barometer shares SPIVA's equal-weighting and its survival-plus-outperformance definition of success ("survived and beat their average passive rival"), but it already benchmarks against the "average passive peer" — i.e. actual passive funds — which is exactly CFR's third adjustment. Also note Ptak discloses the Barometer in the piece rather than hiding it.

Describe the sponsor precisely: the Active Managers Council, the active-management advocacy arm of the Investment Adviser Association (the trade association for SEC-registered investment advisers), not "the IAA, an active-management trade body."

If the article cites the 2,844 vs 4,518 fund-months as proof that dead funds skew losers, add the offsetting facts: 32 of the 78 dead funds (41%) outperformed while alive, and the aggregate gap is driven by headcount (32 vs 46 funds), not longevity — per fund it is 88.9 vs 98.2 months, about 10% apart. Ptak's "lived nearly twice as long" is an aggregate statement only.
Label the Cremers-Fulkerson-Riley paper an unpublished, non-peer-reviewed working paper (draft dated May 4, 2026) every time its numbers are cited.
newContradictions: Ptak's own high-yield census partially SUPPORTS Cremers-Fulkerson-Riley rather than refuting them: 32 of 78 dead high-yield funds (41%) outperformed the index over the portion of the period they lived. SPIVA scores all 78 as failures. The article should not present Ptak's census as a clean refutation of the dead-fund adjustment.

Morningstar's Active/Passive Barometer already benchmarks active funds against the "average passive peer" (actual passive funds), which is exactly the third of the three adjustments Cremers-Fulkerson-Riley demand. So the industry-standard scorekeeper Ptak works for has already conceded one of the paper's three points — while Ptak's article ranks that same benchmark adjustment as the MOST persuasive of the three critiques.

Internal inconsistency in Ptak's high-yield numbers: he reports an average dead-fund lifespan of 8.3 years for 78 funds (implying ~7,769 fund-months), but the two aggregate month totals he gives sum to 7,362 (2,844 + 4,518), implying ~7.9 years. A ~5% gap I could not reconcile from the published text.

Morningstar's chart source notes in the high-yield section say the fund universe is "as of Dec. 31, 2014" while the body text says Dec. 31, 2004. The body text is the internally consistent one (72 survivors + 78 dead = 150); the footnote appears to be a Morningstar typo. Cite the body text, not the chart footnote.

The S&P DJI press release announcing Cremers' own SPIVA award states that SPIVA "scorecards show both asset-weighted and equal-weighted averages, include survivorship bias correction to account for funds that may have merged or been liquidated." S&P has long published asset-weighted RETURNS even though its headline underperformance RATES are equal-weighted and count non-survivors as failures. If the article frames asset-weighting as something SPIVA suppresses, that is too strong.
reasoning:
The stated local extraction files (iaa_spiva.txt et al.) did not exist — the scratchpad was empty and no other session directory held them — so I fetched and extracted every primary document myself rather than relying on any prior extraction.

PRIMARY DOCUMENTS REACHED VERBATIM: (1) The Cremers-Fulkerson-Riley PDF, downloaded from investmentadviser.org (803 KB, 40 pages, PDF 1.7) and converted with `pdftotext -layout`. I read the title page, abstract, executive summary, Table I, and all of Tables 2-7 including the appendix panels. (2) Ptak's Morningstar article, downloaded and tag-stripped to plain text — I read the full body, not a summarizer's rendition. (3) The S&P Dow Jones Indices press release of May 22, 2014 announcing the Third Annual SPIVA Awards, from PR Newswire, read in full around the award citation. (4) Morningstar's Active/Passive Barometer commentary page, for the "survived and beat their average passive rival" success-rate convention.

INDEPENDENT RECOMPUTATION rather than acceptance: I re-derived 55.31 as the exact mean of the twelve 20-year cap-valuation cells in Table 7 Panel A (sum 663.71 / 12). I reconciled Ptak's "nearly one-fifth of the 37-percentage-point improvement" against the paper's own tables — 61.33 (Table 2) - 23.91 (Table 7) = 37.42pp improvement, of which 61.33 - 54.34 (Table 3) = 6.99pp = 18.7% is replication gap. I traced the abstract's 56% to the All Domestic Funds 1-year cell (56.49) rather than assuming it referred to the 20-year headline. I checked each of the three adjustments individually for that category against Tables 4, 5, 6 and confirmed the benchmark adjustment moved the number the wrong way (54.34 -> 56.07) and that the interaction adds +7.85pp versus the sum of individual effects.

WHAT BROKE. Three things. First, the article's biggest error: it generalizes Ptak's investment-grade-intermediate-bond-category statistic into a statement about "the 37pp fixed-income improvement." The fixed-income class figure is a different move (34.25pp) and no replication-error share was computed for it. Second, the SPIVA award attribution is wrong on year, prize level, and paper title — and, worse, on characterization: the awarded paper's headline finding is that indexing improves industry efficiency, which is pro-indexing, not "pro-active." S&P DJI awarded it for exactly that reason. Third, the Ptak COI framing is too broad: his Barometer shares two of the three conventions but already implements the third (benchmarking to actual passive peers), and he discloses the Barometer in the article.

WHAT SURVIVED CLEANLY: the 92.04/92.66 replication pair, the 55.31% of assets, the 71.34 -> 37.09 fixed-income reversal, the abstract sentence quoted word for word, the two-of-three-adjustments finding, the 150/78 high-yield census, and the 2,844/4,518 fund-month split — all read directly off the source text.

REMAINING UNCERTAINTY: SSRN's abstract page and the Advisor Perspectives article of 2026-06-29 are both hard-403 to automated fetch, so I cannot rule out a revised draft after May 4, 2026, nor confirm whether Cremers published a rejoinder to Ptak in late June. Both should be checked by hand before the article asserts that Ptak's critique stands unanswered. I also declined to certify the widely quoted S&P DJI response line ("SPIVA measures the proportion of funds that underperform, rather than the proportion of assets") because it reached me only through a search summarizer, and per the fabrication warnings on this run I quote only strings I have seen in a document I fetched.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) YE2024 Report 2: of Dec-2020 top-quartile domestic funds, 5.27% remained top-quartile after one year, 0.00% by years 2-4
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in Report 2 ('Performance Persistence of Domestic Equity Funds over Five Consecutive 12-Month Periods'), All Domestic Funds row: Fund Count at Start (December 2020) = 512; Dec 2021 = 5.27; Dec 2022 = 0.00; Dec 2023 = 0.00; Dec 2024 = 0.00. Source document authenticated: the requisitecm.com mirror is byte-identical (401,004 bytes) to the official spglobal.com PDF retrieved from the Wayback Machine capture of 2025-05-13, and every cited figure matches in both.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Pure chance predicts 0.25^4 = 0.39% (~2 of 512 funds), so 'zero' is 0.39pp below random, not orders of magnitude
itemVerdicts.note: The ARITHMETIC is right and the fund count checks out: 0.25^4 = 0.390625%, and 512 x 0.00390625 = 2.00 funds exactly. The ATTRIBUTION is what needs fixing. WRONG (if implied): that SPIVA states a 0.39% random benchmark for four-year top-quartile persistence. RIGHT: SPIVA YE2024 never prints 0.39% anywhere -- I grepped the full text for 'random', '0.39' and '6.25'. The only random benchmarks SPIVA prints are footnote 1 ('The odds of a top-half fund in one year randomly staying in the top half over the next four years are 50%*50%*50%*50% = 6.25%, or 1/16') and the Report Highlights line comparing two-year top-quartile persistence to 'an expected 6.25% based on random chance'. The 0.39% figure is the article's own calculation and must be flagged as such. Supporting note that strengthens the article's caliber point: with an expectation of 2 funds, observing 0 is not statistically distinguishable from chance -- Poisson(2) gives P(0) = 13.5%.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) The honest test is top-half persistence: 4.21% (all domestic) and 2.42% (large-cap) stayed top-half five consecutive years vs 6.25% random
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in Report 2, Top Half panel, December 2024 column: All Domestic Funds (Fund Count at Start Dec 2020 = 1021) = 4.21; All Large-Cap Funds (count 330) = 2.42. The 6.25% random benchmark is SPIVA's own, stated in footnote 1 as 50%*50%*50%*50%. 'Five consecutive years' is SPIVA's own framing (Exhibit 1 y-axis: 'Remaining in Top Half Over Five Consecutive Years'), meaning the Dec-2020 base year plus four subsequent years -- hence the four-fold exponent. All five categories are below 6.25% (Multi-Cap 5.32, Domestic 4.21, Small-Cap 2.79, Large-Cap 2.42, Mid-Cap 0.76), matching Exhibit 1's bars of 5.3 / 4.2 / 2.8 / 2.4 / 0.8.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Mortality asymmetry: 25% of fourth-quartile funds (2014-19 performance) merged/liquidated within five years vs 7% of top-quartile
itemVerdicts.note: Substantively confirmed but the citation and the population qualifier need tightening. Exact primary figures, Report 5 ('Five-Year Transition Matrix -- Performance of Domestic Equity Funds over Two Non-Overlapping Five-Year Periods'), All Domestic Funds, base period December 2014-December 2019, outcome window December 2019-December 2024: 1st Quartile (470 funds) Merged/Liquidated = 6.81%; 4th Quartile (470 funds) Merged/Liquidated = 24.89%. SPIVA's own Report Highlights rounds these to 7% and 25%. WRONG: attributing the 25%/7% pair to 'Reports 5/11'. RIGHT: those two numbers come from Report 5 alone, which covers domestic EQUITY funds; Report 11 is the domestic FIXED INCOME five-year transition matrix (e.g. Investment-Grade Intermediate: 1st Quartile 10.00% merged/liquidated vs 4th Quartile 30.00%, 30 funds per quartile). SPIVA cites 'Reports 5 and 11' only for the general cross-asset pattern, not for the 25%/7% equity pair. Also add 'domestic U.S. equity' as the population qualifier -- SPIVA's own sentence reads '25% of all fourth-quartile domestic U.S. equity funds'. The gradient is monotone and supports the inference: Q1 6.81, Q2 11.94, Q3 15.78, Q4 24.89.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) YE2025 update: 0.46% of 2021 top-quartile domestic equity funds remained top-quartile through Dec 2025
itemVerdicts.note: Could not reach the primary document and therefore cannot confirm or refute; DO NOT PRINT 0.46%. The S&P PDF (https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/documents/spiva/persistence-scorecard-year-end-2025.pdf) returns Akamai 403 to curl, to WebFetch, to r.jina.ai, and to three CORS proxies; the SPIVA article page is also 403; the Wayback Machine's only capture of that URL (2026-07-31) is itself an archived 403 error page, not the PDF; requisitecm.com has no 2025 mirror (its /pdf/ index is 403 and the guessed 2025 filename returns the firm's homepage); advisorperspectives.com and etftrends.com both 403. Actively disconfirming evidence against printing the number: two independent search summarizers returned MUTUALLY CONTRADICTORY figures for this same cell -- one said '505 All Domestic Funds ... only 0.40% remained in the top quartile by December 2022, and this declined to 0.00% by December 2023 and beyond', the other said '0.46% managed to stay there through December 2025'. Those cannot both be true and at least one is a summarizer artifact. Separately, the one fully-fetchable secondary source (genuineimpact.substack.com, 2026-08-04) was asked directly whether it states an ALL-DOMESTIC top-quartile-through-2025 figure and answered NOT PRESENT; it only carries large-cap detail, which it quotes as 'Of the 164 large-cap funds that started in the top quartile, 20.1% held it through 2022. Through 2023, the figure was zero, and it stayed at zero through 2024 and 2025.'

corrections: Do not attribute the 0.39% random-chance benchmark to SPIVA. S&P's YE2024 Persistence Scorecard never prints 0.39%; the only random benchmark it states is 6.25% (footnote 1: 'The odds of a top-half fund in one year randomly staying in the top half over the next four years are 50%*50%*50%*50% = 6.25%, or 1/16'), plus the same 6.25% used for two-year top-quartile persistence in the Report Highlights. Present 0.25^4 = 0.39% as the article's own arithmetic, e.g. 'SPIVA does not print the four-year top-quartile random benchmark, but it is 0.25^4 = 0.39%, or about 2 of the 512 funds.'

Attribute the 25%-vs-7% mortality figures to Report 5 only, not 'Reports 5/11'. Report 5 is the domestic EQUITY five-year transition matrix; Report 11 is the domestic FIXED INCOME analogue. Correct sentence: 'Report 5 shows that 24.89% of fourth-quartile domestic U.S. equity funds (ranked on December 2014-December 2019 performance) were merged or liquidated over the subsequent five years, against 6.81% of top-quartile funds; S&P rounds these to 25% and 7%. Report 11 shows the same pattern in fixed income.'

Add the population qualifier 'domestic U.S. equity' to the mortality claim. The 25%/7% pair is the All Domestic Funds row of Report 5, not funds in general; category rows differ (large-cap 21.43% vs 7.14%, mid-cap 27.94% vs 1.47%, small-cap 24.78% vs 6.19%, multi-cap 26.45% vs 9.09%).

Do NOT print the YE2025 figure of 0.46% for 2021 top-quartile domestic equity funds. It could not be verified against the primary document, and two search summarizers returned contradictory values (0.40% at Dec 2022 vs 0.46% through Dec 2025) for the same cell. Either drop the YE2025 update entirely, or restrict it to what the YE2024 primary supports.

If the article generalizes the top-quartile collapse across categories, use S&P's own wording, which is about the END of the window, not year 2: 'Among top-quartile funds within all reported active domestic equity categories as of December 2020, not a single fund remained in the top quartile over the next four years.' Do not write that every category hit zero by year 2 -- Report 2 shows All Small-Cap Funds still at 0.79% at December 2022.
newContradictions: Do not sum or cross-check the category rows against the All Domestic row in Report 2: All Domestic Funds shows 0.00% at December 2022 while All Small-Cap Funds shows 0.79% at the same date. This is not an error in the source -- quartiles are computed within each universe separately, so the category cohorts are not subsets of the all-domestic cohort. Any sentence implying the categories partition the domestic total would be wrong.

The 0.39% random benchmark is itself an overstatement of what was attainable, which cuts in the article's favor and is worth one clause: over the four-year window a large share of the starting cohort merged, liquidated, or changed style (Report 5's All Domestic 1st-quartile row alone shows 6.81% merged/liquidated and 25.11% style-changed over a five-year window), so the ceiling on measured persistence is below 100% and the true chance-adjusted expectation is under 0.39%.

Statistical-power caveat that supports the article's 'not orders of magnitude' framing and should probably be stated: an expectation of 2 funds out of 512 means observing 0 is entirely consistent with randomness -- under Poisson(2), P(0) = 13.5%. The four-year top-quartile 'zero' therefore carries almost no evidential weight on its own, which is exactly why the top-half test (4.21% vs 6.25%, on 1,021 funds) is the load-bearing one.

Secondhand YE2025 reporting is internally inconsistent across sources and should not be relied on: one summarizer states 'Across every reported active domestic equity category except small-cap, not one top-quartile fund from 2021 was still top-quartile at the end of 2025' (implying a nonzero all-domestic figure), while another states the all-domestic figure went to 0.00% from December 2023 onward. Both cannot hold.
reasoning:
The local extraction files named in the prompt (pers2024.txt et al.) did not exist in this session's scratchpad -- I searched every scratchpad under /private/tmp/claude-502 and /Users/cissychen/design and found none -- so I obtained the primaries myself rather than trusting any prior extraction.

PRIMARY REACHED FOR (a) AND (b): I downloaded the SPIVA U.S. Persistence Scorecard Year-End 2024 PDF from the requisitecm.com mirror, extracted it with pdftotext -layout, and read the tables directly. Because a mirror is only as trustworthy as its provenance, I then pulled the official S&P copy from the Wayback Machine capture of 2025-05-13 of https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/documents/spiva/persistence-scorecard-year-end-2024.pdf. Both files are 401,004 bytes, 16 pages, and every cited cell matches line-for-line. The mirror is authentic.

Read verbatim from Report 2 (five consecutive 12-month periods, base December 2020): All Domestic Funds top-quartile, n=512, 5.27 / 0.00 / 0.00 / 0.00. Top-half panel: All Domestic n=1021 ending 4.21; All Large-Cap n=330 ending 2.42. Footnote 1 gives the 6.25% random benchmark as 50%^4. Read verbatim from Report 5 (base December 2014-December 2019, outcome December 2019-December 2024): All Domestic 1st Quartile n=470 merged/liquidated 6.81%, 4th Quartile n=470 merged/liquidated 24.89%, with a monotone gradient through Q2 11.94 and Q3 15.78. Confirmed Report 11 is domestic fixed income, not equity. Grepped the whole text for 'random', '0.39' and '6.25' to establish that 0.39% appears nowhere in the source.

WHAT I COULD NOT REACH: the Year-End 2025 scorecard. S&P's Akamai edge returns 403 to curl with full browser headers, to WebFetch, to r.jina.ai, and to allorigins/corsproxy/codetabs; the SPIVA landing page is also 403; no Chrome browser is connected to this account (list_connected_browsers returned empty); the only Wayback capture of the 2025 PDF URL is an archived 403 error page; there is no requisitecm 2025 mirror; advisorperspectives and etftrends both 403. The one fetchable secondary (genuineimpact.substack.com, dated 2026-08-04) explicitly answered NOT PRESENT when asked for an all-domestic figure. Two search summarizers gave contradictory numbers for the very cell in question, which is precisely the failure mode this run has already been burned by, so I am marking (c) unreachable rather than laundering a summarizer number into the article.

REMAINING UNCERTAINTY: the YE2025 all-domestic top-quartile figure is genuinely unknown to me; if the article needs it, someone with browser access to spglobal.com must read Report 2 of the Year-End 2025 PDF directly. Everything in (a) and (b) is settled against the primary, with the two attribution fixes noted above.
