itemVerdicts.item: (c) No primary source computes the cumulative fee saving attributable to indexation
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as stated: a primary source exists. Vanguard's own published material ('50 years, 50 facts: Indexing since 1976,' corporate.vanguard.com, data through Dec 31, 2025) states verbatim: 'Over one recently ended 25-year period, indexing helped investors save an estimated $570 billion in fees—money that stayed invested and continued compounding.' Methodology: assumes index investors would otherwise have paid the then-prevailing asset-weighted average ACTIVE fund expense ratio; savings = cumulative difference between what index investors actually paid and that counterfactual. RIGHT version: no INDEPENDENT/neutral primary source (ICI, Morningstar) computes a cumulative figure — both only report point-in-time or single-year deltas — but Vanguard (an interested party, the largest index-fund sponsor) does publish a cumulative estimate ($570bn over 25 years) using a specific, disputable counterfactual assumption. If the article states flatly 'no primary source exists,' it must be softened to 'no independent/neutral primary source' and should either cite the Vanguard figure with its conflict-of-interest caveat or explicitly construct its own estimate as originally planned.

corrections: Sub-claim (c) must be qualified: a primary source computing a cumulative fee-saving-from-indexation figure DOES exist — Vanguard's '50 years, 50 facts' (corporate.vanguard.com, data through 12/31/2025) states 'indexing helped investors save an estimated $570 billion in fees' over 'one recently ended 25-year period,' using a counterfactual that assumes index investors would otherwise have paid the prevailing asset-weighted active-fund expense ratio. The article should replace 'there is NO primary source' with 'no independent/neutral primary source' and note the Vanguard figure exists but comes from an interested party (the largest index-fund sponsor) using a specific, disputable counterfactual methodology — it should not be treated as a neutral estimate, and if the article wants a neutral cumulative number it still must construct one explicitly.

Minor precision note for (a): the 1996 and 2025 active/index equity numbers (1.08%, 0.64%, 0.27%, 0.05%) come from ICI's Figure 6 bar-chart data labels rather than narrative sentences; the 2025 endpoints (0.64% active, 0.05% index) are independently corroborated in the report's prose text, but the 1996 starting points (1.08%, 0.27%) rest only on the chart labels — flag this as chart-sourced if precision of provenance matters.
newContradictions: Vanguard's '50 years, 50 facts' page (corporate.vanguard.com/content/corporatesite/us/en/corp/articles/50-years-50-facts-indexing-since-1976.html) claims investors saved a cumulative $570 billion in fees from indexing over a 25-year period ending ~2025 — this is a primary-source cumulative fee-saving figure that the claim group asserted does not exist. It should be treated with caution (interested-party source, specific counterfactual assumption) but cannot be ignored if the article addresses cumulative savings claims.
reasoning: The two local files named in the prompt (ici_per32.txt, msfee2026.txt) did NOT exist in the scratchpad (verified via ls and find — only unrelated files like cfms.txt, pers2024.txt, etc. were present). I reconstructed both from primary PDFs: (1) ICI Research Perspective 32-1 — direct curl to ici.org URLs was blocked by Akamai/Edgesuite ('Access Denied'), so I located the correct URL via WebSearch (https://www.ici.org/system/files/2026-03/per32-01.pdf), fetched it via WebFetch (which internally retrieved and cached the actual PDF binary), then ran pdftotext -layout on the cached binary to get verbatim page text, and saved it locally as ici_per32.txt. (2) Morningstar 2026 US Fund Fee Study — found the correct PDF URL via WebSearch, curl succeeded directly, and I ran pdftotext -layout to produce msfee2026.txt. All numbers in sub-claims (a) and (b) were checked against these verbatim extracted texts, not summaries — I quoted exact sentences and cross-checked chart data labels against corroborating prose sentences where available (index equity 0.05% in 2025, active domestic equity industry average 0.64% in 2025, $15.0bn vs $2.8bn average fund size, Morningstar's 0.80%→0.32% 2006-2025 delta, the $6.8bn one-year-delta framing, and the 0.58% vs 1.00% active-equity asset-weighted/equal-weighted split). Sub-claim (a) and (b) HOLD verbatim. For sub-claim (c) I actively searched (per instructions to hunt for contradicting sources) for any primary source computing a cumulative indexation fee saving, and found one: Vanguard's own '50 years, 50 facts' page states a $570 billion cumulative saving over a 25-year period through Dec 31, 2025, verified verbatim via WebFetch. This directly contradicts the flat claim that 'there is NO primary source' — it exists, though from an interested party (Vanguard, the dominant index-fund sponsor) using a specific counterfactual methodology, so the claim needs qualification to 'no independent/neutral primary source.' Overall verdict is CORRECTED because sub-claim (c), as literally stated, is false, even though (a) and (b) check out cleanly.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Pastor-Stambaugh-Taylor (JFE 2015): +1pp of active-industry share of market cap -> gross fund performance falls ~40bp/yr (extended sample ~20bp)
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim from the paper (NBER w19891 p.17-18 and the Nov-2013 circulated version, identical text): 'consider a one percentage point increase in IndustrySize, which is not too large. In our main sample, this increase in IndustrySize is associated with a sizable decrease in fund performance: 0.0326% per month, or almost 40 bp per year. In the extended sample, the magnitude of the same effect is smaller but still substantial, about 20 bp per year.' IndustrySize is verbatim 'the sum of AUM across all funds in our sample, divided by the total market value of all stocks' = active-MF share of market cap; it 'starts at 2.4% in January 1979, peaks at 18.6% in July 2008, and finishes at 16.8% in December 2011.' Three specification/window details the article must not drop: (i) main sample = 1993-2011, extended sample = 1979-2011 (the 40bp is NOT the full-history number); (ii) the coefficient is from the OLS-with-fund-fixed-effects column (t=-3.60 main, -4.34 extended), with RD point estimates 'virtually identical'; (iii) the dependent variable GrossR is a benchmark-adjusted GROSS return, not a factor alpha, and PST's data END in December 2011 — the 'post-2010 shrinkage' extrapolation is the article's, not PST's. Robustness holds: Pastor, Stambaugh, Taylor and Zhu, 'Diseconomies of Scale in Active Management: Robust Evidence,' Critical Finance Review 11(3-4), 2022, confirm the industry-level result under robust regression. Version caveat: I could not open the paywalled JFE typeset text, but two circulated versions carry identical wording and coefficients.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Cremers-Ferreira-Matos-Starks (JFE 2016): average alpha higher where explicit indexing is bigger, but the interaction shows marginal return to being more active is LOWER there
itemVerdicts.note: Directionally right and the two halves do come from the same table — but the article omits that BOTH results are significant only in Panel B. Verified in the accepted version ('forthcoming in Journal of Financial Economics'), Table 7, dependent variable = yearly benchmark-adjusted (net-return) four-factor alpha, sample 2002-2010. Panel B (country of SALE), column (2): Explicit indexing (%TNA) = +0.1196 (t=4.16); Active share x Explicit indexing (%TNA) = -0.1753 (t=-4.21). Panel A (country of DOMICILE), column (2): +0.0106 (t=0.43) and -0.0351 (t=-0.95) — BOTH INSIGNIFICANT. Verbatim conclusion: 'the coefficient on the interaction between active share and the market share of explicitly indexed funds is negative and significant (in Panel B) ... We thus conclude that the marginal returns to active management are lower in markets with more prevalent and cheaper explicitly indexed funds.' Denominator check: 'Explicit indexing (% TNA) is the market share of explicitly indexed funds as a percentage of the TNA in each country in a given year' — share of country MUTUAL-FUND ASSETS, not market cap.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Fama-French 2010: aggregate gross VW three-factor alpha +0.13%/yr (t=0.40) on 1984-2006
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim (JF 65(5), 2010, p.1921): 'The intercepts in (1) for VW gross returns are quite close to zero, 0.13% per year (t = 0.40) for the three-factor version of (1), and -0.05% per year (t = -0.15) for the four-factor model.' Table II, 1984-2006: VW three-factor gross coef 0.13, t 0.40; VW three-factor NET coef -0.81, t -2.50; CAPM VW gross -0.18 (t=-0.49). 'alpha = minus fees' paraphrase is fair: 'When we add back the costs in expense ratios, alpha estimates for VW gross fund returns are close to zero.' EW gross three-factor is 0.36%/yr (t=0.85) — do not swap EW for VW. Sample window 1984-2006 confirmed.

itemVerdicts.item: (c-ii) Harvey & Liu (JF 2022): the FF bootstrap 'has little or no power to detect the truly outperforming funds'
itemVerdicts.note: The quote is real but the article applies it to the wrong statistic. Verbatim (Harvey and Liu, 'Luck versus Skill in the Cross Section of Mutual Fund Returns: Reexamining the Evidence,' Journal of Finance 77(3), June 2022, p.1946): 'it is perhaps unsurprising that the FF technique has little or no power to detect the truly outperforming funds in our simulation.' WRONG use: citing this as impeaching the +0.13%/yr (t=0.40) aggregate VW gross alpha. RIGHT scope: HL's power result concerns FF's CROSS-SECTIONAL BOOTSTRAP TEST on individual funds' alphas, and is driven specifically by undersampling from FF's minimum of only eight observations ('the FF approach suffers from undersampling'; 'the undersampling of the FF approach causes problems with funds with a small number of observations'). The 0.13%/t=0.40 figure comes from a plain time-series OLS regression on an aggregate portfolio — no bootstrap is involved, and HL never re-estimate it. HL also do not reject FF wholesale: 'we recommend the use of the FF approach with a complete history of returns (i.e., CROSSI_full). It has near-optimal size and much higher test power', and they find the rival KTWW method 'substantially overrejects.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Berk-van Binsbergen (JFE 2015): AUM-weighted mean value added $3.2m/yr (t=5.74), median negative, 57.01% of funds below zero
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers right, WEIGHTING LABEL WRONG. WRONG: 'AUM-weighted mean value added.' RIGHT: it is TIME-weighted — the cross-sectional mean weighted by the number of months each fund exists. Table 3 note verbatim: 'The Cross-Sectional Weighted mean, standard error and t-statistic are computed by weighting by the number of periods the fund exists, that is, they are the statistical properties of S-bar_W defined by (9).' Text verbatim: 'Table 3 provides the time-weighted mean of S_i (given by (9)) in our sample. The average fund added an economically significant $270,000 per month, or $3.2 million annually (in Y2000 dollars).' 0.27 x 12 = $3.24m/yr; t = 5.74 (Vanguard benchmark) / $0.25m and t=3.94 (FFC). The EQUAL-weighted cross-sectional mean is only $0.14m/month (t=4.57). Other side of the table confirmed verbatim: 50th percentile = -0.02 ($m/month) and 'Percent with less than zero 57.01%' (Vanguard) / 59.70% (FFC); text: 'The median fund lost an average of $20,000/month, and only 43% of funds had positive estimated value added ... most funds destroyed value but because most of the capital is controlled by skilled managers, as a group, active mutual funds added value.' Two further caveats: the sample runs January 1977 to March 2011 in Y2000 dollars (it too predates the passive ramp), and value added is dollars extracted from markets that accrue to the MANAGER via fees, not returns to investors. Version caveat: verified identically in NBER w18184 and Rodney White WP 17-14; the JFE 118(1) typeset version is paywalled.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Unterberg, 'Passive Flows, Active Woes' (SSRN 6902444, June 2026): net 4-factor alpha -0.72%/yr (1984-2009) -> -1.82%/yr (2010-24); VW gross alpha ~0 -> -0.66%/yr; industry-level passive-share/active-minus-passive-spread relation flipped sign
itemVerdicts.note: PRIMARY NOT REACHED. papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6902444 serves a Cloudflare 'Verify you are human' interstitial to WebFetch, curl, and a real browser; I am not permitted to complete bot-detection challenges. ResearchGate returns 403; CXO Advisory's writeup is paywalled; the Morningstar US URL given in the article's source list also 403s. What I DID reach at first hand is the author's own site, hannahunterberg.com/research, whose abstract reads verbatim: 'Using U.S. equity fund data (1984-2024), I document a decline in active fund performance after 2010, with average annual four-factor alpha falling by around one percentage point and the previously positive relation between Active Share and performance reversing. These patterns contrast with theories predicting improved performance as the active sector shrinks.' That corroborates the ~1pp magnitude and the existence/date of the paper (UC Irvine Merage; the site lists the Brattle Group PhD Candidate Award, WFA 2026 — NOT the 'Two Sigma Award' a search summarizer asserted), but contains none of the three specific figures. All three DO match the article's named secondhand source word for word — Larry Swedroe, Morningstar, 17 August 2026, readable at morningstar.com.au/funds/how-passive-investing-is-driving-decline-active-fund-alpha: 'average net alpha for active funds fell from negative 0.72% annually (1984-2009) to negative 1.82% annually (2010-24)'; 'before fees the value-weighted active fund sector performed similarly to the market portfolio, with alpha close to zero, during the 1984-2009 period. After 2010, the value-weighted portfolio earns a four-factor gross alpha of negative 0.66% per year'; and '6) The industry-level "returns to scale" relationship also flipped. Historically, a larger passive share of the industry predicted a wider active-minus-passive return spread ... After 2010, a larger passive share predicts a narrower spread.' So the article transcribed its secondhand source faithfully — but these remain secondhand, from an unrefereed June 2026 working paper, and the third item in particular does not appear in the author's own abstract.

corrections: (d) Berk-van Binsbergen: replace 'AUM-weighted mean value added' with 'time-weighted mean value added (weighted by the number of months each fund exists)'. Berk and van Binsbergen's Table 3 note reads: 'The Cross-Sectional Weighted mean, standard error and t-statistic are computed by weighting by the number of periods the fund exists.' The $270,000/month = $3.2m/yr, t=5.74 figure is that time-weighted mean; the equal-weighted cross-sectional mean is $140,000/month (t=4.57). Nothing in the paper is AUM-weighted.

(c) Harvey & Liu: do not deploy the 'little or no power' quote against Fama-French's +0.13%/yr (t=0.40) aggregate VW gross alpha. That number comes from a plain time-series OLS regression on an aggregate portfolio, not from a bootstrap, and Harvey-Liu never re-estimate it. Their power result concerns FF's CROSS-SECTIONAL BOOTSTRAP TEST on individual funds' alphas, and is driven by undersampling arising from FF's minimum of only eight monthly observations per fund. Add the qualifier, and add that Harvey-Liu recommend keeping the FF approach with complete return histories ('near-optimal size and much higher test power') while finding the rival Kosowski et al. method 'substantially overrejects'.

(b) Cremers-Ferreira-Matos-Starks: state that both halves of the result are statistically significant only in Panel B (variables measured by country of SALE). In Table 7 column (2), Panel B: Explicit indexing (%TNA) = +0.1196 (t=4.16), Active share x Explicit indexing (%TNA) = -0.1753 (t=-4.21); in Panel A (country of DOMICILE) the same two coefficients are +0.0106 (t=0.43) and -0.0351 (t=-0.95), both insignificant. Also say that 'explicit indexing' there is a share of a country's MUTUAL-FUND total net assets, not of market cap, and that the dependent variable is a benchmark-adjusted NET-return four-factor alpha over 2002-2010.

(a) Pastor-Stambaugh-Taylor: attach the sample windows to the two numbers — ~40bp/yr is the MAIN sample (1993-2011) and ~20bp/yr the EXTENDED sample (1979-2011), from the OLS-with-fund-fixed-effects specification (t = -3.60 and -4.34). Also state that PST's data end in December 2011, so the inference that the post-2010 contraction 'should have raised gross alpha' is the article's extrapolation beyond PST's sample, not a PST finding.

Terminology: stop using 'active share' for two different things. PST's IndustrySize is the active mutual fund industry's AUM as a share of total stock market capitalization; Cremers-Petajisto 'Active Share' (used in claims (b) and (e)) is a fund-level measure of holdings deviation from benchmark. Claim (e)'s headline reversal is in the latter. Conflating them makes the paragraph read as if one measure flipped sign in two papers.

(e) Unterberg: label all three figures explicitly as reported by Larry Swedroe in Morningstar (17 August 2026), from an unrefereed June 2026 SSRN working paper that could not be opened directly. Note also that the author's own posted abstract states only the ~1 percentage point alpha decline and the reversal of the Active Share-performance relation; the 'industry-level passive share vs active-minus-passive spread flipped sign' item appears only in Swedroe's summary, not in the abstract, and should carry the lowest confidence of the three.

(a)/(e) framing: PST is evidence FOR the Grossman-Stiglitz direction (a smaller active sector implies better gross performance), not against it. If the section is headed 'the evidence runs the wrong way', make explicit that PST supplies the prediction and only Unterberg (secondhand, unrefereed) supplies the post-2010 refutation.
newContradictions: Fama-French 2010's aggregate VW gross alpha and Berk-van Binsbergen's value-added result are not independent confirmations of each other, and neither speaks to the post-2010 period: FF2010's regression sample is 1984-2006 and BvB's fund sample is January 1977 to March 2011. Both end before the passive share of US equity fund assets crossed 50%. Any 'the aggregate was always roughly zero gross' claim is a statement about the pre-ramp era only.

Berk-van Binsbergen measure dollars EXTRACTED FROM MARKETS by managers, which in their own framework accrue to managers as fees rather than to investors as returns. Quoting the positive $3.2m alongside FF2010's alphas as if both describe investor outcomes conflates two different objects.

Cremers-Ferreira-Matos-Starks' 'more indexing, higher average alpha' result is essentially a COMPETITION story (their words: 'enhanced competition by low-cost explicitly indexed funds spurs active funds to deliver better after-fee performance'), i.e. fee and effort discipline within the fund industry, not an informational-efficiency story about price discovery. It is weak support for any claim about indexing and market informativeness.

Evaluated at a typical fund's Active Share, the CFMS Panel B point estimates roughly cancel: 0.1196 - 0.1753 x AS is about zero for AS near 0.68 and negative above it. So the paper does not support 'more indexing means higher alpha for genuinely active funds' — only for benchmark-hugging ones.

Swedroe's Morningstar piece states index funds and ETFs 'have grown from about 19% to over 50% of equity FUND ASSETS since 2010'. If the article reuses that figure, it must not be relabelled as a share of market capitalization or of trading volume.

Unterberg's mechanism (persistent price pressure from passive flows depressing off-benchmark holdings) is a demand/price-impact story that explicitly denies declining manager skill. It therefore cuts against, not for, the version of the index-bubble thesis that says indexing degrades price discovery because informed active managers have exited.
reasoning:
The local extraction files named in the brief (pst.txt, bvb.txt, cfms2016.txt, ff2010real.txt, etc.) do not exist anywhere on this machine — the named scratchpad contains only two unrelated directories (v15_oii, v15venv), and a filesystem-wide find for pst.txt/bvb.txt/cfms2016.txt/ff2010real.txt/spiva-my2025.txt returned nothing. The second real error is scope creep on Harvey-Liu, whose power critique targets FF's cross-sectional bootstrap over individual funds, not the aggregate VW gross-alpha OLS that produces 0.13%/t=0.40. itemVerdicts.item: (a) ICI Research Perspective 32-1 (March 2026): actively managed equity MF asset-weighted expense ratio 1.08% (1996) -> 0.64% (2025); index equity MF 0.27% (1996) -> 0.05% (2025)
itemVerdicts.note: Verified against the actual primary PDF (the local scratchpad file ici_per32.pdf was a Level3/Akamai 'Access Denied' HTML stub, NOT the real document -- re-fetched via WebFetch and re-extracted with pdftotext). Figure 6 ('Average Expense Ratios for Both Actively Managed and Index Mutual Funds Have Fallen') gives equity mutual funds: actively managed 1996=1.08, 2024=0.64, 2025=0.64; index 1996=0.27, 2024=0.05, 2025=0.05. The 2025 endpoints are independently corroborated elsewhere in the same report: Figure 3 states '...the average expense ratio for actively managed domestic equity mutual funds at small fund complexes was 1.00%, higher than the industry average of 0.64%' (note: 'Data only include actively managed equity mutual funds'), and Figure 2's memo row for 'Index equity mutual funds' gives asset-weighted average = 0.05% for 2025. Two independent extraction passes (layout and raw) of the real PDF agree on all four numbers; assignment of 1.08/0.27 to 1996 active/index respectively is internally consistent (active always priced above index throughout the document) and matches known prior-year ICI fee-study series.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Average index equity mutual fund $15.0bn vs average actively managed equity mutual fund $2.8bn (scale/mix partly explains the gap)
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim from ICI report body: 'At year-end 2025, the average index equity mutual fund ($15.0 billion) was substantially larger than the average actively managed equity mutual fund ($2.8 billion).' The report itself attributes the fee gap to three factors -- low turnover, narrower/large-cap-blend investment focus (mix), and economies of scale from larger average fund size -- so the claim's 'scale/mix partly explains the gap' gloss is an accurate abbreviation (it omits the turnover point but adds nothing false).

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Morningstar 2026 US Fund Fee Study: all-fund asset-weighted fee 0.80% (2006) -> 0.32% (2025)
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim from local msfee2026.txt (matches the genuine PDF, 'MANAGER RESEARCH | MAY 2026 / 2026 US Fund Fee Study / Notable fee trends through 2025'): 'Between 2006 and 2025, the asset-weighted average fee fell to 0.32% from 0.80%.'

itemVerdicts.item: (b) '$6.8 billion saved' is a ONE-YEAR delta (2bp x assets in 2025), not cumulative savings from the passive shift
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'We estimate that investors saved nearly USD 6.8 billion in fund expenses last year as the asset-weighted average expense ratio for all US mutual funds and ETFs ticked down to 0.32% in 2025 from 0.34% in 2024.' This is explicitly a single-year (2024->2025, 2bp) delta applied to 2025 assets -- confirmed to be a one-year figure, not a cumulative multi-decade saving. The claim's characterization of it as 'routinely misquoted' as cumulative is a reasonable framing note, not itself a checkable fact from the document, but the underlying one-year-delta description is verbatim-correct.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Active US equity 0.58% asset-weighted vs 1.00% equal-weighted
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'the asset-weighted average expense ratio for active US equity funds was 0.58% in 2025, versus 1.00% when calculating an equal-weighted average.'

itemVerdicts.item: (c) No primary source computes the cumulative fee saving attributable to indexation; article must construct one explicitly if wanted
itemVerdicts.note: Consistent with what both primary sources actually show: ICI's report presents expense-ratio trend lines and fund-size/scale statistics but computes no aggregate dollar 'total saved by indexation' figure; Morningstar's only dollar-saving figure ($6.8bn) is explicitly a one-year snapshot (see above), not a cumulative or passive-attributed figure. No contradicting source of a ready-made cumulative-savings-from-indexation estimate was found in either document. This is a methodological/negative claim rather than a quotable assertion, but nothing in the primary sources contradicts it.

reasoning: Local scratchpad file ici_per32.pdf turned out to be a Level3/Akamai 'Access Denied' HTML error page (verified via `file` and `head -c`), not the real ICI document -- this would have produced a false 'unreachable' or worse, a hallucinated verification, if not caught. Re-fetched the genuine PDF via WebFetch (https://www.ici.org/files/2026/per32-01.pdf, which downloaded a real 1MB binary this time, distinct from the earlier stub), then ran pdftotext -layout and pdftotext -raw locally on the saved binary to get verbatim text, cross-checked in two independent extraction modes. Confirmed: (1) actively managed equity MF asset-weighted expense ratio 1.08% (1996) -> 0.64% (2025) and index equity MF 0.27% (1996) -> 0.05% (2025), corroborated independently by Figure 3 (0.64% 'industry average' for actively managed domestic equity funds, 2025) and Figure 2's memo row (0.05% asset-weighted for index equity funds, 2025) elsewhere in the same document, not just the chart figure being quoted; (2) average index equity MF $15.0bn vs active $2.8bn, verbatim; document itself attributes the gap partly to fund-mix/investment-focus and partly to economies of scale (matches 'scale/mix' framing). For Morningstar, the local msfee2026.txt file was legitimate real extracted text (title header 'MANAGER RESEARCH | MAY 2026 / 2026 US Fund Fee Study' confirmed) and directly verified: 0.80%(2006)->0.32%(2025) all-fund asset-weighted fee; the $6.8bn figure is explicitly stated as a one-year (2024->2025, 2bp) delta, not cumulative; active US equity 0.58% asset-weighted vs 1.00% equal-weighted, verbatim. Sub-claim (c) (no primary source computes cumulative indexation-attributable savings) is a negative/methodological claim consistent with what both documents actually contain -- no aggregate cumulative-savings figure was found in either source, and Morningstar's only dollar figure is explicitly one-year. No corrections needed; all sub-claims verified verbatim or via independent internal corroboration within the primary documents themselves.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) YE2024 Report 2: of 512 Dec-2020 top-quartile All Domestic funds, 5.27% top-quartile at Dec 2021, 0.00% at Dec 2022/2023/2024
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the local primary (pers2024.txt) AND independently re-extracted from pers2024.pdf page 5 with `pdftotext -layout` to rule out extraction garbling. Report 2 row 'All Domestic Funds': Fund Count at Start (December 2020) = 512; December 2021 = 5.27; December 2022 = 0.00; December 2023 = 0.00; December 2024 = 0.00. Internal arithmetic checks: 27/512 = 5.2734% -> 5.27, so the surviving count is exactly 27 funds. The report's own Summary states verbatim: 'Among top-quartile funds within all reported active domestic equity categories as of December 2020, not a single fund remained in the top quartile over the next four years (see Report 2).' Note All Small-Cap was 0.79% at Dec 2022 (not zero at year 2), so the 'zero from year 2 on' statement is true for All Domestic and for the Dec-2024 endpoint across all five categories, but not for every category at every intermediate year.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Random benchmark 0.25^4 = 0.39% (~2 of 512 funds); 'zero' is 0.39pp below random, not orders of magnitude
itemVerdicts.note: Arithmetic exact: 0.25^4 = 0.00390625 = 0.390625%, and 0.390625% x 512 = exactly 2.00 funds. The convention matches SPDJI's own: footnote 1 of the report reads 'The odds of a top-half fund in one year randomly staying in the top half over the next four years are 50%*50%*50%*50% = 6.25%, or 1/16', and Report Highlights uses 6.25% (=0.25^2) as the random benchmark for two subsequent years of top-quartile persistence. So 0.25^4 for four subsequent years is SPDJI-consistent, not an invented null. The article's corrective is if anything too weak: under the null, P(exactly zero of 512) = (1-0.00390625)^512 = 13.5%, i.e. observing zero is entirely unremarkable. And conditioning on the observed path (27 funds alive at Dec 2021), the null predicts 27 x 0.25^3 = 0.42 funds by Dec 2024 - under half a fund.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Top-half persistence: 4.21% (All Domestic) and 2.42% (All Large-Cap) stayed top-half five consecutive years vs 6.25% random
itemVerdicts.note: Report 2, 'Percentage Remaining in Top Half', December 2024 column: All Domestic Funds 4.21 (count at start 1021; 43/1021 = 4.2116%), All Large-Cap Funds 2.42 (count at start 330; 8/330 = 2.4242%). Exhibit 1 plots these as 4.2 and 2.4 against a 6.25 'Expected Persistence Under Random Distribution' line, and is headlined 'Only 2% of All Large-Cap Equity Funds Remained in the Top Half Over a Five-Year Period'. Full Exhibit 1 set: Multi-Cap 5.3, Domestic 4.2, Small-Cap 2.8, Large-Cap 2.4, Mid-Cap 0.8 (Report 2 exact: 5.32/4.21/2.79/2.42/0.76). Corroborated secondhand by Evidence Investor ('Only 4.2% of US funds and 6.1% of European funds remained in the top half over five years'). CALIBER NOTE, not an error: the 6.25% null assumes independence AND survival. Funds that merge/liquidate are mechanically counted as not persisting. Using Report 5's own five-year mortality for the top half of domestic funds (1st quartile 6.81%, 2nd quartile 11.94%; asset-blind equal-weight blend ~9.4%), a survival-adjusted null is ~5.7%, not 6.25%. The 4.21% shortfall survives, but the gap is roughly a third smaller than the naive comparison implies.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Mortality asymmetry: 25% of fourth-quartile funds (2014-19 performance) merged/liquidated within five years vs 7% of top-quartile (Reports 5/11)
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers verified twice. Report Highlights verbatim: 'For example, 25% of all fourth-quartile domestic U.S. equity funds (based on 2014-2019 performance) were either merged or liquidated within the subsequent five years; the comparable figure for top-quartile funds was only 7%. There were similar results among both active equity and active fixed income funds (see Reports 5 and 11).' Report 5 table, All Domestic Funds, Merged/Liquidated column (outcomes Dec 2019-Dec 2024): 1st Quartile 6.81 (32/470), 4th Quartile 24.89 (117/470). ATTRIBUTION CAVEAT: the 25%/7% pair comes from Report 5 (domestic EQUITY) alone. Report 11 is domestic FIXED INCOME and shows the same direction with different magnitudes - IG Intermediate 4th 30.00 vs 1st 10.00; IG Short & Intermediate 26.47 vs 8.82; High Yield 25.00 vs 5.56; Global Income 45.00 vs 15.00. Citing '25% vs 7%' to 'Reports 5/11' jointly would misattribute.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Inference: 'dead funds skew toward losers, which partially validates SPIVA's dead=underperformer convention'
itemVerdicts.note: The DATA is right; the INFERENCE overreaches even with 'partially'. Two problems, both checkable in primary text I read. (1) Category mismatch: Report 5 quartiles are PEER-relative rankings within the active universe, whereas SPIVA's dead=underperformer convention is about the BENCHMARK. Bottom-peer-quartile mortality does not establish that exiting funds trailed their index. (2) A direct counter-primary is sitting in the same scratchpad - Cremers, Fulkerson & Riley, 'How the SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Understates the Performance of Actively Managed Mutual Funds' (iaa_spiva.txt), Section 3.1, verbatim: 'While it is reasonable to expect that most funds exiting the sample have underperformed, Bessembinder, Cooper, and Zhang (2023) demonstrate that a significant portion do not.' And: 'by classifying all exiting funds as underperformers, the Scorecard understates active fund performance.' They quantify it: applying returns over the living period instead, the underperformance rate falls 'by only 0.5% over one year but by 16% over 20 years', and in high yield over 20 years 'decreases from 78% to 52%'. WRONG version: 'dead funds skew toward losers, which partially validates SPIVA's dead=underperformer convention.' RIGHT version: 'dead funds skew heavily toward the worst PEER quartile (24.89% of bottom-quartile domestic equity funds merged or liquidated over 2019-2024 vs 6.81% of top-quartile), so the convention is directionally defensible - but Cremers, Fulkerson and Riley show a significant minority of exiting funds did not underperform, and that treating all of them as failures understates active performance by up to 16 percentage points at 20-year horizons.'

itemVerdicts.item: (c) YE2025: 0.46% of 2021 top-quartile domestic equity funds remained top-quartile through Dec 2025
itemVerdicts.note: COULD NOT REACH THE PRIMARY - DO NOT PRINT THIS NUMBER. spglobal.com/spindices.com now block this environment entirely at the Akamai edge (HTTP 403 'Security Controls Triggered' / 'Access Denied' via curl, via WebFetch, and via a real browser; even the YE2024 PDF URL that the local copy came from now 403s).
