Independent-ish secondhand corroboration exists only for adjacent cells, not this one: two separate sources (a Substack post dated 2026-08-04 and theideafarm) both report 164 large-cap funds top-quartile at end-2021 -> 20.1% through 2022 -> zero from 2023 on; 124 small-cap funds -> 2.4% still top-quartile at end-2025; and 4.5% of above-median large-cap funds staying above median through 2025 vs the 6.25% random expectation. None of them quotes the All Domestic top-quartile row. Sanity check against 0.46%: if the All Domestic starting count is ~505 as one summarizer reports, 0.46% is not attainable at any integer count (1/505 = 0.20%, 2/505 = 0.40%, 3/505 = 0.59%), which is further reason to distrust it.

corrections: DELETE the YE2025 figure. Do not print '0.46% of 2021 top-quartile domestic equity funds remained top-quartile through Dec 2025.' The primary (persistence-scorecard-year-end-2025.pdf) is unreachable - spglobal.com 403s this environment at the Akamai edge, the sole Wayback capture is itself a 403, and no mirror exists. The 0.46% figure surfaced only from a summarizer that had '0.46%' fed to it in the query; a neutrally-queried summarizer returned 0.00% for the same cell, and S&P's own article-page summary reportedly says only small-cap funds had any survivors. If a YE2025 sentence is needed, use only the two figures that two independent secondhand sources agree on, and label them as secondhand: of 164 large-cap funds top-quartile at end-2021, 20.1% held it through 2022 and zero held it from 2023 onward; and 4.5% of above-median large-cap funds stayed above median every year through 2025 against a 6.25% random expectation. Better: cite the YE2024 edition, which is verified verbatim.

Scope the mortality statistic correctly. WRONG: '25% of fourth-quartile funds merged/liquidated within five years vs 7% of top-quartile (Reports 5/11).' RIGHT: '25% of fourth-quartile domestic U.S. EQUITY funds, ranked on 2014-2019 performance, merged or liquidated over the following five years (Dec 2019-Dec 2024), against 7% of top-quartile funds (Report 5; exact values 24.89% and 6.81% of 470 funds each). Report 11 shows the same direction for domestic fixed income with different magnitudes - e.g. 30.00% vs 10.00% for investment-grade intermediate, 25.00% vs 5.56% for high yield.' The 25/7 pair is Report 5 only; attributing it to 'Reports 5/11' jointly is a misattribution.

Fix the inference drawn from the mortality asymmetry. WRONG: 'dead funds skew toward losers, which partially validates SPIVA's dead=underperformer convention.' RIGHT: 'dead funds skew heavily toward the worst-performing PEER quartile, so the convention is directionally defensible - but Report 5 ranks funds against peers, not against a benchmark, and Cremers, Fulkerson and Riley show that treating every exiting fund as a benchmark underperformer materially understates active performance: they write that although most exiting funds did underperform, Bessembinder, Cooper and Zhang (2023) show a significant portion did not, and re-scoring exiting funds over their living period cuts the measured underperformance rate by only 0.5 percentage points at one year but by 16 points at twenty years - from 78% to 52% in high yield.'

Strengthen (and make precise) the random-chance corrective on the 'zero' figure. The article's '0.39pp below random' is correct but understates the case. Add: under the 0.25^4 null, the expected number of survivors from 512 top-quartile funds is exactly 2.0, and the probability of observing exactly zero is 13.5% - so 'zero' is not even a statistically unusual draw. Conditioning on the 27 funds that actually survived year one, the null predicts 0.42 funds by December 2024, i.e. less than one. Also note the null is SPDJI's own: the report's footnote 1 uses 50%^4 = 6.25% for top-half persistence, and its Report Highlights uses 6.25% (= 0.25^2) as the random benchmark for two-year top-quartile persistence.

Add a survival caveat to the 6.25% top-half benchmark. The 6.25% null assumes both independence and survival; funds that merge or liquidate are mechanically scored as not persisting. Using the same report's Report 5 five-year mortality for top-half domestic funds (6.81% of 1st-quartile and 11.94% of 2nd-quartile funds), a survival-adjusted null is roughly 5.7%, not 6.25%. The 4.21% shortfall survives the adjustment, but the gap narrows by about a third - state the observed-vs-null comparison as directional evidence, not as a precise measure of negative skill.

If the article says top-quartile persistence went to zero 'from year 2 on', scope it to All Domestic Funds. Report 2 shows All Small-Cap Funds at 0.79% in December 2022 (year 2). The categorically true statement is S&P's own: no category had a single fund still top-quartile at the December 2024 four-year endpoint.
newContradictions: Cremers, Fulkerson & Riley, 'How the SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Understates the Performance of Actively Managed Mutual Funds' (local file iaa_spiva.txt, Section 3.1) is a direct counter-primary to sub-claim (b)'s inference and was apparently not weighed against it. Verbatim: 'While it is reasonable to expect that most funds exiting the sample have underperformed, Bessembinder, Cooper, and Zhang (2023) demonstrate that a significant portion do not.' And: 'by classifying all exiting funds as underperformers, the Scorecard understates active fund performance.' Quantified impact: underperformance rate falls 'by only 0.5% over one year but by 16% over 20 years'; in high yield over 20 years it 'decreases from 78% to 52%'. It also cites Linnainmaa (2013), 'Reverse survivorship bias', Journal of Finance 68(3), 789-813, for the general point that survivorship corrections can overshoot into reverse bias.

Two web summarizers returned mutually incompatible values for the SAME cell of YE2025 Report 2 (All Domestic Funds, top quartile, December 2025): 0.46% versus 0.00%. The 0.46% appeared only after the figure was placed in the search query, and 0.46% is not attainable at any integer count if the starting universe is ~505 funds. This is a live fabrication risk of exactly the kind flagged in the run's two prior incidents.

Report 5 shows a second, much larger attrition channel the mortality argument ignores: 'Style Changed' runs 25.11% for 1st-quartile and 28.72% for 4th-quartile domestic funds - roughly symmetric across quartiles and larger than the merge/liquidate column for top-quartile funds. Any argument that reads fund disappearance as a performance signal has to account for style reclassification, which carries no such signal and is bigger.
reasoning:
I treated every sub-claim as false until I read the sentence myself, and I re-extracted the key table a second way to guard against a bad PDF conversion.

WHAT I REACHED VERBATIM. The YE2024 U.S. Persistence Scorecard, both as the pre-extracted pers2024.txt and as an independent `pdftotext -layout` pass over pers2024.pdf (page 5 for Report 2, plus Report 5, Report 11, the Summary, Exhibit 1 and footnote 1). The two extractions agree digit for digit, and every percentage reconciles to an integer fund count against the stated denominators - 27/512 = 5.27%, 43/1021 = 4.21%, 8/330 = 2.42%, 32/470 = 6.81%, 117/470 = 24.89% - so the extraction is clean, not garbled. I also read Section 3.1 of the Cremers-Fulkerson-Riley SPIVA critique in the same directory verbatim.

Note on the environment: the scratchpad does not contain the ~200 files the task description promised, and the sandboxed path was empty; the real contents (6 entries) were only visible via /System/Volumes/Data/... Only pers2024 and iaa_spiva were present. So gs1980, pedersen, gk, etc. were not available to cross-check against, and I did not pretend otherwise.

WHAT HOLDS. Sub-claim (a) is exactly right on every number - 512 funds, 5.27%, 0.00% at Dec 2022/2023/2024, 4.21% and 2.42% top-half, 6.25% random. The 0.25^4 = 0.39% null is not the article's invention: it is SPDJI's own convention, stated in footnote 1 (50%^4 = 6.25%) and in Report Highlights (6.25% = 0.25^2 for two years). The arithmetic 0.39% x 512 = exactly 2.0 funds is correct. The corrective is sound and, if anything, too gentle: P(zero survivors) under the null is 13.5%, so zero is not an unusual draw at all. Sub-claim (b)'s numbers are verbatim from Report Highlights and reconcile to Report 5's table.

WHAT DOES NOT HOLD. Two things. First, (b)'s inference. Report 5's quartiles are peer-relative, while SPIVA's convention concerns the benchmark, so the asymmetry is directional support at best - and the counter-primary is sitting in the same directory, unweighed. Second, (c). I could not reach the YE2025 primary by any route: spglobal.com and spindices.com 403 this environment at the Akamai edge for curl, WebFetch and a real browser alike (even the YE2024 URL now 403s); the single Wayback capture of the 2025 PDF is itself an archived 403 with no document text; requisitecm has no 2025 mirror; four proxies fail through to the same 403; and etftrends sits behind a Cloudflare interstitial I will not solve.

The (c) situation is worse than plain unreachability, and this is the finding I would most want carried forward. The 0.46% surfaced only from a summarizer that I had fed '0.46%' in the query - query echo. A neutrally-phrased query returned 0.00% for the identical cell, and a third summarizer reading S&P's own article page returned wording implying only small-cap funds had survivors. On top of that, 0.46% is arithmetically unreachable at any integer count if the denominator is ~505 (1/505 = 0.20%, 2/505 = 0.40%, 3/505 = 0.59%). Only two YE2025 figures have genuine independent secondhand agreement - large-cap 164 funds going to zero from 2023, and 4.5% top-half large-cap persistence - and neither is the claimed cell.

REMAINING UNCERTAINTY. I cannot confirm or refute the YE2025 All Domestic figure; it needs a human with unblocked access to spglobal.com. I found no erratum or revision to the YE2024 edition. One caliber point I would flag even though it was not in the claim as written: the 6.25% top-half null assumes survival, and adjusting it by the report's own top-half mortality (~9.4% over five years) lowers it to ~5.7%, which narrows the observed-vs-random gap by about a third without eliminating it.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Bebchuk & Hirst, Specter of the Giant Three: mean combined Big Three stake in S&P 500 rose 5.2% (1998) → 20.5% (2017)
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in NBER w25914 (= 99 B.U. L. Rev. 721): 'the proportion of S&P 500 shares managed by the Big Three has grown approximately fourfold over the past two decades, from 5.2% in 1998, to 20.5% in 2017.' Table 5 confirms 20.5% is the MEAN (median 19.5%). Russell 3000 counterpart 3.7% → 16.5%.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) The 5.2%→20.5% series includes the Big Three's ACTIVE assets, not just index funds
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed, though the 2019 paper obscures it (Figure 1 is titled 'Percentage of Corporate Equity Held by Big Three Index Funds'). The authors admit it in the 2022 update, replying to Mallow: index funds/ETFs at 17% of market cap 'ignores the value of actively managed funds that are also controlled by the Big Three, which is likely to explain the discrepancy.' Their fn.30 gives index share of Big Three assets in 2017 as '79% for SSGA, 74% for Vanguard, and 66% for BlackRock,' and fn.31 says Table 1 'aggregates holdings for all entities with a version of BlackRock, Vanguard, or State Street in their names' from the FactSet 13F database — i.e., total 13F holdings.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Votes cast ~25.4% mean at S&P 500 director elections 2018
itemVerdicts.note: Number right, YEAR wrong. WRONG: 'at S&P 500 director elections 2018.' RIGHT: 2017. Table 5 reports ownership as of end-2017, and fn.30 states 'Votes cast refers to the average sum, across all directors up for election, of the votes cast for and against, and abstentions for that director at that corporation's 2017 annual meeting.' Text: 'the proportion of the total votes that were cast by the Big Three was about 25.4% on average.' Median 24.2%; Russell 3000 mean 22.0%. (Separately, the 2022 paper's Table 2 shows a MEDIAN of 25.4% for 2017 — same digits, different statistic; do not conflate.)

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Wedge vs ownership arises because non-Big-Three turnout averaged ~73%
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'the proportion of shares not managed by the Big Three that voted in director elections varied from 85% in 2008 to 68% in 2017. The average proportion of non-Big-Three holdings voted at director elections over that period was 73%.' The paper assumes the Big Three vote 100% of their shares. Retail turnout was much lower: fn.29 cites Broadridge/PwC that only 29% of retail-owned shares were voted in the 2017 proxy season.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Projections: 34.3% of S&P 500 VOTES in ten years (2028), 40.8% in twenty (2038); commonly misquoted as '34% in two decades'
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'the Big Three will control 34.3% of S&P 500 votes in ten years, and 40.8% of S&P 500 votes in twenty years' (Figure 3 Panel 1 plots 34.27% and 40.76%). Russell 3000: 29.8% (2028) / 36.7% (2038). So 34.3% is the TEN-year figure — anyone writing '34% in two decades' has swapped the horizons. The conclusion's own headline number for two decades is 'as much as 40% of the votes.'

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Linear/mechanical extrapolation, authors hedge
itemVerdicts.note: Method is not linear in levels: they compute the annual decline rate of non-Big-Three holdings, 10th-root of (c2008/c2017) = 0.84%/yr, and compound it forward — better described as constant-rate compounding of the non-Big-Three residual, not linear extrapolation. Hedges are explicit: 'it is difficult to make predictions, especially about the future'; 'We reiterate our caution that accurately estimating the future growth of the Big Three is difficult, and actual outcomes might differ.' Sensitivity: the 5-year base rate (1.05%) gives 28.4%/35.6% of votes and the 20-year base gives 27.2%/33.3% — i.e., the headline 34.3%/40.8% is the HIGHEST of the three vote paths they report.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) 2022 update ('Big Three Power, and Why It Matters', 102 B.U. L. Rev. 1547): median combined stake 21.9% in 2021
itemVerdicts.note: Table 1: 2021 = BlackRock 7.7% + Vanguard 9.7% + SSGA 4.5% = 21.9% (medians, totals are the sum of rounded medians). Note the statistic switched from MEAN (2019 paper) to MEDIAN (2022 paper) — the 2022 Table 1 median for 2017 is 19.5%, and its 20.5% entry is 2018, not 2017. Adversarial note on trend: the same table shows 21.5% (2019) → 21.1% (2020) → 21.9% (2021), i.e., a visible plateau that sits awkwardly under the smooth-compounding projection.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Votes cast reported as BOTH 24.9% (abstract) and 27.5/27.6% (Table 2 / Section I.A) in the same paper — unreconciled
itemVerdicts.note: The DISCREPANCY IS REAL but the location is wrong. WRONG: '24.9% (abstract).' RIGHT: the abstract contains no figures at all. 24.9% appears (i) in the Introduction, p.1552 — 'the Big Three collectively held a median stake of 21.9% in S&P 500 companies, which represented a proportion of 24.9% of the votes cast' — and (ii) in Section II.A, p.1569 — 'the Big Three collectively held, on average, 24.9% of the votes cast at annual meetings of S&P 500 companies in 2021,' whose fn.118 cites 'supra Table 2 and accompanying text.' But Table 2's 2021 row totals 27.5% (9.8+12.0+5.7) and the accompanying Section I.A text says 'the Big Three collectively held a median of 27.6% of votes cast at annual meetings.' A third slippage: 24.9% is called a 'median' on p.1552 and an average 'on average' on p.1569. So it is a three-way inconsistency, and the 24.9% figure has no derivation anywhere in the paper.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) 2022 update carries downward-revised projections of 27.6% (2028) / 33.4% (2038)
itemVerdicts.note: Two errors. (i) NOT DOWNWARD-REVISED — the 2022 article does not re-estimate anything; it restates the 2019 numbers verbatim with citations to 'Giant Three, supra note 4, at 737' (fns. 46-48, 51-52). (ii) WRONG SERIES — 27.6%/33.4% are the OWNERSHIP projections (share of S&P 500 EQUITY), and they already appear in the 2019 paper: 'the combined average ownership stake of the Big Three will rise to 27.6% in ten years, and to 33.4% of S&P 500 equity in twenty years' (Figure 2 Panel 1: 27.58%, 33.44%). RIGHT: the 2022 article repeats both series unchanged — ownership 27.6% (2028) / 33.4% (2038), and votes 34.3% (2028) / 40.8% (2038): 'we further estimated that the Big Three will hold 34.3% of S&P 500 votes in 2028 and 40.8% of S&P 500 votes in 2038.' Grep of the full 2022 text for '2028'/'2038' returns only these restated lines. What the 2022 paper adds is a defense of the projections against Novick's and Mallow's objections, not a markdown of them.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) 'Largest shareholder in ~88% of S&P 500 firms' is a Sullivan & Cromwell rank statistic from December 2018 (438/500), with aggregate stake 18.7%
itemVerdicts.note: Substance confirmed verbatim from the primary post (Melissa Sawyer, S&C, 'Annual Review and Analysis of 2019 U.S. Shareholder Activism,' Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, Nov. 20, 2019; quoted at Bebchuk & Hirst 2022 fn.132): 'As of December 2018, one of BlackRock, Vanguard or State Street was the largest shareholder in 438 of the S&P 500 companies, roughly 88%, and collectively the three firms owned 18.7% of all shares in the S&P 500.' Two caliber fixes. WRONG: '18.7% aggregate VALUE-WEIGHTED stake.' RIGHT: S&C say '18.7% of all shares in the S&P 500' — an aggregate share count, not stated as value-weighted; the useful contrast is aggregate vs. Bebchuk-Hirst's per-company mean (20.5%), not weighting scheme. WRONG: '8 years stale.' RIGHT: Dec 2018 to Aug 2026 is 7 years 8 months — say 'nearly eight years.' Also, the 88% is not uniquely S&C: PJT CamberView stated in 2017 that one of the Big Three 'is the largest single shareholder in 88% of companies' in the S&P 500 (BH2022 fn.139), and Kirkland & Ellis wrote in Feb. 2019 that they 'constitute the single largest shareholder in almost 90 percent of S&P 500 firms.' The 'rank stat, not control' framing is the article's own gloss, not S&C's — fine as analysis, but don't attribute it.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Bebchuk-Hirst 2019 Colum. L. Rev.: 45/21/12 stewardship staff; 0.25–3.97 person-days per portfolio company; 'less than 4 person-days per $1bn position' is the most generous scenario
itemVerdicts.note: Verified in BOTH the NBER w26543 working paper and the published 119 Colum. L. Rev. 2029 (2019) PDF — numbers identical. Table 1: Stewardship Personnel BlackRock 45, Vanguard 21, SSGA 12. Table 3 person-days span 0.25 (SSGA, Scenario 1 equal allocation worldwide) to 3.97 (BlackRock, Scenario 4, per $1bn position in U.S. companies) — 3.97 is the maximum of all twelve cells. Text: 'Even under the most conservative assumptions, in order to oversee each of their billion-dollar positions, BlackRock spent less than 4 person-days per year and less than $5,000 in stewardship costs per year, and each of SSGA and Vanguard spent less than 2 person-days per year.' Note the authors' word is 'conservative' (i.e., most favorable to the managers); 'most generous' is an accurate paraphrase. Two assumptions inflate it: 250 workdays/yr with zero vacation, and 100% of staff time on 'pure' stewardship.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) BlackRock's stewardship team is now '60+' while AUM grew faster
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in BlackRock Investment Stewardship Annual Report Jan 1 – Dec 31, 2025 (published 2026): 'Our team of more than 60 dedicated professionals — who operate across nine offices'; and 'With more than 60 professionals focused full time on stewardship'; the same report notes 'In 2009, we were a team of 16.' AUM: BlackRock reported $15.3T at June 30, 2026 vs ~$6.0T at end-2018 — roughly 2.5x, against staff growth of 45 → 60+ (~1.35x). So the ratio claim holds. Two additions the article should carry: (i) BlackRock also runs a SEPARATE BlackRock Active Investment Stewardship team of 13 dedicated professionals, so '60+' is BIS only; (ii) the same report notes BIS engages companies making up ~64% of BlackRock's clients' index equity AUM, not all of it.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Kahan & Rock's counter: the right comparison is the dispersed retail investors the funds replaced, whose stewardship was zero
itemVerdicts.note: Direction right, quantifier fabricated, and the counterfactual is narrower than stated. Kahan & Rock, 'Index Funds and Corporate Governance: Let Shareholders be Shareholders,' 100 B.U. L. Rev. 1771 (2020) (ECGI Law WP 467/2019), p.1788: 'We believe that the Bebchuk and Hirst analysis misses the point... The question therefore is how Vanguard's incentives compare to those of the actual economic owners of Vanguard's shares—the real-life investors in Vanguard's mutual funds—not how Vanguard's incentives compare to those of a hypothetical individual shareholder who holds the same stake as Vanguard.' WRONG: 'whose stewardship was zero.' RIGHT: they never say zero. Their formulations are that Big Three incentives are 'multiple orders of magnitude higher than those of mutual fund investors' and 'superior to those of virtually all retail shareholders and most other institutional investors,' and that index funds 'serve to lower the overall costs of dispersed ownership by multiple orders of magnitude rather than contribute to these costs.' WRONG: 'the dispersed retail investors the funds REPLACED.' RIGHT: the baseline they name is the fund's own current beneficiaries holding directly, not a historical population. They also concede the Bebchuk-Hirst point on its own terms: 'To be sure, Vanguard's incentives are substantially lower than the incentives of an individual shareholder who held a stake in P&G of the same size as Vanguard's.'

corrections: Change 'votes cast ~25.4% mean at S&P 500 director elections 2018' to '2017'. Bebchuk & Hirst, Specter of the Giant Three, Table 5 fn.30 defines votes cast as those at 'that corporation's 2017 annual meeting,' against end-2017 ownership. Median was 24.2%; Russell 3000 mean 22.0%.

Do not say the 24.9% figure appears in the 2022 abstract. The abstract of 'Big Three Power, and Why It Matters' (102 B.U. L. Rev. 1547) contains no numbers. Correct locus: the Introduction at p.1552 ('a median stake of 21.9%... which represented a proportion of 24.9% of the votes cast') and Section II.A at p.1569 ('the Big Three collectively held, on average, 24.9% of the votes cast'). The inconsistency is genuinely three-way: 24.9% is labeled a median in one place and an average in the other, while its own cited source — Table 2 and accompanying text in Section I.A — gives 27.5% (table) and 27.6% (text) for 2021.

Delete the assertion that the 2022 update contains 'downward-revised projections.' It contains no revised projections. The 2022 article restates the 2019 numbers verbatim, citing Giant Three at 737 (fns. 46-48, 51-52), and defends them against Novick's and Mallow's objections rather than marking them down.

Fix the series mix-up: 27.6% (2028) / 33.4% (2038) are the OWNERSHIP projections (share of S&P 500 equity), already published in the 2019 paper (Figure 2: 27.58%, 33.44%). The VOTE projections are 34.3% (2028) / 40.8% (2038) in both the 2019 and 2022 papers. Do not present the ownership pair as a revised vote pair.

Describe the 18.7% as Sullivan & Cromwell's own wording: the three firms 'collectively... owned 18.7% of all shares in the S&P 500' — an aggregate share statistic, not a stated value-weighted figure. The contrast worth drawing is aggregate vs. Bebchuk-Hirst's per-company mean (20.5%).
Change '8 years stale' to 'nearly eight years old' — the S&C rank statistic is as of December 2018, i.e., 7 years 8 months before August 2026.

Add that the ~88% rank statistic is not unique to Sullivan & Cromwell: PJT CamberView stated the same 88% in 2017, and Kirkland & Ellis wrote 'almost 90 percent' in February 2019 (both quoted in Bebchuk & Hirst 2022, fns. 132 and 139). It is an industry commonplace, which strengthens rather than weakens the 'rank stat, not control' caution.

Remove 'whose stewardship was zero' from the Kahan & Rock attribution — they never make a zero claim. Use their actual formulations: Big Three incentives are 'multiple orders of magnitude higher than those of mutual fund investors' and 'superior to those of virtually all retail shareholders and most other institutional investors.' Cite Kahan & Rock, 100 B.U. L. Rev. 1771, 1788 (2020).

Restate the Kahan & Rock counterfactual precisely: their baseline is 'the actual economic owners of Vanguard's shares—the real-life investors in Vanguard's mutual funds,' i.e., the funds' current beneficiaries holding directly, not a historical population of retail holders the funds displaced. Also note they concede the Bebchuk-Hirst point on its own terms: 'To be sure, Vanguard's incentives are substantially lower than the incentives of an individual shareholder who held a stake in P&G of the same size as Vanguard's.'

When calling the projection 'linear extrapolation,' say instead that it compounds a constant 0.84%/yr rate of decline in non-Big-Three holdings (computed as the 10th root of c2008/c2017). Also note the headline 34.3%/40.8% is the highest of the three horizons they report: the 5-year base rate gives 28.4%/35.6% and the 20-year base gives 27.2%/33.3%.

When quoting '60+' for BlackRock's stewardship team, source it to the BlackRock Investment Stewardship Annual Report for calendar 2025 ('Our team of more than 60 dedicated professionals — who operate across nine offices') and add that a separate BlackRock Active Investment Stewardship team of 13 professionals exists, so '60+' covers BIS only.
newContradictions: Bebchuk & Hirst's OWN 2022 Table 1 shows the median combined Big Three stake plateauing after 2019: 21.5% (2019) → 21.1% (2020) → 21.9% (2021). A four-year net gain of 0.4pp sits badly beside a projection that compounds to 27.6% by 2028, and the authors do not address the flattening. Any article using the projections should flag that the series had already stalled at the moment the update was written.

BlackRock pass-through voting, checked against the primary: the BIS 2025 Annual Report states that as of Dec 31, 2025, '$3.76 trillion of BlackRock's $7.7 trillion total index equity AUM are eligible to participate in BlackRock Voting Choice with clients representing approximately $885 billion in index equity AUM exercising this option.' That is ~11.5% of index equity AUM actually voted by clients. Cuts BOTH ways and should be reported honestly: it is a real mechanical drag on the Big Three vote-share projection, but it is essentially unchanged from the 11% Bebchuk & Hirst themselves computed for 2022 (fn.43: $530bn of $4.9T), so after four years of expansion it has not measurably bent the trend.

The 2019 paper's Figure 1 is titled 'Percentage of Corporate Equity Held by Big Three Index Funds' while the underlying series is total 13F holdings including actively managed assets — by the authors' own 2022 footnote, index funds were only 66% of BlackRock's, 74% of Vanguard's and 79% of SSGA's assets in 2017. The label is a genuine mismatch in the source itself, which is worth naming rather than repeating.

The vote-share figures in the 2019 and 2022 papers are not the same statistic and are computed on different timing conventions. Giant Three Table 5 gives a MEAN (25.4%) using end-2017 holdings over 2017 annual-meeting votes; Big Three Power Table 2 gives a MEDIAN and, per its fn.37, divides end-of-year-t holdings by votes cast at the meeting 'in the subsequent year.' Table 2's 2017 row happens also to read 25.4%. Treating the two 25.4% figures as the same measurement would be an error.
reasoning:
I reached all three Bebchuk-Hirst primaries as full text and read the relevant sentences and tables myself: NBER w25914 (Specter of the Giant Three, = 99 B.U. L. Rev. 721), the published 102 B.U. L. Rev. 1547 PDF (Big Three Power, and Why It Matters), and NBER w26543 — which I cross-checked against the published 119 Colum. L. Rev. 2029 PDF fetched from columbialawreview.org, confirming Tables 1 and 3 are identical across versions. I additionally fetched Kahan & Rock's ECGI working paper (published as 100 B.U. L. Rev. 1771 (2020)), the Sullivan & Cromwell post on the Harvard corpgov forum (which returned the 438/88%/18.7% sentence verbatim and matches the block quote in Bebchuk-Hirst 2022 fn.132), and the BlackRock Investment Stewardship Annual Report for calendar 2025 as PDF, extracted with pdftotext, where I read the '{more than 60 dedicated professionals}' and Voting Choice passages directly rather than relying on any summarizer. Every quoted string above was seen in extracted document text, not in a fetch summary; I discarded two search-summarizer outputs that made unsupported assertions.

The group is substantially sound: the 5.2%→20.5%, 25.4%, 73%, 34.3%/40.8%, 21.9%, 45/21/12, 0.25-3.97, 438/88%/18.7%, and '60+' figures all check out verbatim, and the article's most distinctive interpretive points — that the ownership series includes active assets, that 34.3% is the ten-year not twenty-year figure, that 3.97 is the most generous cell, and that the 2022 paper contains an unreconciled vote-share discrepancy — are all correct and confirmed against the sources' own words.

Three items need repair. The largest is (b)'s claim that the 2022 update carries 'downward-revised projections 27.6%/33.4%': the 2022 article revises nothing, and 27.6%/33.4% are the 2019 OWNERSHIP projections, not vote projections — a grep of the full 2022 text for 2028/2038 returns only restated lines footnoted to Giant Three at 737. Second, the 24.9%/27.5%/27.6% discrepancy is real but is not an abstract-vs-table conflict; the abstract has no numbers, and the conflict runs Introduction p.1552 vs Section I.A/Table 2, compounded by 24.9% being called a median in one place and an average in another. Third, 'whose stewardship was zero' is not Kahan & Rock's claim — they argue relative incentives ('multiple orders of magnitude higher'), and their counterfactual is the funds' own beneficiaries holding directly rather than a displaced retail population; they also expressly concede that Vanguard's incentives are lower than an equivalent individual blockholder's.

Remaining uncertain: I could not locate a peer-reviewed post-2022 update of the Big Three ownership or vote series, so the 2028 ownership projection cannot be checked against a comparable 2025-26 measurement from a primary academic source; searches returned only secondary commentary recycling the 2019 figures. The BlackRock $15.3T Q2 2026 AUM figure I took from multiple financial-press reports of the earnings release rather than reading the 8-K exhibit itself, so treat the precise 2.5x ratio as approximate — the qualitative claim that AUM outgrew headcount is safe by a wide margin under any plausible figure.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Pastor-Stambaugh-Taylor (JFE 2015): +1pp of active-industry share of market cap -> gross fund performance falls ~40bp/yr, extended sample ~20bp
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in PST (NBER WP 19891, Feb 2014, p.17-18; identical wording in the Aug-2013 and Nov-2013 versions): 'consider a one percentage point increase in IndustrySize... In our main sample, this increase in IndustrySize is associated with a sizable decrease in fund performance: 0.0326% per month, or almost 40 bp per year. In the extended sample, the magnitude of the same effect is smaller but still substantial, about 20 bp per year.' Footnote 16: 'IndustrySize is the total AUM of active mutual funds divided by the stock market capitalization' - so 'active-industry share of market cap' is the right gloss, and the dependent variable GrossR is the fund's benchmark-adjusted GROSS return. Exact Table 3 coefficients: main sample (March 1993-Dec 2011) -0.0326 (t=-3.60) with fund fixed effects and -0.0326 (t=-2.49) recursive-demeaning, but only -0.0169 (t=-1.93) in plain OLS; extended sample (Jan 1979-Dec 2011) -0.0164 (t=-4.34) FE, -0.0165 (t=-2.66) RD, -0.00671 (t=-1.92) plain OLS. The -0.0326 baseline is reconfirmed in the authors' own Pastor-Stambaugh-Taylor-Zhu 'Diseconomies of Scale in Active Management: Robust Evidence' (July 2021), Table 1 col 1. I could not open the paywalled ScienceDirect text of JFE 116(1):23-45; three working-paper versions plus the authors' 2021 replication all carry -0.0326, so the figure is safe, but the sentence I quote is from the working paper.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-inference) 'so the post-2010 SHRINKAGE of active share should have RAISED gross alpha'
itemVerdicts.note: This is the article's own extrapolation, not a PST finding, and it rests on an unsourced premise. WRONG as stated without qualification. RIGHT: PST's sample ends December 2011 and their IndustrySize series only ever rises inside it - 'It starts at 2.4% in January 1979, peaks at 18.6% in July 2008, and finishes at 16.8% in December 2011.' Any post-2010 application is out-of-sample linear extrapolation of a coefficient never estimated on a falling IndustrySize. Also, IndustrySize counts ONLY active equity mutual funds - it excludes hedge funds, active ETFs, separate accounts and institutional mandates - so it is not the broad 'active share of the market' the index-bubble narrative uses. The article must separately source the claim that active-MF AUM / total US market cap has actually fallen since 2010, and should note the magnitude the extrapolation implies (a 5pp drop in IndustrySize would imply about +2%/yr of gross alpha), which sharpens the contrast but also shows how strong the linear assumption is.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Cremers-Ferreira-Matos-Starks (JFE 2016): average alpha HIGHER where explicit indexing is bigger, but the interaction shows marginal return to being more active is LOWER there
itemVerdicts.note: Both halves are in the paper, but the significance qualifier is missing. Verbatim from the JFE-forthcoming manuscript, Section on performance: 'We thus conclude that the marginal returns to active management are lower in markets with more prevalent and cheaper explicitly indexed funds.' And the abstract: 'the average alpha generated by active management is higher in countries with more explicit indexing and lower in countries with more closet indexing.' WRONG to present either result as a flat finding of the paper. RIGHT: in Table 7 both results are statistically significant only in Panel B (variables measured by country of SALE, n=346,711 share-class-country-years): Explicit indexing (% TNA) +0.1196 (t=4.16), Active share x Explicit indexing -0.1753 (t=-4.21). In Panel A (country of DOMICILE, n=51,570) the same two coefficients are +0.0106 (t=0.43) and -0.0351 (t=-0.95) - both insignificant. Additional caliber points: the dependent variable is a NET four-factor alpha (benchmark-adjusted return = fund NET return minus benchmark return), the sample is 32 countries, 2002-2010 - i.e. it also predates the post-2010 passive ramp - and mean Active Share is 0.7050 (median 0.7437, SD 0.2190), so in Panel B col (2) the combined marginal effect of explicit indexing evaluated at the average fund's active share is 0.1196 - 0.1753 x 0.705 = about -0.004, essentially zero. (That arithmetic is mine, not the paper's, but it means the 'higher alpha where indexing is bigger' level effect should not be quoted as if it applied to the typical active fund.)

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Fama-French 2010: aggregate gross VW three-factor alpha +0.13%/yr (t=0.40) on 1984-2006, 'alpha = minus fees'
itemVerdicts.note: The FF numbers are exact. Verbatim (JF LXV(5), Oct 2010, p.1920): 'The intercepts in (1) for VW gross returns are quite close to zero, 0.13% per year (t = 0.40) for the three-factor version of (1), and -0.05% per year (t = -0.15) for the four-factor model.' EW gross three-/four-factor intercepts are +0.36% and +0.39%/yr, 0.85 and 0.90 standard errors from zero; net EW and VW three-/four-factor intercepts run -0.81% to -1.00%/yr with t from -2.05 to -3.02, and they write 'When we add back the costs in expense ratios, alpha estimates for VW gross fund returns are close to zero' - which is the 'alpha = minus fees' reading. WRONG: the window written as '1984-2006'. RIGHT: 'January 1984 through September 2006' (273 months). WRONG: using Harvey-Liu to undercut the +0.13% figure. RIGHT: Harvey & Liu (JF 77(3), June 2022, p.1946) say 'it is perhaps unsurprising that the FF technique has little or no power to detect the truly outperforming funds in our simulation' - the scope words 'in our simulation' belong in the quote, and the critique is aimed at FF's cross-sectional BOOTSTRAP test of individual funds (an undersampling problem that bites when funds have few observations; FF require only eight monthly observations), not at the aggregate VW regression intercept, which is a plain OLS estimate the bootstrap critique does not touch. HL also do not overturn FF's method: 'our general recommendation is to use FF's technique that captures cross-sectional correlations, but to implement it in a way that is consistent with KTWW's approach in which the minimum number of observations is increased.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Berk-van Binsbergen (JFE 2015): AUM-weighted mean value added $3.2m/yr (t=5.74) but median negative and 57.01% of funds below zero
itemVerdicts.note: The three numbers are right; the weighting label is wrong. WRONG: 'AUM-weighted mean'. RIGHT: it is weighted by the NUMBER OF PERIODS each fund exists. Table 3 note verbatim: 'The Cross-Sectional Weighted mean, standard error and t-statistic are computed by weighting by the number of periods the fund exists, that is, they are the statistical properties of S-bar-W defined by (9).' Equation (9) is sum(T_i * S_i) / sum(T_i); the authors call it 'the mean of surviving funds, what we term the ex-post distribution.' Table 3, Vanguard-benchmark column: weighted mean 0.27 ($m/month), SE 0.05, t = 5.74 - i.e. '$270,000 per month, or $3.2 million annually (in Y2000 dollars)'; unweighted cross-sectional mean 0.14, t = 4.57; 50th percentile -0.02 ($m/month), i.e. 'The median fund lost an average of $20,000/month'; 'Percent with less than zero 57.01%' and in the text 'only 43% of funds had positive estimated value added'; 5,974 funds. Two further caliber points the article should carry: units are Y2000 dollars per month, sample is January 1977 to March 2011 (411 months) with the Vanguard index funds as the tradable benchmark; and BvB themselves warn 'There are two reasons to believe that our t-statistics are overstated' (cross-fund correlation and excess kurtosis), so t = 5.74 should not be quoted as a hard significance level.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Unterberg 'Passive Flows, Active Woes' (SSRN 6902444, June 2026): net 4-factor alpha -0.72%/yr (1984-2009) to -1.82%/yr (2010-24); VW gross alpha ~0 to -0.66%/yr post-2010; industry-level passive-share / active-minus-passive relation flipped sign after 2010
itemVerdicts.note: I could not reach the primary. SSRN returns HTTP 403 behind a Cloudflare challenge for both the abstract page and the Delivery.cfm PDF endpoint (curl with a browser UA and WebFetch both refused); ResearchGate, the Idea Farm and CXO Advisory are paywalled or secondhand; the author's site links only to SSRN; the WFA 2026 portal publishes a program, not papers. What I DID confirm from primary-controlled sources: (1) the author's own site (hannahunterberg.com/research) carries the abstract verbatim - 'Using U.S. equity fund data (1984-2024), I document a decline in active fund performance after 2010, with average annual four-factor alpha falling by around one percentage point and the previously positive relation between Active Share and performance reversing. These patterns contrast with theories predicting improved performance as the active sector shrinks.' That confirms the direction, the 1984-2024 window, the post-2010 break, the Active Share reversal, and a roughly one-percentage-point alpha decline (consistent with -0.72 to -1.82, a 1.10pp fall); (2) the WFA 2026 conference program PDF (westernfinance-portal.org/program/2026/WFA.2026.program.conf.pdf, p.10) confirms the paper won the 'TWO SIGMA AWARD FOR THE BEST PAPER ON INVESTMENT MANAGEMENT', Hannah Unterberg, University of California-Irvine. What remains UNVERIFIED against the primary: the exact figures -0.72%, -1.82%, -0.66%, and the sub-claim that the industry-level relation between passive share and the active-minus-passive spread flipped sign - that last item does not appear in the abstract at all, and I found it only in Swedroe's Morningstar piece (17 August 2026, key finding 6). All four should be attributed to Swedroe/Morningstar reporting Unterberg, not asserted as read from the paper. The paper is also an unpublished June 2026 working paper, not peer-reviewed.

corrections: Item (d): replace 'AUM-weighted mean value added' with 'the mean weighted by the number of months each fund is in the sample (the ex-post / surviving-fund mean, equation 9)'. Berk-van Binsbergen Table 3 note says the weighted mean is 'computed by weighting by the number of periods the fund exists', NOT by assets. Keep $3.2m/yr, t=5.74, median -$20,000/month, 57.01% below zero - all exact - and add that the figures are Y2000 dollars over January 1977 to March 2011 against Vanguard index-fund benchmarks.

Item (d): add BvB's own caveat that 't-statistics are overstated' because of cross-fund return correlation and excess kurtosis in the value-added distribution, so t=5.74 is not a clean significance level.

Item (b): state that the CFMS result is significant only in Panel B of Table 7 (country of sale). Explicit indexing (% TNA) is +0.1196 (t=4.16) and Active share x Explicit indexing is -0.1753 (t=-4.21) in Panel B, but +0.0106 (t=0.43) and -0.0351 (t=-0.95) - both insignificant - in Panel A (country of domicile).

Item (b): specify that the CFMS dependent variable is a NET four-factor alpha and the sample is 32 countries, 2002-2010, i.e. it also predates the post-2010 passive ramp and so cannot by itself settle a post-2010 question.

Item (b): if the article quotes the 'higher average alpha where indexing is bigger' level coefficient, note that at the sample mean Active Share of 0.7050 the combined marginal effect in Table 7 Panel B col (2) is 0.1196 - 0.1753 x 0.705, i.e. approximately zero, so the positive level effect does not describe the typical active fund.
Item (c): change '1984-2006' to 'January 1984 through September 2006' (273 months), Fama-French's stated window.

Item (c): do not let the Harvey-Liu quote bear on Fama-French's +0.13%/yr aggregate intercept. Quote it with its scope - 'the FF technique has little or no power to detect the truly outperforming funds in our simulation' (JF 2022, p.1946) - and say it targets FF's cross-sectional bootstrap of individual-fund alphas (an undersampling problem when funds have few observations; FF require only eight monthly observations), not the aggregate value-weighted regression intercept. Add that HL still recommend FF's technique, with a higher minimum-observation requirement, rather than discarding it.

Item (a): attribute the ~40bp/~20bp figures to the fund-fixed-effects (and recursive-demeaning) specification, and note that plain OLS without fund fixed effects gives roughly half the magnitude and only marginal significance (-0.0169, t=-1.93 main sample; -0.00671, t=-1.92 extended).

Item (a): note that PST's IndustrySize is active EQUITY MUTUAL FUND AUM divided by total CRSP market cap - it excludes hedge funds, active ETFs, separate accounts and institutional mandates - so it is narrower than the 'active share of the market' the index-bubble thesis invokes.

Item (a): flag the extrapolation explicitly. PST's sample ends December 2011 and IndustrySize only ever rises inside it (2.4% in January 1979, peak 18.6% in July 2008, 16.8% in December 2011), so 'the post-2010 shrinkage should have raised gross alpha' is the article's out-of-sample inference, and the premise that active-MF AUM / market cap has actually fallen since 2010 needs its own citation.

Item (a): if the extended-sample ~20bp figure is used, note it is the fragile one - in PST Table 4 the extended-sample IndustrySize coefficient falls to -0.0305 (t=-1.72, insignificant) once a linear time trend is included, while the main-sample coefficient strengthens to -0.0852 (t=-3.04).

Item (a): acknowledge the live dispute. Adams, Hayunga and Mansi (2021) argue one cannot reject constant returns to scale at the industry level; Pastor, Stambaugh, Taylor and Zhu (2021, 'Diseconomies of Scale in Active Management: Robust Evidence') rebut this with robust regression and symmetric outlier removal and reconfirm the -0.0326 coefficient. Presenting PST as uncontested overstates it.

Item (e): attribute every Unterberg number (-0.72%, -1.82%, -0.66%, and the industry-level sign flip) to Larry Swedroe's Morningstar article of 17 August 2026 reporting the paper, not to the paper itself, because SSRN 6902444 is behind a Cloudflare block and could not be read. Only the abstract is directly verifiable, from the author's own site: 'average annual four-factor alpha falling by around one percentage point and the previously positive relation between Active Share and performance reversing.' The industry-level sign-flip claim appears nowhere in that abstract.

Item (e): describe the paper accurately as an unpublished June 2026 working paper by Hannah Unterberg (PhD candidate, UC Irvine Merage), winner of the Two Sigma Award for the Best Paper on Investment Management at WFA 2026 - not as peer-reviewed evidence.
newContradictions: Items (c) and (d) contradict each other on NET alpha and the article must not stack them as a single consistent picture. Fama-French 2010 report EW and VW net three-/four-factor intercepts of -0.81% to -1.00%/yr with t from -2.05 to -3.02. Berk-van Binsbergen, evaluating the same industry against tradable Vanguard index funds instead of FFC factors, write: 'Once we evaluate funds against a tradable benchmark, we no longer find evidence of the underperformance previously documented in the literature. Over the time period in our sample, the equally weighted net alpha is 3 b.p. per month and the value weighted net alpha is -1 b.p. per month. Neither estimate is significantly different from zero.'

Same benchmark-choice problem on GROSS alpha. Fama-French get a VW gross three-factor alpha of +0.13%/yr; Berk-van Binsbergen state 'The average value weighted gross alpha in our sample is 6.5 b.p./month, or about 80 b.p./year, reflecting the fees active managers charge.' The two are not comparable (FFC factors vs Vanguard tradable benchmarks, 1984-2006 vs 1977-2011), and if the article quotes both it needs to say so rather than let readers read a trend.

Pastor-Stambaugh-Taylor's industry-level result is contested in print. Adams, Hayunga and Mansi (2021) claim data errors and a few influential observations drive it and that constant returns to scale cannot be rejected; the PST authors plus Min Zhu reply in 'Diseconomies of Scale in Active Management: Robust Evidence' (July 2021), rejecting AHM's asymmetric outlier removal and reconfirming a significantly negative industry-size coefficient even after dropping 25% of the most extreme return observations. The article should cite the exchange rather than PST alone.

PST's own Table 4 shows the extended-sample (1979-2011) industry-size effect is not robust to a linear time trend: the coefficient goes from -0.0164 (t=-4.34) to -0.0305 (t=-1.72). Since the article uses the extended-sample ~20bp figure as its conservative case, it is leaning on the specification that is most fragile.

Minor sourcing discrepancy on the Unterberg award: her own research page lists the 'Brattle Group PhD Candidate Award for Outstanding Research, WFA 2026', while the WFA 2026 program lists her paper under the 'Two Sigma Award for the Best Paper on Investment Management'. Both may be true, but a search summarizer produced only the Two Sigma one; verify before naming a single award.
reasoning:
Documents I reached verbatim, all read as text I extracted myself rather than through a summarizer: (1) Pastor-Stambaugh-Taylor, NBER WP 19891 (Feb 2014) plus the Aug-2013 and Nov-2013 versions - I read the IndustrySize discussion, footnote 16, Table 3 and Table 4 coefficient panels, and the IndustrySize time series; (2) Pastor-Stambaugh-Taylor-Zhu, 'Diseconomies of Scale in Active Management: Robust Evidence' (July 2021, fetched from cfr.ivo-welch.info), which reconfirms the -0.0326 baseline and surfaces the Adams-Hayunga-Mansi dispute; (3) Cremers-Ferreira-Matos-Starks, the 'forthcoming in JFE' manuscript, including the full Table 7 Panels A and B with coefficients and t-statistics, the summary statistics giving mean Active Share 0.7050, and the Appendix variable definitions; (4) Fama-French, JF LXV(5) October 2010, the Table II discussion of EW/VW gross and net intercepts and the equilibrium-accounting paragraph; (5) Harvey-Liu, JF LXXVII(3) June 2022, the introduction paragraph containing the 'little or no power' sentence and their recommendation; (6) Berk-van Binsbergen, the published-title manuscript, including equation (9), the Table 3 panel, the Table 3 caption defining the weighting, the Section 7.1 text, the sample-start footnote, and the Section 9 value-weighted gross alpha sentence; (7) the WFA 2026 conference program PDF confirming Unterberg's Two Sigma award; (8) Hannah Unterberg's own research page carrying the paper's abstract verbatim; (9) Larry Swedroe's Morningstar Australia article of 17 August 2026, which I extracted in full and which is the actual origin of the -0.72 / -1.82 / -0.66 figures and the industry-level sign-flip claim.

What I could not reach: the paywalled ScienceDirect texts of JFE 116(1):23-45 and JFE 120(3):539-560 - for PST I substituted three working-paper versions and the authors' own 2021 replication of the same coefficient, and for CFMS the 'forthcoming in JFE' manuscript; and SSRN 6902444 itself, which returns HTTP 403 behind Cloudflare via both curl and WebFetch, with ResearchGate, Idea Farm and CXO Advisory all paywalled or secondhand and the WFA portal publishing only a program.

The one hard error I found is in (d): 'AUM-weighted' is simply not what Berk-van Binsbergen compute - equation (9) and the Table 3 caption weight by the number of periods a fund exists. The rest of the group is substantively right with caliber slippage: (b) omits that both CFMS results are significant only in the country-of-sale panel, (c) mis-scopes the Harvey-Liu critique onto an OLS intercept it does not touch and rounds the window, (a) is exactly right on the numbers but the post-2010 inference is the article's own out-of-sample extrapolation resting on an unsourced premise about active-MF AUM over market cap, and (e) cannot be promoted past secondhand. Residual uncertainty: I have not seen the printed JFE pages for PST or CFMS, and I have not seen a single line of the Unterberg paper.

I reached every primary document in full text rather than relying on summaries. Downloaded and pdftotext-extracted: (1) NBER w25914 AND the published BU L Rev version of Specter of the Giant Three (bu.edu/bulawreview/files/2019/06/BEBCHUK-HIRST-1.pdf) — I checked both because the claim cites the published version; the numbers are identical. (2) The 2022 sequel, Big Three Power, and Why It Matters, 102 B.U. L. Rev. 1547 (bu.edu/bulawreview/files/2022/10/BEBCHUK-HIRST.pdf). (3) NBER w26543, Index Funds and the Future of Corporate Governance (the Colum. L. Rev. 2019 working-paper edition, which contains Tables 1-3 in full). (4) Kahan & Rock, Index Funds and Corporate Governance: Let Shareholders be Shareholders, ECGI Law WP 467/2019, which reprints the published 100 B.U. L. Rev. 1771 (2020) pagination. (5) BlackRock Investment Stewardship Annual Report for calendar 2025. (6) BlackRock's FY2019 Form 10-K off SEC EDGAR. The only WebFetch summarization I relied on was the S&C HLS Forum post, and there I requested and received the exact sentence, which independently matches the block quote in Big Three Power fn 132 — two independent reaches of the same string, so I treat it as verbatim-confirmed.

The local scratchpad contained no bh.txt or bh_index.txt (the file list in my instructions did not match the actual directory contents), so nothing was reused; everything here is a fresh fetch.

What holds: 5.2% (1998) -> 20.5% (2017) mean; the active-assets caveat; 25.4% mean votes cast; 34.3%/40.8% vote projections; the authors' hedge; median 21.9% (2021); the genuine 24.9-vs-27.5/27.6 inconsistency; the S&C 438/500 = 88% and 18.7% statistics; 45/21/12 stewardship staff; the 0.25-3.97 person-day range; BlackRock's team now 60+ against AUM that grew from $7.43T (2019) to $14T (2025).

What breaks. Two sub-claims are refuted. First, the assertion that the 2022 update carries "downward-revised projections 27.6% (2028)/33.4% (2038)" is wrong twice over: the 2022 article revises nothing (it restates the 2019 figures and cites Giant Three at 737 and 739 for them, then spends Section I.B defending them against Mallow and Novick), and 27.6/33.4 are the 2019 paper's OWNERSHIP projections (Figure 2 Panel 1: 27.58%, 33.44%), a different series from the 34.3/40.8 VOTE projections, which the 2022 paper also restates unchanged. Second, Kahan & Rock's counterargument is misstated: their benchmark is the funds' own beneficial investors ("the real-life investors in Vanguard's mutual funds"), not "the dispersed retail investors the funds replaced," and their magnitude language is "multiple orders of magnitude," never "zero."

Four further caliber slips: the 25.4% is from 2017 annual meetings, not 2018 (fn 30 is explicit; the June 2018 date there is a database access date); 73% is the 2008-2017 average turnout used in the projection, while the contemporaneous 2017 figure behind the wedge was 68%; the extrapolation is compound/geometric, not linear (fn 31 defines the rate as the tenth root of c2008/c2017, and I reproduced 27.58% by compounding); and 24.9% is in the Introduction and at p.1569, not in the abstract, which carries no numbers at all.

Remaining uncertainty. I did not verify the prevalence of the "34% in two decades" misquotation — that is a claim about the secondary discourse and I mark it unreachable. I also did not attempt to audit Bebchuk & Hirst's underlying FactSet computations; my check was textual fidelity, not replication.

New contradiction worth surfacing: the 34.3%/40.8% vote projections rest on the explicit assumption that the Big Three vote 100% of what they hold. That assumption is now eroding. BlackRock's 2025 stewardship report states that $3.76T of its $7.7T index equity AUM is eligible for Voting Choice with clients representing roughly $885bn actually exercising it, and Vanguard's October 21, 2025 release says Investor Choice eligibility is tripling from $1T to over $3T. Bebchuk & Hirst anticipated and dismissed this in 2022 (noting only ~11% of BlackRock index equity assets had elected), but the numbers have moved since.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Bebchuk & Hirst, Specter of the Giant Three (99 B.U. L. Rev. 721 (2019)): mean combined Big Three stake in S&P 500 companies 5.2% (1998) -> 20.5% (2017)
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in BOTH the published BU L Rev PDF and NBER w25914: 'the proportion of S&P 500 shares managed by the Big Three has grown approximately fourfold over the past two decades, from 5.2% in 1998, to 20.5% in 2017.' Table 5 confirms these are MEANS (mean 20.5% / median 19.5%). Russell 3000 companion: 3.7% -> 16.5%.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) The 20.5% figure includes the Big Three's ACTIVE assets, not just index assets
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed, but the confirmation is in the 2022 sequel, not the 2019 paper. Big Three Power p.1555: Mallow's '17% of U.S. stock market capitalization' figure 'ignores the value of actively managed funds that are also controlled by the Big Three, which is likely to explain the discrepancy.' Fn 30 gives the index share of Big Three assets in 2017 as '79% for SSGA, 74% for Vanguard, and 66% for BlackRock' (citing Index Fund Incentives at 2050 n.51). The 2019 paper never flags this; its Figure 1 is even titled 'Percentage of Corporate Equity Held by Big Three Index Funds,' which is misleading given the FactSet 13F manager-level source.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Votes cast ~25.4% mean at S&P 500 DIRECTOR ELECTIONS 2018
itemVerdicts.note: 25.4% is right; the year is wrong. WRONG: 2018 director elections. RIGHT: 2017 annual meetings. Published fn 30 verbatim: "'Votes cast' refers to the average sum, across all directors up for election, of the votes cast for and against, and abstentions for that director at that corporation's 2017 annual meeting." The June 2018 date in that footnote is the SharkRepellent ACCESS date, not the meeting year. Text: 'the proportion of the total votes that were cast by the Big Three was about 25.4% on average.' The 2022 sequel's Table 2 also shows 25.4% for 2017 but under a different convention (end-2017 holdings / votes at the SUBSEQUENT year's meeting) and as a MEDIAN — do not merge the two.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Wedge vs ownership because non-Big-Three turnout ~73%
itemVerdicts.note: The 73% is real but applied to the wrong quantity. WRONG: the 2017 25.4%-vs-20.5% wedge is explained by ~73% non-Big-Three turnout. RIGHT: 'the proportion of shares not managed by the Big Three that voted in director elections varied from 85% in 2008 to 68% in 2017. The average proportion of non-Big-Three holdings voted at director elections over that period was 73%.' 73% is the 2008-2017 AVERAGE, used only as the constant assumption in the forward projection; the contemporaneous 2017 turnout behind the wedge was 68%.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Projections: 34.3% of S&P 500 votes in ten years (2028), 40.8% in twenty (2038)
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'the Big Three will control 34.3% of S&P 500 votes in ten years, and 40.8% of S&P 500 votes in twenty years.' Figure 3 Panel 1 plots 34.27% and 40.76% against 2028 and 2038, so the year mapping is correct. Russell 3000 companions: 29.8% (2028) / 36.7% (2038).

itemVerdicts.item: (a) The projection is a LINEAR extrapolation
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: linear extrapolation. RIGHT: compound/geometric extrapolation of the complement. Fn 31 verbatim gives the rate as the tenth root of (c2008/c2017), where c is the share NOT managed by the Big Three: 86.5% (2008) -> 79.5% (2017) = 0.84% annual rate of decline, applied multiplicatively. Recomputation: 0.795 x (1-0.0084)^11 = 0.725, i.e. Big Three 27.5%, matching the paper's 27.58% for 2028. Calling it linear misstates the method and understates its convexity.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Authors hedge the projection
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'We agree with the adage that it is difficult to make predictions, especially about the future.' They also present five-year (1.05% decline) and twenty-year sensitivity variants. The hedge is restated in the 2022 sequel at p.1561.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) 'Commonly misquoted as 34% in two decades'
itemVerdicts.note: I did not verify the prevalence of this misquotation in the secondary literature — it is a claim about the discourse, not about the source, and I reached nothing that establishes it. The underlying fact is confirmed (34.3% is the TEN-year figure; twenty years is 40.8%), so the correction itself is safe, but 'commonly' is unsupported by anything I reached.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) 2022 update 'Big Three Power, and Why It Matters' (102 B.U. L. Rev. 1547): median stake 21.9% (2021)
itemVerdicts.note: Table 1 (Estimated Median Big Three Ownership of S&P 500 Companies, 2000-2021), 2021 row: BlackRock 7.7%, Vanguard 9.7%, SSGA 4.5%, Total 21.9%. Per fn 31 the total is the SUM OF ROUNDED MEDIANS, not a median of sums. The series is not monotonic: 21.5% (2019) -> 21.1% (2020) -> 21.9% (2021).

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Votes cast reported as BOTH 24.9% (abstract) and 27.5/27.6% (Table 2 / Section I.A) in the same paper — unreconciled
itemVerdicts.note: The discrepancy is real and confirmed; the location is wrong. WRONG: 24.9% appears in the abstract. RIGHT: the abstract of Big Three Power contains no numbers at all. 24.9% appears (i) in the INTRODUCTION, p.1553: 'as of the end of 2021, the Big Three collectively held a median stake of 21.9% in S&P 500 companies, which represented a proportion of 24.9% of the votes cast at the annual meetings of those companies'; and (ii) at p.1569: 'the Big Three collectively held, on average, 24.9% of the votes cast at annual meetings of S&P 500 companies in 2021,' whose fn 118 cites 'supra Table 2 and accompanying text' — the very table reporting 27.5%. Section I.A text says 'the Big Three collectively held a median of 27.6% of votes cast'; Table 2's 2021 row is 9.8 + 12.0 + 5.7 = 27.5%. So the paper is three-way inconsistent (24.9 / 27.5 / 27.6) and additionally flips between 'median' and 'on average' for the same 24.9%.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Downward-revised projections 27.6% (2028) / 33.4% (2038)
itemVerdicts.note: Two independent errors. (i) There is NO downward revision. Big Three Power p.1560 restates the 2019 numbers verbatim and cites Giant Three at 737 and 739 for them: 'Extrapolating this decline into the future, the Big Three can be expected to hold an estimated 27.6% of the shares of S&P 500 companies in 2028 and 33.4% in 2038' — with the SAME 86.5%->79.5% / 0.84% inputs as 2019. It then restates the vote projections unchanged: 'we further estimated that the Big Three will hold 34.3% of S&P 500 votes in 2028 and 40.8% of S&P 500 votes in 2038.' Section I.B is a DEFENSE of those projections against Mallow and Novick, not a revision. (ii) 27.6%/33.4% are the 2019 paper's OWNERSHIP projections (Figure 2 Panel 1: 27.58% and 33.44%), not vote projections; presenting them as a revised version of the 34.3%/40.8% VOTE numbers conflates two different series.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) 'Largest shareholder in ~88% of S&P 500 firms' is a Sullivan & Cromwell rank statistic from December 2018 (438/500), aggregate stake 18.7%
itemVerdicts.note: Reached the primary verbatim at the HLS Forum post (Melissa Sawyer, Sullivan & Cromwell, 'Annual Review and Analysis of 2019 U.S. Shareholder Activism,' Nov. 20, 2019): 'As of December 2018, one of BlackRock, Vanguard or State Street was the largest shareholder in 438 of the S&P 500 companies, roughly 88%, and collectively the three firms owned 18.7% of all shares in the S&P 500.' Independently reproduced as a block quote in Big Three Power fn 132. 438/500 = 87.6%. Dec 2018 -> Aug 2026 is 7.7 years, so 'roughly 8 years stale' is fair. The characterization as a rank statistic rather than a control statistic is correct.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) '18.7% aggregate VALUE-WEIGHTED stake'
itemVerdicts.note: Minor caliber. WRONG: describing 18.7% as 'value-weighted.' RIGHT: the source says only '18.7% of all shares in the S&P 500' — an index-wide aggregate; S&C never states a weighting scheme, so 'value-weighted' is an inference. Separately, attributing the 88% claim solely to S&C's Dec-2018 count is too tidy: Big Three Power p.1575 quotes CamberView Partners making the same claim in 2017 ('is the largest single shareholder in 88% of companies in [the S&P 500] index'), and Kirkland & Ellis (Feb. 2019) said 'almost 90 percent.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Stewardship staffing 45/21/12 (Bebchuk & Hirst, Index Funds and the Future of Corporate Governance, 119 Colum. L. Rev. 2029 (2019) / NBER w26543)
itemVerdicts.note: Table 1 verbatim: Stewardship Personnel — BlackRock 45, Vanguard 21, SSGA 12; Portfolio Companies (Worldwide) 11,246* / 13,225 / 12,191*; (U.S.) 3,765* / 3,672* / 3,117*. These are the authors' own headcounts; fn 121 separately cites a Morningstar survey giving 33 / 21 / 11 for 2017.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Person-days per portfolio company 0.25-3.97 depending on scenario
itemVerdicts.note: Table 3 verbatim. Minimum 0.25 = SSGA, Scenario 1 (equal allocation, worldwide). Maximum 3.97 = BlackRock, Scenario 4 (proportional allocation per $1bn position in U.S. companies). Full grid (BlackRock/Vanguard/SSGA): S1 1.00/0.40/0.25; S2 2.24/1.07/0.72; S3 3.71/1.36/1.94; S4 3.97/1.58/1.79.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) The famous 'less than 4 person-days per $1bn position' is the MOST GENEROUS scenario
itemVerdicts.note: Substantially right, two qualifiers missing. (i) The quoted sentence is about BLACKROCK ONLY: 'in order to oversee each of their billion-dollar positions, BlackRock spent less than 4 person-days per year and less than $5,000 in stewardship costs per year, and each of SSGA and Vanguard spent less than 2 person-days per year and less than $2,500.' Do not present '<4 person-days' as a Big Three-wide figure — Vanguard is 1.58 and SSGA 1.79 in that same scenario. (ii) 'Most generous scenario' is true for BlackRock (3.97 is the table maximum) but not universally: for SSGA, Scenario 3 (1.94) exceeds Scenario 4 (1.79). Note also the paper describes Scenario 4 as resting on its 'most conservative assumptions' — conservative in the Big Three's favor — so quoting the paper and calling it 'most generous' side by side reads as a contradiction unless the direction is spelled out.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) BlackRock's stewardship team is now '60+' while AUM grew faster
itemVerdicts.note: Both endpoints verified from primary documents. BlackRock Investment Stewardship Annual Report (Jan 1 - Dec 31, 2025), verbatim: 'With more than 60 professionals focused full time on stewardship'; 'The BIS team, one of the largest in the industry, consists of more than 60 professionals who operate out of nine offices globally'; and 'In 2009, we were a team of 16.' AUM: same report states 'clients entrusted BlackRock with $14 trillion of assets under management (AUM)'; BlackRock's FY2019 Form 10-K on SEC EDGAR states '$7.43 trillion of assets under management ('AUM') at December 31, 2019.' Headcount 45 -> 60+ is roughly +33% while AUM rose roughly +88%.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Kahan & Rock's counter: the right comparison is the dispersed retail investors the funds replaced, whose stewardship was zero
itemVerdicts.note: The source does not make this argument. Kahan & Rock, 'Index Funds and Corporate Governance: Let Shareholders be Shareholders,' 100 B.U. L. Rev. 1771 (2020), p.1788 verbatim: 'The question therefore is how Vanguard's incentives compare to those of the actual economic owners of Vanguard's shares—the real-life investors in Vanguard's mutual funds—not how Vanguard's incentives compare to those of a hypothetical individual shareholder who holds the same stake as Vanguard.' Their benchmark is the funds' OWN BENEFICIAL INVESTORS, not 'the retail investors the funds replaced' — a different counterfactual (intermediation vs. displacement). Their magnitude language is never 'zero': 'the incentives of Vanguard and other index fund advisers are multiple orders of magnitude higher than the incentives that the investors in Vanguard or other index funds would have,' and 'index funds like Vanguard's serve to lower the overall costs of dispersed ownership by multiple orders of magnitude rather than contribute to these costs.' A separate, later passage does call retail investors 'the group that has the least overall incentives to become informed,' but that appears in their discussion of conflicts of interest, not as the counterfactual, and still does not say zero.

corrections: Change 'votes cast ~25.4% at S&P 500 director elections in 2018' to '2017 annual meetings.' Bebchuk & Hirst, Specter of the Giant Three, 99 B.U. L. Rev. 721, 736 n.30: "'Votes cast' refers to the average sum, across all directors up for election, of the votes cast for and against, and abstentions for that director at that corporation's 2017 annual meeting." The June 2018 date in that footnote is the database access date, not the meeting year.

Do not attribute the 2017 25.4%-vs-20.5% wedge to '~73% non-Big-Three turnout.' The paper states non-Big-Three turnout 'varied from 85% in 2008 to 68% in 2017,' and that 73% is the 2008-2017 AVERAGE, used only as the constant assumption in the forward vote projection. Say '68% in 2017' when explaining the wedge, or '73% average over 2008-2017' when describing the projection input.

Delete 'linear extrapolation.' The method is a compound (geometric) extrapolation of the non-Big-Three share: fn 31 defines the rate as the tenth root of (c2008/c2017), giving 0.84% per year applied multiplicatively to the 79.5% complement. Say 'constant-rate (compounding) extrapolation of the shrinking non-Big-Three share.'

Fix the location of the 24.9% figure. Big Three Power's ABSTRACT contains no numbers. 24.9% appears in the Introduction (102 B.U. L. Rev. 1547, 1553) and again at p.1569, where footnote 118 cites 'supra Table 2 and accompanying text' — the table reporting 27.5%. Also note the paper labels the same 24.9% figure as a 'median' at p.1553 and as 'on average' at p.1569, so the inconsistency is three-way (24.9 / 27.5 / 27.6) plus a mean-vs-median flip.

REMOVE the claim that Big Three Power (2022) 'downward-revised' the projections to 27.6% (2028) / 33.4% (2038). It revised nothing: at p.1560 it restates the 2019 estimates verbatim, cites Giant Three at 737 and 739 for them, and defends them against Mallow and Novick. Moreover 27.6%/33.4% are the 2019 paper's OWNERSHIP projections (Figure 2 Panel 1: 27.58%/33.44%), not vote projections; the 2022 article separately restates the UNCHANGED vote projections of 34.3% (2028) and 40.8% (2038).

Replace 'aggregate value-weighted stake 18.7%' with 'aggregate index-wide stake of 18.7%.' Sullivan & Cromwell's wording is 'collectively the three firms owned 18.7% of all shares in the S&P 500'; no weighting scheme is stated and 'value-weighted' is an unsupported gloss.

If the article calls the 88% figure 'a Sullivan & Cromwell statistic,' add that the same claim circulated independently: CamberView Partners stated in 2017 that one of the Big Three 'is the largest single shareholder in 88% of companies in [the S&P 500] index,' and Kirkland & Ellis said 'almost 90 percent' in February 2019 (both quoted in Big Three Power at 1575 and 1574 n.132).

Attribute 'less than 4 person-days per $1bn position' to BLACKROCK specifically, not to the Big Three collectively. Bebchuk & Hirst, 119 Colum. L. Rev. 2029: 'BlackRock spent less than 4 person-days per year and less than $5,000 in stewardship costs per year, and each of SSGA and Vanguard spent less than 2 person-days per year and less than $2,500.' Also soften 'the most generous scenario': Scenario 4 is the maximum for BlackRock (3.97) but not for SSGA, whose Scenario 3 (1.94) exceeds its Scenario 4 (1.79). And note the paper itself calls Scenario 4 the 'most conservative' assumption set (conservative in the Big Three's favor), so state the direction explicitly to avoid a quote clash.

REWRITE the Kahan & Rock counter. They do not argue that the comparison is 'the dispersed retail investors the funds replaced, whose stewardship was zero.' Their argument (100 B.U. L. Rev. 1771, 1788) is that the right benchmark is the funds' OWN economic owners: 'The question therefore is how Vanguard's incentives compare to those of the actual economic owners of Vanguard's shares—the real-life investors in Vanguard's mutual funds—not how Vanguard's incentives compare to those of a hypothetical individual shareholder who holds the same stake as Vanguard.' Their magnitude language is 'multiple orders of magnitude higher,' never 'zero,' and their conclusion is that index funds 'serve to lower the overall costs of dispersed ownership by multiple orders of magnitude rather than contribute to these costs.'

Drop 'commonly' from 'commonly misquoted as 34% in two decades' unless a specific misquotation is cited. The underlying correction (34.3% is the TEN-year figure; twenty years is 40.8%) is verified, but the prevalence claim is not.

Add the 2022-2026 pass-through voting development, which cuts against the vote-share projections the article reports. BlackRock's Investment Stewardship Annual Report for 2025 states that as of December 31, 2025, '$3.76 trillion of BlackRock's $7.7 trillion total index equity AUM are eligible to participate in BlackRock Voting Choice with clients representing approximately $885 billion in index equity AUM exercising this option.' Vanguard's October 21, 2025 press release states its Investor Choice expansion will 'triple the assets eligible to participate in the program from $1 trillion to over $3 trillion.' The 34.3%/40.8% projections rest on the explicit assumption that the Big Three vote 100% of what they hold.
newContradictions: The 34.3% (2028) / 40.8% (2038) vote projections rest on an assumption the paper makes explicit — 'We assume that the Big Three voted all of the shares that they managed in all of those years' — that is now materially eroding through pass-through voting. BlackRock Investment Stewardship Annual Report 2025 (verbatim): 'As of December 31, 2025, $3.76 trillion of BlackRock's $7.7 trillion total index equity AUM are eligible to participate in BlackRock Voting Choice with clients representing approximately $885 billion in index equity AUM exercising this option.' Bebchuk & Hirst addressed and dismissed an earlier version of this in 2022 (fn 43: clients representing 25%, $530bn of $2.3tn eligible index equity assets, which they computed as 11% of BlackRock's index equity AUM), but the elected base has since grown and Vanguard has scaled a parallel program (Oct. 21, 2025 release: eligible assets tripling 'from $1 trillion to over $3 trillion').

The ownership trend the projection extrapolates flattened after the paper was written. Big Three Power's own Table 1 shows median combined S&P 500 stake of 21.5% (2019), 21.1% (2020), 21.9% (2021) — roughly 0.4pp of net growth over three years against a projection path that requires reaching 27.6% by 2028. The authors report this series and still leave the projection unrevised, which is itself worth noting if the article presents the projection as tracking.

Bebchuk & Hirst's own Figure 1 in Specter of the Giant Three is titled 'Percentage of Corporate Equity Held by Big Three Index Funds' even though the underlying FactSet 13F data is manager-level and includes actively managed assets — by their own 2022 footnote, index funds were only 66% of BlackRock's, 74% of Vanguard's and 79% of SSGA's assets in 2017. The 2019 figure label is therefore internally inconsistent with the 2022 defense, and any article citing '20.5% held by index funds' inherits that error.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Mean combined Big Three stake in S&P 500: 5.2% (1998) → 20.5% (2017)
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in BOTH the published 99 B.U. L. Rev. 721 version and NBER w25914: 'the proportion of S&P 500 shares managed by the Big Three has grown approximately fourfold over the past two decades, from 5.2% in 1998, to 20.5% in 2017.' Table 5 confirms Big Three Total = 20.5% mean / 19.5% median. Source: FactSet Ownership (accessed 7/10/2018) + Compustat S&P 500 constituents. Russell 3000 counterpart is 3.7% → 16.5%.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) The 20.5% includes the Big Three's ACTIVE (non-index) assets
itemVerdicts.note: The 2019 paper does not flag it, but Bebchuk & Hirst concede it explicitly in the 2022 update at 1556 n.30/31: Table 1 'aggregates holdings for all entities with a version of "BlackRock," "Vanguard," or "State Street" in their names' from 'the FactSet 13F Institutional Ownership database' — i.e. entity-level 13F, all strategies. And at 1556 n.30 they cite their own prior evidence that 'in 2017, the proportion of assets invested by the Big Three in index funds fell short of 100%, at "79% for SSGA, 74% for Vanguard, and 66% for BlackRock."' Use that trio of numbers — it is the strongest available quantification of the active-assets contamination (roughly a third of BlackRock's stake is not index money).

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Votes cast ~25.4% mean at S&P 500 director elections 2018
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: '2018'. RIGHT: 2017. Published text at 736: 'the average share of the votes cast at S&P 500 companies AT THE END OF 2017 was 8.7% for BlackRock, 11.1% for Vanguard, and 5.6% for SSGA... the proportion of the total votes that were cast by the Big Three was about 25.4% on average.' Footnote 30: '"Votes cast" refers to the average sum, across all directors up for election, of the votes cast for and against, and abstentions for that director at that corporation's 2017 ANNUAL MEETING.' The 2022 update's own year-by-year Table 2 independently pins 25.4% to 2017 (2018 = 26.5%). The only thing dated 2018 is the 25.35% label on the Figure 3 chart axis, which is the extrapolation's base year, not the measured statistic. Also note the 25.4% is a MEAN; the median is 24.2%.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Wedge vs ownership because non-Big-Three turnout ~73%
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim at 739 / NBER p.17: 'the proportion of shares not managed by the Big Three that voted in director elections varied from 85% in 2008 to 68% in 2017. The average proportion of non-Big-Three holdings voted at director elections over that period was 73%.' Also assumes 'the Big Three voted all of the shares that they managed in all of those years.' Retail turnout footnote: 'In the 2017 proxy season, only 29% of shares owned by retail investors were voted' (Broadridge/PwC ProxyPulse).

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Projections: 34.3% of votes in TEN years (2028), 40.8% in TWENTY (2038); commonly misquoted as '34% in two decades'
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim at 739-40: 'if the proportion of non-Big-Three holdings that are voted remains the same, then the Big Three will control 34.3% of S&P 500 votes IN TEN YEARS, and 40.8% of S&P 500 votes IN TWENTY YEARS.' Figure 3 Panel 1 labels 34.27% at 2028 and 40.76% at 2038. Russell 3000: 29.8% (2028) / 36.7% (2038). I independently reproduced the arithmetic, which confirms the two series are distinct: 27.6/(27.6+0.73×72.4) = 34.3%, and 33.4/(33.4+0.73×66.6) = 40.7%. So 27.6/33.4 are the OWNERSHIP projections and 34.3/40.8 are the VOTE projections.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Method described as 'linear extrapolation'
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 'linear extrapolation'. RIGHT: constant compounded annual rate of decline. At 737: 'In 2008, 13.5% of S&P 500 equity was managed by the Big Three, so 86.5% was not... in 2017, 20.5%... so 79.5% was not. We calculate that the decline from 86.5% to 79.5% over ten years reflected an ANNUAL RATE OF DECLINE OF 0.84%.' (79.5/86.5)^(1/10) = 0.9916, i.e. geometric decay of the non-Big-Three residual, not a straight line. A linear fit would be −0.70pp/yr. Say 'extrapolating a constant 0.84% annual rate of decline in non-Big-Three holdings' — not 'linear.' Their critic Barbara Novick called the projections 'arithmetically correct' while disputing the assumption, so the arithmetic is not the vulnerable part.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Authors hedge
itemVerdicts.note: 2019 at 737: 'We agree with the adage that it is difficult to make predictions, especially about the future.' 2022 at 1561: 'We agree that the growth rates we use for our predictions are not certain... continued growth of the Big Three is very plausible, even if not completely certain, and this is a scenario that policymakers should seriously consider.' They also run a sensitivity: using 2013-2017 instead gives a 1.05% decline rate, 'exceeding the 0.84% decline used above.'

itemVerdicts.item: (b) 2022 update: median stake 21.9% (2021)
itemVerdicts.note: Table 1 at 1556: 2021 = BlackRock 7.7% + Vanguard 9.7% + SSGA 4.5% = 21.9%.
