CAVEAT the article must carry: footnote 31 says 'Estimated medians are rounded to one decimal place; TOTALS IN THE FINAL COLUMN ARE THE SUM OF THE ROUNDED MEDIANS.' A sum of three per-manager medians is not the median combined stake. Do not write '21.9% is the median Big Three stake' — write 'the sum of their three median stakes was 21.9%.' Separately, do NOT splice 20.5% (2017 mean) → 21.9% (2021 sum-of-medians) into one growth series; on the consistent median basis Table 1 runs 19.5% (2017) → 21.9% (2021). Also n.31: the 2022 series uses FactSet 13F data that 'updates the data on which we relied in our earlier work,' so the two papers' series are not strictly comparable.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Votes cast reported as BOTH 24.9% (abstract) and 27.5/27.6% (Table 2 / Section I.A) in the same paper — unreconciled
itemVerdicts.note: Substance CONFIRMED and in fact worse than stated; the attribution is WRONG. WRONG: '24.9% (abstract).' RIGHT: the abstract of 'Big Three Power' contains no numbers at all. 24.9% appears exactly twice, both in body text: the Introduction roadmap at 1552 ('a median stake of 21.9% in S&P 500 companies, which represented a proportion of 24.9% of the votes cast') and Section II.B at 1569 ('the Big Three collectively held, ON AVERAGE, 24.9% of the votes cast at annual meetings of S&P 500 companies in 2021'). The contradiction is sharper than the claim says: footnote 118 sources the 24.9% to 'See supra Table 2 and accompanying text' — but Table 2 reads 27.5% for 2021 and the accompanying text at 1558 says 27.6%. So the paper cites its own table for a number that table does not contain. There is a mean/median tangle too: Table 2 is titled 'Estimated MEDIAN Big Three Ownership... as a Proportion of Total Votes,' but footnote 37 describes computing AVERAGES ('shows the average, across all of the companies in its portfolio... then those results are averaged'), and Table 2's 2017 value (25.4%) equals the 2019 paper's MEAN, not its median (24.2%). Also 9.8+12.0+5.7 = 27.5, so the text's 27.6% does not even match its own table's rounded sum.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) 'Downward-revised projections 27.6% (2028) / 33.4% (2038)'
itemVerdicts.note: REFUTED on two independent counts. (1) NOT downward-revised — not revised at all. 'Big Three Power' Section I.B ('In the Future,' 1560-61) restates the 2019 estimates verbatim and footnotes every one of them to the earlier paper: 'the Big Three can be expected to hold an estimated 27.6% of the shares of S&P 500 companies in 2028 and 33.4% in 2038' (nn.45-48 = 'Bebchuk & Hirst, Giant Three, supra note 4, at 737-41'), and 'we further estimated that the Big Three will hold 34.3% of S&P 500 votes in 2028 and 40.8% of S&P 500 votes in 2038' (nn.50-52 = same). The 0.84% rate and the 73% turnout assumption are carried over unchanged. I checked the full table of contents and grepped for any revised horizon — the 2022 paper contains no updated projection anywhere. (2) MISLABELED — 27.6%/33.4% are OWNERSHIP-SHARE projections, not vote projections, in both papers; they are identical to the 2019 figures at 99 B.U. L. Rev. 738 ('the combined average ownership stake of the Big Three will rise to 27.6% in ten years, and to 33.4% of S&P 500 equity in twenty years'). The vote projections remain 34.3%/40.8%. Delete this sub-claim or rewrite it as: 'the 2022 update did not revise the projections downward — it reprinted the 2019 estimates unchanged.'

itemVerdicts.item: (c) 'Largest shareholder in ~88% of S&P 500' = Sullivan & Cromwell, Dec 2018 data, 438/500, aggregate stake 18.7%
itemVerdicts.note: Fetched the primary and grepped the raw HTML, not a summarizer. Verbatim: 'Concentration of equity ownership, particularly among the largest three index fund providers, continues to be a key component in the activism landscape. As of December 2018, one of BlackRock, Vanguard or State Street was the largest shareholder in 438 of the S&P 500 companies, roughly 88%, and collectively the three firms owned 18.7% of all shares in the S&P 500.' Cite: Melissa Sawyer, Sullivan & Cromwell LLP, 'Annual Review and Analysis of 2019 U.S. Shareholder Activism,' Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, Nov. 20, 2019 (memo published Nov 2019; DATA as of Dec 2018). Quoted in full at 102 B.U. L. Rev. 1572 n.132. Two caliber notes: (i) S&C says '18.7% of all shares in the S&P 500' — an aggregate share count. Calling it 'value-weighted' is your inference; it is defensible (aggregate = value-weighted mean of firm-level stakes) but is not S&C's word, so say 'aggregate' or 'in aggregate they owned 18.7% of all S&P 500 shares.' (ii) 'roughly 88%' is S&C's own rounding of 438/500 = 87.6%. Staleness: Dec 2018 data is ~7.7 years old as of Aug 2026 — 'nearly eight years' is safer than 'eight years.' A near-identical claim in the same paper (1575 n.139) traces to CamberView Partners in 2017, so the statistic was already circulating undated before S&C; I found no updated primary equivalent through 2026-08.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Stewardship staffing 45/21/12; person-days 0.25-3.97; 'less than 4 person-days per $1bn' is the most generous scenario
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed against the PUBLISHED Columbia Law Review PDF (119 Colum. L. Rev. 2029), not just the NBER working paper. Table 1: Stewardship Personnel 45 / 21 / 12; Portfolio Companies (Worldwide) 11,246* / 13,225 / 12,191*. Table 3 person-days: Scenario 1 (equal allocation, worldwide) 1.00/0.40/0.25; Scenario 2 (75% to U.S., per U.S. company) 2.24/1.07/0.72; Scenario 3 (per $1bn worldwide) 3.71/1.36/1.94; Scenario 4 (per $1bn U.S.) 3.97/1.58/1.79. So 0.25 (SSGA, Scenario 1) to 3.97 (BlackRock, Scenario 4) is exactly right. The headline sentence: 'Even under the most conservative assumptions, in order to oversee each of their billion-dollar positions, BlackRock spent less than 4 person-days per year and less than $5,000 in stewardship costs per year, and each of SSGA and Vanguard spent less than 2 person-days per year and less than $2,500.' Your framing is correct: 3.97 is the LARGEST cell in the whole table, so 'less than 4 person-days' is the reading most flattering to the managers — B&H's own word for it is 'most conservative' (i.e. biased against their own thesis). Two notes: the figure is BLACKROCK-SPECIFIC (Vanguard/SSGA are under 2), and VERSION MATTERS — the earlier ECGI/SSRN working paper (Law WP N° 433/2018, July 2019) has DIFFERENT numbers: personnel 33/21/11, Table 3 range 0.16-3.17, and the sentence 'each of the Big Three spends less than 3.5 person-days each year, and less than $4,000.' Cite the published Columbia version or NBER w26543 (Dec 2019), never the July 2019 WP.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) BlackRock's team is now '60+' while AUM grew faster
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim from the primary PDF (BlackRock Investment Stewardship Annual Report, Jan 1 – Dec 31, 2025): 'Our team of more than 60 dedicated professionals — who operate across nine offices — brings decades of experience in corporate governance and stewardship,' and separately 'With more than 60 professionals focused full time on stewardship... In 2009, we were a team of 16.' Same report: 'clients entrusted BlackRock with $14 trillion of assets under management (AUM)' and '$7.7 trillion' in public equity AUM as of Dec 31, 2025. So staff 45 → 60+ is roughly +33% while AUM went from ~$6.5T (end-2018) / ~$7.4T (end-2019) to $14T, roughly doubling. 'AUM grew faster' holds comfortably. One qualifier to add: BlackRock split out a separate BlackRock Active Investment Stewardship (BAIS) team in 2024, '13 dedicated professionals in six offices globally,' so total stewardship headcount is ~73+, not 60+ — the 60+ covers the index/BIS side only, which is the relevant comparison to the 2019 figure but should be stated as such.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Kahan & Rock's counter: the right comparison is dispersed retail investors the funds replaced, whose stewardship was zero
itemVerdicts.note: Read the published 100 B.U. L. Rev. 1771 (2020) in full. Directionally right, materially miscalibrated on both halves. WRONG comparison group: 'the dispersed retail investors the funds replaced.' RIGHT: the fund's own investors — the actual economic owners of the shares. At 1788: 'The question therefore is how Vanguard's incentives compare to those of the ACTUAL ECONOMIC OWNERS of Vanguard's shares — the real-life investors in Vanguard's mutual funds — not how Vanguard's incentives compare to those of a hypothetical individual shareholder who holds the same stake as Vanguard.' Their framing at 1776 is that comparing advisers to 'regular shareholders owning the same stake — a comparison in which advisers will necessarily fare poorly — is a CATEGORY MISTAKE.' The counterfactual is the same investors holding directly rather than through the fund, not a historical population the funds displaced. WRONG magnitude: 'whose stewardship was zero.' K&R never say zero. They say index fund advisers' incentives are 'multiple orders of magnitude higher' than fund investors'; that 'Individual shareholders have notoriously poor incentives' (1789); that retail investors are 'the group that has the least overall incentives to become informed' (1814); and in the conclusion, 'Small individual shareholders, who are least likely to have conflicts of interests, have among the worst incentives to become informed.' Also note they explicitly entertain OTHER comparison groups and do not rest on retail: they benchmark the Big Three against advisers to actively managed funds (Table 1, Table 2 relative-incentive scores) and against public pension funds, concluding 'the relative incentives of the Big Three are by far the strongest in the industry.' Their bottom line is complementarity — 'different institutions have different advantages that complement each other' — not that the Big Three are good because retail was zero.

corrections: Change 'votes cast ~25.4% at S&P 500 director elections in 2018' to '...in 2017.' The published text (99 B.U. L. Rev. 736) says 'at the end of 2017,' footnote 30 says the votes are from 'that corporation's 2017 annual meeting,' and the 2022 update's year-by-year Table 2 puts 25.4% at 2017 and 26.5% at 2018. Only the Figure 3 chart axis carries a 2018 label (25.35%), and that is the extrapolation's base year, not the measured statistic.

Do not call the Bebchuk-Hirst projection a 'linear extrapolation.' They extrapolate a CONSTANT COMPOUNDED ANNUAL RATE of 0.84% decline in non-Big-Three holdings (86.5% in 2008 → 79.5% in 2017), which is geometric decay, not a straight line. A linear fit would be −0.70pp/yr. Their own critic conceded the projections are 'arithmetically correct,' so the arithmetic is not the weak point — the constant-rate assumption is.

DELETE or rewrite the claim that the 2022 update carries 'downward-revised projections 27.6% (2028)/33.4% (2038).' The 2022 paper revised nothing: Section I.B reprints the 2019 estimates and footnotes all four to 'Giant Three, supra note 4, at 737-41.' And 27.6%/33.4% are the OWNERSHIP-share projections in both papers; the VOTE projections are 34.3% (2028)/40.8% (2038), also unchanged. Correct sentence: 'The 2022 update left the projections untouched, reprinting the 2019 figures verbatim.'

Change '24.9% (abstract)' to '24.9% (Introduction at 1552, and again at 1569).' The abstract of 'Big Three Power' contains no numbers. Strengthen the point while you are there: footnote 118 sources the 24.9% to 'supra Table 2 and accompanying text,' but Table 2 reads 27.5% and the accompanying text at 1558 reads 27.6% — the paper cites its own table for a figure that table does not contain. Add that 1569 calls 24.9% an average while Table 2 is titled a median.

Do not present 21.9% (2021) as 'the median combined Big Three stake.' Footnote 31 states 'totals in the final column are the sum of the rounded medians' — a sum of three per-manager medians, not the median of the combined stake. Same caveat applies to Table 2's 27.5%. Write 'the sum of their three median stakes.'

Do not splice 20.5% (2017, mean, 2019 paper) and 21.9% (2021, sum-of-medians, 2022 paper) into one growth series. They are different statistics from different data vintages — footnote 31 says the 2022 series uses FactSet 13F data that 'updates the data on which we relied in our earlier work.' On the consistent median basis, Table 1 runs 19.5% (2017) → 21.9% (2021).

When making the 'includes active assets' point, cite the hard number rather than asserting it: Bebchuk & Hirst concede at 102 B.U. L. Rev. 1556 n.30 that 'in 2017, the proportion of assets invested by the Big Three in index funds fell short of 100%, at "79% for SSGA, 74% for Vanguard, and 66% for BlackRock."' Roughly a third of BlackRock's counted stake is not index money.

For the S&C statistic, say 'in aggregate the three firms owned 18.7% of all S&P 500 shares,' not 'aggregate value-weighted stake.' The memo's words are 'collectively the three firms owned 18.7% of all shares in the S&P 500.' Cite it as Melissa Sawyer, Sullivan & Cromwell, 'Annual Review and Analysis of 2019 U.S. Shareholder Activism,' HLS Forum on Corporate Governance (Nov. 20, 2019), with data as of December 2018. Prefer 'nearly eight years old' to 'eight years stale.'

Attribute the '4 person-days' figure to BlackRock specifically and to the PUBLISHED version. The published Columbia Law Review text reads: 'in order to oversee each of their billion-dollar positions, BlackRock spent less than 4 person-days per year and less than $5,000... and each of SSGA and Vanguard spent less than 2 person-days per year and less than $2,500.' Do not source the staffing numbers to the July 2019 ECGI/SSRN working paper, which has different figures (33/21/11 personnel; person-day range 0.16-3.17; 'less than 3.5 person-days').

Rewrite the Kahan & Rock counter. Their comparison group is the fund's own investors — 'the ACTUAL ECONOMIC OWNERS of Vanguard's shares — the real-life investors in Vanguard's mutual funds — not... a hypothetical individual shareholder who holds the same stake' (1788) — and they call Bebchuk-Hirst's benchmark a 'category mistake' (1776). It is not 'the retail investors the funds replaced.' And they never say retail stewardship was zero: they say individual shareholders have 'notoriously poor incentives' and 'among the worst incentives to become informed.' Add that they also benchmark the Big Three favorably against active-fund advisers and public pension funds, and conclude on complementarity, not on retail's inadequacy.

If the article cites the 2022 update for the person-days figure, note that B&H's own restatement at 1591 drops the denominator — 'BlackRock spent fewer than four person-days per year, and less than $5,000 in stewardship costs' with no 'per $1bn position' — which reads as per-company and is wrong (Scenario 1 gives 1.00 person-day per worldwide portfolio company, Scenario 2 gives 2.24 per U.S. company). Quote the 2019 Columbia sentence, not the 2022 paraphrase.
newContradictions: BlackRock Voting Choice materially undercuts the vote-share extrapolation and is not addressed anywhere in the 2019 or 2022 papers (the program launched January 2022, after both). From the BlackRock Investment Stewardship Annual Report 2025, verbatim: 'As of December 31, 2025, $3.76 trillion of BlackRock's $7.7 trillion total index equity AUM are eligible to participate in BlackRock Voting Choice with clients representing approximately $885 billion in index equity AUM exercising this option.' So ~11.5% of BlackRock's index equity AUM is now voted to client-selected policies rather than by BlackRock, with ~49% eligible. The 34.3%/40.8% projections assume the Big Three vote 100% of what they hold — an assumption stated explicitly at 99 B.U. L. Rev. 739 ('We assume that the Big Three voted all of the shares that they managed'). Any 2026 article using those projections must flag pass-through voting as a live counterforce. Bebchuk & Hirst themselves anticipated the objection only in the separate-accounts form and dismissed it as 'a relatively small minority of the shares' (1559) — that dismissal was written before Voting Choice scaled.

The stewardship-underinvestment critique now has a second, unaccounted team: BlackRock created BlackRock Active Investment Stewardship (BAIS) in 2024, '13 dedicated professionals in six offices globally' per the 2025 BIS report. Total BlackRock stewardship headcount is therefore ~73+, not 60+. This does not overturn the 'AUM grew faster than staffing' point (45 → ~73 is +62% against roughly a doubling of AUM), but the article should not present 60+ as BlackRock's total stewardship staff.

The 2022 update's Table 2 carries an unresolved mean/median labeling defect that the article can use but must not compound: the table is titled 'Estimated MEDIAN Big Three Ownership of S&P 500 Companies, as a Proportion of Total Votes,' while footnote 37 describes computing AVERAGES ('shows the average, across all of the companies in its portfolio... then those results are averaged for each manager and year'). Table 2's 2017 entry (25.4%) equals the 2019 paper's MEAN votes-cast figure, not its median (24.2%) — suggesting the 'median' series is actually a mean series. This is likely the mechanical source of the unreconciled 24.9% vs 27.5% wedge.

The 2019 Giant Three paper contains a table-numbering error in the NBER working paper (w25914) that was fixed in the published version: the NBER text at p.14 says 'Table 4 contrasts (1) the fraction of shares owned... and (2) the fraction of the votes' while the table immediately below is labeled Table 5. The published 99 B.U. L. Rev. 736 reads 'Table 5.' Cite the published version to avoid inheriting the typo.
reasoning:
I reached every primary document verbatim rather than relying on any summarizer, and I deliberately fetched BOTH the working-paper and published versions of each paper because the task flagged version drift in this literature — that precaution paid off.

Documents read verbatim (local extracts plus fresh fetches, all grepped for exact strings): NBER w25914 and the published 99 B.U. L. Rev. 721 (Specter of the Giant Three); NBER w26543, the ECGI Law WP N° 433/2018 July 2019 draft, AND the published 119 Colum. L. Rev. 2029 PDF from columbialawreview.org (Index Funds and the Future of Corporate Governance); the published 102 B.U. L. Rev. 1547 (Big Three Power); the published 100 B.U. L. Rev. 1771 (Kahan & Rock); the raw HTML of the Sullivan & Cromwell HLS Forum post (I re-grepped the HTML with a Python tag-stripper rather than trusting the WebFetch answer, which had returned only fragments); and BlackRock's Investment Stewardship Annual Report for 2025 (5MB PDF, pdftotext'd and grepped).

Findings that changed the verdict. Sub-claim (b)'s "downward-revised projections 27.6%/33.4%" is flatly false and is the one item I would not let through: the 2022 paper's Section I.B reprints the 2019 estimates and footnotes all four of them to "Giant Three... at 737-41," and 27.6/33.4 are the ownership-share projections, not vote projections. I confirmed the two series are genuinely distinct by reproducing the arithmetic myself — 27.6/(27.6+0.73×72.4) = 34.3% and 33.4/(33.4+0.73×66.6) = 40.7% — which is exactly the ownership→votes conversion via the 73% turnout assumption. I also grepped the 2022 paper's full table of contents and searched for any later horizon year; there is no revised projection anywhere in it.

The version check on (d) was the other payoff: the July 2019 ECGI/SSRN draft reports 33/21/11 personnel and a 0.16–3.17 person-day range with the headline "less than 3.5 person-days," whereas the published Columbia version and NBER w26543 report 45/21/12 and 0.25–3.97 with "less than 4 person-days." The claim group's numbers match the published version, so they are right — but only if sourced correctly, hence the correction.

Smaller caliber slips I could confirm against the page: the 25.4% is a 2017 statistic (the published text says "at the end of 2017" and footnote 30 says "2017 annual meeting"; the 2022 update's own year series independently puts 25.4% at 2017 and 26.5% at 2018), the 24.9% is in the Introduction and body, not the abstract (the abstract has no numbers at all), the projection method is compounded rather than linear, and the 2021 "21.9%" is a sum of three per-manager medians by the authors' own footnote.

On (e) I read Kahan & Rock end to end rather than relying on how Bebchuk & Hirst characterize them. The claim's gist survives but the two load-bearing specifics do not: their comparison group is the fund's own investors, not "the retail investors the funds replaced," and they never say retail stewardship was zero — the strongest language is "notoriously poor" and "among the worst incentives."

Two things I want to be explicit about as uncertain. First, the Figure 3 chart in the 2019 paper labels 25.35% at the 2018 tick even though the text pins 25.4% to 2017; I judged the text and footnote authoritative and treated the figure's 2018 as the extrapolation base year, but the paper is genuinely ambiguous on this and a third verifier might read it differently. Second, I could not locate any post-2021 primary update to the "largest shareholder in 88% of S&P 500 firms" rank statistic through 2026-08 — the 2025-vintage sources I saw were all secondary and were simply recirculating the S&C figure without dating it, which corroborates the article's staleness point but is not itself evidence. I did not treat those as sources. I also note the same 88% claim appears in the 2022 paper attributed to CamberView Partners in 2017, predating the S&C memo, so the S&C attribution is one valid provenance rather than the sole origin.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) ASt: airline ticket prices 3-7% higher from panel regressions vs separate-ownership counterfactual
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the cited IESE WP-1169-E (March 23, 2017), p.3: 'Using fixed-effect panel regressions, we find that ticket prices are approximately 3-7% higher on the average US airline route than would be the case under separate ownership.' Also in the conclusion: 'using fourteen years of market-firm-level quarterly panel data, we find that airline ticket prices are 3-7% higher because of common ownership, compared to a counterfactual world in which firms are separately owned, or in which firms entirely ignore their owners' anti-competitive incentives.' The published JF text carries this too: the Committee on Capital Markets Regulation study (June 2025, p.6 n.17) pin-cites 'id. at 1517' quoting 'ticket prices are approximately 3% to 7% higher…than would be the case under separate ownership.'

itemVerdicts.item: (a) ASt: 10-12% is the BlackRock-BGI-merger IV estimate
itemVerdicts.note: IESE WP p.3: 'They indicate that product prices may be 10-12% higher due to common ownership' — describing the difference-in-differences/IV strategy using the hypothetical BlackRock+BGI portfolio combination. Body (Sec. 5.2.2): 'Multiplying the estimates with the average MHHI delta across routes would imply that ticket prices are about 10%-12% higher because of common ownership alone.' Caliber caveats the article should not drop: ASt hedge with 'may be'; the individual post-period coefficients for 2010Q1, 2011Q1 and 2013Q1 are 'positive and economically sizable but not statistically significant', only 2012Q1 and 2014Q1 are individually significant; the pooled four-period coefficient is 0.542 and is 'markedly higher than the effects estimated in panel regressions'.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) ASt: the DIRECT effect of the BGI merger was ~0.5%
itemVerdicts.note: IESE WP-1169-E, Sec. 5.2.2, verbatim: 'the average implied MHHI delta is about 91 HHI points; our estimates thus indicate that ticket prices on the average U.S. airline route increased by about 0.5% as a direct result of the BlackRock-BGI acquisition.' Intro restates it as 'the acquisition itself increased average ticket prices by about half a percent.' Note: I verified the 10-12% and 0.5% figures in the March 2017 IESE working paper (which is the OA version OpenAlex links for the JF article, and is exactly the URL the article cites); Wiley/JSTOR blocked every attempt to reach the typeset JF pages, so I could not independently confirm those two figures survived unchanged into the 2018 print version.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) The published JF 2018 abstract contains no price percentage
itemVerdicts.note: Crossref-registered JF abstract (10.1111/jofi.12698, JF 73(4):1513-1565) reads in full: 'Many natural competitors are jointly held by a small set of large institutional investors. In the U.S. airline industry, taking common ownership into account implies increases in market concentration that are 10 times larger than what is "presumed likely to enhance market power" by antitrust authorities. Within-route changes in common ownership concentration robustly correlate with route-level changes in ticket prices, even when we only use variation in ownership due to the combination of two large asset managers. We conclude that a hidden social cost—reduced product market competition—accompanies the private benefits of diversification and good governance.' No percentage; the only quantified claim is the 10x concentration comparison, and the price language is correlational ('robustly correlate'). Same in the WP abstract.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) DGS (JF 2022): the correlation loads on the market-share half of MHHI-delta, not the ownership half (placebo tests)
itemVerdicts.note: Published JF abstract (10.1111/jofi.13176, JF 77(5):2765-2798), verbatim: 'This paper reevaluates this evidence and shows that the documented positive correlation between common ownership and airline ticket prices stems from the market share component of the common ownership measure, and not the ownership and control components.' Placebo method confirmed from Gerardi-Lowry-Schenone p.26: 'The paper implements a placebo analysis, which shows that the positive correlation between MHHI-delta and airline ticket prices is driven by the market share component of the MHHI-delta measure rather than the ownership and control components,' and their Table entry for Dennis et al. (2022a) lists 'Fixed Effects; Placebo tests', airline, 2001-2014. Minor caliber: DGS name TWO non-market-share components ('the ownership and control components'), so 'the ownership half' is a simplification of a three-way decomposition.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) DGS: bankruptcy treatment attenuates results
itemVerdicts.note: JF abstract: 'We further show that the results are sensitive to measures of investor control and to assumptions about equity holders' ownership and control during bankruptcy.' GLS p.26: DGS 'show that the relationship between common ownership and ticket prices is not robust to alternative measures of investor control and to assumptions about the extent of investor control during bankruptcy periods.' 'Attenuates' is if anything understated relative to the third-party characterization in CCMR (June 2025, p.6): DGS find 'the airline paper's main results disappear under more plausible bankruptcy assumptions' (i.e., assuming pre-bankruptcy stockholders lose cash-flow rights or control). Safer wording: 'not robust to / disappear under alternative bankruptcy control assumptions.'

itemVerdicts.item: (b) The ASt 'Refutation' and DGS 'Surrebuttal' are both unpublished SSRN papers; the exchange is UNRESOLVED in refereed venues as of 2026-08
itemVerdicts.note: OpenAlex and Crossref both classify ASt 'A Refutation of...' (10.2139/ssrn.4158149, and a second posting 10.2139/ssrn.4219441) and DGS 'A Surrebuttal: There Are No Anti-Competitive Effects of Common Ownership in the Airline Industry' (10.2139/ssrn.4307814) as SSRN preprints/posted-content with no journal version, as of this check. The Refutation also circulates as ECGI Finance WP 837/2022 (19 Aug 2022) and CESifo WP 9937 — both non-refereed working-paper series, which reinforces rather than undercuts the claim. Corroborated by GLS's own footnote 27: 'In subsequent work, Azar et al. (2022b) presents a critique of the Dennis et al. (2022a) placebo analysis and Dennis et al. (2022b) responds to that critique.' — recorded with no resolution.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) BCS: between a third and half of the variation in profit weights comes from relative investor concentration, not overlapping ownership
itemVerdicts.note: Backus-Conlon-Sinkinson, 'Common Ownership in America: 1980-2017', accepted AEA manuscript at chrisconlon.github.io/site/common_owner.pdf, verbatim: 'We show that between a third and a half of the variation in the profit weight measure comes not from overlapping ownership as many researchers assume, but instead from relative investor concentration, which we make precise in what follows.' Restated in Sec. II: overlapping ownership 'only makes up a little over half of the empirical variation in common ownership profit weights. The remainder comes from variation in the ability of common owners to exert control, implicitly modeled as a function of investor concentration.' The hosted PDF's abstract matches the Crossref abstract for AEJ:Micro 13(3):273-308 (10.1257/mic.20190389) word-for-word, so it is the accepted version of the published paper. Venue attribution (AEJ:Micro 2021) confirmed.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) BCS: taken literally the theory implies >10% of S&P 500 firms tunneling by 2017, treated as a reductio
itemVerdicts.note: Intro, verbatim: 'Taking the strict form of common ownership seriously, it could be used to micro-found a tremendous increase in markups between 1980 and 2017, and one might also conclude that over 10% of S&P 500 firms are engaging in tunneling behavior by 2017. We find these predictions to be unrealistically strong.' Section IV.A, verbatim: 'the implication of taking the common ownership hypothesis seriously, that in 2017 more than 10% of the S&P 500 is engaging in some form of tunneling behavior, is implausibly strong.' Reductio framing confirmed. One caveat BCS themselves flag: 'unlike our results in Section III, in the later periods, the result depends heavily on our assumptions about gamma.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d) GLS quote: 'relatively little evidence that common ownership causes lower competition'
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG (as presented): an unqualified conclusion attributed to Atlanta Fed WP 2023-17. RIGHT: the sentence carries an essential restrictive clause and an immediate hedge. Atlanta Fed WP 2023-17 / ECGI Finance WP 943/2023 abstract, verbatim: 'Across the newest papers employing the most credible identification techniques, there is relatively little evidence that common ownership causes lower competition. However, further research is necessary before broad conclusions can be reached.' Also STALE CITATION: this is no longer a working paper — it was published as Gerardi, Lowry & Schenone, 'A Critical Review of the Common Ownership Literature,' Annual Review of Financial Economics 16 (Nov 2024): 89-114, DOI 10.1146/annurev-financial-082123-105841, where the wording is 'relatively little evidence has been found that common ownership causes lower competition.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d) COI: two of three GLS authors wrote the replication critique
itemVerdicts.note: GLS authors are Kristopher Gerardi (FRB Atlanta), Michelle Lowry (Drexel), Carola Schenone (UVA); DGS authors are Patrick Dennis, Kristopher Gerardi, Carola Schenone. Gerardi and Schenone are 2 of 3 on both. In the review they cite their own paper in the third person as 'Dennis et al. (2022a)' throughout Sections 5 and 6 with no COI note in the text I read.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) 'Azar & Vives' opposing survey has the mirror COI'
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: there is no Azar & Vives survey or review of the common-ownership literature. Their complete co-authored corpus (OpenAlex, filtered on Azar A5059636061) is: 'General Equilibrium Oligopoly and Ownership Structure' (Econometrica 89(3), 2021 — theory), 'Reply to: Comments on General Equilibrium Oligopoly and Ownership Structure' (Econometrica 2021 — a letter about their own model), 'Common Ownership and the Secular Stagnation Hypothesis' (AEA P&P 2019), 'Oligopoly, Macroeconomic Performance, and Competition Policy' (SSRN), and 'Revisiting the Anticompetitive Effects of Common Ownership' (ECGI Finance WP 827/2022 / SSRN 3805047) — the last is an EMPIRICAL airline paper, not a survey, and is itself still unpublished; I read its ECGI title page and abstract, which opens 'We use data from the U.S. airline industry to test the hypothesis...'. RIGHT mirror-COI surveys, both verified in Crossref: Martin C. Schmalz, 'Common-Ownership Concentration and Corporate Conduct,' Annual Review of Financial Economics 10 (Nov 2018): 413-448 (Schmalz is an ASt co-author — the exact structural mirror of GLS/DGS); and/or Azar, Schmalz & Tecu, 'Research on the Competitive Consequences of Common Ownership: A Methodological Critique,' The Antitrust Bulletin 66(1) (March 2021): 113-122 (3 of 3 authors are the critiqued paper's authors).

corrections: Replace 'Azar & Vives' opposing survey has the mirror COI' — no such survey exists. Azar and Vives never co-authored a review of the common-ownership literature; their joint work is theory (Econometrica 89(3), 2021), an AEA P&P note (2019), and an unpublished empirical airline paper ('Revisiting the Anticompetitive Effects of Common Ownership,' ECGI Finance WP 827/2022, still SSRN-only). The correct mirror-COI survey is Martin C. Schmalz, 'Common-Ownership Concentration and Corporate Conduct,' Annual Review of Financial Economics 10 (2018): 413-448 — an ASt co-author surveying the literature that his own paper anchors. Azar, Schmalz & Tecu, 'Research on the Competitive Consequences of Common Ownership: A Methodological Critique,' The Antitrust Bulletin 66(1) (2021): 113-122, is an even tighter mirror (3 of 3).

Update the Gerardi-Lowry-Schenone citation: it is no longer only Atlanta Fed WP 2023-17 (Nov 2023). It was published as 'A Critical Review of the Common Ownership Literature,' Annual Review of Financial Economics 16 (2024): 89-114, DOI 10.1146/annurev-financial-082123-105841. The published wording is 'relatively little evidence has been found that common ownership causes lower competition.'

Restore the qualifier stripped from the GLS quote. The full sentence is 'Across the newest papers employing the most credible identification techniques, there is relatively little evidence that common ownership causes lower competition,' immediately followed by 'However, further research is necessary before broad conclusions can be reached.' Quoting only the middle clause converts a scoped, hedged finding into a blanket verdict on the literature.

Soften or re-source 'bankruptcy treatment attenuates results.' DGS's own published abstract says the results 'are sensitive to measures of investor control and to assumptions about equity holders' ownership and control during bankruptcy'; GLS say 'not robust to.' If the stronger 'disappear' framing is wanted, attribute it — the Committee on Capital Markets Regulation (June 2025) writes that DGS find the airline paper's 'main results disappear under more plausible bankruptcy assumptions,' but CCMR is an industry-funded body, not a neutral source.

Add ASt's hedge to the 10-12% figure. ASt write that the BGI-merger estimates 'may be 10-12% higher'; in Table 6 the individual post-period coefficients for 2010Q1, 2011Q1 and 2013Q1 are positive but statistically insignificant, with only 2012Q1 and 2014Q1 individually significant. The 10-12% rests on the pooled four-period coefficient (0.542), which ASt themselves call 'markedly higher than the effects estimated in panel regressions.'

Note the sourcing basis for the ASt numbers. The 3-7%, 10-12% and ~0.5% figures were verified verbatim in the March 2017 IESE WP-1169-E (the URL the article cites, and the only OA full text OpenAlex links for the JF article). The 3%-7% figure is separately confirmed at JF p.1517 via a third-party pin cite. The 10-12% and ~0.5% figures could not be checked against the typeset JF 2018 pages (Wiley blocked). Either cite the working paper for those two, or verify the JF page numbers.

If DGS's decomposition is described, say 'the market-share component rather than the ownership AND CONTROL components' — DGS separate ownership from control, so 'the ownership half' collapses a three-way decomposition into two.
newContradictions: Egland, Hearey, Schatzki & Verbeck, 'Reassessing Common Ownership: Corrections to Azar, Schmalz, and Tecu (2018)' (SSRN 3463231, 2019) is a separate data-error critique of ASt that the claim group omits. It carries a COI in the skeptic direction that mirrors the one the article flags for GLS: the authors disclose the research 'was undertaken with the financial support of BlackRock' (per CCMR's footnote 25). If the article is going to score COIs, this one belongs on the board — as does the fact that ASt's Tecu was at Charles River Associates, disclosed in the WP's own first footnote.

Azar & Ribeiro (2024), 'Estimating Oligopoly with Shareholder Voting Models' (CRESSE conference paper, March 2024) is characterized by CCMR as a study 'conducted by one of the original airline paper's authors' that excludes major airline bankruptcy periods and finds the net effect of common ownership by the largest asset managers is a DECREASE in airline ticket prices. If accurate, that is a partial concession from the ASt side and materially changes the 'unresolved standoff' framing. I did NOT reach this primary document — flagging it as a lead requiring verification, not as an established fact.

Committee on Capital Markets Regulation, 'Common Ownership and Prices: A Comprehensive Generalized Study' (June 2025) is a substantial post-2024 entry that the claim group does not mention. It is an advocacy body's product, not a refereed paper, and should be labeled as such if used — but it is the most recent systematic re-examination I found and it comes down hard on the skeptic side.

The COI framing in (d) is structurally sound but should note that it generalizes: essentially every survey in this literature is written by a participant (GLS by DGS authors; Schmalz 2018 and ASt 2021 by ASt authors; Ederer's 'Common Ownership: A Guide for Antitrust Practitioners' by a common-ownership researcher). Presenting GLS-vs-a-single-opposing-survey as a clean two-sided COI pairing understates how uniformly non-neutral the review literature is.
reasoning: I reached primary text verbatim for four of the five documents. (1) Azar-Schmalz-Tecu, IESE WP-1169-E (fetched and pdftotext'd from the cited URL): confirmed 'approximately 3-7% higher... than would be the case under separate ownership' from fixed-effect panel regressions, 'product prices may be 10-12% higher' from the BlackRock-BGI DiD/IV, and 'ticket prices on the average U.S. airline route increased by about 0.5% as a direct result of the BlackRock-BGI acquisition' — plus an abstract containing no price percentage. The published JF 2018 abstract (Crossref, 10.1111/jofi.12698) likewise contains no percentage; its only quantified claim is the 10x concentration comparison and its price language is 'robustly correlate.' (2) Dennis-Gerardi-Schenone JF 2022 abstract (Crossref, 10.1111/jofi.13176): confirmed the market-share-component finding and the bankruptcy sensitivity verbatim; every route to the DGS full text was blocked (Wiley Cloudflare, econstor, the Atlanta Fed URLs are now 404, CESifo), so I corroborated the placebo method from Gerardi-Lowry-Schenone's own description at p.26 and their summary table, which is authored by two of the three DGS authors. (3) Backus-Conlon-Sinkinson (fetched chrisconlon.github.io/site/common_owner.pdf): confirmed 'between a third and a half of the variation in the profit weight measure comes not from overlapping ownership... but instead from relative investor concentration' and 'in 2017 more than 10% of the S&P 500 is engaging in some form of tunneling behavior, is implausibly strong'; the hosted PDF's abstract matches the AEJ:Micro 13(3):273-308 Crossref abstract word-for-word, so it is the accepted version. (4) Gerardi-Lowry-Schenone (the atlantafed.org URL in the source list 404s; I got the identical paper from ECGI Finance WP 943/2023): the quoted sentence is verbatim but scoped by 'Across the newest papers employing the most credible identification techniques' and immediately hedged, and the paper is no longer a working paper — it was published in Annual Review of Financial Economics 16 (2024): 89-114. Publication status of the Refutation and Surrebuttal was checked in both Crossref and OpenAlex: both remain SSRN posted-content with no journal version; the Refutation additionally circulates as ECGI WP 837/2022 and CESifo WP 9937, both non-refereed. The one refutation: I searched OpenAlex's complete Azar work list and the open web and found no Azar-Vives survey of any kind — their joint output is a theory paper, a reply letter, an AEA P&P note, and an unpublished empirical airline paper whose ECGI title page I read directly. The mirror-COI survey the article is reaching for is Schmalz's 2018 Annual Review of Financial Economics piece (verified in Crossref: vol. 10, pp. 413-448) or ASt's 2021 Antitrust Bulletin methodological critique (66:113-122). Remaining uncertainty: I could not open the typeset JF 2018 pages, so the 10-12% and ~0.5% figures are verified only in the March 2017 working paper the article cites (the 3%-7% figure is separately pinned to JF p.1517 through a third-party quotation); and the Azar & Ribeiro (2024) result reported by CCMR is a lead I did not verify at the source.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) ASt: airline ticket prices 3-7% higher in fixed-effect panel regressions vs a separate-ownership counterfactual
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim twice in the article's own cited source (IESE WP-1169-E, 23 March 2017), p.3: 'Using fixed-effect panel regressions, we find that ticket prices are approximately 3-7% higher on the average US airline route than would be the case under separate ownership.' Conclusion repeats: 'using fourteen years of market-firm-level quarterly panel data, we find that airline ticket prices are 3-7% higher because of common ownership, compared to a counterfactual world in which firms are separately owned, or in which firms entirely ignore their owners' anti-competitive incentives.' Independently pin-cited to the PUBLISHED text by the Committee on Capital Markets Regulation (June 2025 study, n.4): 'See id. at 1517 (claiming that "ticket prices are approximately 3% to 7% higher…than would be the case under separate ownership.")' — i.e. the figure survived into JF 73(4):1513-1565 at p.1517. NOTE for the author: earlier drafts of the same paper carried DIFFERENT numbers (the April 2015 CRA-hosted draft says 'at least 10%' from panel-IV; Azar's Nov 2015 FTC Microeconomics Conference slides say '3-11% higher prices' and '0.6%'). Only the 2017/published numbers may be attributed to 'ASt (JF 2018)'.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) 10-12% is the BlackRock-BGI-merger IV estimate, not the panel estimate
itemVerdicts.note: IESE WP-1169-E p.3-4: the DiD/IV strategy 'estimates from this strategy are arguably less affected by endogeneity of ownership and market shares. They indicate that product prices may be 10-12% higher due to common ownership.' Body (Sec. 5.2.2): 'Multiplying the estimates with the average MHHI delta across routes would imply that ticket prices are about 10%-12% higher because of common ownership alone, compared to a counterfactual world in which firms are separately owned.' Conclusion repeats '10-12%'. Caliber note: the paper frames this as a difference-in-differences identification strategy implemented as 2SLS/panel-IV (Table 6 second stage, coefficient 0.542; discrete-treatment instrument version 0.462) — calling it 'the IV estimate' is fair but 'DiD/IV' is more exact. Verified in the green-OA/accepted manuscript, not in the paywalled Wiley typeset pages (Wiley returns 403; no repository copy of the version of record exists per Unpaywall/OpenAlex/CORE).

itemVerdicts.item: (a) The DIRECT effect of the BGI merger was ~0.5%
itemVerdicts.note: IESE WP-1169-E, Sec. 5.2.2: 'the average implied MHHI delta is about 91 HHI points; our estimates thus indicate that ticket prices on the average U.S. airline route increased by about 0.5% as a direct result of the BlackRock-BGI acquisition.' Intro p.4 states the same as 'increased average ticket prices by about half a percent.' (The superseded 2015 draft/slides said 0.6% — do not mix versions.)

itemVerdicts.item: (a) The published JF abstract contains no price percentage
itemVerdicts.note: Published abstract obtained verbatim from two independent indexes of the publisher record (EconPapers/RePEc for JF 73(4):1513-1565, and the Semantic Scholar record for DOI 10.1111/jofi.12698). Full text: 'Many natural competitors are jointly held by a small set of large institutional investors. In the U.S. airline industry, taking common ownership into account implies increases in market concentration that are 10 times larger than what is "presumed likely to enhance market power" by antitrust authorities. Within-route changes in common ownership concentration robustly correlate with route-level changes in ticket prices, even when we only use variation in ownership due to the combination of two large asset managers. We conclude that a hidden social cost—reduced product market competition—accompanies the private benefits of diversification and good governance.' No price percentage anywhere; the only numeric claim is the '10 times larger' CONCENTRATION multiple, not a price effect. The abstract also says only 'robustly correlate', never 'cause'. (The March 2017 WP abstract was already percentage-free, so this is not a publication-stage retreat — if the article implies the % was stripped at publication, that framing is unsupported.)

itemVerdicts.item: (b) DGS (JF 2022): the correlation loads on the market-share half of MHHI-delta, not the ownership half, shown by placebo tests
itemVerdicts.note: Published JF abstract (77(5):2765-2798, via EconPapers/RePEc publisher record), verbatim: 'This paper reevaluates this evidence and shows that the documented positive correlation between common ownership and airline ticket prices stems from the market share component of the common ownership measure, and not the ownership and control components.' Mechanism confirmed verbatim in the authors' own account (Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, 7 Nov 2022, raw HTML read directly): 'we construct two version of HHI∆: The first, uses placebo ownership and control and true airline market shares, and the second uses true ownership and control and placebo market shares… Our results show no significant correlation between ticket prices and the measure of HHI∆ that uses placebo market shares and true ownership and control. However, we find a positive, large and significant correlation between ticket prices and the version of HHI∆ that uses true market shares and placebo ownership.' Precision note: DGS run placebos in BOTH directions (two placebo MHHI-delta variants), not one.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Bankruptcy treatment attenuates DGS results
itemVerdicts.note: Published abstract: 'We further show that the results are sensitive to measures of investor control and to assumptions about equity holders' ownership and control during bankruptcy.' Direction ('attenuates') confirmed verbatim by the authors: 'The AST paper assumes that equity holders retain full control and cash-flow rights over insolvent airlines. We show that alternatively assuming that equity holders of bankrupt airlines either lose cash-flow rights or retain cash flow rights but lose control significantly attenuates the positive correlation between AST's measure of common ownership concentration and airline ticket prices.' Context worth keeping: at least one major airline was in bankruptcy protection in half the quarters of the 2001Q1-2014Q4 sample. Note the abstract pairs bankruptcy with a SECOND sensitivity the claim omits — alternative measures of investor control (control via threat of exit / non-voting-share voice), under which 'the positive correlation between HHI∆ and ticket prices in AST becomes statistically insignificant.'

itemVerdicts.item: (b) The ASt 'Refutation' and DGS 'Surrebuttal' are both unpublished SSRN papers; the exchange is unresolved in refereed venues as of 2026-08
itemVerdicts.note: OpenAlex title searches return only preprints: ASt 'A Refutation of...' = SSRN 4158149 (and a duplicate posting SSRN 4219441), type 'preprint', 2022; DGS 'A Surrebuttal: There Are No Anti-Competitive Effects of Common Ownership in the Airline Industry' = SSRN 4307814, type 'preprint', 2022. No journal version of either exists as of 2026-08. Scan of the 57 works citing DGS published 2024-01-01 onward shows no comment/reply/replication in a refereed venue that adjudicates the exchange. Two small precisions: (i) the Refutation is not SSRN-only — it also circulates as ECGI Finance Working Paper 837/2022 and CESifo Working Paper 9937, still non-refereed; (ii) there is an EARLIER, distinct ASt response, 'Reply to: Common Ownership Does Not Have Anti-Competitive Effects in the Airline Industry' (SSRN 3168095, 2018), so 'the Refutation' should be dated 2022 to avoid conflating the two.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) BCS (AEJ:Micro 2021): between a third and half of the variation in profit weights comes from relative investor concentration, not overlapping ownership
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the AEJ manuscript hosted by Conlon (chrisconlon.github.io/site/common_owner.pdf), intro: 'We show that between a third and a half of the variation in the profit weight measure comes not from overlapping ownership as many researchers assume, but instead from relative investor concentration, which we make precise in what follows.' Section III adds the cross-sectional figure: 'the role of relative investor concentration is greatest in the cross–section, representing over 45% of the variation.' Publication confirmed: American Economic Journal: Microeconomics 13(3):273-308, 2021, DOI 10.1257/mic.20190389.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Taken literally the theory implies >10% of S&P 500 firms tunneling by 2017, which BCS treat as a reductio
itemVerdicts.note: Intro, verbatim: 'one might also conclude that over 10% of S&P 500 firms are engaging in tunneling behavior by 2017. We find these predictions to be unrealistically strong.' Section V, verbatim: 'the implication of taking the common ownership hypothesis seriously, that in 2017 more than 10% of the S&P 500 is engaging in some form of tunneling behavior, is implausibly strong.' Caveat the article should carry: BCS explicitly flag this result as the FRAGILE one — 'unlike our main results, this finding is sensitive to the specification of control weights' (and 'in the later periods, the result depends heavily on our assumptions about γ'). Do not present the tunneling reductio as equally robust to their main decomposition.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) GLS: 'relatively little evidence that common ownership causes lower competition'
itemVerdicts.note: The quoted string is real but the claim drops the qualifier that carries the whole caliber, and the citation is stale/dead. WRONG as stated: a bare 'relatively little evidence that common ownership causes lower competition' attributed to Atlanta Fed WP 2023-17 (that URL 404s). RIGHT: the abstract reads 'Across the newest papers employing the most credible identification techniques, there is relatively little evidence that common ownership causes lower competition. However, further research is necessary before broad conclusions can be reached.' The conclusion scopes it the same way: 'A survey of the current literature, in particular those papers that have successfully gone through peer review and are now published in top tier academic journals, provides relatively little evidence that common ownership causes anti-competitive behavior among publicly traded firms. Nevertheless, it remains possible that common ownership has anti-competitive effects in other settings.' Also: this is no longer only a Fed working paper — it was peer-reviewed and published as Gerardi, Lowry & Schenone, 'A Critical Review of the Common Ownership Literature,' Annual Review of Financial Economics 16 (Nov 2024): 89-114, DOI 10.1146/annurev-financial-082123-105841. Verified text from the ECGI Finance WP 943/2023 PDF (identical paper, SSRN 4630765); the Atlanta Fed URL given in the claim group returns a 404 HTML page.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Two of three GLS authors wrote the replication critique (skeptic-direction COI)
itemVerdicts.note: Gerardi and Schenone are 2 of the 3 authors of both Dennis, Gerardi & Schenone (JF 2022) and Gerardi, Lowry & Schenone. The review discusses their own JF paper in the third person ('Dennis et al. (2022a)') in both the body and the conclusion without an in-text disclosure of authorship overlap, which strengthens the article's COI point.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) 'Azar & Vives' opposing survey has the mirror COI'
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: there is no Azar & Vives survey of the common-ownership literature. Checked the full OpenAlex work lists for both José Azar (A5059636061) and Xavier Vives (A5041656278) from 2018 on: their only joint common-ownership outputs are 'General Equilibrium Oligopoly and Ownership Structure' (Econometrica 2021) plus its Reply, 'Common Ownership and the Secular Stagnation Hypothesis' (AEA P&P 2019), and 'Revisiting the Anticompetitive Effects of Common Ownership' (SSRN 3805047 / ECGI Finance WP 827/2022). I read the ECGI PDF: it is an EMPIRICAL airline study, abstract verbatim — 'We use data from the U.S. airline industry to test the hypothesis, consistent with the general equilibrium oligopoly model of Azar and Vives (forthcoming), that inter-industry common ownership should be associated with lower prices in product markets… We also find that common ownership by the "Big Three" (BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street) is associated with lower airline prices, while common ownership by shareholders other than the Big Three is associated with higher prices.' Not a survey, and its Big Three finding cuts AGAINST the index-bubble framing rather than mirroring it. RIGHT: the actual mirror-COI survey is Martin C. Schmalz, 'Common-Ownership Concentration and Corporate Conduct,' Annual Review of Financial Economics 10 (Nov 2018): 413-448 — a pro-side literature review by an ASt co-author, in the same Annual Review series that later published GLS. (Schmalz also has 'Recent Studies on Common Ownership, Firm Behavior, and Market Outcomes,' Antitrust Bulletin 2021.)

corrections: Replace 'Azar & Vives' opposing survey' with 'Schmalz's opposing survey.' There is no Azar-Vives survey of the common-ownership literature. The mirror-COI survey is Martin C. Schmalz, 'Common-Ownership Concentration and Corporate Conduct,' Annual Review of Financial Economics 10 (2018): 413-448 — a pro-side review by an Azar-Schmalz-Tecu co-author, published in the same Annual Review series that later carried the Gerardi-Lowry-Schenone review. Azar & Vives (ECGI Finance WP 827/2022, 'Revisiting the Anticompetitive Effects of Common Ownership') is an empirical airline study, not a survey, and it finds that common ownership by the Big Three is associated with LOWER airline prices — cite it only for that, never as a survey.

Restore the qualifier on the Gerardi-Lowry-Schenone finding. The abstract says 'Across the newest papers employing the most credible identification techniques, there is relatively little evidence that common ownership causes lower competition. However, further research is necessary before broad conclusions can be reached.' The conclusion scopes it to 'those papers that have successfully gone through peer review and are now published in top tier academic journals' and adds 'it remains possible that common ownership has anti-competitive effects in other settings.' Do not quote the middle clause as a blanket verdict on the whole literature.

Update the Gerardi-Lowry-Schenone citation. The Atlanta Fed URL in the source list (atlantafed.org/-/media/documents/research/publications/wp/2023/11/08/17--critical-review-of-common-ownership-literature.pdf) is dead — it returns a 404 page, not a PDF. The paper is now peer-reviewed and published: Kristopher Gerardi, Michelle Lowry & Carola Schenone, 'A Critical Review of the Common Ownership Literature,' Annual Review of Financial Economics 16 (November 2024): 89-114, DOI 10.1146/annurev-financial-082123-105841. A working, free copy of the identical text is the ECGI Finance Working Paper 943/2023 PDF (ecgi.global/sites/default/files/working_papers/documents/acriticalreviewofthecommonownershipliterature.pdf). Describing it as merely a Fed working paper understates its status.

Date the Azar-Schmalz-Tecu response as the 2022 'Refutation' and note its working-paper homes. There are two distinct ASt responses to Dennis-Gerardi-Schenone: an earlier 'Reply to...' (SSRN 3168095, 2018) and 'A Refutation of...' (SSRN 4158149, 2022, also ECGI Finance WP 837/2022 and CESifo WP 9937). Both, plus the DGS 'Surrebuttal' (SSRN 4307814, 2022), remain unrefereed as of August 2026 — 'unpublished SSRN papers' is right, but say 'and non-refereed working-paper series' so a reader who finds the ECGI/CESifo versions does not think they are published.

Add the fragility caveat to the Backus-Conlon-Sinkinson tunneling reductio. BCS themselves write that 'unlike our main results, this finding is sensitive to the specification of control weights' and that in later periods 'the result depends heavily on our assumptions about gamma.' Their main decomposition result (a third to a half of profit-weight variation from relative investor concentration) is the robust one; the >10%-tunneling figure is the deliberately fragile reductio. Do not present the two as equally solid.

Pin the Azar-Schmalz-Tecu numbers to the 2017/published version and say which estimator produced each. Earlier drafts of the same paper reported materially different figures — the April 2015 draft says 'at least 10%' from panel-IV, and Azar's November 2015 FTC Microeconomics Conference slides say '3-11% higher prices' and a '0.6%' merger effect. Only the accepted/published numbers (3-7% panel fixed-effects; 10-12% from the BlackRock-BGI difference-in-differences implemented as 2SLS; about 0.5% as the direct effect of the acquisition itself) may be attributed to 'ASt (JF 2018).' Prefer 'difference-in-differences/IV' over bare 'IV' for the 10-12%.

When making the point about the published abstract, say precisely what it does and does not contain. It carries no price percentage, and its only numeric claim is that common ownership implies concentration increases '10 times larger' than the antitrust threshold — a concentration multiple, not a price effect. It also says only that within-route changes 'robustly correlate' with price changes, never that they cause them. But note the March 2017 working-paper abstract was already percentage-free, so do not imply the percentage was stripped out at the publication stage.

Add the second Dennis-Gerardi-Schenone sensitivity alongside bankruptcy. Their published abstract says the results are sensitive both 'to measures of investor control' and 'to assumptions about equity holders' ownership and control during bankruptcy'; under alternative control mechanisms (threat of exit, or voice available to all equity owners regardless of voting designation) the positive correlation 'becomes statistically insignificant.' Reporting only the bankruptcy channel understates their critique.

Optionally add the concession Azar-Schmalz-Tecu themselves make in the 2022 Refutation, that they 'do not claim a causal interpretation of their panel regression estimates.' This is the cleanest way to show how much of the original claim its own authors now defend, and it is quoted with a pin cite in the Committee on Capital Markets Regulation's June 2025 study.
newContradictions: No Azar & Vives survey of the common-ownership literature exists. Their joint 2022 output on this topic (ECGI Finance WP 827/2022) is an empirical airline study whose headline finding — 'common ownership by the "Big Three" (BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street) is associated with lower airline prices, while common ownership by shareholders other than the Big Three is associated with higher prices' — points the opposite way from the index-bubble thesis. If the article uses Azar-Vives at all, this finding is the thing to report, and it is awkward for the pro-thesis side.

Gerardi-Lowry-Schenone is no longer an unrefereed Fed working paper. It passed peer review and appeared in Annual Review of Financial Economics 16 (Nov 2024): 89-114. That weakens any framing that treats the skeptic side as the merely-grey-literature side of the exchange, and it means the COI point has to be made about a peer-reviewed review article rather than a Fed WP.

A further replication critique of Azar-Schmalz-Tecu the article does not mention: Egland, Hearey, Schatzki & Verbeck, 'Reassessing Common Ownership: Corrections to Azar, Schmalz, and Tecu (2018)' (SSRN 3463231, Oct 2019, Analysis Group), which reports that correcting any one of three assumptions (asset-manager incentives, control and cash-flow rights during bankruptcy, and industry-structure change over time) eliminates statistical significance. Note this is consulting-firm work and, like DGS, carries its own directional interest; I did not reach its full text.

Kennedy, O'Brien, Song & Waehrer (2017) is a separate structural-model critique cited in the Gerardi-Lowry-Schenone review: it estimates a structural model in which the common-ownership measure is derived directly from theory and finds the ASt results do not hold. If the article treats DGS as the only serious challenge, that is too narrow.

Committee on Capital Markets Regulation, 'Common Ownership and Prices: A Comprehensive Generalized Study' (June 2025) extends the analysis economy-wide rather than industry-by-industry, and pin-cites the ASt 2018 published text at p.1517. It is an advocacy body with an obvious directional interest, so use it for the pin cite rather than for its conclusions; but its existence means the literature has moved past 2023 and the article should not describe the skeptic case as ending with the 2022 exchange.
reasoning:
Primary documents reached and read verbatim: (1) Azar-Schmalz-Tecu, IESE Working Paper WP-1169-E, 23 March 2017 — the exact URL the claim group cites, and the green-OA version that OpenAlex/Unpaywall/Semantic Scholar all attach to DOI 10.1111/jofi.12698; downloaded and converted with pdftotext, and I read the abstract, the introduction's summary of results, Section 5.2.2 on the BlackRock-BGI strategy, and the conclusion. (2) The published Journal of Finance abstract for ASt, obtained independently from two indexes of the publisher record (EconPapers/RePEc and the Semantic Scholar graph API) — Wiley itself returns 403 to both WebFetch and curl. (3) The published Journal of Finance abstract for Dennis-Gerardi-Schenone 77(5):2765-2798 via EconPapers/RePEc. (4) The Dennis-Gerardi-Schenone authors' own account of their paper on the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, fetched as raw HTML and stripped locally so I read the source text rather than a summarizer's rendering — this is where the placebo construction and the word 'attenuates' are verified. (5) Backus-Conlon-Sinkinson, the AEJ:Micro manuscript at chrisconlon.github.io/site/common_owner.pdf, read in full at the relevant passages; publication metadata cross-checked against the AEA article page (13(3):273-308, 2021). (6) Gerardi-Lowry-Schenone via the ECGI Finance WP 943/2023 PDF, after the Atlanta Fed URL in the claim group returned a 404 HTML page; abstract and conclusion read verbatim. (7) Azar & Vives, ECGI Finance WP 827/2022, abstract read verbatim to establish that it is an empirical paper and not a survey. (8) The ASt 2022 Refutation via the ECGI PDF. (9) Azar's November 2015 FTC conference slides and the April 2015 CRA-hosted draft, fetched specifically to test the version-drift warning — and they did carry different numbers (3-11%, 'at least 10%', 0.6%), which is why I insisted on a published-text pin cite rather than accepting the working paper alone.

Publication-status checks were done against structured APIs rather than search summaries: OpenAlex title searches confirm the Refutation and Surrebuttal exist only as SSRN preprints; a scan of the 57 works citing DGS published 2024-01-01 or later found nothing adjudicating the exchange in a refereed venue; Crossref confirmed the Gerardi-Lowry-Schenone Annual Review publication and the Schmalz 2018 Annual Review survey.

Everything in (a), (b) and (c) checks out verbatim. The one substantive failure is in (d): 'Azar & Vives' opposing survey' names a document that does not exist. Azar and Vives have no survey; their 2022 joint paper is an empirical airline study, and its Big Three result runs against the thesis the article is building. The mirror-COI survey the sentence is reaching for is Schmalz (2018) in Annual Review of Financial Economics. Two further defects in (d): the Atlanta Fed URL is dead, and the paper is no longer a working paper but a peer-reviewed Annual Review article — so the COI point stands but must be aimed at a refereed review. The GLS quotation is also stripped of its scoping clause, which matters because the unqualified version reads as a verdict on the whole literature when the authors restrict it to the newest, best-identified, peer-reviewed papers and explicitly decline to draw broad conclusions.

Residual uncertainty, stated plainly: I could not open the Wiley typeset pages of ASt (JF 2018). The 3-7% figure is nonetheless confirmed in the published text at p.1517 through a direct pin cite and quotation in the Committee on Capital Markets Regulation's June 2025 study. The 10-12% and ~0.5% figures I verified only in the March 2017 accepted/green-OA manuscript that the claim group itself cites as its source. Unpaywall labels that manuscript 'submittedVersion', so there is a small residual risk those two figures were revised between March 2017 and the August 2018 issue; the fact that the 3-7% figure survived verbatim into p.1517 makes that unlikely but does not exclude it. I did not find a repository copy of the version of record anywhere (OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, CORE all point back to the same IESE working paper). I also did not read the full text of Egland et al. (2019), which I raise only as a contradicting source the article omits, not as verified evidence.
