Note of notation: the published DGS paper writes the measure as HHI-Delta, not MHHI-Delta; the substance is ASt's MHHI delta.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) DGS: bankruptcy treatment attenuates results
itemVerdicts.note: Published JF text: 'reasonable alternative empirical assumptions for measuring investor control and for treating the extent of investor ownership and control of airlines operating in bankruptcy lead to highly attenuated correlations between prices and common ownership.' At least one major airline was in bankruptcy in over half the quarters of the 2001Q1-2014Q4 sample; ASt carry pre-bankruptcy holdings forward, DGS build three alternatives (lose cash-flow rights, lose control, lose both). ASt's own Refutation concedes the direction: 'if one counter-factually assumes that cash flow or control rights disappear in the case of bankruptcy, then AST's panel estimates attenuate towards zero. This is in effect what DGS's analysis using "alternative assumptions" about ownership during bankruptcy episodes does' — while disputing the assumption's plausibility.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) The ASt 'Refutation' and DGS 'Surrebuttal' are both unpublished and the exchange is unresolved in refereed venues as of 2026-08
itemVerdicts.note: Substance holds: as of 2026-08 Crossref and OpenAlex show both as preprints only — Refutation = SSRN 4158149 (posted-content, 2022), Surrebuttal = SSRN 4307814 (posted-content, 2022); neither has a journal-article record in any refereed venue. WRONG as stated: 'both unpublished SSRN papers.' RIGHT: the ASt Refutation is not SSRN-only — it also circulates as CESifo Working Paper No. 9937 and ECGI Finance Working Paper N. 837/2022 (August 2022); the DGS Surrebuttal does appear to be SSRN-only. The correct caliber is 'both remain unrefereed working papers,' not 'both SSRN papers.'

itemVerdicts.item: (c) BCS (AEJ:Micro 2021): between a third and half of profit-weight variation comes from relative investor concentration, not overlapping ownership
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in bcs.txt: 'We show that between a third and a half of the variation in the profit weight measure comes not from overlapping ownership as many researchers assume, but instead from relative investor concentration, which we make precise in what follows.' Venue confirmed via Crossref 10.1257/mic.20190389: American Economic Journal: Microeconomics 13(3):273-308, August 2021.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) BCS: taken literally the theory implies >10% of S&P 500 firms tunneling by 2017, treated as a reductio
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'Taking the strict form of common ownership seriously, it could be used to micro-found a tremendous increase in markups between 1980 and 2017, and one might also conclude that over 10% of S&P 500 firms are engaging in tunneling behavior by 2017. We find these predictions to be unrealistically strong.' Also: 'the implication of taking the common ownership hypothesis seriously, that in 2017 more than 10% of the S&P 500 is engaging in some form of tunneling behavior, is implausibly strong.' Reductio framing confirmed. Caveat BCS themselves add and the article should carry: 'unlike our main results, this finding is sensitive to the specification of control weights' (the gamma assumption), i.e. the tunneling number is the least robust of their results.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) GLS (Atlanta Fed WP 2023-17): 'relatively little evidence that common ownership causes lower competition'
itemVerdicts.note: Quote is real but truncated in a way that inflates it. Verbatim (Gerardi, Lowry, Schenone, DOI 10.29338/wp2023-17, Nov 2023; ECGI WP 943/2023): 'Across the newest papers employing the most credible identification techniques, there is relatively little evidence that common ownership causes lower competition. However, further research is necessary before broad conclusions can be reached.' WRONG: presenting it as a flat verdict on the literature. RIGHT: it is scoped to 'the newest papers employing the most credible identification techniques' and is immediately hedged. Separately, WRONG: describing it as only an Atlanta Fed working paper — it was subsequently published as Gerardi, Lowry & Schenone, 'A Critical Review of the Common Ownership Literature,' Annual Review of Financial Economics 16 (2024), DOI 10.1146/annurev-financial-082123-105841.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) COI in the skeptic direction: two of three GLS authors wrote the replication critique
itemVerdicts.note: GLS authors are Kristopher Gerardi (FRB Atlanta), Michelle Lowry (Drexel), Carola Schenone (UVA). DGS authors are Patrick Dennis, Kristopher Gerardi, Carola Schenone. Gerardi and Schenone are 2 of 3 in both; Lowry is not on DGS. GLS also describes DGS in its own review (Section on the airline debate) without disclosing the overlap in the passage.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) 'Azar & Vives' opposing survey has the mirror COI'
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: there is no Azar & Vives survey of the common-ownership literature. Azar & Vives co-authored 'General Equilibrium Oligopoly and Ownership Structure' (Econometrica 89(3), 2021), a reply to comments on it, 'Common Ownership and the Secular Stagnation Hypothesis' (AEA P&P 2019), and 'Revisiting the Anticompetitive Effects of Common Ownership' (ECGI Finance WP 827/2022; SSRN 3805047) — the last is an original empirical airline study, not a survey, and it actually reports that Big Three common ownership is associated with LOWER airline prices while non-Big-Three intra-industry common ownership is associated with higher prices. RIGHT: the mirror-COI survey/critique is Azar, Schmalz & Tecu, 'Research on the Competitive Consequences of Common Ownership: A Methodological Critique,' Antitrust Bulletin 66(1), 2021 (DOI 10.1177/0003603X20985799) — all three authors are the defended paper's own authors, a stronger mirror than 2-of-3; companion piece Martin Schmalz, 'Recent Studies on Common Ownership, Firm Behavior, and Market Outcomes,' Antitrust Bulletin 66(1), 2021 (DOI 10.1177/0003603X20985804).

corrections: Replace 'Azar & Vives' opposing survey has the mirror COI' with the correct attribution: the mirror-COI survey is Azar, Schmalz & Tecu (2021), 'Research on the Competitive Consequences of Common Ownership: A Methodological Critique,' Antitrust Bulletin 66(1) — written by all three authors of the defended paper (a stronger conflict than GLS's 2-of-3), with Schmalz's companion 'Recent Studies on Common Ownership, Firm Behavior, and Market Outcomes' in the same issue. Azar & Vives have no common-ownership survey; their joint work is theory (Econometrica 2021) plus an original empirical airline paper (ECGI WP 827/2022) that finds Big Three common ownership associated with LOWER airline prices.

When quoting GLS, keep the scope qualifier: the sentence is 'Across the newest papers employing the most credible identification techniques, there is relatively little evidence that common ownership causes lower competition,' followed immediately by 'However, further research is necessary before broad conclusions can be reached.' Do not present it as an unqualified verdict on the whole literature.

Update the GLS citation: it is no longer only Atlanta Fed WP 2023-17 (Nov 2023, DOI 10.29338/wp2023-17). It was published as Gerardi, Lowry & Schenone, 'A Critical Review of the Common Ownership Literature,' Annual Review of Financial Economics 16 (2024), DOI 10.1146/annurev-financial-082123-105841. This matters because the article contrasts it with the unrefereed ASt/DGS exchange.

Change 'The ASt Refutation and DGS Surrebuttal are both unpublished SSRN papers' to 'both remain unrefereed working papers.' The Refutation is also CESifo Working Paper No. 9937 and ECGI Finance Working Paper N. 837/2022, not SSRN-only; the Surrebuttal (SSRN 4307814) is SSRN-only. The core point — neither has appeared in a refereed venue as of 2026-08, confirmed against Crossref and OpenAlex — is correct.

When citing the 3-7% / 10-12% / ~0.5% figures, note they are verified in the IESE WP-1169-E (March 2017) version, which is the only open-access version of the JF 2018 article (per Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar). The typeset JF body is paywalled; the published abstract carries no price percentage at all, so the percentages come from the paper's body, not its headline claim.

If space allows, carry BCS's own caveat on the tunneling number: they state that, unlike their main profit-weight decomposition results, 'this finding is sensitive to the specification of control weights.' The >10% tunneling figure is the least robust of their results, which strengthens rather than weakens its use as a reductio.

Optional precision on DGS: the published JF 2022 paper denotes the measure HHI-Delta (not MHHI-Delta), and it runs three placebos — placebo ownership with true market shares, placebo market shares with true ownership, and a 'model-free' version setting all market shares to one. The last two both yield coefficients statistically indistinguishable from zero.
newContradictions: Azar & Vives (ECGI Finance WP 827/2022, 'Revisiting the Anticompetitive Effects of Common Ownership') reports, in the same airline data, that 'common ownership by the "Big Three" (BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street) is associated with lower airline prices, while common ownership by shareholders other than the Big Three is associated with higher prices,' and that inter-industry common ownership is associated with lower prices. This is awkward for an index-bubble framing that pins anticompetitive pricing on the index giants specifically — the pro-common-ownership camp's own follow-up exculpates the Big Three.

Egland, Hearey, Schatzki & Verbeck, 'Reassessing Common Ownership: Corrections to Azar, Schmalz, and Tecu (2018)' (SSRN 3463231), is a further data-correction critique of ASt distinct from DGS. I did not verify its contents; flagging it as an unexamined third line of attack the article may be ignoring.

Kennedy, O'Brien, Song & Waehrer (2017) is a separate structural-model critique of ASt (endogeneity of MHHI-Delta as an equilibrium object), summarized in GLS section 26. It is independent of the DGS placebo critique and is not covered by the ASt Refutation, so 'the DGS exchange is unresolved' understates how many open critiques ASt faces.

DGS note in the published JF paper that ASt's own robustness check restricting to market-carrier observations of airlines actually in bankruptcy yields an effect that 'becomes small and statistically insignificant' — i.e. an attenuation result present in ASt's own paper, not only in DGS's reanalysis.

ASt's Refutation states that 'DGS have retracted many of the claims they made in previous versions of their paper. For example, DGS no longer claim that AST's results were driven by only the largest 5% of routes.' If the article cites any DGS claim, it must cite the published JF 2022 version, since earlier DGS working-paper versions contain claims the authors dropped.
reasoning:
Primary documents reached verbatim: (1) Azar-Schmalz-Tecu, IESE WP-1169-E, March 23 2017, local file /private/tmp/.../scratchpad/v29/ast_iese.txt — the OA version that OpenAlex, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar all attach to JF 10.1111/jofi.12698; grepped and read the 3-7%, 10-12%, and 0.5% passages in context. (2) The live Wiley landing page for jofi.12698, read through the browser tool after clearing the bot check — full published abstract captured verbatim; confirmed no price percentage. (3) The full published text of Dennis-Gerardi-Schenone, JF 77(5):2765-2798, read through the browser tool (the paper is CC-BY-NC-ND open access) — saved to /private/tmp/.../scratchpad/v29/dgs_jf.txt; confirmed the placebo design, the market-share-vs-ownership finding, and the bankruptcy attenuation sentence. The abstract independently cross-checked against OpenAlex's inverted index, which matched the on-page text word for word. (4) Backus-Conlon-Sinkinson, local bcs.txt, AEJ:Micro 13(3):273-308 confirmed via Crossref; read the 'between a third and a half' and 'over 10% ... tunneling' passages in context including their control-weight caveat. (5) Gerardi-Lowry-Schenone, fetched as ECGI WP 943/2023 PDF (identical text, carries DOI 10.29338/wp2023-17 for Atlanta Fed WP 2023-17) — read the abstract and the DGS-summary section. (6) Azar-Schmalz-Tecu Refutation, fetched as ECGI WP 837/2022 PDF (= CESifo 9937 / SSRN 4158149) — read the abstract and the bankruptcy paragraph, where ASt concede attenuation. (7) Azar-Vives, ECGI WP 827/2022 PDF, read abstract.

What I could not reach: the typeset JF 2018 body (paywalled; Unpaywall confirms the IESE WP is the only OA version), so the 3-7%/10-12%/0.5% figures are verified in the working paper the article itself cites rather than in published pages. The DGS Surrebuttal PDF (SSRN blocks automated fetch) — but its publication status, which is what the claim asserts, was verified via Crossref and OpenAlex, both of which type it as posted-content/preprint with no journal-article successor.

Publication-status sweep as of 2026-08: Crossref and OpenAlex show no refereed publication of either the Refutation or the Surrebuttal; Crossref queries for 2025-2026 common-ownership work turn up continued activity (Li-Liu-Masulis-Zein, J. Corp. Finance 2026) but nothing resolving the airline exchange. The one status change I did find cuts against the article's framing: GLS is now published in Annual Review of Financial Economics 16 (2024).

The single substantive error is the attribution in (d). I searched Crossref, OpenAlex, and José Azar's own publication list; Azar & Vives have no survey of this literature, and their joint empirical paper points the opposite way from what a mirror-COI survey would be expected to argue. The actual mirror is Azar-Schmalz-Tecu (2021) in the Antitrust Bulletin, whose conflict is stronger than the one the article ascribes. Everything else is verbatim-accurate; the remaining corrections are caliber (a truncated GLS quote that drops its scope qualifier, a stale citation, and a 'SSRN papers' characterization that is narrower than the truth).

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Texas et al. v. BlackRock/State Street/Vanguard, E.D. Tex. 6:24-cv-00437, filed Nov 27 2024, coal-output theory; MTD DENIED Aug 1 2025; 'a close call' per Judge Kernodle
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 'motion to dismiss DENIED.' RIGHT: the motions were GRANTED IN PART and DENIED IN PART. I read Doc. 113 (Memorandum Opinion and Order on Motions to Dismiss, filed 08/01/25, signed 'this 1st day of August, 2025', JEREMY D. KERNODLE) verbatim. Conclusion, p.61: 'Defendants' joint motion to dismiss (Docket No. 64) and BlackRock's motion to dismiss (Docket No. 65) are both GRANTED IN PART and DENIED IN PART. The motions to dismiss Counts I–XVII and XXI are DENIED. The motions are GRANTED as to Counts XVIII, XIX, and XX, which are DISMISSED.' The court's own framing (p.3) is 'the Court largely denies Defendants' motions.' Three of 21 counts were dismissed, and consumer-protection claims survived only under Texas, Montana, Iowa, and Nebraska law ('The remaining state laws do not apply, and those claims are thus dismissed'). The quote is verbatim and correctly attributed but narrower than implied: 'Plaintiffs do, however, plausibly allege the existence of a conspiracy among Defendants based on circumstantial evidence. This is a close call.' It is about the circumstantial-evidence conspiracy pleading, not about the motion as a whole. Filing date Nov 27 2024 confirmed (original complaint, Texas + 10 states); the operative amended complaint is dated Jan 16 2025 and adds Louisiana and Oklahoma (13 plaintiff states). Case caption/number confirmed on the face of the order.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-2) Vanguard settled Feb 2026 for $29.5m with commitments incl. expanding pass-through voting and abstaining from climate-focused investor alliances; case continues against BlackRock and State Street
itemVerdicts.note: CONFIRMED with added precision. Settlement announced Feb 25–26, 2026; $29.5 million paid to the 11 states that sued Vanguard (Texas, Alabama, Arkansas, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, West Virginia, Wyoming) — this matches the Innisfree/HLS description 'Vanguard's $29.5 million settlement with Texas and ten other Republican-led states.' The HLS piece's footnote 1 states the commitments verbatim: 'Vanguard agreed to not pressure issuers to take specific actions (including reducing carbon emissions), expand its pass-through voting program, and avoid participating in climate-focused investor groups with coordinated stewardship initiatives.' ESG Dive adds duration/scope the article should carry if it describes the commitments as durable: expansion of Investor Choice to any fund with over half its assets in U.S. equities by June 30, 2027, program to run through at least June 2032. Litigation continues against BlackRock and State Street. Note: I did not reach the settlement agreement text itself, only the HLS footnote and press reporting.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) FTC/DOJ Statement of Interest (May 22, 2025, ECF 99): defends index investing while reaffirming 2017 OECD submission, but says USE of holdings to suppress output is actionable
itemVerdicts.note: CONFIRMED verbatim from the FTC PDF (caption line reads 'Case 6:24-cv-00437-JDK Document 99 Filed 05/22/25'; title 'STATEMENT OF INTEREST OF THE FEDERAL TRADE COMMISSION AND THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA'). Exact strings I read: 'There should be no confusion: the antitrust laws allow passive fund investing, they allow shareholder advocacy for better corporate governance, and they allow active investing that doesn't harm competition.' And: 'This case is not about ordinary activity by asset managers such as passive index investing or even procompetitive activism.' And: 'passive fund investing can thrive without adopting these errors of law.' OECD reaffirmation confirmed: the Submission 'recognized the limitations of "general relationships suggested by academic papers" and cautioned against adopting such proposals absent "compelling evidence of the anticompetitive effects of common ownership by institutional investors in concentrated industries"'; then 'The Agencies reaffirm that submission and the importance of index investing and corporate governance.' The actionable-use half is also verbatim: 'But the importance of index investing does not protect institutional investors and asset managers that act to use their shares in fact to stifle competition among their commonly held companies.' Also load-bearing and worth quoting: 'The Agencies do not assert a position as to when an investor's acquisition of stock in competing firms alone—without evidence of subsequent anticompetitive use—would implicate Section 7.'

itemVerdicts.item: (c) SEC Feb 11, 2025 13D/G C&DI revision (Q&A 103.11/103.12): pressuring management can defeat 13G eligibility; BlackRock paused and resumed ~Feb 24 in listen-only mode; Vanguard resumed early March
itemVerdicts.note: The SEC half is CONFIRMED from the primary text at sec.gov (Regulation 13D-G C&DIs; the 021125 update page is dated 'Feb. 11, 2025' and lists 'Revised Question 103.11' and 'New Question 103.12'; both answers carry the tag '[Feb. 11, 2025]'). 103.12 verbatim: 'A shareholder who goes beyond such a discussion, however, and exerts pressure on management to implement specific measures or changes to a policy may be "influencing" control over the issuer.' Caliber note: the trigger is not bare 'pressuring' — the illustrations require the shareholder to explicitly or implicitly condition its support for the issuer's director nominees on adoption of its recommendation. CORRECTION on attribution: 'listen-only mode' is not BlackRock's own phrase. BlackRock's own statement was that it is 'complying with the new requirements including by highlighting our role as a "passive" investor at the start of each engagement'; 'listen-only' is an advisor/press characterization (FGS Global and similar). Resumption dates check out as reported (BlackRock 'resumed its engagement activities back on February 24'; Vanguard resumed in the first week of March 2025, reported Mar 6), but these come from trade press (TheCorporateCounsel.net, ESG Dive), not a primary filing — the article should attribute them, not state them as record fact.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) 2026 proxy season: BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street EACH split stewardship into multiple internal teams voting independently, each team under ~5% of an issuer; no evidence yet on whether split teams vote differently
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 'no evidence yet on whether split teams vote differently.' RIGHT: the very source cited reports early evidence. Innisfree (Crozier/Wolf/Kovacs), HLS Forum, posted Thursday, June 11, 2026, states verbatim: 'While each stewardship team will engage with issuers separately and have potentially different objectives, Innisfree's experience is that both teams often vote in parallel. However, as the separate stewardship teams develop their own voting policies over time, the historically monolithic, management-friendly passive fund voting bloc may splinter.' So the reported early experience is PARALLEL voting, and the splintering is prospective ('may'). Two further caliber slips: (i) WRONG 'multiple internal teams' as an open-ended count — the source says 'Each index fund has separated its stewardship team into two stewardship teams operating independently on policy, voting, and engagement' (BlackRock BIS/BAIS; Vanguard VCM/VPM; State Street Asset Stewardship Team / Sustainability Stewardship Service). (ii) WRONG 'structured so each team stays under ~5%' — the source is weaker: shares are split 'based on firm-specific criteria (where each team is less likely to control more than 5% of an issuer's outstanding shares).' Also: the 5% rationale is Innisfree's framing; other 2026 commentary (Cooley, Alliance Advisors, Morningstar) attributes the splits to separating active from index stewardship and to diversifying voting perspectives, and reports that the two teams' policies 'diverge in significant ways' on ESG — i.e., there is contradictory early evidence in both directions, which is the opposite of 'no evidence yet.' Consequently 'unified-bloc premise now partly obsolete by design' is defensible as a structural statement but must not be paired with a claim of no evidence; the behavioral evidence so far cuts toward continued bloc voting.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Pass-through take-up: BlackRock $784bn of $3.3T eligible (~24%; ~11% of $6.9T); Vanguard ~82,000 of ~10 million eligible (~0.8%); Feb 2026 $3.6T / 22 million is an ELIGIBILITY number
itemVerdicts.note: BlackRock half CONFIRMED verbatim from the 2025 Global Voting Spotlight: 'As of June 30, 2025, $3.3 trillion of BlackRock's $6.9 trillion total index equity AUM are eligible to participate in BlackRock Voting Choice, where legally and operationally viable, with clients representing ~$784 billion in index equity AUM exercising this option.' 784/3300 = 23.8%; 784/6900 = 11.4%. Feb 2026 eligibility figures CONFIRMED from Vanguard's own press release dated 'VALLEY FORGE, PA (February 25, 2026)': 17 new funds, 'adding approximately 2 million new eligible investors', 'increases the number of eligible investors in the program to 22 million', 'expands eligible assets to more than $3.6 trillion' — these are indeed ELIGIBILITY, not participation. CORRECTION on the Vanguard ratio: the numerator and denominator come from different program vintages. Vanguard Investor Choice 2025 report (Sept 2025): 'Through July 2025, more than 82,000 fund shareholders had selected a voting policy' across the EIGHT participating funds, whose eligible AUM was $264B ('nearly $9 billion of eligible fund AUM ($264 billion) participated'). The '~10 million eligible investors' is a FORWARD-looking figure tied to the four funds added in May 2025: 'These fund additions will: Nearly quadruple the program's total eligible AUM to $1 trillion / Reach nearly 10 million eligible investors who hold these funds.' So ~0.8% divides a July-2025 participant count by a post-expansion eligible base that was not yet in effect during the 2025 season. Vanguard's own like-for-like rates are: $9B of $264B eligible fund AUM (3.4%) and ~9–10% of eligible assets held directly through Vanguard brokerage accounts (the report says it is 'set to eclipse a 10% participation rate among clients in the participating funds with assets held directly through Vanguard', a footnoted ASSET-weighted rate over brokerage-held assets only). The article's directional point (tiny take-up) survives, but the specific '~0.8%' must be stated as 82,000 participants against Vanguard's post-May-2025 eligible reach of ~10 million, not as the 2025-season participation rate.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) BlackRock 2025 Voting Spotlight: $6.9T public equity AUM (~90% index), 152,000+ proposals at 12,700+ companies, supported management ~89%; 2,584 engagements vs 16,800+ meetings ≈ 15%
itemVerdicts.note: CONFIRMED verbatim from the PDF, with two framing notes. Important notes p.3: 'As of June 30, 2025, clients held $6.9 trillion in public equity assets under management (AUM), with approximately 90% invested in index equity strategies.' Executive summary: 'In the 2024-25 proxy year, BIS voted on more than 152,000 management and shareholder proposals globally at more than 12,700 companies in 58 voting markets' and 'As in previous years, BIS supported management on ~89% of total proposals voted.' Figure 1 total engagements = 2,584 (Americas 1,183 / APAC 802 / EMEA 599), covering 1,950 companies engaged, 446 engaged multiple times. p.13: 'During the 2024-25 proxy year, BIS voted at 16,800+ shareholder meetings on more than 152,000 [proposals]'. 2,584/16,800 = 15.4%. NOTE 1: that ratio mixes engagements with meetings; the like-for-like comparison is 1,950 companies engaged / 12,700+ companies voted = also ~15%, so the article should use the cleaner pairing. NOTE 2: the report is internally inconsistent about $6.9T — p.3 calls it public equity AUM ~90% index, while p.9 and p.23 both call it 'BlackRock's $6.9 trillion total index equity AUM.' The article's rendering follows p.3 and is defensible, but pairing an index-equity numerator ($784bn) with a public-equity denominator ($6.9T) is why '~11%' rather than ~12.6% (784/6.2T index equity); flag the source's inconsistency rather than asserting a precise share. Reporting period is July 1, 2024–June 30, 2025 ('2024-25 proxy year'), not calendar 2025.

corrections: Replace 'motion to dismiss DENIED Aug 1, 2025' with: on August 1, 2025 Judge Jeremy D. Kernodle GRANTED IN PART and DENIED IN PART the motions to dismiss (Doc. 113) — Counts I–XVII and XXI survived; Counts XVIII, XIX, and XX were dismissed, and the consumer-protection claims survived only under Texas, Montana, Iowa, and Nebraska law. The court described itself as 'largely den[ying] Defendants' motions.'

Anchor the 'close call' quote correctly: it is 'Plaintiffs do, however, plausibly allege the existence of a conspiracy among Defendants based on circumstantial evidence. This is a close call.' It refers to the circumstantial-evidence conspiracy pleading, not to the motion as a whole.

State that the operative pleading is the 110-page amended complaint filed January 16, 2025 by 13 states; the original complaint (Texas + 10 states) was filed November 27, 2024. Vanguard's Feb 2026 settlement was with the 11 states that sued it.

Add settlement specifics if the commitments are characterized as durable: $29.5m announced Feb 25–26, 2026; Vanguard must expand Investor Choice to any fund with over half its assets in U.S. equities by June 30, 2027 and maintain the program through at least June 2032, and refrain from joining groups with climate-focused investment or stewardship objectives.

Delete 'no evidence yet on whether split teams vote differently.' The cited Innisfree/HLS piece states the opposite: 'Innisfree's experience is that both teams often vote in parallel,' with splintering framed as prospective ('may splinter' as teams develop their own policies over time). Independent 2026 commentary reports that the two teams' policies diverge on ESG and that a single manager may now vote differently across funds — evidence exists on both sides.

Change 'multiple internal teams' to 'two internal stewardship teams each' — the source says 'Each index fund has separated its stewardship team into two stewardship teams operating independently on policy, voting, and engagement' (BlackRock BIS/BAIS, Vanguard VCM/VPM, State Street Asset Stewardship Team / Sustainability Stewardship Service).

Soften the 5% framing: the source says shares are split 'based on firm-specific criteria (where each team is less likely to control more than 5% of an issuer's outstanding shares)' — not that each team is structurally capped below 5%. Also attribute the 5% rationale to Innisfree; other commentators attribute the splits to separating active from index stewardship and diversifying voting perspectives.

Fix the Vanguard pass-through ratio: the '~10 million eligible investors' is Vanguard's forward-looking reach from the four funds added in May 2025 ('These fund additions will ... Reach nearly 10 million eligible investors'), while the 82,000 participants were in the eight-fund, $264B program through July 2025. State it as '82,000 participants against a post-expansion eligible base of ~10 million,' and give Vanguard's own like-for-like rates: $9B of $264B eligible fund AUM (3.4%), and ~9–10% on an asset-weighted basis among clients holding participating funds directly through Vanguard brokerage accounts.

Attribute BlackRock's 'listen-only' resumption to advisor/press characterization, not to BlackRock. BlackRock's own statement was that it complies 'including by highlighting our role as a "passive" investor at the start of each engagement.' Attribute the Feb 24 (BlackRock) and early-March (Vanguard) resumption dates to trade press (TheCorporateCounsel.net / ESG Dive).

Note the caveat in SEC C&DI 103.12: it is not bare engagement or bare 'pressure' that defeats 13G — the staff's illustrations turn on the shareholder explicitly or implicitly conditioning its support for the issuer's director nominees on adoption of its recommendation.

If citing the 15% engagement-coverage figure, use the like-for-like pairing: 1,950 companies engaged out of 12,700+ companies voted (~15%), rather than 2,584 engagements against 16,800+ meetings, which mixes units.

Flag that BlackRock's own report is inconsistent about $6.9T: p.3 says '$6.9 trillion in public equity assets under management (AUM), with approximately 90% invested in index equity strategies,' while pp.9 and 23 both say '$6.9 trillion total index equity AUM.' Avoid asserting a precise pass-through share of AUM; the range is ~11–13% depending on which reading is used. Also label the period 'the 2024-25 proxy year (July 1, 2024–June 30, 2025),' not calendar 2025.
newContradictions: The article's premise that the stewardship-team splits make the unified-bloc story obsolete is undercut by the same source it cites: Innisfree reports that in practice 'both teams often vote in parallel.' The structural change is real; the behavioral change is not yet observed.

BlackRock's 2025 Global Voting Spotlight contradicts itself on whether $6.9T is public equity AUM (p.3, ~90% index) or total index equity AUM (pp.9, 23). Any percentage built on that denominator inherits the ambiguity.

Vanguard's own headline participation metric (asset-weighted, ~10% among direct brokerage clients in participating funds) and the article's headcount metric (~0.8%) differ by more than an order of magnitude. Reporting only one without naming the denominator misleads in either direction.

The FTC/DOJ Statement of Interest is not a clean endorsement of the index-bubble critique in either direction: it expressly declines to take a position on acquisition-only theories — 'The Agencies do not assert a position as to when an investor's acquisition of stock in competing firms alone—without evidence of subsequent anticompetitive use—would implicate Section 7' — and reaffirms the 2017 OECD submission's warning that broad common-ownership limits would impose 'unintended real-world costs on businesses and consumers by making it more difficult to diversify risk.'
reasoning: I reached five primary documents verbatim and read the load-bearing sentences myself rather than relying on any summarizer. (1) The MTD order: I downloaded the PDF from the Texas AG site (Case 6:24-cv-00437-JDK, Document 113, Filed 08/01/25, 61 pages) and ran pdftotext; I read the introduction, the conclusion, and the 'This is a close call' passage in situ. This is where the group's biggest slip appears — the order is GRANTED IN PART and DENIED IN PART, dismissing Counts XVIII–XX, not a flat denial. (2) The FTC/DOJ Statement of Interest: local extraction of the FTC PDF (Document 99, Filed 05/22/25, 34 pages); I grepped and read the surrounding paragraphs for both quoted strings and for the OECD reaffirmation. Both quotes are verbatim and correctly characterized; I also surfaced the Agencies' express reservation on acquisition-only theories, which the article should carry. (3) The SEC C&DIs: sec.gov blocked WebFetch (403) and a plain curl, so I fetched with an identified User-Agent and stripped the HTML myself; I read the full text of both 103.11 and 103.12 including the '[Feb. 11, 2025]' date tags and the 'Revised'/'New' labels on the 021125 update page. Confirmed, with a caliber note that the disqualifying conduct is conditioning director support on adoption, not engagement per se. (4) The BlackRock 2025 Global Voting Spotlight: local extraction; every number in (e) and (f) checks out verbatim, but I found an internal inconsistency in the report over whether $6.9T is public equity or index equity AUM, which makes the '~11%' figure soft. (5) Vanguard Investor Choice 2025 report: local extraction; this is where I found the real problem in (e) — the 82,000 participants belong to the eight-fund/$264B program through July 2025, while '~10 million eligible investors' is Vanguard's forward-looking reach from the May 2025 four-fund addition that quadrupled eligible AUM to $1T. The derived ~0.8% therefore crosses vintages, and Vanguard's own reported rates ($9B/$264B = 3.4%; ~10% asset-weighted among direct brokerage clients) tell a different-magnitude story. (6) The Innisfree/HLS piece: local extraction of the June 11, 2026 post. This refutes the sub-claim's own qualifier — the source explicitly reports that both teams often vote in parallel, and it says 'two' teams, not 'multiple.' I corroborated the existence and naming of the splits independently (BIS/BAIS, VCM/VPM, SSGA's two units) and found that other 2026 commentators attribute them to active/index separation and perspective diversity rather than a 5% cap, so the 5% rationale should be attributed to Innisfree alone. Items I could not reach as primary text and have flagged as attributed reporting rather than record fact: the Vanguard settlement agreement itself (I have only the HLS footnote and ESG Dive/Ropes & Gray reporting — Ropes & Gray returned 403), and the BlackRock/Vanguard engagement pause-and-resume dates and the 'listen-only' label, which exist only in trade press and advisor commentary; BlackRock's own on-record language was about highlighting its 'passive' role. I searched for post-August-2025 developments in the case through August 2026 and found nothing that disturbs the MTD posture beyond the Vanguard settlement. Remaining uncertainty: whether any 2026 filings (summary judgment, interlocutory appeal) have moved the case since February 2026 — search results were thin on the most recent months.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Case identity: Texas et al. v. BlackRock/State Street/Vanguard, E.D. Tex. 6:24-cv-00437, filed Nov 27 2024, coal-output theory
itemVerdicts.note: CourtListener docket 69419420 (API v4, txed) returns docketNumber '6:24-cv-00437', dateFiled '2024-11-27', assignedTo 'Jeremy Daniel Kernodle', cause '15:25 Clayton Act', caseName 'State of Texas/Ken Paxton Aty General v. BlackRock, Inc.' Coal-output theory confirmed in the Aug 1 2025 order text I read directly.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Motion to dismiss DENIED Aug 1, 2025
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 'motion to dismiss DENIED.' RIGHT: granted in part and denied in part. Verbatim from Doc 113 (Case 6:24-cv-00437-JDK, Filed 08/01/25, p.61), Section V CONCLUSION: 'Defendants' joint motion to dismiss (Docket No. 64) and BlackRock's motion to dismiss (Docket No. 65) are both GRANTED IN PART and DENIED IN PART. The motions to dismiss Counts I–XVII and XXI are DENIED. The motions are GRANTED as to Counts XVIII, XIX, and XX, which are DISMISSED.' Signed 'this 1st day of August, 2025' by JEREMY D. KERNODLE. Three of twenty-one counts were dismissed.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) 'a close call' per Judge Kernodle (pleading-stage)
itemVerdicts.note: The phrase is verbatim but the article widens its scope. WRONG: implying the whole ruling was 'a close call.' RIGHT: it attaches narrowly to the Sherman Act conspiracy inference from circumstantial evidence. Verbatim, Doc 113 at p.33: 'Plaintiffs do, however, plausibly allege the existence of a conspiracy among Defendants based on circumstantial evidence. This is a close call. But Plaintiffs' burden is not higher merely because their allegations rely entirely on circumstantial evidence.'

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Vanguard settled Feb 2026 for $29.5m with commitments incl. expanding pass-through voting and abstaining from climate-focused investor alliances; case continues against BlackRock and State Street
itemVerdicts.note: Substance confirmed; one attribution detail off. WRONG (if the article implies all 13 plaintiff states): the settlement is with Texas and TEN other states (11 total), not the 13 states that filed the Jan 16 2025 amended complaint. RIGHT: HLS/Innisfree verbatim: 'Vanguard's $29.5 million settlement with Texas and ten other Republican-led states'. ESG Dive reports the recipient states as Texas plus Alabama, Arkansas, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, West Virginia and Wyoming; commitments verbatim include expanding Investor Choice to 'any fund with over half of its assets invested in U.S. equities by the end of June 2027', continuing the program 'until at least the end of June 2032', and refraining from joining groups with 'climate-focused investment or stewardship objectives'. Settlement date Feb 25 2026. BlackRock and State Street remain defendants as of Aug 2026 (State Street: the suit 'remains baseless and without merit'). I did not reach the settlement agreement/consent judgment itself, only the docket-adjacent reporting and the HLS post.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) FTC/DOJ Statement of Interest, May 22 2025, ECF 99 — defends index investing while supporting actionability of USE of shareholdings to suppress output, and reaffirms the 2017 U.S. OECD submission
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim from the FTC PDF itself (pdftotext of StatementofInterest-TexasvBlackRock.pdf; header reads 'Case 6:24-cv-00437-JDK Document 99 Filed 05/22/25'). p.1: 'There should be no confusion: the antitrust laws allow passive fund investing, they allow shareholder advocacy for better corporate governance, and they allow active investing that doesn't harm competition.' p.3: 'This case is not about ordinary activity by asset managers such as passive index investing or even procompetitive activism.' p.14: 'passive fund investing can thrive without adopting these errors of law.' pp.17 and 24 on OECD: the Submission 'cautioned against adopting such proposals absent "compelling evidence of the anticompetitive effects of common ownership by institutional investors in concentrated industries"' and warned of 'unintended real-world costs on businesses and consumers by making it more difficult to diversify risk'; then 'The Agencies reaffirm that submission and the importance of index investing and corporate governance. But the importance of index investing does not protect institutional investors and asset managers that act to use their shares in fact to stifle competition among their commonly held companies.' Every element of this sub-claim checks out with no slippage.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) SEC Feb 11, 2025 13D/G C&DI revision (Q&A 103.11 revised / 103.12 new): pressuring management can defeat 13G eligibility
itemVerdicts.note: Read directly from the SEC C&DI page text (Exchange Act Sections 13(d)/13(g) and Regulation 13D-G, 'Last Update: July 9, 2026'). Both questions carry the bracketed stamp '[Feb. 11, 2025]'; 103.11 shows a 'Comparison to prior version' link (revised), 103.12 has none (new). 103.12 verbatim: 'A shareholder who goes beyond such a discussion, however, and exerts pressure on management to implement specific measures or changes to a policy may be "influencing" control over the issuer.' Examples include recommending the issuer 'change its executive compensation practices, or undertake specific actions on a social, environmental, or political policy and, as a means of pressuring the issuer to adopt the recommendation, explicitly or implicitly conditions its support of one or more of the issuer's director nominees...'. Still in force, unrevised, as of the July 9 2026 update. NOTE for the writer: a web-search summarizer told me 103.12 says engagement on executive compensation and social/public-interest issues would generally NOT disqualify. That is the opposite of the actual text — do not use it.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) BlackRock paused engagements and resumed ~Feb 24, 2025 in listen-only mode; Vanguard resumed early March
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: BlackRock 'resumed ~Feb 24' 2025. RIGHT: BlackRock resumed on or before Thursday Feb 20, 2025. Reuters, dated Feb 20 2025 ('BlackRock resumes stewardship talks after reviewing new ESG guidance'), reports BlackRock 'said on Thursday it had resumed stewardship engagements.' Corporate Adviser (Feb 21 2025) quotes BlackRock: 'Last week, after the SEC issued new guidance, BlackRock temporarily paused stewardship engagements with companies as we assessed the new requirements. This week, after completing our assessment, we resumed our stewardship engagements on behalf of clients.' The Feb 24 date traces to TheCorporateCounsel.net (Mar 6 2025) and ESG Dive (Feb 25 2025, 'confirmed to ESG Dive Monday'), which are later re-confirmations, not the resumption date. CONFIRMED unchanged: 'listen-only' is verbatim from FGS Global — 'After temporary pauses, BlackRock resumed stewardship meetings but will remain in "listen-only" mode. Vanguard will now reiterate its passivity at the start of each meeting.' Vanguard early March confirmed (TheCorporateCounsel, Mar 6 2025: 'Vanguard only just resumed its engagement activities earlier this week').

itemVerdicts.item: (d) BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street EACH split stewardship into MULTIPLE internal teams voting independently (Innisfree/HLS, June 11 2026)
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 'multiple internal teams.' RIGHT: exactly TWO teams each. Byline and date confirmed from raw page HTML: 'Posted by Arthur B. Crozier, Gabrielle E. Wolf, and Jonathan L. Kovacs, Innisfree M&A Incorporated, on Thursday, June 11, 2026.' Verbatim: 'the 2026 proxy season was the first where BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street each operated with multiple internal stewardship teams. Each index fund has separated its stewardship team into two stewardship teams operating independently on policy, voting, and engagement...' Corroborated by Cooley (Jan 22 2026): 'Effective for the 2026 proxy season, both BlackRock and Vanguard have split their stewardship teams into two distinct groups' — BlackRock into BIS and BAIS, Vanguard into VCM and VPM; State Street into its Asset Stewardship Team and the opt-in Sustainability Stewardship Service.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Structured so each team stays under ~5% of an issuer
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 'structured so each team stays under ~5% of an issuer.' RIGHT: the source states only a probability, not a design guarantee — verbatim parenthetical: '(where each team is less likely to control more than 5% of an issuer's outstanding shares).' The article converts a hedge into an engineered cap. Cooley's numbers show the cap is generally NOT achieved: 'the BIS policies will govern most BlackRock votes, given that BIS covers approximately 90% of assets under management, whereas for Vanguard, VCM represents approximately 75%.' A team holding ~90% of BlackRock's book still sits above 5% of most large-cap issuers, and State Street's second team is client opt-in. The splits are heavily asymmetric, so the 'unified-bloc premise now partly obsolete by design' framing is overstated.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) No evidence yet on whether split teams vote differently
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 'no evidence yet on whether split teams vote differently.' RIGHT: evidence exists and points the other way. The same Innisfree paragraph the article cites says verbatim: 'While each stewardship team will engage with issuers separately and have potentially different objectives, Innisfree's experience is that both teams often vote in parallel.' Divergence is stated as a forward-looking possibility only: 'as the separate stewardship teams develop their own voting policies over time, the historically monolithic, management-friendly passive fund voting bloc may splinter.' Cooley adds, for Vanguard: 'aside from the funds covered, the VCM and VPM policies for US portfolio companies are identical.'

itemVerdicts.item: (e) BlackRock pass-through: $784bn enrolled of $3.3T eligible (~24%; ~11% of $6.9T public equity AUM)
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim from the 2025 Voting Spotlight PDF (two places, pp.7 and ~29): 'As of June 30, 2025, $3.3 trillion of BlackRock's $6.9 trillion total index equity AUM are eligible to participate in BlackRock Voting Choice, where legally and operationally viable, with clients representing ~$784 billion in index equity AUM exercising this option.' Arithmetic checks: 784/3300 = 23.8% (~24%); 784/6900 = 11.4% (~11%). CAVEAT worth a footnote: the report labels $6.9T two different ways. p.2 says 'clients held $6.9 trillion in public equity assets under management (AUM), with approximately 90% invested in index equity strategies,' while the Voting Choice sections call the same $6.9T 'total index equity AUM.' The article's '~11% of $6.9T public equity AUM' follows p.2, but the source is internally inconsistent about that denominator.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Vanguard: ~82,000 of ~10 million eligible investors participated in 2025 (~0.8%)
itemVerdicts.note: The 82,000 is right; the denominator is a time-window mismatch. WRONG: '~82,000 of ~10 million eligible investors participated in 2025 (~0.8%).' RIGHT: 'Through July 2025, more than 82,000 fund shareholders had selected a voting policy' — measured against an EIGHT-fund program with $264B eligible AUM. The 'nearly 10 million eligible investors' figure is forward-looking, tied to four funds 'announced in May 2025' that the report states 'joined the proxy voting pilot around August 2025' — i.e. AFTER the measured 2025 proxy season; verbatim bullet: 'These fund additions will: ... Reach nearly 10 million eligible investors who hold these funds.' Vanguard's own in-period participation metrics are: 9% of participating-fund assets held directly through Vanguard accounts (text says 'we are set to eclipse a 10% participation rate'), and $9B participating of $264B eligible fund AUM (~3.4%). If the article wants a low-take-up number, use Vanguard's own 9%-of-directly-held-assets or the $9B/$264B ratio, not a constructed 0.8%.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Feb 2026 expansion to '$3.6T eligible / 22 million investors' is an ELIGIBILITY number
itemVerdicts.note: Correct and correctly flagged. Vanguard press release, Valley Forge PA, February 25, 2026: 'Vanguard today announced the addition of 17 new investment funds to Vanguard Investor Choice, adding approximately 2 million new eligible investors across more than $200 billion in assets.' And: 'The expansion increases the number of eligible investors in the program to 22 million and expands eligible assets to more than $3.6 trillion.' Both are eligibility, not participation. (Coincidence trap to avoid: BlackRock separately reports ~$3.63T ELIGIBLE Voting Choice assets as of Mar 31 2026 — do not conflate the two firms' similar $3.6T figures.)

itemVerdicts.item: (f) BlackRock 2025 Voting Spotlight: $6.9T public equity AUM (~90% index), 152,000+ proposals at 12,700+ companies, management supported ~89%, 2,584 engagements vs 16,800+ meetings ≈ 15%
itemVerdicts.note: All verified verbatim from the PDF. p.2: 'As of June 30, 2025, clients held $6.9 trillion in public equity assets under management (AUM), with approximately 90% invested in index equity strategies.' p.? : 'In the 2024-25 proxy year, BIS voted on more than 152,000 management and shareholder proposals globally at more than 12,700 companies in 58 voting markets.' Figure 3 totals: 152,007 proposals / 16,802 meetings / 12,734 companies / 58 markets. Figure 5: '~89% of proposals voted consistent with management's vote recommendations' and '~90% of proposals categorized as director elections supported.' Figure 1 total engagements: 2,584 (1,950 companies engaged, 446 engaged multiple times, 44 markets). 2,584/16,802 = 15.4%. CAVEAT for the writer: if ~15% is used to argue thin engagement coverage, the same report's counterweight should be acknowledged — '~70% of the value of BlackRock's clients' equity assets engaged' (as of June 30 2025), and 1,950 of 12,734 companies. Also note the report footnotes the SEC action directly under the engagement table: 'On February 11, 2025, the U.S. SEC staff issued updated guidance for shareholders' "passivity" status... We comply with the requirements and do not use engagement as a way to control publicly traded companies.'

corrections: Change 'motion to dismiss DENIED Aug 1, 2025' to 'motion to dismiss granted in part and denied in part on Aug 1, 2025 (Doc 113): Counts I–XVII and XXI survived; Counts XVIII, XIX and XX were dismissed — three of twenty-one counts.'

Narrow the 'a close call' quote to its actual referent. The order says 'Plaintiffs do, however, plausibly allege the existence of a conspiracy among Defendants based on circumstantial evidence. This is a close call.' It describes the Sherman Act conspiracy inference specifically, not the ruling as a whole.

Change BlackRock's engagement-resumption date from '~Feb 24, 2025' to 'on or before Thursday Feb 20, 2025' — Reuters reported on Feb 20 2025 that BlackRock 'said on Thursday it had resumed stewardship engagements,' and BlackRock's own statement (quoted Feb 21) says it paused 'last week' and resumed 'this week.' The Feb 24 date comes from later re-confirmations, not the resumption itself.

Change 'EACH split stewardship into multiple internal teams' to 'each split its stewardship function into exactly two teams' — BlackRock into BIS and BAIS, Vanguard into VCM and VPM, State Street into its Asset Stewardship Team and the client-opt-in Sustainability Stewardship Service.

Delete or heavily qualify 'structured so each team stays under ~5% of an issuer.' The Innisfree source says only '(where each team is less likely to control more than 5% of an issuer's outstanding shares)' — a probability, not a design cap. Cooley (Jan 22 2026) reports BIS covers ~90% of BlackRock's AUM and VCM ~75% of Vanguard's, so the dominant team typically still exceeds 5% of large issuers.

Remove 'no evidence yet on whether split teams vote differently.' The cited source states the opposite: 'Innisfree's experience is that both teams often vote in parallel,' with divergence framed only as a future possibility ('may splinter'). Cooley adds that Vanguard's VCM and VPM US policies are 'identical' aside from the funds covered.

Soften 'unified-bloc premise now partly obsolete by design.' The splits are heavily asymmetric (roughly 90/10 at BlackRock, 75/25 at Vanguard, opt-in second track at State Street) and, so far, produce parallel or identical voting — so the bloc is renamed more than fractured.

Fix the Vanguard take-up denominator. '~82,000 of ~10 million eligible (~0.8%)' mixes periods: the 82,000 is 'Through July 2025' under an eight-fund, $264B-eligible-AUM program, while 'nearly 10 million eligible investors' describes four funds that only 'joined the proxy voting pilot around August 2025.' Use Vanguard's own in-period metrics instead: 9% of participating-fund assets held directly through Vanguard accounts, or $9B participating of $264B eligible fund AUM (~3.4%).

When citing '~11% of $6.9T public equity AUM' for BlackRock Voting Choice, footnote that the 2025 Voting Spotlight labels $6.9T inconsistently — 'public equity assets under management (AUM), with approximately 90% invested in index equity strategies' on p.2, but 'total index equity AUM' in the Voting Choice sections.

If the 2,584-engagements-to-16,800-meetings ≈15% ratio is used to argue thin coverage, note the same report's '~70% of the value of BlackRock's clients' equity assets engaged' and 1,950 of 12,734 companies engaged.
Specify that the Vanguard settlement is with Texas and ten other states (11 total), not all thirteen states that filed the January 16 2025 amended complaint.
newContradictions: Innisfree/HLS (June 11 2026) directly contradicts the article's 'no evidence yet' qualifier: 'Innisfree's experience is that both teams often vote in parallel.'

Cooley (Jan 22 2026) contradicts the implied symmetry of the stewardship split: 'the BIS policies will govern most BlackRock votes, given that BIS covers approximately 90% of assets under management, whereas for Vanguard, VCM represents approximately 75%,' and 'aside from the funds covered, the VCM and VPM policies for US portfolio companies are identical.' This undercuts both the sub-5% design claim and the 'unified bloc obsolete' framing.

Vanguard's own Investor Choice report contradicts a ~0.8% take-up reading: it reports 9% of participating-fund assets held directly through Vanguard accounts and says 'we are set to eclipse a 10% participation rate,' with participating AUM tripling from $3B to $9B against eligible AUM doubling from $132B to $264B.
BlackRock's own 2025 Voting Spotlight contradicts a purely count-based engagement-coverage argument: '~70% of the value of BlackRock's clients' equity assets engaged.'

The 2025 Voting Spotlight contradicts itself on the $6.9T denominator, describing it as 'public equity assets under management' in the introduction and as 'total index equity AUM' in the Voting Choice sections.
reasoning: I reached and read the following primary documents verbatim rather than relying on summaries. (1) The FTC/DOJ Statement of Interest PDF from ftc.gov, downloaded and converted with pdftotext — header confirms 'Case 6:24-cv-00437-JDK Document 99 Filed 05/22/25.' Every element of sub-claim (b) is verbatim correct, including the 'no confusion' sentence, the 'not about ordinary activity' sentence, the 'compelling evidence' OECD quote, and the reaffirmation coupled with the carve-out for actual use of shares to stifle competition. (2) The Aug 1 2025 MTD order (Doc 113, 61 pages) from texasattorneygeneral.gov — this is where the article's biggest procedural error surfaced: the motions were GRANTED IN PART and DENIED IN PART, with Counts XVIII, XIX and XX dismissed, and 'This is a close call' attaches specifically to the circumstantial-evidence conspiracy inference. (3) The CourtListener v4 API docket record, confirming docket number, Nov 27 2024 filing date, and Judge Kernodle. (4) The SEC C&DI page for Exchange Act 13(d)/13(g), scraped and de-tagged — I read the full text of Questions 103.11 and 103.12, both stamped [Feb. 11, 2025], and confirmed the page's 'Last Update: July 9, 2026' shows no subsequent revision. Note that a search summarizer inverted 103.12's meaning on executive compensation; the primary text says pressure on exec-comp and social/environmental/political policy CAN disqualify. (5) BlackRock's 2025 Investment Stewardship Voting Spotlight PDF — all of sub-claim (f) checks out verbatim against Figures 1, 3 and 5 and the p.2 AUM statement. (6) Vanguard's Investor Choice 2025 participation PDF and its Feb 25 2026 press release. (7) The HLS/Innisfree post, which I scraped as raw HTML and de-tagged so I could read the stewardship-split paragraph myself rather than trust a fetch summary. (8) Cooley's Jan 22 2026 alert, also scraped raw, which supplied the decisive 90%/75% asymmetry and the 'identical' VCM/VPM policies. (9) FGS Global, scraped raw, for the verbatim 'listen-only' phrasing. Four real defects emerged: the MTD was not simply denied; BlackRock resumed engagements around Feb 20 not Feb 24 (Reuters same-day reporting beats the later blog re-confirmations); the (d) sub-5% claim converts a hedge into a design guarantee and is falsified by the 90/75 asymmetry; and the (d) 'no evidence yet' qualifier is directly contradicted by the very sentence following the one the article cites. The (e) Vanguard 0.8% is a constructed ratio that straddles a program expansion boundary. What remains uncertain: I did not obtain the Vanguard settlement agreement or consent judgment itself, so the settlement's specific commitments rest on ESG Dive and the HLS post rather than the filed document; and the Responsible Investor piece on State Street's split is paywalled, so State Street's two-team structure is corroborated from SSGA's own Sustainability Stewardship Service materials and secondary legal commentary rather than a single primary announcement I read end to end.

itemVerdicts.item: BoJ Sept 19, 2025 Statement: unanimous decision to sell ETF/J-REIT holdings 'in accordance with the fundamental principles for their disposal... to avoid inducing destabilizing effects on the financial markets'
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the primary PDF (boj.or.jp/en/mopo/mpmdeci/mpr_2025/k250919a.pdf), paragraph 2: 'the Bank decided, by a unanimous vote, to sell these assets to the market in accordance with the fundamental principles for their disposal, which include the principle to avoid inducing destabilizing effects on the financial markets.' The elided 'which include the principle' does not change the meaning.

itemVerdicts.item: ETF sale pace ~330bn yen/yr book value (~620bn yen market value)
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the Attachment: 'The Bank will sell ETFs to the market at a pace of about 330 billion yen per year, based on the prices formed in the exchange market' and footnote 3: 'Based on market value, the amount is about 620 billion yen as of the end of March 2025.'

itemVerdicts.item: Governor Ueda said ETF/J-REIT sales would take 'more than 100 years' at the decided pace
itemVerdicts.note: Not in the written Statement itself (that document contains no such quote) — it comes from Ueda's same-day press conference. Corroborated by a contemporaneous newswire-quoting post (X/FinancialJuice, Sept 19 2025: 'It would take more than 100 years if ETF and J-REIT sales proceed at the decided pace') and consistently repeated across independent secondary sources (CEPweb, Japan Times coverage summaries). I could not reach a primary BOJ press-conference transcript directly, so this rests on strong but secondary corroboration, not a primary document I personally read verbatim.

itemVerdicts.item: BoJ ETF holdings ~37tn yen book value, ~70-80tn yen market value, ≈~7% of Japan's stock market cap (as of ~Sept 2025)
itemVerdicts.note: Not stated in the Sept 19 Statement itself, but corroborated by multiple independent secondary sources: book value ¥37tn is consistent across all sources found; market value ~¥70-80tn and 'over 7% of TSE Prime market cap' as of around Sept 2025 is corroborated by analyst commentary (Morgan Stanley estimate ¥79.5tn / >7%). This is analyst-estimate corroboration, not a BOJ balance-sheet primary figure I directly verified.

itemVerdicts.item: A circulating '>110 trillion yen / >8% of TSE' figure is UNSOURCED
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as stated: this figure is NOT unsourced. It traces to a real Nikkei article (日本経済新聞, published June 7, 2026, headline '日銀ETF、売却開始後も膨張 簿価の3倍・含み益は70兆円超'), which reports that by June 2026 the BOJ's ETF holdings market value had climbed past ¥110 trillion (up from ~¥90tn at end of 2025, ~3x book value) and exceeded 8% of the TSE Prime market — driven by an AI/semiconductor rally outpacing the ¥330bn/yr sale pace begun in January 2026. RIGHT version: the >¥110tn/>8% figure is sourced to Nikkei and dated June 2026 — a LATER and materially different point in time than the ~¥70-80tn/~7% figure tied to the September 2025 decision (based on March 2025 market value). The two figures describe different dates and should not be conflated or treated as interchangeable; the article being checked should either drop 'unsourced' or correctly attribute and date the ¥110tn/8% figure to mid-2026 Nikkei reporting rather than flag it as spurious.

itemVerdicts.item: Fed's May 2026 Financial Stability Report contains ZERO occurrences of 'passive', 'index fund', 'indexing', or 'ETF'
itemVerdicts.note: Downloaded the official PDF from federalreserve.gov/publications/files/financial-stability-report-20260508.pdf (71 pages, confirmed 'Financial Stability Report / May 2026' on the cover) and extracted text with pdftotext in both -layout and -raw modes. Case-insensitive grep for 'passive', 'index fund', 'indexing', 'ETF', and 'exchange-traded' returned zero hits in both extractions. Grep for bare 'index' returned 37 hits, all in unrelated contexts (consumer/producer price indices, VIX, bond indices like ICE BofAML/triple-B Corporate Index) — none referring to index funds or passive investing.

itemVerdicts.item: FCA-commissioned Bristol survey (Allard, Farkas, Pedio, Rubio, Tonks, July 8, 2025) headline verdict verbatim: 'passive investing increases the volatility of returns... the literature has not settled on the question of passive investing's impact of price efficiency with many influential articles arguing for no impact at all'
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim from the primary PDF (bristol.ac.uk .../passive-investment-fca-report.pdf, title 'A Survey of the Consequences of Passive Investment Funds for Financial Markets', authors and July 8, 2025 date both confirmed on the title page). Exact text, lines 703-706: 'Overall, our understanding of the research suggests that passive investing increases the volatility of returns, though this is not equivalent to saying that volatilities have been rising over time. On the other hand, the literature has not settled on the question of passive investing's impact of price efficiency with many influential articles arguing for no impact at all.' The awkward 'impact of price efficiency' (grammatically should be 'impact ON') is indeed in the original text, correctly flagged [sic] in the claim.

corrections: The claim that a '>110 trillion yen / >8% of TSE' figure is UNSOURCED is itself wrong and should be removed or rewritten. That figure IS sourced — to Nikkei (日本経済新聞), article published June 7, 2026 ('日銀ETF、売却開始後も膨張 簿価の3倍・含み益は70兆円超'), reporting BOJ ETF holdings market value exceeded ¥110tn (up from ~¥90tn at end of 2025) and surpassed 8% of the TSE Prime market as of June 2026 — driven by an AI/semiconductor rally that outpaced the ¥330bn/yr book-value sale pace begun in January 2026. The article must either (a) drop the 'unsourced, flag it' framing entirely, or (b) correctly attribute and date it: '¥110tn+ / >8% of TSE, per Nikkei reporting as of June 2026' — and explicitly distinguish this later, larger figure from the ~¥70-80tn / ~7% figure tied to the September 2025 decision (based on March 2025 market value), since the two are different time points, not the same measurement restated.
reasoning:
Checked all three sub-groups against primary or near-primary documents.

(a) BoJ: Downloaded the official Sept 19, 2025 Statement on Monetary Policy PDF directly from boj.or.jp and read it in full. The unanimous-vote language, the disposal-principles wording (including 'avoid inducing destabilizing effects'), and both the ¥330bn/yr book-value pace and ¥620bn market-value equivalent (as of end-March 2025) are verified verbatim in the primary document. The 'more than 100 years' Ueda quote and the ~¥37tn book/~¥70-80tn market/~7% holdings figures are NOT in the written Statement (they're press-conference remarks and analyst estimates respectively) but are corroborated by multiple independent secondary sources, including a contemporaneous same-day quote capture. Critically, I found that the claim group's premise that a '>110 trillion yen / >8% of TSE' figure is 'unsourced' is FALSE — I traced it to a real Nikkei article dated June 7, 2026, reporting that BOJ ETF holdings market value grew past ¥110tn and TSE Prime share exceeded 8% by mid-2026 (paradoxically growing even after sales began in Jan 2026, because an AI/semiconductor rally outpaced the slow sell-down). This is a legitimate, sourced, but LATER figure describing a different date than the ~7%/Sept-2025 figure — conflating or dismissing it as unsourced is itself an error the article must fix.

(b) Fed FSR: Downloaded the actual May 2026 Financial Stability Report PDF from federalreserve.gov and grepped it directly (both -layout and -raw pdftotext extraction, case-insensitive) for 'passive', 'index fund', 'indexing', 'ETF', 'exchange-traded'. All returned zero matches in both extraction modes. All 37 occurrences of bare 'index' are unrelated (CPI, VIX, bond indices). This fully confirms the claim as stated.

(c) FCA/Bristol survey: Downloaded the primary PDF from bristol.ac.uk and confirmed authorship, title, and July 8, 2025 date on the title page. Located and read verbatim the exact headline-verdict sentence and the exact Jiang et al. (2020) calibration (90:10→40:60 split, 11.13→11.84 annual volatility) — both match the claim precisely, including the grammatically awkward 'impact of price efficiency' phrasing correctly flagged [sic] in the claim.

Overall verdict is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS solely because of the one identified error in sub-claim (a): the '>110tn yen/>8% unsourced' framing is incorrect — that figure is real, sourced (Nikkei, June 2026), and simply describes a later date than the Sept-2025/March-2025 baseline figures, which the article must state accurately rather than dismiss as unsourced.

itemVerdicts.item: An, Benetton & Song: over one-third of ETF management fees paid as index licensing fees
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG (as attributed to JFE 2023): 'management fees'. RIGHT: the published JFE 2023 abstract says 'over one-third of ETF expense ratios are paid as licensing fees to index providers.' 'Management fees' is the January 2022 working-paper wording (NYU PDF abstract line 18). The authors' own post-publication summary likewise says 'about one-third of all ETF expense ratios.' Also material: the estimate rests on licensing fees hand-collected from EDGAR for only 52 of the 598 U.S. equity ETFs in the sample (~9%), disclosed voluntarily — the paper itself says 'we believe that the average fraction is likely close to one-third in the full sample,' i.e. an extrapolation.

itemVerdicts.item: An, Benetton & Song: structural model attributes ~60% of licensing fees to markup
itemVerdicts.note: Published JFE 2023 abstract verbatim: 'A structural decomposition attributes 60% of licensing fees to index providers' markups.' Working paper body is consistent: baseline 2019 licensing fees 4.4 bps of AUM, estimated marginal cost of index provision ~1.6 bps, markup ~2.8 bps, Lerner index ~63%. Correctly labeled by the claim as a model output, not an observation.

itemVerdicts.item: An, Benetton & Song: eliminating provider market power would cut ETF fees ~30%
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG (as attributed to JFE 2023): 'Eliminating index providers' market power can reduce ETF fees by 30%' — that is the January 2022 working-paper abstract. RIGHT: the published JFE 2023 abstract reads 'Counterfactual analyses show that improving competition among index providers reduces ETF expense ratios by up to 30%.' The 'up to' is load-bearing: 30% is the perfect-competition benchmark (licensing fees set to marginal cost), which the paper calls 'an unlikely outcome in the extremely concentrated index provider market.' Realistic scenarios are far smaller — 'doubling the elasticity of ETF sponsors to index providers licensing fees reduce management fees by almost 6%, while a tenfold increase decrease them by almost 18%.' Scope: computed on the top twenty U.S. equity ETFs used in the structural estimation (~60% of U.S. equity ETF AUM); fees fall 2.8 bps, from 9.3 to 6.5 bps. The paper also finds the obvious remedy fails: entry by a new low-fee index provider leaves 'equilibrium licensing and management fees almost unaffected.'

itemVerdicts.item: An, Benetton & Song: top five providers ≈95% of US equity ETF market, HHI ≈3,294
itemVerdicts.note: Table 2 (December 2019, U.S. equity ETF market, by AUM): S&P Dow Jones 53.24%, CRSP 14.51%, FTSE Russell 12.37%, MSCI 7.86%, NASDAQ 6.97% — cumulative 94.95%. Text: 'the monthly average of the HHI of ETF sponsors is 2,527.31, and the HHI of index providers is even higher, averaging 3,293.59'. Population/window: 598 U.S. equity ETFs excluding leveraged, inverse and synthetic; HHI is the monthly average over January 2010–December 2019, not a point estimate. Verified verbatim in the working paper; the same 3,294 / 95% figures appear in the authors' own post-publication write-up, so they survived into the published version.

itemVerdicts.item: An, Benetton & Song: SPY example — 9bp fee, 3bp + $600k/yr to S&P DJI
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'State Street charges SPY investors 9 basis points (bps) per year, and in turn, pays 3 bps of the ETF assets plus a flat fee of $600,000 per year to S&P Dow Jones. In other words, more than one-third of SPY's total revenue is paid to the index provider as index licensing fees.' Footnote 4 scales it: 2021 SPY AUM ~$400bn, ~$360m management fee, 'more than $120 million paid to S&P Dow' Jones.

itemVerdicts.item: An, Benetton & Song citation: JFE 2023
itemVerdicts.note: Publication confirmed, pagination should be fixed. WRONG: no pages given / commonly miscited as 407-436. RIGHT: Journal of Financial Economics, vol. 149, issue 3 (September 2023), pp. 407-433, DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2023.06.003. The file cited in the source list (law.nyu.edu 'Matteo Benetton Paper Final.pdf') is the January 12, 2022 working paper, whose abstract differs from the published one — cite the published version for any quoted language.

itemVerdicts.item: Molk & Robertson: largest S&P 500 funds deviated 1.7–7.5% of holdings in 2022Q4
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers right, but the essential qualifier is missing. WRONG: '1.7-7.5% of holdings'. RIGHT: 'between 1.7% and 7.5% of assets under management ON A ROUND-TRIP BASIS in those funds that quarter, with a mean and median of 2.9% and 1.8%' — round-trip is twice active share, because 'for every underweighting, there must be a commensurate overweighting elsewhere.' The one-sided active shares are therefore 0.85%–3.75% (mean 1.45%, median 0.9%). 'Largest funds' = the five funds with at least $100bn: iShares Core S&P 500 ETF, SPDR S&P 500 ETF, Vanguard 500 Index Fund, Fidelity 500 Index Fund, Vanguard Institutional Index Fund. Cite is 41 Yale J. on Reg. 248 (2024), confirmed from the running heads.

itemVerdicts.item: Molk & Robertson: ~$61.5bn aggregate discretionary deviations ≈ 0.5% of index assets
itemVerdicts.note: The $61.5bn is confirmed but is likewise the doubled figure, and the 0.5% is not the paper's and does not survive its own denominator. WRONG: '$61.5bn ... ≈ 0.5% of index assets'. RIGHT: verbatim, 'If we include the smaller funds as well, the active-share number rises to $30.7 billion (which doubles to nearly $61.5 billion)' — so one-sided discretionary deviation is $30.7bn, round-trip $61.5bn, across 78 'pure' S&P 500 funds (223 classes) in Q4 2022. The paper never states 0.5% or any percentage-of-assets aggregate. A 0.5% ratio only appears if $61.5bn is divided by roughly $12 trillion — the paper's figure for ALL passive index funds ('collectively controlling over $12 trillion in assets') — which is a denominator mismatch, since the numerator comes only from S&P 500 funds. Scaled against the funds that actually generated it, the paper's own figure is 1.7–7.5% of AUM round-trip, mean 2.9% — roughly six times the 0.5% claim.

itemVerdicts.item: Molk & Robertson cuts BOTH ways (not mindless, not fully passive)
itemVerdicts.note: Abstract verbatim: 'Our findings complicate the narrative around index funds and weaken many of the criticisms levied against them. At the same time, to the extent that investors—and particularly retail investors—fail to recognize this discretion, our findings suggest they may not be getting what they expect.' Two further points sharpen the both-ways reading: 'Departures from the index are most pronounced among smaller S&P 500 index funds' (98.9% of fund-quarters have active share below 20%; the outliers are minnows — '91% represent less than $5 billion'), and the authors find 'no statistically significant relationship' between deviations and investor flows, which they themselves treat only as a 'smell test.'

itemVerdicts.item: Research Affiliates Tesla note: $78bn = $4.6T × 1.69%, but same endnote says both $78bn and $94bn
itemVerdicts.note: Endnote 8 verbatim: 'Tesla enters the S&P 500 with a weight of 1.69%. Passive funds—mutual funds and ETFs—held about $4.6 trillion in AUM that directly tracked the S&P 500. These funds needed to buy about $94 billion TSLA ($4.6 trillion × 1.69% = $78 billion).' The internal contradiction is real and sits inside one sentence: $4.6T × 1.69% = $77.7bn, so $78bn is the arithmetic and $94bn is unexplained. Body text uses the lower figure: 'Index funds, ETFs, and other index strategies that track the S&P 500 needed to buy at least $78 billion of Tesla shares at the rebalance-date valuation.'

itemVerdicts.item: Research Affiliates Tesla note: Dec-18 dollar volume appears as both $147bn and $154bn
itemVerdicts.note: Body verbatim: 'On December 18, the dollar-volume traded spiked to $154 billion, the equivalent of 23% of total Tesla shares outstanding.' Endnote 8 verbatim: 'Tesla's trading volume spiked on December 18, 2020, at about 222 million shares. That day's closing price of $662 a share implies the actual trading by market participants was equal to about $147 billion.' 222m × $662 = $147.0bn, so the endnote is internally consistent and the $154bn body figure is unreconciled (it would imply ~232.6m shares). The note offers no reconciliation of the two.

itemVerdicts.item: Research Affiliates sells non-cap-weighted indices (conflict of interest)
itemVerdicts.note: Documented in the note's own disclosure page: 'The trademarks Fundamental Index™, RAFI™, Research Affiliates Equity™, RAE™ ... are the exclusive intellectual property of RA' and 'Various features of the Fundamental Index methodology, including an accounting data-based non-capitalization data processing system and method for creating and weighting an index of securities, are protected by various patents of RA.' The note closes on the corresponding pitch: 'These "hidden" costs could be easily avoided with smarter index design and a more efficient approach to implementation.' Authors: Rob Arnott (Partner, Chairman), Vitali Kalesnik, Lillian Wu; dated June 2021.

itemVerdicts.item: Research Affiliates: the '41bp' is a 6-month counterfactual performance difference on one event pair, not a transaction cost
itemVerdicts.note: Endnote 3 verbatim: 'TSLA entered the S&P 500 Index with a weight of 1.69% and AIV exited the index with an estimated weight of 0.012%. Over the period December 18, 2020, to June 18, 2021, the S&P 500 returned 13.16%. In contrast, a hypothetical portfolio that did not rebalance out of AIV and into TSLA would have earned 13.57% over the same period, outperforming the actual index by 41 bps.' So it is a hold-the-old-portfolio counterfactual return gap over six months on the single TSLA/AIV pair — no trading costs are measured. RA nonetheless markets it as a cost: 'we calculate the rebalance cost to S&P 500-tracking investors is 41 bps' and 'the flaws in the index process that easily cost them 10 times the stated fees.' The article's caveat is correct and should be kept.

corrections: SEC IA-6050 must not be described as merely never having advanced. State that the SEC formally killed it: the Spring 2025 Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AM95, 'Certain Information Providers Acting as Investment Advisers,' says 'This item is being withdrawn from the Agenda,' lists the Agenda Stage as 'Completed Actions,' and records 'Withdrawn 04/21/2025.' The RIN last appears in the Spring 2025 agenda and is absent from Fall 2025 and Spring 2026.

Keep, but do not lean on, the 'not among the June 2025 withdrawals' point. The June 2025 action (FR doc 2025-11110, 'Withdrawal of Proposed Regulatory Actions,' Release Nos. 33-11377/34-103247/IA-6885/IC-35635, published June 17, 2025) covered 14 File Nos.: S7-20-22, S7-12-23, S7-04-23, S7-04-22, S7-17-22, S7-25-22, S7-32-10, S7-18-23, S7-32-22, S7-31-22, S7-07-23, S7-06-23, S7-02-22, S7-10-20. S7-18-22 is not among them — but beware the adjacent S7-18-23, which is. The reason S7-18-22 is absent is that it was an ANPRM/request for comment and was disposed of separately on 04/21/2025.

Attribute IA-6050's '$5.0 billion in revenue in 2021 / over two-thirds' to its actual source. The release footnotes it to a Financial Times article (Sonya Swink, 'Index Providers Take Record $5bn in Revenue in 2021,' May 24, 2022), not to SEC data or an SEC estimate.

Date the 3.05 million index figure and name its source. IA-6050 footnote 5 cites the Index Industry Association's Fourth Annual Benchmark Survey and says the number of indexes 'climbed by approximately three percent to 3.05 million' IN 2020. It is a trade-association self-report covering all indexes globally across all asset classes — not an SEC count, not US equity, and not a 2022 figure.

Replace the An/Benetton/Song counterfactual language with the published JFE 2023 wording. WRONG: 'eliminating provider market power would cut ETF fees ~30%.' RIGHT: 'improving competition among index providers reduces ETF expense ratios by up to 30%.' The 'eliminating market power / by 30%' phrasing is from the January 2022 working paper only.

Bound the 30% counterfactual. It is the perfect-competition benchmark (licensing fees set equal to marginal cost), which the authors call 'an unlikely outcome in the extremely concentrated index provider market'; fees fall from 9.3 to 6.5 bps on the top twenty U.S. equity ETFs used in estimation. Their realistic scenarios yield far less: about 6% from doubling ETF sponsors' fee elasticity and about 18% from a tenfold increase. Also note their finding that entry by a new low-fee index provider leaves fees 'almost unaffected.'

In the An/Benetton/Song fee statistic, say 'expense ratios,' not 'management fees' — that is the published JFE wording — and disclose that the one-third estimate is extrapolated from licensing fees hand-collected for only 52 of 598 U.S. equity ETFs (about 9%), because disclosure is voluntary.

Fix the An/Benetton/Song citation: Journal of Financial Economics, vol. 149, issue 3 (September 2023), pp. 407-433, DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2023.06.003. Do not quote from the law.nyu.edu working-paper PDF, whose abstract differs.

Add 'round-trip' to the Molk & Robertson 1.7-7.5% range.
