Their sentence is 'between 1.7% and 7.5% of assets under management on a round-trip basis,' mean 2.9% and median 1.8%; round-trip is twice active share, so the one-sided deviations are 0.85%-3.75%. 'Largest funds' means the five funds with at least $100bn: iShares Core S&P 500 ETF, SPDR S&P 500 ETF, Vanguard 500 Index Fund, Fidelity 500 Index Fund, Vanguard Institutional Index Fund.

Drop or fix the '≈0.5% of index assets' gloss on Molk & Robertson's $61.5bn — the paper states no such percentage. The $61.5bn is itself the doubled round-trip figure; the one-sided active share is $30.7bn ('the active-share number rises to $30.7 billion (which doubles to nearly $61.5 billion)') across 78 'pure' S&P 500 funds in Q4 2022. A 0.5% ratio requires dividing by roughly $12 trillion of all index-fund assets, a denominator far larger than the S&P 500 funds that produced the deviations. If a percentage is wanted, use the paper's own: 1.7-7.5% of those funds' AUM on a round-trip basis, mean 2.9%.

Strengthen the Molk & Robertson 'cuts both ways' point with their actual second edge: deviations are concentrated in small funds (98.9% of fund-quarters have active share under 20%; 91% of the high-deviation observations are funds under $5bn), and the authors find no statistically significant flow response to deviations — which they explicitly call only a 'smell test.'

Note that the Research Affiliates PDF has moved: researchaffiliates.com now 302-redirects to rafi.com. The live URL is https://www.rafi.com/content/dam/ra/publications/pdf/832-revisiting-teslas-addition-to-the-sp500.pdf (the researchaffiliates.com PDF link in the source list returns an HTML interstitial, not the document).
newContradictions: Research Affiliates' own two figures for the same quantity cannot both be right and the note never reconciles them: endnote 8 says passive funds 'needed to buy about $94 billion TSLA ($4.6 trillion × 1.69% = $78 billion)' — $4.6T × 1.69% is $77.7bn, so the $94bn is unsupported by the note's own arithmetic, while the body text uses 'at least $78 billion.' Any article using the $78bn number should say the source's own headline figure in the same sentence is 22% higher.

Research Affiliates' Dec-18 dollar volume is $154bn in the body but 'about $147 billion' in endnote 8, where 222 million shares × $662 = $147.0bn. The endnote's arithmetic is right; the body's $154bn would require ~232.6m shares. This matters because the $147bn vs $78bn gap is what RA uses to argue 'closet indexers likely needed to buy a similar, if not larger, amount,' and the note's own explanation for the residual is different again — 'Many large institutional investors own the S&P 500 in separately managed accounts, which accounts for the difference.'

RA frames the 41 bps as a trading/rebalance cost — 'the rebalance cost to S&P 500-tracking investors is 41 bps' and 'flaws in the index process that easily cost them 10 times the stated fees' — but endnote 3 shows it is purely a six-month return differential between the actual S&P 500 (13.16%) and a hypothetical portfolio that skipped one rebalance (13.57%). No transaction costs are measured anywhere in the note, and the disclosure page concedes 'No allowance has been made for trading costs or management fees.'

The An/Benetton/Song paper is often cited as evidence that breaking index-provider market power would meaningfully cut investor costs, but the same paper finds the market-based remedy fails: entry of a new low-fee index provider leaves 'equilibrium licensing and management fees almost unaffected,' consistent with Morningstar's Open Indexes Project having 'little effects.' The 30% figure requires perfect competition, which the authors call unlikely; their own realistic policy lever (mandatory disclosure of licensing fees, footnote 37) is untested in the model.

Molk & Robertson is a genuinely two-edged source, but note that its headline dollar figure ($61.5bn) and its headline percentage range (1.7-7.5%) are BOTH round-trip doubles. Anyone quoting them alongside a one-sided quantity — e.g. comparing to a fund's active share, or to index assets — is double-counting by construction.

SEC IA-6050 as a source is weaker than its 'SEC found' framing suggests: its two most-quoted numbers are footnoted to a Financial Times story ($5.0bn / two-thirds) and a trade-association press release (3.05 million indexes). The only figure sourced to SEC staff work is the China A-shares 4-5.5% range, from DERA's July 2020 Risk Spotlight.
reasoning: Primary documents reached and read verbatim, not via summarizers: (1) IA-6050 full text (Conformed to Federal Register version, 32 pp.) — confirmed the two-thirds/$5.0bn sentence at p.5, footnote 5 (3.05 million, IIA 2020), footnote 10 (FT sourcing), footnote 45 (China A-shares 4%-5.5%), and the closing 'Dated: June 15, 2022.' (2) reginfo.gov RIN 3235-AM95 rule pages for pubIds 202504/202510/202604, read as raw HTML stripped locally — the Spring 2025 entry carries 'This item is being withdrawn from the Agenda', stage 'Completed Actions', and timetable 'ANPRM 06/22/2022 87 FR 37254 ... Withdrawn 04/21/2025'; the publication history ends at Spring 2025, so it is absent from Fall 2025 and Spring 2026. (3) federalregister.gov API raw JSON for the June 2025 withdrawal — one matching document, 'Withdrawal of Proposed Regulatory Actions', published 2025-06-17, whose docket_ids list 14 file numbers; S7-18-22 is not among them (S7-18-23 is, a likely source of confusion). (4) An/Benetton/Song January 12, 2022 working paper (law.nyu.edu PDF, local an.txt) — confirmed HHI 3,293.59, Table 2 cumulative 94.95%, SPY 9bp/3bp/$600,000, 60% markup (4.4bp licensing vs 1.6bp marginal cost), the 30% perfect-competition counterfactual with its 6%/18% realistic alternatives, and the ineffective-entry result. (5) Published JFE abstract retrieved verbatim from OpenAlex and cross-checked against Crossref — 'expense ratios', 'structural decomposition', 'improving competition ... by up to 30%' — establishing the version drift from the working paper's 'management fees' / 'Eliminating index providers' market power ... by 30%'. Biblio confirmed as 149(3):407-433, DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2023.06.003. (6) Molk & Robertson full Yale J. Reg. PDF (local mr.txt) — abstract, p.253 intro paragraph with the 'round-trip basis' qualifier and mean/median 2.9%/1.8%, and the p.276 passage giving $25.8bn / ~$52bn for large funds and $30.7bn / ~$61.5bn for all funds, Table 1 summary statistics, and the five-fund composition of the >=$100bn group. (7) Research Affiliates Tesla note — the researchaffiliates.com PDF URL in the source list now returns an HTML interstitial; the live PDF is at rafi.com and was fetched and converted locally, giving verbatim endnote 3 (13.16% vs 13.57%, 41 bps), endnote 8 ($4.6T, 1.69%, $94bn/$78bn, 222m shares, $662, $147bn), the body's $154bn and 'at least $78 billion', the 'rebalance cost ... 41 bps' framing, and the RAFI/Fundamental Index trademark-and-patent disclosure establishing the conflict. Remaining uncertainty, stated honestly: I could not obtain the full text of the published JFE version (Elsevier returns 403 despite the article being CC-BY, and Unpaywall lists no repository copy), so the body numbers for (b) — HHI 3,294, top-five 95%, SPY 9/3bp/$600k — are verified verbatim only in the January 2022 working paper. The authors' own post-publication write-up reproduces 3,294, the 95% five-provider figure, and the SPY 9bp/3bp/$600,000 sentence, and uses 'expense ratios' consistently with the published abstract, which is strong but secondary corroboration that those body figures survived. I also did not independently verify the total AUM of Molk & Robertson's 78-fund sample; my conclusion that their $61.5bn corresponds to roughly 3% (round-trip) rather than 0.5% rests on the paper's own reported percentages (1.7-7.5%, mean 2.9%), not on an outside AUM estimate.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Case caption/venue/filing date: Texas et al. v. BlackRock/State Street/Vanguard, E.D. Tex. 6:24-cv-00437, filed Nov 27 2024, coal-output theory
itemVerdicts.note: CourtListener docket 69419420 (primary): court txed, docketNumber 6:24-cv-00437 (full: 6:24-cv-00437-JDK), dateFiled 2024-11-27, cause '15:25 Clayton Act', assignedTo Jeremy Daniel Kernodle. Docket entry 1 = COMPLAINT filed by State of Montana and State of Texas/Ken Paxton, entered 11/27/2024. ECF 113 opinion confirms the theory: Count I alleges Defendants 'unlawfully acquired and used stock in violation of Section 7 of the Clayton Act' to 'constrain coal output.'

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Motion to dismiss DENIED Aug 1, 2025
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 'motion to dismiss DENIED.' RIGHT: granted in part and denied in part. ECF 113 (read directly from the RECAP PDF), Section V. CONCLUSION, verbatim: 'To summarize, Defendants' joint motion to dismiss (Docket No. 64) and BlackRock's motion to dismiss (Docket No. 65) are both GRANTED IN PART and DENIED IN PART. The motions to dismiss Counts I–XVII and XXI are DENIED. The motions are GRANTED as to Counts XVIII, XIX, and XX, which are DISMISSED.' Signed 1 August 2025 by Kernodle. The core Clayton Act §7 and Sherman Act §1 counts survived; three counts were dismissed. Contemporaneous press correctly said 'mostly rejects' / '18 of 21 counts.'

itemVerdicts.item: (a) 'a close call' per Judge Kernodle (pleading-stage)
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in ECF 113 at p.33: 'Plaintiffs do, however, plausibly allege the existence of a conspiracy among Defendants based on circumstantial evidence. This is a close call. But Plaintiffs' burden is not higher merely because their allegations rely entirely on circumstantial evidence.' CALIBER NOTE: the phrase is scoped to the sufficiency of the circumstantial-evidence conspiracy pleading, not to the ruling as a whole; do not render it as 'the judge called the case a close call.'

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Vanguard settled Feb 2026 for $29.5m; commitments incl. expanding pass-through voting and abstaining from climate-focused investor alliances; case continues against BlackRock and State Street
itemVerdicts.note: Settlement agreement PDF (texasattorneygeneral.gov/sites/default/files/images/press/Settlement_1.pdf) §1.12: 'Settlement Amount' means twenty-nine million and five hundred thousand U.S. dollars ($29.5 million).' §4.1: 'Vanguard will use commercially reasonable efforts to make proxy voting choice available to investors in funds accounting for at least 50% percent of assets invested in U.S. Equity Investments'; §4.3: 'continue offering proxy voting choice at least through the end of June 2032.' §5.6: 'Vanguard and its U.S.-domiciled subsidiaries will withdraw from PRI and will not participate in any organization that advocates for the setting of specific output or emissions targets or levels or that requires its members to make commitments specific to achieving climate-focused investment or stewardship objectives such as NZAM, Ceres, or Climate Action 100+.' Docket: ECF 147 stipulation and ECF 148 order, both 02/26/2026, dismissing all claims against Vanguard with prejudice; BlackRock and State Street each answered the Second Amended Complaint on 03/06/2026, so the case continues against them. Minor date caveat: Vanguard/press announced Feb 25, 2026; the court order is Feb 26, 2026. SCOPE CAVEAT: §4.1's threshold is aggregate (funds accounting for ≥50% of U.S. equity assets), NOT 'any fund with over half its assets in U.S. equities' — that paraphrase circulates in secondary coverage and is wrong.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) FTC/DOJ Statement of Interest, May 22 2025, ECF 99: defends passive index investing verbatim
itemVerdicts.note: Read from the FTC PDF text. Cover page: 'Document 99 Filed 05/22/25', 'STATEMENT OF INTEREST OF THE FEDERAL TRADE COMMISSION AND THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA.' Verbatim p.2: 'There should be no confusion: the antitrust laws allow passive fund investing, they allow shareholder advocacy for better corporate governance, and they allow active investing that doesn't harm competition.' Verbatim p.3: 'This case is not about ordinary activity by asset managers such as passive index investing or even procompetitive activism.' Also p.14: 'passive fund investing can thrive without adopting these errors of law.'

itemVerdicts.item: (b) FTC/DOJ reaffirm the 2017 U.S. OECD Submission (broad common-ownership limits lack compelling evidence) while supporting that USE of horizontal shareholdings to suppress output is actionable
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim pp.17–18: the Submission 'recognized the limitations of "general relationships suggested by academic papers" and cautioned against adopting such proposals absent "compelling evidence of the anticompetitive effects of common ownership by institutional investors in concentrated industries." U.S. OECD Submission, ¶¶ 3, 15.' It 'also cautioned against creating across-the-board limitations on common ownership given the potential for "unintended real-world costs on businesses and consumers by making it more difficult to diversify risk."' Then: 'The Agencies reaffirm that submission and the importance of index investing and corporate governance. But the importance of index investing does not protect institutional investors and asset managers that act to use their shares in fact to stifle competition among their commonly held companies.' And p.24: 'The Agencies do not assert a position as to when an investor's acquisition of stock in competing firms alone—without evidence of subsequent anticompetitive use—would implicate Section 7.' Every element of the sub-claim checks out.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) SEC Feb 11, 2025 13D/G C&DI revision (Q&A 103.11/103.12): pressuring management can defeat 13G eligibility
itemVerdicts.note: SEC update notice page (…-021125) reads: 'Compliance and Disclosure Interpretations: Regulation 13D-G / Feb. 11, 2025 / (UPDATED 2/11/25) / Section 103. Rule 13d-1 / Revised Question 103.11 / New Question 103.12.' Live C&DI page: both answers carry the stamp '[Feb. 11, 2025]' and are still in force (page last updated July 9, 2026 — no later revision to 103.11/103.12; the July 11, 2025 and July 9, 2026 updates touched other Q&As). 103.12 verbatim: 'A shareholder who goes beyond such a discussion, however, and exerts pressure on management to implement specific measures or changes to a policy may be "influencing" control over the issuer.' Examples include recommending removal of a staggered board, a majority-voting standard, eliminating a poison pill, changing 'executive compensation practices,' or 'specific actions on a social, environmental, or political policy' while conditioning director support on adoption.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) BlackRock paused engagements and resumed ~Feb 24 in listen-only mode; Vanguard resumed early March
itemVerdicts.note: PAUSE confirmed: Semafor, Feb 18 2025, verbatim: 'BlackRock called off scheduled engagement meetings with companies after the Securities and Exchange Commission last week walked back guidance…' VANGUARD confirmed: TheCorporateCounsel.net (March 2025): 'BlackRock resumed its engagement activities back on February 24, while Vanguard only just resumed its engagement activities earlier this week' — early March. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) DATE: WRONG to state '~Feb 24' as settled. Bloomberg/RTTNews ran 'BlackRock Reportedly Restarts Talks With Companies Following SEC Guidance' dated February 21, 2025 04:36 EST, i.e. resumption was already reported by Feb 21; Feb 24 comes from a single secondary blog. RIGHT: 'resumed within roughly a week, by late February 2025.' (2) 'LISTEN-ONLY MODE' IS UNSUPPORTED. I could not find that phrase in any reachable primary or secondary source — not the ESG Dive piece, not Semafor, not the RTTNews/Nasdaq piece, not TheCorporateCounsel, not BlackRock's own 2025 Voting Spotlight (grep for 'listen' returns only unrelated prose). It appears only inside web-search summarizer output, which is exactly the fabrication pattern flagged in this run. RIGHT, attested wording (BlackRock spokesperson to Bloomberg, quoted verbatim by ESG Dive): 'We are complying with the new requirements including by highlighting our role as a "passive" investor at the start of each engagement. BlackRock does not use engagement as a way to control publicly traded companies.' BlackRock's own 2025 Voting Spotlight footnote says the same: 'We comply with the requirements and do not use engagement as a way to control publicly traded companies.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Innisfree/HLS forum June 11 2026: BlackRock, Vanguard, State Street EACH split stewardship into multiple internal teams voting independently
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim from the raw HTML of corpgov.law.harvard.edu/2026/06/11/2026-proxy-season-trends-the-fracturing-of-shareholder-power/ (authors Arthur B. Crozier, Gabrielle E. Wolf, Jonathan L. Kovacs, Innisfree M&A; June 11, 2026): 'Following regulatory and political pressure, the 2026 proxy season was the first where BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street each operated with multiple internal stewardship teams. Each index fund has separated its stewardship team into two stewardship teams operating independently on policy, voting, and engagement…' PRECISION NOTE: 'multiple' = exactly TWO per firm in the source; write 'two' rather than the vaguer 'multiple.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Structured so each team stays under ~5% of an issuer
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as a blanket statement about all three firms. RIGHT: true for Vanguard, false for BlackRock, unevidenced for State Street. The source sentence is a hedged parenthetical: '(where each team is less likely to control more than 5% of an issuer's outstanding shares)' — not a flat assertion. Primary EDGAR check I ran: (i) VANGUARD — Vanguard Group Inc.'s own Schedule 13G/A (accession 0000102909-26-002704, filed 2026-03-30) reports 0 shares / 0% and carries the comment 'On January 12, 2026, The Vanguard Group, Inc. went through an internal realignment. In accordance with SEC Release No. 34-39538 (January 12, 1998), certain subsidiaries or business divisions… will report beneficial ownership separately (on a disaggregated basis)… The Vanguard Group, Inc. no longer has, or is deemed to have, beneficial ownership over securities beneficially owned by such subsidiaries.' The successors, VANGUARD CAPITAL MANAGEMENT LLC (CIK 2100119) and VANGUARD PORTFOLIO MANAGEMENT LLC (CIK 2100121), each file their own 13Gs: at Macy's (both filed 2026-07-31) VCM reports classPercent 4.96 (13,069,479 sh) and VPM reports 4.94 (13,002,621 sh) — deliberately just under 5% each, ~9.90% combined. (ii) BLACKROCK — the split does NOT keep both under 5%: at NETSTREIT Corp., BlackRock, Inc. (CIK 2012383) reports classPercent 13.9 (13,535,141 sh, filed 2026-07-08) and BlackRock Portfolio Management LLC (CIK 2052113) reports classPercent 5.8 (5,621,525 sh, filed 2026-07-17). (iii) STATE STREET — no disaggregation is visible at all: State Street Corporation still files a single consolidated 13G (e.g. Becton Dickinson, filed 2026-08-07, classPercent 5.4), and EDGAR full-text aggregation for SCHEDULE 13G filings Apr–Aug 2026 shows only one State Street reporting entity. Note also that the underlying splits differ in kind by firm (BlackRock: BIS index vs BAIS active, effective Jan 1 2025 per its own Voting Spotlight footnote; State Street: core Asset Stewardship vs a Sustainability Stewardship Service), so 'each structured to stay under 5%' is not a description that fits all three.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Ownership unchanged; unified-bloc premise now partly obsolete by design
itemVerdicts.note: Ownership unchanged is directly supported: Vanguard's 13G/A comment states the disaggregated subsidiaries 'pursue the same investment strategies as previously pursued by The Vanguard Group, Inc. prior to the realignment,' and VCM 4.96% + VPM 4.94% at Macy's reconstitutes the same ~9.9% stake. 'Partly obsolete by design' is fair as to the reporting/voting structure — but see the next item, because in practice the bloc has not yet fractured.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) No evidence yet on whether split teams vote differently
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 'no evidence yet.' RIGHT: the very source cited reports early evidence, and it points the other way. Innisfree/HLS, verbatim: 'While each stewardship team will engage with issuers separately and have potentially different objectives, Innisfree's experience is that both teams often vote in parallel. However, as the separate stewardship teams develop their own voting policies over time, the historically monolithic, management-friendly passive fund voting bloc may splinter.' So the correct framing is: as of the 2026 season the split is structural, and the two teams have so far tended to vote in parallel; divergence is a forward-looking possibility ('may splinter'), not an observed fact. The same article adds, on the related pass-through channel: 'in Innisfree's experience, pass-through voting has not meaningfully impacted stewardship voting at Vanguard, BlackRock, or State Street.'

itemVerdicts.item: (e) BlackRock pass-through: $784bn enrolled of $3.3T eligible (~24%; ~11% of $6.9T public equity AUM)
itemVerdicts.note: BlackRock 2025 Investment Stewardship Voting Spotlight, verbatim (pp.7 and 29): 'As of June 30, 2025, $3.3 trillion of BlackRock's $6.9 trillion total index equity AUM are eligible to participate in BlackRock Voting Choice, where legally and operationally viable, with clients representing ~$784 billion in index equity AUM exercising this option.' Arithmetic checks: 784/3,300 = 23.8% (~24%); 784/6,900 = 11.4% (~11%). DOCUMENT-INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY worth a footnote: p.3 of the same report calls the $6.9T 'public equity assets under management (AUM), with approximately 90% invested in index equity strategies,' while pp.7/29 call the identical $6.9T 'total index equity AUM.' Both cannot be right; the ~11% is unaffected either way, but do not present '$3.3T of $6.9T public equity AUM' as the report's own wording.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Vanguard ~82,000 of ~10 million eligible investors participated in 2025 (~0.8%)
itemVerdicts.note: Vanguard 'INVESTOR CHOICE 2025 Investor participation and preferences' PDF, verbatim: 'Through July 2025, more than 82,000 fund shareholders had selected a voting policy'; and, on the four funds added in May 2025, 'Reach nearly 10 million eligible investors who hold these funds.' Vanguard's Sept 10, 2025 press release: 'Over 82,000 Vanguard investors participated in Investor Choice during the 2025 proxy season – more than double the 2024 total.' 82,000/10,000,000 = 0.82%. DENOMINATOR CAVEAT (not an error, but the article should disclose it): Vanguard's own preferred metrics are far higher — 'we are set to eclipse a 10% participation rate among clients in the participating funds with assets held directly through Vanguard,' and by assets 'nearly $9 billion of eligible fund AUM ($264 billion) participated,' i.e. ~3.4%. The ~0.8% is the article's own head-count construction against the broadest eligibility base.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Feb 2026 expansion to '$3.6T eligible / 22 million investors' is an ELIGIBILITY number
itemVerdicts.note: Vanguard press release, Feb. 25, 2026, verbatim: 'Vanguard today announced the addition of 17 new investment funds to Vanguard Investor Choice, adding approximately 2 million new eligible investors across more than $200 billion in assets. The expansion increases the number of eligible investors in the program to 22 million and expands eligible assets to more than $3.6 trillion.' Both figures are explicitly eligibility, not participation — the article's characterization is exactly right, and this is the correct guard against the common misreading.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) BlackRock 2025 Voting Spotlight: $6.9T public equity AUM (~90% index); 152,000+ proposals at 12,700+ companies; supported management ~89%
itemVerdicts.note: All verbatim from the Voting Spotlight PDF. p.3: 'As of June 30, 2025, clients held $6.9 trillion in public equity assets under management (AUM), with approximately 90% invested in index equity strategies.' (Footnote 2: ~50% of total equity AUM in iShares ETFs plus a further 39% in institutional index strategies.) p.9-ish: 'In the 2024-25 proxy year, BIS voted on more than 152,000 management and shareholder proposals globally at more than 12,700 companies in 58 voting markets.' Figure 5: '~89% of proposals voted consistent with management's vote recommendations' and '~90% of proposals categorized as director elections supported.' MISSING QUALIFIER the article must add: these are BIS-only, Benchmark-Policies-only figures. The report states 'Clients representing approximately three quarters of public equity AUM entrust BIS to apply the Benchmark Policies' and expressly excludes clients voting via BlackRock Voting Choice (~$784bn), the Climate and Decarbonization Stewardship program (~$158bn), and all BAIS (active) activity. Pairing '$6.9T' directly with '152,000+ proposals voted' implies BIS votes the whole book; it votes roughly three quarters of it.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) 2,584 engagements vs 16,800+ meetings voted ≈ 15%
itemVerdicts.note: The number survives but the construction mixes units. Verbatim sources: Figure 1 'Total | Engagements 2,584 | Companies engaged 1,950 | Companies engaged multiple times 446 | Markets engaged 44'; and p.14 'During the 2024-25 proxy year, BIS voted at 16,800+ shareholder meetings on more than 152,000 management and shareholder proposals in 58 voting markets.' WRONG construction: 2,584 engagement conversations ÷ 16,800 shareholder meetings — a conversation count over a meeting count, and 446 companies were engaged more than once, so 2,584 overstates reach. RIGHT construction, like for like, from the same report: 1,950 companies engaged ÷ 12,700+ companies at which BIS voted ≈ 15%. (It happens to land on the same ~15%: 2,584/16,800 = 15.4%, 1,950/12,700 = 15.4%.) Use the companies-to-companies version.

corrections: Do not write that the motion to dismiss was 'denied.' ECF 113 (Aug 1, 2025) states verbatim: 'Defendants' joint motion to dismiss (Docket No. 64) and BlackRock's motion to dismiss (Docket No. 65) are both GRANTED IN PART and DENIED IN PART. The motions to dismiss Counts I–XVII and XXI are DENIED. The motions are GRANTED as to Counts XVIII, XIX, and XX, which are DISMISSED.' Write: the core Clayton Act §7 and Sherman Act §1 counts survived; three of twenty-one counts were dismissed.

Scope the 'close call' quote correctly. Judge Kernodle's 'This is a close call.' (ECF 113 at 32–33) attaches specifically to whether plaintiffs plausibly pleaded a conspiracy on purely circumstantial evidence — not to the ruling as a whole. Quote it in that sentence's context: 'Plaintiffs do, however, plausibly allege the existence of a conspiracy among Defendants based on circumstantial evidence. This is a close call.'

Delete 'listen-only mode.' That phrase could not be located in any primary or reachable secondary source (Semafor Feb 18 2025, ESG Dive, RTTNews/Nasdaq Feb 21 2025, TheCorporateCounsel March 2025, BlackRock's own 2025 Voting Spotlight); it surfaces only in web-search summarizer output. Replace with BlackRock's attested statement: 'complying with the new requirements including by highlighting our role as a "passive" investor at the start of each engagement.'

Soften the BlackRock resumption date. '~Feb 24' rests on a single secondary blog; Bloomberg/RTTNews reported resumption on February 21, 2025. Write 'resumed within about a week, by late February 2025' rather than asserting Feb 24.

Do not state that all three managers structured the split so each team stays under 5%. Primary EDGAR filings: Vanguard yes (Vanguard Capital Management LLC 4.96% and Vanguard Portfolio Management LLC 4.94% of Macy's, both filed 2026-07-31, after The Vanguard Group Inc. zeroed out its own 13Gs citing a January 12, 2026 'internal realignment' under SEC Release No. 34-39538); BlackRock no (BlackRock, Inc. 13.9% and BlackRock Portfolio Management LLC 5.8% of NETSTREIT Corp., July 2026 — both above 5%); State Street no evidence (State Street Corporation still files a single consolidated 13G, e.g. 5.4% of Becton Dickinson on 2026-08-07). Attribute the 5% framing to Innisfree's hedged parenthetical — '(where each team is less likely to control more than 5% of an issuer's outstanding shares)' — and note it is verified only for Vanguard.

Reverse the 'no evidence yet on whether split teams vote differently' claim. The cited Innisfree/HLS piece says the opposite: 'Innisfree's experience is that both teams often vote in parallel.' Divergence is framed as prospective — 'as the separate stewardship teams develop their own voting policies over time, the historically monolithic, management-friendly passive fund voting bloc may splinter.' Write: the split is structural, but through the 2026 season the two teams have generally voted in parallel; fragmentation is a forecast, not an observation.

Say 'two' stewardship teams per firm, not 'multiple.' The source is explicit: 'Each index fund has separated its stewardship team into two stewardship teams operating independently on policy, voting, and engagement.'

Fix the engagement-reach ratio's units. Use 1,950 companies engaged ÷ 12,700+ companies voted ≈ 15% (both figures from the Voting Spotlight), not 2,584 engagements ÷ 16,800 meetings. 2,584 counts conversations, and 446 companies were engaged more than once, so it overstates reach even though both quotients round to ~15%.

Add the BIS-only qualifier to the BlackRock voting figures. The 152,000+ proposals / 12,700+ companies / ~89% management support cover only BIS under its Benchmark Policies. The report states 'Clients representing approximately three quarters of public equity AUM entrust BIS to apply the Benchmark Policies,' and expressly excludes BlackRock Voting Choice clients (~$784bn), the Climate and Decarbonization Stewardship program (~$158bn) and all BAIS (active) activity. Do not present these counts as covering the full $6.9T.

Footnote the $6.9T labelling inconsistency inside BlackRock's own report: p.3 calls it 'public equity assets under management (AUM), with approximately 90% invested in index equity strategies,' while pp.7 and 29 call the same $6.9T 'total index equity AUM.' The ~11% pass-through figure is unaffected, but do not attribute '$3.3T of $6.9T public equity AUM' to the document as its own phrasing.

Disclose the Vanguard 0.8% denominator choice. 82,000 of ~10 million eligible investors is arithmetically right, but Vanguard's own published metrics are ~10% participation among direct-brokerage clients in participating funds and ~$9bn of $264bn (3.4%) of eligible fund AUM across the eight originally participating funds. State which denominator is being used.

Correct the scope of Vanguard's settlement voting commitment if it is described. Settlement §4.1 is an aggregate threshold — 'commercially reasonable efforts to make proxy voting choice available to investors in funds accounting for at least 50% percent of assets invested in U.S. Equity Investments' — not 'any fund with over half its assets in U.S. equities' (a paraphrase circulating in law-firm coverage). §4.3 fixes the commitment 'at least through the end of June 2032.' The alliance commitment is §5.6: withdraw from PRI and not participate in organizations such as NZAM, Ceres, or Climate Action 100+.

Use precise Vanguard settlement dates: announcement and press coverage Feb 25, 2026; joint stipulation (ECF 147) and the court's order of dismissal with prejudice (ECF 148) both Feb 26, 2026; Paxton press release Feb 26, 2026.
newContradictions: The cited Innisfree/HLS article directly contradicts the article's own 'no evidence yet on divergent voting' framing: 'Innisfree's experience is that both teams often vote in parallel.' The same article also undercuts any story that pass-through voting is eroding the bloc: 'in Innisfree's experience, pass-through voting has not meaningfully impacted stewardship voting at Vanguard, BlackRock, or State Street. While the funds offer pass-through voting to an increasing number of their investors, most investors either do not opt-in or opt-in to the stewardship team's vote.'

Primary EDGAR filings contradict the uniform 'sub-5% by design' story: BlackRock, Inc. reported 13.9% of NETSTREIT Corp. on a Schedule 13G filed 2026-07-08 with BlackRock Portfolio Management LLC separately at 5.8% (filed 2026-07-17). BlackRock's disaggregation therefore did not produce sub-5% buckets, and State Street Corporation has not disaggregated at all (single 13G, 5.4% of Becton Dickinson, filed 2026-08-07).

BlackRock's own 2025 Voting Spotlight is internally inconsistent about $6.9T, calling it 'public equity assets under management (AUM), with approximately 90% invested in index equity strategies' on p.3 and 'total index equity AUM' on pp.7 and 29. Any article quoting that figure inherits the ambiguity.

The engagement figures cut against a 'monolithic engaged owner' picture more sharply than the article's 15% suggests, and in a way the article should not overstate either: BIS held 2,584 engagements but reached only 1,950 distinct companies (446 engaged more than once) while voting at 12,700+ companies and 16,800+ meetings — and those vote counts exclude Voting Choice, Climate and Decarbonization, and all BAIS-voted active holdings.

The BlackRock/BAIS split predates the 2026 'fracturing' narrative: BlackRock's own Voting Spotlight footnote says 'As of January 1, 2025, BlackRock's stewardship policies are developed and implemented separately by BIS and BlackRock Active Investment Stewardship (BAIS),' i.e. a year before the 2026 proxy season the Innisfree piece frames as the first with multiple teams. The three firms' splits also differ in kind (BlackRock index/active; State Street core/sustainability; Vanguard adviser-entity disaggregation), so 'each split its stewardship team' flattens three different reorganizations.
reasoning:
I verified this group almost entirely from primary documents rather than secondary reporting, and I re-fetched raw HTML/PDF wherever a summarizing fetch was involved, because two fabricated-quote incidents were flagged for this run.

Primary documents reached verbatim: (1) FTC/DOJ Statement of Interest, ECF 99, filed 05/22/25 — local extraction in the scratchpad v30 directory, all four quoted passages located exactly, including the OECD-submission reaffirmation on pp.17–18 and 24. (2) ECF 113, the Aug 1 2025 Memorandum Opinion and Order — pulled the actual PDF from CourtListener RECAP (gov.uscourts.txed.234523.113.0.pdf) and read the conclusion and the 'close call' page directly. (3) The full CourtListener docket for 6:24-cv-00437 (docket_id 69419420), which gave me the Nov 27 2024 filing date, the June 9 2025 MTD hearing with DOJ/FTC counsel present, ECF 147/148 (Vanguard dismissal, Feb 26 2026), and the March 6 2026 answers by BlackRock and State Street. (4) The Vanguard settlement agreement PDF hosted by the Texas AG, with §§1.12, 4.1, 4.3, 5.6 read verbatim. (5) SEC C&DI 103.11 and 103.12 in full, plus the dated update-notice page — retrieved by using an SEC-compliant declared User-Agent after generic fetches returned 403. (6) BlackRock's 2025 Investment Stewardship Voting Spotlight, local extraction, every figure located. (7) Vanguard's 2025 Investor Choice participation report and both the Sept 2025 and Feb 2026 press releases. (8) The Innisfree/HLS forum article, re-fetched as raw HTML and grepped, because my first read of it came through a summarizing fetch.

The most productive adversarial step was not accepting the Innisfree 5% parenthetical on its face. I went to EDGAR and pulled actual 2026 Schedule 13G XML: Vanguard Group Inc. has zeroed its own 13G positions citing a January 12, 2026 internal realignment under SEC Release No. 34-39538, and its two successors report 4.96% and 4.94% of Macy's — a textbook sub-5% pair. But BlackRock's two reporting entities report 13.9% and 5.8% of NETSTREIT, and State Street still files one consolidated 13G at 5.4% of Becton Dickinson. So the 'each team under 5%' design is real at Vanguard, false at BlackRock, and unevidenced at State Street. That is the single largest caliber problem in the group after the motion-to-dismiss mischaracterization.

Four things are genuinely wrong rather than merely imprecise: the MTD was granted in part, not denied; 'no evidence yet on divergent voting' is contradicted by the article's own cited source; 'listen-only mode' is unattested anywhere I could reach and looks like summarizer confabulation; and the sub-5% structure does not generalize across the three firms. Everything in (b) and (e), and the numeric core of (f), checks out verbatim.

Residual uncertainty: I could not open the Bloomberg piece behind its paywall, so the Feb 21 vs Feb 24 BlackRock resumption date rests on the RTTNews syndication timestamp versus TheCorporateCounsel's account — hence my recommendation to hedge rather than pick. I also did not obtain a primary State Street stewardship-structure disclosure; my conclusion there is that no 13G disaggregation exists, which is evidence of absence in the beneficial-ownership channel only, not proof that State Street did not reorganize its stewardship teams internally as Innisfree describes.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) SEC IA-6050 quote: 'three index providers account for over two-thirds of the market for indexes, totaling approximately $5.0 billion in revenue in 2021'
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim exact at p.5 of the Federal-Register-conformed release (sec.gov/files/rules/other/2022/ia-6050.pdf), sourced to fn.10 (Sonya Swink, FT, May 24, 2022). GLOSS REQUIRED, not a correction: the underlying Burton-Taylor study (press release May 12, 2022) states 'Global index revenues increased 23.1% in 2021, totaling a record $5 billion' and separately 'FTSE Russell, S&P Dow Jones Indices and MSCI account for more than 2/3rds of total index revenue.' So $5.0bn is the WHOLE industry's 2021 revenue; the three providers took roughly two-thirds of it (~$3.4bn). The SEC sentence is grammatically ambiguous — do not render it as 'the three providers earned $5.0 billion.'

itemVerdicts.item: (a) IA-6050 index count ~3.05 million
itemVerdicts.note: Footnote 5: '(noting that in 2020, the overall number of indexes climbed by approximately three percent to 3.05 million)', citing Index Industry Association, Fourth Annual IIA Benchmark Survey (Oct. 28, 2020). Caliber note: it is a 2020 IIA-survey figure carried in a footnote, not a 2022 SEC count.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) IA-6050 China A-shares 4-5.5% weights post-inclusion
itemVerdicts.note: Footnote 45, verbatim: '(noting that the weight of Chinese A shares in the three emerging market indexes ranged between 4% and 5.5% after completion of each index's inclusion process)', citing SEC DERA, Risk Spotlight: U.S. Investors' Exposure to Domestic Chinese Issuers (July 6, 2020). Release date confirmed: 'Dated: June 15, 2022.' (published 87 FR 37254, June 22, 2022).

itemVerdicts.item: (a) The request NEVER became a proposed rule; absent from Spring 2026 SEC agenda; not among the June 2025 withdrawals
itemVerdicts.note: Three sub-parts confirmed, one framing WRONG. CONFIRMED: no NPRM ever issued — reginfo.gov RIN 3235-AM95 timetable shows only ANPRM 06/22/2022 (87 FR 37254), comment end 08/16/2022, comment period reopened 10/18/2022 (87 FR 63016), end 11/01/2022. CONFIRMED absent from the current 2026 SEC Agency Rule List on reginfo.gov (~40 items, none is 3235-AM95); the RIN's 'published in the following Unified Agenda(s)' list terminates at Spring 2025. CONFIRMED not among the June 2025 withdrawals: FR doc 2025-11110, 'Withdrawal of Proposed Regulatory Actions' (Release Nos. 33-11377; 34-103247; IA-6885; IC-35635; pub. June 17, 2025) lists File Nos. S7-20-22, S7-12-23, S7-04-23, S7-04-22, S7-17-22, S7-25-22, S7-32-10, S7-18-23, S7-32-22, S7-31-22, S7-07-23, S7-06-23, S7-02-22, S7-10-20 and RINs 3235-AM32/AM45/AM57/AM62/AM91/AM96/AN08/AN14/AN15/AN18/AN24/AN25/AN27/AN29 — S7-18-22 and 3235-AM95 appear in neither list. WRONG framing: 'it simply never reached proposal stage / is absent from the agenda' understates the record. It was AFFIRMATIVELY WITHDRAWN. The Spring 2025 Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AM95 ('Certain Information Providers Acting as Investment Advisers') reads: 'The Division was considering recommending that the Commission propose rules related to the role of certain third-party service providers and the implications for the asset management industry. This item is being withdrawn from the Agenda.' Agenda Stage of Rulemaking: 'Completed Actions'; Timetable: 'Withdrawn 04/21/2025'. RIGHT version: withdrawn from the regulatory agenda on April 21, 2025, separately from and two months before the June 2025 formal withdrawal of 14 NPRMs (which it was not part of, because it never was an NPRM).

itemVerdicts.item: (b) An, Benetton & Song: over one-third of ETF management fees paid as index licensing fees
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as attributed to 'JFE 2023': the published JFE abstract (vol. 149, iss. 3, pp. 407-433, doi 10.1016/j.jfineco.2023.06.003) says 'over one-third of ETF EXPENSE RATIOS are paid as licensing fees to index providers.' RIGHT for the January 12, 2022 working paper at the law.nyu.edu URL, whose abstract says 'over one-third of ETF management fees.' Underlying estimate confirmed verbatim in the WP: 'We estimate that the index licensing fees comprise about one-third of all ETF management fees that ETF sponsors collect from ETF investors. This fraction has also increased steadily, from 31.4% in 2010 to 35.7% in 2019.' MATERIAL CAVEAT the claim omits: licensing fees are disclosed voluntarily and 'only about 10% of ETFs in our sample disclose their licensing fees'; the authors themselves flag 'this limitation and possible selection bias.'

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Structural model attributes ~60% of licensing fees to markup; eliminating provider market power would cut ETF fees ~30% (model counterfactuals, not observations)
itemVerdicts.note: 'MODEL counterfactuals, not observations' is CORRECT and the right caliber. But the wording is the working paper's, not the JFE's. WRONG (as 'JFE 2023'): 'A structural model ... suggests that 60% of licensing fees are index providers' markups. Eliminating index providers' market power can reduce ETF fees by 30%' — that is the Jan 2022 WP abstract. RIGHT (JFE 2023 published abstract): 'A structural decomposition attributes 60% of licensing fees to index providers' markups. Counterfactual analyses show that improving competition among index providers reduces ETF expense ratios by up to 30%.' The published version adds 'up to' and swaps 'eliminating market power' for 'improving competition' and 'fees' for 'expense ratios.'

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Top five providers ~95% of US equity ETF market; HHI ~3,294
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the WP and reproduced in the authors' HLS Forum adaptation of the accepted version (Aug 8, 2023). Table 2 (Dec 2019, U.S. equity ETF market): S&P Dow Jones 53.24%, CRSP 14.51%, FTSE Russell 12.37%, MSCI 7.86%, NASDAQ 6.97% — cumulative 94.95%. HHI: 'Over our sample period, the monthly average of the HHI of ETF sponsors is 2,527.31, and the HHI of index providers is even higher, averaging 3,293.59.' Sample Jan 2010-Dec 2019, so 3,294 is a TIME-SERIES AVERAGE, not a point-in-time figure. The claim's 'US equity ETF market' framing is actually more precise than the paper's own loose sentence ('about 95% of the entire ETF market').

itemVerdicts.item: (b) SPY example: 9bp fee, 3bp + $600k/yr to S&P DJI
itemVerdicts.note: WP p.2 verbatim: 'State Street charges SPY investors 9 basis points (bps) per year, and in turn, pays 3 bps of the ETF assets plus a flat fee of $600,000 per year to S&P Dow Jones.' Figure 1 caption: 'The licensing fees is 3 bps of AUM + $600,000 per year' as of December 2019. Same figures reproduced in the authors' Aug 2023 HLS Forum piece, so they survived into the published version. Minor: SPY's actual gross expense ratio is 9.45bp; the paper rounds to 9.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Molk & Robertson: largest S&P 500 funds deviated from the index by 1.7-7.5% of holdings in 2022Q4
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers right, qualifiers dropped. RIGHT (p.253): 'they represent between 1.7% and 7.5% of assets under management on a ROUND-TRIP BASIS in those funds that quarter, with a MEAN AND MEDIAN of 2.9% and 1.8%, respectively.' Three omissions matter: (i) round-trip = twice the computed active share (the paper defines active share as half the cumulative deviation); (ii) 'largest funds' = the five funds with at least $100 billion in total NAV (iShares Core S&P 500, SPDR S&P 500, Vanguard 500 Index, Fidelity 500 Index, Vanguard Institutional Index); (iii) it is a percentage of ASSETS UNDER MANAGEMENT, not 'of holdings.' Sample: 78 'pure' S&P 500 funds / 223 classes, 2015Q1-2022Q4.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) ~$61.5bn aggregate discretionary deviations ~= 0.5% of index assets
itemVerdicts.note: $61.5bn CONFIRMED verbatim (p.275): 'the active share by large funds ... represented almost $25.8 billion ... the total deviation from the index by these funds represented nearly $52 billion. If we include the smaller funds as well, the active-share number rises to $30.7 billion (which doubles to nearly $61.5 billion).' '0.5% of index assets' is WRONG and is NOT in the paper — Molk & Robertson compute no percentage-of-assets figure at all, saying only 'While this number is small relative to the total size of these funds, it nevertheless represents a substantial amount of discretionary management.' RIGHT: against the correct denominator (S&P 500 index-fund assets — the five >=$100bn funds alone held roughly $2 trillion in 2022Q4, and $52bn/$2T is consistent with the paper's reported 2.9% mean / 1.8% median round-trip), $61.5bn is roughly 2-3% of those funds' assets, not 0.5%. 0.5% is obtained only by dividing by the $12.5 trillion ALL-index-fund figure the paper cites elsewhere ('Index funds ... constituting $12.5 trillion in assets, or 43% of total mutual fund market, at the beginning of 2022') — a population mismatch (all index funds vs. S&P 500 funds). Either drop the percentage, state it as ~2-3% of the sample funds' assets, or make the all-index-fund denominator explicit.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Cuts BOTH ways (not mindless, not fully passive)
itemVerdicts.note: Supported by the abstract verbatim: 'Our findings complicate the narrative around index funds and weaken many of the criticisms levied against them. At the same time, to the extent that investors—and particularly retail investors—fail to recognize this discretion, our findings suggest they may not be getting what they expect.' Plus the body's 'small relative to the total size of these funds ... nevertheless ... a substantial amount of discretionary management.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d) RA Tesla note: $78bn forced-buy rests on $4.6T x 1.69%, but the same endnote says both '$78 billion' and '$94 billion'
itemVerdicts.note: Endnote 8 verbatim: 'Tesla enters the S&P 500 with a weight of 1.69%. Passive funds—mutual funds and ETFs—held about $4.6 trillion in AUM that directly tracked the S&P 500. These funds needed to buy about $94 billion TSLA ($4.6 trillion x 1.69% = $78 billion).' Body p.4: 'Index funds, ETFs, and other index strategies that track the S&P 500 needed to buy at least $78 billion of Tesla shares at the rebalance-date valuation.' The arithmetic checks ($4.6T x 1.69% = $77.7bn); the $94bn is unexplained. NEW PROBLEM the claim misses: the $4.6T is explicitly a year-end-2019 figure ('As of year-end 2019, approximately $4.6 trillion of investment capital was directly tracking the S&P 500 and another $6.6 trillion was benchmarked to the index'), applied to a December 2020 event — a stale denominator, understating the forced buy on its own terms.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Dec-18 dollar volume appears as both $147bn and $154bn
itemVerdicts.note: Both refer to December 18, 2020. Endnote 8: 'Tesla's trading volume spiked on December 18, 2020, at about 222 million shares. That day's closing price of $662 a share implies the actual trading by market participants was equal to about $147 billion.' Body p.4: 'On December 18, the dollar-volume traded spiked to $154 billion, the equivalent of 23% of total Tesla shares outstanding.' 222M x $662 = $147.0bn; $154bn implies ~232.6M shares. Uncorrected across two RA renderings of the same PDF (one generated 09/23/2022, one generated 07/03/2024).

itemVerdicts.item: (d) The '41bp' is a 6-month counterfactual performance difference on one event pair, not a transaction cost
itemVerdicts.note: Endnote 3 verbatim: 'TSLA entered the S&P 500 Index with a weight of 1.69% and AIV exited the index with an estimated weight of 0.012%. Over the period December 18, 2020, to June 18, 2021, the S&P 500 returned 13.16%. In contrast, a hypothetical portfolio that did not rebalance out of AIV and into TSLA would have earned 13.57% over the same period, outperforming the actual index by 41 bps.' So it is a six-month return differential on the single TSLA/AIV addition-deletion pair. IMPORTANT: RA itself labels it a cost — pull-quote: 'The December 2020 S&P 500 rebalance out of AIV and into TSLA cost investors 41 bps in the first six months, and the cost may go higher'; body: 'A pensioner with a $100,000 allocation to the S&P 500 is about $410 poorer as the result of the December 21 index rebalance.' The article's caveat is therefore correct and necessary, but should be phrased as correcting RA's own framing, not as describing it.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) RA sells non-cap-weighted indices (conflict of interest); note dated June 2021
itemVerdicts.note: Date confirmed on the PDF masthead: 'June 2021', authors Rob Arnott, Vitali Kalesnik, Lillian Wu. COI confirmed structurally from the note's own disclosure block: 'The trademarks Fundamental Index(TM), RAFI(TM), Research Affiliates Equity(TM), RAE(TM) ... are the exclusive intellectual property of RA ... Various features of the Fundamental Index methodology, including an accounting data-based non-capitalization data processing system and method for creating and weighting an index of securities, are protected by various patents of RA.' The note's own pull-quote pitches the remedy it sells: 'Smarter index design and more-efficient implementation could help investors' tracking traditional indices avoid these hidden costs.' The note carries NO explicit conflict-of-interest statement linking the argument to RA's commercial index products — the COI is inferable only from the trademark/patent boilerplate.

corrections: SEC IA-6050 did not merely fail to advance — it was affirmatively withdrawn. Replace 'the request never became a proposed rule and quietly dropped off the agenda' with: 'No proposed rule ever followed. The SEC withdrew the item (RIN 3235-AM95, Certain Information Providers Acting as Investment Advisers) from its regulatory agenda on April 21, 2025; the Spring 2025 Unified Agenda entry states "This item is being withdrawn from the Agenda" and lists it under Completed Actions. It was separate from the June 17, 2025 formal withdrawal of fourteen pending rule proposals (Release Nos. 33-11377; 34-103247; IA-6885; IC-35635), which covered only items that had reached proposal stage; File No. S7-18-22 is not on that list. It is absent from the SEC's Spring 2026 (Atkins) agenda.'

Do not present the SEC's '$5.0 billion in revenue in 2021' as the three providers' revenue. The Burton-Taylor study the SEC's FT source reports on states that GLOBAL index revenues totaled a record $5 billion in 2021, and that 'FTSE Russell, S&P Dow Jones Indices and MSCI account for more than 2/3rds of total index revenue' — i.e. roughly $3.4bn of the $5.0bn. Quote the SEC sentence, then gloss it: '$5.0bn is the whole industry's 2021 revenue; the three take more than two-thirds of it.'

The IA-6050 '3.05 million indexes' figure is a 2020 Index Industry Association survey number carried in footnote 5 ('in 2020, the overall number of indexes climbed by approximately three percent to 3.05 million'), not a 2022 SEC count. Attribute it as such.

If citing An, Benetton & Song as 'JFE 2023,' use the published wording, not the January 2022 working paper's. WRONG: 'over one-third of ETF management fees are paid as licensing fees'; 'eliminating provider market power would cut ETF fees ~30%.' RIGHT (JFE 149(3):407-433): 'over one-third of ETF expense ratios are paid as licensing fees to index providers'; 'A structural decomposition attributes 60% of licensing fees to index providers' markups'; 'Counterfactual analyses show that improving competition among index providers reduces ETF expense ratios by up to 30%.' Note the 'up to.' The law.nyu.edu URL currently cited IS the working paper (dated January 12, 2022), so either cite it as the working paper or cite the JFE version and use its numbers.

Add the disclosure caveat An/Benetton/Song themselves make: licensing fees are disclosed voluntarily and 'only about 10% of ETFs in our sample disclose their licensing fees,' with the authors acknowledging 'this limitation and possible selection bias.' The one-third figure rests on that 10% subsample.

State that An/Benetton/Song's HHI of 3,294 is the monthly (time-series) AVERAGE over January 2010-December 2019 for index providers in the U.S. equity ETF market (precisely 3,293.59), not a point-in-time number; and that the top-five 95% figure is cumulative AUM share as of December 2019 (94.95%).

Molk & Robertson's 1.7-7.5% must carry its qualifiers: it is round-trip active share (twice the computed active share), for the five funds in fund families holding over $100 billion, measured as a percentage of assets under management (not 'of holdings'), in 2022Q4, with mean 2.9% and median 1.8%.

Delete or fix '≈0.5% of index assets.' Molk & Robertson state no such percentage; the paper's only framing is 'this number is small relative to the total size of these funds.' Against S&P 500 index-fund assets the $61.5bn is roughly 2-3%, not 0.5%. The 0.5% figure only results from dividing by the $12.5 trillion ALL-index-fund total quoted elsewhere in the paper — the wrong population. Either write '~2-3% of these funds' assets' or make the all-index-fund denominator explicit.

Explain how Molk & Robertson's $61.5bn is built: aggregate active share across all 78 funds was $30.7bn, which 'doubles to nearly $61.5 billion' on a round-trip basis; the five largest funds alone accounted for $25.8bn one-way / ~$52bn round-trip.

Add to the Research Affiliates critique that the $4.6 trillion denominator is explicitly a YEAR-END 2019 figure ('As of year-end 2019, approximately $4.6 trillion of investment capital was directly tracking the S&P 500') applied to a December 2020 event — a stale base that understates the forced buy on the note's own logic, compounding rather than explaining the unexplained $94bn.

When calling the 41bp 'not a transaction cost,' note that Research Affiliates itself calls it one ('the December 2020 S&P 500 rebalance out of AIV and into TSLA cost investors 41 bps in the first six months'; 'A pensioner with a $100,000 allocation to the S&P 500 is about $410 poorer'). Frame the point as correcting RA's label, not describing it: endnote 3 defines the 41bp as the gap between the S&P 500's actual 13.16% return and a hypothetical un-rebalanced portfolio's 13.57% over Dec 18, 2020-Jun 18, 2021 — a six-month return differential on one addition/deletion pair.

If describing the RA conflict of interest, be precise: the note contains no conflict-of-interest disclosure. The commercial interest is visible only in the trademark/patent boilerplate (Fundamental Index(TM), RAFI(TM), and patents on 'an accounting data-based non-capitalization data processing system and method for creating and weighting an index of securities') and in the note's own remedy pitch, 'Smarter index design and more-efficient implementation could help investors' tracking traditional indices avoid these hidden costs.'
newContradictions: Research Affiliates' $4.6 trillion is a year-end-2019 figure ('As of year-end 2019, approximately $4.6 trillion of investment capital was directly tracking the S&P 500 and another $6.6 trillion was benchmarked to the index'), yet it is used to size a December 2020 forced buy — a full year after, during which the S&P 500 rose materially. This stale-denominator problem is separate from, and additional to, the $78bn/$94bn discrepancy, and neither the note nor the claim group flags it.

The RA note's numerical inconsistencies were never corrected: both the September 2022 and July 2024 regenerations of the same PDF (retrieved via the Internet Archive) carry the identical '$94 billion TSLA ($4.6 trillion x 1.69% = $78 billion)' sentence and the identical $147bn/$154bn split.

SEC IA-6050's headline '$5.0 billion in revenue in 2021' is ambiguous and, read naturally, misattributes the whole index industry's revenue to the three named providers. Burton-Taylor's own release (May 12, 2022) shows $5bn is total global index revenue and the top three take 'more than 2/3rds' of it. Any article quoting the SEC sentence without a gloss inherits the ambiguity.

The reginfo.gov timetable for RIN 3235-AM95 labels the 06/22/2022 publication an 'ANPRM' and the 10/18/2022 reopening an 'NPRM Comment Period Reopened,' but the SEC release itself is styled ACTION: 'Request for comment' and no NPRM was ever issued. The agenda's own labeling is loose; rely on the release text, not the reginfo action names.

Molk & Robertson's aggregate $61.5bn is dominated by the five largest funds ($52bn of it, i.e. ~85%), so the headline figure is not evidence of widespread discretion across the 78-fund sample — the sample's largest active shares belong to tiny funds ('91% represent less than $5 billion'; max active share 92.24%), whose dollar impact is trivial. The dollar figure and the percentage figure describe two disjoint groups and should not be blended.

An/Benetton/Song's HHI of 3,294 and 95% concentration are computed within the U.S. equity ETF market only — a subset of the index-licensing market the SEC's two-thirds/$5bn revenue figures describe. The two concentration statistics measure different populations (ETF tracking-assets share vs. global index revenue share) and should not be presented as corroborating each other.
reasoning:
Reached and read all four primary documents in full text, not summaries. The scratchpad files named in my brief (an.txt etc.) did not exist in this session's directory, so I downloaded everything fresh.

(1) SEC IA-6050: retrieved sec.gov/files/rules/other/2022/ia-6050.pdf (SEC blocks generic UAs; succeeded with an identifying UA), pdftotext -layout, 1,623 lines. Located the two-thirds/$5.0bn sentence at p.5, the 3.05 million index count at footnote 5, the China A-shares 4-5.5% at footnote 45, and 'Dated: June 15, 2022.' Cross-checked the $5.0bn against the Burton-Taylor press release (prnewswire, May 12, 2022), which shows the $5bn is total global index revenue with the top three taking more than two-thirds. For rulemaking status I pulled reginfo.gov's RIN 3235-AM95 pages for pubIds 202504 (Spring 2025), 202510, and 202604 — the Spring 2025 entry states the item 'is being withdrawn from the Agenda,' Agenda Stage 'Completed Actions,' Timetable 'Withdrawn 04/21/2025,' with no NPRM in the timetable; the 2026 pages return no entry, and the current 2026 SEC Agency Rule List (~40 items) does not contain the RIN. For the June 2025 withdrawals I pulled the Federal Register API and then the raw text of FR doc 2025-11110 and read the full File No. and RIN header lists — S7-18-22 / 3235-AM95 are absent.

(2) An, Benetton & Song: downloaded the law.nyu.edu PDF and confirmed it is the January 12, 2022 WORKING PAPER, not the JFE article. Verified verbatim: Table 2 (Dec 2019, U.S. equity ETF market) cumulative 94.95%; HHI monthly average 3,293.59 over Jan 2010-Dec 2019; SPY 9bps with 3bps + $600,000/yr to S&P DJI; one-third of management fees with the 31.4%->35.7% trend and the 10%-disclosure selection-bias caveat. Then compared against the published version: OpenAlex returned the Elsevier abstract for doi 10.1016/j.jfineco.2023.06.003 (JFE 149(3):407-433), which uses 'expense ratios,' 'structural decomposition,' and 'improving competition ... reduces ETF expense ratios by up to 30%' — materially different wording from the working paper the claim quotes. Corroborated independently by the authors' own HLS Forum adaptation (Aug 8, 2023), which likewise says 'about one-third of all ETF expense ratios.' I could not obtain the full JFE PDF (ScienceDirect 403, Semantic Scholar 429/not found, no OA copy), so the published-version check rests on the Elsevier-supplied abstract plus the authors' HLS summary rather than the article body; the HHI/95%/SPY figures appear unchanged in both.

(3) Molk & Robertson: downloaded the Yale J. Reg. PDF (2,946 lines). Verified the abstract and p.253 text for 1.7-7.5% and $61.5bn, and the p.275 construction ($25.8bn -> ~$52bn for large funds; $30.7bn -> ~$61.5bn overall). Searched the full text for '0.5%' and for any percentage-of-assets framing: none exists. The paper's only comparative statement is 'small relative to the total size of these funds.' The nearest denominators in the paper are $12.5T (ALL index funds, beginning of 2022) and $7T (global S&P 500-tracking assets, fn.19); 61.5/12,500 = 0.49%, which is almost certainly where 0.5% came from and is the wrong population. Against the sample's own funds (the five >=$100bn funds alone were roughly $2T in 2022Q4, consistent with the paper's own 2.9% mean round-trip on ~$52bn) the ratio is ~2-3%.

(4) Research Affiliates: researchaffiliates.com serves a destination-gate HTML page instead of the PDF, so I retrieved it through the Internet Archive and extracted twice, obtaining two different RA regenerations (generated 09/23/2022 and 07/03/2024) with identical substantive text. Confirmed endnote 8's self-contradicting sentence, the $147bn vs $154bn split (both for Dec 18, 2020, with 222M x $662 = $147.0bn), endnote 3's definition of the 41bp as a 13.57% vs 13.16% six-month return differential, and the disclosure block's Fundamental Index/RAFI trademarks and non-capitalization-weighting patents. Also found the year-end-2019 vintage of the $4.6T denominator, which the claim group does not mention.

Remaining uncertainty: I did not read the body of the published JFE article, only its abstract (Elsevier via OpenAlex) and the authors' HLS Forum adaptation, so I cannot rule out that some in-text numbers shifted between the working paper and publication beyond the abstract wording I documented. My ~2-3% recomputation of the Molk & Robertson ratio uses fund AUM I estimated from the paper's own internal consistency ($52bn round-trip at a reported 2.9% mean), not a figure the paper prints; the defensible finding is that 0.5% is not in the paper and is inconsistent with the paper's own reported percentages, whatever the exact right number is. My web-search budget was exhausted before I could check for post-publication critiques or replications of Molk & Robertson.

itemVerdicts.item: SEC Request for Comment IA-6050 (June 15, 2022): 'three index providers account for over two-thirds of the market for indexes, totaling approximately $5.0 billion in revenue in 2021'
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the conformed Federal Register version, IA-6050 / IC-34618 / File No. S7-18-22, RIN 3235-AM95, at p.5 (local copy /private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-cissychen-design/0f8bdcde-3464-42f4-af17-1552808c31d6/scratchpad/v31/ia6050.txt lines 259-261): 'Although there are many indexes available and no formal barriers to becoming an index provider, three index providers account for over two-thirds of the market for indexes, totaling approximately $5.0 billion in revenue in 2021.' Date confirmed: 'Dated: June 15, 2022' (line 1611); comments due Aug 16, 2022; published 87 FR 37254 (June 22, 2022). CALIBER FLAG (not an error in the quote, but a trap for the article's gloss): SEC footnote 10 sources the figure to Sonya Swink, 'Index Providers Take Record $5bn in Revenue in 2021,' Financial Times (May 24, 2022). The $5.0bn is the WHOLE index-provider industry's 2021 revenue; the three providers account for over two-thirds OF THAT (~$3.4bn). The article must not say the three providers earned $5.0bn.

itemVerdicts.item: Index count ~3.05 million
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed but with a provenance caveat. It is not an SEC count and not a 2022 count. IA-6050 footnote 5 (ia6050.txt line 228) cites the Index Industry Association's Fourth Annual Benchmark Survey (Oct 28, 2020) '(noting that in 2020, the overall number of indexes climbed by approximately three percent to 3.05 million)'. So: ~3.05 million indexes as of the IIA's 2020 survey, cited by the SEC in 2022.

itemVerdicts.item: China A-shares 4-5.5% weights post-inclusion
itemVerdicts.note: IA-6050 footnote 45 (ia6050.txt lines 1185-1189), citing SEC Division of Economic and Risk Analysis, 'Risk Spotlight: U.S. Investors' Exposure to Domestic Chinese Issuers' (July 6, 2020): '(noting that the weight of Chinese A shares in the three emerging market indexes ranged between 4% and 5.5% after completion of each index's inclusion process)'. Exact wording is 'between 4% and 5.5%' — the range applies to three emerging-market indexes, i.e. the A-share weight WITHIN the EM index, not within any global or US index.

itemVerdicts.item: IA-6050 never became a proposed rule; absent from the current (2026) SEC agenda; not among the June 2025 withdrawals
itemVerdicts.note: Central assertion HOLDS, but two labels are wrong and one material fact is missing. (1) NEVER A PROPOSED RULE — CONFIRMED. reginfo.gov RIN 3235-AM95, Spring 2025 agenda (pubId=202504), timetable lists only: ANPRM 06/22/2022 (87 FR 37254); ANPRM Comment Period End 08/16/2022; NPRM Comment Period Reopened 10/18/2022 (87 FR 63016); NPRM Comment Period End 11/01/2022. No NPRM was ever issued. (2) NOT IN THE JUNE 2025 WITHDRAWALS — CONFIRMED. I read the full text of 'Withdrawal of Proposed Regulatory Actions,' Release Nos. 33-11377; 34-103247; IA-6885; IC-35635, 90 FR (June 17, 2025), FR doc 2025-11110. It covers File Nos. S7-20-22; S7-12-23; S7-04-23; S7-04-22; S7-17-22; S7-25-22; S7-32-10; S7-18-23; S7-32-22; S7-31-22; S7-07-23; S7-06-23; S7-02-22; S7-10-20 and RINs 3235-AM32, AM45, AM57, AM62, AM91, AM96, AN08, AN14, AN15, AN18, AN24, AN25, AN27, AN29. Neither S7-18-22 nor RIN 3235-AM95 appears. (NOTE the near-miss: S7-18-23 IS on the list; S7-18-22 is not. Do not confuse them.) (3) MISSING FACT — the item was NOT merely left dormant. The Spring 2025 Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AM95 places it under 'Completed Actions' with the abstract 'The Division was considering recommending that the Commission propose rules related to the role of certain third-party service providers and the implications for the asset management industry. This item is being withdrawn from the Agenda.' and a timetable row 'Withdrawn 04/21/2025'. (4) WRONG AGENDA LABEL — 'Spring 2026 SEC agenda' is not what it is called. reginfo.gov's current publication is Publication ID '2026' (pubId=202510); OIRA released it July 3, 2026 and Chairman Atkins issued his statement July 7, 2026; the Reg Flex portion printed at 91 FR 53164 (Aug 14, 2026), Release Nos. 33-11416; 34-105483; IA-6963; IC-36153, File No. S7-2026-16, data current as of May 12, 2026. Absence CONFIRMED: I pulled the full SEC rule lists for the current publication in both the active (prerule/proposed/final) and completed stages — RIN 3235-AM95 appears in neither.

itemVerdicts.item: An, Benetton & Song (JFE 2023): over one-third of ETF management fees are paid as index licensing fees
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG (as attributed to JFE 2023): 'over one-third of ETF MANAGEMENT FEES'. RIGHT: the published JFE version says EXPENSE RATIOS. Published abstract verbatim (OpenAlex/Crossref, DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2023.06.003, JFE vol. 149, iss. 3, Sept 2023, pp. 407-433): '(iii) over one-third of ETF expense ratios are paid as licensing fees to index providers.' The 'management fees' wording is from the Jan 12, 2022 working paper (the law.nyu.edu PDF the article cites; local an.txt lines 18, 106-107), which the published version rewrote throughout. Second caliber flag: 'over one-third' is generous. The authors' own account of the published paper (Harvard corpgov post, Aug 8, 2023, raw page text) says 'We estimate that the index licensing fees comprise about one-third of all ETF expense ratios that ETF issuers collect from ETF investors. This fraction has also increased steadily over time, from 31.4% in 2010 to 35.7% in 2019.' It is BELOW one-third at the start of the sample. Third flag: the estimate rests on a voluntary-disclosure subsample — 'only about 10% of ETFs in our sample disclose their licensing fees' — with acknowledged possible selection bias.

itemVerdicts.item: An, Benetton & Song: structural model attributes ~60% of licensing fees to markup; eliminating provider market power would cut ETF fees ~30% (MODEL counterfactuals, not observations)
itemVerdicts.note: 60% CONFIRMED. Published abstract: 'A structural decomposition attributes 60% of licensing fees to index providers' markups.' (WP an.txt line 20: 'A structural model ... suggests that 60% of licensing fees are index providers' markups.') Supporting figures: 2019 implied licensing fees 4.4 bps of AUM, estimated marginal cost ~1.6 bps, markup ~2.8 bps, Lerner index ~63%. The article's framing as a MODEL counterfactual is correct and important. 30% NEEDS A QUALIFIER. WRONG: 'eliminating provider market power would cut ETF fees ~30%' as the paper's headline result. RIGHT (published abstract, verbatim): 'Counterfactual analyses show that improving competition among index providers reduces ETF expense ratios by up to 30%.' 'Up to' is load-bearing because the paper runs TWO counterfactuals with opposite results: entry by a new low-fee index provider leaves fees 'almost unaffected' (they cite Morningstar's 2016 Open Indexes Project as the real-world analogue), and only the PERFECT-COMPETITION counterfactual delivers 30% — 'with perfectly competitive index providers, ETF marginal costs decrease by about 2.8 bps, and the ETF expense ratios decline by a similar amount, which represents a 30% reduction relative to the baseline scenario. In dollar amount, this decrease will generate approximately $700 million in yearly savings for ETF investors.' The WP's blunter 'Eliminating index providers' market power can reduce ETF fees by 30%' was softened for publication.

itemVerdicts.item: An, Benetton & Song: top five providers ~95% of US equity ETF market, HHI ~3,294
itemVerdicts.note: an.txt Table 2 (Dec 2019, U.S. equity ETF market, by AUM): S&P Dow Jones 53.24%, CRSP 14.51% (cum. 67.75%), FTSE Russell 12.37% (cum. 80.12%), MSCI 7.86% (cum. 87.98%), NASDAQ 6.97% (cum. 94.95%). HHI: 'the monthly average of the HHI of ETF sponsors is 2,527.31, and the HHI of index providers is even higher, averaging 3,293.59' — a monthly/time-series average over Jan 2010-Dec 2019, rounded to 3,294 in the intro. Population: U.S. EQUITY ETFs only (not all ETFs, not fund assets generally, not market cap). Retained in the published version per the authors' Harvard corpgov post.

itemVerdicts.item: An, Benetton & Song: SPY example — 9bp fee, 3bp + $600k/yr to S&P DJI
itemVerdicts.note: an.txt Figure 1 and text (as of December 2020): 'State Street charges SPY investors 9 basis points (bps) per year, and in turn, pays 3 bps of the ETF assets plus a flat fee of $600,000 per year to S&P Dow Jones. In other words, more than one-third of SPY's total revenue is paid to the index provider as index licensing fees.' Retained verbatim in the authors' published-version account. Their scaling illustration: SPY AUM ~$400bn in 2021 -> ~$360m in fees to State Street, >$120m to S&P DJI.

itemVerdicts.item: Molk & Robertson (Yale J Reg 2024): largest S&P 500 funds deviated from the index by 1.7-7.5% of holdings in 2022Q4
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers CONFIRMED, denominator/basis wording needs fixing. WRONG: '1.7-7.5% of holdings'. RIGHT (mr.txt p.253, 41 Yale J. on Reg. 248, 253 (2024)): '...they represent between 1.7% and 7.5% of assets under management ON A ROUND-TRIP BASIS in those funds that quarter, with a mean and median of 2.9% and 1.8%, respectively.' Round-trip = twice active share, because (footnote 110) 'mathematically an underweight must be combined with an overweight.' The article should also carry the mean/median (2.9%/1.8%), since 7.5% is the extreme of the range, and should note the paper's own framing that departures are LARGEST among smaller funds, smaller among megafunds. Abstract wording: 'even among the largest S&P 500 funds, holdings differed from the index by a total of between 1.7% and 7.5% in the fourth quarter of 2022.'

itemVerdicts.item: Molk & Robertson: ~$61.5bn aggregate discretionary deviations ~ 0.5% of index assets
itemVerdicts.note: $61.5bn CONFIRMED; the '0.5%' is NOT in the paper and the ratio is a population mismatch. The string '0.5%' does not appear anywhere in the article text (I grepped the full 190KB extraction). Paper, p.275: 'in the fourth quarter of 2022 ... the active share by large funds (those associated with fund families representing over $100 billion in investor capital) represented almost $25.8 billion in investor capital. Moreover, the active share is only half of the total deviation from the index ... Accordingly, the total deviation from the index by these funds represented nearly $52 billion. If we include the smaller funds as well, the active-share number rises to $30.7 billion (which doubles to nearly $61.5 billion).' A 0.5% ratio requires a ~$12.3T denominator, which matches the paper's ALL-INDEX-FUNDS figures ('over $12 trillion in assets' in the abstract; '$12.5 trillion in assets, or 43% of total mutual fund market, at the beginning of 2022' at p.249) — but the $61.5bn numerator comes ONLY from S&P 500 index funds. Like-for-like, using the paper's own footnote 19 ('Globally, over $7 trillion in assets tracks the S&P 500,' citing the S&P 500 Factsheet, S&P DJI, Sept 30, 2022), $61.5bn is ~0.9%. Against the paper's actual sample (78 'pure' S&P 500 funds, 223 classes; fund-level mean NAV $23.63bn, 2,087 fund-quarters over 2015Q1-2022Q4) the ratio is materially higher still — on the order of 2%, consistent with the reported mean round-trip deviation of 2.9%. The paper's own qualitative gloss is 'this number is small relative to the total size of these funds, it nevertheless represents a substantial amount of discretionary management.'

itemVerdicts.item: Molk & Robertson cuts BOTH ways (not mindless, not fully passive)
itemVerdicts.note: Correct characterization and it is the authors' own. Abstract: 'Our findings complicate the narrative around index funds and weaken many of the criticisms levied against them. At the same time, to the extent that investors—and particularly retail investors—fail to recognize this discretion, our findings' [raise concerns]. Also: 'we find no meaningful relationship between these deviations and investment flows' (i.e., investors do not appear to police the discretion), and p.254: 'our evidence suggests that these titans of asset management may have a more important role to play in corporate governance than is currently assumed.' Citation confirmed: 41 Yale J. on Reg. 248 (2024).

itemVerdicts.item: Research Affiliates Tesla note (June 2021): $78bn forced-buy rests on $4.6T x 1.69%, and the same endnote says both '$78 billion' and '$94 billion'
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed verbatim from the actual PDF (retrieved via web.archive.org; researchaffiliates.com serves an interstitial HTML page instead of the PDF to non-browser clients — anyone re-checking must use the Wayback copy). Arnott, Kalesnik & Wu, 'Revisiting Tesla's Addition to the S&P 500: What's the Cost, Before and After?' (June 2021). Endnote 8, verbatim: 'Tesla enters the S&P 500 with a weight of 1.69%. Passive funds—mutual funds and ETFs—held about $4.6 trillion in AUM that directly tracked the S&P 500. These funds needed to buy about $94 billion TSLA ($4.6 trillion x 1.69% = $78 billion).' The self-contradiction is inside ONE sentence: the prose says $94 billion, the parenthetical arithmetic gives $78 billion ($4.6T x 1.69% = $77.7bn). Body text (p.4) uses the other figure: 'Index funds, ETFs, and other index strategies that track the S&P 500 needed to buy at least $78 billion of Tesla shares at the rebalance-date valuation.' ADDITIONAL FLAG the article should carry: the $4.6T is stale — 'As of year-end 2019, approximately $4.6 trillion of investment capital was directly tracking the S&P 500 and another $6.6 trillion was benchmarked to the index' — applied to a December 2020 event.

itemVerdicts.item: RA Tesla note: Dec-18 dollar volume appears as both $147bn and $154bn
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed, and the two figures sit in different places, not in the same endnote. Body (p.5): 'On December 18, the dollar-volume traded spiked to $154 billion, the equivalent of 23% of total Tesla shares outstanding.' Endnote 8: 'Tesla's trading volume spiked on December 18, 2020, at about 222 million shares. That day's closing price of $662 a share implies the actual trading by market participants was equal to about $147 billion.' 222m x $662 = $147.0bn, so the endnote is internally consistent and the body's $154bn is the outlier. RA reconciles the gap to index demand with: 'Many large institutional investors own the S&P 500 in separately managed accounts, which accounts for the difference.'

itemVerdicts.item: RA sells non-cap-weighted indices (conflict of interest)
itemVerdicts.note: True, and evidenced inside the note itself — but note the piece carries NO explicit conflict-of-interest statement. The only disclosure is the trademark/patent paragraph: 'The trademarks Fundamental Index(TM), RAFI(TM), Research Affiliates Equity(TM), RAE(TM) ... are the exclusive intellectual property of RA ... Various features of the Fundamental Index methodology, including an accounting data-based non-capitalization data processing system and method for creating and weighting an index of securities, are protected by various patents of RA.' So the article is right that RA has a commercial interest in the conclusion that cap-weighted indexing imposes hidden costs, but should not imply RA disclosed it as a conflict.

itemVerdicts.item: RA Tesla note: the '41bp' is a 6-month counterfactual performance difference on one event pair, not a transaction cost
itemVerdicts.note: Exactly right, and RA's own wording makes it explicit even while calling it a 'cost': 'How much did the S&P 500 rebalance into TSLA cost investors? If a hypothetical investor did not rebalance into TSLA and held the S&P 500 at the pre-rebalance allocation, the investor would have been 41 basis points (bps) ahead of the rebalanced S&P 500 in the first six months after the rebalance, and likely that return advantage is not the end of the story. A pensioner with a $100,000 allocation to the S&P 500 is about $410 poorer as the result of the December 21 index rebalance.' Window: Dec 21, 2020 rebalance to the June 18, 2021 close. Single event pair: TSLA added (1.69% weight), AIV deleted (est. 0.012% weight); AIV's relative return advantage over TSLA was 78.6% (160.20/89.70). RA's separate, broader estimate of the ongoing drag is '20-40 bps' per year, derived from '2-4% of annual turnover' times 'an avoidable 1,000 bp performance drag' — the article must not conflate the 41bp one-event number with that annualized range.
