corrections: An, Benetton & Song is cited as JFE 2023, so use the PUBLISHED wording: 'over one-third of ETF EXPENSE RATIOS are paid as licensing fees to index providers' — not 'management fees'. The 'management fees' phrasing appears only in the Jan 12, 2022 working paper (the law.nyu.edu PDF), which the Journal of Financial Economics version (vol. 149, iss. 3, Sept 2023, pp. 407-433, DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2023.06.003) rewrote throughout.

Do not write 'eliminating provider market power would cut ETF fees ~30%' as the paper's finding. The published abstract says 'Counterfactual analyses show that improving competition among index providers reduces ETF expense ratios by UP TO 30%.' The 'up to' matters: the paper runs two counterfactuals and they disagree. Entry by a new low-fee index provider leaves licensing fees and expense ratios 'almost unaffected' (the authors point to Morningstar's 2016 Open Indexes Project as the real-world confirmation); only the perfect-competition counterfactual yields the 30% figure (~2.8 bps, ~$700 million/year in investor savings). If the article wants the strong version, it must attribute it to the working paper, not to JFE 2023.

Qualify the 'over one-third' licensing-fee share. The authors' own description of the published result is 'about one-third,' rising 'from 31.4% in 2010 to 35.7% in 2019' — it is below one-third at the start of the sample. Also disclose the population: the estimate rests on the roughly 10% of ETFs that voluntarily disclose licensing fees in EDGAR filings, a selection bias the authors acknowledge.

Fix the Molk & Robertson deviation basis. The 1.7%-7.5% figure is 'between 1.7% and 7.5% of assets under management ON A ROUND-TRIP BASIS' — i.e. twice active share, since every underweight implies an offsetting overweight — not '1.7-7.5% of holdings'. Include the mean and median (2.9% and 1.8%), and note the range applies to the largest S&P 500 funds in 2022Q4 while deviations are LARGER among smaller funds.

Drop or reframe '$61.5bn ≈ 0.5% of index assets'. That ratio is not in Molk & Robertson (the string '0.5%' does not appear in the article) and it mixes populations: the $61.5bn numerator is round-trip deviation by S&P 500 index funds alone, while a 0.5% ratio requires a ~$12.3 trillion denominator, which matches the paper's ALL-index-funds figures ('over $12 trillion'; '$12.5 trillion in assets, or 43% of total mutual fund market, at the beginning of 2022'). Like-for-like, using the paper's own footnote 19 ('Globally, over $7 trillion in assets tracks the S&P 500,' S&P DJI Factsheet, Sept 30, 2022), $61.5bn is roughly 0.9%; measured against the 78 'pure' S&P 500 funds in the paper's actual sample it is on the order of 2%, consistent with the reported 2.9% mean round-trip deviation. Also state the construction explicitly: $61.5bn = the $30.7bn aggregate active share doubled.

Add the missing regulatory fact to the IA-6050 passage: the request for comment was not merely left to lapse — RIN 3235-AM95 was formally WITHDRAWN FROM THE UNIFIED AGENDA effective April 21, 2025. The Spring 2025 agenda entry lists it under 'Completed Actions' with the abstract 'The Division was considering recommending that the Commission propose rules related to the role of certain third-party service providers and the implications for the asset management industry. This item is being withdrawn from the Agenda.' The article's two negative claims remain true (it never reached the proposed-rule stage; it was not among the June 2025 proposed-rule withdrawals), but 'never proposed, quietly dormant' understates what happened.

Fix the agenda label. There is no 'Spring 2026 SEC agenda.' The relevant document is the SEC's 2026 Regulatory Agenda (reginfo.gov Publication ID '2026', pubId 202510), released by OIRA on July 3, 2026 with Chairman Atkins's statement on July 7, 2026; the Regulatory Flexibility Act portion was printed at 91 FR 53164 (Aug 14, 2026), Release Nos. 33-11416; 34-105483; IA-6963; IC-36153, File No. S7-2026-16, with data current as of May 12, 2026. RIN 3235-AM95 appears in neither the active nor the completed SEC rule list of that publication.

When identifying the June 2025 withdrawal release, cite it precisely and do not confuse the file numbers: 'Withdrawal of Proposed Regulatory Actions,' Release Nos. 33-11377; 34-103247; IA-6885; IC-35635, published June 17, 2025. It covers File Nos. S7-20-22, S7-12-23, S7-04-23, S7-04-22, S7-17-22, S7-25-22, S7-32-10, S7-18-23, S7-32-22, S7-31-22, S7-07-23, S7-06-23, S7-02-22, S7-10-20. Note that S7-18-23 is on that list and S7-18-22 (the index-provider request) is not — the two are one digit apart.

Do not let the SEC's '$5.0 billion' read as the three big providers' revenue. IA-6050 footnote 10 sources it to Sonya Swink, 'Index Providers Take Record $5bn in Revenue in 2021,' Financial Times (May 24, 2022): $5.0bn is the entire index-provider industry's 2021 revenue, of which the three account for over two-thirds (~$3.4bn).

Attribute the '~3.05 million indexes' figure correctly. It is not an SEC or 2022 count: IA-6050 footnote 5 cites the Index Industry Association's Fourth Annual Benchmark Survey (Oct 28, 2020), 'noting that in 2020, the overall number of indexes climbed by approximately three percent to 3.05 million.'

State the RA Tesla arithmetic precisely: the $78bn and $94bn contradiction occurs inside a SINGLE SENTENCE of endnote 8 — 'These funds needed to buy about $94 billion TSLA ($4.6 trillion x 1.69% = $78 billion)' — while the body text (p.4) uses 'at least $78 billion.' The $147bn/$154bn discrepancy is across locations, not within one endnote: the body says Dec 18 dollar volume 'spiked to $154 billion,' while endnote 8's own inputs (222 million shares at a $662 close) give '$147 billion.' Add that the $4.6 trillion base is a YEAR-END 2019 figure applied to a December 2020 event.

Keep the RA 41bp firmly framed as what it is: a hypothetical six-month return difference between holding the pre-rebalance S&P 500 and the rebalanced index, over Dec 21, 2020 to June 18, 2021, on the single TSLA-add/AIV-delete pair — not a transaction cost, not annualized, and not a general estimate. RA's separate general estimate of the drag is '20-40 bps' a year, built from '2-4% of annual turnover' times 'an avoidable 1,000 bp performance drag'; do not merge the two.

If the article calls RA's index business a conflict of interest, note that the Tesla note itself contains no conflict-of-interest disclosure — only a trademark/patent paragraph identifying RAFI/Fundamental Index as RA's 'accounting data-based non-capitalization data processing system and method for creating and weighting an index of securities.' Say RA has an undisclosed commercial interest, not that RA disclosed one.

Add the sourcing caveat for anyone re-verifying the RA note: researchaffiliates.com now serves an HTML interstitial ('Choose your destination') at the PDF URL to non-browser clients. The retrievable primary text is the Wayback copy at https://web.archive.org/web/2023id_/https://www.researchaffiliates.com/content/dam/ra/publications/pdf/832-revisiting-teslas-addition-to-the-sp500.pdf
newContradictions: Version drift in An, Benetton & Song is real and runs in the direction of weaker claims. The article cites 'JFE 2023' but uses working-paper numbers/wording. WP (Jan 12, 2022) abstract: 'over one-third of ETF management fees ... Eliminating index providers' market power can reduce ETF fees by 30%.' Published JFE abstract: 'over one-third of ETF expense ratios ... Counterfactual analyses show that improving competition among index providers reduces ETF expense ratios by up to 30%.' Anyone reading the published paper will not find the article's sentence.

An, Benetton & Song's own results undercut a common policy inference drawn from them: their entry counterfactual finds that a new low-fee index provider leaves fees 'almost unaffected,' and they cite Morningstar's 2016 Open Indexes Project as real-world confirmation that entry alone does not discipline this market. The 30% number requires assuming away index-provider market power entirely, which no policy lever does.

Molk & Robertson's headline deviation number is a round-trip (double-counted) measure. Their aggregate active share across all S&P 500 funds in 2022Q4 is $30.7bn; $61.5bn is that figure doubled. Any comparison the article draws to single-direction quantities (e.g. dollar volume, market caps of Dollar General/Target, 'discretionary buying') is comparing a 2x number to a 1x number. The paper itself makes the Dollar General/Target comparison, so this is the paper's rhetorical choice, not the article's — but the article should not compound it.

Molk & Robertson does not support a strong 'index funds are secretly active' reading at the megafund level: 98.9% of fund-quarter observations have active share below 20%, 16 of the 24 exceptions belong to a single fund (Rydex S&P 500), the largest fund-quarter with active share above 5% had only $27.6bn in AUM, and 'with rare exceptions, all the S&P 500 index funds in our sample have low tracking error.' The discretion is real but concentrated in small funds.

The RA Tesla note's internal numbers do not reconcile with its own narrative of forced index demand: endnote 8 puts total Dec-18 market trading at ~$147bn against a stated index need of $78-94bn, and RA itself attributes the gap to separately managed accounts — i.e. the note concedes it cannot cleanly separate index-mandated buying from everything else on that day.

The SEC's own IA-6050 footnote 44 cites a contrary source on the index-effect literature — 'But see Maria Kasch and Asani Sarkar, Is There an S&P 500 Index Effect?' — so the request for comment is not itself an SEC endorsement of a persistent index-inclusion price effect. Any article using IA-6050 to support the index-effect claim should note the SEC hedged it.
reasoning:
I reached every primary document verbatim except the published PDF of An/Benetton/Song, which ScienceDirect blocks (403); for that one I used the Crossref and OpenAlex records of the published abstract plus the raw HTML of the authors' own Harvard corpgov write-up of the published paper, curled directly and parsed locally so no summarizer stood between me and the text.

(a) SEC IA-6050. Read the conformed FR version locally (ia6050.txt). The two-thirds/$5.0bn sentence, the 3.05 million index count (footnote 5, IIA Oct 2020 survey), and the 4%-5.5% China A-share range (footnote 45, SEC DERA Risk Spotlight July 6, 2020) are all exact. Date 'Dated: June 15, 2022' confirmed. For the regulatory status I went to reginfo.gov rather than trusting search summaries — the Spring 2025 agenda entry (pubId=202504) for RIN 3235-AM95 shows the full timetable (ANPRM only, never an NPRM) and, crucially, 'Withdrawn 04/21/2025' under Completed Actions, which the claim omits. I then pulled the SEC's complete current-publication rule lists (active and completed) and confirmed AM95 is in neither; the current publication is pubId=202510, displayed as Publication ID '2026', not 'Spring 2026'. I read the full text of the June 17, 2025 withdrawal release (FR doc 2025-11110) and enumerated its 14 file numbers and 14 RINs — AM95/S7-18-22 absent, with the S7-18-23 near-miss noted.

(b) An/Benetton/Song. Local an.txt is the Jan 12, 2022 working paper, not the JFE version. Every number the claim lists (95%/94.95% cumulative Dec 2019 US equity ETF share, HHI 3,293.59 monthly average Jan 2010-Dec 2019, SPY 9bp/3bp+$600k as of Dec 2020, one-third, 60%, 30%) is verbatim in the WP. The published version differs on two wordings — 'expense ratios' for 'management fees' and 'up to 30%' for a flat 30% — which is exactly the version-drift trap flagged in my instructions.

(c) Molk & Robertson. Full text locally (mr.txt). The 1.7%-7.5%, mean 2.9%/median 1.8%, and $61.5bn all check out, but the deviation basis is 'of assets under management on a round-trip basis' and $61.5bn is explicitly the $30.7bn active share doubled. I grepped for '0.5%' and 'half a percent' across the whole document: absent. Reverse-engineering the ratio gives a ~$12.3T denominator, matching the paper's all-index-funds figures rather than S&P 500-tracking assets — a numerator/denominator population mismatch. Using the paper's own footnote 19 ($7T+ tracking the S&P 500) the like-for-like ratio is ~0.9%.

(d) Research Affiliates. researchaffiliates.com serves an HTML interstitial at the PDF URL, so the local ra.pdf/ra2.pdf are unusable HTML shells — a good example of why the local-file shortcut needs checking. I retrieved the real PDF from the Wayback Machine and extracted it. Every element of the claim is confirmed word for word, including the single-sentence $94bn/$78bn contradiction in endnote 8 and the $154bn (body) vs $147bn (endnote, = 222m shares x $662) split. I additionally found that the $4.6T base is a year-end 2019 figure applied to a December 2020 event, and that the note's only relevant disclosure is a trademark/patent paragraph, not a conflict statement.

Remaining uncertainty: I could not open the published JFE PDF itself, so I cannot rule out that a figure like the HHI or the SPY example was revised between the WP and print — though the authors' own August 2023 write-up of the published paper reproduces 3,294, the ~95% top-five share, and the 9bp/3bp+$600k SPY figures unchanged, which makes revision unlikely. I also did not independently verify the FT (paywalled) or the SEC DERA Risk Spotlight behind the SEC's footnotes; I verified only that the SEC characterizes them as the article says.
